units.la: QVVM sæpius ante biennium, Illustres & generosi Domini, & amicorum literis & sermone omnium nuncius afferretur percrebruisse in vniuersa Polonia vestra rumorem constantissimum, sed tamen (ut in his rebus fieri solet) ἀνέφαλον, Illustrissimos Principes, Comites Palatinos, Dominos gratiosissimos (quorum in fide & clientela annos quasi viginti quinque vixi per voluntatem Dei) ab orthodoxa veritate turpiter defecisse, & in Arianorum atque Samosatenianorum partes transfugisse, graviter sanè tuli & iniquo animo tam impudens hominum maleuolorum factum: præsertim cùm id quod res est probè animaduerterem, istum rumorem ab aduersarijs orthodoxæ fidei nostræ (quam ex Scripturis hausimus) certo consilio profectum esse, vt cùm eadem opera de existimatione Principum nostrorum & nostra omnium detraherent, tum bonam inprimis iuuentutem ab huius Academiæ aditu, & a diuinæ illius veritatis, quam profitemur, studio & cognitione abercerent: prout nefaria sua commenta administri Satanæ in alienam perniciem venditant simplicis veritatis loco. Sed eo me longè grauius affecit proximo superiore anno super-
units.tr: Some two years ago, Illustrious and noble lords, a rumour reached me again and again by letters from friends and by the report of everyone, that a very persistent rumour had spread through all your Poland; but, as usually happens in such matters, it was without head or foundation. It said that the most illustrious princes, the counts palatine and most gracious lords (in whose faith and clientage I have, by the will of God, lived for about twenty-five years) had shamefully fallen away from the orthodox truth and gone over to the party of the Arians and Samosatenes. I took this very hard indeed, and with a troubled mind, at such a shameless deed of ill-disposed men. Especially since I clearly perceived what was the case: that this rumour had been launched by the adversaries of our orthodox faith (which we have drawn from the Scriptures) with a deliberate purpose, so that while at the same time they might disparage the reputation of our princes and of us all, they might above all draw good young men away from entrance to this Academy and from the study and knowledge of that divine truth which we profess. In just this way the servants of Satan peddle their wicked inventions in place of the simple truth, to the ruin of others. But a grief of much greater weight affected me in the year just before, when...

units.la: (··) 2 aeniens dolor, quum mihi nunciatum esset de obitu Illustris & generosi Domini, D. Ioannis Hlebowitij, Palatini Trocensis, &c. memoriæ sanctissimæ, parentis vestri, non vobis solum familiæ, toti, sed ipsi quoque patriæ & Ecclesiæ toti luctuosissimo. Nam illum quidem antegressum dolorem animi mei leuabat hæc consolatio, quòd rei & rumoris falsi vanitatem aperta veritas sic ementiebatur palam, vt illud ipsum consilium improbissimum tam impudenter mentiendi considerem in auctores suos statim recasurum. (quid enim veritate fortius?) quam ad rem etiam aliquid adiumenti me sciebam allaturum edita Defensione illa, quam aduersus philosophicas Samosateni, Arij, aliorumque orationes, libello uno comprehensas, rogatu bonorum quorundam exaraueram, vt extaret istis in locis constans orthodoxæ fidei nostræ de sancta Trinitate documentum.
units.tr: ...a sorrow that came upon me when it was announced to me of the death of the illustrious and noble lord, Mr. John Hlebowitius, Palatine of Troki, etc., of most holy memory, your parent, a loss most mournful not only to your family and all of it, but to the fatherland itself and to the whole Church. For that earlier grief of my mind was eased by this consolation: that the open truth so plainly exposed the emptiness of the matter and the false rumour, that I reflected that this most wicked plan of lying so shamelessly would soon fall back upon its own authors (for what is stronger than truth?). I also knew that the publication of that Defence, which I had written at the request of certain good men against the philosophical arguments of Samosatenes, Arius and others, comprised in a single little book, would bring some help in these places, so that there might stand a firm witness of our orthodox faith concerning the holy Trinity.

units.la: Hunc verò mærorem, perceptum de illa migratione sanctissimi & grauissimi viri parentis vestri ad Dominum, quid leuare posset, non æquè facile animaduertebam: cum eum omni officio ac potius pietate in Deum, Ecclesiam, fidem patriamque prælu-xisse omnibus, dum vixit, recordarer; sed heroem auctoritate parem, qui eadem fide, zelo, veritate, ac curabat ipse, doctrinam Christi colere & procurare videretur, vix quemquam post se, dum ex hac vita excessit, reliquisse. Atque hæc me quidem cura tenuit sollicitum quàm diutissimè, de salute popularium vestrorum cogitantem, donec quorundam amicorum literis sum factus certior de futuro ad nos aduentu vestro. Nam huius rei expectatio mærentem animum meum non mediocriter recreauit, cum & spectatissimum prudentiæ illius paternæ monimentum hoc fore considerem, & pignus pietatis vestræ, in qua felicissimè adhuc cura diligentiaque summa grauissimi testis parentis vestri adoleuerût G.V. in Domino. Nunc verò, quandoquidem hoc aduentu vestro desiderij mei expectationem quodammodo expleuistis, & in hac pietatis veritatisque palæstra pedem posuistis, quod faustum & felix: id mihi unum restare
units.tr: But what could relieve this sorrow, arising from the departure of that most holy and most grave man, your parent, to the Lord, I did not so readily perceive: since I recalled that he had shone before all, while he lived, with every duty and rather with piety towards God, the Church, the faith and the fatherland; yet, as a hero equal in authority, who seemed to cultivate and promote the doctrine of Christ with the same faith, zeal and truth that he himself cared for, he had left scarcely anyone like himself behind when he departed from this life. And this anxiety held me troubled for a very long time, as I thought about the salvation of your countrymen, until by the letters of certain friends I was made aware of your coming to us in the future. For the expectation of this matter greatly refreshed my sorrowing mind, since I considered that this would be a most conspicuous monument of that paternal prudence, and a pledge of your piety, in which, so far happily, the care and great diligence of your most grave parent, a witness, have grown up. In the Lord. Now, since by this coming of yours you have in some measure fulfilled my expectation, and have set foot in this arena of piety and truth, which is auspicious and happy, the one thing that remains for me is...

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: restare videtur faciendum, ut V. G. gratuler de aduentu ve-stro, omnem benedictionem a Deo & Seruatore nostro exoptem vobis, meáque officia (si quæ a me V. G. Il. digna & grata proficisci possunt) spondeam & deferam. Sed quid? adhuc pudibundus sum, inurbanus, ἀχρόικ; nequeo austeriorem illam speciem (fateor) quam mihi natura indidit ac confirmauit educatio, hac ætate mea ingrauescente abstergere. Quapropter unum mihi visum est facere. A studijs subsidium petij inurbanitatis istius & horridulæ rusticitatis meæ, librúmque a me recens vestrorum hominum causa perscriptum meo nomine ad Ill. G.V. allegaui. Etenim iamdiu vestra illa Polonia suis quidem beata bonis, sed malis importatis aliunde & per alios misera, iamdiu Lithuania cum ingenijs perditissimis conflictatur, quæ vltro ipsa ruunt in perniciem suam & alios in eamdem labem summo labore, diligentia, contentione, & peruicacia sollicitant sermonibus, exemplis, & scriptis, omnémque lapidem (quod aiunt) mouent vt socios mali sui quamplurimos adiungant sibi.
units.tr: It seems that one thing remains to be done: to congratulate Your Illustriousness on your arrival, to wish you every blessing from God our Savior, and to pledge and offer my services (such as I can offer that are worthy and acceptable to Your Illustrious Grace). But what? I am still bashful and unpolished, ἀχρόικ [achroikos]; I cannot, I confess, wipe away that rather austere manner which nature gave me and upbringing confirmed, now that I am growing older. Therefore I thought of one thing to do. I have sought help from my studies against this unpolished manner and my rough rusticity, and I have dedicated to Your Illustrious Grace, in my own name, a book I recently wrote for the sake of your countrymen. For that Poland of yours, though blessed in its own goods, has long been wretched through evils imported from elsewhere and through other men; and Lithuania has long been troubled by most desperate minds, who rush headlong into their own ruin and, with great labor, diligence and zeal, and with stubbornness, urge others into the same downfall by speech, example and writing, and move every stone (as they say) to win as many companions in their evil as they can.

units.la: Hoc autem malum (quod est profecto grauissimum) quum audiuissem iamdiu, afficiebar grauissimè Christiana popularium vestrorum commiseratione, & virum aliquem auctoritate grauem, scientia rerum diuinarum instructum, fortémque & generosum Christi militem optabam exsistere, qui gladio diuini verbi in virtute & demonstratione spiritus illud expugnaret. Vt autem multis hinc inde scriptis ad me antehac transmissis comperi tantis malis non admodum obsisti, nedum compesci alieno studio, nec sua infirmitate ipsa concidere, sed populi imperiti mentes in dies infici rationis humanæ & popularitatis inani specie, quæ falsis istis dogmatis inest quamplurimùm: eò me tandem compulerunt Dei auctoritas, bonorum postulationes, meáque ipsius conscientia, vt de excutiendis & confutandis ex Dei verbo impuris aliquot scriptionibus serió cogitarem, in quibus arcem & præsidium istius mali videbam præcipuè collocari. Rationibus naturalibus & humanis orthodoxam doctrinam de sancta Trinitate oppugnarunt: breuiter confutaui, ostendens physicis legibus non expendi metaphysicas; multo minus res diuinas physicis aut metaphysicis, & tamen eos ipsos Physicae admiratores etiam in re physica non raro alucinari. Auctoritatibus Scripturae sacrae detortis ad suum illud consilium obtinendum inscite atque impie abutuntur: Easdem auctoritates male ab illis alio abripi, auctoritate Scripturae ipsius demonstraui, quemadmodum fieri omnino a nobis necesse est ad iustam Scripturae veritatisque diuinae (quae una & uniformis est) intelligentiam. Vnum ad confutationis iustae rationem desiderari praeterea videbatur: nempe ut qui loci a nobis adducuntur ad demonstrationem diuinae & orthodoxae veritatis, eos ab iniquis falsisq; interpretationibus istorum vindicaremus. Istius autem generis neque apud venerandam illam antiquitatem (quod mihi quidem constare posset) neque hac memoria nostra scriptum vllum argumento tam exiguo, aut arte lubrico vix puto extitisse, quam illud est quod ante annos aliquot Senensis cuiusdam opera in manus primum multorum fuit disseminatum, deinde vero & typis exaratum, postremo etiam opera singulari amplius recognitum, cuius manuscriptum exemplar fuit Tiguro transmissum ad me. In hoc enim scripto sanctissimum illud primum caput in Euangelio Ioannis mysteriisque diuinis confertissimum, ineptis argutiis atque impiis interpretationibus ex tota haeresewn colluuie, quae unquam extiterunt, collectis turpissime maculatur, & accumulantur omnia quae ab istis hominibus adferenda impietati suae unquam adferripetuerunt. Hoc igitur scriptum utrumque, impressum & manuscriptum excutiendum suscepi, & ex verbo Dei sine offensa cuiusquam aut acerbitate animi confutandum. Atque hanc confutationem, Illustres & generosi Domini, in praesentia allego ad vos: scriptum vobis συνηδυτικὸν de aduentu vestro, publicum vestrae pietatis studiorumque testem, certissimum obseruantiae meae erga Ill. G. V. iudicem, & veritatis diuinae pro eo ac potui vindicem
units.tr: When I had heard of this evil, which is indeed most grievous, I was deeply moved by a Christian pity for your countrymen, and I longed that some man of weighty authority, learned in divine things, and a brave and noble soldier of Christ, would arise to overcome it with the sword of the divine Word in the power and demonstration of the Spirit. But as I learned from the many writings sent to me hitherto from various places, these evils have not been much resisted, still less checked by the zeal of others, nor have they fallen of their own weakness; rather the minds of the unlearned people are being infected day by day under the empty appearance of human reason and popularity, which is very much present in these false doctrines. At last the authority of God, the requests of good men, and my own conscience compelled me to think seriously of examining and refuting, from the Word of God, some impure writings, in which I saw that the stronghold and defense of this evil was chiefly located. They attacked the orthodox doctrine of the holy Trinity with natural and human arguments; I briefly refuted them, showing that metaphysical matters are not to be weighed by physical laws, much less divine things by physics or metaphysics, and that those very admirers of physics often go astray even in physical matters. They misuse the passages of holy Scripture, twisted to obtain their purpose, foolishly and impiously; I demonstrated from Scripture itself that those same passages are wrongly dragged by them in another direction, as it must altogether be done by us for a right understanding of Scripture and of divine truth, which is one and uniform. Besides this, one thing seemed still lacking for a just refutation: namely, that we should vindicate from unfair and false interpretations those passages which we bring forward to demonstrate divine and orthodox truth. Now, of this kind, I think there has hardly existed, either in that venerable antiquity (as far as I could ascertain) or in our own memory, any writing so slight in its argument, or so slippery in its craft, as that which some years ago, through the work of a certain Sienese, first came into the hands of many, was then spread abroad and printed, and finally was revised again with particular care; a manuscript copy of it was sent to me from Zurich. For in this writing that most holy first chapter of the Gospel of John, most rich in divine mysteries, is most shamefully defiled by silly subtleties and impious interpretations gathered from the whole sewer of heresies that have ever existed, and all the things that these men have ever sought to bring forward for their impiety are heaped together. I have therefore undertaken to examine both this writing, printed and manuscript, and to refute it from the Word of God, without offense to anyone or bitterness of spirit. And this refutation, Illustrious and noble Lords, I now dedicate to you: a writing to you, συνηδυτικόν [synēdytikon], on your arrival, a public witness of your piety and studies, a most certain judge of my observance towards Your Illustrious Grace, and a vindicator of divine truth, as far as I have been able.

units.la: cem religiosissimum futurum apud vestros: quorum saluti consultum cupio in Christo Seruatore nostro. V. itaque Ill. G. rogo quàm possum studiosissimè, vt cùm meum hunc laborem vobis gratulatorium æquo animo a me accipiatis ipsi, tum pro insigni studio pietatis illius vestræ, sanctáq; zelotypia erga Deum, Ecclesiam, patriámque vestram (quem zelum iamdiu ab Illustri & generoso heroe parente vestro acceptum colitis diligentissimè) efficiatis vt quicunque fructus ex hoc scripto potest obtingere, ad populares vestros (quorum causa hoc elaboratum est maximè) transmittatur, fiántque illi eiusdem salutis viaq; salutaris, quam fide optima ex Scripturis docemus, participes in Christo Iesu Domino & Seruatore nostro. Deus V. Ill. G. protegat virtute sui Spiritus ab omni malo, & in omni bono confirmet augeátque ad laudem gratiæ gloriosæ suæ.
units.tr: ...most religious for your people, whose welfare I desire to be considered in Christ our Saviour. I therefore beg you, most illustrious and noble Sir, as earnestly as I can, that you would both receive from me with a willing mind this my labour, offered as a congratulatory gift to you, and, in view of that remarkable zeal of piety of yours and your holy jealousy for God, the Church and your country (a zeal you have diligently cherished since it was first received from your illustrious and noble father, the hero), see to it that whatever fruit can come from this writing be sent on to your fellow citizens, for whose sake this work has been chiefly undertaken; and may they become partakers, in Christ Jesus our Lord and Saviour, of that same salvation and of the way of salvation which we teach from the Scriptures in the purest faith. May God protect your Illustrious Lordship by the power of his Spirit from all evil, and confirm and increase you in all good, to the praise of his glorious grace.

units.la: TERTIA DEFENSIO CATHOLICAE DOCTRINAE DE S. TRINITATE PERSONARVM IN VNITATE ESSENTIAE DEI.
units.tr: THIRD DEFENCE OF THE CATHOLIC DOCTRINE CONCERNING THE HOLY TRINITY OF THE PERSONS IN THE UNITY OF THE ESSENCE OF GOD.

units.la: DE summo omnium grauissimoq; mysterio, de Deo dicturus, atque defensurus verae pietatis & Christianae religionis arcem a periculosis eorum cuniculis qui ratione humana freti conantur labefactare veritatis diuinae fidem, primùm Deum optimum maximum doctorem veritatis auctoremque fidei nostrae orthodoxae oro supplex, & meam ipsius & legentium omnium mentem a natiua caecitate liberet, animosq; a studiis omnibus siue fluctuantibus ignoratione, siue aduersantibus infirmitate & malitia, potenter vindicet in Christo Iesu virtute aeterna Spiritus; vt de veritate diuina secundum veritatem, ipso duce & doctore solo, pie sancte & sobrie posssimus quaerere, eam quaerentes inuenire ex promissione ipsius, inuentam condere magis magisque in thesauro cordis nostri, & conditam ad aedificationem fratrum nostrorum expromere, quod gloriae Dei ipsius & Seruatoris nostri inseruiat. Expugnauimus ante per Dei gratiam duo impedimentorum genera quibus Samosateniani, Ariani, alii, tum sibiipsis ad cognoscendam veritatem Dei praecludunt viam, tum aliis obstitunt vehementissimè in via veritatis, ne assequantur salutarem illam cognitionem veritatis quam ex verbo Dei, id est, Scriptura sacra didicimus. Nam obiicientibus naturae lucem & argumenta ex ea sumta, ostendimus eam lucem nihil nisi tenebras esse, cum luce diuina comparatam, & argumenta eius non ad peruestigandam maiestatem gloriamque Dei, sed ad redarguendam vanitatem nostram & inscientiam pertinere. Deinde verò quia speciem aliquam Scripturæ solent obtendere, cuius auctoritatibus principia sua naturalia & rationis in diuinis plane cæcutientis semina student confirmare, modum exposuimus quo sanctissimæ illæ purissimæq; auctoritates Scripturæ a sordibus & inquinamentis ipsorum defendantur, & integra Dei veritas in ouili Christi ex eiusdem Scripturæ fontibus conseruetur. Nunc tertium restat opus confutationis absoluendum: nempe vt quos Scripturæ locos ad sanctissimi & augustissimi huius mysterii declarationem a nobis allatos iidem artifices suis corruptelis infpurcant, & abripiunt a germana ipsorum interpretatione, eosdem restes veritatis, quam colimus docemúsque, esse demonstremus. Hoc igitur consilium nostrū Deo auctore effecturi ad gloriam ipsius, assertionémque veritatis, & tam multarum animarum salutem quæ his telis in Sarmatia maximè appetitæ fluctuant miserrimè, & a vero Deo in falsa hominū commenta tradúcuntur: argumentum vnum ad manum sumsimus confutandum, in quo sic apertè omnia doctrinæ suæ initia descripserunt, vt nihil mihi quidem ad tenendam eam desiderari amplius videatur posse. Cùm enim firmissimam certissimámque totius huius mysterii declarationem primo capite Euangelii Ioannis exstare animaduerterent, omneis ingenii sui neruos quam potuerunt maximè contenderunt, vt lucem illius sumo suarum interpretationum obscurarent, & multiplice πολυλογία simplicitatem, mendacio veritatem Christi obruerent. Huius autem illorum scripti duo ad me exempla fuerunt perlata: quorum vnum, tempore (si bene coniicio) vetustius aliquanto, fuit commissum typis studio & opera auctoris, alterum posterius siue ab auctore, siue a certo homine auctoris necessario limatius & accuratius exaratum, tum, quod per manus multorum (vt solent isti) submis-sum est, vt peritos semper fugeret, imperitos vero plurimum falleret. Quapropter vtrumque scriptum visum est nobis suo ordine & fide optima coniungere, vt aliis scriptis antehac fecimus: sperantes fore (quod olim dicebat Irenæus) vt quo magis erunt ex scriptis ipsorum cognita, eo sint magis attendentibus piis & consideratis <bl>Κάλως</bl>. Fecimus autem hoc ordine, vt primum impresi, tum vero Manuscripti verba haberentur: quibus responsa Defensionis nostræ coniunctim subiecimus, ne idem sæpius a nobis repeti cum tædio legentium oporteret.
units.tr: Since I am about to speak of God, the highest and most weighty of all mysteries, and to defend the citadel of true piety and the Christian religion against the perilous tunnels of those who, relying on human reason, try to undermine faith in divine truth, I first humbly pray to God the best and greatest, the teacher of truth and author of our orthodox faith, that he free both my own mind and the minds of all readers from their native blindness, and powerfully vindicate our souls, in Christ Jesus and by the eternal virtue of the Spirit, from all those studies which waver through ignorance or stand opposed through weakness and malice; so that we may inquire into divine truth according to truth, with him alone as our guide and teacher, piously, holily and soberly, and, seeking it, may find it according to his promise, store up what we have found ever more deeply in the treasury of our heart, and, once stored, bring it forth for the building up of our brothers, so that it may serve the glory of God himself and of our Saviour. Earlier, by the grace of God, we overcame two kinds of obstacles by which the Samosatenes, the Arians and others block for themselves the way to knowing the truth of God, and also most vehemently obstruct others on the way of truth, so that they do not attain that saving knowledge of truth which we have learned from the Word of God, that is, from holy Scripture. For when they objected the light of nature and arguments drawn from it, we showed that this light, compared with divine light, is nothing but darkness, and that its arguments serve not to search out the majesty and glory of God but to refute our own vanity and ignorance. Then, because they are wont to put forward some appearance of Scripture, and try to confirm by its authorities their natural principles and the seeds of reason, which are plainly blind in divine matters, we set out the method by which those most holy and most pure authorities of Scripture are defended from their filth and pollution, and the whole truth of God is preserved in the fold of Christ from the springs of the same Scripture. Now there remains a third task of refutation to be completed: namely, to show that the passages of Scripture which we have adduced for the declaration of this most holy and most august mystery, and which these craftsmen defile with their corruptions and drag away from their genuine interpretation, are indeed the true witnesses of the truth which we worship and teach. Therefore, with God as our author, we shall carry out this plan for his glory and the assertion of the truth, and for the salvation of so many souls, which, struck by these weapons in Sarmatia, are most wretchedly tossed about and led away from the true God into human inventions. We have taken up for refutation one argument, in which they have so openly set out all the beginnings of their doctrine that, as far as I am concerned, nothing more seems to be needed to refute it. For when they noticed that the firmest and most certain declaration of this whole mystery stands in the first chapter of the Gospel of John, they strained every nerve of their wit as hard as they could, to darken the light of that chapter by their own interpretations, and to overwhelm the simplicity of Christ's truth with a manifold verbiage and falsehood. Two copies of their writing were brought to me: one of them, somewhat older in time (if I guess rightly), was committed to print by the zeal and work of the author; the other, later, was written out more polished and carefully, either by the author or by a certain man necessarily of the author's circle, and, since it was sent through many hands (as is their custom), it always shuns the learned and deceives the unlearned most of all. Therefore we thought it right to join both writings in their own order and in good faith, as we have done with other writings before, hoping (as Irenaeus once said) that the more they are known from their own writings, the more they will be pleasing to pious and thoughtful readers. We have arranged it so that the printed words come first and then the words of the manuscript, to which we have added together the replies of our Defence, so that we need not, to the weariness of readers, repeat the same things often.

units.la: Samosateni Præfatio. I.
units.tr: Preface of Samosatenus. I.

units.la: CVM plerique abutantur hoc Ioannis capite ad hominum commenta stabilienda de filio Dei Christo, quem fingunt æternum, bis genitum, duarum naturarum, incarnatum, hocque contra omnem veritatem faciant: quo non tantum tota Scriptura de Christo Filio Dei obscuratur, corrumpitur, atque pervertitur, sed etiam ille Christus Dei Filius a Mose, Prophetis, & in toto veteri Testamento prænunciatus, & a pijs omnibus semper ante exspectatus, qui posteà de Spiritu sancto conceptus, ex Maria natus, pro nobis passus & mortuus, funditus exstirpatur: quin & secundus Deus introducitur, ad abolendum illum solum, verum, altissimumque Deum Patrem Christi: Quare ne pii patiantur se abduci ab illo uno solo Deo Patre, & a Christo etiam unico eius filio, quem nobis Pater de cælo commendauit, breuiter summas tantum rerum in hoc capite controuersarum attingam.
units.tr: Since many people misuse this first chapter of John to establish their human inventions about the Son of God Christ, whom they imagine as eternal, twice begotten, of two natures, and incarnate, and in doing so they act against all truth, the result is not only that the whole of Scripture concerning Christ the Son of God is obscured, corrupted and perverted, but also that the Christ, the Son of God, who was foretold by Moses, the Prophets and the whole Old Testament, and who was always awaited in advance by all the godly, who afterwards was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of Mary, and suffered and died for us, is utterly uprooted. Moreover, a second God is introduced, in order to abolish that one true, most high God, the Father of Christ. Therefore, lest the godly suffer themselves to be drawn away from that one God the Father, and from Christ also, his only Son, whom the Father commended to us from heaven, I will briefly touch only the main points of the controversy in this chapter.

units.la: M s. Præfatio.
units.tr: Manuscript Preface.

units.la: Quoniam quæ dicenda sunt, fortasse vti noua & hactenus inaudita, suspecta prima fronte videbuntur: ante quàm ergo scriptum hoc legatur, paucula quædam præfari visum est, quæ scilicet & suspicionem tollere possint, & simul ad eius intelligentiam non mediocrem lucem afferre. Primùm ergo quicquid de Ebione & Cerintho vulgo iactatur, figmentum esse censebitur: nempe quòd Ioannes contra eos qui Christum ante Mariam esse negabant, suum scripserit Euangelium. Nam ultra quòd nihil solidi ad eius probationem in medium adfertur, non desunt etiam efficaces rationes quæ diversum sentire cogant.
units.tr: Since what must be said may seem suspicious at first sight, perhaps because it is new and hitherto unheard of, before this writing is read it seems right to preface a few things, which can both remove suspicion and at the same time bring no small light to its understanding. First, therefore, whatever is commonly bandied about concerning Ebion and Cerinthus will be judged to be an invention: namely, that John wrote his Gospel against those who denied that Christ existed before Mary. For, besides the fact that nothing solid is brought forward in support of this, there are also not lacking effective arguments that compel the opposite view.

units.la: Causa autem huiusce erroris fuit falsa quorundam imaginatio. Cùm enim viderent sic Ioannem primo hoc cap. appellare Christum verbum Deum, audirent mundum per ipsum esse creatum, carnem denique esse factum, & huiusmodi alia; non intelligentes veram Euangelistæ mentem, cœperunt nescio quid altius ac divinius mente concipere, quàm Ioannes intelligere voluerit: nempe Christum esse æternum Dei filium, æqualem in omnibus Deo Patri, & secundam in Trinitate personam, immò ipsissimum Deum omnipotentem.
units.tr: The cause of this error, however, was a false imagining on the part of some. For when they saw that John in the first chapter calls Christ the Word, God, that they heard that the world was created through him, and that he became flesh, and other things of this kind, not understanding the true mind of the Evangelist, they began to conceive something higher and more divine than John had wished them to understand: namely, that Christ is the eternal Son of God, equal in all things to God the Father, and the second person in the Trinity, indeed the very God, almighty.

units.la: Sed si itares haberet ut dicunt, certè divina Scriptura alicubi clarè, apertè, ac sine verborum involucris & ambagibus ista docuisset. Mirum siquidem esset Ioannem & cæteros, Euangelistas, Apostolos, omnes in re tanti momenti (nam ad salutem pertinere contendunt) nihil penitus scripsisse: maximè cùm in multis aliis describendis longè minoris momenti & ad salutem non usque adeò necessariis occupentur. Et, si alii omnes hæc prætermisissent, certè Lucas diligentissimus scriptor annotasset, qui magna cum diligentia (ut ipsemet scribit) omnibus ab initio peruestigatis perfectè de Iesu Christo scripsit. Nimium ergo grandem ipsi & aliis scriptoribus iniuriam faciunt, qui ipsos aliquid prætermisisse asserunt quod ad salutem pertineat. Ut & aliud quod vehementer urget, nempe non alium Messiam a nobis ad salutem exspectandum ac credendum esse, quàm eum qui a Prophetis descriptus & promissus promissus fuerat, nempe ex semine Dauidis. Atqui Prophetae nunquam dixerunt venturum Messiam qui esset verus Deus & homo, sed simpliciter ex semine Dauidis. Aduertendum est praeterea, quod quando in Instrumento nouo fit mentio, Christum fecisse mundum, omnia condidisse, &c. non haec ad materialia & visibilia esse trahenda, vt ipsi faciunt, sed solummodo ad spirituale suum regnum, quod appellatur mundus, domus, orbis, Ioan. 3. Hebr. 2. vt fusius infra probabimus: siquidem Christus spiritualis rex est, non carnalis: datus a Deo Patre ad aedificandum, faciendum, creandum spirituale regnum hoc, quod est Ecclesia. Sicut enim Moses, vt minister, inquit Paulus Hebr. 3. fuit fidelis in tota domo sua, ita Christus, tanquam Filius administrauit domum ipsius, cuius domus sumus nos.
units.tr: But if the matter were as they say, surely Holy Scripture would have taught these things somewhere clearly, openly, and without veils of words and circumlocutions. It would indeed be strange if John and the other Evangelists and Apostles had written nothing at all on a matter of such great importance (for they contend that it pertains to salvation), especially since they occupy themselves in describing many other matters of far less importance and not so necessary for salvation. And if all the others had passed over these things, surely Luke, the most diligent writer, would have noted them, who, as he himself writes, with great diligence, having investigated everything carefully from the beginning, wrote perfectly about Jesus Christ. They therefore do a very great injustice to him and to the other writers when they assert that they passed over something that pertains to salvation. There is also another point which they press vehemently: that we are not to expect or believe in any other Messiah for salvation than the one who was described and promised by the Prophets, namely from the seed of David. Yet the Prophets never said that the coming Messiah would be a true God and man, but simply from the seed of David. Furthermore, it must be noted that when mention is made in the New Testament of Christ making the world, creating all things, etc., these things are not to be drawn to material and visible things, as they do, but only to his spiritual kingdom, which is called world, house, orb (John 3; Heb. 2), as we will prove more fully below: for Christ is a spiritual king, not a carnal one, given by God the Father to build, make and create this spiritual kingdom, which is the Church. For just as Moses, as a servant, says Paul in Heb. 3, was faithful in all his house, so Christ, as a Son, administered his own house, of which house we are.

units.la: Quantum vero ad Ebionem & Cerinthum attinet, in quorum odium Ioannem scripsisse asseritur, id ab omni veritate alienum videtur. Si enim ita res haberet, verisimile non est Ioannem rem hanc tam leuiter silentio praeteriisse, quin saltem vel semel haereticos huiusmodi nominaret. Quod si videmus ipsum tam acriter in Apocalypsi Nicolaitarum facta reprehendisse, quomodo hac in historia Ebionitarum & Cerinthi falsa dogmata non reprehendisset? Cur nusquam clare testatur ipsum Christum natura Deum esse simul & hominem? cur huiusmodi haereticos deuitandos & cauendos esse non admonuit? Verum quod Ioannes horum in scribendo nullam habuerit rationem, vel ex eo euidentissime apparet, quod in fine suae historiae rationem reddens in quem finem scripserit, non alium fuisse tradit quam vt homines credant Christum esse filium Dei, & ita credendo vitam haberent aeternam. Nam hic opportunum fuisset Euangelistae aliquid contra pestiferos hos homines scribere. Poterat enim ita dicere, vt credatis Christum esse filium Dei coaeternum, consubstantialem cum Patre, ac in omnibus coaqualem, & ita credendo vitam æternam habeatis. Sed quid pluribus opus est? Quod demum requiritur, benigne Lector, illud est, ut omni persuasione hactenus concepta spoliatus huc accedas, ac libero iudicio iuxta normam verbi Dei iudices, fusis primùm ad Deum ardentibus precibus. Hac siquidem sola ratione veritatem assequere. Vale.
units.tr: Concerning Ebion and Cerinthus, in whose hatred John is said to have written, this seems entirely alien to the truth. For if things were so, it is not likely that John would have passed over the matter so lightly in silence, without at least once naming heretics of this kind. But if we see that he reproved the deeds of the Nicolaitans so sharply in the Apocalypse, how would he not have reproved the false doctrines of the Ebionites and Cerinthus in this narrative? Why does he nowhere clearly testify that Christ himself is by nature God and man at once? Why did he not warn that heretics of this kind are to be avoided and guarded against? Indeed, that John had no regard for these men in writing is most evidently apparent from this, that at the end of his history, giving the reason for which he wrote, he declares that his purpose was none other than that men should believe that Christ is the Son of God, and so by believing have eternal life. For here it would have been fitting for the Evangelist to write something against these pestilent men. He could have said: "that you may believe that Christ is the Son of God coeternal, consubstantial with the Father, and coequal in all things, and so by believing you may have eternal life." But why are more words needed? What is finally required, kind reader, is that you approach this with all persuasion hitherto conceived set aside, and judge with a free mind according to the rule of the Word of God, first pouring out fervent prayers to God. For by this method alone you will attain the truth. Farewell.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: THE ORTHODOX.

units.la: VTRAMQVE hanc præfationem, Christiane Lector, hoc loco visum est coniungere, tum vt ex ipsarum inter se comparatione videas quantum momenti secundæ curæ prioribus ad oppugnandam veritatem Dei adiecerint, tum vero vt ad vtramque vna & eadem opera simul respondeam, nequando actum agi sæpius oporteat. Equidem non dubito quin austera illa frons & censoria quasi virgula, quæ priore illa præfatione cœperat occupari, multorum animos pietati ferió dantium operam in ipso limine offenderit: adeò superciliosè iudicium suum de plerisque omnibus, de nostra communi fide, & de Iesu Christo Seruatore nostro enunciat. Sed postquã hoc malum euentus præter opinionem auctoris comprobauit, tum manus altera sperans (quod dici solet) δλ' ἑτέρων ἀμεινόνων, est admota, subiectáque præfationi ua; in qua, prioris illius austera simplicitate remota, lenius instillantur & propinantur imbibenda, quæ prius epotare & exhaurire vno spiritu multorum animi renuerant, fastidierántque. Sed missa arte, quam quiuis de vulgo potest animaduertere, ne artem sectari putemur aut dicamur ipsi, (quam hic laudare non possumus) ad argumentum ipsum veniamus. In priore sua præfatione exponit Samosatenus caput controuersiæ, cuius causa se ad istud scriptionis genus adductum fuisse pronunciat. nunciat. Id autem vt commodius singuli queant percipere, hoc syllogismo breuiter concludemus: Qui filiū Dei aeternum, bis genitum, duarum naturarum, & incarnatum fuisse docent, hi contra omnem veritatem absurda statuunt quàm plurima: Hoc faciunt Orthodoxi, qui primo capite Ioannis in eam sententiam abutuntur: Hi ergo absurda statuunt quàm plurima. Negamus simpliciter omneis huius argumentationis partes. Nec propositio maior, nec assumtio vera: proinde nec in conclusione plus veritatis est. Ac de minore quidem ex professo agitur posteà in scripto reliquo: singula itaque membra suo ordine & loco expendentur. De maiore videamus. Hæc illa, inquit, absurda sunt quæ inde consequuntur. 1. quòd tota Scriptura de Christo filio Dei obscuratur, corrumpitur, atque peruertitur. 2. quòd Christus ille Dei Filius funditus exstirpatur. 3. quòd secundus Deus introducitur ad abolendum illum solum verum, altissimumq; Deum Patrem Christi. Atqui his omnibus Samosatenus principium petit, vt loquuntur Scholastici. Nam primùm negamus horum absurdorum quicquam ex orthodoxa illa doctrina consequi quam sanctè profitemur: neque vlla vis argumentorum non modò vera, sed ne probabilis quidem adferri potest, vnde hæc absurda, quæ obiiciuntur nobis, neri aut necti possint. Deinde verò hæc ipsa absurda, quæ tam graviter Samosatenus in nos visus est intorquere, per necessariā consequutionem ex doctrina ipsius singula confici affirmamus, certisq; tum auctoritatibus diuini verbi, tum argumentationibus possumus convincere. Sed quia hîc τὸ ἀναπόδεικτον a nobis petitur, præstat loquentem Samosatenum audiamus, & nouis suis interpretationibus, quas ausus est comminisci, alterum nobis Euangelium, alterum Christum, & Deum alterum adornantem.
units.tr: It seemed right to join these two prefaces together here, Christian reader, partly so that from comparing them you can see how much weight the second effort added to the first in its attack on the truth of God, and partly so that I can answer both at once, lest the business have to be repeated again and again. I have no doubt that the stern brow and the censor's rod, which the first preface had begun to wield, offended at the very threshold the minds of many who earnestly devote themselves to godliness, so haughtily does he pronounce his judgement on nearly all men, on our common faith, and on Jesus Christ our Saviour. But since the outcome has shown that this evil went beyond the author's intention, a second hand has been applied, hoping (as the saying goes) but from better men [δλ' ἑτέρων ἀμεινόνων]. It has been added to the preface, and in it the harsh simplicity of the first is set aside. Things that the minds of many had refused to swallow and drain in one gulp, and had found distasteful, are now poured in more gently and offered to be drunk. But let this artifice go, which any ordinary person can notice, so that we are not thought to pursue art, or to be called artful ourselves (which we cannot praise here), and let us come to the matter itself. In his first preface Samosatenus sets out the heart of the controversy, and he declares that this was the reason he was driven to this kind of writing. So that each reader may grasp it more easily, we shall sum it up briefly in this syllogism: Those who teach that the Son of God is eternal, twice begotten, of two natures, and incarnate, maintain a great many absurdities contrary to all truth. The Orthodox do this, who abuse the first chapter of John to that opinion. Therefore they maintain a great many absurdities. We simply deny all the parts of this argument: neither the major premise nor the minor is true, and so there is no more truth in the conclusion. The minor premise will be dealt with expressly later in the remaining writing, so each part will be weighed in its own order and place. Let us look at the major premise. These, he says, are the absurdities that follow from it: (1) that the whole of Scripture concerning Christ the Son of God is obscured, corrupted, and perverted; (2) that that Christ, the Son of God, is utterly uprooted; (3) that a second God is introduced to abolish that one true and most high God, the Father of Christ. Yet Samosatenus begs the question in all of these, as the Schoolmen say. For first, we deny that any of these absurdities follows from that orthodox doctrine which we piously profess, and no force of argument, not only true but not even probable, can be brought to show how these absurdities that are thrown at us could be fastened or tied to it. Then again, we affirm that these very absurdities, which Samosatenus has been so eager to hurl at us, are each produced from his own doctrine by necessary consequence, and we can convince him of this both by sure testimonies of the divine Word and by argument. But since he here demands from us what is not proved, it is better to hear Samosatenus himself, who has dared to devise, with his new interpretations, another Gospel, another Christ, and another God for us.

units.la: Posteriore præfatione interpolaturus illud asperius scribendi genus artifex, insinuatione vtitur ῥητεχνῶς, quam nos in medio relinquemus. Nemo enim homo tam hebes atque obesus est, qui nesciat de re noua atque inaudita auctorem potius & scholam veritatis, quàm hominem ignotum & aliud agentem audiri oportere. Auctorem habemus veritatis Deum, qui instrumento Scripturæ suæ instruxit domum suam, & in ea iam olim seruos suos de hoc mysterio informauit. Hic veritas vniformis & docentis, & doctrinæ, & discentium quos docet Deus: veritas Catholica in consensione sanctorum posita, quam hic Samosatenus non dubitat oppugnare. Insinuet se nouator iste: at sapientia & veritas Dei incompitis clamat, cuius vocem cum orthodoxa illa & prisca Ecclesia agnoscimus. Huic vero insinuationis modo non bene conueniunt præsidentes illæ Samosateni affirmationes duæ, quas perinde cupit Ecclesiæ obtrudere atque aphorismos omnium certissimos & indubitatas plane demonstrationes. Prior est, figmentum esse quod vulgo iactatur de Ebione & Cerintho, aduersus hos puta Ioannem scripsisse Euangelium: posterior falsam imaginationem, quamuis vetustâ, esse, quæcunque Orthodoxi adferunt ad huius capitis intelligentiam, de filio Dei. Cùm autem propositionum illarum argumenta a Samosateno in præfatione reliqua ὕστερον πρότερον adferantur, eodem ordine de illis dicemus paucis. Male hoc caput intelligi, & contra mentem Ioannis ex eo doceri, Christum æternum Dei filium esse, Deo Patri æqualem in omnibus, secundam in Trinitate personam, ipsissimum omnipotentem Deum, hanc denique puram putam imaginationem esse, tribus argumentis probare nituntur, quæ ordine exponemus. Primum: Si hoc verum esset, diuina Scriptura alicubi clarè & aperte docuisset, præser-tim sim cùm ad salutem contendant pertinere: Non fecerunt autem, ne Ioannes quidem aut Lucas: Non igitur verum. Maiorem concedimus: etsi non est simpliciter ac per se necessaria. Nam vel unus apertus locus, ut hic ipse est, ad diuinam auctoritatem satis. Quid enim? nónne semel dicta veritas a Deo tam est veritas & fidem nostram obligans, quàm millies recantata? nónne quum primùm semel fuisset dicta, & veritas diuina fuit, & audientis Adami obstrinxit fidem? Minor salsissima est: fecerunt enim Apostoli & Euangelistae passim; fecit Ioannes hoc loco, & singulis fermè capitibus: fecit Lucas cap. 1. & 2. prout singulari opere (si Deus volet) ostendemus, ne idem centies repeti oporteat. Sic ergo conclusio falsa.
units.tr: Intending to alter that harsher style of writing in a later preface, the craftsman uses insinuation artfully [ῥητεχνῶς], which we shall leave aside for now. For no one is so dull or so dense as not to know that about a new and unheard-of matter one should listen to an author and a school of truth, rather than to an unknown man who is up to something else. We have God as the author of truth, who equipped his house with the instrument of his Scripture and instructed his servants about this mystery in it long ago. Here truth is uniform, in the one who teaches, in the teaching, and in the learners whom God teaches: it is the Catholic truth, founded on the agreement of the saints, which this Samosatene does not hesitate to attack. Let this innovator insinuate himself: but the wisdom and truth of God cries out openly, and we recognise its voice in that orthodox and ancient Church. But those two assertions of Samosatene that lead his argument do not fit well with this method of insinuation. He wants to force them on the Church as if they were the most certain aphorisms and plainly indubitable demonstrations. The first is that the story commonly repeated about Ebion and Cerinthus is a fiction, namely that John wrote his Gospel against these men. The second is that whatever the Orthodox put forward to explain this chapter concerning the Son of God is a false imagining, however old. Since Samosatene gives the arguments for these propositions later in the preface, in a hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον] order, we will deal with them briefly, in the same order. They try to prove with three arguments, which we shall set out in turn, that this chapter is badly understood, and that it is taught from it against John's mind, that Christ is the eternal Son of God, equal to God the Father in all things, the second person in the Trinity, the very almighty God; and finally that this is a pure fancy. First: If this were true, divine Scripture would have taught it somewhere clearly and openly, especially since they contend that it pertains to salvation. But Scripture did not do so, not even John or Luke. Therefore it is not true. We grant the major premise, though it is not simply and in itself necessary. For one plain passage, such as this very one, is enough for divine authority. For what? Is a truth once spoken by God not as much a truth, binding our faith, as one repeated a thousand times? When it was first spoken once, was it not already divine truth, and did it not bind the faith of Adam, who heard it? The minor premise is utterly absurd. For the Apostles and Evangelists did so everywhere; John did so in this place and in almost every chapter; Luke did so in chapters 1 and 2, as we will show in a separate work (if God wills), so that the same point need not be repeated a hundred times. So the conclusion is false.

units.la: Secundum: Apostoli & Euangelistae eum Messiam excipi & credi voluerunt, qui a Prophetis descriptus & promissus fuerat: Fuerat autem promissus ex semine Davidis, non autem Deus verus & homo: Hunc ergo excipi & credi voluerunt. Maior verissima est: Minor salsissima: quemadmodum vel ex Esaiae 7. & sequentibus confirmatur. Nã propterea dictus est Immanuel, ut si θεάνθρωπον dicas, id est, Deum & hominem in unitate personae. Solus certè Propheta Esaias (ut alios taceamus) plus satis argumentorum legentibus orthodoxis est suppeditaturus, unde huius affirmationis vanitatem, & affirmantium (ut ita dicam) ἀπάτωρ θεὸς redarguant. Sed haec alias. Neque haec ergo conclusio verior superiore est. Tertium: Quae de Christo praedicantur, secundum conditionem regis & regni praedicantur, & ita accipienda sunt: Conditio regis & regni spiritualis est: ergo spiritualiter praedicantur, & ita accipienda. Hinc, Christus fecisse mundum, omniaque per ipsum facta praedicantur: haec igitur praedicata spiritualiter sunt accipienda. Prosyllogismi utraque propositio est valde ambigua. Nam Christus rex, & Christi regnum bifariam di-
units.tr: Second: The Apostles and Evangelists wished that the Messiah be received and believed as the one described and promised by the Prophets. But he had been promised as from the seed of David, not as true God and man. Therefore they wished that this one be received and believed. The major premise is most true; the minor is most absurd, as is confirmed even from Isaiah 7 and the following chapters. For he was therefore called Immanuel, so that you may call him theanthropos [θεάνθρωπον], that is, God and man in unity of person. Certainly the prophet Isaiah alone (to say nothing of the others) will supply readers who are orthodox with more than enough arguments to refute the vanity of this assertion and of those who assert it, (so to speak) the fatherless god [ἀπάτωρ θεὸς]. But these matters belong elsewhere. Nor is this conclusion any truer than the previous one. Third: What is predicated of Christ is predicated according to the condition of king and kingdom, and must be understood accordingly. The condition of the king and kingdom is spiritual; therefore what is predicated of Christ is predicated spiritually and must be understood so. Hence, it is said that Christ made the world, and that all things were made through him: these things, therefore, must be understood spiritually. Both premises of this prosyllogism are very ambiguous. For Christ the king, and the kingdom of Christ is said in two ways

units.la: b citur: primùm respectu vniuersalis regni, quod regnum diuinum atque æternum est, commune Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti in vnitate essentiæ: secundò respectu singularis regni, quo vt Rex Mediator, regnum obtinet Ecclesiæ suæ in persona sua: quorum prius a natura habet, posterius a dispensatione diuina. Præterea loquutio ambigua item est, secundum conditionem regis & regni prædicari, & accipi, & quæcunque in hanc sententiam a Samosateno dicuntur. Nam siue prædicata hæc enuncientur de rege, qui subiectum est, siue de regno, quod obiectum, siue de administrationis modo, quæ relatiua actio regis ad regnum est, hæc conditio ambiguè dicitur. Rex, quà Deus, semper spiritualis est: quà Mediator, non item: assumsit enim corpus, & in eo regnat, in quo etiam fecit & passus est ea corporaliter quæ ex historiis Euangelicis cognouimus. Regnum vtrumuis dixeris, si obiectum materiámque in qua regnat Christus, respicias, non nisi æquiuocè dici potest secundum conditionem regis: cùm secundum essentiam, potentiam, operationem, & affectiones quaslibet res subiectæ ipsæ inter se plurimum differant, & omnes a conditione regis sui absint quàm longissimè: soli homini cum suo rege conuenit identitate naturæ, quà homo est similis fratribus suis excepto peccato. Modus, si ad formam essentialem regni & administrationis vtriusque huius respexeris, omnino spiritualis est: si ad cætera, summè varius spiritualiter & corporaliter, prout illa Dei sapientia est πολυποικίλως. Cùm ergo conditio regis & regni huius secundum hoc spiritualiter, secundum illud aliter fit accipienda, prout prædicatur varie, omnino sequitur hic Samosatenum ex ambiguo fallere: aut (si aliter placet) inconsequentem argumentationem a non distributo ad distributum exstruere. Nam vt maiorem veram esse demus secundùm ea quæ modò distinximus, particularis futura est & indefinita: Minor itidem particularis, nec alia ratione vera quàm si dixeris, conditionem regis & regni ex parte, non vniuersè, spiritualem esse. Indefinitè autem, vel sine vniuersali signo a genere ad speciem quis nescit tantùm negantia duci argumenta posse? Sic falsam esse vides, Samosatene, argumentationem tuam. Euerso autem prosyllogismo, quid iam consequente syllogismo facias? Quæ Christus fecisse prædicatur, spiritualiter sunt accipienda: Christus fecisse mundũ, omnia prædicatur: Mundus ergo, omnia spiritualiter. Maior indefinitè vera, sed particularis: si fiat vniuersalis, salsissima futura est. Et hic ergo ex particularibus concluditur ἀσυλλογίςως. Siquidē porrò sic pugnaturus es, omnib. iudicibus vincéris, qui solus currens tibi videris vincere. Quæ de mundi, orbis, domus interpretatione adfert παρέργως, nihil ad rē, neq; ex veritate. sed de eis alibi. Quæ de Ebione & Cerintho narrantur, déque Ioannis consilio Euangeliū perscripturi, aliqua ex parte falsa sunt, & huius scriptoris produnt ἀνιςοφησίαν. Nam primùm nomen Ebion non est viri proprium, sed Hebræum vocabulum & Syrum, appellatiuè pauperem significans, vt ipse Eusebius inter reratus est. Hinc plurali numero Ebionim dicti, vulgo Ebionæi, fratres pauperes siue mendicantes, a sectæ illius modo. Quapropter non Ebionem, sed Ebionæos a Samosateno dici oportuit: nisi forte Ebionem, vt Epiphanius, singulariter per enallagen pronunciauerit, & ad caput istius ordinis respexerit. Huius rei ignoratione posteriores scriptores Ebionem viri proprium nomen putauerunt. Secundò non abest a falso, quòd vnam solùm causam, cur Ioannes scripserit ista, in medium protulit, cùm duæ ab orthodoxis Patribus adducantur passim: vna, vt quæ alii Euangelistæ prætermiserant de Christo dicenda, siue a Christo gesta, etiam ante quàm Baptistes in vincula coniectus esset, ab eo perscripta haberentur; quod Ecclesiæ in Asia rogauerant: altera, vt erroribus quos disseminabat Satan occurreret. Priorem copiosè narrat Eusebius libro 3. historiæ Ecclesiasticæ, cap. 23. & Augustinus commodè notauit his verbis: Ioannes est reliquus, qui iam non restat cui conferatur. Quicquid enim singuli dixerunt, quæ ab aliis non dicta sunt, difficile est vt habeat aliquam repugnantiæ quæstionem. Idem Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, alii. Hanc tamen omissi à Samosateno indignum fuit. Postremò falsum est ad Ebionem & Cerinthum solummodò respexisse: & quòd in odium eorum scripsisse dicitur, odiosum. vt enim veritas mendacib[?]us omnibus, sic præco veritatis præconibus quibuslibet mendaciorum obsistit, & veritatis παραχαράκτης aduersatur.
units.tr: is said in two ways: first, with respect to the universal kingdom, which is divine and eternal and common to the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in unity of essence; second, with respect to the particular kingdom by which he, as Mediator King, holds the kingdom of his Church in his own person. The former he has by nature, the latter by divine dispensation. Moreover, the phrase "to be predicated and understood according to the condition of the king and kingdom" is ambiguous, and so is everything Samosatenus says to this effect. For whether these predicates are stated of the king, who is the subject, or of the kingdom, which is the object, or of the manner of administration, which is the king's relative action toward the kingdom, the word "condition" is used ambiguously. The king, as God, is always spiritual; as Mediator he is not, for he assumed a body and reigns in it, and in it he also did and suffered bodily those things that we know from the Gospel histories. You may call the kingdom either, if you look at the object and the matter in which Christ reigns, but it can only be said, equivocally, to be according to the condition of the king. For according to essence, power, operation and all affections, the subjects themselves differ greatly among themselves, and all are as far as possible from the condition of their king. Only man agrees with his king in the identity of nature, in that he is a man like his brethren, apart from sin. As for the manner, if you look at the essential form of the kingdom and of this twofold administration, it is wholly spiritual; if you look at the rest, it is very varied, spiritually and bodily, as that wisdom of God is [πολυποικίλως] manifoldly. Therefore, since the condition of this king and kingdom must be understood spiritually in one respect and otherwise in another, as it is predicated variously, it entirely follows that Samosatenus here deceives by an ambiguity, or (if you prefer another way) builds an inconsequential argument from the undistributed to the distributed. For even if we grant that the major is true according to what we have just distinguished, it will be particular and indefinite. The minor is likewise particular, and is true in no other way than if you say that the condition of the king and kingdom is spiritual in part, not universally. But who does not know that arguments drawn indefinitely, or from genus to species without a universal sign, can only prove negatives? Thus you see, Samosatenus, that your argument is false. Moreover, once the prosyllogism is overturned, what will you accomplish by the conclusion that follows? "What Christ is said to have done must be understood spiritually; Christ is said to have made the world, and all things; therefore the world and all things are spiritual." The major is indefinitely true but particular; if it were made universal it would be most absurd. So here too a conclusion is drawn from particulars [ἀσυλλογίστως] without syllogism. Indeed, if you continue to argue in this way, you will be conquered by all judges, you who seem to yourself the only one running and winning. What he brings forward about the interpretation of "world," "orb" and "house" is [παρέργως] in passing, has nothing to do with the matter, and does not follow from the truth; but of these elsewhere. What is told about Ebion and Cerinthus, and about John's purpose in writing his Gospel, is in part false, and betrays the folly [ἀνοησίαν] of this writer. For first, the name Ebion is not a man's proper name, but a Hebrew and Syriac word, signifying a poor man as a common noun, as Eusebius himself has rightly observed. Hence in the plural they are called Ebionim, commonly Ebionites, poor brethren or beggars, from the manner of that sect. Therefore Samosatenus ought to have called them not Ebion but Ebionites; unless perhaps, like Epiphanius, he used the singular by enallage and referred to the head of that order. Later writers, through ignorance of this matter, thought Ebion was a man's proper name. Secondly, it is not free from falsehood that he brings forward only one reason why John wrote these things, when two are commonly adduced by the orthodox Fathers: one, that things concerning Christ which the other Evangelists had omitted should be recorded, including deeds of Christ done even before the Baptist was cast into prison, which the churches in Asia had asked him to write down; the other, that he should oppose the errors which Satan was spreading. Eusebius relates the first at length in book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 23, and Augustine remarked it aptly in these words: "John is the last, and there is no one left to whom he may be compared. For whatever the others said, which were not said by the rest, it is hard for it to have any appearance of contradiction." Chrysostom, Cyril and others say the same. Yet it was unworthy of Samosatenus to pass over this. Lastly, it is false that he looked only to Ebion and Cerinthus, and it is odious to say that he wrote "out of hatred for them." For as truth opposes all lies, so the herald of truth opposes every herald of lies, and resists the [παραχαράκτης] counterfeiter of truth.

units.la: Non autem ad hos duntaxat respexisse locupletissimus testis vnus de multis nobis futurus est Irenæus, auctor idoneus & ab antiquitate summa: qui Ebionæos quidem in hac causa minimè, sed Nicolaitas, Cerinthũ, & alios aliquot diserte nominat. Omnia igitur talia, inquit circumscribere volens discipulus Domini, & regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quòd sit vnus Deus omnipotens, qui per verbum suum omnia fecit, & visibilia & invisibilia: significans quoque, per quod verbum Deus creationem perfecit, per idem etiam salutem iis qui in creatione sunt hominibus præstitisse, sic inchoauit in ea quæ est secundum Euangelium institutione, In principio erat Verbum, &c. Et paulo post. omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt: in omnibus ergo est & hæc quæ secundum nos est conditio, siue creatio. Quæ verba eo de industria adduco, vt antiquitatis vera sententia de tertio illo Samosateni argumento videatur, quod antè refellimus. Vt autem falsum illud esse vincat quod in opinione est vulgi, rationibus quatuor abutitur. Prima: non fuisset fuissēt Ioannes tam leuiter præteriturus silentio rē hanc, quin saltem hæreticos nominasset. Negatur consequens: nam primùm alia est ratio scribendi Euangelii, alia epistolæ, aut cuiuscunque scripti alterius. Euangelio veritas narratur simpliciter, quod Ioannes fecit: epistolis, aliis sic narratur veritas, ut in contraria excurratur singulari applicatione. Deinde si vel unum hæretici hominis nomen in Euangelium inferciri fuisset alienum, quanto magis, si plura, quæ eodem tempore in veritatem Christi insurgebant? Huius autem rei Iustinus, Irenæus, alii testes sunt, ab antiquo illo, non ab hoc perturbato & factionibus feruente seculo; non unum inquam, sed varios fuisse aduersarios. Tum fuisset illud alienum a Christiana prudentia & charitate factum; quæ sic veritatem Dei asserit, ut mendacia ipsa auctorúmque nomina non prodat foras, sed prodeuntia foras tum demum publicè excipit ut veritatis, charitatis, prudentiæque Christianæ rationibus senserit conuenire. Postremò tu ipse, Samosatene, respondes, quum exemplum Nicolaitarum adducis. At Nicolaitas palàm traducit, quidni etiam istos? Nam Cerinthus synecdochicè comprehenditur Nicolaitarum nomine, a quibus didicerat. Demonstrat illud ibidem Irenæus non obscurè, dicens, Hanc fidem annuncians Ioannes Domini discipulus, volens per Euangelii annunciationem auferre eum qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, & multo prius ab iis qui dicuntur Nicolaitæ, qui sunt vulgo (ἀπόσπασμα) eius quæ falsò cognominatur scientia; &c. De Ebionæis, hoc loco nullum verbum. Secunda ratio: Cur Ioannes nusquam clarè testatur Christum natura simul esse Deum & hominem? Hoc idem argumentum est primum, quod huius præfationis principio confutauimus. Itaque actum ne agamus, tantùm Irenæi verba adferam ibidem posita: Secundum nullam, inquit, sententiam hæreticorum, verbum Dei caro factum est. Siquis enim regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quòd sine carne & impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei verbum & qui est in superioribus Christus. Hoc signum hæreticorum iam illo tempore habebatur. Tertia ratio: Cur huiusmodi hæreticos devitandos & cavendos esse non admonuit? Respondeo vt ante, non esse istud opus Euangelicæ historiæ: non fuisse futurum prudentiæ & charitatis Christianæ opus, eum hominem palàm configere calamo qui se vltrò & turpiter non dedisset palàm: doctrinam falsam fuisse satis retectam, tum propositá veritate luculentissima, tum notato principe illius falsitatis qui palàm mendacia sua & impietatem notandam præbuerat, vt fit in Apocalypsi iterato Nicolaitarum nomine. Quarta: hanc causam scribendi Euangelii non adfert Ioannes, sed ita solùm dicit, Hæc scripta sunt, vt credatis Iesum esse Christum illum, Filium illum Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Immò verò hæc causa non Cerinthum quidem singulariter, sed omnes hæreticos attingens communiter, illis verbis diserte expressa est, quum Dei veritas speciatim aduersus mendacia hæreticorum qui tum exstiterant distincte asseritur. Nam eorum alij personam, alij beneficium Christi indignè lacerabant. Qui personam, aut Iesum esse negabant Christum, aut Christum diuidebant, aut negabant Filium Dei, aut illum negabant quem Apostoli & Euangelistæ docuerat: Qui beneficium, aut omnino in eum credi negabant oportere, aut credentibus ab eo vitam æternam fore: quæ omnia Irenæus libro 1. & 3. narrat copiosissimè. Quum ergo diceret Ioannes, hæc scripta sunt, vt credatis Iesum esse Christum illum, &c. nónne quasi digito omneis illas hæreses commonstrabat, vt Ecclesiam in veritate aduersus mendacia hominum confirmaret? Atque hæc virtus est historiæ Euangelicæ, ab epistolarum & Apocalypseos natura differens. Nam in his mendacia quoque notauit diligentissimè, in Euangelio puram expressit veritatem. Atque hanc in sua præfatione vtinam Samosatenus imitatus esset: nam a veritate ablufit plurimùm, vt iis quæ modò sunt dicta euicimus.
units.tr: Yet that he did not look only to these, Irenaeus, a most weighty witness, one of many we shall have, a reliable author and of the highest antiquity, will make plain. He does not name the Ebionites in this matter at all, but he clearly names the Nicolaitans, Cerinthus and several others. "All such things," he says, wishing to set aside the Lord's disciple and to establish the rule of truth in the Church, "that there is one almighty God, who through his Word made all things, both visible and invisible; signifying also that through the same Word by which God accomplished creation, he also bestowed salvation on those men who are in creation; he thus began in that institution which is according to the Gospel, In the beginning was the Word, etc." And a little later: "All things, he says, were made through him; in all, therefore, is also this condition which pertains to us, or creation." I cite these words deliberately, so that the true view of the Fathers on that third argument of Samosatenus, which we refuted above, may appear. To prove that what is commonly believed is false, he relies on four arguments. The first: "John would not have passed over this matter so lightly in silence, without at least naming the heretics." I deny the consequence. For first, the manner of writing a Gospel is different from that of an epistle or any other writing. In a Gospel the truth is narrated simply, as John did; in epistles and other writings the truth is narrated in such a way that the contrary errors are attacked by a particular application. Next, if even a single heretic's name would have been out of place to insert into the Gospel, how much more would several be, who at the same time rose against the truth of Christ? Irenaeus, Justin and other witnesses testify to this, from that ancient age, not from this disturbed century seething with factions; I say there were not one but various adversaries. Then it would have been a thing alien to Christian prudence and charity, which asserts the truth of God in such a way as not to publish the lies themselves and the names of their authors, but, when they come forth, publicly to meet them only as the reasons of truth, charity and Christian prudence seem to require. Lastly, you yourself, Samosatenus, answer when you bring up the example of the Nicolaitans: "But he names the Nicolaitans openly, why not these too?" For Cerinthus is comprehended by synecdoche under the name of the Nicolaitans, from whom he had learned. Irenaeus shows this plainly in the same place, saying: "John, the Lord's disciple, announcing this faith, wishing by the proclamation of the Gospel to take away from men the error sown by Cerinthus, and much earlier by those who are called Nicolaitans, who are the common offshoot [ἀπόσπασμα] of what is falsely called knowledge," etc. Of the Ebionites there is not a word in this place. The second argument: "Why does John nowhere clearly testify that Christ is at once God and man by nature?" This is the same argument that we first refuted at the beginning of this preface. So, lest we repeat ourselves, I will bring only the words of Irenaeus set down in the same place: "According to no opinion of the heretics was the Word of God made flesh. For if anyone examines the rules of all of them, he will find that the Word of God is introduced by all of them as without flesh and impassible, and Christ as he who is above." This was already at that time a mark of the heretics. The third argument: "Why did he not warn that such heretics are to be avoided and guarded against?" I answer as before: this was not the task of the Gospel history; it would not have been a work of Christian prudence and charity to name openly a man who had not openly and shamefully given himself up; the false doctrine had been sufficiently refuted, both by the most clear setting forth of the truth and by the noting of the leader of that falsehood, who had openly exhibited his lies and the impiety to be noted, as happens in the Apocalypse, where the name of the Nicolaitans is mentioned again. The fourth: "John does not give this reason for writing the Gospel, but says only: These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is that Christ, that Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name." Indeed, this reason touches not Cerinthus singularly but all heretics in common, and it is expressed plainly in those words, since the truth of God is distinctly asserted against the lies of the heretics who then arose. For some of them shamefully tore apart the person, others the benefit of Christ. Those who attacked the person either denied that Jesus is the Christ, or divided the Christ, or denied the Son of God, or denied him as the Apostles and Evangelists had taught him. Those who attacked the benefit either denied that one ought to believe in him at all, or said that eternal life would not come to believers from him; all these things Irenaeus relates most fully in books 1 and 3. Therefore, when John said, "These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is that Christ," and so on, did he not, as it were with his finger, point out all those heresies, so as to confirm the Church in the truth against the lies of men? And this is the virtue of the Gospel history, which differs from the nature of the epistles and of the Apocalypse. For in these he also noted the lies most diligently, while in the Gospel he set forth the pure truth. Would that Samosatenus had imitated this in his preface! For he has strayed very far from the truth, as we have proved by what has just been said.

units.la: SAMOSATENUS. 2. In principio.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 2. In the beginning.

units.la: VOCE principii æternitatem quidam significari volunt: alii verò tempus ante conditum mundum. Sed nihil horum intelligit Ioannes. Tempus enim Euangelii, quo cæptum est a Christo prædicari, designat nomine principii seu initii; quemadmodum ipse Ioannes alibi hoc aperte comprobat dicēs, sed & vos testabimini (Christus ait ad Apostolos) qui mecum ab initio estis: sic, hæc vobis initio non dixi, quia fui vobiscum. Vox ἀρχὴ vtrobique posita, vt Ioannis cap. 1. Sed & Marcus ab eadem voce & re incipit Euangelium suū, ἀρχὴ seu principium Euangelii Christi nominans. Sic & Lucas quoque orditur suum Euangelium, eadem voce vsus: Sicut, inquit, nobis tradiderunt qui a principio spectatores erant & ministri sermonis, visum est quoque mihi omnia ab initio tibi describere. Sic Actor. 1. de eodem initio scribit, quando (inquit) Iesus cœpit facere & docere, incipiens a baptismo Ioannis. Sic Actor. 11. illapsus est Spiritus sanctus in eos, quemadmodum & in nos ἐν ἀρχῇ, ab initio: certè non ab æterno, nec ante conditum mundum, sed tempore ministerii, quando missus fuit. Eadem voce vtitur describens hunc sermonē Christum hominem, Quod erat a principio, quod audiuimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus & manus nostræ contrectauerunt de sermone vitæ. De Christo verbo, visibili oculis, palpabili manibus, qui ex Maria natus est, loquitur. Nam ille æternus qui singitur, a nemine vnquam palpatus ab æterno, vel post legitur, neque vnquam auditus. Caterum ostendant qui aliter sentiunt, alicubi Scripturam sub nomine principii æternitatem designasse. Quod si ostendere solido aliquo testimonio non poterunt, quid temere pronunciant, detorquentes genuinas vocum significationes?
units.tr: Some want the word "beginning" to signify eternity, and others want it to signify the time before the world was made. John means neither. By the "beginning" he designates the time of the Gospel, when Christ began to be preached, as John himself plainly shows elsewhere when he says: "But you also will bear witness (Christ says to the apostles), because you have been with me from the beginning" [John 15:27]; and again: "I did not say these things to you at the beginning, because I was with you" [John 16:4]. The word ἀρχὴ [beginning] is used in both places, as in John 1. Mark also begins his Gospel with the same word and the same matter, naming it "the beginning [ἀρχὴ], or principle, of the Gospel of Christ." Luke too begins his Gospel with the same word: "as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also to describe all things to you from the beginning." Acts 1 likewise writes of this same beginning: "when Jesus began to do and teach, beginning from the baptism of John." In Acts 11 the Holy Spirit fell on them "just as on us at the beginning [ἐν ἀρχῇ]": certainly not from eternity, nor before the world was made, but at the time of his ministry, when he was sent. John uses the same word when he describes this Word, the man Christ: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life." He speaks of Christ the Word, visible to the eyes, tangible to the hands, who was born of Mary. For that eternal being whom they imagine was never touched by anyone from eternity, nor is he read of afterward, nor was he ever heard. Let those who think otherwise show that Scripture somewhere designates eternity under the name of beginning. If they cannot show this by any solid testimony, why do they rashly pronounce, twisting the genuine meanings of the words?

units.la: M S.
units.tr: M S.

units.la: Qui hoc loco principii nomine Christi æternitatem designare volunt, manifeste erroris conuincuntur, tum quòd nulla Scripturæ auctoritate fulcitur, tum quòd omni rationi aduersatur. Neque enim datur principium sine principio: sed principium solum datur in his rebus quæ principiū habere possunt. At æternitas nulla admittit principium: immo quum principium dico, consequenter ac necessario æternitatem excludo. Nomen ergo principii hoc loco non æternitatem, sed ordinem earum rerum respicit, quas Ioannes de Iesu Christo dilectissimo Dei filio descripturus est. Imitatúsque est Ioannes hac in re Mosem & Marcum Euangelistam, qui historias suas describentes similiter ab hoc nomine principii exordium sumpserunt. Et sanè mirum est, quòd cùm Theologi fere omnes passim deprædicent, nullum interpretationis genus melius ac securius inueniri posse, quàm si Scriptura per eamdemmet scripturam exponatur, hoc tamen loco sui ipsorum obliti valere iussa Scripturæ diuinæ auctoritate suis somniis indulgent. Causa autem huius erroris fuit, quòd Verbum hoc, cuius sit a Ioanne mentio, finxerunt esse quemdam æternum ac consubstantialem Dei filium, immo ipsummet æternum Deum omnis principij expertem. Sed quàm vanum hoc sit, infrà videbitur.
units.tr: Those who want the name "beginning" in this place to designate the eternity of Christ are plainly convicted of error, both because it is supported by no authority of Scripture and because it runs counter to all reason. For there is no beginning without a beginning; a beginning is given only in those things which can have a beginning. But eternity admits no beginning; indeed, when I say "beginning," I consequently and necessarily exclude eternity. The name "beginning" in this place therefore refers not to eternity but to the order of those events which John is about to describe concerning Jesus Christ, the most beloved Son of God. In this matter John imitated Moses and the Evangelist Mark, who, describing their histories, likewise took their starting point from this same name of beginning. And indeed it is remarkable that, although nearly all theologians everywhere proclaim that no method of interpretation is better or safer than to explain Scripture by Scripture itself, yet in this place they forget themselves, and, disregarding the authority of the divine Scripture, indulge their dreams. The cause of this error, however, is that they have fashioned this Word, of whom John speaks, to be a certain eternal and consubstantial Son of God, indeed the eternal God himself, free from all beginning. But how vain this is will be seen below.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOX.

units.la: Hîc verò Samosatenus in ipso limine, commodo suo & interpretationes adfert, & argumentationes a nostris (vt quidem videri cupit) fabricatas. Sic enim adfingit: Principium Principium istis hominibus aut est æternitas, aut tempus ante mundum conditum: Sermo ille fuit in principio: In æternitate igitur, & ante mundum conditum. Maiorem negat allata alia principij interpretatione & exemplis eius: atque vt negationem suam amplius confirmet, Gualteri adhibet testimonium, tamquam si æquiuocatione non obscura, & ab hominibus quoque nostris oculatioribus perspecta soleremus aut vellemus in rebus tantis (quod absit) illudere. Ne multa, Samosatene, dum hæc impingis hominibus nostris, peccas trifariam: 1. ea quæ ad interpretationem loci iustam coniungimus, prout re sunt coniunctissima, ad fallaciam tuam diuidendo. 2. vocis interpretationem, quæ a nostris non est nec vnquam fuit, nobis adfingendo. 3. nouam quandam atque inauditam homonymiam siue æquiuocationem, vbi nulla est nec esse aut videri potest, aucupando. Singula hæc itaque videamus: tum vero tu ipse videris quid futurum sit hac interpretatione tua.
units.tr: Here Samosatenus, at the very threshold, brings forward interpretations that suit his purpose, along with arguments which he claims (as he wishes it to appear) were made up by our people. For he adds this: "Principium: for these people, the beginning is either eternity or the time before the world was created. That Word was in the beginning. Therefore it was in eternity, and before the world was created." He denies the major premise, citing another interpretation of principium and examples of it. To confirm his denial further, he adduces the testimony of Walter, as though we were accustomed, or wished, to trifle with such great matters through an equivocation that is not obscure and is clear even to the sharper-sighted of our own people (God forbid!). To be brief, Samosatenus: while you assail our people with these claims, you err in three ways. (1) By dividing, to suit your fallacy, what we rightly join together in the interpretation of the passage, since in fact the parts are most closely connected. (2) By attributing to us an interpretation of the word which was never ours and is not ours now. (3) By seeking out a new and unheard-of homonymy or equivocation where there is none and none can be seen. Let us look at each of these in turn. Then you yourself will see what will follow from this interpretation of yours.

units.la: 1. Fallaciam diuisionis, vt vocant, his verbis commissam demonstramus hoc modo: Quicunque tum ex illis orthodoxis Patribus, tum ex nostris æternitatem personæ Christi hoc Ioannis loco docuerunt, ij non ex voce principij sola, sed ex prædicato (vt loquuntur) toto asseruerunt æternitatem λόγος, quum dicitur, erat in principio: contra quàm tu, Samosatene, adfingis nobis. Sic enim illi, & rectè, sunt ratiocinati: Qui iam erat in principio, ante principium est: erat autem in principio λόγος, Scriptura teste: ante principium igitur est.
