Quid? nónne hoc vides ex illo consequi necessario, & hunc λόγον ante principium exstitisse? Auctores vetustos & recentiores si opus esset adducere, facerem sane libenter: sed exstant in manibus omnium. Itaque dicā Augustini verbis, Quid ait Euangelista? in principio erat verbum. Si erat, non est factum, vt ista omnia per ipsum fierent
units.tr: (1) We show the fallacy of division, as it is called, committed in these words, in the following way. Whoever, whether among those orthodox Fathers or among our own people, have taught the eternity of the person of Christ from this passage of John, they did not base the eternity of the Logos on the word principium alone, but on the whole predicate (as they put it) when it is said, "was in the beginning." This is contrary to what you, Samosatenus, impute to us. For they reasoned thus, and rightly: "He who already was in the beginning is before the beginning. But the Logos was in the beginning, as Scripture testifies. Therefore he is before the beginning." What? Do you not see that this necessarily follows, and that this Logos existed before the beginning? If it were necessary to bring forward ancient and more recent authors, I would gladly do so, but they are in everyone's hands. So I will use Augustine's words: "What does the Evangelist say? In the beginning was the Word. If he was, he was not made, so that all these things were made through him

units.la: c & sine ipso nihil. Si ergo erat in principio verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat verbum: si non potes cogitare quid sit, differ ut crescas, &c. Item Chrysostomi, Hoc in loco, erat, proprium non solum significat, sed erat in principio, & verbum erat. Quemadmodum igitur, est, verbum si de homine dicatur, praesens duntaxat tempus significat: sin autem de Deo, sempiternum atque perpetuum: itidem & erat. Nam quum de humana natura habetur sermo, praeteritū tempus, & hoc ipsum finitum: quando vero de Deo, aeternitatem ipsam ostendit. Concludā illis Basilij luculentissimis: Audi Euangelium, in principio erat. Quod si erat in principio, quando non erat? utrum horum impietate desleam, an inscientia horream? Sed, inquiunt, antequam gigneretur, non erat. Scilicet nouisti quando sit genitus, ut aliquid anterius possis inferre tempori? istud enim quod dicis, ante, vox est temporis, alterū tempus alteri anteponens ad antiquitatē. Qui autem cum ratione conueniat, eū qui fecit tempus generatione habere subiectam temporalib. appellationibus? In principio igitur erat. Nisi a voce erat, discesseris, nullum profecto aditum isti blasphemiae improbae daturus es. Atq; haec iudicio meo satis, ad fallaciā diuisionis, qua Samosatenus vtitur, demonstrandam. 2. Falsam interpretatione adfingi hominib. nostris vt aperte demonstremus, quid alia probatione opus est, quàm a Samosateno ipso? falsum est quod dicit, voce principij aeternitatem quidam significari volunt, alij vero tempus ante conditum mundum. Nam primum quid est tempus ante conditum mundum, si tempus dicitur, nisi χρόνῳ & αἰῶνι, & ipsa aeternitas? Ex vno falso duo facit, vt videatur habere plura quae in nobis reprehendat, & specie apud imperitos obtendit contradictionis. Sed posteriorem puduit istius ineptiae, vt ms. ostendit comparatio. Valeat igitur, quum posteriore cura Samosatenus sustulerit. Secundo vix vllus est rerum Theologicarum,
units.tr: and without him nothing was made. If therefore the Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word: if you cannot grasp what it is, defer it until you grow..." And Chrysostom: "In this place, 'was' signifies not only what is proper, but 'was in the beginning' and 'the Word was.' Just as 'is', when said of a man, signifies only the present tense, but when said of God, signifies what is everlasting and perpetual, so too 'was'. For when the discourse concerns human nature, it signifies past time, and that finite; but when it concerns God, it shows eternity itself." I will conclude with the most lucid words of Basil: "Hear the Gospel: in the beginning was. But if he was in the beginning, when was he not? Shall I lament this impiety, or shudder at this ignorance? But, they say, before he was begotten he was not. Surely you know when he was begotten, so that you can introduce something earlier than time? For what you say, 'before', is a word of time, placing one time before another in antiquity. But how does it agree with reason that he who made time should be subject, by being begotten, to temporal terms? Therefore in the beginning he was. Unless you depart from the word 'was', you will certainly never give any entrance to that wicked blasphemy." In my judgment, this is enough to demonstrate the fallacy of division that Samosatenus uses. (2) To show plainly that a false interpretation is attributed to our people, what other proof is needed than Samosatenus himself? It is false, what he says: "Some wish that by the word principium eternity is signified, others the time before the world was created." For first, what is "the time before the world was created", if it is called time, but time [χρόνῳ] and age [αἰῶνι], and eternity itself? From one falsehood he makes two, so that he may seem to have more things in us to find fault with, and so that by a show of contradiction he may impress the unlearned. But he was ashamed of the latter absurdity, as the comparison shows. Let it stand, then, since Samosatenus has removed it by later care. Secondly, there is hardly anyone skilled in theological

units.la: Homil. 2. in Ioan.
units.tr: Homily 2 on John.

units.la: Homil. in principium Euangelij Ioan. gicarum, aut etiam naturaliū peritus mediocriter, qui ita sentiat aut doceat,vt a Gualtero rectè affirmatur:sed quicunque ad hunc locum de æternitate dixerunt,ij non ad nudam vocem principij, sed ad propositionem hanc coniunctam, erat in principio, respexerunt, vt antè ostendimus. Postremò vt demus fuisse nonnullos qui ita simpliciter principium definiuerint, at iniquum est profecto vtrumq; istud: tum particularem Titij aut Mæuij interpretationem omnibus tribui, vt omnes reprehendantur quamuis aliud sentientes, cùm ex particulari non possit confici vniuersale, nisi forte particularia omnia simul comportentur: tum verò alias interpretationes ab omnibus doctis vno consensu positas reticeri. Quam re qua fide faciat, Samosatenus viderit. Quæ autem interpretationes? fortasse dixerit. Dicam paucis,ne quid dissimulem. Duæ interpretationes olim a Patribus fuerunt allatæ: vna simplex, quâ affirmant, vt antè vidimus: altera subtilior, quam non affirmatè dicunt, sed hypotheticè suppeditant,nectentes ex consequentia. Simplex est hæc: principium esse hoc loco principiatorum (sic enim liceat loqui ad relationis commoditatē) id est,eorum omnium quæ principiū habent in tempore,adeoq; primum ipsius temporis terminū, momentum, seu punctū, quo coepe-runt esse tempus,locus,creatio, & res creatæ tempore & loco. In hoc principio, inquiunt, iam erat Sermo ille,de quo Ioannes instituit dicere: ergo ante tempus, locum, creationem , & res creatas omneis. Hæc simplicissima verissimáque interpretatio; ad quam omnes vno consensu respexerunt, quamuis diuerso (vt fit) interpretationis modo. Altera autem interpretatio est relationis ad intus, vt vocant, a Patribus orthodoxis, non vt primaria,sed vt secundaria semper vsurpata: nō vt propria, sed vt adhærens propriæ: quum illi dicerent, in principio, id est, in Patre, qui principium est originarium siue Pater Filij. Quam interpretationem eo adferimus, vt Samosateniani videant nos bona fide agere, nec quicquam dissimulare velle quod ad causam hanc adferri possit. Quòd si falsam esse hanc interpretationem contenderint, facile respondebimus, primùm veram atque simplicem praecessisse: tum aliud esse si dere dixeris simpliciter, aliud si de loci interpretatione: rem enim veram esse, quòd Pater fit principium Filij, & Filius fit in Patre, sed hanc interpretationem propriam horum verborum non esse; propriam magis sequentium illorum, & sermo erat apud Deum, vt postea exponemus. Atque haec ita se habere vel vnus Cyrillus, auctor grauissimus, in hunc locum testis est. Nos itaque omnes vno consensu cum veritate & cum Ecclesia orthodoxa propriam interpretationem amplectimur, & certa fide colimus. Quapropter cùm neque veras, neque omneis omnium interpretationes hic noster attulerit, iniquè facit qui ex insufficiente enumeratione falsóque suppositio aequiuocationes struit, & falsi probationes a nobis exigit dicens, ostendant qui aliter sentiunt, alicubi Scripturam sub nomine principij æternitatem designasse, &c. Sed iam de aequiuocatione videamus.
units.tr: Homily on the beginning of John's Gospel: fairly skilled in theological or even natural matters, who thinks or teaches as Walter rightly affirms. But whoever have spoken of eternity on this passage, they did not look to the bare word principium, but to this joined proposition, "was in the beginning," as we showed above. Finally, grant that there were some who defined principium simply in this way: it is surely unfair both to ascribe the particular interpretation of Titius or Maevius to everyone, so that all are blamed though they think otherwise (since a universal cannot be made from a particular unless all the particulars are brought together), and to pass over in silence the other interpretations which all learned men have set down with one consent. With what good faith Samosatenus does this, let him see. But which interpretations? Perhaps he will ask. I will say briefly, so as not to conceal anything. Two interpretations were once offered by the Fathers: one simple, which they affirm, as we saw above; the other more subtle, which they do not state outright but offer hypothetically, drawing it by consequence. The simple one is this: principium in this place means the beginning of the things that have a beginning (for so one may speak, for the convenience of the relation), that is, of all things which have their beginning in time; and so the first limit of time itself, the moment or point at which time, place, creation, and created things began to be. In this beginning, they say, the Word of whom John undertook to speak already was. Therefore before time, place, creation, and all created things. This is the simplest and truest interpretation, to which all look with one consent, though in different ways of interpreting, as happens. The other interpretation concerns the relation to what is within, as they call it, used by the orthodox Fathers not as primary but always as secondary: not as proper, but as adhering to the proper. For they said "in the beginning," that is, in the Father, who is the originating beginning, or the Father of the Son. We bring forward this interpretation so that the Samosatenians may see that we act in good faith and wish to conceal nothing that could be brought to this cause. But if they contend that this interpretation is false, we will easily reply that the true and simple one came first. Then it is one thing if you speak simply, and another if you speak of the interpretation of place. For the thing is true, that the Father is the beginning of the Son, and the Son is in the Father; but this is not the proper interpretation of these words. It belongs more properly to what follows, "and the Word was with God," as we will explain later. That these things stand so, Cyril alone, a most weighty author, bears witness on this passage. So we all, with one consent, together with the truth and the orthodox Church, embrace the proper interpretation and hold to it with certain faith. Wherefore, since he has brought forward neither the true interpretations nor all the interpretations of all, he acts unfairly who builds equivocations out of an insufficient enumeration and a false supposition, and who demands from us proofs of falsehood, saying: "Let those who think otherwise show that somewhere Scripture, under the name of principium, designates eternity," and so on. But now let us see about the equivocation.

units.la: 3. Nouam & inauditam aequiuocationem a Samosateno quaeri vbi nulla est, etsi iam satis superiore loco ostendimus producta vera & genuina verborum Ioannis interpretatione, amplius tamen a consilio Euangelistae, a perpetuo consensu Ecclesiae orthodoxae, a natura rei, & a conditione loci ipsius adhuc demonstrari potest. Consilium Ioannis hoc fuit, vt quae ab aliis Euangelistis non fuerant diserte exposita de Christo Seruatore nostro, inprimis autem veritatem personae illius aduersus haereses falsas, quae post tempus aliorum Euangelistarum natae sunt, afferret: vt in praefationem fecundam obseruauimus. Nam hæreses quàmplurimas Satan excitauerat aduersus veritatem personæ Christi, vt labefaceret doctrinam Euangelij: quarum aliæ negabant Iesum esse Christum aut λόγον, aliæ λόγον esse, aliæ æternum esse, aliæ subsistere personaliter, aliæ esse in Patre, aliæ hanc personam Deum esse vel diuinam personam, aliæ coniunctim esse personam diuinam æternum in se subsistentem, & exsistentem in Patre, alii creatorem esse vniuersitatis, aliæ sustentantem atq; gubernantem, alii homines illustrantem & agentem virtute diuina sua secundùm modum naturæ & gratiæ tum communis, tum etiã particularis in homines deriuatæ, aliæ denique, vel potius omnes (vt ante ex Irenæo docuimus) incarnatum esse, & personam vnam Θεάνθρωπον, Deum & hominem in vnitate personæ: quas omneis hæreses iã eo tempore succreuisse demonstrat Irenæus, qui successit proximè sanctorum Apostolorum tempora (vt ipse ait libro 3. & 5. aduersus hæreses) & discipulorū Ioannis auditor fuit. His ergo hæresibus & consimilibus per Spiritum Dei cupiens Ioannes obsistere, vt Apostolus Christi, singula hæc confirmauit: Iesum esse Christum & λόγον, quû diceret, ὁ λόγος, ille sermo, ac non alter: esse λόγον, erat æternum esse, erat in principio: subsistere personaliter & esse in Patre, hic Sermo erat apud Deum: esse Deum seu diuinam personam, hic Sermo erat Deus: personam diuinã vnam & eamdem esse in se subsistentem æternúmq; exsistentem in Patre, hic erat in principio apud Deum: eumdem esse λόγον ᾧ δημιουργὸν sermonem & opificē siue creatorem mundi, omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est: commune principium esse, sustentans & gubernans omnia, in quo viuimus, mouemur, & sumus, in ipso vita erat: homines verò illustrans & gubernans communiter & singulariter secundùm naturam & gratiam suam, hæc vita erat lux hominum, &c. incarnatum esse, & Deum verum hominem verum in vnitate personæ, non autem alium Deum aliúmq; hominem, nec alium Iesum aliúmq; Christum, & hic Sermo factus est caro, &c. Negabit Samosatenus hoc consilium Ioanni fuisse propositum: scilicet quia aduersatur causæ quam obtendit. Sed de prisca illa historia vtri parti magis crediturí sunt boni? Patribus illis, qui partim ijsdem proximisque temporibus vixerunt, partim continua seculorum serie hanc doctrinam a maioribus acceptam posteris per manus tradiderunt, an hominibus nouis? Illorum quidem proprium fuit veram historiam tradere qui aut viderunt ipsi, aut proximè ab his accepe-runt: isti possunt, homines noui, cudere, sia tradita (vt faciunt aperte) discesserint. Atque hoc secundum illud est argumentum, quo ante diximus nouam istam æquiuocationem conuelli & confutari oportere: quòd hic perpetuus fuit consensus Ecclesiæ illius orthodoxæ in veritate huius doctrinæ constanter retinenda contra particulares ἐπροσθὲς καλίας eorum hominum quos insanis spiritus interdum excitauit. Nam ex eo Patrum sanctorum consensu tum occasionem foris ab hæreticis ex parte oblatam, tum pium Ioannis Apostoli & Euangelistæ consilium ac finem, tum inuictam denique huius doctrinæ veritatem per Spiritum Dei cognoscimus.
units.tr: 3. A new and unheard-of equivocation is sought by Samosatenus where none exists. Although we have already shown above, from a sound and genuine interpretation of John's words, that it does not exist, it can be shown further from the purpose of the Evangelist, from the unbroken agreement of the orthodox Church, from the nature of the matter, and from the context itself. John's purpose was to set forth, concerning our Saviour Christ, what the other Evangelists had not expressed clearly, and above all to assert the truth of his person against the false heresies that arose after the time of the other Evangelists, as we noted in the second preface. For Satan had stirred up very many heresies against the truth of Christ's person in order to undermine the doctrine of the gospel. Some denied that Jesus is Christ or Word [λόγος]; some that he is the Word; some that he is eternal; some that he subsists personally; some that he is in the Father; some that this person is God, or a divine person; some that he is jointly a divine person, eternal, subsisting in himself and existing in the Father; some that he is the creator of the universe; some that he sustains and governs it; some that he enlightens and acts upon men by his divine power, according to the manner of nature and of grace, both common and particular, derived to men; and finally, or rather all of them (as we taught above from Irenaeus), some that he was incarnate, and that there is one person, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπον], God and man in unity of person. Irenaeus, who came immediately after the times of the holy Apostles (as he himself says in book 3 and book 5 against the heresies), and who was a hearer of John's disciples, shows that all these heresies had already sprung up in his time. John, therefore, desiring by the Spirit of God to withstand these heresies and similar ones, as an Apostle of Christ, confirmed each of these points: that Jesus is Christ and the Word, when he says the Word [ὁ λόγος], that Word, and not another; that he is the Word, was eternal, was in the beginning; that he subsists personally and is in the Father, this Word was with God; that he is God, or a divine person, this Word was God; that the one and same divine person subsists in himself and eternally exists in the Father, this was in the beginning with God; that he is the same Word [λόγον], the Maker [δημιουργὸν], the Word and workman or creator of the world, all things were made by him, and without him was not anything made that was made; that he is the common principle, sustaining and governing all things, in whom we live, move, and have our being, in him was life; and that he enlightens and governs men, both in common and individually, according to his nature and grace, this life was the light of men, etc.; that he was made flesh, and is true God and true man in unity of person, and not another God and another man, nor another Jesus and another Christ, and this Word was made flesh, etc. Samosatenus will deny that this purpose was set before John, namely because it is opposed to the cause he puts forward. But in that ancient history, which of the two sides will good men rather believe? Those fathers who lived partly in the same and nearby times, and partly through a continuous succession of ages handed down to posterity this doctrine received from their forebears; or new men? It belonged to those who either saw these things themselves or received them closely from those who did to relate true history. The new men, by contrast, can fabricate, and they have openly departed from what was handed down. This is the second argument by which, as we said before, this new equivocation ought to be refuted and overthrown: that there was a constant consensus of that orthodox Church in holding firmly to the truth of this doctrine against the particular inventions of those men whom an insane spirit has sometimes stirred up. For from that agreement of the holy Fathers we learn, on the one hand, the occasion offered from outside by the heretics, on the other, the pious purpose and aim of the Apostle and Evangelist John, and finally the invincible truth of this doctrine, through the Spirit of God.

units.la: Sed ne forte Samosatenus hoc loco (vt solent isti) crimi-netur, nos ab auctoritate hominum argumentari, huic testimonio in rebus diuinis habendam non esse fidem (etsi Dei testimonio caruisse illos quis dicat?) videri quid Christus, quid Deus, quid Scriptura dicat, oportere: iam tertium illud affirmamus, ipsius rei natura quæ agitur æquiuocatione istam euerti, quam Samosatenus cupit obtrudere. Hanc autem rei naturam verbis Chrysosto-miiam mi iam ante satis expressimus principio fermè segmenti huius: quæ verba ita plana sunt, ut nihil a nobis ad illustrationem eorū possit accedere. Agitur de persona diuina: res ergo æterna agitur, quæ non supponitur temporali principio (vt ita loquar) sed magis præponitur. Hanc vero æternam personam quorsum diceret Ioannes fuisse in principio prædicationis Euangelicæ? Si negabit diuinam personam esse (vt facit) nos affirmamus, & pòst vbi de hac re agitur, id est, sequente loco demonstrabimus. Summa, verum est illud Logicorum dictum, Talia esse subiecta, qualia permittuntur esse a prædicatis suis commodè intellectis: & vicissim, talia esse prædicata, qualia esse a subiectis permittuntur: quia alterū circumscriptione quamdā alterius in veris enunciatis cōplectitur. Hic autē de subiecto diuino, id est, æterno agitur, & quidem de rebus essentialibus eius, quę dicuntur de eo per se: Sic ergo prædicatum accipi, non angustius fieri necesse est.
units.tr: But lest perhaps Samosatenus here (as such men usually do) accuse us of arguing from the authority of men, and say that in divine matters the testimony of men is not to be trusted, and that one must see what Christ, what God, and what Scripture says (though who would say those men lacked the testimony of God?), we affirm, thirdly, that the very nature of the matter under discussion overturns the equivocation which Samosatenus wishes to impose. We have already expressed this nature of the matter in Chrysostom's words near the beginning of this section, and those words are so plain that nothing from us could add to their clarity. The matter concerns a divine person; therefore it concerns an eternal thing, which is not supposed to have a temporal beginning (so to speak) but is rather placed before all time. But why would John say that this eternal person was at the beginning of the evangelical preaching? If Samosatenus denies that he is a divine person (as he does), we affirm that he is, and we will demonstrate it later, where this matter is treated, that is, in the following section. In sum, the saying of the logicians is true: subjects are such as their predicates, rightly understood, allow them to be; and conversely, predicates are such as the subjects allow them to be, because the one embraces the other within a certain limitation in true propositions. Here, however, the subject is divine, that is, eternal, and indeed the predicates concern its essential things, which are said of it in themselves. So to take the predicate in this way, there is no need to make it narrower.

units.la: Nunc de natura & conditione loci ipsius videamus. Principiū, ait ille, tempus est illud Euangelij, quo cœptum est a Christo prædicari: & locos adfert ad dicti tui confirmationem. Ego vero (vt taceā, quòd tu ipse euertis hanc restrictionē tuā segmento 4. vt in eum locū dicturi sumus) vtrumq; nego ad hunc locum pertinere, determinationē principij, & locos istos qui ad determinationem probandā adducuntur. Probamus hoc modo: Quod per se indeterminatū est, eius varia est ac multiplex pro ratione locorū determinatio: Ita est autē principiū per se. Ergo variæ determinationis capax. Tum quod, variæ est determinationis capax, id ex loco ipso determinatur, nō autē ex alijs locis, nisi forte idē dixerint re aut analogia: Principiū est variæ determinationis capax: Ex loco ipso igitur determinandū, non autē ex alijs qui nec re, nec analogia dicunt idē. His autē locis (vltimū si exceperis, de quo tuo ordine posteà) idē non dici probo tum ex Samosatenis ipsius confessione, tum ex ipsis Scripturæ verbis.
units.tr: Now let us look at the nature and context of the passage itself. The beginning, he says, is that time of the gospel when Christ began to be preached, and he brings passages to confirm what you say. I, indeed (to say nothing of the fact that you yourself overturn this restriction of yours in section 4, as we shall say when we come to that place), deny that either the determination of the beginning, or those passages that are brought to prove this determination, pertain to this place. We prove it thus: What is indeterminate in itself has a varied and manifold determination according to the reasons of the places; but the beginning is such in itself. Therefore it is capable of varied determination. Moreover, what is capable of varied determination is determined from the place itself, not from other places, unless perhaps they say the same thing in fact or by analogy. The beginning is capable of varied determination. Therefore it must be determined from the place itself, and not from other places which say the same thing neither in fact nor by analogy. I prove that these passages (except the last one, which we will take up in its own order later) do not say the same thing, both from Samosatenus's own admission and from the words of Scripture itself.

units.la: Hîc enim agitur de Sermone Dei absolutè & de illius esse: illic de relatione temporaria, sine qua nulla humana actio apud alios institui ficriqué, aut ab alijs obseruari potest. Non igitur necessaria est hæc determinatio, petita ex alijs locis & differentibus. Non necessariam esse docui: docebo non esse iustam. Eorum quæ per se indeterminata sunt iusta est determinatio quæ ex loco sumitur: nempe ex subiecto prædicato, & adiunctis ipsorum: Non conuenit autem subiecto, prædicato, vel adiunctis hæc determinatio: non iusta igitur. Subiecto non conuenit: nam hîc agitur de eo Sermone qui est ὑφιστάμενος, subsistens in se, existens in Patre, & Deus cum Patre. Nec prædicato conuenit: nam de eo dicitur quod erat, quod erat apud Deum, & quod erat Deus in principio: quæ omnia de Deo enunciata omne principium temporale transcendunt. Nec adiunctis conuenit: etenim de eo dicitur, quod omnia per ipsum facta sunt, quod in ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum, &c. quorum alia ante principium sunt, nempe quæcunque essentialia personæ ipsius, alia inde a principio temporis, nempe quæ relationem habent ad res creatas & factas in tempore. Negat Samosatenus? atqui res ipsa loquitur, verba sunt euidentissima, & post suo ordine glossemata illius confutabimus: quem in locum, ne longiores simus, & ne actum (quod aiunt) agi oporteat, lectorem reijcimus. Quid? quod etiam inepta est hæc interpretatio? nam tibi, Samosatene, quid est illud, in principio erat sermo? nempe erat tempore Euangelij, quo coeptum est a Christo Euangelium prædicari. Et quis, quaeso, ita loquitur? homo ille erat, quo tempore coepit Rempub. administrare, concionari, peregrinari, &c. Id quidem per conuersionem dici potest, quum de rei existentia forte dubitatur: concionabatur, erat igitur: nam ab est tertij adiecti (vt loquuntur) ad est secundi adiecti valet consequentia. Sed vt vice versa loquatur quisquam, erat ille quum coepit concionari, inceptissimum est, puerile est, non solùm Apostolo, sed etiam viro indignum qui modò ratione vti possit. Quemadmodum si dicimus, omnia per Christum facta sunt in principio, erat igitur, iusta conclusio est: sin autem dicamus, erat quum omnia per ipsum fierent, nihil insulsius. Atque id tamen, Samosatene, vt probes, adducis locos aliquot, futiliterque operam consumis in falso illo tuo glossemate ac puerili dicto alienis probationibus & nihil ad rem facientibus confirmando. Vides nec esse necessariam, nec iustam, sed ineptam interpretationem tuam. Restat vt vnum aliquid addam, quod tu ipse facilè animaduerteris. Erat Christus, inquis, quum coepit praedicare. Agnosco: quid autem? non ante erat? Erat certè, quum coepit Ioannes praedicare: hic autem praedicauit ante Christum. Neque id solùm, sed erat etiam ex quo coepit in mundo esse, id est, ex quo conceptus est, natus, &c. Quòd si erat in principio praedicationis suæ, & fuit ante principium illud, quis iam non videt loquutione hac, erat in principio, non excludi tempus quod isti principio praecesserit? Itaque non est cur ægrè Samosatenus ferat, si vel ipso annuente ita concludimus; Qui erat in principio hoc, ante hoc principium erat: Sermo erat in principio: Ergo & ante principium fuit. Est autem principium hoc temporis, & eorum omnium quæ sunt in tempore: fuit ergo hic Sermo ante principium temporis, rerumque temporalium omnium. Quæ cùm ita sint, falsam esse interpretationem Samosateni huius, alienam probationem (loci enim qui adducuntur, nihil ad rem) & inanem conclusionem affirmamus: quod omnes boni visuri sunt. Turpiter verò ex loco 1. Ioan. 1. disputator noster πως λογίζεται, quū ex natura vna Christi & proprietatibus ipsius concludit ad tollendam naturam alteram cum suis proprietatibus. Primùm enim locum interpretatur malè, deinde etiam argumentatur exeo malè. Dicit Ioannes, quod erat a principio, &c. nempe, ait iste, principio prædicationis. Si solùm tunc fuisse dicit, negamus, & negari oportere ante ostendimus nouum istud reftrictionis genus: falsum enim. Si iam ante fuit (vt certè fuit) quando fuisse dicendus est? Respondet Ioannes, Sermo est vita æterna, & vita æterna: Vita æterna erat in principio apud Patrem: Sermo igitur erat in principio apud Patrem. Negat iste. cur autem? nam de Christo verbo, visibili oculis, palpabili manibus, qui ex Maria natus est, loquitur: non igitur de æterno. Consequens fallum, quia vtrumque de Christo verum est diuersa ratione. Propterea enim dicit Ioannes primùm de natura vtraque distinctè, tum verò de persona ex naturis duabus constante. De diuina dicit, quod erat a principio: de humana, quod audiuimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, & manus nostræ contrectarunt: vtrumque verò ad vnitatem personæ eiusdem pertinere ostendit subdens, de Sermone illo vitæ: non enim totum Sermonis auditum est, visum, &c. sed tantùm de eo aliquid. Ergo ex falsa loci interpretatione Samofatenus argumentatur falsò, posita natura vna alteram tolli eximians. Quid ergo? an tibi, Samofatene, hæc propositio placet? Qui visibilis & palpabilis est, is non est inuisibilis & impalpabilis. Nos verò ita respondemus: si secundùm idem dixeris, concedimus: sunt enim membra hæc contradictoria. Sin minùs, quid obstat quin vt Aethiops niger & albus est, ita homo sit idem visibilis & palpabilis secundùm hoc, & contrà secundùm illud? Homo secundùm naturam corporis, visibilis & palpabilis est: secundùm naturam spiritus sui, minimé: idem ergo visibilis, & inuisibilis. Hoc ipsum eodem iure de Christo dicisto dicimus: nam quod erat a principio, id est inuisibile: quod assumsit in tempore, id auditum, visum, spectatum, & contrectatum est. Eadem igitur persona secundum illud inuisibilis, secundum hoc visibilis est. Impium vero genus illud argumentationis est, ex quo sententiam suam hic Samosatenus se putat confirmare, quum ait, Ille aeternus qui fingitur, a nemine vnquam palpatus ab aeterno, vel post legitur, neque vnquam auditus. Nunquam hoc argumento quisquam vsurus est, quin supponat principium ἀδεων, siue sciens prudens, siue imprudens faciat: nempe qui non est palpatus ab aeterno, eum non esse aeternum: & (quod amplius) qui nunquam palpatus est, neque auditus, eum ne esse quidem. Sine hoc axiomate inconsequens futura est tota Samosateni argumentatio. Hoc autem principium & axioma ridiculum non Epicurus, non Diagoras atheos, non Theodorus Cyrenaicus ausus est dicere, quod Samosatenus imprudens occupauit. Sed hic in tota hac quaestione varijs modis errat, & supponit opinionum monstra: 1. Christum non esse aeternum Deum, &c. quod suo loco alibi (si Deus volet) demonstrabimus. 2. non assumpsisse in tempore humanam carnem in vnitatem personae, vt fit Immanuel. 3. illum aeternum non fuisse corporaliter auditum, visum, spectatum, palpatum, &c. quod de natura illa aeterna verum, de persona falsum est. Posterioris editionis eadem plane ratio est. Nam principium pro aeternitate accipi posse negat, & confirmat: damus. Tum principium restringit ad ordinem rerum quae in tempore de Christo praedicantur, exemplo Mosis & Marci: nos confutauimus, exemplaque dissimilia esse docuimus. Postremo miratur Theologos vir acutus a sua illa regula hic discedere, qua dicunt, nullum interpretationis genus melius ac securius in-
units.tr: For here the discussion concerns the Word of God absolutely and his being, whereas there it concerns a temporal relation, without which no human action can be undertaken among others or observed by others. So this determination, drawn from other passages and different things, is not necessary. I have shown that it is not necessary; I shall now show that it is not just. A determination taken from the context is the just one for things that are indeterminate in themselves: namely from the subject, the predicate and their adjuncts. But this determination fits neither the subject, the predicate nor the adjuncts; therefore it is not just. It does not fit the subject, for the Word here discussed is hypostatic, subsisting in himself, existing in the Father, and God with the Father. Nor does it fit the predicate, for of him it is said that he was, that he was with God, and that he was God in the beginning*; all these statements about God transcend every temporal beginning. Nor does it fit the adjuncts, for of him it is said that all things were made through him, that in him was life, and that the life was the light of men, and so on. Some of these things are before the beginning, namely whatever is essential to his person; others are from the beginning of time, namely those that have a relation to created things made in time. Does Samosatenus deny this? Yet the matter itself speaks, the words are most plain, and I will afterwards refute his glosses in their proper place; to that place, lest I be too long and lest (as they say) the same thing be done twice, I send the reader. What is more, this interpretation is absurd. For tell me, Samosatene, what does in the beginning was the Word mean? Surely it means that he was at the time of the Gospel, when the Gospel began to be preached by Christ. And who, I ask, speaks like that? A man was at the time when he began to administer the commonwealth, to preach, to travel abroad, and so on. Such a usage may indeed be put the other way round when the existence of a thing is in doubt: he preached, therefore he was; for the inference from is of the third adjective (as they say) to was of the second holds. But for anyone to speak the other way round, he was when he began to preach, is most inept, childish, and unworthy even of an apostle, or of any man who can use reason. Just as if we say, all things were made through Christ in the beginning, therefore he was, the conclusion is sound; but if we say, he was when all things were being made through him, nothing could be more insipid. Yet, Samosatene, to prove this you bring forward a few passages and waste your effort in confirming that false gloss of yours and that childish saying by proofs foreign to the matter and irrelevant to it. You see that your interpretation is neither necessary nor just, but absurd. It remains for me to add one thing, which you yourself will easily notice. Christ was, you say, when he began to preach. I agree. But what then? Was he not before? He certainly was when John began to preach; yet John preached before Christ. And not only that, but he also was from the time he began to be in the world, that is, from the time he was conceived, born, and so on. But if he was at the beginning of his preaching, and was before that beginning, who does not now see that by this phrase, was in the beginning, the time that preceded that beginning is not excluded? Therefore Samosatenus has no reason to be vexed if we conclude, even with his own assent, as follows: He who was in this beginning was before this beginning. The Word was in the beginning. Therefore he was also before the beginning. Now this is the beginning of time and of all things that are in time; therefore this Word was before the beginning of time and of all temporal things. Since these things are so, we affirm that this interpretation of Samosatenus is false, his proof foreign to the matter (for the passages he cites have nothing to do with it), and his conclusion empty; all good men will see this. But our disputant reasons [πως λογίζεται] shamefully from 1 John 1, when from the one nature of Christ and its properties he concludes to the removal of the other nature with its properties. For first he interprets the passage badly, and then he argues badly from it. John says that which was from the beginning, and so on; namely, says he, the beginning of preaching. If John says only that he was then, we deny it, and I have already shown that this new kind of restriction must be denied, for it is false. If he was already before (as certainly he was), when is he to be said to have been? John answers: the Word is eternal life, and eternal life: eternal life was in the beginning with the Father; therefore the Word was in the beginning with the Father. He denies this. But why? Because, he says, John is speaking of Christ the Word, visible to the eyes, tangible to the hands, who was born of Mary, and therefore not of the eternal Word. The consequence is false, because both are true of Christ in different respects. For John speaks first of each nature separately, and then of the person constituted of two natures. Of the divine nature he says that which was from the beginning; of the human, that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and which our hands have handled; and he shows that both pertain to the unity of the same person by adding concerning that Word of life: for it is not the whole Word that was heard, seen, and so on, but only something of him. Therefore Samosatenus argues falsely from a false interpretation of the passage, supposing that the one nature is destroyed by the other. What then? Does this proposition please you, Samosatene? What is visible and tangible is not invisible and intangible. We answer thus: if you mean in the same respect, we grant it, for these members are contradictory. But if not, what prevents a man from being at once visible and tangible in one respect and, on the contrary, invisible in another, just as an Ethiopian is both black and white? A man according to the nature of his body is visible and tangible; according to the nature of his spirit, by no means: the same man is therefore both visible and invisible. We say the same of Christ by the same right: for that which was from the beginning is invisible; that which he assumed in time was heard, seen, looked upon, and handled. The same person, therefore, is invisible according to the one and visible according to the other. Impious indeed is that kind of argument, by which Samosatenus thinks he confirms his opinion, when he says: That eternal one who is feigned was never touched by anyone from eternity, or afterwards is read of, nor was he ever heard. No one will ever use this argument without presupposing the axiom [ἀδεων], whether he does so knowingly or unknowingly: namely, that one who was not touched from eternity is not eternal; and (what is more) one who was never touched nor heard is not even existent. Without this axiom the whole argument of Samosatenus will be inconsequent. But this principle and axiom, so ridiculous, neither Epicurus, nor Diagoras the atheist, nor Theodorus the Cyrenaic dared to state; Samosatenus has taken it up unwittingly. But in this whole question he errs in various ways, and presupposes monstrous opinions: 1. that Christ is not the eternal God, and so on, which I shall demonstrate elsewhere in its own place, if God wills; 2. that he did not assume human flesh in time into the unity of the person, so that he became Immanuel; 3. that the eternal one was not bodily heard, seen, looked upon, handled, and so on, which is true of that eternal nature but false of the person. The reasoning of the later edition is plainly the same. For he denies that beginning can be taken for eternity, and he confirms this; we grant it. Then he restricts beginning to the order of things that are predicated of Christ in time, citing the example of Mark and Moses; we have refuted this and shown that those examples are dissimilar. Finally, the clever man wonders that the theologians depart here from their own rule, by which they say that no kind of interpretation can be better and safer than when Scripture is explained by the same Scripture; this, he says, we have not observed in this passage. We acknowledge the first proposition, provided that ambiguity is guarded against. For the same Scripture must be the same not only in word but also in fact and in analogy, so that the defence…

units.la: M & ueniri posse, quàm si Scriptura per eamdem scripturam expo-natur: id a nobis in hoc loco minimè obseruari. Prio-rem propositionem agnoscimus, si ab æquiuocatione caueatur. Eamdem enim scripturam non voce solùm oportet esse, verumetiam reipsa & analogia, vt defensio-nis secundæ segmento 13. ostendimus: nec aliter iustã esse ex loco vno expositionem alterius. Etsi autem loci illi, Mosis inquam & Marci, vocem eamdem habent, tamen nullam reipsa & analogia cum hoc habent conuenien-tiam, vt de hoc iudicium fieri ex illis possit. Quòd si hæc distinctio nō obseruabitur, nulla fermè pagina est in scripturis sacris, ex qua absurda plurima grauissimáq; non sint consequutura, facta confusione sensus propter vnius eiusdémq; vocis occupationem. Regula ergo, quam Samosatenus iactat, a nobis facit: qui non miramur verissimam hanc regulam ab ipso minimè seruari; sed monemus vt seruata hac eadem regula deinceps magis discat sapere in rerum sacrarum inuestigatione, & similia similibus nō secundùm literam solùm, sed magis secundùm veritatem expendat spiritualitérq; diiudicet, spiritualia cum ijs quæ spiritualia sunt coniungendo, vt Apostolus præcipit, non autem corporalia & temporalia (vt hic facit) cum spiritualibus atque æternis confundendo.
units.tr: ...can be obtained than if Scripture is explained by the same Scripture; this is what we do not observe in this place. We acknowledge the first proposition, provided that it is safeguarded against equivocation. For the same Scripture must be the same not only in words but also in fact and in analogy, as we showed in the thirteenth section of the Second Defence; and otherwise the exposition of one passage by another is not legitimate. Yet those passages, I mean those of Moses and Mark, have the same wording, but they have no real agreement with this passage in fact or analogy, so that no judgment can be formed about this passage from them. But if this distinction is not observed, there is almost no page of Holy Scripture from which many absurd and very grave consequences would not follow, the sense being confused by the appropriation of one and the same word. So the rule which Samosatenus boasts of is our rule. We do not marvel that he himself by no means keeps this most true rule; rather we advise him that, keeping this same rule, he should learn to be wiser in the investigation of sacred things, and weigh like things with like not merely according to the letter but more according to the truth, and judge spiritually, joining spiritual things with those that are spiritual, as the Apostle commands, and not confounding bodily and temporal things (as he does here) with spiritual and eternal things.

units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 3.

units.la: Erat verbum.
units.tr: The Word was.

units.la: VERBI nomine putant denotari aliquem filium æternum, per quem Deus omnia ageret sub veteri Testamento, & loquutus fuerit cum Patribus. Sed hæc commenta hominum refutant multi loci Scripturæ; & præcipuè Actor. 13. capite, quòd omnia quæ erant facta & promissa in vetere Testamento vnus ille Deus Pater præstiterit, & filium etiam eduxerit ex femine femine Davidis: Et Hebr. 1. cap. dicitur Deum olim sub vetere Testamento loquutum per Prophetas, nunc autem novissimis temporibus, id est, sub novo Testamento loquutum per filium: & Actor. 1. Lucas dicit se scribere quae coepit Iesus docere & facere, nihil unquam scribens de gestis Christi sub vetere Testamento. Nos vero Sermonem seu Verbum esse dicimus Christum hominem visibilem ex Maria natum, qui voluntatem paternam homines docuit: unde etiam, quod prologuutor esset paternorum mandatorum, nomen habet Sermonis vel Verbi. Qui enim hic Verbum appellatur, alio in loco a Ioanne & aliis vocatur eodem sensu Magister, praeceptor, doctor, Apostolus confessionis nostrae, Pontifex, imago Dei inconspicui: quae omnia Christus homo expressit tum dictis, tum factis, &c. Sed & omnes loci Scripturae, quicunque de hoc Verbo loquuntur, non intelligunt aliquem Christum aeternum ante Mariam, vel binaturium, sed hunc de quo loquimur hominem: ut 1. Ioan. 1. Sermonem seu Verbum describit visibile, palpabile, quod & auditum est, Christum intelligens hominem. Sic Actor. 13. Sermo salutis vocatur, qui ignoratus ab Hierosolymitanis, condemnatus & occisus est. Sic Apoc. 19. amictus veste sanguinolenta, cuius nomen SERMO DEI. Hi loci omnes hominem Christum Verbum esse docent, Sermonem videlicet illum qui docendo loquebatur, non aliquem aeternum, qui nihil docuisse legitur.
units.tr: By the name Word, they think, is meant some eternal Son, through whom God acted under the Old Testament and spoke with the Fathers. But many passages of Scripture refute these fictions of men, and especially Acts 13, where it is said that all the things that were done and promised in the Old Testament that one God, the Father, accomplished, and that he also brought forth his Son from the seed of David. And Hebrews 1 says that God formerly spoke under the Old Testament through the prophets, but now in the last times, that is, under the New Testament, he has spoken through the Son; and Acts 1, Luke says that he writes of what Jesus began to teach and do, never writing anything about the deeds of Christ under the Old Testament. But we say that the Word or Speech is Christ, a visible man born of Mary, who taught men the will of the Father; hence also he has the name of Speech or Word because he was the spokesman of the Father's commands. For he who is here called the Word is elsewhere called by John and others, in the same sense, Teacher, Instructor, Doctor, the Apostle of our confession, High Priest, the image of the invisible God; and Christ the man expressed all these things, both by words and deeds, and so on. But also all the passages of Scripture which speak of this Word do not understand some eternal Christ before Mary, or one with two natures, but this man of whom we speak; as 1 John 1, which describes the Word or Speech as visible, tangible, which was also heard, meaning Christ the man. So Acts 13 calls him the word of salvation, who was disregarded by the Jerusalemites, condemned and killed. So Revelation 19 speaks of him clothed in a blood-stained garment, whose name is THE WORD OF GOD. All these passages teach that the man Christ is the Word, that is, that Speech which, by teaching, spoke, not some eternal being, who is never read to have taught anything.

units.la: Praeterea interpretes in expositione huius nominis, Verbum, variant: in genere autem concordant, quod Verbum sit quidam aeternus Dei filius, sine initio a Patre genitus ante omnia saecula, coaeternus, consubstantialis, ac per omnia Patri coaequalis, secunda in Trinitate persona: & huiusmodi alia quaedam comminiscuntur. Sed hoc fuit merum humanum inventum. Ex divinis enim Scripturis haec nunquam probare poterunt: immò tota Scriptura aduersatur. Ioannes ergo Verbi nomine ipsum Dominum Iesum Christum Dei filium intelle-xit: non tamen respectu alicuius naturæ aut substantiæ, sed tantummodò ratione officij, quo ipse Dei Filius vsus est in ma-nifeftando Euangelio Dei Patris fui verbo. Nam nihil omni-no Christus, quantum ad fui naturam ac substantiam, nobis profuisset, nisi Euangelij arcanum annunciaffet. Et obserua hanc esse ipsius Ioannis peculiarem phrafim: habet enim Ioan-nes peculiares quasdam phrafes, quibus nemo alius scripto-rum Ecclesiasticorum vtitur. Nam in tota Scriptura non in-uenitur Christum appellatum fuisse Verbum, præterquàm ab ipso Ioanne: nec alia ratione id factum est, quàm quòd ipsius officio ac opera nobis ipsum Euangelij verbum, quòd prius la-tebat, innotuit. Est enim Metonymia, seu denominatio: nam ideò (vt dictum est) Christus Verbum dicitur, quia Dei iussu verbum Euangelij nobis primus ex sinu Patris annuncia-uit. In hanc sententiam Ioannes ipse in sua Apocalypsi cap. 19. hoc Verbi nomine vsus est, quum dixit Verbum esse no-men Christi. Caterùm quod magnam lucem adfert huic loco est, quòd omnia nomina quæ ipsi Christo posita inueniun-tur, non ratione alicuius naturæ aut substantiæ æternæ, sed ra-tione solùm officij ac effecti fuerunt indita. Nuncupatur enim lux mundi, via, veritas, vita, ostium, pastor bonus, Iesus, Christus, magister, vitis vera, panis viuus, agnus Dei, aduo-catus, Sacerdos, iustificatio, sanctificatio, resurrectio, Ponti-sex, ac infinitis aliis nominibus. Quemadmodum ergo nomi-nafta quæ recensuimus (nam huiusmodi nominibus ipse Ioannes fere omnibus metaphoricè vtitur præter aliorum Scriptorum morem) rei aliquid nouæ non adferunt, quam & cæteri Euangelistæ & Apostoli non tradiderint: eadem ratione dicendū est hoc loco, Verbi nomine nihil noui ab aliis scriptoribus adferre: æquè enim istis omnibus nominibus metaphoricè vti-tur Ioannes: ita vt vel hinc discere liceat, in rebus ad salutem pertinenpertinentibus non anxiè nobis laborandum esse in inquirendo quid in substantia Christus sit, sed quid ratione multorum beneficiorum ac effectuum nobis attulerit ac profuerit. Summa ergo est hæc: Scripturus Ioannes de Domino Iesu Christo Dei filio, mundíque Redemptore, nec non & de spirituali mundo spiritualiter per eum instaurato, altius ab origine, vel ante ipsius Christi manifestationem orditur dicens, In principio erat Verbum, id est, Christus Dei filius in principio sui Euangelij, antequàm ad suos veniret & manifestaretur, erat, id est, versabatur, & id quidem per triginta annos, in mundo apud Iudæos, illíque de nomine & facie notus erat: nam vulgo habebatur ac appellabatur filius Iosephi fabri. Sed quòd ipse Iesus esset Dei filius, annunciaturúsque esset Euangelium Dei, Verbum hoc ipsum omnibus prorsus ignotum erat. Ideò sequitur, Et verbum erat apud Deum.
units.tr: Moreover, the interpreters differ in their explanation of this name, Word; but they agree in general that the Word is a certain eternal Son of God, begotten without beginning by the Father before all ages, coeternal, consubstantial, and in all things equal to the Father, the second person in the Trinity; and they invent other things of this kind. But this was pure human invention. For they could never prove these things from the divine Scriptures; indeed the whole of Scripture is opposed to them. John therefore by the name Word understood the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, yet not with respect to any nature or substance, but only by reason of the office which the Son of God himself exercised in manifesting the Gospel, the Word of his Father. For Christ, as to his nature and substance, would have profited us nothing at all, unless he had announced the mystery of the Gospel. And observe that this is John's own peculiar phrase; for John has certain peculiar phrases which no other writer of ecclesiastical works uses. For in the whole of Scripture it is not found that Christ was called the Word except by John himself; nor was it done for any other reason than that by his office and work the Word of the Gospel itself, which previously lay hidden, became known to us. It is a metonymy, or a denomination: for Christ is called the Word (as has been said) because, at God's command, he first announced to us the word of the Gospel from the bosom of the Father. John himself uses this name Word in this sense in his Apocalypse, chapter 19, when he says that the Word is the name of Christ. But what brings great light to this passage is that all the names which are found applied to Christ himself were given not by reason of any eternal nature or substance, but only by reason of office and effect. For he is called the light of the world, the way, the truth, the life, the door, the good shepherd, Jesus, Christ, teacher, the true vine, the living bread, the Lamb of God, advocate, priest, justification, sanctification, resurrection, high priest, and by countless other names. Therefore, just as the names we have listed (for John uses almost all such names metaphorically, contrary to the custom of other writers) bring nothing new about the thing, which the other Evangelists and Apostles did not also hand down, so by the same reasoning it must be said here that by the name Word he brings nothing new beyond the other writers: for John uses this name metaphorically just as he does all those others. So from this one may learn that in matters pertaining to salvation we need not labour anxiously in inquiring what Christ is in substance, but what he has brought and profited us by the many benefits and effects. The sum therefore is this: John, about to write of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and Redeemer of the world, and also of the spiritual world spiritually restored through him, begins higher, from the origin, or before the manifestation of Christ himself, saying: In the beginning was the Word, that is, Christ, the Son of God, at the beginning of his Gospel, before he came to his own and was made manifest, was, that is, dwelt, and that indeed for thirty years, in the world among the Jews, and was known to them by name and face; for he was commonly regarded and called the son of Joseph the carpenter. But that Jesus himself was the Son of God, and was about to proclaim the Gospel of God, this Word itself was altogether unknown to all. Therefore it follows: And the Word was with God.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: Hîc pium Lectorem rogo ad duo capita seorsim velit attendere: vnû, quid prior ille Samosatenus reticeat: alterum, quid dicat. Quid reticeat, iam antè ostendimus: nempe verbum, erat: cuius vim certo consilio dissimulat, de qua superiore loco dicebamus ex sanctorum Patrum testimonio. Hoc autè suo commodo, vel potiús incommodo imperitorû reticet: qua fide, nouit & cognoscet Dominus. Omnino tamen factum absurdû esse posterior Samosatenus vidit: ac propterea interpretationem adiecit illius verbi quam prior dissimulauerat. Iam quid dicat, videamus. Hoc autem duobus membris concluditur: nam primùm doctrinam nostram adfert oppugnátq;: deinde adfert & confirmat suam. In adferenda doctrina nostra (de vocibus enim curiosè nolo contendere, ad rem aducerto) sic definit Verbum, quà persona diuina est solum, vt illud belle dissimulet quod sanctè credimus profitemurque, Verbum hoc esse carnem factum, personam vnam ex duabus naturis constitutam. Cur autem dissimulat? quia non credit, neque rationibus eius commodat quòd credimus: at nos tamen credimus, quod a disputante (si modò bona fide velit disputare) minimè dissimulari oportuit. Iniquè igitur. Nam si vtrumq; profitemur in vnitate personæ (profitemur autem) certè vnum ponendo alterum minimè tollimus: atque hinc tamen profluere, hic hærere, huc spectare singula ipsius argumenta omnes visuri sunt, qui æquo animo & sine præiudicato ad rem aduerterint. Atque hæc causa est, cur omissa parte de qua inter nos convenit, Deum his vltimis temporibus nobiscum per Filium loquutum esse, eam solum oppugnat quam nos de Christo ante aduentum ipsius in carne affirmamus, Deum in Testamento vetere omnia per hunc Sermonem egisse & loquutum esse cum Patribus. Hoc enim si vicerit, alterum illud eádem se putat obtinere, si tum non fecit aut dixit quicquam, ergo non fuisse tunc: ac proinde multo minùs veram affirmationem nostram de æternitate eius haberi oportere. Doctrinam nostram de Verbo, Filio æterno Dei, per quem olim Pater egit omnia, tribus oppugnat locis. Ex primo, qui est Actor. 13. duas argumentationes colligit. Prior, in hunc modum: Quod Deus Pater fecit in Testamento vetere, non fecit Filius: Deus Pater promisit & praestitit omnia in Testamento vetere: non ergo Filius. Maior omnino falsa est, & contradictoria sanctissimis illis certissimisque Christi propositionibus, Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor: item, quæcunque Pater facit, hæc etiam Filius pariter facit. Priore omnis temporum, posteriore omnis operationum in res creatas diuisio tollitur. Grauiter itaque erratur in hac argumentatione,
units.tr: Here I ask the pious reader to attend separately to two points: first, what that former Samosatene passes over in silence, and second, what he says. What he passes over I have already shown: namely the word was, whose force he deliberately dissembles, and which I discussed in the earlier passage from the testimony of the holy Fathers. He passes it over for his own convenience, or rather to the disadvantage of the unlearned; with what good faith, the Lord knows and will know. Yet the later Samosatene saw that the omission was altogether absurd, and therefore added an explanation of the word that the former had dissembled. Now let us see what he says. It falls into two parts: first he brings forward our doctrine and attacks it, then he brings forward and confirms his own. In presenting our doctrine (for I do not wish to quarrel over words, I come to the matter), he defines the Word only as a divine person, so as cleverly to hide what we holy believe and profess: that this Word was made flesh, one person constituted from two natures. Why does he hide it? Because he does not believe it, and his arguments do not suit what we believe. Yet we do believe it, and a disputant who wishes to argue in good faith ought by no means to conceal it. He acts unfairly, then. For if we profess both natures in the unity of the person (and we do profess it), certainly by affirming the one we do not in the least remove the other. Yet all who consider the matter calmly and without prejudgment will see that each of his arguments flows from this, clings to this, and aims at this. And this is the reason why, having passed over the point on which we agree, that God in these last times has spoken with us through the Son, he attacks only what we affirm of Christ before his coming in the flesh: that God in the Old Testament did all things through this Word and spoke with the fathers. For if he wins this point, he thinks he has won the other as well: if then the Word did or said nothing, therefore he was not then; and consequently our true affirmation of his eternity ought much less to be held. He attacks our doctrine of the Word, the eternal Son of God through whom the Father once did all things, in three places. From the first, which is Acts 13, he draws two arguments. The first runs thus: What God the Father did in the Old Testament, the Son did not do; God the Father promised and performed all things in the Old Testament; therefore not the Son. The major premise is wholly false and contradicts those most holy and certain sayings of Christ: My Father worketh hitherto, and I work; likewise, whatever the Father does, these the Son also does in like manner. By the former the whole division of times is removed; by the latter, the whole division of operations upon created things. Therefore he errs gravely in this argument,

units.la: Ioan. 5. mentatione, quum de operatione per omnia & in omne tempus communi diuisio statuitur. Est enim communis operatio, vna eademq; est Patris & Filij. Non est autem Samosatenus nescius, a communi ad particulare argumenta quæuis negantia, affirmantia vero vniuersa solum recte confici. Itaque si dixeris, Filius nihil promisit, nec præstitit in Testamento vetere, optime consequetur, nec Pater igitur. E contrario autem si dixeris, Pater promisit olim & præstitit omnia, consequetur iusta consequentia, ergo & Filius: nam Pater & Filius operantur vsque adhuc, & quæcunque facit Pater, ea Filius pariter facit. Posterior argumentatio sic habet: Qui ex semine alicuius est, non ante fuit quam educeretur ex femine: Filiū eduxit Pater ex femine Dauidis: ergo non ante fuit. In hac Samosatenus itidem παραλογίζεται. Nam primum Maior propositio physica seu naturalis est, de simplice & naturali homine vera naturaliter: hoc autem quid ad supernaturale & diuinum opus? quum itaque de Christo agitur, non aliter vera est hæc propositio, quàm si adiceceris, quà ex femine alterius est, non ante fuisse quàm educeretur ex femine. Deinde Minor insidiosa est, latente æquiuocatione: Filium enim Samosatenus intelligit appellari Christum respectu naturæ humanæ, quam solam habeat, & habere a Patre. Falsum, vt ante diximus: & falsò ex naturæ vnius positione statuens remotionem alterius, eam sibi videtur tollere: nam vt parte vna essentiali rei cuiuscunque posita, altera non tollitur, sed contrà necessariò ponitur ad constituendum totum: sic natura vna essentiali Christi posita, altera non tollitur, sed contrà, ex quo illa est, ponitur eadem necessariò ad constitutionem personæ. Postremò etiam errat, quum naturæ vnius propria attribuit alteri, eáque de toto persona prædicari iubet. Filius non ante est, inquit, quàm pro-
units.tr: John 5. when he sets up a division of operation into all things and all times as if it were common. For the operation is common, one and the same of the Father and the Son. Nor is the Samosatene unaware that arguments denying something of the particular from the common are sound, but that only affirmations made of the universal are rightly drawn. So if you say, The Son promised nothing and performed nothing in the Old Testament, he will rightly conclude, nor then the Father. On the other hand, if you say, The Father promised and performed all things long ago, the just conclusion follows, therefore the Son too: for the Father and the Son work even until now, and whatever the Father does, the Son does in like manner. The latter argument runs thus: Whoever is of the seed of someone, was not before he was brought forth from the seed; the Father brought the Son forth from the seed of David; therefore he was not before. In this too the Samosatene likewise παραλογίζεται (reasons fallaciously). For first, the major premise is a physical or natural proposition, true naturally of a simple and natural man; but what has that to do with a supernatural and divine work? When Christ is in question, this proposition is true only if you add: in so far as he is of another's seed, he was not before he was brought forth from that seed. Next, the minor premise is deceptive, with a hidden equivocation: the Samosatene understands the Son to be called Christ with respect to the human nature alone, which he has, and has from the Father. This is false, as we said before; and by inferring from the positing of one nature the removal of the other, falsely, he thinks he removes it. For just as when one essential part of anything is posited, the other is not removed but on the contrary is necessarily posited to constitute the whole, so when one essential nature of Christ is posited, the other is not removed but on the contrary, from which the former is, the same is necessarily posited for the constitution of the person. Lastly, he also errs when he attributes to one nature what belongs to the other, and bids that what belongs to one nature be predicated of the whole person. The Son is not before, he says, than he is brought forth by the Father;

units.la: e ducatur a Patre: Filium eduxit Pater ex femine Dauidis, nem-pe secundum naturam humanam quam eduxit: Ergo non ante fuit: certè secundum eam naturam qua ex semi-ne Dauidis est. Nobis verò pari iure licebit argumenta-ri, & vere: Filium Pater ante, immo æternum genuit: ergo ante, immo æternum est, nempe quà persona diuina est, Sermo æternus æterni Patris. Probationes posteà videbimus. Ex secundo loco, qui est Hebr. 1. sic argu-mentatur: Deus olim per Prophetas loquutus est, his verò vltimis temporibus & nunc per Filium: Non ergo Filius olim loquutus est, ac ne fuit quidem. Negatur vterque conclu-sionis locus. Prior locus, non esse olim loquutum Filiū, cuidenter fallit ex elenchi ignoratione, quia non secun-dum idem & eodem modo Filius in Testamento vetere & nouo loquutus est. Nam olim quidem loquutus est vt Sermo Dei, at non in carne assumta personaliter: post autem loquutus est vt Sermo factus caro, & in carne (in qua Filius Dei venerat) patefactus: quod ipse Apostolus interpretatur principio cap. 2. eiusdem epistolæ. Olim loquutus est, quà Sermo Deus solùm: vltimis verò tem-poribus loquutus est, quà Deus & homo, in vnitate per-sonæ ex assumente persona & assumta natura constitutę. At nos ediuerso ita statuimus, Deus Pater olim & tempo-ribus vltimis loquutus est, ergo & Filius: nam communis est (vt paulo ante diximus) operatio Patris & Filij, atque hic pariter facit quæcunque facit Pater. Posterioris conclusionis, Filium ne fuisse quidem, falsitas reuinci-tur maiore apposita. Ea est huiusmodi, homo qui non lo-quitur, non est. Alia dari non potest iusta argumentatio-num lege. At primùm quid magis falsum? quid absur-dius ad ferri potest? nam si homo est, est igitur, quamuis nihil dicat: prædicatum est contrarium subiecto. Deinde mutus homo est, & non loquitur: nam mutus est. Ta-cens cens non loquitur, etsi homo est: sed tacet. Postremò hoc dicitur de homine qui tantùm homo, homo φιλὸς, vel de homine simplice: Nos autem hunc Sermonem Dei non simplicem nudùmque hominem, sed Immanuelem agnoscimus, id est, Deum & hominem: quid hîc simile? Proinde ita religiosè credimus & docemus: Sermo, quà Sermo Dei est, a principio loquutus est cum Patre: quà homo factus est, his vltimis demum temporibus secundùm humanam illam naturam, quam assumfit, loquutus est. Malè itaque ex naturæ vnius modo concluditur de personæ totius conditione: quod vitiosum esse & ἀσυλλόγιστον ante docuimus. Ex tertio loco (est autem ille Actor. 1.) sic argumentatur: Lucas dicit se scribere quæ cœpit Iesus docere & facere, & nihil vnquam scribit de gestis Christi sub Testamento vetere: nec igitur fuit Christus sub Testamento vetere, nec gessit quicquam. Atqui fallacia est in hac comparatione duplex. Primùm enim res secundùm humanitatem assumtam, & in eadem a Christi persona doceri & geri cœptas respexit Lucas, vt historia Euangelica ipsius demonstratur: hîc vero Samosatenus de persona in se ἀσυλλογίστως accipit: sic a dicto secundùm quid (vt vocant) concludit simpliciter. Deinde res diuersas diuerso tempore gestas conturbat elenchi ignoratione, & a non distributo ad distributum concludit vitiosè: aliæ enim res sub Testamento vetere gestæ sunt, & aliæ sub nouo. De rebus autem sub hoc, id est, huius tempore, non sub illo gestis Lucas loquutus est. Postremò id plane alienum est (vt Scholastice loquar) quòd ab auctoritate negatiuè ἀσυλλογίζεται: hoc non dicit Lucas, non ergo fuit Sermo, neque hoc a Sermone gestum. Quis sanus sic argumentetur? fieri enim potest, vt id fuerit, factùm ve fit quod nemo dicat aut scribat: fieri etiam potest, vt dicat ille quod hic non dixerit, prout ab Euangelistis videmus factum. Hic ergo gladius plumbeus. At dicit Lucas, de omnibus quæ cæpit Iesus facere & docere: nihil ergo excipitur. Verum est: propterea quum Lucas non dicat de omnibus simpliciter, sed circumscriptionem adhibeat dicens, quæ cæpit Iesus facere & docere, vniuersalem istam ex determinatione intelligimus, ne fallaciam diuisionis (quò te Samosatene, non vides ruere) committamus. Sic enim ostendit Lucas aliud esse, si quis de omnibus Christi operibus sermonibusque scribere velit vniuersè; aliud verò, si de ijs operibus quæ certo modo, id est, in assumta carne, certóque tempore, nimirum Euangelij post assumtam carnem facere & docere cœpit in persona sua, & continuauit facere & docere in persona Apostolorum seruorum suorum, ex quo sursum in cœlum receptus est. Nam principiū Euangelicæ veritatis Christo tribuitur, quod principium Euangelio suo Lucas describit: continuatio prædicationis illius, Apostolis consequente ordine tributa est, cuius continuationis historiam Lucas secundo libro pertexuit, qui Acta Apostolorum inscribitur. Hæc ergo argumentationum genera qui sciens prudens obijcit, sciens prudens fallit: qui imprudens, fallitur: sed neutrum a nobis scientibus videntibúsque probari bona fide potest. In adferenda & confirmanda doctrina sua quid Samosatenus agat, videamus. Primùm adfert Sermonis huius, de quo Ioannes agit, interpretationem & definitionem quamdam: esse Christum hominem visibilem, ex Maria natum, &c. quæ nos omnia non solùm damus, sed etiam religiosè ex verbo Dei affirmamus. At definitio hæc imperfecta est, si ad mentem Samosateni respexeris: quæ alia mente ab homine orthodoxo & pio enunciata non æquè iniusta aut imperfecta haberetur. Pius enim hæc legens & dicens, Christum intelliget verè Deum vere hominem in vnitate personæ: hic verò Christum hominem dicens, hominem solùm intelligit. Deinde illud etiam pius optima fide annuet, eò quod proloquuntor est paternorum mandatorum, nomen habere Sermonis vel Verbi: sed hic intelligit ea solùm de causa Sermonem appellari, &c. id est, Sermonem esse non essentialem natura genitum a Patre, sed accidentarium, & ita solùm ab officio dictum: quod nos freti veritate negamus, & auctoritate Scripturæ. Atque eadem quoque est probationum ratio, quæ pòst adferuntur: hæ ex appellationibus Christi, illæ ex prædicationib. de Christo enunciatis sumtæ. In ijs enim abeo quod dicitur de vna natura eius, vel potiùs de persona eius secundùm naturam vnam, id est, humanam quam assumfit, argumentatur & concludit de toto personæ, contra omneis iustas, vt antè diximus, argumentandi leges. Falsa itaque conclusio est totius Sermonis huius, in qua positione naturæ vnius esse statuitur remotionem alterius. Vt enim positio materiæ non est remotio formæ, & positio partis vnius de toto aliquo essentialis non est remotio alterius: sic etiam in Christo posita natura vna alteram non sequitur tolli, cùm vtraque coeat in constituenda persona Christi Domini & Seruatoris nostri. Christus enim Deus & homo, ac non homo solùm ab Ecclesia creditur colitúrque. Etsi (vt in transcursu moneam) de appellationibus Christi quæ hîc congestæ habentur, vnam oportet excipi, quòd Christus imago Dei inconspicui appellatur. Nam cæteræ appellationes quidem respiciunt ad nos, & ad nos simplicem relationem habent. Magister enim, præceptor, doctor, & Apostolus confessionis nostræ eo dicitur, quòd instituat nos: Pontifex vel Sacerdos, quòd reconciliet nos: omnia ex operatione dicta. Sed quum imago Dei inconspicui dicitur, duplex respectus est, vnus personæ, alter operationis. Personæ respectus est, quà Christus imago essentialis est Patris, perfecta, & Patrem perfectè exprimens, persona personam, vt Defensionis 2. segmento 6. docuimus. Operationis vero respectus est ex proprietate personæ profluens, quòd Christus imago essentialis Patris nos informat de veritate, & nos renouans in spiritu mentis nostræ facit vt omnes retecta facie gloriam Domini, vt in speculo, intuentes transformemur in eamdem imaginem ex gloria in gloriam. Atque hæc duo sic conueniunt in persona Christi, vt alterum altero minimè destruatur, quia illud est principium huius, hoc verò nihil est aliud quàm actus ex illo principio indesinenter profluens: quemadmodum dispensatio operationum in nos cum proprietate personarum inter se, œconomia externa cum interna suum commensum & conuenientiam habet quodammodo. Sed (vt eò redeamus vnde digressi sumus) quia non satis animaduertere forte imperitiores possunt, quò illa verba pertineant, eo quod proloquuntor est paternorum mandatorum, nomen habere Sermonis vel Verbi: id aperte opus est explicari, vt singuli videant veram quidem hanc rationem esse ex Scripturis sacris, sed neque solam esse, neque sufficientem ad tanti mysterij explicationem. Igitur Sermo quum dicitur, aut absolutè, aut relatè dicitur. Nam duos habet terminos, vt loquuntur vulgo, terminum a quo, & terminum ad quem: quorum prior terminus recentioribus Logicis fundamentum, posterior verò terminus simpliciter appellatur. Itaque Sermo ratione quidem duplex, sed reipsa vnus est. Absolutè dicitur, quum sermonis essentialis (nam de essentiali hic agitur, non autem de enunciato, qui accidentarius est) id est, λόγω in mente, velut in suo principio, positi ad suum fundamentum habetur ratio. Relatè autem dicitur, quum termini vtrisque
units.tr: "The Son is not before he is brought forth by the Father." The Father brought forth the Son from the seed of David, namely according to the human nature which he brought forth. Therefore he did not exist before? Certainly not according to that nature by which he is of the seed of David. We, however, may with equal right and truth argue: the Father begot the Son before, indeed from eternity; therefore the Son is before, indeed from eternity, namely as he is the divine person, the eternal Word of the eternal Father. We shall see the proofs later. From the second passage, which is Hebrews 1, he argues thus: "God spoke at various times through the prophets, but in these last times, and now, through the Son. Therefore the Son did not speak in former times, and indeed did not even exist." Both conclusions are refuted at their point. The first, that the Son did not speak in former times, plainly fails through ignorance of the point at issue, because the Son did not speak in the same way and in the same respect under the Old Testament and the New. For in former times he spoke as the Word of God, but not personally in the assumed flesh; afterwards he spoke as the Word made flesh, and made manifest in the flesh in which the Son of God had come. The Apostle himself explains this at the beginning of the second chapter of the same epistle. He spoke in former times as the Word of God only; in the last times he spoke as God and man, in the unity of a person constituted of the assuming person and the assumed nature. We, on the contrary, hold thus: "God the Father spoke in former times and in the last times; therefore the Son also did," for the operation of Father and Son is common (as we said a little before), and here likewise whatever the Father does, the Son does too. The falsity of the second conclusion, that he did not even exist, is refuted by adding the major premise. It is of this kind: "a man who does not speak is not." No other form of argument is allowed by the rules of just reasoning. But first, what could be more false? What could be carried to a more absurd lengths? For if he is a man, he is, although he says nothing; the predicate is contrary to the subject. Next, a dumb man is a man and does not speak, for he is dumb; a silent man does not speak, though he is a man, but he is silent. Finally, this is said of a man who is merely a man, a mere [ψιλὸς] man, or of a simple man. But we acknowledge this Word of God not as a simple and bare man, but as Immanuel, that is, God and man. What is similar here? Accordingly we believe and teach with such piety: the Word, as the Word of God, has spoken from the beginning with the Father; as he became man, he has spoken in these last times according to that human nature which he assumed. It is therefore wrongly concluded from the condition of one nature to the condition of the whole person, which we have shown before to be faulty and [ἀσυλλόγιστον] unreasoned. From the third passage (which is Acts 1) he argues thus: "Luke says that he writes of what Jesus began to do and teach, and he never writes anything of the deeds of Christ under the Old Testament. Therefore Christ did not exist under the Old Testament, and did nothing." Yet the fallacy in this comparison is twofold. First, Luke had regard to things done and taught as to the assumed humanity, and as begun in the person of Christ in that humanity, as the Gospel history demonstrates. But here Samosatenus takes it of the person in himself [ἀσυλλογίστως], unreasoningly; thus from a statement made in a certain respect (as they call it) he concludes absolutely. Next, he confuses things done at different times through ignorance of the point at issue, and concludes faultily from the undistributed to the distributed term: for some things were done under the Old Testament and others under the New. Luke, however, spoke of things done under this, that is, in this time, not under that. Finally, it is quite out of place (to speak scholastically) that he argues negatively from authority: "Luke does not say this; therefore it was not the Word, nor was this done by the Word." Who in his right mind would argue so? For it can happen that something was, or is done, which no one says or writes; it can also happen that one writer says what another has not said, as we see done by the Evangelists. So this is a leaden sword. But Luke says, "of all things which Jesus began to do and teach"; nothing is therefore excepted. This is true: but since Luke does not say "of all things" simply, but adds a limitation, saying "which Jesus began to do and teach," we understand that universal from the determination, lest we commit the fallacy of division (whither you rush, Samosatenus, you do not see). For Luke thus shows that it is one thing if someone wishes to write of all the works and words of Christ universally, and another if he writes of those works which he began to do and teach in a definite manner, that is, in the assumed flesh, at a definite time, namely the Gospel after the flesh was assumed, in his own person, and continued to do and teach in the person of his Apostles, his servants, from the time he was received up into heaven. For the beginning of the Gospel truth is ascribed to Christ, which beginning Luke describes in his Gospel; the continuation of that preaching is ascribed to the Apostles in their following order, the history of which continuation Luke wove in his second book, which is entitled the Acts of the Apostles. Therefore whoever knowingly and deliberately objects with these kinds of argument knowingly and deliberately deceives; whoever does so unknowingly is deceived; but neither can be proved in good faith by us, who know and see. Let us see what Samosatenus does in producing and confirming his doctrine. First he offers an interpretation and a certain definition of this Word of whom John speaks: that Christ is "a visible man, born of Mary," etc., all of which we not only grant but also religiously affirm from the word of God. But this definition is imperfect if you look to the mind of Samosatenus; uttered in another mind by an orthodox and pious man it would not be held equally unjust or imperfect. For a pious man reading and saying these things understands Christ as truly God and truly man in the unity of person; but he who says "Christ the man" understands only a man. Next, the pious man will also assent in good faith to this, that "because he is the proclaimer of the Father's commands, he has the name of Word or Speech"; but he understands that he is called Word only for this reason, etc., that is, that the Word is not begotten of the Father essentially by nature, but accidentally, and so named only from his office. This we, relying on the truth and the authority of Scripture, deny. And the same is the manner of the proofs which are afterwards adduced: these are taken from the appellations of Christ, those from the predications made concerning Christ. For in them he argues and concludes from what is said of one nature of his, or rather of his person according to one nature, namely the human which he assumed, to the whole of the person, against all just rules of reasoning, as we said before. The conclusion of this whole discourse is therefore false, in which it is laid down that the positing of one nature is the removal of the other.
