For just as the positing of matter is not the removal of form, and the positing of one part of some whole which is essential is not the removal of the other, so also in Christ, the positing of one nature does not entail that the other is removed, since both come together to constitute the person of Christ our Lord and Saviour. For Christ is believed and worshipped by the Church as God and man, not as man only. Although (let me note in passing) among the appellations of Christ gathered here one must be excepted, namely that Christ is called "the image of the invisible God." For the other appellations indeed refer to us and have a simple relation to us. "Teacher," "instructor," "doctor," and "Apostle of our confession" are so called because he instructs us; "High Priest" or "Priest" because he reconciles us; all are said from operation. But when he is called "the image of the invisible God," there is a twofold respect: one to the person, the other to the operation. The respect to the person is that as Christ is the essential image of the Father, perfect, and expressing the Father perfectly, person for person, as we taught in the second segment of the Defence, section 6. The respect to the operation flows from the property of the person, namely that Christ, as the essential image of the Father, informs us of the truth, and renewing us in the spirit of our mind, makes us all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, to be transformed into the same image from glory to glory. And these two agree in the person of Christ in such a way that the one is in no way destroyed by the other, because the former is the principle of the latter, and the latter is nothing other than an act flowing unceasingly from that principle; just as the arrangement of the operations towards us, together with the proper character of the persons among themselves, the external economy with the internal, has in some way its own measure and agreement. But (to return to where we digressed) since perhaps the more unskilled cannot sufficiently notice to what those words refer, "because he is the proclaimer of the Father's commands, he has the name of Word or Speech," it is clearly necessary to explain it, so that each may see that this reason is indeed true from the holy Scriptures, but is neither the only one nor sufficient for the explanation of so great a mystery. Therefore when Word is spoken of, it is spoken either absolutely or relatively. For it has two terms, as they commonly say: the term from which, and the term to which; of which the former is called by the more recent logicians the foundation, and the latter simply the term. Thus the Word is twofold in aspect, but one in reality. It is spoken absolutely when the reason of the essential word (for we are dealing here with the essential, not the uttered word, which is accidental) is considered as posited in the mind, as in its principle, with respect to its foundation, that is, as [λόγω] reason. It is spoken relatively when the terms of both

units.la: 2. Cor. 3. usque ratio reipfa conuenit atque obseruatur. Hoc in rebus corporeis λόγον habentibus est cuidentiffimum: in spiritualibus analogicè obseruandum. Nam exempli causa, Angeli & formæ intelligentiæq; cœlestes tum in sese λόγον suum vel sermonem habent, quem manat & gignit intelligentia, & est de esse (vt loquuntur) ipsius, tum suum sermonem alij alijs exponunt προφορικῶς: etsi non hoc corporali, sed spirituali & intellectuali modo. Hoc posito, iam quid Samofatenus dicat, animaduer-tant pij. Est quidem sermo Dei Christus, sed respectu fo-lum (vt illevult) posterioris termini. Habent quidem homines, habent Angeli suum λόγον absolutè, eúmque essentialem intelligentiæ suæ: habent & λόγον relatè. Sed Deus relatè solùm habet, Christus sermo Dei relatè solùm est. Deus bone, quid audio? tantámne insaniam animos hominum occupare, vt Sermonem absolutum illum ac essentialem sibi inesse, non Deo statuant! Hoc ego quidem non dico, inquiet Samofatenus. Immo verò, mihomo, hoc ipsum. Nam fi Christus eo solùm est Sermo Dei, quòd paternorum mandatorum (vt tu loqueris) proloquutor est, relatè solùm est Sermo, & Deus relatè solùm Sermonem habet. Quòd fi dixeris, Deo nihilominùs suum sermonem absolutum esse & internum λόγον, vide & attende quàm multa concurrant absurda, eáque grauissima: ergo re aliud est sermo abso-lutus & internus, aliud Christus: ergo Deo sermones reipfa duo sunt: ergo Deus non est fimpliciffimus: Et sermo ille absolutus, quem dicis non esse Christum, is ipse est qui erat in principio, qui erat apud Deum, qui erat Deus (nam quicquid est in Deo Deus est, aut Deus (quod absit) non erit fimpliciffimus) qui erat in principio apud Deum, per quem omnia facta sunt, &c. Si non, ergo Deus fine sermone absoluto fuerit, fecerítq; omnia:
units.tr: 2 Cor. 3 ... the thing itself agrees and is observed. In bodily things that have a logos this is most plain; in spiritual things it must be observed by analogy. For example, angels and heavenly forms and intelligences both have in themselves their own logos or speech, which flows from and is begotten by their understanding and belongs to their being (as they say), and they also express their speech to one another outwardly (prophorikōs), though not in a bodily but in a spiritual and intellectual manner. This being laid down, let the godly note what Samosatenus says. Christ is indeed the Word of God, but only with respect (as he wills it) to the second term. Men have, and angels have, their own logos absolutely, which is essential to their understanding; they have also a logos relatively. But God has it only relatively, and Christ, the Word of God, is only relatively a word. Good God, what do I hear? Can such madness take hold of men's minds that they hold that God does not have that absolute and essential Word in himself! "I do not say this," Samosatenus will reply. But indeed, my friend, this very thing. For if Christ is the Word of God only because he is the spokesman of the Father's commands (as you put it), then he is a word only relatively, and God has a word only relatively. But if you say that God nonetheless has his own absolute speech and inner logos, see and consider how many absurdities follow, and very grave ones. Therefore, in reality, the absolute and inner word is one thing and Christ is another; therefore God has two words in reality; therefore God is not most simple. And that absolute word, which you say is not Christ, is the very one who was in the beginning, who was with God, who was God (for whatever is in God is God, or else God (far be it) would not be most simple), who was in the beginning with God, through whom all things were made, and so on. If not, then God was without an absolute word and yet made all things:

units.la: omnia: ergo res creatæ eo præstabunt creatori suo, quòd sermonem absolutè habent quem sermonem non habet Deus. Innumera denique absurda sunt ex tuo illo dogmate consequentia, quæ colligi in hunc locum possunt, & quæ tu, Samosatene, resipiscentia fugies, site recolligas. Vide autem quàm id certò breuiterque possis perficere: Qui Sermo erat in principio, erat apud Deum, erat Deus, is Sermo Dei absolutus & essentialis est: Christus sermo ille est qui erat in principio, erat apud Deum, & erat Deus: Christus ergo Sermo Dei absolutus & essentialis est. Sic partem quam dicis, agnoscimus: quam negas, ostendimus. Et si autem posterius scriptum reipsa cum priore conuenit, quia tamen nouum pigmentum superiori adiectum est, & axiomata quædam a veritate discrepantia, de ijs quoque dicendum paucis. Obijcit primùm interpretes in expositione huius nominis, Verbum, variare: idque vt incertam esse doctrinam nostram redarguat. Possem quidem multò maiore varietatem Samosateno obijcere, & velut contra dictoriam eius doctrinâ aperte reuincere: sed optimus erit ad eam rem segmento sequente locus. Varij sunt, at non contradictorij; diuersi, at non aduersi hoc loco interpretes. Cur autem? quia Christus vario respectu Sermo Dei ac multiplice appellatur: sic huic respectus vnus, illi alter sese obtulit, ex quo Sermonem interpretaretur. Eorum præcipui duo, quos antè expositimus, ab vtroque Sermonis termino, vt Nazianzenus optimè obseruauit: accedunt aliquot secundarij, tamquâ riui ex capitibus istis duobus dimanantes, nimirum ex termino a quo, vt vocant, & termino ad quem. Sed hi omnes respectus reipsa conueniunt, in genere concordant, vt hic ipse loquitur. Hoc igitur obesse non potest causæ nostræ, sed magis admirabilitatem multiformis illius sapientiæ Dei ostendere. Descriptionem Verbi accipimus: cipimus: sed commentum negamus esse. Esse commentum Samosatenus affirmat duobus argumentis: probari non posse ex Scripturis: Scripturam adversari. Prius falsum: nam ut de hoc loco & sequentibus taceam, quod Esaias de Iehova magnifice praedicauit, id Ioannes de Christo affirmat dictum: Christus ergo Iehova est, aeternus Deus, essentialis Deus. Alia suo tempore adferemus: hoc in praesentia satis. Posterius similiter falsum: nam quod Scriptura affirmat, id non adversatur Scripturae: alioqui Scriptura ipsa pugnaret secum: hoc autem Scriptura affirmat: quomodo Scripturae adversetur? Christum non respectu personae in se (hoc enim malo, quam quod Samosatenus pronunciat) sed tantummodo ratione officij Verbum appellari, falsum: atque hoc perspicue paulo ante nos demonstrauisse confidimus. Ridicule vero hoc suum paradoxum confirmat, dicens, nihil omnino Christum, quantum ad sui naturam ac substantiam, nobis fuisse profuturum, nisi Euangelij arcanum annunciasset. Nam primum profuisset, ut prodest omnibus communiter, sed non profuisset nobis salutariter. Secundo hic quidem vnus modus est, sed non solus, quo prodest nobis. Postremo si hoc modo prodest quantum ad naturam & substantiam suam (ut Samosateni vtamur verbis) prodest igitur. Non est autem hic solus modus: non igitur solo hoc modo prodest nobis in persona sua. Quid? quod diuinitus prodest? salute? gloria? quas res Deus solus sibi vindicat, nec se alteri cuiquam daturum affirmat per Prophetas constantissime. His subijciuntur axiomata, & determinationes pro auctoritate a Samosateno factae: quas esset neglecturus, nisi me imperitiorum ratio commoueret. Primum axioma: hanc esse Ioannis peculiarem phrasin: nam in tota Scriptura Christum non appellari Verbum, praeterquam ab ipso Ioanne. Modestiam tuam, Samosatene, desidero. Testes apud Romanos olim solenni formula modestiae suae indice non dicebant affirmate pro testimonio, sed verbo Arbitror utebantur, vt narrat Tullius. Quid, si hic diceres, non obseruaui, non memini, si bene obseruaui, aut aliquid simile? Ferrem facilius dictum, & laudarem modestiam tuam in errore tuo. Nam qui sic affirmate dicit, negat se amplius doceri velle: quod in homine nato est insolens. Sed, vt ad rem, credo ego te non obseruauisse: iniquè tamen concludis, mihi homo: non obseruaui, non est igitur, & hanc conclusionem tuam sic nobis offers, vt olim Sibyllae folium. Ego vero contrà, hanc Ioannis peculiarem phrasin esse nego: & alios in Scripturis affirmo vti. Non dicam Christum Angelum Iehouae, Angelum foederis appellari analogica appellatione & idem significante: sed verbum vel Sermo Iehouae diserte appellatur in Scriptura, his verbis: reuelauit se Iehoua Samuelî Silunte in sermone Iehouae: item, propter Sermonem tuum, & secundum animum tuum praestas has omneis res maximas (nam Sermonem hic de persona dici, non autem de transeunte verbo) ostendit eiusdem laudationis antigraphum 1.Chron. 17.) item, Spiritus Iehouae loquutus est in me, & Sermo eius per linguam meam: item, sum vobiscum, dictum Iehouae exercituum, Cum Verbo, quo pepigeram vobiscum exeuntibus vobis ex Aegypto, & Spiritu meo stante in medio vestri. Haec non obseruauerat Samosatenus: sunt tamen a Scriptura, & in Scriptura sunt, quibus vanitas huius axiomatis facile ostenditur. Hoc autem verbum non solum respectu officij, verumetiam ortus a Patre, vt Filius Patris aeterni aeternus est, appellari ante satis confirmauimus. De Metonymia & denominatione Samosatenus viderit: Ego neque hic Metonymiam aut denominationem vllam video: neque ab optimae notae auctoribus,
units.tr: ...then created things will excel their Creator in this, that they have an absolute word, which God does not have. Finally, countless absurdities follow from that dogma of yours, which can be gathered together at this point, and which you, Samosatenus, will flee by repentance or else gather up. See how certainly and briefly you could establish this: That Word which was in the beginning, was with God, was God, is the absolute and essential Word of God: Christ is that Word which was in the beginning, was with God, and was God: therefore Christ is the absolute and essential Word of God. Thus we acknowledge the part you state; the part you deny we show. And although the later writing agrees in substance with the earlier, yet because a new embellishment has been added to the former, and certain axioms discordant with the truth, these too must be discussed briefly. He first objects that the interpreters vary in explaining this name, Word, and uses this to prove that our doctrine is uncertain. I could indeed bring against Samosatenus a much greater variety, and openly refute his teaching by its own contradictions; but the next section will be a better place for that. The interpreters here are various but not contradictory, diverse but not opposed. Why so? Because Christ is called the Word of God in many respects and in many ways: thus one respect presented itself to one, another to another, from which they interpreted the Word. The principal of these are two, which we set out above, taken from each of the two terms of the Word, as Nazianzen observed very well; there are also some secondary ones, like streams flowing from those two heads, namely from the term from which and the term to which, as they are called. But all these respects agree in substance; "they agree in genus," as he himself puts it. This therefore cannot harm our cause, but rather shows the wonder of that manifold wisdom of God. We accept the description of the Word, but we deny that it is a fiction. Samosatenus asserts that it is a fiction, on two grounds: that it cannot be proved from the Scriptures, and that Scripture opposes it. The first is false: for, to pass over this passage and those that follow, what Isaiah magnificently proclaimed of Jehovah, John affirms was said of Christ: Christ therefore is Jehovah, the eternal God, the essential God. We shall bring other proofs in their proper place; this is enough for now. The second is likewise false: for what Scripture affirms does not oppose Scripture, otherwise Scripture would contradict itself; but Scripture affirms this; how then could it oppose Scripture? That Christ is called the Word with respect to his office only, and not with respect to his person in himself (for this I prefer to what Samosatenus pronounces), is false; and we trust we have shown this clearly a little above. He also ridiculously confirms his paradox by saying that Christ would have profited us nothing at all as to his nature and substance, unless he had announced the mystery of the gospel. For first, he would have profited in the way he profits all men in common, but he would not have profited us savingly. Second, this is indeed one way, but not the only way, in which he profits us. Last, if he profits in this way as to his nature and substance (to use Samosatenus's own words), then he profits; but this is not the only way; therefore he does not profit us in his person only in this way. What of the fact that he profits us divinely? In salvation, in glory, things which God alone claims for himself and constantly affirms through the prophets that he will not give to any other. To these are added axioms and determinations made by Samosatenus on his own authority, which I would have neglected, had not the reasoning of the unlearned moved me. The first axiom: that this is the peculiar phrase of John; for in the whole of Scripture Christ is not called the Word, except by John himself. I desire your modesty, Samosatenus. Witnesses among the Romans formerly, as Tully relates, did not state their testimony affirmatively with the solemn formula of modesty, but used the word I think. What if you were to say here, "I have not observed, I do not remember, if I have observed well," or something like that? I would bear the statement more easily, and I would praise your modesty even in your error. For he who speaks thus affirmatively declares that he no longer wishes to be taught, which is unusual in a man born. But, to the point, I believe you did not observe it; yet you wrongly conclude, my good man: I have not observed, therefore it is not so; and you offer us this conclusion of yours as the Sibyl's leaf was once offered. I, on the contrary, deny that this is John's peculiar phrase, and I affirm that others also use it in the Scriptures. I will not say that Christ is called the Angel of Jehovah, the Angel of the covenant, by an analogical appellation with the same meaning; but the Word or Speech of Jehovah is expressly called so in Scripture, in these words: Jehovah revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh in the word of Jehovah; likewise, for thy word's sake, and according to thine own heart, thou hast wrought all these great things (for here Word is said of a person, not of a passing word; this is shown by the parallel of the same praise in 1 Chron. 17); likewise, The Spirit of Jehovah spoke in me, and his word was in my tongue; likewise, I am with you, saith Jehovah of hosts, with the word which I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit remaining in the midst of you. Samosatenus had not observed these; yet they are from Scripture and are in Scripture, and by them the vanity of this axiom is easily shown. Moreover, we have already sufficiently confirmed that this name is applied not only with respect to office, but also, as born of the Father, that the Son is eternal as the Father's eternal Son. Let Samosatenus see to the matter of metonymy and denomination: I see here neither metonymy nor any denomination, nor do I hear that by writers of the best note,

units.la: 1.Sam.3. 2.Sam.7. 2.Sam.23 Aggaei 2. auctoribus, etiam Grammaticis, Metonymiam denominationem audio appellari: nam denominatio μετωνυμία est.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 3; 2 Sam. 7; 2 Sam. 23; Hag. 2. By authors, even grammarians, I hear that metonymy is called denomination, for denomination is [μετωνυμία] metonymy.

units.la: Secundum axioma, quod luculentum vocat, huiusmodi est: omnia nomina Christo imposita, non ratione alicuius naturæ aut substantiæ, sed ratione solùm officij ac effecti fuisse indita. Negamus hoc axioma vniuersale esse, & ei rectè apponi vniuersale signum. Nam Christus appellatur Filius hominis respectu naturæ, non officij aut effecti vllius: atque eodem iure Filius Dei vel Filius Patris appellatur respectu naturæ æternæ illius quam habet a persona Patris in vnitate essentiæ: eodem vnigenitus. Sic etiam Iehouam ab Esaia dicianté ostendimus, quod essentiæ est nomen, ac non officij: vt & κυρίῳ nomen, quà Iehouæ interpretamentum est, Græcè accipi Defensionis 2. segmento 13. docuimus. Falsum igitur axioma, nec semper verum, quod Samosatenus audacter affirmauit. Exempla quæ adfert agnoscimus. Sed in ijs tamen variè fallitur. Horum enim primùm quædam attributa sunt, quæ causam cum effectis, principium cum operationibus continent & connotant (vt loquuntur) complexione quadam necessaria. Nam lux vera est secundùm veritatem naturæ essentia sua: lux mundi est communicatione gratiæ: & eodem modo veritas. Et certè cùm vnica sit veritas, & vera lux vnica, non potest Filius quin sit idem cum Patre, aut duplex veritas & lux vera (quod absit) futura est; primaria Patris, & secundaria Filij. Et ita appellatur Sermo, respectu naturæ & operationum ipsius. Secundò etiam in eo fallitur, quòd istis omnibus nominibus metaphoricè Ioannem vti dicit: sunt enim alia propria, vt veritas, Iesus, Christus, Magister, & similia: alia analogica, vt lux (nam lux etiam spiritualis est) Sacerdos, Pontifex: alia denique metaphorica, vt a Samosateno appellantur.
units.tr: The second axiom, which he calls luminous, is this: all names given to Christ were bestowed not on account of any nature or substance, but solely on account of office and effect. We deny that this axiom is universal, and we deny that a universal sign is rightly attached to it. For Christ is called Son of man with respect to nature, not with respect to any office or effect; and by the same right he is called Son of God or Son of the Father with respect to that eternal nature which he has from the person of the Father in unity of essence; and likewise only-begotten. So too we have shown that Jehovah, as Isaiah speaks of him, is a name of essence and not of office; and we have taught, in the second part of the Defence, section 13, that the Greek name [κύριος] Lord, which is the interpretation of Jehovah, is to be understood in the same way. The axiom is therefore false, and not always true, as Samosatenus boldly asserts. We acknowledge the examples he brings, but in them he errs in various ways. First, some of these are attributes which contain and connote (as they say) the cause together with its effects, and the principle together with its operations, by a certain necessary complex. For the true light is true by the truth of its nature, which is its essence; it is the light of the world by the communication of grace; and it is the same with truth. Indeed, since there is one truth and one true light, the Son cannot fail to be the same as the Father, or else there would be (God forbid) a twofold truth and true light, a primary one of the Father and a secondary one of the Son. And so he is called Word with respect to his nature and his operations. Secondly, he also errs in saying that John uses all these names metaphorically. For some are proper, such as truth, Jesus, Christ, Teacher, and similar names; others are analogical, such as light (for light is also spiritual), priest, high priest; and finally others are metaphorical, such as those which Samosatenus calls such.

units.la: Postremò, cùm non fit adæquata planè istorum nomi-num ratio, quod hic supponit pro vero & indubitato, fe-quitur non valere axioma illud consectarium, eamdem omnium istorum nominum rationem esse. Quòd fi hanc demus eamdem esse, tamen hac Verbi appellatio-ne & interpretatione nihil noui adferimus, quod non cæteri Euangelistæ & Apostoli tradiderint, qui Christum filium Dei, vnigenitum, Dominum (id est, Iehouam) appella-runt, & in quorum numero Apostolus ad Hebræos dicit Sermonem Dei viuum & efficacem esse, diiudicantem cogi-tationes & conceptiones cordis: nec vllam rem creatam esse quæ non manifesta fit in conspectu ipsius, sed omnia esse nuda & patentia oculis ipsius: quæ verba de Sermone fubfiften-te necessarium est accipi. Tertium axioma ex præceden-tibus (quæ falsa esse ostendimus) infert Samofatenus: nempe non anxie nobis laborandum esse quærendo quid Chri-ftus in substantia fit, sed quid ratione multorum beneficiorum ac effectuum nobis attulerit profuerit que. Axioma impiû simul & impudens. Nam primùm quod Scriptura ex-ponit nobis, impium fuerit de eo cognoscendo nô anxiè laborare: hoc autem, quid Christus in substantia fit, Scriptura diligentissimè exponit nobis. Præterea quàm nauiter impudentem eum oportet esse, qui in fe respiciat alienis ornatum beneficijs, in auctorem verò beneficio-rum minimè, vt eum cognoscat & agnoscat ex officio suo? Nouit bos possessorem suum, & asinus præsepe do-mini fui: hic de Deo suo, sancto Israelis cognoscendo minimè laboraturus est. Postremò fi vllum est argu-mentum, quo ad refipifcentiam, fidem, charitatem ac-cendamur, illud est inprimis habendum, quòd Christus filius Dei propter nos homines inaniuit sese, & prout Deus est natura, sic gratia edidit operationes diuinas hu-mano generi salutareis. De hoc fundamento qui non anxiè laborari docent oportere, ij salutis veritatem, neglecta salutis causa, de mentibus hominum vt decutiant anxiè videntur laborare. Nam cùm actiones sequantur eorum conditionem qui agunt, & perfectæ operationes non nisi a perfectis auctoribus præstari possint, vtrumque certum est, ignorato auctore nunquam bene cognosci qualitatem operationum, & contrà non bene expensis operationibus non bene agnosci causam efficientem illarum. Quod malum in Samosateno & grege ipsius animaduertimus, qui salutem nostram diuinum opus confitetur verbis; sed reipsa diuinum opus non agnoscit, quum de effectore non vult ita anxiè laborari, vt eum diuinum & reuera Deum agentem cognoscamus. Restat iam postremus locus de summa horum verborum, in principio erat verbum, interpretatione, quam prior Samosatenus certo consilio in hunc locum dissimulauerat. Sed quia hæc ipsa summa ijsdem prope verbis in loco sequente, & eadem plane sententia exponitur, hoc totum quicquid est eodem sumus reiecturi.
units.tr: Lastly, since the account of these names is not at all adequate, which he assumes as true and beyond doubt, it follows that the consequence he draws, that all these names have the same account, does not hold. But even if we grant that it is the same, we bring forward nothing new in this naming and interpretation of the Word, which the other evangelists and apostles have not handed down, who call Christ the Son of God, the only-begotten, the Lord (that is, Jehovah); and among them the Apostle to the Hebrews says that the Word of God is living and effective, judging the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and that no created thing is hidden in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes; words which must necessarily be understood of the Word subsisting. The third axiom Samosatenus infers from the preceding (which we have shown to be false), namely: we need not labour anxiously in seeking what Christ is in substance, but what he has brought and profited us by reason of his many benefits and effects. An axiom at once impious and shameless. For first, what Scripture sets out for us, it would be impious not to labour anxiously to know; and Scripture sets out most diligently for us what Christ is in substance. Moreover, how brazenly shameless must he be who looks to himself, adorned with the benefits of others, but not at all to the author of the benefits, so as to know and acknowledge him as his duty requires? The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's manger; yet this man will not labour at all to know his God, the Holy One of Israel. Lastly, if there is any argument that stirs us to repentance, faith and love, it is above all this: that Christ the Son of God emptied himself for us men, and, as he is God by nature, so by grace he put forth divine operations that are saving for mankind. Those who teach that we need not labour anxiously over this foundation seem, by neglecting the cause of salvation, to labour anxiously to shake the truth of salvation out of men's minds. For since actions follow the condition of those who perform them, and perfect operations can only be performed by perfect authors, both points are certain: that without knowing the author the quality of the operations is never well known, and conversely that without carefully weighing the operations the efficient cause of them is not well recognised. We observe this fault in Samosatenus and his band, who confess in words that our salvation is a divine work, but in fact do not recognise it as a divine work, since they are unwilling to labour so anxiously over the agent that we come to know him as divine and truly God acting. There remains now the last point, the interpretation of the sum of these words, in the beginning was the Word, which Samosatenus earlier deliberately passed over in this place. But since this same sum is set out in almost the same words, and with exactly the same meaning, in the following place, we shall reject the whole of it together there.

units.la: SAMOSATENVS. 4.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 4.

units.la: Et Verbum erat apud Deum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum.
units.tr: And the Word was with God. This was in the beginning with God.

units.la: Qvi Christum æternum tuentur, his verbis abutuntur, vt statuant Christum fuisse realiter in cœlo ante mundum conditum, cùm nulla Scriptura hoc doceat. Pij verò facilè vident 1. Petri 1. ad præordinationem hoc referri, tum ad promissionem, & figuras, & umbras, sacrificia & oblationes in quibus prænunciatus & præfiguratus fuit Christus. Sic se ante Abrahamum fuisse dicit ille homo Christus, Ioan. 8. non enim alius ibi loquitur. Ab initio enim mundi, ante Abrahamum erat promissus, cognitus, & exspectatus. Erant typi varij eius & sacrificia, quibus præfigurabatur Christus, sine quibus nunquam pij adoraturi Deum in cœtus coibant. Quare etiam Abraham diem Christi futuri, non ipsum Christum præsentem, videre cupiuit; quem in promissione tunc & figuris videbat, eius natiuitatem, mortem, & resurrectionem, & quæ nomine nostro facturus erat exspectans. ² Sic Patres eumdem Christum habebant in cibum sub typis: eumdem enim cibum habuerunt quem nos, teste Paulo 1.Cor.10. Petra enim erat Christus, qui sequebatur eos post venturus: non vt nos, quos iam præcesserat. Sic & baptismum nobiscum communem habebant, vt probat inibi Paulus. ³ Certè Christi caro, qui est cibus omnium electorum (non aliqua eius æterna deitas) tunc non fuit reipsa: nondum enim erat Maria, ex qua natus est. ⁴ Ad eumdem quoque modum respectans Ioannes in Apocalypsi cap. 13. dixit Agnum fuisse occisum ab origine mundi in typus & sacrificijs, & vmbris: in pijs quoque, vt in Abele occiso: quem admodum & nunc occiditur & persequutionem patitur in fidelibus suis membris (quod etiam ipse Christus contra Paulum persequentem Ecclesiam testatur) quamquam hic præsens nobiscum non versetur carne, vt tangi possit: & crucifigitur ab Antichristo, Apocal. 11. & ab impijs, ⁵ qui eum conculcant & crucifigunt denuò, Hebr. 6. Sed & ipse Paulus optimus interpres horum docet Hebr. 11. quomodo illi promissa adepti sunt, eminus omnia conspicati. ⁶ Qui quoque doctiorum Neotericorum sententias quærunt eadere, videant (etiamsi in hac re aduersarios nostros) Caluinum, Bucerum in hos locos, Marloratum quoque, qui omnium fere huius seculi sententias collegit, & Castalionem in nouo eius Testamento. ⁷ Fuisse ergo Verbum apud Deum docet: sed addit, in principio, id est, sui ministerij & officij tempore, vt audisti. In illo enim principio Christus cœpit esse nobis Verbum, & magister, & Propheta, prædicans mandata paterna. In hoc ergo principio erat apud Patrem, nondum notus hominibus, sed soli Patri.
units.tr: Those who defend an eternal Christ abuse these words to maintain that Christ really existed in heaven before the world was made, although no Scripture teaches this. Godly readers, however, easily see that 1 Peter 1 refers this to predestination, and also to the promise, the types and shadows, and the sacrifices and offerings in which Christ was foretold and foreshadowed. In this sense the man Christ says in John 8 that he was before Abraham, for he speaks of nothing else there. From the beginning of the world, before Abraham, he was promised, known and awaited. He had various types and sacrifices, by which Christ was foreshadowed, and without which the godly never assembled to worship God. Hence Abraham too longed to see the day of the Christ who was to come, not the Christ present to him; he saw him in the promise and the figures then, and awaited his birth, death and resurrection, and what he was going to do on our behalf. ² In this way the Fathers had the same Christ as food under types, for they had the same food as we do, as Paul testifies in 1 Cor. 10. For the rock was Christ, who was to come after them, not as he had already come for us. So too they shared baptism with us, as Paul proves there. ³ Certainly the flesh of Christ, who is the food of all the elect, was not really present at that time (it is not some eternal deity of his), for Mary, from whom he was born, did not yet exist. ⁴ In the same way John, looking back in Revelation 13, said that the Lamb was slain from the beginning of the world in types, sacrifices and shadows; also in the godly, as in Abel when he was slain. Likewise he is now slain and suffers persecution in his faithful members (as Christ himself testifies against Paul, who persecuted the Church), although he is not here with us in the flesh so that he could be touched; and he is crucified by the Antichrist (Rev. 11) and by the ungodly, ⁵ who trample him underfoot and crucify him again (Heb. 6). But Paul himself, the best interpreter of these things, also teaches in Heb. 11 how they obtained the promises, seeing all things from afar. ⁶ Those also who seek the opinions of the more learned of the moderns to agree with them should look at Calvin and Bucer on these passages (though they are our opponents in this matter), Marlorat too, who has gathered almost all the opinions of this age, and Castellio in his New Testament. ⁷ So John teaches that the Word was with God, but he adds, in the beginning, that is, at the time of his ministry and office, as you have heard. For in that beginning Christ began to be the Word to us, and teacher, and prophet, proclaiming the commands of the Father. In this beginning, then, he was with the Father, not yet known to men, but only to the Father.

units.la: Non enim ab hominibus agnoscebatur esse Messias, qui tam vilis, ex Nazareth, ex Iosepho, fabri filius reputabatur, pro Dei filio & Messia non habebatur, cui omnes primores contradicebant: & in causa mortis hic titulus, quasi ab illo falsò usurpatus, Christo obiicitur. Non fuit notus Ioanni: quia etsi venerat ad manifestandum eum Israeli, dicit tamen, Et ego non noveram eum. Non noverant eum & Israelitæ, ut Ioannes testatur, in medio vestrum stat quem vos nescitis. Immo & Apostolis ignotus erat, quem nec moriturum, nec etiam resurrecturum credebant, sine quo Christus agnosci non poterat verè: immo non tantum Christum, sed & eius officium, facta, & verba non agnoscebant, neque intelligebant, ut multi loci Evangelij docent, Ioan. 13. & 20. Eodem spectat & illud, quando fratres suadent Christo, ut se manifestet mundo. Sed & ipse Christus nolebat sciri ante tempus, quum vetaret non tantum daemonijs, quæ eiiciebat, de se prædicare, sed & illis quos sanabat, Marc. 9. Matth. 8. Transfigurationem quoque, quasi præcipuè ante mortem esse Dei filium unigenitum demonstrauit, silentio præterire ad resurrectionem usque iussit. Nam plenaria eius patefactio, quæ erat apud Deum, pertinebat ad resurrectionem, vbi absorpta cruce, morte, & exinanitione, filium esse suum potenter per spiritum sanctificationis per resurrectionem declarauit Pater, ut Paulus docet Roman. 1. Nemo enim ita ex morte seruatus est, ut resurgeret viueret que perpetuò, quemadmodum Christus, Roman. 6. nemo accepit potestatem in cœlo & in terra, ut Christus de se testatur post resurrectionem, Matth. 28. nemo etiam sedit ad dexteram Dei præter hunc, Marc. 16. hæc autem omnia post resurrectionem facta. Quare etiam illud testimonium Dauidis Psalm. 2. ego hodie genui te, non æternæ generationi, sed Christo rediuiuo consentienter aptat Paulus, quia ibi iam exemtus omni cruce, filius Dei esset plenariè declaratus, Act. 13. ut & Rom. 1. hoc ipsum & Ioannes dicit cap. 7. spiritum quoq non fuisse tunc datum antequàm Christus glorificaretur, id est, priusquàm Filius esse Dei plenè demonstraretur. Actorum quoque cap. 10 hoc ipsum comprobat dicens, hunc Deus suscitauit tertio die, effecitque vt manifestus fieret toti populo, sed testibus prius designatis qui comederunt & biberunt vnà cum eo postea. Quare etiam quadraginta diebus manens apud suos10 manifestauit se cis vere: postea verò perfectius, quum Spiritum sanctum docendum misit, Actor. 1. & 2. 11 Certum ergo est, Christum in principio fuisse apud Deum, non fuisse cognitum plenè ab initio non tantùm a plebe, sed etiam ab Apostolis. Sed & Ioannes apertis verbis hoc comprobat primæ primo, quum scribit vitæ illum Sermonem, quem viderunt, audiuerunt, contrectarunt (ne quis alium fingat æternum, inuisibilem, impalpabilem) fuisse apud Patrem, id est, in principio non notum hominibus: ideòque statim addit per antithesin, sed postea hæc vita patefacta est, vt iam audisti ex multis locis.
units.tr: Indeed he was not recognised by men as the Messiah, for he was regarded as so lowly, from Nazareth, the son of Joseph the carpenter, and was not held to be the Son of God and the Messiah. All the leading men opposed him, and this title, as if falsely claimed by him, was thrown up against Christ as the cause of his death. He was not known to John, for although he had come to make him manifest to Israel, he still says, "I did not know him." The Israelites did not know him either, as John testifies: "Among you stands one whom you do not know." Indeed he was unknown even to the Apostles, who did not believe he would die or even rise again, and without this Christ could not truly be known. Not only Christ himself, but also his office, deeds and words, they did not recognise or understand, as many passages of the Gospel show (John 13 and 20). To this also belongs the fact that his brothers urged Christ to reveal himself to the world. But Christ himself did not want to be known before the time, when he forbade not only the demons, whom he cast out, to speak about him, but also those whom he healed (Mark 9; Matt. 8). He also showed that the transfiguration, which was particularly before his death, was a sign that the only-begotten Son of God should be passed over in silence until the resurrection. For the full revelation of him, which was with God, belonged to the resurrection, when, the cross, death and humiliation having been swallowed up, the Father declared by the resurrection that he was his Son in power, through the Spirit of sanctification, as Paul teaches in Rom. 1. For no one has been saved from death in such a way as to rise and live forever, as Christ did (Rom. 6). No one received power in heaven and on earth, as Christ testifies of himself after the resurrection (Matt. 28). No one else sat at the right hand of God besides him (Mark 16), and all these things happened after the resurrection. Hence Paul also fittingly applies David's testimony in Ps. 2, "Today I have begotten you," not to the eternal generation, but to the Christ restored to life, because then, freed from all the cross, the Son of God was fully declared (Acts 13), as also in Rom. 1. John himself says the same in chapter 7, that the Spirit too was not yet given before Christ was glorified, that is, before the Son of God was fully shown. In Acts 10 he proves this very thing, saying that God raised him on the third day and caused him to be made manifest to the whole people, but to witnesses previously chosen, who ate and drank with him afterwards. Hence also, remaining with his own for forty days, he showed himself to them truly, but more perfectly afterwards, when he sent the Holy Spirit to teach (Acts 1 and 2). ¹¹ It is certain, then, that Christ was in the beginning with God, and that he was not fully known from the start, not only by the common people but also by the Apostles. John too proves this plainly in 1 John 1, when he writes that the Word of life, whom they saw, heard and handled (so that no one may imagine another eternal, invisible, impalpable one), was with the Father, that is, in the beginning not known to men. Therefore he immediately adds by way of contrast, "but afterwards this life was made manifest," as you have heard from many passages.

units.la: Non dissimilis quoque phrasis est Matth. 13. Nonne omnes sorores eius sunt apud nos? Eadem Græca vox, ἀδελφαὶ ἡμῶν, nobis nota. Sic quum Christus rogaretur a Caiapha de doctrina, Matth 26. & Marc 14. respondit, vt de ea quæ illis nota esse debuit, semper docui apud vos in templo, Ioan. 18. Sic Galat. 2. non cessi ad momentum, vt veritas Euangelij permaneret apud vos, id est, vt vobis integra & nota esset. Sed & communis loquendi modus hoc indicat, quum quæ nescimus & certa esse putamus, respondemus Apud Deum illa esse abscondita, Deù illa scire, nos latere quæ apud Deum sunt: vt contrà scimus quæ ille vult esse apud nos. Sic apud se habere, sibi tantùm nota esse dicimus, apud se loqui: vt de Pharisæo, Luc. 18. Apud Deum sunt omnia quæ futura sunt, necdum sunt etiam: vt iudicium futurum, Antichristi abolitio, & Babylonis ruina: nihil enim illi vel occultum, vel non præsens, vt nobis hominibus. Quòd si verò Ioannes voluisset intelligere, Christum in principio fuisse apud Deum in cælo, tunc quoque quum scriberet beret hoc Ioannes, post ascensionem Christi, erat in cælo Chri-stus. Dixisset ergo & fuisse, & nunc esse apud Deum in cælo Christum, non tantum in principio. Mentiretur enim fuisse illum in principio, quum & tunc longè post principium illud esset in eodem cælo, quum scriberet hoc Ioannes. 12 Sed animaduerte eiusmodi phrases in Scripturis idem sonare: fuit apud Deum, est in Patre, est ex Deo, est in sinu Patris, est in cælo, a Deo processit, a Deo venit, a Patre exiuit, descendit de cælo, pro a Deo edoctus & sanctificatus.
units.tr: A similar phrase is found in Matt. 13: "Are not all his sisters with us?" The same Greek word, [ἀδελφαὶ ἡμῶν], is familiar to us. So too when Christ was questioned by Caiaphas about his teaching (Matt. 26 and Mark 14), he answered as if about what they ought to have known: "I always taught openly in the temple" (John 18). Likewise in Gal. 2, "we did not yield for a moment, that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you," that is, that it might be whole and known to you. Common usage also indicates this: when we do not know something which we nevertheless think is certain, we answer that it is hidden with God, that God knows those things, and that what is with God is hidden from us; conversely we say that we know what he wants to be with us. Likewise we say that to have something with oneself means only that it is known to oneself, or to speak with oneself, as of the Pharisee in Luke 18. Everything that is going to be in the future is with God, even though it does not yet exist: such as the future judgment, the abolition of the Antichrist, and the ruin of Babylon. For nothing is hidden from him or absent from him, as it is for us men. But if John had wished to mean that Christ was in the beginning with God in heaven, then when John was writing this, after Christ's ascension, Christ was in heaven. He would then have said that Christ both was and now is with God in heaven, not only in the beginning. For he would be lying in saying that Christ was in the beginning, since long after that beginning he was in the same heaven when John was writing this. ¹² But observe that such phrases in the Scriptures have the same sense: he was with God, he is in the Father, he is from God, he is in the bosom of the Father, he is in heaven, he proceeded from God, he came from God, he went out from the Father, he came down from heaven, for he was taught and sanctified by God.

units.la: M S.
units.tr: M S.

units.la: Et Verbum erat apud Deum.
units.tr: And the Word was with God.

units.la: ID est, Iesus Christus Dei filius, uti verbum, antequam veniret ad suos Iudæos, ac manifestaretur, tantummodo soli Deo notus erat, hominibus autem prorsus ignotus. In hanc sententiam Ioannes Baptista dicebat, ego baptizo vos aqua: in medio vestrum stat quem vos nescitis: ipse, &c. Immo ipsemet Ioannes hac ratione ipsum ignorabat: proinde dicebat, Et ego nesciebam eum, sed ut manifestaretur in Israël, propterea ego veni aqua baptizans, &c. Et ideo etiam veluti digito ipsum demonstrabat dicens, Ecce agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi. Et notum est hanc dictionem, apud, in hanc significationem vsurpari. Nam in hancmet sententiam ipse Ioannes epistola 1. cap. 1. ita scribit, & annunciamus vobis vitam æternam quæ erat apud Patrem & manifestata est nobis, &c. Et observa locum illum Ioannis plurimum facere ad intelligentiam primæ partis huius capitis. Sed & cæteri Apostoli, & præcipuè Paulus verbum hoc fuisse apud Deum absconditum, & postmodum hominibus revelatum clarissimè demonstrant. Ad hæc Ephes. 3. ita legitur, Et in lucem proferam omnibus quæ sit communio mysterij quod erat in Deo absconditum a seculis: & in eadem epistola cap. 1. habetur Deum nobis patefecisse arcanum voluntatis suæ iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuerat in semetipso, vsque ad dispositionem plenitudinis temporum, vt omnia per Christum restauraret. Et 2. Tim. 1. dicit gratiam Euangelij nobis fuisse datam ante tempora aeterna, sed palam factam esse per apparitionem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui & mortem aboleuit, & in lucem produxit vitam & incorruptibilitatem per Euangelium. Et ad Titum cap. 1. Deum ante tempora saecularia promisisse, sed patefecisse temporibus suis verbum per praedicationem, &c. Petrus quoq; epistola 1. cap. 1. dicit praeordinatum quidem fuisse Christum ante conditum mundum, sed manifestatum fuisse hodiernis temporibus propter nos, & catera.
units.tr: That is, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as the Word, before he came to his own, the Jews, and was made manifest, was known to God alone, and was altogether unknown to men. John the Baptist spoke to this effect: "I baptize you with water; in the midst of you stands one whom you do not know; he is..." etc. Indeed John himself was ignorant of him in this way, and so he said, "And I did not know him, but that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water," etc. For this reason he also pointed him out, as it were with his finger, saying, "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world." It is well known that the word "with" [apud] is used in this sense. For John himself, in the same sense, writes in 1 John 1: "And we declare to you eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us," etc. Observe that this passage of John contributes greatly to understanding the first part of this chapter. The other Apostles, and especially Paul, also clearly show that this Word was hidden with God and afterwards revealed to men. Eph. 3 reads thus: "And I will bring to light for all what is the fellowship of the mystery which was hidden in God from the ages." And in the same letter, chapter 1, it is said that God has made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he had purposed in himself, unto the dispensation of the fullness of times, that he might restore all things through Christ. And 2 Tim. 1 says that the grace of the Gospel was given to us before the eternal times, but has been made plain by the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, who both abolished death and brought to light life and immortality through the Gospel. And Titus 1 says that God promised before the world's ages, but in his own times revealed the Word through preaching, etc. Peter also, in 1 Pet. 1, says that Christ was indeed foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifested in these last times for our sake, and the rest.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: NVNC se demum Samosatenus amplius aperit, qui verbi erat interpretationem superiore membro dissimulauerat. Huius autem verbi perspecta significatione, tota haec quaestio facilem exitum, spero, habitura est. Quapropter ordinem hunc seruari video a nobis oportere, vt primum dicamus de antecedentis membri, quam Samosatenus voluit, interpretatione: secundo de interpretatione eiusdem verbi in hoc vtroque, quod praefixit, membro: tertio denique de veritate interpretationum eius. In antecedente membro vel propositione Euangelistae, aut idem significatum verbi erat Samosatenus seruari voluit, aut sensit alterum. De significato altero sensisse vix est credibile, aut id fide mala hoc loco dissimulauerit: quamuis rationibus illius forte futura fuisset commodior altera interpretatio ad oppugnandam (vt facit) veritatem. Concludemus itaque, breuitatis causa, illic Samosatenum a priore membro ad hunc locum interpretationem huius verbi erat (quod est membrorum rum omnium commune) reiecisse: proinde eodem modo illic quoque accipi oportere. Atque hac in sententia verbis MS. omnino confirmamur. De veritate autem illius interpretationis postea communiter in horum locorum declaratione videbimus. Quas igitur verbi erat interpretationes adferat, cognoscamus. Si verbi illius erat vnicam interpretationem Samosatenus prior attulisset (cuius periculo posterior magis didicit sapere, & melius cauere sibi) ratio nobis foret expeditior ad mentem ipsius assequendam & peruestigandam rei veritatem. Sed ita se hic inuoluit varijs interpretationibus, vt ego quidem mirari satis non possim hominem fuisse ausum haec sua volucria & instabilia cogitata in hunc modum conscripta luci & typis publice committere. Etenim primo in loco haec ipsa sunt illius verba: Pÿ facile vident 1. Petri 1. ad praeordinationem hoc referri, tum ad promissionem, & figuras, & vmbras, sacrificia & oblationes, in quibus praenunciatus & praefiguratus erat Christus. Secundo autem his verbis vtitur: fuisse ergo Verbum apud Deum docet, sed addit, in principio, id est, sui ministerij & officij tempore, vt audisti. In illo enim principio Christus esse coepit nobis Verbum, & Magister, & Propheta, praedicans mandata paterna. In hoc ergo principio erat apud Patrem, nondum notus hominibus, sed soli Patri: nor enim ab hominibus agnoscebatur esse Messias, &c. Postremo autem corollarium in fine adhibet, vt putauit ipse, δογματικώτατον: vt ego sentio, & vere sentio, περιφδοξότατον, quum dicit, Animaduerte eiusmodi phraseis in Scripturis idem sonare: fuit apud Deum, est in Patre, est ex Deo, est in sinu Patris, est in coelo, a Deo processit, a Deo venit, a Patre exiuit, descendit de coelo: pro a Deo edoctus & sanctificatus. Haec ipsa verba, quibus Samosatenus vtitur: quorum ex primo loco duæ exsurgunt interpretationes verbi iftiuserat: vna, erat præordinatus, aut (si cui magis placet) erat præordinatione: altera verò, promissus erat, prænunciatus, & præfigura-tus. Ex secundo, consimiliter duæ: nam prima Ioannis propositio, in principio erat Verbum, hoc modo exponitur, esse cœpit nobis verbum, & Magister, & Prophe-ta,prædicans mandata paterna: secunda verò illa,&Verbum erat apud Deum, hoc significare dicitur, in hoc principio erat apud Patrem, nondum notus hominibus, sed soli Patri. Ex tertio, vna: erat apud Deum, pro eo quod est, edoctus est & sanctificatus est a Deo, nempe vt docendi apud præceptorem discipuli locari solent.
units.tr: Now at last Samosatenus opens himself more fully, he who had concealed the interpretation of the word was in the preceding clause. Once the meaning of this word is clearly grasped, I hope the whole question will have an easy outcome. Accordingly, I see that we ought to keep this order: first, to speak of the interpretation of the preceding clause, which Samosatenus wished to take in a certain way; second, of the interpretation of the same word in each of the two clauses he has put forward; and third, finally, of the truth of his interpretations. In the preceding clause, or proposition, of the Evangelist, Samosatenus wished either to keep the same meaning of the word was, or he meant another. It is hardly credible that he meant the other meaning, or else he dissembled it here out of bad faith, although for his arguments another interpretation would perhaps have been more convenient for attacking (as he does) the truth. We will conclude, therefore, for the sake of brevity, that there Samosatenus rejected from the former clause the interpretation of this word was (which is common to all the clauses), and so it must be understood in the same way there as well. And we are wholly confirmed in this opinion by the words of MS. But we will see later, in the common explanation of these passages, what the truth of that interpretation is. Let us therefore learn what interpretations of the word was he brings forward. If Samosatenus had first offered a single interpretation of that word was (at whose peril the later man learned to be wiser and to guard himself better), our way to grasping his mind and investigating the truth of the matter would be easier. But he entangles himself here with such various interpretations that I cannot sufficiently wonder that the man dared to commit these flighty and unstable thoughts, written in this manner, to the light and to the press for public view. For first, in the place itself, these are his own words: They easily see that 1 Peter 1 refers this to foreordination, and also to promise, and to the figures and shadows, sacrifices and offerings, in which Christ was foretold and foreshadowed. Second, he uses these words: So the Word was with God, he teaches, but he adds, in the beginning, that is, at the time of his ministry and office, as you have heard. For in that beginning Christ began to be to us the Word, and Teacher, and Prophet, preaching the Father's commandments. In this beginning, therefore, he was with the Father, not yet known to men, but only to the Father; for he was not acknowledged by men to be the Messiah, etc. Finally, at the end he adds a corollary, which he thought to be most dogmatic [δογματικώτατον]; as I judge, and truly judge, it is most vainglorious [περιφδοξότατον], when he says: Notice that such phrases in the Scriptures have the same sense: was with God, is in the Father, is from God, is in the bosom of the Father, is in heaven, went forth from God, came from God, went out from the Father, came down from heaven: that is, was taught and sanctified by God. These are the very words Samosatenus uses. From the first passage two interpretations of this word was arise: one, was foreordained, or (if anyone prefers) was by foreordination; the other, was promised, foretold, and foreshadowed. From the second, similarly two: for the first proposition of John, "In the beginning was the Word," is explained thus: he began to be to us the Word, and Teacher, and Prophet, preaching the Father's commandments; and the second, "And the Word was with God," is said to mean this: in this beginning he was with the Father, not yet known to men, but only to the Father. From the third, one: "was with God," in the sense of "was taught and sanctified by God," just as disciples are customarily placed with their teacher to learn.

units.la: Quid Samosatenum, obsecro, impulit,vt exundante ingenij sui flumine tam multos atque multiplices interpretationum riuos profunderet, omnésque eodem in loco affirmaret? Atqui omnes simul constare non possunt, vtcunque se hic interpres huc illuc conetur vertere: pugnant enim reipsa inter se, ac non solum interpretationis modo. Si enim de præordinatione sunt ista, quæ penes Deum est & abæterno est, non sunt de prænunciatione & promissione apud homines figurata, quæ penes homines est,& inde a creatione est solum. Si de hac dicuntur, vicissim certe de præordinatione apud Deum non possunt accipi: hæc enim rationem habent inter se toto cœlo (vt aiunt) dissidentem, cùm toti enunciato & singulis membris fermè eius diuersam tribuant significationem. Quòd si de eo accipiantur, quòd Christus nobis Verbum esse cœpit, quid iam huic loco cum præordinatione, aut cum promissione ac præfiguratione illa? Aliter plane hicprincipium, quàm illic accipitur, aliter verbum erat. Si de eo quòd innotuit, postquàm nobis Verbum esse cœpit, vt hic quidem argute sibi videtur loqui, omnia ruunt antecedentia. Si denique de eo quòd edoctus a Patre & sanctificatus dicitur apud ipsum, valeant interpretationes reliquæ: nam si hoc dixit Ioannes (vnum autem aliquid eum dixisse necesse est) certè reliqua illa hoc quidem in loco non dixerit. Miseret me profecto Samosateni huius; qui aut Ioannem ita putauit desipere, vt vno verbo in eodem loco tam multa diuersa pugnantiáque dixerit, aut pios sibi res vsqueadeò diuersas atque differentes eumdem in locum affirmanti præsumsit credituros. Atque huius mali posteriorem Samosatenum ita puduit, vt ab ista varietate insulsa discesserit: sed hanc reduuiam non est medicatus anulus ipsius, vtcunq; pretiosu n esse putauerit. Nunc expendamus istarum interpretationum dissidentium inter se veritatem, vt tertio loco recepimus.
units.tr: What, I beg you, impelled Samosatenus to pour forth so many and manifold streams of interpretations from the overflowing river of his wit, and to assert them all in the same passage? Yet they cannot all stand together, however this interpreter tries to turn them this way and that; for in fact they fight among themselves, and not merely in the mode of interpretation. For if these things concern foreordination, which lies with God and is from eternity, they do not concern promise and foreshadowing among men, which lies with men and is from creation only. If they are said of the latter, then in turn they cannot be understood of foreordination with God; for these have a relation to each other that is, as they say, worlds apart, since he assigns to the whole statement and almost to each of its clauses a meaning quite different from the others. But if they are taken to mean that Christ began to be the Word to us, what then has this passage to do with foreordination, or with that promise and foreshadowing? Here "beginning" is taken quite differently than there, and "was" differently too. If they refer to what became known after he began to be the Word to us, as he seems cleverly to himself to say here, then all the preceding interpretations collapse. Finally, if they refer to what is said of him as taught and sanctified by the Father, with him, then the remaining interpretations may stand; for if John said this (and he must have said one thing), then surely those others he did not say in this place. I truly pity this Samosatenus, who either thought John so foolish that in one word in the same place he said so many diverse and conflicting things, or presumed that pious readers would believe one who asserts such utterly diverse and different things in the same place. And the later Samosatenus was so ashamed of this evil that he withdrew from this silly variety; but his ring did not cure this relapse, however precious he may have thought it. Now let us weigh the truth of these mutually disagreeing interpretations, as we have taken up in the third place.

units.la: Harum igitur interpretationum nulli cum mente sancti Apostoli & Euangelistæ Ioannis hoc in loco dicimus conuenire. Id quidem non negamus, Christum ab æterno fuisse præordinatum; a seculo promissum, prænunciatum, & præfiguratum: quum coepit nobis prædicare in carne, tum fuisse nobis Verbum vel Sermonem Patris, & Magistrum, & Prophetam singulari modo præterquàm ante fuerit: Patri fuisse ante notum quàm hominibus; a Deo Patre omnia accepisse, edoctum & sanctificatum esse, & si qua sunt eiusmodi. Sed ea omnia, & singula huius loci negamus esse. Hanc autem negationem nostram cùm Samosatenus ipse inconstantia sua probat & instabili incertóque interpretationum modo, tum verò ipsius rei natura quæ agitur, & consilium Ioannis Euangelistæ, & verba ipsius, & alij denique loci confirmant luculentissimè, in quibus orthodoxa planè sententia & interpretatio nostra statuitur.
units.tr: Of these interpretations, then, we say that none agrees with the mind of the holy Apostle and Evangelist John in this place. We do not deny that Christ was foreordained from eternity, promised and foretold and foreshadowed from the beginning of the world; nor that when he began to preach to us in the flesh, he was to us the Word or Speech of the Father, and Teacher, and Prophet in a unique way beyond what he had been before; nor that he was known to the Father before he was known to men, that he received all things from God the Father, was taught and sanctified, and whatever else is of that kind. But we deny that all these things, each and every one, are the meaning of this passage. Our denial is confirmed not only by Samosatenus' own inconsistency and his unstable and uncertain manner of interpreting, but also, and most clearly, by the nature of the matter under discussion, the purpose of the Evangelist John, his own words, and other passages, in which the orthodox view and our interpretation are plainly established.

units.la: Samosateni huius instabilitatem in exponendo hoc loco incertissimam modò demonstrauimus.
units.tr: We have already shown how very unstable and uncertain Samosatenus is in expounding this passage.

units.la: Nam quod uno in loco exstruit, id eodem (ne longius abcamus) destruit imprudens altera interpretatione. Quapropter nihil opus est amplius, ut in destruendis & labefactandis interpretationibus illius operā consumamus, cum ille nobis suam tam strenuè commodet, suóque iumento malum accersat sibi. Omnino incertam hominis istius mentem esse oportuit, quæ incertas expositiones tam multas fluctuans attulerit. Atque hac ratione plurimùm homines contentiosi, noui Hyperboli, aut ostentabundi Thrasones abutuntur, quibus facilè non ausis obloqui: sed veritatis percipiendæ & tradendæ amantes abstinent diligentissimè.
units.tr: For what he builds up in one place, he, heedless, tears down in the same place (not to go further afield) with another interpretation. Therefore there is no need for us to spend any more effort on overthrowing and undermining his interpretations, since he so eagerly provides us with the means himself and brings ruin upon his own beast of burden. That man's mind must surely have been unsettled, to have produced so many uncertain expositions, wavering back and forth. In this way, contentious men, new Hyperbolus or boastful Thrasos, very often take advantage, since they are not easily opposed; but those who love to grasp and hand on the truth keep most carefully away from such things.

units.la: Rei naturam, quæ agitur, omnibus istis interpretationibus hoc quidem in loco aduersari demonstramus in hunc modum. Agitur de suppositovno, seu persona Christi, ut ipse agnoscit disputator noster: & ordine agitur ab Euangelista. Quale hoc sit suppositum, ex Chrysostomo ante audiuimus, & quid prædicationes flagitent quæ fiunt de hoc suppositō. Negabit Samosatenus. Nobis verò, ut alias probationes omneis taceamus, solus ordo satis futurus est ad reuincenda commenta ipsius. Nam orsus ab æternitate Apostolus ad principium temporis venit, a principio ad progressum, a progressu ad complementum: eum denique ordinem in hac narratione de Christo obseruauit, quem nemo religiosus non est summè admiraturus; nemo nisi religionis expers, ex quo viderit, neglecturus.
units.tr: We show in this way that the nature of the matter under discussion stands against all these interpretations in this passage. The subject is one supposit, or person, of Christ, as our disputant himself acknowledges; and the Evangelist treats it in order. What this supposit is, we heard earlier from Chrysostom, and what the predications made of this supposit require. Samosatenus will deny it. But for us, to pass over all other proofs, the order alone will be enough to refute his inventions. For beginning from eternity, the Apostle comes to the beginning of time, from the beginning to the progress, from the progress to the completion; in short, he observed in this narrative about Christ that order which no devout person will fail to admire greatly, and which no one lacking religion, once he has seen it, will neglect.

units.la: Orditur ab æternitate & ijs quæ de natura sunt huius Sermonis diuini in se, his verbis, In principio erat Sermo ille, & Sermo erat apud Deum, & Sermo erat Deus: Hic erat in principio apud Deum. Ad principium temporis venit, quum se foris explicauisse dicit in creatione & operationibus erga res creatas, illis, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est. Ab hoc principio ad progressum gressum 'transiens, commodissimè distribuit illius tem-pora, & exponit prouidentiam eius inde a creatione po-tentissimè sustentantem & gubernantem omnia, inpri-mis autem homines communi & particulari virtute se-cundum naturæ legem ab ipso positam, tum ante pec-catum, dicens, In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum; tum vero post tristem hominis lapsum, etiam perstan-tem in sua illa communi & singulari sustentatione & gu-bernatione hominum, quamuis indignissimorum : pri-mùm quidem ordinariè naturæ & gratiæ testimonijs, Et lux ista in tenebris lucet,& tenebræ eam non comprehende-runt: deinde verò extraordinariè, & modo singulari gra-tiæ, tum præmisso signo anteambulonis seu præcursoris sui, dicens, Fuit quidam missus a Deo, cui nomen Ioannes, & cætera, quæ διαχερτικῶς per modum hyperbati ab Euan-gelista Ioanne adiecta sunt: tum priore aduentu gratioso ipsius in carne, Et Sermo ille caro factus est, &c. post quem aduentum commoratus est inter suos, eisque se contem-plandum & recognoscendum gradatim & successiuè (vt loquuntur) præbuit plenus gratiæ & veritatis. Nam ex eo demum aduentu ministerium illud consequutum est, de quo Samosatenus ait Christum nobis factum esse Ver-bum, & Magistrum, & Prophetam, proloquendo verba pa-terna. Iam verò cum hoc diuino ordine & plane incom-parabili, si placet, comparetur istius ordo imaginarius. Quàm verè dixeris, ἑρεα πολλα μεταξύ! Sanè quamcun-que expendamus ex eius interpretationibus, confusa, præpostera, peruersa omnia. Ac propterea vir, si quis-quam, δωδεκαμήχαν hæc ad præordinationem, illa ad promissa & figuras & typos, alia ad communicationem & exhibitionem præsentem, nonnulla ad notitiam, quæ-dam ad institutionem & sanctificationem personæ rapit: & vno denique loco nomen principij fine fine variat, verbúmq; illud vnicum erat tam distorquet miserè, vt nul-la vnquam certa apud homines futura sit mentis aut loci interpretatio, si hæc admittantur atque obtineant. Sed vt tam multis omissis, vnam aliquam, eámque omnium quas hic adfert speciosissimam producamus: age, fingamus hæc dixisse Ioannem (a quibus tamen ὃς ὃ̀ πάντων pius animus semper abhorrebit) prout Samosateno se-mel, ac non semper video placuisse, & Manuscripto confirmari: In principio ministerij Euangelici erat quidem Verbum vel Sermo ille seipsum patefaciens & voluntatem Patris: sed erat apud Deum soli Patri notus, & idem erat Deus præordinatione & institutione a Deo Patre facta, per gratiosam communicationem illius. Hic, inquam, Sermo erat in principio illius ministerij apud Patrem, id est, soli Patri notus, hominibus autem minimè. Omnia per ipsum facta, id est, instaurata sunt spiritali instauratione: & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est ad hanc instaurationem pertinens, & quæ sequuntur. Tandem verò his omnibus positis, quum veniturad il-lum locum, Et Sermo ille factus est caro, quis homo non videt ineptissimum ordinem (ne quid dicam grauius) huic Euangelistæ & Euangelio ipsius affictum esse? Pura puta certè est synchysis in sacra hac narratione, si obtinebit istorum hominum interpretatio. Atque hæc vniuersè de ordine huius narrationis satis. De consilio autem Ioannis quid dicturi sumus? nempe idipsum quod antè segmento 2. statuimus: nam alterum altero sunditus euertitur. Aut ergo illud consilium Ioannis euersa huius Samosateni sententia stare necesse, aut e contrario hac consistente ruere: adeò sunt inter se contradicentia. Sed de hac reconsido eo in loco satis a nobis fuisse dictū pro instituto nostro. Quamobrem de verbis videamus. Principij igitur & Verbi seu Sermonis voces quid proprie hoc loco designent, suprà ostendimus segmento 2. & 3. & quàm turpiter in principio exponendo hic nouator offendat, paulo ante euicimus. Iam nobis excutienda restat hoc quidem in loco primum verbi erat, deinde loquutionis huius vtriusque, in principio erat Sermo, & hic erat in principio apud Deum, interpretatio, & iusta significatio. Verbi erat significationem aut propriam esse, aut figuratam necesse est: Si propria, aut esse καληγορημένῳ, quam secundi adiecti vocant, aut συγκατηγορημένῳ siue (vt alijs placet) συγκατηγορηματικῶ, quæ tertij adiecti appellatur. Verbum autem est vel erat κατηγορούμενον, aut prædicatur de substantia quæ est reipsa & exsistit per se, aut de accidente, quod ratione inest in alio, non autem exsistit per se. Ens enim de substantia & de accidente dicitur ἀναλόγως. Hic de substantia agi inter nos convenit. Itaque omisso accidente, de essentiali modo ἕ εἶναι videndum est. Hoc genus essendi (vt ita loquamur) vel exsistendi est triplex in rebus creatis omnibus: vnū, quod commune; alterum, quod speciale, tertium denique quod indiuiduale vocant. Secundùm primum genus, substantiæ ab accidentibus disparantur, & simpliciter dicuntur esse: secundùm alterum, species disparantur substantiarum inter se, & dicuntur substare: secundùm tertium denique, primæ substantiæ vel indiuidua subsistentia distingui solent, & dicuntur subsistere: hæc autem indiuidua subsistentiæque, si ratione præditæ sunt, personæ appellantur. Iam de primo illo genere seu modo essendi solùm hic non agi, inter nos quoque (vt puto) convenit. De secundo agi, Samosatenum ipsum vix dicturum puto: cùm hic quæstio sit non de specie vlla, aut etiam de indiuiduo secundùm rationem speciei solùm, sed de indiuiduo vno certo secundùm rationem (vt ita dicam) indiuidualem ipsius, secundùm quam hoc vnum suppositum erat in principio,& apud Deum, & Deus,&c.Quæ cùm ita sint, verbum erat hoc loco aut est κατηγορούμενον tertio modo, aut π͂ρωτοκατηγορούμενον, aut denique figuratum. Esse autem π͂ρωτοκατηγορούμενον, & simplicem prædicationis copulam, simpliciter nego: & multis argumentis Ioannes docet manifestissimè. Nam si erat in principio, si erat apud Deum, si erat Deus, si erat in principio apud Deum, erat igitur: ac proinde hoc Verbum erat perinde significat ac si Ioannes dixisset, hic Sermo erat non solùm primo modo (hic enim analogicè communis est omnium entium, puta essentiarum & accidentium) non solùm item secundo modo, siue communi, siue speciali (horum enim prior omnium substantiarum communis est, posterior speciei cuiusque proprius) sed erat tertio modo, id est, erat unum suppositum, & subsistebat individualiter. Atque hoc probatur eo, quòd Deus est Ens vniuocè (vt loquuntur) non communi cum entibus lege, non genus, non species, sed essentia ὑπερούσιος, ens entium, & principium principiorum omnium. In principio autem & ante principium nihil erat quàm Deus essentia ὑπερούσιος, nihil quod non esset Deus. Nam aliquid aliud præter Deum ante principium omnium statuere, id non piorum prudentiúmque placitum, sed furentium Manichæorum est delirium. Erat autem in principio Sermo, & apud Deum, & Deus: erat igitur, id est, subsistebat persona Sermonis in principio apud Deū Deus, apud Patrem Filius. Hæc a se videns Samosatenus commodè eludi non posse, subterfugit nova ratione & inaudita quadam, affirmans ea secundum quid & figuratè dici, quæ tam simpliciter proprieque ab Euangelista fuerunt dicta quàm quod maximè. Principium, ait ille, secundùm quid dicitur: & verbum erat, figuratè, quamuis non eo sublata subsistentia Verbi. Erat enim Sermo aut præcognitione & præordinatione apud Deum, aut promissione, aut exhibitione, aut declaratione & manifestatione publica, aut denique institutione & sanctificatione a Patre. Itaque principium secundùm præcognitionem ad æternitatem spectat, secundùm promissionem ad primordia humani generis, secundùm exhibitionem ad primordia humanæ naturæ Christi, secundùm declarationem manifestationémque ad primordia ministerij illius, secundùm institutionem denique & sanctificationem a Patre, ad tempus Baptismi, quo Christus diuinitus inauguratus est, quum super eum Spiritus sanctus descendisset, testante e cœlo Patre. Ergo hoc primum nobis, Samosatene, affirmas non esse propriam & simplicem huius loci interpretationem: deinde verò & illud ostendis, te in multiplice varietate istarum interpretationum pendere animi, quam earum tenere debeas. Sic incertus doces, & rem tibi incertam doces: ecquis proprie isto docendi modo reddatur certior? Ego verò contrà & nominis principium simplicem, & verbi erat proprijssimam adfirmo esse hoc in loco significationem, & loquutionem quamque proprie accipi oportere. De nomine principij, relatiuum esse ad res principiatas (vt ita vocemus) antè vicimus segmento 2. Verbum erat accipi quàm proprijssimè demonstrabimus tribus argumentis. Vnum hoc esto: Omnium vocum in sermone nostro naturalis potius quàm ficta, propria quàm figurata seruanda est significatio, nisi aut rei forte, id est, subiecti, aut loci natura postulauerit, id est, prædicationis & adiunctorum eius. Et verbi, erat, igitur naturalis propriáq; tenenda significatio. Quòd si forte Samosatenus dixerit, aliud rei naturam postulare, id ego consentiente veritate, & boni omnes qui res diuinas aliquo pacto sapiunt, negaturi sumus. Taceo quod antè satis docuimus, id rei naturā omnino flagitare, vt propria seruetur huius verbi significatio. Quid? quòd nosterhic Samosatenus titubans, ex tot figuratis suis interpretationibus quam eligat nescit, & altera subruit alteram præinscientia? Proprium igitur hoc verbum, & de Sermone Dei exponendum proprie. Sed & loquutiones ipsas proprie accipi iubent tum rei natura, tum loquutionum modus, tum denique alij consimiles loci. Ex rei natura quæ agitur has loquutiones proprias esse vincimus, quia res diuina agitur, ac non accidentaria. Deo enim quid accidat? aut qui accidat Deus? Nam quicquid Deus in Scripturis ὑποστατικῶς, non autem προσωπικῶς aut συγχωρητικῶς esse dicitur, aut Deo inesse prædicatur, id ex communi omnium consensu essentiale est. Hic autem agitur de eo Sermone qui erat in principio, & apud Deum, & Deus: essentialis igitur prædicatio. Nec refert quod Samosatenus potest regerere, hoc ab Ioanne non dici simpliciter, sed ita dici, erat in principio, erat apud Deum, erat Deus, &c. Nam si erat in principio (vt ante diximus) si erat apud Deum, eratque Deus, erat igitur: & quidem erat non accidentali, sed essentiali ratione, quia erat in principio, erat apud Deum, & erat Deus: nam quod erat in principio, apud Deum, Deus, id accidens esse non potest, aut Deo insunt accidentia. Est autem simplicissimus: expers igitur accidentium, ab æterno, in æternum. De modo vero loquutionum quid dicturi sumus? Certè hæ loquutiones aut propriæ dicendæ sunt, aut figuratæ schemate vel tropo: Non autem figuratæ, nec schemate, nec tropo: Propriæ igitur. Quòd si figuratas Samosatenus dixerit schemate, quo tandem? obsecro. Non pleonasmo: quid enim pressius, ac minus redundans. Non ellipsi: quid enim plenius? Non denique enallage: quid enim rectius? Atqui ad hos tres fontes capitaque pertinent omnes figurarum riui. Sin tropo figuratas ratas dixerit, quisnam ille sit audiamus. Non enim redundant hæ loquutiones per synecdochen: non deficiunt per metonymiam, aut metalepsin vllam: non mutationem tropicam induunt μεταφορικῶς. sed omnia de Deo & secundùm Deum proprie simpliciterque enunciantur. Proprie autem? immo proprissimé: quid enim magis proprium, quàm quod dicitur vniuocé? Quid autem magis vniuocè, quàm quum vox vniuoca per se, de Deo proprie est enunciata? Sic autem hoc loco se habet hæc vox, sic loquutio tota. Nam λόγος vniuocè appellatur Sermo, id est, persona illa Filij vnigeniti, quem Pater de se in se gignit: æquiuocè autem in nobis dicitur essentialis facultas illa quam mens de se in se generat συναιδίως. Tum verbum erat vniuocè de eo prædicatur, qui reuera Deus est. Cùm enim sit Deus non προπικῶς aut συγχωρητικῶς, sed ὑπάρχων, (vt loquitur Paulus) siue ὑπαρκτικῶς, omnino eum in se & per se esse entem (vt ita dicamus) substantem, & subsistentem necesse est, & ita de eo dici vniuocè: cætera autem æquiuocè entia, substantia, & subsistentia ab eo communi vel vniuersali principio appellari. Sic ergo erat in principio Sermo, & apud Deum, & Deus proprie, magis inquam proprie quàm vnquam dici de re vlla possit: immo hoc proprie, cætera æquiuocé. Locos autem consimiles ad huius rei demonstrationem adferri quid attinet? Nam hic ipse locus est euidentissimus. Tum pleni sunt Scripturæ sacrosanctæ libri, plenæ illorum paginæ exemplis vocum, & testimonijs ad hanc rem pertinentibus. Certè quum Apostolus inquit, Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem est, & in se-cula, eumdem modum ostendit ad Christum pertinere ἔναγ, τῆς οὐσίας, ἡ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, eumdem,inquam,affirmat modum de essentia & substantia & subsistentia
units.tr: He begins with eternity and with what this divine Word is in itself, in these words: In the beginning was that Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: he was in the beginning with God. He comes to the beginning of time when he says that the Word showed himself outwardly in creation and in his works toward created things: All things were made by him, and without him was made nothing that was made. Passing from this beginning to the progress of events, he distributes the times of the Word most fittingly and sets forth his providence, which from creation onward most powerfully sustains and governs all things, and especially human beings, by a common and particular power, according to the law of nature established by him. This applies both before sin, when he says, In him was life, and the life was the light of men, and after the sad fall of humankind, when his common and singular sustaining and governing of human beings continued, though they were most unworthy. First, indeed, this happened ordinarily, through the testimonies of nature and grace: And that light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. Then it happened extraordinarily and in a singular mode of grace, with a sign of his forerunner or precursor placed first, when he says, There was a man sent from God, whose name was John, and the rest, which the evangelist John added by way of hyperbaton [διαχερτικῶς]. Then came his gracious first coming in the flesh: And that Word was made flesh, and so on. After this coming he dwelt among his own, and presented himself to them to be contemplated and recognised gradually and successively (as they say), full of grace and truth. For it was from that coming that the ministry followed, of which Samosatenus says that Christ was made the Word for us, and Teacher, and Prophet, proclaiming the words of the Father. Now let his imaginary order be compared, if you like, with this divine and wholly incomparable order. How truly you could say, many things lie between [ἔρεα πολλὰ μεταξύ]! Indeed, whatever we weigh from his interpretations, all is confused, preposterous and perverse. Therefore this man, if anyone, drags these things, full of twelve contrivances [δωδεκαμήχανα], to forethought, those to promises, figures and types, others to communication and present exhibition, some to knowledge, and others to the institution and sanctification of the person. Finally, in one place he varies the word beginning at every turn, and so wretchedly twists that single word was that no interpretation of mind or place will ever be certain among human beings, if these things are admitted and prevail. But, to pass over many things, let us bring forward one, the most specious of all that he offers here. Come, let us suppose that John said these things (though a pious mind will always abhor such things), just as it seems to have pleased Samosatenus once, and not always, and as it is confirmed by a manuscript: At the beginning of the evangelical ministry there was indeed the Word, or that Word, making himself known and the will of the Father; but he was with God, known only to the Father, and he was God by the forethought and institution made by God the Father, through the gracious communication of that Word. This Word, I say, was at the beginning of that ministry with the Father, that is, known only to the Father, but not to human beings. All things were made through him, that is, restored by a spiritual restoration; and without him was made nothing that was made pertaining to this restoration, and so on.
