Finally, when all these things have been laid down, and we come to that place, And that Word was made flesh, what man does not see that a most absurd order (not to say anything more severe) has been fastened upon this evangelist and his Gospel? Surely there is pure synchysis in this sacred narrative, if this interpretation of those men is to prevail. These things in general about the order of this narrative are enough. But what shall we say about the purpose of John? Namely, the very thing we established earlier in segment 2: for the one overturns the other from the foundations. Either John's purpose must stand with the overthrow of this opinion of Samosatenus, or, on the contrary, if this opinion stands, that purpose must fall; so contradictory are they to each other. But I have said enough about this matter in its own place, as my plan requires. Therefore let us look at the words. What the words beginning and Word or Speech properly designate in this place, we have shown above in segments 2 and 3, and how shamefully this innovator goes astray in explaining beginning, we have proved a little earlier. Now what remains for us to examine in this place is first the word was, and then the interpretation and true meaning of both expressions, in the beginning was the Word, and he was in the beginning with God. The meaning of the word was must be either proper or figurative. If proper, it is either a predicate of the kind they call the second adjunct [καληγορημένῳ, i.e. κατηγορούμενον], or a co-predicate [συγκατηγορημένῳ], or, as others prefer, a co-predicative [συγκατηγορηματικῷ], which is called the third adjunct. The verb is or was, as a predicate [κατηγορούμενον], is either said of a substance that exists in itself and subsists through itself, or of an accident, which is in another by reason and does not exist through itself. For being [ens] is said of substance and of accident analogically [ἀναλόγως]. Here we agree that the discussion concerns substance. So, leaving aside accident, we must consider the essential mode of being [τὸ εἶναι]. This kind of being, or existing (if we may so speak), is threefold in all created things: one common, another special, and a third which they call individual. According to the first kind, substances are distinguished from accidents and are said simply to be. According to the second, species of substances are distinguished from one another and are said to subsist in something. According to the third, finally, the first substances or individual subsistences are usually distinguished and are said to subsist; and these individual subsistences, if they are endowed with reason, are called persons. Now we agree, I think, that the first kind or mode of being is not what is at issue here. As to the second, I do not think Samosatenus himself would say it applies, since the question here is not about any species, or even about an individual only according to the nature of a species, but about one definite individual according to what I may call its individual nature, according to which this one suppositum was in the beginning, and with God, and God, and so on. Since these things are so, the verb was in this place is either a predicate in the third mode, or a primary predicate, or finally figurative. That it is a primary predicate and a simple copula of predication, I simply deny; and John teaches this most clearly by many arguments. For if he was in the beginning, if he was with God, if he was God, if he was in the beginning with God, then he was: and so this verb was signifies in the same way as if John had said, this Word was not only in the first mode (for in this sense it is common to all beings analogically, namely substances and accidents), nor only in the second mode, whether common or special (for the former is common to all substances, the latter proper to each species), but was in the third mode, that is, was one suppositum and subsisted individually. And this is proved by the fact that God is being univocally (as they say), not by a common law with beings, not as a genus, not as a species, but as a supersubstantial essence [ὑπερούσιος], the being of beings, and the principle of all principles. Moreover, in the beginning and before the beginning there was nothing but God, a supersubstantial essence, nothing that was not God. For to posit anything other than God before the beginning of all things is not the view of the godly and wise, but the raving of the furious Manichaeans. But the Word was in the beginning, and with God, and God: he was therefore, that is, the person of the Word subsisted in the beginning with God as God, and with the Father as the Son. Samosatenus, seeing that he cannot conveniently escape these points, evades them by a new and unheard-of device, asserting that those things are said in a qualified sense and figuratively, though they were stated by the evangelist as simply and properly as possible. The beginning, he says, is said in a qualified sense; and the verb was is figurative, though the subsistence of the Word is not thereby removed. For the Word was either with God in foreknowledge and forethought, or in promise, or in exhibition, or in public declaration and manifestation, or finally in institution and sanctification by the Father. So the beginning, according to foreknowledge, refers to eternity; according to promise, to the first beginnings of the human race; according to exhibition, to the first beginnings of Christ's human nature; according to declaration and manifestation, to the first beginnings of his ministry; and according to institution and sanctification by the Father, to the time of Baptism, when Christ was inaugurated by divine authority, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him, the Father bearing witness from heaven. Therefore, Samosatenus, you first assert to us that this is not the proper and simple interpretation of the passage; and then you also show that, amid the manifold variety of these interpretations, you hang in doubt about which of them you ought to hold. Thus you teach uncertainly, and you teach an uncertain matter: can anyone be made more certain by a teaching method of this kind? I, on the contrary, affirm that the simple meaning of the noun beginning and the most proper meaning of the verb was are what is required in this place, and that every expression ought to be taken properly. As to the noun beginning, we showed earlier in segment 2 that it is relative to the things that have a beginning (as we may call them). That the verb was must be taken most properly, we will demonstrate by three arguments. Let this be the first: In our speech, the natural meaning of all words is to be kept rather than a feigned one, and the proper rather than the figurative, unless the nature of the thing, that is, of the subject, or of the place, that is, of the predicate and its adjuncts, demands otherwise. The verb "was" therefore must keep its natural and proper meaning. But if Samosatenus should say that the nature of the thing demands something else, we, with the agreement of truth and of all good people who have some understanding of divine things, will deny it. I pass over what we have sufficiently taught above, that the nature of the thing wholly requires that the proper meaning of this verb be kept. What of this: that our Samosatenus, wavering, does not know which of his many figurative interpretations to choose, and undermines one by another, with no foresight? Therefore this word is proper, and must be explained properly of the Word of God. But the expressions themselves are required to be taken properly both by the nature of the thing, and by the manner of the expressions, and finally by other similar passages. By the nature of the thing under discussion we conquer that these expressions are proper, because the matter is divine and not accidental. For what can happen to God? Or what accident can befall God? For whatever in the Scriptures is said to be in God substantially [ὑποστατικῶς], and not personally [προσωπικῶς] or by concession [συγχωρητικῶς], or is predicated as inhering in God, that is essential by the common consent of all. But here we are dealing with that Word which was in the beginning, and with God, and was God: therefore the predication is essential. Nor does it matter what Samosatenus may object, that John does not say this simply, but says it thus: he was in the beginning, he was with God, he was God, and so on. For if he was in the beginning (as we said before), if he was with God, and was God, then he was: and indeed he was not by an accidental but by an essential reason, because he was in the beginning, he was with God, and he was God; for what was in the beginning, with God, and God, cannot be an accident, nor do accidents inhere in God. But he is most simple; therefore he is free from accidents, from eternity to eternity. What shall we say about the manner of the expressions? Surely these expressions must be called either proper or figurative by scheme or trope. But they are not figurative, either by scheme or by trope: therefore they are proper. But if Samosatenus should call them figurative by scheme, by which scheme, I beg you? Not by pleonasm: for what is more concise and less redundant? Not by ellipsis: for what is fuller? Not finally by enallage: for what is more correct? Yet all the streams of figures derive from these three sources and heads. But if he should call them figurative by trope, let us hear what trope he means. For these expressions are not redundant by synecdoche, nor deficient by metonymy or any metalepsis, nor do they take on a tropical change metaphorically; rather, everything is stated properly and simply about God and according to God. Properly? Indeed most properly: for what is more proper than what is said univocally? And what is more univocal than when a univocal word is stated of God properly, in itself? For this word, and this expression as a whole, stands thus here. For logos is applied univocally to the Word, that is, to that person of the only-begotten Son whom the Father begets from himself in himself; but in us the essential faculty which the mind generates from itself in itself, co-eternally [συναιδίως], is called word only equivocally. Then the verb was is predicated univocally of him who is truly God. For since he is God, not personally or by concession, but existing [ὑπάρχων], as Paul says, or actually [ὑπαρκτικῶς], he must necessarily be a being that stands and subsists in himself and through himself (if we may so speak), and so is univocally said of him; while the other things are called beings, substances and subsistences equivocally, from that common or universal principle. So then the Word was in the beginning, and with God, and God, properly; indeed more properly than anything can ever be said of any thing: or rather, this is said properly, and the others equivocally. But what is the point of bringing forward similar passages to demonstrate this? For this very passage is most evident. Moreover, the books of holy Scripture are full, their pages full of examples of words and testimonies pertaining to this matter. Certainly, when the Apostle says, Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, he shows that the same manner belongs to Christ, in essence, substance, and subsistence; he affirms, I say, the same manner of essence, substance and subsistence, and this eternal (as I may say) identity of them. For what is more the same than what is most simple? And what is more simple than God? And the Apostle wished to make this affirmation most clearly evident from the fact that, with a single word, he refers to three distinct members, although…

units.la: Philip. 2. Christi, æternáque (vt ita dicam) identitate earum. quid enim magis idem est, quàm quod simplicissimum? quid magis simplex, quàm Deus? Et suam hanc affirmationem Apostolus ex eo cōstare voluit euidentissimè, quod vnico verbo ad tria membra distincta, quamuis ἐξαιρέτως suppresso, vtitur: nam vbi verbum deficit, substantiuum ex naturæ lege & Hebræorum constante vsu oportet intelligi. Eadem quoque ratione dicebat Ioannes, hic est verus Deus & vita æterna, postquam de pijs fidelibusque affirmasset dicens, sumus in verace illo, in Filio Dei Iesu Christo: nempe quia in illo sumus participatione gratiæ, qui in se est veritas & vita æterna diuinæ suæ naturæ immutabili veritate. Sic idem sese prædicat esse resurrectionem & vitam, esse viam veritatem & vitam, esse lucem mundi, &c. nam qui ita est, cum esse omnino necesse est, & quidem esse ὄντως, ὑπωδῶς, ἡ ὑποστατικῶς, essentia, subsistentia, & subsistentia, prout distinguunt Scholastici. Sed hæc in præsentia satis: quæ alibi (si Deus volet) copiosius persequemur. Statuimus igitur nullo pacto hic figuratam esse verborum Ioannis significationem ex communi iure. Nunc age, de particularibus istis interpretationibus singillatim quoque videamus. Prima. In principio, inquit Samosatenus, prædicationis suæ erat Verbum vel Sermo Patris, id est, Christus Iesus præordinatione. Vide acumen hominis. Præordinationem, Samosatene, si opponis rei existentiæ, vt certè fieri necesse est, falsum est quod dicis. Nam in principio prædicationis suæ, qua Christus ipse in carne prædicauit Euangelium, iam fuit Christus re & existentia, ac non præordinatione solum. Si coniungis quorsum ista tua interpretatio? & quorsum hæc Euangelista dixerit? In principio prædicationis erat, & erat præordinatus. Belle sane, vt ante segmento 2. arguimus. Dices fortasse, hanc interpretationem ad secundum eundum membrum, hic Sermo erat apud Deum, non autem ad primum pertinere. Ergo te hoc non reticuisse oportuit: nam quis posset? quis velit diuinare? Sed esto, de secundo dixeris. An vero hunc Sermonem fuisse apud Deum praeordinatione statuesin principio praedicationis suae? nam propterea praecauit Apostolus, quum iterato diceret, hic erat in principio apud Deum. Quod si fuit praeordinatione, non igitur re fuit & existentia. Atqui reipsa exstitit, vt ante dicebamus, quum praedicare coepit: nam quid operetur qui non est? Si re exstitit, non ergo praeordinatione solum. Sin vtroque, amabo te, quid attinuit praeordinationis solius meminisse? & principium illud ab vtro sumes? nam praeordinationis non est principium, cum in Deo aeterna sit: existentiae vero humanitatis, & praedicationi principium temporale est. Quinetiam, vt amplius dicamus, si secundum hanc praeordinationem fuisse dicitur qua fuit, eadem quoque ratione fecisse & fuisse aliis, qua se communicauit cum illis, dicendus est. Nempe omnia per hunc facta fuerint, praeordinatione: in ipso vita fuerit omnium, praeordinatione: lux fuerit hominum, praeordinatione: & in tenebris praeordinatione luxerit: ad suos praeordinatione venerit: & credentibus, quotquot acceperunt ipsum, dignitatem illam contulerit praeordinatione, vt filij Dei fierent: omnia denique ad versum vsque illum, & Sermo ille caro factus est, praeordinatione fuerit, fecerit, praestiterit, non autem reipsa compleuerit horum quicquam.
units.tr: Philip. 2. of Christ, and of their eternal (so to speak) identity. For what is more the same than what is most simple? And what is more simple than God? The Apostle wished this assertion of his to rest on a plain point: he uses one word for three distinct members, with the word understood in its eminent sense [ἐξαιρέτως] but left unexpressed. Where the word is lacking, the substantive must be understood, by the law of nature and the settled usage of the Hebrews. In the same way John also said, this is the true God and eternal life, after he had said of the godly and faithful, we are in him that is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. We are in him by participation in grace, and he is in himself the truth and eternal life, by the unchangeable truth of his divine nature. So too he declares of himself that he is the resurrection and the life, that he is the way, the truth and the life, that he is the light of the world, and so on. For he who is so must of necessity be, and indeed be really [ὄντως], substantially [οὐσιωδῶς], or subsistently [ὑποστατικῶς], in essence and in subsistence, as the Schoolmen distinguish. But this is enough for the present; what remains we shall, God willing, pursue more fully elsewhere. We conclude, therefore, that the meaning of John's words is in no way figurative here by the common law of language. Now let us look at these particular interpretations one by one. First: In the beginning, says Samosatenus, of his preaching, the Word or Speech of the Father was, that is, Jesus Christ by predestination. See the man's sharpness! Samosatenus, if you set predestination against real existence, as you must do, then what you say is false. For at the beginning of his preaching, when Christ himself in the flesh preached the Gospel, he was already Christ in reality and existence, not in predestination alone. If you join the two, what is the point of your interpretation, and why would the Evangelist have said this? In the beginning of the preaching he was, and he was predestined. Very fine indeed, as we argued before at section 2. You may perhaps say that this interpretation applies to the second member, this Speech was with God, and not to the first. Then you ought not to have passed over this; for who could guess it? who would wish to divine it? But grant that you spoke of the second. Do you really mean that this Speech was with God by predestination at the beginning of his preaching? For that is why the Apostle was careful to repeat, this was in the beginning with God. But if he was so by predestination, then he was not so in reality and existence. Yet he did in fact exist, as we said before, when he began to preach: for what can one who is not do? If he existed in reality, then not by predestination alone. If in both ways, then pray tell, why did you bother to mention predestination alone? And from which of the two will you take that beginning? For predestination has no beginning, since it is eternal in God; but the existence of the humanity and its preaching have a temporal beginning. Moreover, to say more: if he is said to have been so by this predestination, then by the same reasoning he must be said to have made all things and to have been for others in the way he communicated himself to them. Namely, all things were made through him by predestination; in him was the life of all things by predestination; he was the light of men by predestination, and shone in darkness by predestination; he came to his own by predestination; and to those who believed, as many as received him, he gave by predestination the dignity of becoming sons of God; in short, everything up to the verse and the Word was made flesh happened, was made, was performed by predestination, and not in reality did he accomplish any of these things.

units.la: Secunda. Quod si ad secundam interpretatione Samosatenus venerit, fuisse illum promisso, praenunciatione, praefiguratione (horum enim ratio communis est) nihil inde assequuturus est. Nam ea ipsa, quae modo ad praeordinationem diximus, ad hunc locum ex aequo pertinent, cum omnia sint in ideis, vt loquuntur, posita: Si promisso, prænunciatione, præfiguratione fuit,non ergo fuisse existentia: si exstitit re, non ergo promisso, &c. si vtroque, ergo superuacaneam hanc festiuam distinctionem esse: tum eodem modo sequentia omnia ad versum vsque 14. restringi oportere,nisi ineptam & putidam ὑςτερολογίαν in verbis Euangelistæ placet statuere. Hoc autem Samosateno qui placeat? nam interpretatur diuerso modo. Nec illud igitur placere ipsi oportuit. Tertiæ & quartæ interpretationis modum coniungit Samosatenus, quum ait, in principio sui ministerij & officij Christus esse cœpit nobis Verbum, & Magister, & Propheta, prædicans mandata paterna: & in hoc principio erat apud Patrem, nondum notus hominibus, sed soli Patri. Hæc fermè Samosateni verba, quæ anteà iam satis falsi reuicimus. Nam glossema est supposititium, quum additur istud, nobis: nec probari potest. Etenim Christus (vt verbis Samosateni vtar) cœpit nobis esse Verbum,quum per Baptismū cum initiauit Pater.ac priùs quidem Ioanni Baptistę non innotuerat: sed tum eodem momento, in illo, inquam, principio diuinitus illi innotuit Christus, & alijs postridie per illum,contraquàm hic ausus est affirmare. Tum enim dicebat Ioannes, ego non nouera eum: sed qui misit me vt baptizarem aqua, ille mihi dixerat,super quem videris Spiritum descendentem ac manentem super eum, hic est qui baptizat Spiritu sanƈto. Ego igitur vidi, & testor hunc esse Filium illũ Dei. Præterea hîc adtexitur interpretatio iusto verborum ordini, quem antè demonstrauimus, aduersaria. Primùm enim agitur de Sermone, vt in ipso est:tum de operationibus ipsius, quæ inde a creatione ad tempus illud vsque quo venit in carnem, exstiterunt: postremò autem de aduentu in carnem. At noster hic antagonistes veritatis præire vult ante hæc omnia locum de notitia Sermonis illius, postquàm in carnem aduentauit.
units.tr: Second. If Samosatenus comes to his second interpretation, that he was by promise, by announcement, by prefiguration (for these have a common sense), he will gain nothing from it. For the very things we have just said about predestination apply equally to this place, since all things, as they say, are laid up in ideas. If he was by promise, announcement, or prefiguration, then he was not in existence; if he existed in reality, then not by promise and so on; if in both ways, then this pleasing distinction is superfluous. Likewise, all that follows up to verse 14 would have to be restricted in the same way, unless one is willing to set up an inept and foolish hysterologia in the words of the Evangelist. But why would this please Samosatenus? For he interprets it in a different way. Therefore he ought not to be pleased with this either. Samosatenus joins the third and fourth interpretations together when he says: In the beginning of his ministry and office, Christ began to be to us the Word, both Teacher and Prophet, proclaiming the commands of the Father; and in this beginning he was with the Father, not yet known to men, but known to the Father alone. These are nearly Samosatenus' own words, which we have already sufficiently refuted as false. For the addition to us is a spurious gloss, and cannot be proved. Indeed, Christ (to use Samosatenus' words) began to be the Word to us when the Father initiated him by baptism; and before that he was not made known to John the Baptist. But at that very moment, in that beginning, I say, Christ was made known to him by God, and to others the next day through him, contrary to what this man has dared to assert. For John then said: I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water told me, upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. I therefore saw it, and testify that this is the Son of God. Besides, here the interpretation is set against the proper order of the words, which we showed before. For first the Evangelist speaks of the Speech as it is in itself; then of its operations, which came into being from creation up to the time when it came into the flesh; and lastly of its coming in the flesh. But our antagonist here, an enemy of the truth, wants the passage about the knowledge of that Speech to come before all these things, after it had come into the flesh.

units.la: Quid autem est capiti ocream (quod aiunt) tibiæque galeam aptare, nisi hoc est? Deinde nescio quis vnquam istum docuerit hunc interpretationis modum, erat, id est, cœpit esse: hoc nulla ratione, exemplo, auctoritate iusta defendi potest. Adde, quòd si cœpit esse verbum administratione sua quod ante non fuit, iniquum est secundum membrum & huic oppositum (vt quidem Samosateno placet) ad cognitionem rapi, & idem verbum variè accipi in ijs membris quæ inter se comparantur. Dicitur autem respectu nostri fuisse, id est, cœpisse prædicare: Dei verò respectu, fuisse, id est, Deo Patri soli fuisse cognitum. Quid? quòd ante Sermo fuit Deo cognitus, quàm obiret administrationem suam? quàm veniret in carne? addo etiam, quàm omnia per ipsum facta essent? quæ omnia suo ordine deinceps a Ioanne affirmantur. etsi a Samosateno studio quidem maximo, sed frustrà detorquentur alió. Quinta interpretatio eiusdem modi est plane, & rationibus ijsdem refellitur: quas, ne longiores simus, æquo Lectori & pietatis amanti ex antecedentib. reuocandas in hunc locum permittimus.
units.tr: But what is this, but (as they say) fitting a greave to the head and a helmet to the leg? Then I do not know who ever taught this method of interpretation, that was means began to be. This cannot be defended on any sound ground, by example or by authority. Add that, if the Word began to be by his administration what he was not before, it is unfair (as Samosatenus would have it) to drag the second member, set over against the first, into the sense of recognition, and to take the same word in different senses in the members that are compared with one another. It is said that he was with respect to us, that is, he began to preach; but with respect to God, he was, that is, he was known to God the Father alone. What then? Was the Speech known to God before he undertook his administration? Before he came in the flesh? I add: before all things were made through him? All these things John afterwards affirms in their order, although Samosatenus, with great zeal but in vain, twists them another way. The fifth interpretation is of the same kind and is refuted by the same arguments, which, lest we be too long, we permit the fair-minded reader who loves godliness to recall from what has gone before and apply to this passage.

units.la: Enimuero si Deus erat idem qui erat apud Deum, quomodo edoctus & sanctificatus est a Patre, quà erat Deus? Hæc attributa Christi sunt quà homo, non quà Deus: hîc autem a Ioanne agitur de Christo quà Deus, non quà homo. Nam quà erat in principio, & apud Deum, & Deus, & operatus est vt Deus, hoc Ioannes exponit versibus 13. pòst ad humanitatem assumtam transit, in versu 14. Hæc qui non vident quum docentur, eos voluntaria cæcitas in luce præpedit, non humana infirmitas. Tu verò, ô lux mundi, tenebras istas discute, eosque dirige in luce qui tui sunt propter nomen & veritatem tuam. Atque hæc generatim de horum verborum interpretatione. Nunc videndum est, quia multa quoque in hunc locum a veritate aliena varijs modis infarcta sunt, vt ea breuiter & suo ordine destringamus.
units.tr: Indeed, if God was the same who was with God, how was he taught and sanctified by the Father, in so far as he was God? These attributes belong to Christ as man, not as God; but here John speaks of Christ as God, not as man. For what he was in the beginning, and with God, and God, and what he worked as God, John sets out in verses 1–3; afterwards he passes to the humanity assumed, in verse 14. Those who do not see this when it is taught are hindered by a wilful blindness in the light, not by human weakness. But you, O light of the world, dispel those shadows, and direct in the light those who are yours, for your name's sake and your truth. These are the general points on the interpretation of these words. Now we must see, since many things foreign to the truth have also been crammed into this passage in various ways, that we may dispatch them briefly and in order.

units.la: 1. Falsò & vitiosè hic locus de Abrahamo adducitur. Non enim hæc Christus simpliciter dicit de prænunciatione & præfiguratione aduentus & carnis suæ, quem diem vidit Abraham & lætatus est, vt ante pronunciauerat, sed de persona dicit, quæ persona erat in principio, & apud Deum, & Deus, quamuis suo tempore patefacienda in carne: non, inquam, de modo reuelationis & cognitionis ipsius, sed de esse (vt ita loquamur) personali suo. Probatur hypothesi. Nam postquam Christus Iudæis dixerat, Abraham Pater vester gestiuit vt videret diem hunc meum, & vidit, atque gauisus est, Iudæi regesserunt Christo, quinquaginta annos nondum habes, & Abrahamum vidisti? sic argumentantes, fieri non potest vt homo necdum quinquagenarius sit visus Abrahamo, aut Abrahamum ipse viderit: tu autem necdum es quinquagenarius: itaque de persona Christi, tamquam homine solùm iudicabant. His respondet Christus, se non λεπτὸν hominem & factum in tempore haberi oportere, sed longè superiorem humana conditione, quæ ante oculos erat, agnoscendum: nam etsi persona ipsius, quà homo, necdum est quinquagenaria, personam tamen æternam esse, quæ iam subsistiterit ante Abrahami tempus: personam ipsius diuinam esse atque æternam hypostasin, sed συμπάσχοντ humanitatem eius. Atque hoc ipsum, quod Samosatenus negat, Iudæi intelligentes ex Christi verbis, eò insaniæ atque furoris eruperunt, vt lapides humo sustulerint in eum coniecturi. Quòd si forte aduersarius iste obiecerit, Christum de die illo suo, quo Sermo factus est caro & conuersatus est inter nos, loquutum esse, quem diem Abraham prænunciatione, promissione, præfiguratione viderit: itaque fore vt ineptè Christus ad alium sermonem transfilisse videatur, nisi de eadem re eodémque modo sequentia illa enunciaue-rit: nos ergo ineptè hæc verba transferre alió, & præter sententiam illius: speciosa quidem hæc, sed falsa argumentatio futura est. Non enim Christus ipse ad hunc sermonem transgressus est per se, & sine occasione vita, vt de natura sua Ὑπερανθρωπίνη gloriaretur temere: sed ineptè & impiè Iudæi ipsi eò transiuerant dicentes, quinquaginta annos nondum habes, &c. quorum ineptiā a Christo refelli oportuit. Ineptè ergo insciteque Iudæi ab instituto sermone discesserant: sed ijs Christus ex veritate respondit sapientissimè, æternitatem afferens non carnis illius promissæ & præfiguratæ, sed personæ suæ, quæ in tempore promissam illam & præfiguratam assumsit carnem. Huius verò personæ immutabilem veritatem secundùm esse ipsius vt amplius confirmaret, non dicit Christus, ego fui aut eram: sed diuino modo loquitur πρὸ τοῦ ἀμετακλήτου illius significante, Antequam Abraham fieret, vel esset, ego sum. In hoc autem loco & sequentibus quàm plurimis pium Lectorem velim obseruare, quàm sit falsa huius disputatoris nostri argumentatio, qua fretus velut Orci galea (quod aiunt) hunc locum & alios accumulat. Sic enim ille: Qui prænunciatur, præfiguratur, promittitúrque, tantisper dum prænunciatur, non est: Christus prænunciatus fuit in Testamento vetere, &c. non fuit igitur. Falsissima est argumentatio. Ecquis te vnquam, Samosatene, docuit ab eo quod secundùm quid (vt loquuntur Scholastici) ad dictum simpliciter valere consequentiam? Nam maior & minor secundùm adventum ipsius in carne de Christo enunciantur: conclusio affirmat simpliciter. Nempe sic te auctore licebit argumentari: Qui prænunciatur fore medicus, non est: qui prænunciatur fore catholicus, non est: qui prænunciatur fore caro, siue in carne non est. Id quidem verum est, perlonam illam non esse medicam, non esse catholicam, non esse in carne, dum vere prænunciatur. Nam si est ita, falsò prænunciatur fore: sin verè prænunciatur, nondum ita est. Sed cum qui medicus, qui catholicus, qui in carne futurus est (futura enim est resurrectio, unde peti exemplum potest) propterea non esse, id est, subsistere, quis homo sanæ mentis possit concludere? Ab est enim tertij adiecti, ut vocant, ad est secundi tum demum consequentia valet, quum accidens positiuum de substantia prædicatur: ex priuantibus verò, aut ideis atque umbraculis non valet. In hoc autem genere promissa & præfigurationes sunt. Suppositum est homo, quum nondum homo iste medicus, aut catholicus est: sic etiam suppositum est Christus, quum nondum esset in carne. Subiectum prius est assumto, hypostasis enhypostato. Itaque secundum subiectum, suppositum, siue hypostasin, antequàm Abraham esset, Christus est: secundum carnem assumtam & enhypostaton, Christus Iudæos alloquens non erat quinquagenarius. Falsum ergo illud Samosateni {sic ὁμοιωματικὸν} dicentis, Sic se ante Abrahamum fuisse dicit ille homo Christus Ioan. 8. non enim alius loquitur: ab initio enim mundi, ante Abrahamum erat promissus, cognitus, & exspectatus. Non enim Christus, quà Deus, fuit præfiguratione, sed antequàm Abraham esset, immo ab æterno est: contrà verò, quà homo, vel secundum carnem, ad quam Iudæi contumaciter intendebant acie oculorum suorum, non fuit reipsa ante illam temporum plenitudinem: sed præordinatione, prænunciatione, promissione, typo, & si quid aliud est quo id exprimamus quod volumus, Christum hominem fuisse concedimus. Non ergo persona Filij Dei simpliciter, id est, quà æternus Dei filius & Deus, præfigurata est (fuit enim ante figuras & umbracula quæuis æternus Dei Sermo) sed Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus, quà assumsit carnem, & in carne sua fecit ac pertulit quæcunque fuerunt opus ad salutem nostram. Aut etiam (si aliter placet) non ratione eiusdem Christum eodem tempore fuisse & non fuisse affirmamus: sed fuisse illū secundum æternam hypostasin, non fuisse autē secundum humanitatem illā quam æterna hypostasis assumsit in tempore. Atque hic ille scopulus est, in quem Samosatenus offendit hoc loco atque sequentibus. Non enim alius tum Iudæos alloquutus est quàm qui ante Abrahamum est, non alia persona, sed idem ipse Christus, licet alia ratione & modo, nimirum in assumta carne. Ac proinde pater ille Abraham utrumque vidit: & Christum præsentem, quà Sermo Dei Patris coæternus est, & ante Abrahamum est: & diem illum Christi vidit quo Christus inaniuit sese formam serui assumta, obediensque factus est ad mortem usque crucis. Vidit autem fide Christum præsentem reipsa, quà Deus: nam fides index est eorum quæ no videntur, ut qua videmus Deum: Diem vero futurum illum, Christi in carne futuri, gesturi, & perpessuri quæ sunt ad salutem nostram fide eadem vidit in spe præordinationem cernente, promissis hærente, & typis ac umbraculis obsignata, donec in re exhiberetur Ecclesiæ Dei. Itaque non cupiuit solùm videre Christum, aut diem illum (hoc enim verbo Samosatenus suum illud dogma sufflaminandum putauit esse) sed utrumque ratione diuersa vidit, atque lætatus est, ut ipse Christus diserte pronunciauit.
units.tr: 1. This passage is wrongly and falsely applied to Abraham. Christ is not simply speaking here of the foreshadowing and prefiguring of his coming and his flesh, the day which Abraham saw and rejoiced in, as he had said before. He is speaking of the person, who was in the beginning, and with God, and was God, although he was to be revealed in the flesh at his own time. I say he is speaking not of the mode of the person's revelation and knowability, but of his personal being, so to speak. This is proved from the context. After Christ had told the Jews, "Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad," the Jews answered Christ, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Arguing thus, they meant that a man not yet fifty could not have been seen by Abraham, nor could he have seen Abraham; and since you are not yet fifty, they judged concerning the person of Christ as a man only. To this Christ replies that he must not be regarded as a mere man made in time, but must be acknowledged as far above the human condition which was before their eyes. For although his person as man was not yet fifty years old, his person was eternal, and had already subsisted before the time of Abraham. His person is divine and an eternal hypostasis, but his humanity suffers together with it [συμπάσχοντα]. The Jews understood this very point, that Samosatenus denies, from Christ's words, and they broke out into such madness and fury that they picked up stones from the ground to throw at him. But if perhaps this opponent should object that Christ was speaking of that day of his, on which the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, the day which Abraham saw by prophecy, promise and prefiguring, and that therefore Christ seems to have passed foolishly to another subject unless he had declared the following words about the same matter and in the same way, then we are foolishly transferring these words elsewhere and against their meaning. This argument would be specious but false. For Christ himself did not pass to this subject of his own accord, without occasion, so as to boast rashly of his own nature as superhuman [ὑπερανθρωπίνη]. Rather, the Jews themselves had foolishly and impiously turned to it, saying, "You are not yet fifty years old," and so on, and Christ had to refute their foolishness. The Jews, then, foolishly and ignorantly departed from the subject of the discussion, but Christ answered them from the truth most wisely, asserting an eternity not of that flesh which was promised and prefigured, but of his own person, which in time assumed that promised and prefigured flesh. To confirm further the unchanging truth of this person according to his being, Christ does not say, "I was" or "I used to be," but speaks in a divine manner, signifying that unchangeable [πρὸ τοῦ ἀμετακλήτου] state: "Before Abraham was, or existed, I am." In this passage and in very many that follow, I would have the pious reader observe how false is the argument of this disputant of ours, relying on which, as they say, he piles up this passage and others, as if wearing the helmet of Orcus. For he speaks thus: "What is foretold, prefigured and promised, is not, for as long as it is only foretold; Christ was foretold in the Old Testament, etc.; therefore he was not." The argument is most false. Who ever taught you, Samosatenus, that a consequence drawn from what holds in a certain respect (as the Scholastics say, secundum quid) holds absolutely for the thing said? For the major and minor premises are said of Christ with respect to his coming in the flesh, while the conclusion affirms absolutely. In this way, with you as authority, it will be permitted to argue: "What is foretold to be a physician is not; what is foretold to be catholic is not; what is foretold to be flesh, or to be in the flesh, is not." This is indeed true, that the person is not a physician, is not catholic, is not in the flesh, while he is truly foretold. For if it were so, he would be falsely foretold to be; but if he is truly foretold, he is not yet so. But who of sound mind could conclude from this that someone who is going to be a physician, going to be catholic, going to be in the flesh (for the resurrection is future, and an example may be taken from that), is therefore not, that is, does not subsist? The consequence from the third added term (as they call it) to the being of the second holds only when a positive accident is predicated of the substance; but it does not hold from privations, or from ideas and shadows. Promises and prefigurings belong to this kind. The supposit is a man before this man is a physician or catholic; so too the supposit Christ existed before he was in the flesh. The subject is prior to the assumed, the hypostasis to the enhypostatic. Therefore, according to the subject, the supposit or hypostasis, Christ existed before Abraham was; according to the assumed and enhypostatic flesh, Christ speaking to the Jews was not fifty years old. Therefore that statement of Samosatenus, [ὁμοιωματικὸν] (in the manner of a likeness), "That man Christ says that he was before Abraham, John 8," is false; for it is not another who speaks. For from the beginning of the world he was promised, known and awaited before Abraham. For Christ, as God, was not before by prefiguring; rather, before Abraham was, indeed from eternity, he is. On the other hand, as man, or according to the flesh, toward which the Jews obstinately directed the keen sight of their eyes, he was not in reality before that fullness of time. But we concede that Christ was man by predestination, prophecy, promise, type, and whatever else there is by which we may express what we mean. Therefore we do not affirm that the person of the Son of God simply, that is, as the eternal Son of God and God, was prefigured (for the eternal Word of God existed before all figures and shadows); rather, the Mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus the man, was prefigured, insofar as he assumed the flesh and in his flesh did and suffered whatever was necessary for our salvation. Or even (if it pleases otherwise) we do not affirm that Christ was and was not at the same time with respect to the same thing; rather, he was according to the eternal hypostasis, but was not according to that humanity which the eternal hypostasis assumed in time. And this is the rock on which Samosatenus stumbles in this passage and those that follow. For it was no other than he who is before Abraham who addressed the Jews at that time; it was not another person, but the same Christ, though in another respect and mode, namely in the assumed flesh. And so that father Abraham saw both: Christ present, insofar as the Word of God the Father is coeternal and is before Abraham; and he saw that day of Christ, on which Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. He saw Christ present in reality, as God, by faith; for faith is the evidence of things not seen, as by faith we see God. But that future day, of Christ who was to come in the flesh, to act and to suffer the things which are for our salvation, he saw by the same faith, in hope, discerning the predestination, cleaving to the promises, and sealed by types and shadows, until it should be exhibited in reality to the Church of God. Therefore he desired not only to see Christ, or that day (for Samosatenus thought that this word must be applied to restrain his own dogma), but he saw both, in different ways, and rejoiced, as Christ himself plainly declared.

units.la: 2. Eundē Christum vere habuerunt in persona Patres, sed non in assumta carne: eundem, inquam, ratione personæ, deitatis & humanitatis ipsius; sed non eodem modo, vt ante docuimus. Sophistica itaque est hæc argumentatio, vt & sequentes omnes loci in fallaciam elenchi incidunt, quia tempora ante & post carnem a Christo assumtam inter se conturbantur. His enim substantia communis est in persona Christi, & communis ratio: nam personam suam Christus tradidit Spiritu, Patres acceperunt fide: sed modus differens, exhibendae in persona carnis alius quàm exhibitę. Dicerem de eo quòd locum illum 1. Cor. 10. Bibebant ex sequente spirituali petra, hic exponit sequente, id est, post ventura: subtiliter sane. Sed hanc ego festucam non moucro. Grauiora, & quae magis cum argumento sunt coniuncta persequar.
units.tr: 2. The Fathers truly had the same Christ in person, but not in the assumed flesh: the same, I say, in respect of his person, deity and humanity; but not in the same way, as we taught before. This argument is therefore sophistical, and all the following passages fall into the fallacy of refutation, because the times before and after Christ assumed the flesh are confused with one another. For there is a common substance in the person of Christ, and a common reason: Christ gave his person by the Spirit, and the Fathers received it by faith; but the mode differs, since the flesh was to be exhibited in the person in one way, and was exhibited in another. I could say something about the passage 1 Cor. 10, "they drank of the following spiritual rock," where he explains "following" as meaning "things to come after," and that is certainly subtle. But I will not stir this trifle. I will pursue more serious matters, which are more closely connected with the argument.

units.la: 3. Ad eundem lapidem semper offendit miser. Non erat Christi caro: sed erat Christus seu persona Christi, quae persona post suo tempore carnem assumsit & aptauit sibi. Vt enim anima hominis sibi assumit & adunat corpus in matris utero natura formatum in vnitatem personae, sic persona Christi suam humanitatem vnione personali aptauit sibi. Eo est ratio dissimilis, quòd anima naturaliter non est persona, & quòd praeformatum corpus assumit sibi: Christi vero persona est, eáque aeterna, quae post suo tempore humanitatem fecit assumendam. Turpis vero fallacia diuisionis est, quum Samosatenus his verbis vtitur, caro Christi cibus omnium electorum est, non aliqua eius aeterna deitas. Nam res omnino coniungendas distrahit, & opponit componendas, carnem, & Spiritū, qui est ipsa deitas & vis diuina Christi. In materiali hoc cibo quis nescit duo concurrere? nempe alimentum hoc materiale & instrumentale huic vitae accommodum, & verbum benedictionis a Domino? Non enim ex solo pane viuit homo, sed ex omni verbo prodeunte ab ore Dei. Similiter in carne Christi duo opus est obseruari: primùm carnem, vt caro est alimentum spirituale & instrumentum spiritualis vitae: deinde spiritum, id est, deitatem vimque diuinam Christi, per quam caro illa viua est atque viuifica, vt caro Christi, caro inquam aeternae deitatis eius. Christus itaque viuificat & per se in se, quoscunque viui-ficat: Per se, virtute spiritus vel deitatis suæ: in se vero, instrumento etiam carnis seu humanitatis suæ. Spiritus enim is est qui viuificat, caro non prodest quicquam, nisi quà caro Filij Dei est & diuina caro. Eo differunt hæc duo inter se, quòd materialis cibus in se nec principium vitæ, nec causam efficientem habet, sed principium & causa efficiens vitæ Deus est, qui vim attribuit foris: caro autem Christi principium vitæ spiritualis habet in persona, vnione personali Spiritus, id est, deitatis cum carne: qua gratia vnionis vim carni intus attribuit spiritus, vt viuifica sit, Cyrillo teste, saluis vtriusque naturæ proprietatibus: quia in ipso omnis plenitudo deitatis habitat corporaliter. Hæc duo quisquis opponit, discerpit Christum. Hic enim vnus est. Mediator Dei & hominum vnitate personæ, qua muis e duabus naturis, ex quo assumsit carnem, constitutæ.
units.tr: 3. The wretched man always stumbles over the same stone. Christ's flesh did not exist, but Christ, or the person of Christ, existed, and this person later, in its own time, assumed flesh and fitted it to itself. For just as the soul of a man takes to itself and joins to itself a body formed by nature in the mother's womb, into unity of person, so the person of Christ fitted his humanity to himself by personal union. The comparison fails in this respect: the soul is not naturally a person, and it takes to itself a body already formed, whereas the person of Christ is a person, and an eternal one, which in its own time made the humanity to be assumed. But it is a foul fallacy of division when Samosatenus uses these words: the flesh of Christ is the food of all the elect, not some eternal deity of his. For he tears apart things that must be joined together and sets against each other things that must be combined, namely the flesh and the Spirit, who is the very deity and divine power of Christ. Who does not know that two things come together in this material food: first, this material and instrumental nourishment suited to this life, and second, the word of blessing from the Lord? For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Likewise in the flesh of Christ two things must be observed: first the flesh, insofar as the flesh is spiritual food and an instrument of spiritual life; then the Spirit, that is, the deity and divine power of Christ, through which that flesh is living and life-giving, as the flesh of Christ, I say, the flesh of his eternal deity. Christ therefore quickens both through himself and in himself whomever he quickens: through himself, by the power of his Spirit or deity; in himself, also by the instrument of his flesh or humanity. For it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing, except insofar as it is the flesh of the Son of God and divine flesh. These two differ in this way: material food has in itself neither the source of life nor the efficient cause, but God, who gives the power from outside, is the source and efficient cause of life. The flesh of Christ, however, has the source of spiritual life in the person, by the personal union of the Spirit, that is, of the deity, with the flesh; by the grace of this union the Spirit imparts to the flesh a power within, so that it is life-giving, as Cyril testifies, the properties of each nature being preserved, because in him dwells all the fullness of the deity bodily. Whoever sets these two against each other tears Christ apart. For he is one, the Mediator between God and men, by the unity of person, constituted of the two natures from the time he assumed flesh.

units.la: 4. Duo hic desideramus: vnum, quòd ex ambiguo loco non secus argumentatur Samosatenus, quàm si indubitata certáque apud omneis esset hæc interpretatio: alterum, quòd duas interpretationes vni loco aptat inter se diuersissimas. Locum ambiguum esse inter cæteros docet Aretas his verbis, ἐν ὑπογεγραμμένῳ... (Greek). & quæ sequuntur. id est, hyperbaticè hoc intelligendum est, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitæ agni mactati: nam quorum scripta sunt nomina, a iactis fundamentis mundi scripta sunt. Ambiguitas igitur in eo est, quòd illa verba, (Greek) a iactis fundamentis mundi, hi referunt ad participium proximum, occisi vel mactati, vt hic Samosatenus facit, & complures alij: illi ad verbum, scripta sunt, vt facit Aretas, & confirmat dicens, nam quorum nomina scripta sunt in libro vitæ agni malati, eorum nomina a iactis mundi fundamentis scripta sunt, & contrà: agni verò cædes non fuit inde a iactis fundamentis mundi. Hanc interpretationem ne ipse quidem Samosatenus tam piam esse negauerit quàm altera illa est: atque haud scio an etiam verior ac simplicior dicenda sit. Primùm ergo quid responsurus est Samosatenus, si negare interpretationem illam placuerit? etenim verba in ambiguo sunt, ut iam ostendimus. Deinde ut illa concedatur, quid tandem ex ea confecturus est? Agnus, inquit, fuit occisus ab origine mundi in typis & sacrificijs & umbris: ergo fuit agnus in typis & sacrificijs & umbris, non autem realiter & substantialiter. Atqui hoc genus argumentationis puerile esse atque inefficax ante ostendimus, quû ab est tertij adiecti ad est secundi (ut vocant) in priuantibus ideisque nectitur consequentia. Tamquam si de aegroto, cuius sectionem medicus matutino pingens chirurgum cautionis ergò docuerit, postquam dixeris aegrotum hunc fuisse a matutino sectum, ex eo concludat alter, hunc ergo aegrotum fuisse in typo, non realiter & substantialiter: aut etiam concludat alius, fuisse illum a matutino solum, ac non ante. Atqui, vir bone, & ante vir fuerit necesse est, quàm secaretur, pingeretúrque, & ante aegrotauerit. Quid ergo ex hoc argumentationis modo concluseris? Etenim ante fuit Agnus quàm occideretur, ante fuit persona quàm caro Agni: quinetiam ante fuit ipsa caro Agni quàm occideretur propter peccata nostra; neque tum demum coepit Agnus esse, quando occisus est: quod ex singulari isto argumentationis genere sequi oporteret. Quòd autem huic suæ interpretationi alteram diuersissimam coniungit aduersarius orthodoxæ huius doctrinæ, nihil ad rem facit. Agnus, inquit, fuit occisus in pijs, ut in Abele occiso, &c. Et quorsum ista? Contendit iste ante fuisse Christum praeordinatione, nenon existentia: promissione, non exhibitione; figuris, nō veritate; spe(vt ita dicam)non re. Iam vero vt illud probet, restim ex arena nectens dicit eum in piis, ut in Abele, aliisque occidi, & ab origine mundi occisum esse. Quid ista, obsecro, οἰκείωσις (vt vocarunt Patres) siue ἐφαρμοσις, id est, appropriatio & applicatio perpessionum quas sustinere fideles oportuit, ad sermonem institutum? Nam ex ea, Samosatene, dic amabo te, an vnquam Christum Iesum inde a principio non fuisse probaturus es? Etenim οἰκειώσεις & applicationes istę relationis sunt, & relationis secundum esse, vt appellantur vulgo, eiusque mutuae: in qua omnia simul oportet exister, caput, membra, compagemque siue coagmentationem & applicationem eorum inter se spirituali modo. Quemadmodum ergo ad calefactionem statui ignem calefacientem & calefactam materiam necesse est: item ad viuificationem poni spiritum viuificantem & corpus viuificatum: sic ad applicationem istarum perpessionum caput applicans & membrum applicatum oportet exister, & simul quidem existere, nisi falsam relatorum naturam esse nostr hic Samosatenus docuerit. Cum autem haec falsa dici nullo iure possit, accipio dictum huius disputatoris: & ex eo affirmo contra sententiam ipsius, ergo Christum iam fuisse Abelis tempore, si in Abele occisus est. Nam si in Abele occisus est Christus, omnino certe fuerit occisus vt caput in membro: est autem occisus, vel Samosateno teste: fuit igitur occisus vt caput in membro: & fuit igitur. Pergam vlterius eodem duce, vel potius indice: Nunc Christus occiditur & persecutionem patitur in fidelibus membris suis: est igitur. Quod si dixerit ille, est quidem nunc, ex quo Verbum caro factum, vel Deus in carne patefactus: sed ante non fuit, quum tamē occideretur secundum quendam modum: respondebo, atque idem hic dicitur de eodem, & eodem modo, etsi de diuerso tempore: ergo dicti ciusdem de eodem, & dicti eodem modo ratio eadem tenenda est. Tunc occisus fuit: fuit igitur: Nunc occiditur in suis: est igitur, & est in suis. Occisus fuit, occiditurque in pijs: fuit igitur, & est in illis. Sed carnem tunc non habuit, dixerit ille: quid ad nos? fuit tamen omnino, fuit: nam si non fuit, non fuit occisus: si fuit occisus, fuit igitur: &, si fuit occisus in illis, fuerit in illis necesse est, fuerítque vnius ad alterum applicatio, quam ante ostendimus. Quid vero, quòd Samosatenus causam nostram impru-dens adiuuat dicendo, quamquam hic praesens non versetur nobiscum carne, ut tangi possit? Sic enim arguo ex istis verbis: Christus igitur, quamuis absens carne, tamen in pijs occiditur, vt praesens spiritu & deitate sua. Nam absentem nec in se, nec in alio constat occidi posse: Christus in suis potuit & potest occidi: immo occisus fuit atque occiditur: non igitur absens: si non absens, praesens igitur. Quòd si praesens, aut carne praesens, aut spiritu: non autem carne, ac ne nunc quidem, vt ipse quoque Samosatenus agnoscit: praesens ergo spiritu. At Christus in Abele occisus est: praesens ergo in Abele spiritu. Spiritum autem quum dico, nolo mihi spiritualem daxat modum, sed subsistentiam ipsam intelligi, vel spiritualem substantiam, quae carni (id autem est, substantiae carnis) opponitur. Alioquin Abeli hic in terris agenti viuentique nec carnem Christi adfuisse, quae nondum erat, nec carnalem modum, qui citra subiectum esse non poterat, inter nos conuenit. Quorsum ergo Samosatenus a natura vna argumentatur ad alteram? ad perfectam ab ea quae per se imperfecta est? ad assumentem personam a natura assumta? si non erat humanitas Christi, non ergo fuisse deitatem? si non erat Christus secundum humanitatem, non ergo fuisse Deum? quod genus argumenti nobis tacentibus refellit natura ipsa, & nos iam satis ante refellimus. 5. Ad eamdem applicationem hic locus Hebr. 6. pertinet, quam nota 4. supra tradidimus. Nam vt Christus in Abelo fuit occisus olim, sic Christum in Abelo occidit Cain, eumque impij crucifigunt denuo, exacerbantes & prouocantes spiritum illius. Actio enim & passio conueniunt in vna substantia motus, & vnus sunt motus numero, licet inter se differant secundum varios agentis & patientis habitus. Quapropter etiam Grammatici verbum actiuum solent passiuo resoluere, & contrá. Hic ergo nihil promouet sua verborum accumulatione. De loco item Hebr. 11. iam ante diximus. Etsi quid est, cur iste locus in hanc sententiam proferatur? A nobis facit, Samosatenum confodit. Promissa adepti sunt, inquit. Recte: si adepti, realiter igitur habuerunt, ac non typicè & figuratiuè inaudiuisse dicendi sunt solùm. Sic enim ibidem Apostolus versu 33. per fidem regna debellarunt, exercuerunt iustitiam, assequuti sunt promissiones, &c. Rursum vero, non sunt adepti promissa, sed eminus ea conspicati, ne seorsim a nobis consummarentur: hoc est, rem quidem, & substantiam ipsam promissionum in sese habuerunt, sed non singulas promissionum partes secundum perfectiorem modum earum & complementum in Christo. Vtrumq; ergo verum est, quia non est vtrumque ratione eiusdem dictum. Etenim (vt paucis omnia complectamur) Dei promissionum in sedere summa est haec, ero Deus tuus & semini tui: medium promissionum, Christus, in semine tuo, inquit, sibi sunt benedicturae omnes gentes: obiectum reale (vt vocant) tum aeternum, puta, coelestis haereditas, tum vero temporale sacramentum, haereditas terrena scilicet: modus differens, nempe ad complementum per initia & progressus varios pertinens: adiuncta denique, promissiones particulares & effecta illarum. In his autem promissionibus alia sunt communia omnium, idque aut quouis, aut suo tempore: alia vero particularia temporum, aut personarum etiam singularia. Omnium in omni tempore communia sunt hæc: summa foederis substantia: medium illius, persona Christi, quamuis necdum assumta carne olim: & efficacitas ipsius. Suo tempore communia sunt hæc: obiecta, cum Iudaeis olim terrena, tum omnibus coelestis hæreditas, quam modo possidemus fide, vt olim possidebat Abraham: & persona Christi his temporibus vltimis facta caro, siue in carne patefacta. Particularia temporum fuerunt ista: primum quod Abraha, Isaac, Iacob, & alij, vsquedum populus fuit missus in possessionem Chananæ, non sunt adepti hæreditatem promissam terræ, quam ex facto, antequam morerentur, possidentes obtinerent: sed eminus promissa conspicati, postquam ipsis fuissent persuasa, & ea amplexi fuissent, ac profecti hospites se & aduenas in terra Chananæ (huc enim respexit Apostolus versu 13. quem versum hic artificiose obducit Samosatenus, & in alium sermonem rapit quam Apostolus sibi voluerit) deinde etiam particulares suorum temporum fuerunt modi, quibus Deus per initia, progressus, & complementa vsus est in docendis, & ostendendis, & præstandis reipsa promissis suis, vt idem Apostolus ibidem asserit. Postremo autem singulares promissiones sunt personis factæ, quas illæ singulari gratia & beneficio Dei adeptæ sunt. Atque hæc quidem a Samosateno, si veritati studet, distingui oportuit. Nam duplex est hoc loco peccatum quod in Christum committit & Ecclesiam eius: vnum, quod personam Christi ante carnem assumtam fuisse negat, quem errorem paulo ante perspicuè confutauimus: alterum, quod sacramentum vel signum confundit cum re sacramenti, quamuis hæc ab Apostolo inter se distinguantur luculentissime. Hæc-
units.tr: 4. Here we have two problems. First, Samosatenus argues from an ambiguous passage as if this interpretation were certain and accepted by everyone. Second, he fits two very different interpretations to one passage. That the passage is ambiguous Aretas himself teaches, in these words: "it is to be understood hyperbatically: those whose names are not written in the book of life of the slain Lamb; for those whose names are written, they were written from the foundation of the world." It is to be understood hyperbatically, those whose names are not written in the book of the life of the Lamb that was slain: for those whose names are written, their names were written from the foundation of the world. The ambiguity lies in this: the words from the foundation of the world may be taken with the nearest participle, slain or sacrificed, as Samosatenus does and many others do, or with the verb were written, as Aretas does, and he confirms it by saying: for those whose names are written in the book of the life of the slain Lamb, their names were written from the foundation of the world, and conversely: but the slaying of the Lamb did not happen from the foundation of the world. Samosatenus himself could not deny that this interpretation is as pious as the other, and I am not sure it should not be called the truer and simpler of the two. First, then, what will Samosatenus reply if it pleases him to deny that interpretation? For the words are ambiguous, as we have already shown. Next, suppose that interpretation is granted: what will he infer from it? The Lamb, he says, was slain from the beginning of the world in the types and sacrifices and shadows: therefore the Lamb was in the types and sacrifices and shadows, but not really and substantially. But we showed earlier that this kind of argument is childish and worthless, since the consequence is drawn from the third adjunct to the second, as they call it, in privatives. It is like this: a physician, painting in the morning the cut of a patient whose incision he had taught the surgeon to make for caution's sake, tells you that this patient was cut in the morning; from this another man concludes, therefore this patient was in the type, not really and substantially; or another concludes that he was cut only in the morning and not before. But, my good sir, he must have been a man before he was cut and painted, and must have been sick before that. What then will you conclude from this mode of argument? For the Lamb existed before he was slain, the Person existed before the flesh of the Lamb; indeed the flesh of the Lamb itself existed before it was slain for our sins; nor did the Lamb begin to be only when he was slain, which is what this peculiar kind of argument would require. As for the fact that the adversary of this orthodox doctrine joins to his interpretation another very different one, it has nothing to do with the matter. The Lamb, he says, was slain in the pious, as Abel was slain, etc. And to what purpose is this? He contends that Christ existed before, by predestination but not by existence, by promise but not by exhibition, by figures but not by truth, by hope, so to speak, but not in reality. Now, to prove this, he weaves a rope of sand and says that he was slain in the pious, as in Abel and others, and was slain from the foundation of the world. What, I ask, is this οἰκείωσις (as the Fathers called it), or ἐφαρμοσις, that is, the appropriation and application of the sufferings which the faithful had to bear, to the subject under discussion? For, Samosatenus, tell me, please, will you ever prove that Christ Jesus did not exist from the beginning? These appropriations and applications belong to relation, and to relation according to being, as it is commonly called, and to its mutual form; in which all things must exist together: the head, the members, and the joining or coupling and application of them to one another in a spiritual manner. Just as, for heating, there must be a fire that heats and a matter that is heated, and likewise for quickening there must be a Spirit that quickens and a body that is quickened, so for the application of those sufferings there must exist a head applying and a member applied, and they must exist together, unless this Samosatenus teaches that the nature of correlatives is false. But since this cannot rightly be called false, I accept the assertion of this disputant, and from it I affirm, against his own view, that Christ was already present in the time of Abel, if he was slain in Abel. For if Christ was slain in Abel, he certainly was slain as the head in the member: but he was slain, even by Samosatenus's testimony: therefore he was slain as the head in the member, and therefore he was. I will go on with the same guide, or rather informer: Now Christ is slain and suffers persecution in his faithful members: therefore he is. If he should answer that indeed he is now, since the Word was made flesh, or God was manifested in the flesh, but before he was not, although he was slain in a certain manner, I will reply that the same is said of the same, and in the same manner, though at a different time; therefore the same reasoning about the same subject and the same manner must be kept. He was slain then: therefore he was. Now he is slain in his own: therefore he is, and is in his own. He was slain and is slain in the pious: therefore he was, and is in them. But, he will say, he did not then have flesh: what is that to us? Still he was in every way, he was; for if he was not, he was not slain; if he was slain, he was; and if he was slain in them, he must have been in them, and there was an application of the one to the other, which we showed before. And what of the fact that Samosatenus, unwittingly helping our cause, says: although he is not present with us here in the flesh, so that he could be touched? For I argue from these words thus: Christ, then, though absent in flesh, is nevertheless slain in the pious, as present in spirit and his deity. For it is agreed that one who is absent can be slain neither in himself nor in another: Christ could be and can be slain in his own, indeed he was slain and is slain: therefore not absent: if not absent, then present. But if present, then present either in flesh or in spirit: not in flesh, and not even now, as Samosatenus himself admits: therefore present in spirit. But Christ was slain in Abel: therefore present in Abel in spirit. When I say spirit, I do not want to be understood as only a spiritual manner, but the subsistence itself, or a spiritual substance, which is set over against flesh (that is, the substance of flesh). Otherwise, it is agreed between us that neither the flesh of Christ, which did not yet exist, nor the fleshly mode, which could not exist without a subject, was present to Abel living and acting here on earth. Why then does Samosatenus argue from one nature to another? From the imperfect to the perfect? From the assuming person to the nature assumed? If the humanity of Christ did not exist, then was not the deity either? If Christ did not exist according to his humanity, then was he not God either? This kind of argument nature itself refutes, even while we are silent, and we have already refuted it sufficiently before. 5. The passage Heb. 6. belongs to the same application, which we set out in note 4 above. For as Christ was once slain in Abel, so Cain slew Christ in Abel, and the wicked crucify him again, provoking and exasperating his Spirit. For action and passion meet in one substance of motion, and the motions are one in number, although they differ according to the various dispositions of the agent and the patient. That is why grammarians are accustomed to resolve an active verb into a passive, and the reverse. So he gains nothing here by his piling up of words. Concerning Heb. 11 I have already spoken earlier. But what reason is there for this passage to be put forward for this opinion? It favours us and stabs Samosatenus. They obtained the promises, he says. Rightly so: if they obtained them, they had them in reality, and they are not to be said to have only heard of them typically and figuratively. For the same Apostle says in verse 33: through faith they subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, etc. But on the other hand: they did not obtain the promises, but saw them afar off, lest they should be made perfect apart from us: that is, they had indeed the thing itself and the substance of the promises, but not each part of the promises according to their more perfect mode and their completion in Christ. Both statements are therefore true, because they are not both spoken in the same respect. For (to sum up everything briefly) the sum of God's promises is this: I will be your God and the God of your seed; the means of the promises is Christ, in your seed, he says, all nations shall be blessed: the real object (as they call it), partly eternal, namely the heavenly inheritance, and partly temporal, a sacrament, namely the earthly inheritance; the mode, which differs, that is, pertaining to completion through the beginnings and various progressions; and finally the adjuncts, the particular promises and their effects. Among these promises some are common to all, either at all times or at their own time; others are particular to certain times, or even singular to particular persons. The following are common to all at all times: the substance of the covenant as a whole; its means, the person of Christ, although the flesh had not yet been assumed in the past; and its efficacy. The following are common at their own time: the objects, earthly for the Jews of old, and for all the heavenly inheritance, which we now possess by faith, as Abraham formerly possessed it; and the person of Christ, made flesh, or manifested in the flesh, in these last times. The following were particular to times: first, that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the others, until the people were sent into possession of Canaan, did not obtain the promised inheritance of the land, which they would have held by actual possession before they died, but, having seen the promises from afar, after they had been persuaded of them and had embraced them, they lived as strangers and sojourners in the land of Canaan (for the Apostle looked to this in verse 13, a verse which Samosatenus cunningly distorts and drags into another meaning than the Apostle intended). Then there were also the particular modes of their own times, by which God, through beginnings, progressions and completions, dealt in teaching, showing, and actually fulfilling his promises, as the same Apostle asserts in the same place. Lastly, singular promises were made to persons, which they obtained by the singular grace and benefit of God. These distinctions, if Samosatenus were concerned with the truth, ought to have been made by him. For there is a double sin that he commits here against Christ and his Church: one, that he denies that the person of Christ existed before the assumption of the flesh, an error we clearly refuted a little earlier; the other, that he confuses the sacrament or sign with the thing of the sacrament, although the Apostle most clearly distinguishes these two. These things—

units.la: Hæc autem vt assequatur, in duplicem ignorationem elenchi prolapsus est, quum eos sermones qui nec rationem eiusdem, nec de eodem tempore sunt habiti, licentiissimè conturbauit. Nam omnes quidem pij substantiam sederis promissionumque in Christo, & efficacitatem illius iam olim perceperunt, ac proinde communia & particularia promissa adepti sunt secundùm rationem istam, Hebr. 11. 33. Sed ratione modi quàm plurima distingui necesse est, quæ secundùm tempora illi omnium minimè, isti ex parte, hi autem omnino assequuti sunt. Sic Abraham, Isaac, Iacob promissam terram non obtinuerunt, quamuis rem promissam certè obtinuerint quæ designabatur sacramento terræ: posteri illorum re simul cum signo adepti sunt, sed tamen ex parte & tenuiore quodam ac obscuriore modo: hæc autem omnia ad nos secundùm veritatem planiùs his temporibus vltimis peruenerunt, & planissimè secundo aduentu Christi in omnibus consummanda. Secundùm hos igitur gradus instituta comparatione, fit vt etiam ijdem respectu vario promissiones adepti & non adepti dicantur in Scripturis sacris, & hoc tempore dici possint.
units.tr: Yet in order to achieve this, he has fallen into a twofold ignorance of the argument, since he has recklessly confused sayings that were neither spoken about the same thing nor at the same time. For all the godly have indeed long since perceived the substance of the covenant and of the promises in Christ, and its efficacy, and so they have obtained the common and particular promises according to that reasoning (Heb. 11. 33). But in the manner of obtaining them there must be many distinctions, for the ancients obtained them least of all in respect of time, these in part, and the latest generation completely. Thus Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did not obtain the promised land, although they certainly obtained the thing promised that was signified by the sacrament of the land. Their posterity obtained the thing together with the sign, but in part, and in a thinner and more obscure manner. All these things have come to us more plainly in truth in these last times, and will be most plainly consummated at the second coming of Christ. Therefore, when the comparison is drawn according to these degrees, it follows that the same people, with varying respects, are said in the holy Scriptures both to have obtained and not to have obtained the promises, and can be so described in this time.

units.la: 6. Testimonia hominum nostrorum, quæ cum Samosateno dicuntur facere, adduci peruelim: ego quidem exstare nego apud horum bonorum quemquam: siqua rapiuntur in eam sententiam, grauissima fit viris bonis iniuria.
units.tr: 6. I should very much like the testimonies of our own people, which they say favour Samosatenus, to be cited. For my part I deny that any of these good men has such testimony. If any are wrested to that opinion, a most grievous injury is done to good men.

units.la: 7. Præposterè. Ordinem ab Ioanne institutum hic Samosatenus inuertit, vt causam suam hac specie adiuuet. Nam tria illa prædicata de vno eodemque Sermone coniungi & continentia vno in loco haberi interfuit, vt Sermonem illum subsistentiam æternam esse, & apud Patrem esse vt subsistentia a Patre distinctum, & Deum esse, vnum videlicet essentia cum Patre, intelligeremus. Hæc autem certo consilio in loco hoc discerpuntur, vt locus ille amplissimus de vnitate essentiae Patris & Filij (a quo homi-nes isti, vt a clamore fures, maximè sibi metuunt) latitare posset, aut certè molli & subdolo traiectu quodam eneruari: quemadmodum sequente loco videmus factum. De prioris autem loci interpretatione iam ante diximus segmento 1. & 2. eamque falsi reuicimus. Nam neque Sermonis vocabulum sic posse aut debere accipi docuimus, neque verbum erat, neque nomen principij: sed aliena a vocibus, membris, adiunctis, argumento denique toto interpretamenta adferri. Ac proinde nec verborum expositioni cum veritate diuina conuenit, nec illi ipsi doctrinae quam Samosatenus studuit expositione sua confirmare. In illo, inquit principio Christus coepit esse nobis Verbum, & Magister, & Propheta, praedicans mandata paterna. Hoc enunciatum est simpliciter falsum, si ad rem ipsam veritatemq; Christi respexeris: sin ad modum docendi in assumta carne, cum certa quadam cautione concedimus, quia nec sic quidem simpliciter est verum. Christus ante docuit quàm carnem assumfisset, nimirum spiritu & diuinitate sua: Christus non ante quàm assumfisset carnem, docuit in carne, id est, humanitate sua. Vtrumque verum. De posteriore conuenit: priorem ergo affirmationem auctoritate Scripturae (etsi iam ante segmento 3. fecimus) ostendamus. Ecce, inquit Dominus, ego mitto Angelum siue nuncium coram facie tua, qui seruet te in via hac, & introducat te in locum illum quem parau. Caue tibi a facie eius, & ausculta voci eius, ne irritato eum: nam non effet condonaturus defectionem vestram, quia nomen meum est in eo: sed omnino ausculta voci eius, vt facias quicquid eloquuturus sum, &c. Angelus siue nuncius in hoc loco dux, seruator, cofummator fidei, vt Heb.12. condonans peccata dicitur, in quo nomen Dei est, id est qui sermo Deus sit (vt Ioannis vtamur verbis) Sermo Iehouae, idémq; Ie- houa
units.tr: 7. Out of order. Samosatenus here inverts the order set by John, so that he may help his cause by this appearance. For it was important that those three predicates concerning one and the same Word be joined and held together in one place, so that we might understand that the Word is an eternal subsistence, and was with the Father as a subsistence distinct from the Father, and was God, namely one in essence with the Father. But in this place they are torn apart by deliberate design, so that that most ample passage on the unity of essence of the Father and the Son (of which these men, as thieves from a shout, are most afraid) might lie hidden, or at least be weakened by some soft and deceitful transposition, as we see was done in the following passage. Concerning the interpretation of the former passage we have already spoken in sections 1 and 2, and have refuted that falsehood. For we have shown that the word Word cannot be taken or ought not be taken in this way, nor the verb was, nor the noun beginning; rather, interpretations foreign to the words, the clauses, the context, and finally to the whole argument, are brought in. And therefore his exposition of the words agrees neither with divine truth, nor does it confirm by his exposition that very doctrine which Samosatenus was eager to establish. "In that beginning," he says, "Christ began to be for us the Word, and the Teacher, and the Prophet, proclaiming the commands of the Father." This statement is simply false, if you look to the thing itself and the truth of Christ. But if you look to the manner of teaching in the assumed flesh, we grant it with a certain caution, because even so it is not simply true. Christ taught before he had assumed flesh, namely by his Spirit and divinity. Christ, not before he had assumed flesh, taught in the flesh, that is, by his humanity. Both are true. The latter point is agreed; therefore let us show the former affirmation by the authority of Scripture (although we did so already in section 3). "Behold," says the Lord, "I send an Angel, or messenger, before your face, who shall keep you in this way and bring you into the place which I have prepared. Beware of his face, and hear his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not pardon your transgression, because my name is in him; but hear his voice, and do whatever I shall speak, etc." The Angel or messenger in this place is the leader, the keeper, the consummator of faith, as in Heb. 12, who is said to pardon sins, and in whom is the name of God, that is, who is the Word God (to use John's words), the Word of Jehovah, and the same Jehovah.

units.la: Exod. 23. houa cum Patre. Item,transmittam omnem bonitatem meā ante faciem tuam, & proclamabo nomen Iehouæ coram te: & altero loco qui huic respondet, transiens itaq; Iehoua ante faciem eius proclamauit, Iehoua, Iehoua,&c. Videmus hic Iehouam proclamantem de Iehoua, Deum de Deo, vt Sermonem illius. Et alibi, reuelauit se Iehoua Samueli Silunte per Sermonem Iehouæ. En tibi personas treis in vnitate essentiæ: Iehouam reuelatum, aut reuelantem sese, Spiritum sanctum: Sermonem reuelantem, qui idem Iehoua, Filium: & Patrem Sermonis, Iehoua, cuius propterea Sermo seu Verbum in prisicis Scripturis appellatur. Sic etiam Dauid, Propter Verbum, inquit, vel Sermonem tuum, & secundum animum tuum fecisti totam hanc amplitudinem: quæ verba, nequi sit tergiuersationi locus, Spiritus sanctus prouidentissimè in repetitione explicauit hoc modo: Iehoua, propter Seruum tuum, & secundum animū tuum,&c. Hoc autem illud Verbū, hic ipse Sermo, qui Ecclesiam Iudæorū docebat & ducebat olim, is ipse est Sermo de quo hic Ioannes loquitur, Dominus Christus Iesus: & de quo insigne illum Prophetæ locum (vt alios taceā) intelligi oportere confirmat Euangelista, dicens, Vt impleretur quod dictum est per Esaiam Prophetam dicentem, Ecce seruus ille meus, quem elegi, &c. Et Apostolus ait, Christus, vt filius, domui suæ præest: cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & spem illam de qua gloriamur, ad finem vsque firmam tenuerimus. Quapropter sicut dicit Spiritus ille sanctus, hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obdurate corda vestra. Quibus profecto verbis suum illud seculum quoque ad vocem Christi religiosè audiendam nobiscum excitabat. Deinde paulo post, Christi participes facti sumus, si modo principium illud quo sustentamur, firmum tenuer mus ad finem vsque, Interim dum dicitur, hodie si vocem eius audieritis, &c. Sed quid multis opus est? Vnica illa sancti Apostoli Petri epistola optimè cōfirmat
units.tr: Exod. 23. Jehovah with the Father. Likewise: "I will make all my goodness pass before your face, and I will proclaim the name of Jehovah before you"; and in another place which answers this, "And Jehovah passed by before his face and proclaimed, Jehovah, Jehovah," etc. We see here Jehovah proclaiming about Jehovah, God about God, as his Word. And elsewhere, "Jehovah revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh" through the Word of Jehovah.
