Behold three persons in unity of essence: Jehovah revealed, or revealing himself, the Holy Spirit; the Word revealing, who is the same Jehovah, the Son; and the Father of the Word, Jehovah, whose Word or Speech is therefore called in the ancient Scriptures. So also David: "For your Word's sake, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness." Lest there be room for evasion, the Holy Spirit, most providently, explained these words in the repetition in this way: "Jehovah, for your Servant's sake, and according to your own heart, etc." Now this Word, this very Speech, who in former times taught and led the Church of the Jews, is the same Speech of whom John speaks here, the Lord Christ Jesus. And the evangelist confirms that the famous prophecy (to say nothing of others) must be understood of him, saying: "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, saying, Behold my servant whom I have chosen," etc. And the Apostle says: "Christ, as a son, is over his house, whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the hope of which we glory unto the end. Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says, Today if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." By these words truly he also roused that age along with us to hear the voice of Christ religiously. Then a little after: "We have become partakers of Christ, if we hold firm the beginning by which we are sustained unto the end. Meanwhile, while it is said, Today if you will hear his voice," etc. But why need there be more? That one epistle of the holy Apostle Peter confirms best

units.la: Exodi 33. Exod. 34. 1. Sam. 3. 2. Sam. 7. 1. Chron. 17. Esa. 42. Matt. 12. Hebr. 3. non coepisse Christum Prophetam in hominibus agere, & instituere verbo Ecclesiam suam, quum in carne manifestus esset, sed ab omni seculo, ex quo Prophetae & prophetiae sunt (sunt autem inde a principio humani generis) Spiritum Domini Iesu Christi doctorem in populo Dei exstitisse. Nam agens de Prophetis Petrus cap. 1. sic ait, Scrutantes in quem, aut cuiusmodi temporis articulum praenuncius ille Spiritus Christi, qui erat in ipsis, declararet euentu-ras Christi perpessiones, & gloriam illas consequuturam. Item postea, Quapropter etiam continetur in Scriptura, ecce pono Sione lapidem in imo angulo, electum, pretiosum: cui qui credit, non pudefiet. Huic enim dicenti & voluntatem Patris enuncianti creditur, id est, Sermoni aeterno Dei. Cuius rei applicatione & accommodatione luculentissima vtens Petrus in verbis sequentibus dicit, vobis igitur est honori qui creditis: immorigeris vero, lapis quem reprobauerunt aedificatores hic factus est caput anguli, & lapis ad quem impingitur, & petra offendiculi. Haec autem Dauidis & Esaiae verba tum ad prisca tempora, vt Prophetae ipsi aperte clamant, tum ad haec vltima quibus Christus in carne aduenit, pertinent. Et capite sequente, mortificatus quidem est Christus carne, viuificatus autem spiritu: per quem etiam spiritibus immorigeris qui sunt in carcere profectus praedicauit olim, quum semel exspectaret Dei patientia in diebus Noë. &c. His alios insuper locos essemus addituri, nisi horum euidentia atque commoditas futura satis apud bonos veritati probandae & confirmandae videretur: alijs enim ne tota quidem Scriptura satis. Concludimus itaque Dominum Iesum Christum illum ipsum Sermonem aeternum esse Dei Patris, in quo & per quem Adamo & prisci illis sanctisque Patribus inde a principio voluntatem suam declarauit Pater: ac non tum demum coepisse Christum, quum in carne vixit diuinumque illum lum & salutarem Apostolatum obijt quem Euangelistæ & Apostoli speciatim descripserunt in Testamēto nouo. Alterius loci, & Sermo erat apud Deum, itidem se habet interpretatio. Nam neque in se verum illud dictum, neque germanum est huius loci interpretametum, quum hic nouus interpres dicit, in hoc principio erat apud Patrem, nondum notus hominibus, sed soli Patri. Non enim ab hominibus agnoscebatur esse Messias, &c. Ac primùm quidem hoc sibi Ioannem Euangelistam noluisse suprà iam demonstrauimus, neq; huius loci, horum verborum esse: quapropter plura non sumus de hac parte adiecturi. Sed dictum istud si placuerit simpliciter hoc sensu expendere, omnino aut falsum, aut ambiguum est. Nam falsum est, si vniuersè: ambiguum, si indefinitè acceperis, & particularis interpretationis, ex qua nihil concludi potest. Vniuersè autem a Samosateno dici ex eo iudicamus, quòd & oppositionem facit inter Deum & homines in hoc argumento, & voce, soli, exclusiua diserte vtitur. Etenim qui nondum notum hominibus Christum, sed soli Patri fuisse dicit, homines excludit vniuersos. Hoc autem falsum est, & repugnans Scripturæ sacræ veritati. Hæc quidem vera sunt: nemini homini Christum fuisse notū naturali luce: tum personam Christi, quà Filius Dei est, soli Patri cum Spiritu sancto fuisse notam essentialiter. Sed ad neutrum horum Samosatenum respexisse, quum ista scriberet, res ipsa loquitur. Fuit autem Christus notus hominibus iam eo tempore per cœlestem illam & supernaturalem lucem, partim singulari, partimq; cōmuni reuelatione. Zachariæ quidē certè, Iosepho, Mariæ virgini, Simeoni, Annæ, Elisabethæ, Magis, Pastoribus, aliisque iamdiu ante innotuerat, quàm ministerium illud suum officiúmque Prophetæ capesseret: similitérque Ioanni Baptistæ, quum id proximè Christus obiturus esset. His omnibus ergo innotuerat Christus singulari revelatione. Communi autem revelatione, viáq; ministerij in Ecclesia instituti, fuit in ipso principio cognitus a discipulis Ioannis Baptistæ Christus, quum magistrum suum illi audiuisent dicentem, ecce agnus Dei: & iterum, ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi: quemadmodum a Ioanne Euangelista narratur euidentissime. Hoc igitur si vniuersè a Samosatceno dictum est, vt est, quis bonus probare possit, tam densa nube testium in sacris Scripturis reclamante? Quòd si indefinitè placeat accipere, quid est nisi hoc illudere est? Si enim hominibus quibusdam notus, & aliis ignotus in illo principio fuit, vtrumque certè verum est: &, si quibusdam notus, non ergo soli Deo notus, quod iste nouus auctor tam confidenter affirmauit, sed Deo fuerit notus, & quibuscunque reuelauit Pater. Non enim agnoscebatur Messias ab illis hominibus, qui iis solùm oculis carnis cernebant: sed ab ijs tamen agnoscebatur, quorum oculos Pater noster qui est in cœlis illustrabat. Itaque frustra Samosatenus narrationes accumulat de ijs qui Christum functionis principio non nouerant: cum ex indefinita enunciatione, quæq; vera ex parte est, & ex parte falsa, coficiat vniuersalem, & tamquam ex vniuersali id quod sibi vult concludat vniuersè: quod repugnat iustæ argumentationum legi. Quemadmodum autem communem enunciationem, sic proximè sequentem congeriem exemplorum vitiosam esse paucis demonstrabimus. Nam primus exemplorum locus est de ijs qui carnis solùm & sensus oculos habuerunt, non autem mentis a diuina luce. Hoc verò concesserimus, & sanctè affirmamus vltro. De Ioanne Baptista quod adfert, duobus modis fallit in exemplo vno. Nam primùm cognoscendi verbo æquiuocè abutitur. Baptistes enim Christum iamdiu cognouerat fide, ətiq non cognouerat personam determinatè secundùm secundum carnem. Hæc autem cognitio secundum carnem quantula pars cognitionis est? obsecro. Deinde vero confundit tempora illius notitiæ, vt illudat imperitis. Baptista enim Christum quidem non cognouerat defacie secundum carnem, antequam ad ipsum veniret Christus: quo de tempore dicit, & ego non noueram eum: sed ante tamen ille cognouit Christum, quàm initium Christus faceret ministerij: adde etiam quàm initiaretur Baptismo, vt in ministerio illo suo consecraretur. Cur enim dixisset Ioannes, ego opus habeo baptizari a te, & tu venis ad me? Iam tum ergo conspexerat Spiritum descendentem vt columbam, & manentem super ipsum, quum necdum baptizatus esset, eúmq; hoc signo de facie pernouerat, quem iamdiu fide didicerat. Ex his ita concludo necessaria consequentia: Principium ministerij Christi fuit post Baptismum: ante Baptismum Ioannes cognouit Christum: ergo ante principium ministerij. Falsum igitur quicquid hic a Samosateno de Ioannne Baptista dicitur. De Israelitis eadem ratio: horum enim alij fide non agnoscebant Christum, alij ne de facie quidem: atque ad hoc genus notitiæ externæ secundum carnem maximè spectabat Ioannes dicendo, in medio vestrum stat, quem vos nescitis. Insidiæ ergo hic struuntur æquiuocatione: tâquam si quis diceret, non nouerant Christum de facie: omnino ergo non nouerant. quod genus ratiocinationis quis probet? Nec dissimile est, quod de Apostolis postea subijcitur, & aliis exemplis sequetibus hic argutatus est. Vt enim patefactioni Christi qua se ipse patefecit, ita etiam cognitioni hominum suus fuit modus per sua tempora momentáque distinguendus. Non autem plenè facta est, siue (vt Samosatenus loquitur) non plenaria ab initio fuit Christi patefactio: nec cognitio igitur plenaria fuit. Primùm itaque communes quasi notiones, principia, & prima quasi
units.tr: Exodus 33; Exod. 34; 1 Sam. 3; 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chron. 17; Isa. 42; Matt. 12; Heb. 3. Christ did not begin to act as Prophet among men or to establish his Church by the Word only when he was made manifest in the flesh. Rather, from the beginning of the world, since there have been prophets and prophecy (and these have existed from the beginning of the human race), the Spirit of the Lord Jesus Christ has been the teacher among the people of God. For Peter, speaking of the prophets in chapter 1, says: Searching what, or what manner of time, the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow. Again later: Wherefore it is also contained in Scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a stone, chosen and precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. For it is this One, who speaks and declares the will of the Father, who is believed, that is, the eternal Word of God. Peter, using the application and accommodation of this matter very clearly, says in the following words: To you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders rejected, the same is made the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence. These words of David and Isaiah refer both to the earlier times, as the prophets themselves plainly cry out, and to these last times in which Christ came in the flesh. And in the next chapter: Christ indeed suffered in the flesh, but was quickened by the Spirit: by which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison, which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, and so on. We would add other passages besides these, were it not that these are plain and clear enough to prove and confirm the truth before good men; for to others not even the whole of Scripture is enough. We conclude, therefore, that the Lord Jesus Christ is that same eternal Word of God the Father, in whom and through whom the Father declared his will to Adam and to the ancient and holy Fathers from the beginning. Christ did not then first begin to exist when he lived in the flesh and discharged that divine and saving apostleship which the Evangelists and Apostles described in detail in the New Testament. The interpretation of the other passage, and the Word was with God, is likewise faulty. For that statement is neither true in itself nor the genuine meaning of this text, since this new interpreter says: In this beginning he was with the Father, not yet known to men, but to the Father alone. For he was not recognised by men as the Messiah, and so on. First, we have already shown above that John the Evangelist did not intend this, and that it does not belong to this place or these words; therefore we will not add more on this part. But if it pleases us to weigh that statement simply in this sense, it is either wholly false or ambiguous. It is false if taken universally; ambiguous if taken indefinitely, as a particular interpretation from which nothing can be concluded. We judge that Samosatenus meant it universally, because he sets up an opposition between God and men in this argument and expressly uses the exclusive word alone. For one who says that Christ was not yet known to men, but to the Father alone excludes all men. But this is false and contrary to the truth of holy Scripture. It is true that Christ was known to no man by natural light; and that the person of Christ, as he is the Son of God, was known essentially to the Father alone with the Holy Spirit. But the matter itself shows that Samosatenus was looking to neither of these points when he wrote these things. Christ was in fact known to men even at that time, through that heavenly and supernatural light, partly by a singular revelation and partly by a common one. Certainly to Zechariah, Joseph, the virgin Mary, Simeon, Anna, Elisabeth, the Magi, and the shepherds, and to others, Christ had been made known long before he took up his ministry and the office of Prophet. So too to John the Baptist, when Christ was about to undertake it. Christ therefore had become known to all these by a singular revelation. By common revelation, and by the way of the ministry established in the Church, Christ was known from the very beginning by the disciples of John the Baptist, when they heard their master say: Behold the Lamb of God; and again, Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sin of the world, as John the Evangelist very plainly relates. If, then, this was said by Samosatenus universally, as it is, what good man could prove it, when so thick a cloud of witnesses in the holy Scriptures cries out against it? But if he chooses to take it indefinitely, what is this but mockery? For if Christ was known at that beginning to some men and unknown to others, both things are certainly true; and if he was known to some, then he was not known to God alone, as this new author so confidently asserted, but was known to God and to whomever the Father revealed him. For he was not recognised by those men who saw only with the eyes of the flesh; but he was recognised by those whose eyes our Father who is in heaven enlightened. Therefore Samosatenus heaps up his stories in vain about those who did not know Christ at the start of his office; since from an indefinite statement, which is partly true and partly false, he builds a universal one, and from this universal he draws the conclusion he wants universally, which is contrary to the law of just argument. But as I have shown the general statement to be defective, so I will show in a few words that the following heap of examples is defective too. The first example is of those who had only the eyes of the flesh and the senses, not the eyes of the mind enlightened by divine light. We concede this, and readily affirm it. As to what he brings forward about John the Baptist, he is deceived in one example in two ways. First, he misuses the word to know in an equivocal sense. For the Baptist had known Christ by faith long before, though he had not known his person definitely according to the flesh. And how small a part of knowledge is this knowledge according to the flesh, I ask you? Second, he confuses the times of that acquaintance, to deceive the unlearned. For John had indeed not known Christ by sight according to the flesh before Christ came to him, which is the time he refers to when he says: And I knew him not; but nonetheless John knew Christ before Christ began his ministry, and even before he was initiated by baptism so as to be consecrated to that ministry. For why would John have said, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? Already then he had seen the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, while he was not yet baptized; and by this sign he had known from sight the one whom he had long before learned through faith. From this I conclude by a necessary consequence: The beginning of Christ's ministry was after baptism; before baptism John knew Christ; therefore before the beginning of the ministry. Whatever is said here by Samosatenus about John the Baptist is therefore false. The same reasoning holds about the Israelites: some of them did not recognise Christ by faith, and some not even by sight. And it was to this kind of external knowledge according to the flesh that John chiefly looked when he said: There standeth one among you, whom ye know not. Snares are therefore laid here by equivocation, as if someone were to say: They did not know Christ by sight; therefore they did not know him at all. Who would approve such a form of reasoning? What follows, about the Apostles, and the other examples he argues through after this, is not unlike. For just as the manifestation of Christ, by which he revealed himself, had its own mode, so the knowledge of men had to be distinguished by its own times and stages. Yet the manifestation was not complete, or, as Samosatenus puts it, Christ's manifestation was not full from the beginning; therefore the knowledge was not full either. First, then, we will set out the common notions, the principles, and the first, as it were,

units.la: Matth. 3. femina de persona, fine, officio, modo, omnibúsq; Christi beneficiis fide les habuerunt, quibus principiis non actus, sed potentia infuit plenariæ illius cognitionis; re ipsa tamen & actu vera, iusta, & salutaris habentibus ipsam. Deinde huius cognitionis principia femináque procedente tempore, secundùm patefactionem Christi & piorum comprehensionē, scse profuderunt explicaueruntque in credentibus singulis, tanquam ex veris principiis processus veri, vt ex veris feminibus verae plantae in Christum insitae per fidem assurgerent: quod noster hic Samofatenus non videtur animaduertisse, quum de Apostolis non sine contumelia dicit, quem nec moriturum, neq; etiam resurrecturum credebant, sine quo Christus agnosci non poterat vere. At tu, miser, nec vere Christum nouisti, nec plene: Apostoli tum vere nouerunt, nō plene: prout nos quoque hoc tempore cognoscimus, tum demum & vere simul & plene cogniturí, quum Christus (qui vita nostra est) apparebit, & nos cum ipso patefiemus in gloria. Hic enim ex parte cognoscimus, ex parte prophetamus, vt cum Paulo dicam. Itaque cognouerunt Apostoli, & non cognouerunt Christū: cognouerunt cognitione inchoata & sensim augescente, nō cognouerunt perfecta: ab illa vero ad hanc cognitionem per suos progressus & gradus contenderunt vera cognitione, quamuis plenaria (vt vocas) minimè. Iam nevides, Samofatene? iamne lentis fallaciam tuam? fallaciam dico, siue fallaris ipse, siue prudens fallas. Vtrum sit, nouit Dominus, & reposcet: nos vero συμπάσχομεν. Nam secundùm hos gradus & patefactio a Christo fuit humano captui accomoda, & cognitio in Christianis adaucta est vera vere, & contendendo ad plenitudinem perfectionémq; suam adolescens. Atque in hunc modum sequenteis omnes locos (ne longiores simus) exponi & conciliari necesse est. Sic enim falso concluditur: non plene nouerunt, non nouerunt igitur: nam etsi non plenè, aliquatenus tamen cognouerant: est enim maius & minus scientiæ, principium & progressus, est pars & totum suum. Tu verò non ignoras a parte ad totum in quantitate (vt loquuntur) non valere consequentiam. Sed de his satis. 8. Exinanitionem si rectè acciperet iste, resipiscenti ex animo gratularer: sed repugnant sequentia. Duo itaque hic certo consilio confunduntur, quæ Paulus optimè distinxit: inanitio personæ, & submissio in persona inanita. Inanitionem personæ describit his verbis Apostolus, Quum esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam parem esse cum Deo: sed ipse inaniuit se, formam serui accepta similis hominibus factus. Submissionem personæ in se inanitæ, illis, Et habitu compertus vt homo ipse se submisit, factus obediens vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Inaniuit ergo se, quum æternus Dei Filius verus Deus, essentia infinitus, immortalis, &c. carnem assumsit in vnitatem personæ, tanquam si ex illa infinitate sua se ad nihilum redegisset. Submisit autem se persona inanita, quum subiectus Legi diceret, in lege tua scriptum est de me, ecce me, o Deus, vt facia voluntatem tuam. Itaque Christus resurrectione crucem quidem & mortem absorpsit plenè, inanitionem verò nō item: etsi præter veritatem hoc loco affirmatur. 9. Negamus Apostolum eo loco & testimonio agere de resurrectione Christi, sed tantum de excitatione, id est, præstatione illius quem Patribus olim promiserat, nempe seminis benedicti vel personæ Christi. Duo enim distinctè probat Apostolus ad antegressæ orationis suæ confirmationem: vnum, Christum esse exhibitum: alterum, eundem ex mortuis suscitatum esse. Exhibitum esse probat a genitura illa temporali, quam sua die perfecit Deus, vt Psalmo 2. scriptum est. Suscitatum ex mortuis probat sequentibus dicens. Quòd autem excitauerit eum a mortuis,
units.tr: Matth. 3. They had faith concerning the person, the purpose, the office, the manner, and all the benefits of Christ. In these principles there was not actual knowledge but the power of that full knowledge, yet they were in fact and in act true, right, and saving for those who possessed them. Then, as time went on, the principles and seeds of this knowledge, according to the manifestation of Christ and the understanding of the pious, poured themselves out and unfolded in each of the believers, as true growth proceeds from true principles, so that true plants grafted into Christ through faith might rise from true seeds. Our Samosatenus here does not seem to have noticed this, when he says of the Apostles, not without insult, "whom they did not believe would die or even rise again, and without whom Christ could not truly be recognised." But you, wretched man, have known Christ neither truly nor fully. The Apostles knew him truly, though not fully, just as we also know him at this time; and we shall know him both truly and fully only when Christ, who is our life, appears, and we are revealed with him in glory. For, as I may say with Paul, "we know in part and we prophesy in part." Thus the Apostles knew and did not know Christ: they knew him with an inchoate knowledge that gradually increased, not a perfect one; and from that knowledge they pressed on to this one through their progress and stages, by true knowledge, though by no means full knowledge, as you call it. Do you see now, Samosatenus? Do you see your deceit? I say deceit, whether you are deceived yourself or deceive knowingly. The Lord knows which it is and will require it; but we suffer with you. For according to these stages both the revelation from Christ was adapted to human capacity, and knowledge in Christians grew truly in truth, advancing toward its fullness and perfection. And in this way the following passages must be explained and reconciled (so that I do not go on too long). For this is the false conclusion: "they did not know fully, therefore they did not know"; for even if not fully, they had nevertheless known in some measure. There is a greater and a lesser knowledge, a beginning and a progress, a part and a whole. You, however, are not unaware that in quantity (as they say) the inference from part to whole does not hold. But enough of this.

units.la: Hebr. 10. non amplius reuersurum in sepulcrum, ita dixit, &c. Aliud autem excitare simpliciter, ἀνιστάναι γενικῶς, aliud excitare ex mortuis, ἀνιστάναι ἐκ νεκρῶν εἰδικῶς. Non enim quisquis excitatur, idé excitatur ex mortuis: sed contrà quisquis excitatur ex mortuis, is excitari dicedus est. Genus enim de specie prædicatur, non contrà. Quòd si exempla Samosatenus desideraverit, sunt quidem veteris Testamenti multa: sed quia verbi Græci exemplo opus est, e Nouo paucula adferemus. Matth. 22.24. siquis mortuus fuerit nõ habens filios, eius frater ducet affinitatis iure vxorem eius, & ἀναστήσει, suscitabit semè fratri suo. Act. 3.22. Moses dixit Patribus, Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus Deus vester ex fratribus vestris, sicut me, ἀναστήσει, inquit. & versu 26. ad eundem locum respiciens, vobis primum Deus quum excitasset Filium suum Iesum, misit qui benediceret vobis, &c. Sic etiam Act. 7.37. Atque haud scio an coniugatum nomen τῆς ἀναστάσεως in hunc modum exponi oporteat Act. 1. 22. quum Apostoli vnum eorum fieri dicerent testem excitationis Christi oportere: qua in doctrina versatur ministerium & Apostolatus illorum, vt postea vers. 25. ab ipsis appellatur. Sed quid multis opus est? Ipse Paulus disertis verbis tuetur & munit interpretationem hanc, quum altero post versu aduersatiuam illam adhibet, Quòd autem excitauerit eum ex mortuis, &c. Falsa igitur argumentatio ex falsa interpretatione. Quamquam si etiam concederetur iste interpretationis modus (vt plerisq; accidit) nihil tamen amplius ex ea consequeretur, quàm quod ante nota 7. in eadem causa ostendimus: nempe tum quidem plus innotuisse Christum, sed non propterea fugisse ante illud tempus omnem hominum notitiam. Sequentium item locorum quos Samosatenus adducit, eadem ratio: quapropter pium Lectorem breuitatis ergo ad notam 7. reijcimus. 10. An ergo priùs se Christus falsò & imaginarie, rie, id est, Marcionitice manifestauerat? Certè ante resur-rectionem se tam verè manifestauit Christus, quàm post resurrectionem fecit; licet non adeò plenè siue plenaria manifestatione, vt idem ante loquutus est. Hæc ergo nihil ad rem, nisi vt fucum imperitis. Conclusio est ambigua, & ex negatis confutatisq; principijs. Nam neque principij vocem sic accipi vt Samosateno placet, neque phrasin illam, erat apud Deum, suprà demonstrauimus: sed hūc ipsum glossarium, captata ambiguitate vbi nulla est, & voces & loquutiones detorquere de sanctissimo hoc mysterio propriè enunciatas. Principium restringit noua & inaudita determinatione: esse apud Deum figuratè accipit: nos vtrumque freti veritate negamus & confutauimus. Atque hæc causa est, cur de eadem affirmatione laborans Samosatenus vnum adhuc testimonium pro auctario adfert, & nouam illius loquutionis, erat apud Deum, interpretationem exemplis fulcire tentat. De testimonio videamus. Primùm agnoscimus Filium & secundùm essentiam (quæ tota est in Filio, & tota in Patre) & secundùm personalitatem (vt ita loquamur) soli Patri cum Spiritu sancto æternùm esse cognitum cognitione diuina & perfectissima, quantam ne Angeli quidem in coelis assequuntur: nam infinita est. Secundò & hoc agnoscimus, creatam illam cognitionem quam Deus Pater cum suis creaturis de Filio communicat, non plenè, sed quasi per gradus successiuè cum eis communicari, & ab eis percipi: ac proinde sua esse principia tum communicationis, tum comprehensionis illius, quæ principia sui progressus solent excipere pro demensu donationis Christi. Postremò etiam illud agnoscimus ad creatam hanc cognitionem pertinere, quòd Deus ipse de ea communicet, nòsq; de ea comprehendamus, quæ ad esse, ad virtutem, ad sermones, ad actiones, & ad perpessiones Christi salutareis pertinent, vcrè, breuiter, & perspicuè in Scri-pturis sacris. Sed negamus locos qui de esse ipsius agunt, eos de virtute, sermonibus, actionibus, & perpessionibus exponi oportere, aut contrà, sed suam cuiq; loco germa-nam interpretationem conseruari: ex quibus tamen per iustam consequentiam doctrinas erui alias de aliis ratio & veritas diuina postulant. Est autem locus ille & Sermo erat apudDeum, proprie de ipso esse huius sermonis dictus, ac proinde primò & per se de esse illius exponendus, vt ante ostendimus. Quòd siquis ab eo quod quid est argu-mentationes volet de virtute, potentiáq; & consimilibus aliis efficere, non equidem impedio: sed quid sibi velit quisque locus, id primum videri iudico oportere: quid inde conficiatur, prognatam quæstionem esse. Idem de loco 1. Ioan. 1. qui hic adducitur, omnino statuimus. Nam primum subsistentiam æternam personæ Christi Ioannes asserit his verbis, Quod erat a principio. Deinde naturam
units.tr: Hebr. 10. He said that he would no more return to the sepulchre, &c. But to raise up simply is one thing [ἀνιστάναι γενικῶς, to raise up generally], and to raise up from the dead is another [ἀνιστάναι ἐκ νεκρῶν εἰδικῶς, to raise up from the dead specifically]. For not everyone who is raised up is therefore raised from the dead; on the contrary, whoever is raised from the dead is to be said to have been raised. For the genus is predicated of the species, not the reverse. If Samosatenus wants examples, there are indeed many from the Old Testament, but since the Greek word itself needs illustrating, we will cite a few from the New. Matth. 22.24: "If anyone dies without having children, his brother shall take his wife by right of kinship, and [ἀναστήσει] shall raise up seed to his brother." Act. 3.22: "Moses said to the fathers, The Lord your God will raise up [ἀναστήσει] for you a Prophet from among your brethren, like unto me." And in verse 26, looking back to the same passage: "God, having raised up [ἀναστήσας] his Son Jesus, first sent him to bless you," &c. So also Act. 7.37. And I do not know whether the cognate noun [τῆς ἀναστάσεως] in Act. 1.22 ought not to be explained in this way, where the Apostles say that "one of them must be made a witness of the resurrection [τῆς ἀναστάσεως] of Christ"; the ministry and apostleship of these men consists in this teaching, as is afterwards called by them in verse 25. But why need we say more? Paul himself, in plain words, supports and fortifies this interpretation when, in the next verse but one, he adds that contrasting clause, "But that he raised him up from the dead," &c. The argument is therefore false because the interpretation is false. Yet even if this manner of interpretation were granted (as it often is), nothing more would follow from it than what we showed earlier in note 7 on the same point: namely that Christ was then more fully made known, but that he had not on that account escaped all human knowledge before that time. The same reasoning applies to the later passages that Samosatenus adduces; therefore, for the sake of brevity, we refer the pious reader to note 7. 10. Did Christ then manifest himself falsely and imaginarily before, that is, in the manner of Marcion? Certainly Christ manifested himself before the resurrection as truly as he did after it, although not so fully or with a complete manifestation as he later spoke. These points, therefore, have nothing to do with the matter, except to throw dust in the eyes of the unlearned. The conclusion is ambiguous and rests on principles that have been denied and refuted. For neither is the word "beginning" to be taken as Samosatenus wishes, nor have we shown above that the phrase "was with God" is to be taken in that sense; rather, he twists these words and expressions, which were properly spoken of this most holy mystery, into a gloss, seeking an ambiguity where there is none. He restricts "beginning" by a new and unheard-of qualification, and he takes "was with God" in a figurative sense. We, relying on the truth, deny and refute both. And this is the reason why Samosatenus, struggling over the same assertion, brings forward yet one more testimony as an addition, and tries to support with examples his new interpretation of the phrase "was with God." Let us look at the testimony. First, we acknowledge that the Son, both according to the essence (which is wholly in the Son and wholly in the Father) and according to his personhood (so to speak), has been known eternally by the Father alone, together with the Holy Spirit, with a divine and most perfect knowledge, such as not even the angels in heaven attain; for it is infinite. Secondly, we also acknowledge that the created knowledge of the Son which God the Father communicates with his creatures is not imparted to them fully, but is communicated and received by them successively, by degrees; and accordingly that there are principles of this communication and of this apprehension, which usually receive their progress according to the measure of Christ's gift. Lastly, we also acknowledge that it belongs to this created knowledge that God himself communicates of it, and that we apprehend those things which pertain to the salvation of Christ, in his being, power, words, actions and sufferings, truly, briefly and clearly in the holy Scriptures. But we deny that passages which speak of his being should be explained of his power, words, actions and sufferings, or the reverse, but that each passage keeps its own proper interpretation; from these, nevertheless, other doctrines are drawn by just consequence from one another, as reason and divine truth require. Now that passage "and the Word was with God" is spoken properly of the very being of this Word, and therefore must first and in itself be explained of his being, as we showed before. If anyone wishes to draw from what something is arguments about power, might and similar things, I indeed do not hinder him; but I judge that it must first be seen what each passage means, and that what follows from it is a question that arises afterwards. We hold exactly the same about 1 John 1, which is cited here. For first John asserts the eternal subsistence of the person of Christ in these words, "which was from the beginning." Then [he asserts] the nature assumed into the unity of the same person, which confirmed to the eyes, ears, minds and hands of men, concerning that Word made flesh, those things that we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and which our hands have handled, concerning the Word; for they did not see this Word as the Word...

units.la: assumtam in vnitatem eiusdem personæ, quæ aureis ho-minum, oculos, mentes, manus de illo Sermone carne fa-cto confirmauit, illis, quod audiuimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, & manus nostræ contrectarunt de Sermone: hunc enim Sermonem nō viderunt quà sermo, sed quà caro: nempe quatenus seipsum Sermo in sua hu-manitate videndum, spectandum, tractandúmq; propo-suit illis. Tertiò proprietatem essentialem Sermonis hu-ius explicat, quòd Sermo vita sit, vel Sermo vitæ (nam v-trouis modo exposueris, non magni interest) & hac pro-prietate sua nobis salutaris, nimirum vitam habens in se essentialiter, eámq; nobis per gratiam conferens. Po-stremò finem subijcit, vt & vos communionem habeatis no-biscum, &c. Tertium autem illum de vita locum, vt no-bis apprimè salutarem, Ioannes persequitur accuratis-simè interiecto membro parenthęto in hanc sententiam. Illa vita, inquit, quæ formaliter vita est & Sermo Dei, ac proinde a natura hominibus ignota plane propter infinitatem illius & tenuitatem vitiosi ratemq; nostram, illa patefacta est, & Deus in carne factus conspicuus, vt ait Paulus: & ita quidem patefacta, vt tum ipsi eam viderimus secundum carnem assumtam quæ panis est vitæ, tu etiam testemur vt spectatores ipsius & testes a Deo in Ecclesia dati, & annunciemus, vt præcones ibidem ab eo instituti, vitā illā æterna: quæ & sine principio est in se secundum rationem temporis, vt quæ a principio erat apud Patrem, & secundum tempus patefacta est nobis sine fine futura tum in se ipsa proprietate essentiæ & naturæ suæ, tum in nobis (qui communionem habemus cum ipso) communicatione gratiæ. Quid hoc tanto mysterio diuinius? Ecce autem, inquit Samosatenus, erat apud Patrem, id est, ignotus erat hominibus. Nego fuisse ignotum: non enim id continuo sequitur, si non fuit plane notus, fuisse ignotum. Præterea nego eam sententiam huius loquutionis esse, erat apud Patrem: propriam affirmo esse, iniquè figuratam effici; quæ omnia ante commonstrauimus. At, inquit, absurdum est alium fingere æternum, inuisibilem, impalpabilem. Fateor. Nestorianum est, impium, si alium æternum, inuisibilem, impalpabilem, & alium factum in tempore, visibilem, & palpabilem esse docueris. Id verò absurdum non est, si eumdem Christum, eumdem Sermonem vitæ secundum aliud & aliud sic esse dixeris. Non enim est alius Iesus, & alius Christus, aut simpliciter alius & alius: sed in vno eodemque Christo est aliud & aliud. Est enim vna persona Christi, secundum deitatem æterna, inuisibilis, impalpabilis per essentiam suam: & secundum carnem vel humanitatem suam assumtam eadem persona, ac non alia, in tempore facta, visibilis, & palpabilis creditur: quemadmodum Scripturæ domcent. Vt autē nō est absurdū, nec credētibus pijs absurdū videri potest, cp Sermo factus est caro: sic absurdū nulla ratione dici aut videri potest, cp Sermo proprietates habet diuinas, & humanas caro: nō magis, inquā, absurdū, quàm illud in vnoquoq; nostrū absurdum est, animæ suas qualitates spiritales cōstare, & suas corpori. Quod verū esse quis vel Samosatenus vel fungus nesciat? At Ioānes, inquit, ideò statim addit per antithεsin, sed postea hæc vita patefacta est. Respōdeo, hìc Samosatenus translilit ad genus alterū hac sua argumētatione, a substātia nempe ad modū accidentarium. Nam de substantia personæ & modo substantiali eius agit Apostolus. Substantia est natura duplex, Sermonis seu vitæ & carnis assumtæ: modus substātialis est diuinæ quidē illius, cp nō potest homini aut creaturæ vlli in hac vita patescere secundùm essentiāsuā: humanæ, quòd patet omnibus. His naturis adunatis personaliter, Sermo in se ἀφανῆς factus est in carne φανερῶς. Hic ergo ille substātialis modus, vel personalis est. Noster verò nouus hic interpres modū facit accidentarium: non enim de esse & modo illius, sed de cognitione aliena, qua ipse notus est, intelligit: nō de eo quod actu est in se, suaqȝ per se virtute explicat, sed de eo quod aliena potentia cognoscitur. Atqui Deus est actus purus & simplicißimus: hic autem Sermo est Deus: actus igitur est, neque potentia, sed actu subsistit in se. Quod si fuit tempus quum non subsisteret, potentiâ certè, non actu fuit. Non igitur Deus est. Est autem Deus: actu igitur, non potentia est: ac proinde nunquam fuit tempus, quum non subsisteret. De hac autem subsistentia Sermonis vitæque æternæ à Ioanne agitur: quæ vita in seipsa si potentiâ est, non est æterna: est autem æterna in se: actu igitur, ac nō potentiâ æterna est. Quapropter non per antithεsin hæc verba oportet intelligi, & vita patefacta est, sed per synthεsin potiùs, vt ita loquamur: prout exponitur verbis sequenquentibus,quum Ioannes dicit, Sermo ille seu vita illa aeterna erat apud Patrem, subsistens nimirum in se, & pate-facta est nobis in carne, quam adiunxit sibi & assumsit in unitatem personae. Quid? si quis dixerit, foetus erat apud matrem, an hoc quisquam interpretabitur, cognitus erat soli matri? nonne potius locutio, ut proprie sonat, de subsistentia exponi debet? Certe: nā sive cognitus sit aliis, sive incognitus, apud ea subsistit: primum hoc est naturae ordine, ut sit, etiam incognitus: secundum, ut cognoscatur esse tum declaratione, quando fovetur intus, tum vero nativitate, quando in lucem editur ante oculos omnium. Quod de misero foetu humano natura docet, id tu, Samosatene, de Filio Dei aeterno (quamuis incomparabili modo) negaueris? Quemadmodum autem foetus est apud matrem (ut in hoc simili consistamus) sive soli matri cognitus, sive aliis etiam per sermonis, veteri, aliorumque signorum revelationem: & primum quidem soli matri est a natura notus, deinde aliis a matre innotescit: ac proinde concludi non potest iusta consequentia, est apud matrem, ergo soli matri cognitus: sic etiam Sermo Patris esse apud Patrem dicitur, sive soli Patri cognitus, sive aliis praeterea: Ac primum quidem soli Patri est cognitus, deinde vero aliis per revelationem Patris, quam revelationem Pater inde a creatione fecit per sua incrementa & progressus: proinde concludi nō potest, est Sermo apud Patrem, ergo cognitus soli Patri: quam tamen interpretationem Samosatenus pro germana venditat. Nisi quis forte παραδόξως illud axioma tueri velit: quisquis apud aliquem est, ei soli cognitum esse apud quem est. Qua ratione futurum est, quum homo Italus apud Polonum est, ut Polono soli sit cognitus. Utinam vero, utinam hic Samosatenus noster ei soli apud quem erat innotuisset, ac non sese aliis noscendum quàm plurimis modis ac perniciosissimis praebuisset. Pergit Samosatenus, At, inquit, non dissimiles quoque phrases in Scripturis exstat, Matth. 13. & 26. &c. Respondeo, non modo non dissimiles, sed eadem plane loquutiones sunt quæ à Samosateno adferuntur: sed falsa omnium interpretatio. Nam horum neutrum est necessarium, ut apud aliquem esse significet ei notum esse hominem soli apud quem est, & ut notum esse alicui sit apud eum esse. Prioris loquutionis hæc sunto exempla: sunt feræ, sunt homines apud feras, nec tamen solis feris noti: sunt homines alij apud alios, nec solis ijs noti apud quos sunt: item sunt angeli apud homines, sunt apud angelos, nec tamen ijs solis noti apud quos dicuntur esse: immo (ut dicam aliquid grauius) sunt apud ignotos etiam ignoti. Et tibi, Samosatene, apud aliquem esse, & ei soli, soli inquam notum esse, sunt idē? De posteriore videamus. Quàm multos noui, Deus bone, qui non sunt apud me! qui nunquam fuerunt apud me! qui non sunt in viuis! Tu quoque, Samosatene, fieri potest ut patrem tuum noueris, si forte quum adoleuisses superstes fuit, & iam non sit apud te. Sunt denique præsentes apud me noti: at etiam absentes noui, & a me dissitos longissimé. Re ergo & ratione hæ loquutiones inter se differunt: nec idem esse possunt. Non negamus conjunctas esse posse, nempe ut antecedens & consequens. Non raro enim accidit, ut prius ad me quis veniat & sit apud me, quàm sit mihi cognitus. Sed si ita est, primum non sunt idem; quia non sunt idem antecedens & consequens. Secundò ne re quidem necessariò sunt inter se idem; quia non est cohærentia illorum aut consequentia semper necessaria: nam utrumque fieri potest, ut & mihi innotescat qui nunquam sit apud me, & sit apud me qui nunquam cognoscatur a me. Postremò quid si hæc duo toto genere differre demonstremus? Certè esse apud aliquem, secundum hominem est τῷ λόγῳ, in prædicamento Vbi: cognosci ab aliquo, passionis est. Itaque nulla ratione sunt idem, cum sint ἀπόλυθα, & quidem μὴ ἀναγκαῖα, & ἐπιφογενῆ. Falsæ igitur omnes interpretationes illæ, quæ a Samosateno in aliquot Noui Testamenti locos productæ sunt. Nam licet id concedamus, nota fuisse illa de quibus hæc loquutio ijs in locis enunciatur: nunquam tamen Samosatenus inde consecuturus est idem esse si dixeris, sunt apud nos, & nota sunt nobis. Atque hoc ipsum, velit nolit, cogitur agnoscere, dum his verbis vtitur: Sic quum Christus rogaretur a Caiapha de doctrina, Matth. 26. & Marc. 14. respondit vt de ea quæ illis nota esse debuit, Semper docui apud vos in templo, &c. O vim veritatis, quæ latere non potuit, quin aducrsum pectus Samosateni transfoderet. Apud quos docuit Christus doctrinam suam, apud illos nota esse debuit. Debuit autem? ergo non fuit cognita, quamuis esse cognita debuerit. Antecedens fuit, quòd apud illos Christus docuit doctrinam suam: consequens, non quòd apud illos cognita fuerit, sed quòd esse debuerit. Ex tuis ipsius verbis, Samosatene, vinco alterum esse antecedens, alterum consequens: tum eorum consequentiam (vt ante dixi) non semper esse necessariam, sed contingentem solum, cum hic fuerit antecedens, consequens vero nō fuerit, sed esse debuerit. Atque hæc inter se idem te auctore dicemus esse? Deus meliora. Dices fortasse, at in diuinis alia est ratio. Esto sanè: tu igitur, mi homo, cur adducis, aliam rationem qui esse vides? Verum tamen vt alia sit ratio humanarum diuinarumque rerum, est tamen qualiscunque analogia, cuius causa hæ loquutiones enunciatæ sunt, retinenda. Eam, si placet, vide. Esse apud hominem humanitus, reipsa est λόγος. Filium esse apud Patrem est περιχώρησις diuinæ, vt orthodoxi Patres nominant, quæ in personis diuinis habet quasi rationem λόγος, quum demittuntur sermones per quamdam analogiam ad rationem naturæ nostræ. Esse apud hominem, est antecedens re & tempore, notum esse homini est consequens: at esse Filium apud Patrem, & notum esse Patri, non differunt re & tempore (nam alioqui Deus nec simplicissimus, nec æternus esset) sed ratione solum, quo in discrimine rationis posita est analogia. Postremo esse apud hominem, & cognitum esse homini, non habent consequentiam inter se necessariam, quia reipsa alterum sine altero inter homines esse potest: nam ignotus apud aliquem esse potest, & qui apud aliquem est fieri potest ut non cognoscatur. Quapropter etiam ex analogia hæc duo, apud Deum esse, & Deo soli cognitum esse Filium, ratione omnino differunt.
units.tr: Taken up into the unity of the same person, the Word, which by those things that were heard, seen, looked upon, and handled by human ears, eyes, minds and hands confirmed the Word made flesh: that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word. For they saw this Word not as Word but as flesh, namely, insofar as the Word in his humanity offered himself to them to be seen, looked upon and handled. Thirdly, he explains the essential property of this Word, that the Word is life, or the Word of life (it does not matter much which way you put it), and by this property of his he is salutary to us, since he has life in himself essentially and confers it on us through grace. Lastly, he adds the purpose: that you also may have fellowship with us, and so on. John pursues this third point, about life, which is most salutary for us, with great care, inserting a parenthetical clause to this effect: That life, he says, which is formally life and the Word of God, and therefore by nature plainly unknown to men because of its infinity and our feeble and sinful reason, that life has been made manifest, and God, made visible in the flesh, as Paul says. And it has been made manifest in such a way that we have seen it, according to the flesh assumed, which is the bread of life; and that you also may testify to it as its eyewitnesses and as witnesses given by God in the Church, and may proclaim that eternal life to others as heralds appointed by him there. That life, which is without beginning in itself according to the reckoning of time, since it was from the beginning with the Father, has also, in time, been made manifest to us, and will be without end, both in itself by the property of its essence and nature, and in us who have fellowship with him by the communication of grace. What could be more divine than this great mystery? But, says the Samosatene, behold, it was with the Father, that is, it was unknown to men. I deny that it was unknown; for it does not at once follow that, if it was not plainly known, it was unknown. Moreover, I deny that this is the sense of the expression was with the Father; I affirm that it is its proper sense, and that it is wrongly distorted into a figure; all of this we have shown before. But, he says, it is absurd to imagine another who is eternal, invisible, impalpable. I grant it. It would be Nestorian and impious if you taught that one is eternal, invisible and impalpable, and another was made in time, visible and palpable. But it is not absurd if you say that the same Christ, the same Word of life, is so in one respect and in another. For there is not one Jesus and another Christ, or simply one and another; but in one and the same Christ there is one thing and another. For there is one person of Christ, eternal according to the deity, invisible and impalpable through his essence; and according to the flesh or assumed humanity, the same person, and not another, is believed to have been made in time, visible and palpable, as the Scriptures teach. And just as it is not absurd, nor can it seem absurd to believing men, that the Word was made flesh, so it can by no reasoning be said or seen to be absurd that the Word has divine properties and the flesh human ones. No more absurd, I say, than it is absurd in each of us that our spiritual qualities subsist in our souls and our bodily ones in our bodies. Who, even the Samosatene or some dolt, does not know that this is true? But John, he says, adds at once, by way of antithesis, but afterwards this life was made manifest. I answer that the Samosatene here passes to another kind by this argument of his, namely from substance to accident. For the Apostle is speaking of the substance of the person and his substantial mode. Substance is the twofold nature, of the Word or life, and of the assumed flesh. The substantial mode is that of the divine nature, which cannot be made manifest to any man or creature in this life according to its essence, and that of the human nature, which is open to all. With these natures united personally, the Word was made invisible in himself and visible in the flesh. This, then, is the substantial, or personal, mode. But our new interpreter makes it an accidental mode; for he understands it not of the being and mode of that life, but of the knowledge of others by which he himself is known; he explains it not of what he is in himself and by his own power, but of what is known by another's power. But God is pure and most simple act; this Word is God; therefore he is act, not potency, and subsists in himself by act. If there was a time when he did not subsist, he was certainly in potency, not in act. Therefore he is not God. But he is God; therefore he is in act, not in potency; and consequently there never was a time when he did not subsist. And it is of this subsistence of the Word and of eternal life that John is speaking: this life, if it is in itself in potency, is not eternal; but it is eternal in itself; therefore it is eternal in act, not in potency. Therefore these words, and this life was made manifest, must be understood not by antithesis but rather, so to speak, by synthesis, as the following words explain: when John says that the Word, or that eternal life, was with the Father, subsisting, that is, in itself, and was made manifest to us in the flesh, which he joined to himself and assumed into the unity of the person. What then? If someone says, the foetus was with the mother, will anyone interpret this as meaning that it was known only to the mother? Is not the expression rather to be explained, as its words properly sound, of subsistence? Certainly: for whether it is known to others or unknown, it subsists with the mother. First, by the order of nature it is so, even if unknown; second, it is known to be there, first by the sign of the mother's quickening it within, and then by birth, when it is brought into the light before the eyes of all. What nature teaches of the wretched human foetus, will you, Samosatene, deny of the eternal Son of God (though in an incomparable manner)? But just as the foetus is with the mother (let us stay with this comparison), whether it is known only to the mother or also to others through the revelation of speech, of signs, and so on, first it is known by nature to the mother alone, and then it becomes known to others from the mother; and therefore no sound consequence can be drawn that it is with the mother, therefore it is known only to the mother. So too the Word is said to be with the Father, whether known only to the Father or to others besides. At first he is known only to the Father, and afterwards to others through the revelation of the Father, which revelation the Father has made from the creation onward by his increases and progress. Therefore it cannot be concluded that the Word is with the Father, therefore known only to the Father; yet the Samosatene puffs up this interpretation as genuine. Unless perhaps someone wishes to defend that axiom, paradoxically: whoever is with someone, is known only to the one with whom he is. By that reasoning, when an Italian man is with a Pole, he will be known only to the Pole. Would that this our Samosatene had become known only to him with whom he was, and had not made himself known to very many in the most pernicious ways! The Samosatene goes on: But, he says, similar phrases are also found in the Scriptures, Matt. 13 and 26, and so on. I answer that they are not merely not dissimilar, but are plainly the very same expressions that the Samosatene cites; but his interpretation of all of them is false. For neither of these must mean that to be with someone signifies that the man is known to the one with whom he is, and that to be known to someone is to be with him. Here are examples of the first kind: there are wild beasts, there are men among wild beasts, and yet they are not known only to the beasts; there are men with other men, and yet they are not known only to those with whom they are; likewise there are angels with men, there are angels with angels, and yet they are not known only to those with whom they are said to be. Indeed (to say something more weighty) there are some unknown ones with unknown ones. Do to be with someone and to be known to that one alone mean the same thing to you, Samosatene? Let us look at the second. How many have I known, good God, who are not with me! who never were with me! who are not among the living! You too, Samosatene, may have known your father, if perhaps he survived your growing up, and yet he is no longer with you. Finally, there are those who are present with me and known, and there are those whom I know though absent and very far from me. Therefore these expressions differ both in fact and in reason, and cannot be the same. We do not deny that they can be joined, namely as antecedent and consequent. For it often happens that someone comes to me first and is with me before he is known to me. But if so, first, they are not the same, because the antecedent and consequent are not the same. Second, they are not necessarily the same in fact either, because their connection or consequence is not always necessary; for it can happen both that someone becomes known to me who never is with me, and that someone is with me who is never known by me. Lastly, what if we show that these two differ in their whole kind? Certainly to be with someone, as a man is, belongs in reason to the category of where [ὑπὸ τὸ λόγῳ, in the predicament Ubi]; to be known by someone is a passion. Therefore they are in no way the same, since they are [ἀπόλυθα], and indeed [μὴ ἀναγκαῖα] and [ἐπιφογενῆ]. Therefore all those interpretations are false which the Samosatene has drawn from some passages of the New Testament. For even if we grant that those things of which this expression is uttered in those passages were known, the Samosatene will never thereby get to the point that if you say, they are with us, and they are known to us, these are the same. And this very thing, whether he likes it or not, he is compelled to admit when he uses these words: So when Christ was asked by Caiaphas about his teaching, Matt. 26 and Mark 14, he answered as about something that ought to have been known to them: I have always taught among you in the temple, etc. O the power of truth, which could not stay hidden, but pierced the Samosatene's breast! Christ taught his doctrine among those to whom it ought to have been known. But ought it? Then it was not known, although it ought to have been known. The antecedent was that Christ taught his doctrine among them; the consequent was not that it was known to them, but that it ought to have been. From your own words, Samosatene, I prove that one is the antecedent and the other the consequent; and that their consequence (as I said before) is not always necessary but only contingent, since here there was an antecedent without the consequent, which ought to have followed. And will we say, on your authority, that these are the same? God forbid. You will perhaps say, but in divine matters the reasoning is different. Granted indeed: but then, my good man, why do you bring in another reasoning when you see it is different? Yet even though the reasoning of human and divine things is different, there is still some kind of analogy, for the sake of which these expressions were uttered, and it must be kept. Look at it, if you please. To be with a man, in the human manner, is in fact a [λόγος], an ordinary connection. To be the Son with the Father is the divine [περιχώρησις], as the orthodox Fathers call it, which in the divine persons has something like the character of the [λόγος], when words are sent down by a certain analogy to the measure of our nature. To be with a man is antecedent in fact and in time; to be known to a man is the consequent. But to be the Son with the Father, and to be known to the Father, do not differ in fact and in time (for otherwise God would be neither most simple nor eternal), but only in reason, and it is in this difference of reason that the analogy lies. Lastly, to be with a man and to be known to a man do not have a necessary connection with each other, because in fact one can be with men without the other; for someone can be unknown to someone with whom he is, and someone who is with someone may happen not to be known. Therefore, even by this analogy, these two things, to be with God and to be the Son known to God alone, differ entirely in reason.

units.la: Aliud ad stabiliendam hanc interpretationem argumentum, quod Samosatenus adducit, est a communi loquendi modo: quum quæ nescimus & certa putamus esse, illa respondemus apud Deum esse abscondita, &c. Verum, si loquutionem Græcam, sicut Ioannes scripsit, Græca lance Samosatenus expendisset, cauisset profecto ipse sibi, ne in fallaciam figuræ dictionis incideret: quemadmodum hoc loco facit, vsum Græcæ præpositionis πρὸς & Latinæ apud confundendo. Nam etsi interdum hæ duæ præpositiones inter se communicant significatione, frequentius tamen aliud hanc quàm illam significare comperisset. Ex quo sequitur, tum quæ de Latino apud hîc narrantur nihil efficere, tum proprietatem Græci vocabuli πρὸς seruari oportere. Πρὸς autem, vt tradunt Grammatici, & Varinus ex Eustathio & Esychio colligit, πρὸς τὸ ἐμψυχον κίνησιν, ἢ ὕπαρξιν, ἢ ἐνέργειαν denotat, hoc est, aut motum, aut existentiam, aut actum, qui ad rem animatam viuentémque respiciat. Hîc autem de Deo viuente agitur: vnus ergo ex istis modus in hac loquutione obseruandus. Non autem de motu, non de energia dicitur Sermonis monis apud Patrem, vel Samosateno iudice: igitur de existentia. Si enim de motu aut energia diceretur, & dici concederet, eâdem hæc etiam concessurus esset, Sermonem per se substitisse, Deo motum aut energiam alienam accidisse (cùm istis hominibus Sermo non sit Deus essentialiter) ac proinde non esse Deum immutabilem, simplicissimum, & alia multa quæ apud omneis in confesso sunt. Cùm itaq; dicantur ista de existentia personæ Christi in Patre, quo iure ad cognitionem ea Samosatenus referat, qua Sermo est Patri cognitus? Hoc neque existentiæ, neque motus, neque actus, neque actionis est, sed passionis puræ. Passionem verò hac constructione dici hactenus ignorauerunt probati auctores Græci: quid ergo hac interpretatione facias? Quòd si etiam ea exempla, quæ in hunc locum Samosatenus contulit, amplius expenderit, duo hæc comperturus est: primùm ubicunque εστι ὁ λόγος, hanc interpretationem quam modò diximus, seruari oportere: secundò ubicunque aliter accipitur Latinum apud, id non præpositione πρὸς, sed potius παρὰ, vt Luc. 1. 37. expressum a Græcis legi. Non enim, si Græcè illud velis exprimere, apud Deum sunt omnia, &c. conuenienter & κυριολεκτῶς dixeris, πρὸς Θεὸν πάντα ἐστι, sed παρὰ Θεῶ. Frustra igitur de accumulandis exemplis partim alienis, partimque malè intelleƈtis & tortis Samosatenus laborauit. ἐδὲν ὑμέςς. Postremum argumentum est a voce, erat. Dixisset ergo Ioannes, inquit ille, & fuisse & nunc esse in cælo Christum apud Deum, non tantùm fuisse in principio. Mentiretur enim, &c. tamquam si diceret, Quisquis eum qui fuit & est, fuisse dicit, mentitur: Ioannes Sermonem, qui secundùm illud dogma vestrum fuit & est, fuisse dicit: & non mentiatur secundùm vestram hypothesin? Respondeo duobus modis. Primùm etiam in rebus creatis & naturalibus maior est salsissima, & oppositum in appofito, vt vocant, continet. Nam quisquis personam aut rem aliquam fuisse dicit, no negat proprie eamdem esse; præsertim quum temporalis aliqua accedit determinatio, vt quum dicit Ioannes, in principio erat: determinatè enim de Sermone agitur, quà erat iam in principio, & apud Deum, & Deus. Quum autem ex præteriti simplice affirmatione, id est, sublata determinatione, præsens remotio rei statuitur, fuit, non est igitur: hæc non propria loquutio, sed figurata, quam noematicam Quinctilianus vocat, dicenda est: vt quum Romani dicerent, vixit, & similia multa. Quapropter optimè Logici docuerunt, a parte ad totum in quantitate non valere consequentiā: nec conclusionem fore necessariam, si ita dixeris, fuit, non igitur est, nec erit: est, ergo nec fuit, nec erit: erit, nec fuit igitur, nec est. Secundò in rebus diuinis, atque adeò in Metaphysicis, quoties περὶ ὑπάρξεως earum agitur (quam præpositione περὶς demonstrari ante docuimus) siue de earum existentia, pro ratione subiecti prædicatum oportet accipi. Cùm autem res Metaphysicæ secundùm existentiam ipsarum nunquam intereant; omnino prædicatum, quocunque tempore verbum enuncietur de existentia, omnia tempora facultate subiecti complectitur: erat, vel fuit spiritus, Angelus, &c. ergo est & erit. Hæc autem ratio in rebus metaphysicis necessariò si obtinet, multo magis eam in diuinis seruari necesse est: erat Sermo in principio apud Deum, est igitur & erit qui in principio erat. Malitiosa itaque, horrenda, impia est corum calumnia, qui a natura rerum intereuntium argumentationes de diuinis, id est æternis immutabilibusque, nectunt, & falsis etiam in rerum natura suppositionibus oppugnāt veritatem Dei. Nam Deus est extra & supra omne tempus: sed balbutientes de eo tempora enunciamus, quia aliter non possumus. Etsi in hoc temporum vsu orthodoxi doxi Patres conuenienter Scripturæ,& religiosè plurimū illud obseruarunt, vt verbum substantiuum per tempus præsens de æterna Dei immutabilitate diceretur: de æternitate sine principio, per præteritum: de æternitate sine fine, per futurum: de omni denique æternitate & immutabilitate eius, per omnia tempora : vt Apoc. 1. qui est, qui fuit & qui futurus est: quod appellatione Iehouæ Hebræi designabant, vt Defensione 2. diximus (segmento 13). Hîc autem, cùm non simpliciter dicatur, erat, sed addatur determinatio, in principio, quis homo non videt ex natura determinationis istius præteritum tempus, non autem præsens aut futurum, hoc loco fuisse vsurpandum? Atque hæc de argumentis Samosatieni, quàm potuit fieri breuissimé.
units.tr: Another argument that Samosatenus brings forward to support this interpretation is drawn from ordinary usage: when we do not know something but think it certain, we answer that it is hidden "with God," and so on. But if Samosatenus had weighed the Greek expression, as John wrote it, on Greek scales, he would certainly have guarded himself against falling into a fallacy of expression, as he does here by confusing the use of the Greek preposition πρὸς with the Latin apud. For although these two prepositions sometimes share a meaning, he would have found that more often one means something other than the other. It follows that what is said here about the Latin apud proves nothing, and that the proper force of the Greek word πρὸς must be kept. Now πρὸς, as the grammarians teach, and as Varinus gathers from Eustathius and Hesychius, denotes with a living thing [πρὸς τὸ ἐμψυχον] a motion, or a existence, or an action [κίνησιν, ἢ ὕπαρξιν, ἢ ἐνέργειαν], that is, either motion, or existence, or action that bears upon a thing that is animate and alive. Here, however, the living God is spoken of, so one of these modes must be observed in this expression. But, by Samosatenus's own judgement, it is not said of motion, nor of energy, that the Word was with the Father; therefore it is said of existence. For if it were said of motion or energy, and he were to concede that it is said, he would also concede the same thing: that the Word subsisted by itself, and that motion or energy foreign to God happened to God (since for these men the Word is not essentially God), and consequently that God is not immutable, most simple, and many other things that are agreed upon by all. Since, then, these things are said of the existence of the person of Christ in the Father, by what right does Samosatenus refer them to knowledge, by which the Word is known to the Father? This belongs neither to existence, nor to motion, nor to act, nor to action, but to pure passion. Yet the approved Greek authors have so far not known a passive use of this construction. What, then, will you accomplish by this interpretation? And if he had weighed more carefully the examples that Samosatenus brought together for this passage, he would discover two things. First, wherever ἐστι ὁ λόγος occurs, the interpretation we have just given must be kept. Secondly, wherever the Latin apud is taken in another sense, it is expressed by the Greeks not with πρὸς but rather with παρὰ, as in Luke 1:37. For if you wished to express in Greek "with God all things are possible," you would not speak properly and κυριολεκτῶς with πρὸς Θεὸν πάντα ἐστι, but with παρὰ Θεῶ. Samosatenus therefore laboured in vain to heap up examples, some foreign to the point and some badly understood and twisted. [ἐδὲν ὑμέςς] The last argument is taken from the word erat. "John would have said," he says, "that Christ both was and now is in heaven with God, not merely that he was in the beginning. For he would be lying," and so on, as if one were to say: "Whoever says that he who was and is, has been, lies; John says that the Word, who according to your dogma was and is, has been; and does he not lie according to your hypothesis?" I answer in two ways. First, even in created and natural things the greater part is most insipid, and in the matter at hand it contains the opposite of what it says. For whoever says that a person or thing has been does not deny that it is properly the same; especially when some temporal determination is added, as when John says "in the beginning was." For the Word is spoken of in a determinate way, as already being in the beginning, and with God, and God. But when from a simple affirmation of the past, that is, with the determination removed, a present remoteness of the thing is asserted ("it was, therefore it is not"), this is not proper speech but figurative, which Quintilian calls noematic, as when the Romans said "he lived" and many similar things. Therefore the logicians have rightly taught that in quantity the inference from part to whole does not hold, nor would the conclusion be necessary if you said: "it was, therefore it is not, nor will be; it is, therefore it neither was nor will be; it will be, nor was, therefore it is not." Secondly, in divine things, and indeed in metaphysical ones, whenever their περὶ ὑπάρξεως is treated (which we showed earlier is indicated by the preposition περὶ), that is, their existence, the predicate must be taken according to the nature of the subject. But since metaphysical things never perish with respect to their existence, the predicate, whatever tense the verb is stated in when speaking of existence, embraces all times by the capacity of the subject: "a spirit, an angel, etc., was or has been, therefore it is and will be." If this reasoning necessarily holds in metaphysical things, it is much more necessary that it be kept in divine things: "the Word was in the beginning with God; therefore he who was in the beginning is and will be." Malicious, horrible, and impious, then, is the calumny of those who bind arguments about divine things, that is, eternal and immutable ones, to the nature of perishable things, and who attack the truth of God with suppositions false even in the nature of things. For God is outside and above all time; but we, stammering, speak of times about him, because we cannot do otherwise. Yet in this use of tenses the orthodox Fathers, agreeing with Scripture, have very religiously observed that the substantive verb is said in the present tense of God's eternal immutability; of eternity without beginning, in the past tense; of eternity without end, in the future; and finally of all his eternity and immutability, through all tenses; as in Rev. 1: "who is, who was, and who is to come," which the Hebrews signified by the name Jehovah, as we said in our second Defence (section 13). Here, however, since it is not simply said "was," but the determination "in the beginning" is added, what man does not see, from the nature of this determination, that the past tense and not the present or future must be used in this passage? And so much for the arguments of Samosatenus, stated as briefly as possible.

units.la: 12. Axioma istud & corollarium a Samosateno additum summam hominis audaciam ostendit in corrumpendis Scripturæ locis, & veritati repugnat planè. Nam primùm duo confunduntur locorum genera, quorum differentiam vel pueri videre possunt. Vnum genus est relationis internæ, Filij ad Patrem: alterum, relationis externæ, Filij a Patre ad homines: quarum prior relatio mutua, posterior non mutua appellatur. Relationis internæ sunt ista, erat apud Deum, est in Patre, est in sinu Patris, est in cælo: Externæ verò hæc, est ex Deo, a Deo processit, a Deo venit, a Patre exiuit, descendit de cælo, & si qua sunt eiusmodi. Nam mutua quidem est relatio, & quidem realis (vt vocant) Filij ad Patrem, & Patris ad Filium, at non item Dei ad creaturas suas: quæ cùm a Deo omnino pendeant, relationem ad ipsum realem habent, non Deus ad ipsas. Secundò etiam in ijs quæ relationis internæ sunt, confunduntur dicta de subsistentia personali καὶ' ἀλλήλου περιχώρησιν (vt vocabant Patres) cum dictis de communitate essentiæ ac proprietatum ipsius. Nâ loquutiones istæ, Sermo erat apud Deum, Ioan. 1. ego sum in Patre, & Pater est in me, Ioan. 14. de subsistetia personali, & καληλῳ existentia: hæ vero, est in sinu Patris, est in cælo, Ioan. 1. & 3. de communi scientia rerum diuinarum omnium dicuntur figuratè, quæ scientia essentialis est, non autem particulariter ad hanc personam aut illam pertinens. Quum enim diceret Ioannes, vnigenitus ille Filius qui est in sinu Patris, ille exposuit nobis, humano loquendi modo oportebat, Filio sinum Patris, id est, consilia intima & singula sine exceptione amantissimè esse exposita, tanquam si quis Filius hic de sinu Patris sui blandissimè & familiarissimè depromeret. Quum item diceret Filium hominis in cælo esse, humano loquedi more per metalepsin consequentis demonstrauit Christus, sibi præsentissimam esse rerum omnium cœlestium diuinorumque mysteriorum scientiam plane diuinam, vt qui in terra agens versaretur in cœlis, & nihil non in cœlis cognosceret. Hæc ipsi loci ita confirmant manifesto, vt cæcum esse vltrò oporteat qui lucem huius interpretationis e loco natam depulerit.
units.tr: 12. This axiom and corollary added by Samosatenus show the great audacity of the man in corrupting passages of Scripture, and they plainly contradict the truth. For first, two kinds of passages are confused, the difference between which even boys can see. One kind is of internal relation, of the Son to the Father; the other of external relation, of the Son from the Father to men. The former relation is called mutual, the latter non-mutual. Of internal relation are such statements as "was with God," "is in the Father," "is in the bosom of the Father," "is in heaven"; of external relation are these: "is from God," "proceeded from God," "came from God," "went out from the Father," "came down from heaven," and any others of that kind. For the relation of the Son to the Father, and of the Father to the Son, is mutual and indeed real (as they say), but the relation of God to his creatures is not likewise; since these depend wholly on God, they have a real relation to him, but God does not have one to them. Secondly, even among those things that belong to internal relation, statements about personal subsistence and the mutual indwelling [καὶ' ἀλλήλου περιχώρησιν] (as the Fathers called it) are confused with statements about the community of essence and of its properties. For such expressions as "the Word was with God" (John 1), "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me" (John 14), speak of personal subsistence and of existence in the one [καληλῳ]; but "is in the bosom of the Father," "is in heaven" (John 1 and 3), are said figuratively of the common knowledge of all divine things, which knowledge is essential, not belonging particularly to this person or that one. For when John said, "that only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us," the human manner of speaking required that the intimate and individual counsels of the Father's bosom be set forth without exception by the Son, as if some son were to draw from his father's bosom most lovingly and most familiarly. Likewise, when Christ said that "the Son of man is in heaven," he showed in human manner, by metalepsis of the consequent, that his knowledge of all heavenly things and of the divine mysteries was most present to him, a knowledge plainly divine, so that, while acting on earth, he was in heaven and knew nothing that was not in heaven. These very passages confirm this so clearly that he must be blind who, though the light of this interpretation arises from the passage itself, rejects it.

units.la: Tertiò in iis quæ externæ relationis sunt, par etiam conturbatio a Samosateno inuecta est. Ista enim omnia, est ex Deo, siue a Deo, Ioan. 6. 46. Ego a Deo profectus sum, & veni, siue processi & veni, Ioan. 8. 42. ego exiui a Deo, Ioan. 16. 27. ista inquam relationem vtramque denotant, internam & externam: sed ad externam respiciunt maximè, atque ad eam terminantur. Est enim Deus Pater (vt loquuntur) terminus a quo est, processit, venit, exiuit Filius: et autē in nobis idem Filius, venit, processit, exiuit ad nos, velut terminum ad quem: quia ad nos docendum, redimendū, & seruandum a Patre missus est: ad hunc enim finem officiumque maximè Christus illis in locis respexerat. Ille autem postremus locus, descendit de cælo, interdum illud idem significat, interdum aliud. Idem quum significat, dicitur synecdochicè, quia etiam Pater & Spiritus dicuntur cuntur descendere, vt Genes. 11. & alibi: Christus autem descendens de coelo, a Patre creditur descendere, quia idem Filius qui descendit e coelo, a Patre venit, vt Ioan. 6. Quum autem aliud significat, est νόημα ἀνθρώπινον, vt Ioan. 3. (de noemate paulo ante ex Quinctiliano diximus) & nihil aliud significat quàm mysteria regni coelorum inde allata exponere: vt contrà ascendere in cælum metaphoricè est eadem mysteria penitus recognoscere, & habere ea tamquam in numerato singula. Sic enim Christus loquutus est Ioan. 3. 12. Si terrena dixi vobis, & non creditis, quomodo si cælestia dixero vobis, credetis? & huius dicti rationem Nicodemo afferens, nullus enim ascendit in cælum, inquit, nisi qui descendit de cælo, nempe Filius hominis qui est in cælo. Postremò quòd has omneis loquutiones Samosatenus promiscuè interpretatur pro eo quod est, a Deo edoctus & sanctificatus est, id certè nimis dilutum ad exprimendam tanti mysterij & dispensationis illius diuinæ dignitatè: cùm his ferme singulis loquutionibus & summa illa ac diuina planè relatio inter Patrem & Filium in vnitate essentiæ concludatur, & Patris in Filio communicatio cum suis creaturis, inprimis autem cum electis omnibus demonstretur omnimoda ad gloriam suam, nõ autem doctrinæ solùm (quod iste putat) & sanctificationis in ipso. Sed vt nunc sunt tempora, nihil bonum istis hominibus, nisi interpolatum ex miseris priscorum haereticorum ruderibus. Alterum scriptum nihil est aliud quàm superioris epitoma. Nam resectis ijs quæ aut displicebant, aut nocitura causæ videbantur, vnicam interpretationem retinuit quam magis probandam iudicauit, & nos confutauimus. Sed eamdem incudem nolumus tundere. Quòd autem postea aliquot comportat locos, quorum alij de verbo scripto, non de Sermone æterno Dei, alij de Christo sic argumentantur, manifestatum fuisse illum his vltimis temporibus, tum ergo fuisse primum: haec quàm sint puerilia & ludicra, ex antecedentibus facilè quiuis cognituruς est. Nam priore argumentationis genere, per æquiuocationem fallit: posteriore, nulla est consequentia, sed falsa plane argumentatio nectitur, vt copiosè nota i.segmenti huius ostendimus.
units.tr: Thirdly, in the matters of external relation, Samosatenus has also brought in an equal confusion. For all these expressions, "is from God, or from God" (John 6:46), "I came out from God, and I came" (John 8:42), "I came out from God" (John 16:27), denote both relations, internal and external; but they chiefly look to the external one and are terminated in it. For God the Father (as they say) is the terminus a quo: the Son went forth, came, and came out; and again in us the same Son came, went forth and came out to us, as the terminus ad quem, because he was sent by the Father to teach, redeem and save us; for it was to this end and office that Christ chiefly looked in those places. That last place, "came down from heaven," sometimes signifies the same thing, sometimes something else. When it signifies the same, it is used synecdochically, since the Father and the Spirit are also said to come down (as in Genesis 11 and elsewhere); but Christ, coming down from heaven, is believed to come down from the Father, because the same Son who came down from heaven came from the Father (John 6). When it signifies something else, it is a human conception (νόημα ἀνθρώπινον), as in John 3 (we spoke of this notion a little earlier from Quintilian), and it signifies nothing other than to set forth the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven brought from there; so on the contrary, "to ascend into heaven" is metaphorically to know those mysteries thoroughly and to have each of them as if counted out in hand. For so Christ spoke in John 3:12: "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" and, giving the reason for this saying to Nicodemus, he said: "For no one ascends into heaven, except him who came down from heaven, namely the Son of man who is in heaven." Lastly, that Samosatenus interprets all these expressions indiscriminately as meaning that he was taught and sanctified by God, is certainly far too weak to express the dignity of so great a mystery and of that divine dispensation; since almost each of these expressions concludes that most high and divine relation between Father and Son in unity of essence, and shows the communication of the Father in the Son with his creatures, and above all with all the elect, to his entire glory, and not only of doctrine (as he thinks) and sanctification in him. But as things now are, nothing is good for those men unless it is patched together from the wretched rubbish of the old heretics. The other writing is nothing but an epitome of the earlier one. For, having cut out those things which displeased or seemed harmful to his cause, he kept the single interpretation which he judged more worthy of approval, and we have refuted it. But we do not wish to hammer the same anvil again. As for his later gathering of several passages, some of which argue from the written Word, not from the eternal Word of God, and others argue from Christ that he was manifested in these last times, and therefore that he was first then: how puerile and ludicrous these are, anyone may easily recognise from what has gone before. For in the first kind of argument he deceives by equivocation; in the second, there is no consequence at all, but a plainly false argument is strung together, as we showed at length in the note of this section.
