units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 5.

units.la: Et Sermo illè erat Deus.
units.tr: And the Word was God.

units.la: ARTICVLVS additus est Sermoni, vt subiectum esse de quo Deus praedicatur, intelligatur. Absolutè nomen Dei in Scripturis tribuitur interdum Christo; Patri verò per se primò, quia unus & solus Deus est, praeter quem nullus est alius, qui sit à seipso altissimus, & ex quo omnia. Reliquos ergo omnes, quicunque sint tandem siue Dij, siue Domini, ex illo esse oportet: hoc illi omnes debent, ipse autem a nullo pendens hoc nemini debet, 1. Cor. 8. ¹ Quare & Deus Deorum dicitur, & Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, caputq; eius, Ephes. 1. & 1. Cor. 11. ² Dicitur & solus esse super omneis, per omnia, & in omnibus, Ephes. 4. a nullo factus, nec constitutus, nec electus, nec praeordinatus, nec sanctificatus a quoquam, nec exaltatus, nec missus, vel obediens alicui factus: nullum enim se maiorem habet. ³ Quae omnia praedicta Christo filio Dei ex Maria nato, non alteri, tribuit apertè Scriptura: talemque nobis pingit, vt qui omnia a Patre accepta habeat, & ipse totus Patris sit: ab eo enim est factus filius ex semine David, ex muliere, Roman. 1. Galat. 4. ab eo est factus Dominus & Christus, Actor. 2. cui Pater dedit nomen supra omne nomen, vt adoretur, eo quòd Patri obediens fuit ad mortem crucis, Philip. 2. factus nobis sapientia, iustitia, pax a Deo, 1. Cor. 1. Est a Deo quoque datus nobis Magister & Pastor, vt doceat, nequis audiens illum aberret: datus Seruator, Rex, & caput, ne quem perdat: quare & in eo thesauri omnes sunt abscondIti scientiae Dei, Coloss. 2. & tanta potenta potentia (dominium enim in cælo & in terra a Patre habet, Matth. 28.) ut neminem fallat, ut omneis sibi datos seruet, + eáq; ratione Dominus verè dicatur & Rex, tum Deus noster a Patre vnctus: cui & omnia subiecit (seipsum tantùm excipiendo) ut postremò nos regnumq; suum, deiectus hostibus & morte, reddat Deo & Patri, ex quo accepit, ut sit ille Deus omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15. Hæc est Christi solius prærogatiua & dignitas, quam totam a Patre accepit: in qua illi nemo, post illum unum Deum Patrem, æquandus. Et hac ratione, & non alia, Filius Dei est Deus, Dominus, & Christus, Rex, Sacerdos, caput, Propheta, quòd a Deo sit hoc totum factus, nobisque datus, constitutus, & sanctificatus, & ab æterno destinatus, ut esset Messias, Seruator, omniumq; Dominus, & per quem omnia nobis largiretur Pater. Hoc qui de Christo non sentit, & tamen illum a seipso Deum esse credit, duos Deos inducit, & Patrem summa afficit contumelia.
units.tr: The article has been added to the Word, so that it is understood as the subject of which God is predicated. The name of God is absolutely ascribed in Scripture sometimes to Christ; but to the Father, properly and primarily, because he is the one and only God, besides whom there is no other, who is from himself most high, and from whom all things are. Therefore all the rest, whatever they may be, whether gods or lords, must be from him; all of them owe this, but he, depending on no one, owes this to no one (1 Cor. 8). Hence he is also called the God of gods, and the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the head of Christ (Eph. 1; 1 Cor. 11). He is also said to be the one over all, through all, and in all (Eph. 4); made by no one, constituted by no one, chosen by no one, predestined by no one, sanctified by no one, exalted by no one, sent by no one, nor made obedient to anyone: for he has no one greater than himself. All these things which are predicated of Christ, the Son of God born of Mary, and not of another, Scripture plainly ascribes to him; and it paints him as one who has all things received from the Father, and who himself wholly belongs to the Father: for he was made by him a son of the seed of David, of a woman (Rom. 1; Gal. 4); by him he was made Lord and Christ (Acts 2); to whom the Father gave a name above every name, that every knee should bow to him, because he was obedient to the Father unto the death of the cross (Phil. 2); made to us wisdom, righteousness and peace from God (1 Cor. 1). Also a teacher and minister has been given to us by God, that he may teach, lest anyone who hears him should go astray: given as Saviour, King and head, lest he lose anyone; wherefore in him are all the treasures hidden of the knowledge of God (Col. 2); and with such power (for he has dominion in heaven and on earth from the Father, Matt. 28), that he deceives no one, that he keeps safe all who have been given to him; and on this ground he is truly called Lord and King, and then our God, anointed by the Father; to whom he also subjected all things (excepting himself alone), so that finally, having cast down his enemies and death, he may restore us and his kingdom to God and the Father, from whom he received it, that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15). This is the sole prerogative and dignity of Christ, all of which he received from the Father; in which no one, after the one God the Father, is to be equated with him. And for this reason, and no other, the Son of God is God, Lord and Christ, King, Priest, head, Prophet, because he has been made all this by God, and given, appointed and sanctified to us, and destined from eternity to be the Messiah, Saviour, and Lord of all, and through whom the Father would bestow all things on us. Whoever does not think this of Christ, and yet believes that he is God of himself, introduces two Gods, and puts the greatest insult upon the Father.

units.tr: And the Word was God.

units.la: HOC nomen, Deus, apud Hebræos non est nomen substantiæ proprium aut personæ, sed auctoritatis, dignitatis, ac beneficentiæ. Apud Græcos θεὸς dicitur, quòd opem ferat: unde antiquitas nihil aliud existimabat esse Deum, quàm prodesse mortalibus: & ideò vocabant illum Deum, qui aliquid ad vitæ commoda attulisset. Inde etiam ortum est prouerbium, homo homini Deus. In diuinis autem literis quando hoc nomen tribuitur illi summo omnium auctori Deo, tunc nihil aliud significat quàm ipsum Deum agnoscendum esse profonte, origine, liberatore, atque largitore omnium bonorum. Aliquando tribuitur Angelis ac hominibus, quatenus ab illo primo omnium auctore ad aliquam functionem, honorem, & potestatem euehuntur: non enim alia ratione Angeli & Principes diy vocantur. Sic Moses constituitur Deus super Pharaonem, &c. Quantum verò ad Christum attinet, asserere ipsum ita Deum esse ut habeatur pro illo summo altissimóque omnium auctore, extrema est impietas. Nam in Scripturis diuinis solus ille Pater invisibilis ac omnipatens Iehoua hoc honore insignitur. Ideò Paulus ad Corinthios dicebat, Quamuis sint multi dij, &c. tamen nobis vnus est Deus, nempe Pater ille a quo omnia, & vnus Iesus Christus per quem omnia. Item 1. ad Timoth. 2. Vnus enim est Deus, vnus etiam Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus. Est quidem & Christus Deus, at non ille primus a seipso Deus. Christus ergo Deus esse dicitur ratione sanctificationis, honoris, ac potestatis, gloriæ demum, ac maiestatis ab illo primo altissimóque omnium auctore Patre Deo acceptæ. Non est tamen Christus redigendus in ordinem Angelorum ac hominum, qui hoc Dei nomine insigniti fuere: quia longè maiorem ac excellentiorem honorem, potestatem, gloriam, ac maiestatem a Deo Patre suo accepit, quàm nemo alius, nec omnes simul qui nominati sunt, siue ex Angelis, siue ex hominibus fuerint. Hoc ipsum in genere probat ex comparatione facta per Paulum ad Hebr. inter ipsum Christum Dei filium ac Angelos ac Mosem. Legitur præterea spiritum accepisse sine mensura, ita ut de eius plenitudine omnes acceperint: item quòd Pater omnia in manum illi dederit: item data fuit illi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra. Paulus ad Philipp. scribit Deum extulisse illum, ac illi dedisse nomen quod est supra omne nomen, ut in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur cælestium, terrestrium, & infernorum. Quin ibidem Paulus subiungit in quem finem ista omnia ipsi dederit Deus: nempe, inquit, ut omnis lingua confiteatur quòd Dominus Iesus est Christus ad gloriam Dei Patris. Locus hic tam clarus est, ut iure cavillari non possit: quod si bene teneatur, solui facilè poterunt omnes alij loci qui de Christi dignitate & excellentia loquuntur: nam ita semper intelligi debent, ut altissimo illi Patri Deo omnium auctori sua sit salua gloria. Idem Paulus ad Colos. 1. dicit esse imaginem invisibilis Dei, Dei, primogenitum omnis creaturæ, in ipso creata esse omnia tum quæ in terris, tum quæ in cælis, visibilia & invisibilia, thronos, dominationes, principatus, & potestates: omnia per illum & in illum creata esse, & ipsum esse ante omnia, ac in ipso omnia consistere: esse caput corporis Ecclesiæ, principium, primogenitum ex mortuis: ipsum in omnibus primas tenere. Et ne quis putaret huiusmodi prærogatiuas ac excellentias esse ipsius Christi proprias, statim sese declarans ibidè subdit: Quoniam, inquit, placuit Deo in ipso omnem plenitudinem inhabitare, ac per ipsum omnia reconciliare sibi. Idem Paulus ad Hebr. dicit ipsum esse splendorem Dei, ac characterem substantiæ eius, portaréque omnia verbo suo potenti, & quæ sequuntur. Sunt & alia in hanc sententiam testimonia: sed præcipua allegasse sufficiat. Duo tamen subiungam, quæ sunt ipsius Ioannis: in Apocal. vbi dicit, Dignus est Agnus accipere omnem virtutem ac diuitias, sapientiam, ac fortitudinem, honorem, gloriam, ac benedictionem.
units.tr: The name God, among the Hebrews, is not a proper name of substance or of person, but of authority, dignity and beneficence. Among the Greeks it is called God [θεὸς], because it brings help. Hence antiquity thought that being God was nothing other than benefiting mortals, and so they called God whoever had brought something for the conveniences of life. Hence also the proverb arose: man is God to man. In the divine letters, however, when this name is given to that highest author of all, God, it signifies nothing other than that God himself is to be acknowledged as the source, origin, deliverer and bestower of all good things. Sometimes it is given to angels and men, insofar as they are raised by that first author of all to some office, honour and power: for angels and princes are called gods (dii) for no other reason. Thus Moses is set up as God over Pharaoh, etc. As for Christ, to assert that he is God in such a way that he is held to be that highest and most exalted author of all is the utmost impiety. For in the divine Scriptures that Father alone, invisible and all-present, Iehovah, is marked with this honour. Therefore Paul said to the Corinthians: "Although there are many gods," etc., "yet for us there is one God, that Father from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ through whom are all things." Likewise 1 Tim. 2: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Christ is indeed God, but not that first God from himself. Christ is therefore said to be God by reason of sanctification, honour and power, and finally of glory and majesty received from that first and highest author of all, God the Father. Yet Christ is not to be reduced to the order of angels and men, who have been marked with this name of God, because he has received a far greater and more excellent honour, power, glory and majesty from God his Father than anyone else, or all those named together, whether from among angels or men. Paul proves this in general from the comparison he makes in Hebrews between Christ the Son of God himself and the angels and Moses. It is further read that he received the Spirit without measure, so that all have received of his fullness; likewise that the Father has given all things into his hand; likewise that all power in heaven and on earth was given to him. Paul writes to the Philippians that God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. Indeed Paul adds there for what end God gave him all these things: namely, he says, that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is Christ, to the glory of God the Father. This passage is so clear that it cannot rightly be carped at; and if it is well held, all the other passages that speak of Christ's dignity and excellence can easily be resolved, for they must always be understood so that the glory of that most high Father, God the author of all, remains safe. The same Paul in Col. 1 says that he is the image of the invisible God, God, the firstborn of every creature, that in him were created all things, both those on earth and those in the heavens, visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers: that all things were created through him and in him, that he is before all things and in him all things consist; that he is the head of the body of the Church, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, and that he holds the first place in all things. And lest anyone think such prerogatives and excellences are proper to Christ alone, he immediately goes on to declare himself there: "For," he says, "it pleased God that in him all fullness should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself." The same Paul in Hebrews says that he is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his substance, and that he bears all things by his powerful word, and so on. There are other testimonies to this effect, but it is enough to have cited the principal ones. I will add two more, which are John's own. In the Apocalypse he says: "Worthy is the Lamb to receive all power and riches, wisdom and strength, honour, glory and blessing."

units.la: Sed quod omnem scrupulum eximit, est alterum: quia quum in Ioanne Christus ipse a Iudæis accusaretur, quòd se Deum faceret, respondit, Nonne scriptum est in Lege, ego dixi, dii estis? Si illos dixit Deos ad quos sermo Dei factus est, & non potest solui Scriptura: quem Pater sanctificauit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis blasphemare, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum? Quibus verbis non negauit se Deum esse, sed deitatis ac filiationis suæ rationem explicuit, eámque primariam ac verissimam: & quia homo erat, non aliam deitatis filiationisq; rationem sibi tribuit, quàm quæ à Deo per sanctificationem sibi, vti homini, concederetur. Ista auctoritas tam perspicua ac clara est, vt siquis illam cauillari contendat, plus quàm peruicacissimum se prodat.
units.tr: But the other passage removes every scruple. When in John the Jews accused Christ himself of making himself God, he answered: "Is it not written in your Law, I said, you are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, do you say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world?" By these words he did not deny that he is God, but explained the nature of his deity and sonship, and that the primary and truest nature. And because he was a man, he ascribed to himself no other nature of deity and sonship than that which was granted to him, as a man, by God through sanctification. This authority is so plain and clear that whoever sets out to cavil at it shows himself more than most obstinate.

units.la: Quòd si Moses, Aaron, ac Principes dii sunt dicti propter auctoritatem ac potestatem a Deo sibi concessam, quanto magis Dei filius Christus tam præclaris ac stupendis virtutibus a Patre Deo suo exornatus erit omnium Dominus ac Deus? Ideò Petrus in Actis dicebat, certò sciat tota domus Israël, quod hunc Iesum fecerit Deus Christum ac Dominum, quem vos crucifixistis. Hinc mirum non est, si Pater ille gloriæ in Apostolicis literis vocatur Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi: sed omnium clarissimè apud Paulum, & præcipuè Ephes. 1. cap. Sed quid, quod magister ipse veritatis Christus ore proprio apertissimè dixit? ascendo ad Patrem meum & Patrem vestrum, Deum meum & Deum vestrum. Immo etiam collocatus ad dexteram Dei Patris gubernat Dei Ecclesiam, non uti principalis auctor ac Dominus, sed veluti vicarius. Propterea in die iudicij restituet (quemadmodum scripsit Paulus) regnum Patri, subditúsq; illi erit. Adde quod Christus nusquam docuit se esse Deum illum omnium auctorem, sed semper in omnibus suis verbis ac factis omnem laudem & honorem Patri Deo suo detulit, ut ex Evangelistarum scriptis liquet. Unde perpetuò notandum est, quod omnes prærogativæ ac excellentiæ, quæ in Scripturis Christo attribui leguntur, non uti Deo illi summo omnium auctori, sed uti Mediatori nobis a Deo constituto attribuendæ sunt. Et hac ratione nunquam errari poterit. Et si rogetur, quando Christus a Patre Deo suo huiusmodi potestatem, gloriam, ac maiestatem acceperit, divus Petrus epist. 2. cap. 1. exponit. Accepit enim, inquit, a Deo Patre honorem ac gloriam voce delapsa ad eum huiusmodi, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui, ipsum audite: & hanc vocem, inquit, nos audiuimus, quum essemus cum ipso in monte sancto. Habes igitur, qua ratione Christus sit Deus.
units.tr: But if Moses, Aaron and the princes are called gods because of the authority and power granted them by God, how much more will God's Son Christ, adorned by his Father God with such splendid and wonderful virtues, be the Lord and God of all? So Peter said in the Acts: let all the house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. Hence it is no wonder that in the apostolic letters that Father of glory is called the God of our Lord Jesus Christ; and most clearly of all in Paul, and especially in Eph. 1. But what of the fact that Christ, the teacher of truth himself, said most plainly with his own mouth: "I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God"? Indeed, even seated at the right hand of God the Father, he governs the Church of God, not as the principal author and Lord, but as a vicegerent. Therefore in the day of judgment he will hand over the kingdom to the Father (as Paul wrote), and will be subject to him. Add that Christ nowhere taught that he himself is that God, the author of all, but in all his words and deeds he always gave all praise and honour to his Father, his God, as is clear from the writings of the Evangelists. Hence it must always be noted that all the prerogatives and excellences that are read as ascribed to Christ in the Scriptures are to be ascribed to him not as to that highest God, the author of all, but as to the Mediator appointed for us by God. By this rule one will never go wrong. And if it is asked when Christ received such power, glory and majesty from his Father God, the divine Peter explains it in 2 Pet. 1: for he received, he says, honour and glory from God the Father, when a voice came down to him of this kind: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." And this voice, he says, we heard, when we were with him on the holy mountain. You have, therefore, the reason why Christ is God.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOX.

units.la: Quòd hæc verba Samosatenus prior de sua fede transtulit, non temere id, sed artificiosè & certo consilio factum, vt in antecedentem locum monuimus. Sic enim se putauit facilius assequuturum quod tentat: nimirum vt persuadeat non esse Christum (quod ex Scripturis docemus) cemus) a principio λόγου Dei Patris, nec esse a principio apud Deum; sed ex quo a Patre missus est & perfunctus apud homines vocatione sua, factum esse ab illo Deum, id est, non natura, sed voluntate, non essentialiter, sed effectiuè, non per se, sed per communicationem a Patre, nō propriè, sed figuratè Deum appellari. Horret animus cogitantis & reputantis istam audaciam, qua & Dei gloria traditur alteri quàm vero & essentiali Deo, contra quàm apud Prophetas centies iurauit Deus; & tota Scriptura de Christo Filio Dei æterno obscuratur, corrumpitur, atque peruertitur, vt verbis Samosateni vtar, & Christus Dei filius exstirpatur funditus, & secundus Deus extra essentiam Dei introducitur ad abolendum illum solum verum Deum essentia vnicum, personis trinum, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum; & fides nostra ac communis salus, quæ finis est fidei nostræ, labefactatur quàm indignissimè. Sed ad rem. De articulo quod dicit, bene est: Et illud bene, quòd nomen Dei (addo etiam Iehouæ nomen extra essentiam incommunicabile, quia est essentiæ) absolutè in Scripturis tribuitur interdum Christo. At sequentia ferme omnia captionum laqueis abundant, vt quum ait, Patri verò per se primò tribuitur, quia vnus & solus Deus est, præter quem nullus est alius qui sit a seipso altissimus, & ex quo omnia. Quapropter primum membrorum singulorum, tum verò vniuersæ argumentationis veritatem exponemus. Nomen Dei Samosatenus ait Patri primò per se tribui. Ac Dei quidem nomen tribui personæ Patris, inter nos conuenit: sed primò & per se quum dicitur, aut diuinæ essentiæ, aut personæ respectu dicitur & notionalis actus ipsius, vt vocant Scholastici. Respectu diuinæ essentiæ, quæ vnica est trium personarum communis, non solùm Pater, sed & Filius, & Spiritus sanctus primò & per se Deus est. Nam vt particulare secundùm Logicos nec deminuit, nec dilatat rationem communis, sic personæ vnius ratio rationem immutare non potest essentiæ. Respectu verò personæ & notionalis actus quem operatur persona Patris in gignendo Filio & spirando Spiritu, Pater, qui secundùm essentiæ vnius communitatem Deus est cum Filio & Spiritu sancto, non primò & per se Deus dicendus est, si proprie ex relationis natura velimus loqui; sed primò & per se Pater: ac proinde Deus Pater, vt in Scripturis appellatur passim, secundùm essentiam Deus, secundùm personam actúmque suum notionalem Pater. Itaque si dixeris, Qui Deus est, primò & per se Deus est; verissima est propositio eáque communis Patri, Filio, & Spiritui sancto. Si item, Pater primò & per se Deus est, & hæc verissima: nā commune de particulari dicitur citra exclusionem communicantium, Filij, & Spiritus sancti, essentiale de persona: cùm etiam commodè eodem iure possimus dicere, Filius primò & per se Deus est, itémque Spiritus sanctus. Sed fallit hoc loco Samosatenus duobus modis: primùm quòd in hac propositione, nomen Dei Patri primò per se tribui, tacitè inesse statuit vocem exclusiuam solùm, eámque vi istarum vocum, primò per se, quodammodo contineri: secundò quòd istas voces, primò & per se, aliter accipit, & alio respectu, quàm conuenit argumento. Prius salsissimum est. Quid enim? an ignorat iste voces communes, ac non singulares & individuales, in re Logica spectari oportere? Singulare est Petrus, Ioannes, &c. commune homo. De Petro, de Ioanne quum agit Logicus, secundùm rationem communis agit, puta hominis, animalis, &c. Quemadmodum autem Petrus e ratione hominis non excludit Ioannem, sic etiam persona e ratione deitatis siue essentiæ diuinæ non excludit personam. Etenim quis argumentantem in hunc modum audiat? nes est homo: non igitur Petrus homo est. Homo est animal: leo igitur non est animal. Multo minus audiendus a nobis fuerit qui dicet, Pater est primò & per se Deus: Filius ergo non est primò & per se Deus. Posterius vitium (æquiuocatio enim indigna atque insci ta est) quicquid obtendatur, non magis poterit excusari. Vnum alteri primò tribuitur, quòd illius est sine alia consequutione vlla accedente: per se verò tribuitur, quod non per accidens. Illo consequutio prioritatis naturæ (vt vocant) excluditur: hoc, ratio accidentium. Deus de Patre dicitur: & consequitur natura primò, vt Pater sit Deus, non autem vice versa, vt Deus sit Pater solus exclusò Filio & Spiritu sancto: quia prædicatum non est adæquatum, vt loquuntur, cùm Deus sit commune totius essentiæ, & vox Pater sit individualis personæ. Hoc illud est quod Logici appellant dici primò de aliquo, aut primò alicui tribui. Vafre autem illudit, tamquam præstigijs, iste ἀτερμόλογος confundens terminos artium, quum vocem primò Logicè vsurpatam de consequutione vocum in sermone nostro, ad naturam subiecti transfert, adfirmans nomen Dei Patri primò tribui, quia videlicet primus tempore, & causa, & dignitate est, adeóque verus Deus solus, vt ipse loquitur illudens veritati. Logicè enim primò de Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto prædicatur nomen Dei: Theologicè verò secundum distinctionem personarum quam ex Scripturis didicimus, & proprietates notionales ipsarum, Pater primò vel potiùs (nam illud non sine vitio dicitur) primus Deus est non tempore, consequutione, aut dignitate, sed ordine naturæ, quà est Pater Filij, & spirans Spiritum: cui naturæ etiam respondet œconomia, id est, dispositio interna & externa dispensatio, vt orthodoxi Patres olim loquuti sunt. Logicus, quid de quo dicatur etiam primò, observat Logicè: Theologus, quid sit quod dicitur, obferuat Theologicè in Logica enunciatione. Eadem que que fallacia est in vocibus, per se, quæ in hac enunciatione sunt. Aliud enim est per se dici, prædicatum puta de subiecto, aliud per se esse, subiectum puta quod agitur: quæ duo tamen Samosatenus confundit inscienter, an malitiosé? Per se autem dicuntur de subiecto, siue prædicantur, primum quæcunque insunt in eo quod quid est, hoc est, & in subiecto, & in definitione illius: sic Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, Spiritus sanctus est Deus: prædicatum istud, Deum esse, de subiecto per se dicitur, nimirum quia prædicatum essentiale est, qui primus apud Logicos eorum est quæ per se dicuntur modus. Secundò per se dicuntur de subiecto ea prædicata quæ subiecto insunt, & ita quidem insunt ut definiri aliter nó possint quàm mentione subiecti facta. Sic Deus est summum bonum, creator, & siqua sunt eiusmodi. Hic enim prædicata ista subiecto insunt, eáque definiri siquando opus est, non aliter definias quàm Dei mentione facta. Nam & summum bonum, & Creator Deus est: nec alia via summum bonum & Creator rectè definiri potest. Tertiò per se de subiecto dicuntur, quæ non dicuntur de subiecto alio aliquo, sed ipsius subiecti ὑπαρξιν, existentiam & ipsum esse substantiarum siue primarum, siue secundarū denotant. Sic homo est, id est, subsistat: Ioannes est, id est, subsistit. Deus est, id est, subsistat: Pater est, Filius est, id est, subsistit. Atque hic modus dicendi per se, communis est omnium enunciationum basis, & fundamentum summum. Postremo autem per se de subiecto dicuntur, quæ propter ipsa insunt subiecto: quo in genere externæ causæ, efficiens & finalis, earumque effecta continentur. His enim conditio siue limitatio eiusmodi inter subiectum & attributum conficitur, ut attributum illud non possit intelligi nisi facta mentione subiecti, cui sua conditio adiuncta est. Dicam cam familiarius diuerso ordine. Per se prædicationes dicuntur quatuor modis: quorum duo sunt de esse subiecti, duo de ratione illius. De esse subiecti dicuntur, primùm ὑπαρξις, existentia, subiectum puta substare aut subsistere: atque hic modus Aristotelis Logicorumq; tertius: secundò quod essentiale est subiecti, pertinens ad definitionem & constitutionem illius: atq; hic modus illorum primus. De ratione verò subiecti prædicantur, primùm ἴδιον vel accidens (vt vocant) proprium, quod definiri citra subiecti mentionem non potest: atq; hic secundus illis modus: deinde causans & causatum, qui postremus est illorum modus. Secundùm modum hyparxeos & Deus per se est, vt substantia vel essentia ὑπόστασις, & Pater per se est, vt subsistentia siue persona subsistens in vnica illa essentia Dei, & Filius per se est, & Spiritus sanctus consimiliter: subsistit enim vnaquæq; persona in vnitate essentiæ. Secundum τὸ ἀυτῶδες, & Deus est Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus: & e diuerso Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, & Spiritus sanctus Deus, & quidem Deus per se subsistens in vnitate essentiæ. Secundùm τὸ ἰδίωμα, Pater non dicitur Deus per se (nam hoc ad modum illum minimè pertinet) sed Pater per se, siue principium æternùm gignens Filium: & Filius quoque non dicitur Deus per se, sed Filius appellatur æternùm genitus à Patre. Secundùm τὸ αἴτιον non nisi improprie Pater Deus per se appellari potest, vt causa Filij: quia nomen causæ videtur importare diuersitatem substantiæ, & dependentiam quamdam vnius ab altero, adeoque differentiam inter causam & id cuius est causa secundùm perfectionem aut virtutem aliquam. Hinc fit vt Deus per se de Patre prædicari non possit, tanquam si paternitas ipsius causa esset cur sit Deus: cùm Pater, quà Deus ac nō persona solùm, vnica sit causa causarum & principium principiorum a nemine pendens, sed habens omnia a se dependetia. Pater ergo substat per se, vt Deus, & subsistit vt persona: similiterque Filius substat per se vt Deus, & subsistit vt persona καθ' ὑπαρξιν: & Spiritus sanctus consimiliter. Κατὰ τὸ χρονῶδες autem Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, Spiritus sanctus Deus: nomen Dei per se de personis subsistentibus praedicatur. Quicunque dicendi per se praeterea sunt modi, ij ad quæstionem hanc minime pertinent. Sed hic latet SamosatenIana captio, quòd loquutione hac per se, vt voce primò ante abutitur. Nō enim simpliciter illud per se & Logicè accipit, sed altera interpretatione studiosè insidiatur piorū mentibus, vt statim intelligant Patrem esse Deum primò & per se, id est, non ab alio: Filium vero non a se aut per se, sed ab alio esse Deum communicatione gratiæ. Hoc Samosateni consilium esse demonstrant verba proximè sequentia, quum ait, nullus est alius qui sit a seipso Altissimus, &c. Atqui, vir bone, non ignoras aliud esse per se dici Logicè, aliud per se esse, cùm illud prædicationum modu spectet, hoc naturam rerum. Tum etiam nec illud ignoras, aliud loquutione per se, aliud loquutione a se solere significare, cùm illud essentiæ, hoc sit originis. Apage istas argutias & sphingas verborum, quibus nō perducūtur ad veritatem, sed circumuenIuntur imperiti. Sequitur, quia unus & solus Deus est: ambiguè, vt & Defensione 2. ostendimus. Nam hæc verba aut de Deo essentialiter dicuntur, aut de persona Patris. Si de Deo essentialiter, nihil verius: nam etiam Deus essentialiter sancta & adoranda Trinitas appellatur. Sin de persona Patris, iterum ambiguè. Nam illa verba, vnus & solus, aut subiecto hærent, vnus & solus Pater (exclusò videlicet Filio & Spiritu sancto) est Deus, aut prædicato, Pater est vnus & solus Deus. Prius negamus: nam & Filius Deus est, & Spiritus sanctus est Deus vt Pater. Posterius distinguimus: aut enim accipitur Deus essentialiter, tialiter, Pater est is Deus, id est, ea persona deitatis, quae deitas est vnus & solus Deus essentialiter: atque hoc verissimum: aut praedicatum accipitur personaliter vt determinatum subiecto, quasi dicas, persona Patris vnic• est vnus & solus Deus: quam enunciationem Deo ipso auctore pernegamus. Addit, praeter quem nullus est alius qui sit a seipso altissimus, & ex quo omnia. Quod enunciatum verum agnoscimus de Deo essentialiter, de persona Patris distinguimus. Nam si verbum est secundum naturam essentiae dicitur pro eo quod Scholastici dicunt substare, cum vna sit essentia Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti, eaque a nullo sit omnino Filius & Spiritus sanctus, secundum essentiam a nullo sunt vt Pater, vel (vt Samosatenus loquitur) a seipsis sunt: nam sunt cum Patre vnum. Sinautem secundum rationem personae dicitur, nullus est alius, pro eo quod est subsistit, & fit eius cum Filio & Spiritu sancto comparatio, cum persona Patris fit a nullo, persona Filij fit a Patre, & persona sancti Spiritus ab vtraque, vere dicitur de Patre instituta illa personarum comparatione inter se, nullum esse alium qui sit a seipso, id autem est, a nullo: sola enim persona Patris a nullo est. De altissimi nomine iam ante diximus Defensionis 2. segmento 6. Illud vero quod post adijcitur, & ex quo omnia, captiosum est duobus modis: tum quia omnia quum dicuntur, relatio fit proprie & oppositio Dei ad creaturas, hic vero oppositionem instituit etiam Patris ad Filium & Spiritum sanctum, & appellatione omnium ipsum quoque Filium complectitur, per quem sunt omnia & qui est supra omnia ὑπερ́ανος: tum quia ex Patre solo, tamquam Deo solo (excluso Filio & Spiritu sancto) omnia affirmat esse: id est, opus essentiae totius, ac proinde commune personarum in essentia subsistentium singulare statuit esse personae Patris: contra quam praecipiunt Logici ex communi efficiens particulare, vt iam aliquoties antehac diximus. Hic vero dicturi sunt, atqui haec singula ipsissima sunt Scripturæ verba, Ioan. 17. 3. & 1. Cor. 8. 4. & 1. Tim. 2. 5. & aliis praeterea locis. Scripturam sacram agnoscimus: sed confunduntur quæ diuisa sunt, & germana eorum sententia omittitur. De his autem singulis Scripturæ locis in Defensione 2. diximus segmento 4. & 10. & alibi passim. Ex Ioannis 17. hic nunquam probaturus est solum Patrem esse Deum, solam inquam personam Patris, sed Patrem esse Deum illum qui solus est essentia Deus: quod etiam personæ Filij & Spiritus sancti commune est. Quod si rem Samosatenus penitius introspexerit, videbit a se fallacia diuisionis comittii in hac sua interpretatione. Nam hæ voces, illum esse solum verum Deum, non de solo Patre, sola persona illius prædicantur, sed ἀπὸ κοινῶς de Patre & Filio sunt enunciatæ: vt cognoscant, inquit, te & quem misisti Iesum Christum esse illum solum verû Deum, personas videlicet distinctas in vnitate essentiæ. Sic autem de Christo accipi oportere, qui cum sit natura Deus, œconomia vel dispensatione propter nos homines & salutem nostram seipsum exinaniuit, demonstrant ea quæ proximè sequuntur versu 5. glorifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum ea gloria, quam habui apud te prius quàm hic mundus exisseret: quæ verba ad prædordinationem referri est iniquissimum, & a vocibus illis, quam habui apud te, &c. totàque substantia verborum Christi alienissimum. Illa quoque, 1. Cor. 8. nullus est Deus alius nisi vnus, sanctissimè credimus atque confitemur. Nam Deus essentialis est appellatio: esse est subsistere, hic de essentia dictum; non autem subsistere, quod personarum est, in quibus subsistat essentia, & de quibus essentia dicitur. Demonstrat hoc Paulus oppositione idolorum essentiæ cum Deo, Scimus, inquit, idolum nihil esse in mundo, & nullum esse Deum alium nisi nisi vnum: confirmat sequente exegesi ; Nam etiamsi sint qui dicantur dij & in cœlo & in terra (sed æquiuocè dicātur, licet non sint dij & domini vt Deus) sicut sunt dij multi & domini multi (nempe qui dicuntur esse, non autem sunt vt Deus & dominus noster est) Nobis tamen vnus est Deus, Pater ille, ex quo hæc omnia, & nos in ipsum: & vnus Dominus Iesus Christus, per quem hæc omnia, & nos per ipsum. Dixerit fortasse, at fit oppositio Dei Patris & Domini IesuChristi. Negamus: neque oppositio ista pertinuisset quicquam ad consilium Apostoli sermonemque instituturn. Oppositio fit duplex: non Dei Patris, & Filij, sed vna Dei Patris & rerum creatarum, altera Domini gubernantis & rerum gubernatarum. Deus autem quum Pater dicitur oppositione ad creaturas, Pater dicitur essentialiter: ac proinde Pater, Filius, & Spritus sanctus communis est rerum creatarum Pater, vt in Scripturis nominatur passim, Deuter. 32.6. Matth.5.&6.&7. Iacobi 3.9.& alibi. Hic enim Deus non personaliter relatione ad Filium, sed essentialiter oppositione ad creaturas appellatur Pater: quapropter etiā optimè huic causa efficiens & finalis cùm rerum omnium, tum sanctæ Ecclesiæ tribuitur, a quo hæc omnia, & nos in ipsum. Atque hæc oppositio prior. Altera oppositio ad medium quoque spectat, quo resomes a Deo factæ & propter ipsum, eodem auctore a principio ad finem suum perducuntur, vt Deus sit omnia in omnibus. Medium autem est dominium & regnum salutare Christi: mediator Dominus, natura quidem Deus, sed intermedius tamen Dominus diuina dispensatione & voluntaria, per quem hæc omnia, & nos per ipsum a principio ad finem illum dirigimur. Vt ergo de Patris nomine, sic etiam de voce Domini statuimus. Modo enim ad essentiam respicit, secundùm quam Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus Dominus vnus appellatur, est enim natura dominus: modo ad perso-
units.tr: That Samosatenus transferred these words to his own faith in the first place was no accident. As we noted in the preceding passage, he did it deliberately and by design. He thought he would more easily achieve what he was attempting in this way, namely to persuade us that Christ is not from the beginning the Word (λόγου) of God the Father, nor from the beginning with God (as we teach from the Scriptures). Rather, from the time he was sent by the Father and had completed his calling among men, he became God, that is, not by nature but by will, not essentially but effectively, not in himself but by communication from the Father, and he is called God not properly but figuratively. My mind shudders when it considers and weighs this audacity, by which the glory of God is handed over to another than the true and essential God, contrary to what God swore a hundred times through the Prophets. The whole of Scripture concerning Christ the eternal Son of God is obscured, corrupted and perverted, to use Samosatenus' own words, and Christ the Son of God is rooted out utterly, and a second God is introduced outside the essence of God, to abolish that one true God, one in essence and three in persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Our faith and our common salvation, which is the goal of our faith, are shaken most unworthily. But to the matter. He says, "it is well" about the article, and it is well that the name of God (I add also the name Jehovah, which is incommunicable outside the essence, because it belongs to the essence) is at times attributed absolutely to Christ in the Scriptures. But almost everything that follows is full of snares of sophistry, as when he says: but to the Father, first and of himself, is attributed the title, because he is the one and only God, besides whom there is no other who is the Most High of himself, and from whom are all things. Therefore we shall set out the truth of each clause, first of the individual parts and then of the whole argument. Samosatenus says that the name of God is attributed to the Father first and of himself. We agree that the name of God is attributed to the person of the Father. But when it is said first and of himself, it is said either with respect to the divine essence or with respect to the person and its notional act, as the Scholastics call it. With respect to the divine essence, which is one and common to the three persons, not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit are God first and of themselves. For just as the particular, according to the logicians, neither diminishes nor enlarges the notion of the common, so the notion of one person cannot alter the notion of the essence. But with respect to the person and the notional act which the person of the Father performs in begetting the Son and breathing the Spirit, the Father, who is God together with the Son and the Holy Spirit by the commonness of the one essence, is not to be called God first and of himself, if we wish to speak properly from the nature of the relation; rather he is to be called Father first and of himself. Accordingly, God the Father, as he is commonly named in the Scriptures, is God according to the essence and Father according to his person and his notional act. So if you say, "He who is God is God first and of himself," the proposition is most true, and it is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, if you say, "The Father is God first and of himself," this too is most true, for the common is predicated of the particular without excluding those who share it, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the essential is predicated of the person. Indeed, by the same right we may fittingly say, "The Son is God first and of himself," and likewise, "The Holy Spirit is God first and of himself." But Samosatenus deceives in this place in two ways. First, he assumes that the exclusive word alone is tacitly present in this proposition, "the name of God is attributed first and of himself to the Father," and that it is in some way contained in the force of these words "first and of himself." Second, he takes these words "first and of himself" in a different sense and with a different reference from what the argument requires. The first is most false. For what? Does he not know that common terms, not singular and individual ones, must be regarded in logic? "Peter" and "John" are singular; "man" is common. When the logician speaks of Peter or John, he speaks according to the notion of the common, for example of man or animal. And just as Peter, by the notion of man, does not exclude John, so the person, by the notion of deity or the divine essence, does not exclude the other persons. For who would listen to someone arguing in this way: "Peter is a man; therefore Peter is not a man. A man is an animal; therefore a lion is not an animal"? Much less should we listen to the one who says, "The Father is God first and of himself; therefore the Son is not God first and of himself." The second fault (for it is an equivocation, unworthy and unskilled) cannot be excused by any pretext. One thing is attributed to another first when it belongs to that other without any further consequence attaching; it is attributed of itself when it is not so by accident. The first excludes the consequence of priority of nature (as they call it); the second excludes the nature of accidents. "God" is said of the Father, and by the nature of the thing it follows first that the Father is God, but not conversely, that God is the Father alone, excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the predicate is not coextensive, as they say, since God is common to the whole essence, while the word Father is the individual of a person. This is what the logicians call being said first of something, or being attributed first to something. But this crafty man, that ἀτερμόλογος (the word-twister), plays tricks like a conjuror, confusing the terms of the arts. When he takes the word "first", used logically of the order of words in our speech, and transfers it to the nature of the subject, he asserts that the name of God is attributed first to the Father, because he is evidently first in time, cause and dignity, and so is the only true God, as he himself speaks, mocking the truth. For logically the name of God is predicated first of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alike. Theologically, however, according to the distinction of persons which we have learned from the Scriptures, and their notional properties, the Father is first, or rather (for that is not said without fault) he is the first God, not in time, sequence or dignity, but in the order of nature, inasmuch as he is the Father of the Son and breathes the Spirit. To this order of nature there also corresponds the economy, that is, the internal disposition and external dispensation, as the orthodox Fathers of old spoke. The logician observes logically what is said of what, even if it is said first; the theologian observes theologically what the thing is that is said, in a logical statement. The same fallacy lies in the words "of himself" that occur in this statement. For it is one thing to be said of itself, that is, for a predicate to be asserted of a subject, and another thing to be of oneself, that is, for the subject of which something is said to exist of itself. Yet Samosatenus confuses these two, ignorantly or maliciously? Now there are several ways in which something is said of a subject "of itself", or predicated of it. First, whatever is contained in the what-it-is of the thing, that is, both in the subject and in its definition: thus the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God. This predicate, "to be God", is said of the subject of itself, because it is an essential predicate, which among the logicians is the first mode of what is said of itself. Second, those predicates are said of a subject of itself which belong to the subject, and belong to it in such a way that they cannot be defined otherwise than by mentioning the subject. So God is the highest good, the creator, and whatever else is of that kind. For these predicates belong to the subject, and if they must be defined at any time, you cannot define them except by mentioning God. For both the highest good and the creator are God, and the highest good and the creator cannot be rightly defined in any other way. Third, those things are said of a subject of itself which are not said of some other subject, but which signify the existence of the subject itself, and its very being, whether of primary or secondary substances. Thus "man is", that is, subsists; "John is", that is, subsists. "God is", that is, subsists; "the Father is", "the Son is", that is, subsists. This mode of saying "of itself" is common to all statements and is their highest basis and foundation. Last, those things are said of a subject of itself which belong to the subject on account of themselves. Under this kind are contained the external causes, efficient and final, and their effects. For by these a condition or limitation of this sort is formed between subject and attribute, so that the attribute cannot be understood unless the subject is mentioned, to which its condition is joined. I shall state this more familiarly and in a different order. Predications of themselves are said in four ways, two of which concern the being of the subject, and two its nature. Those concerning the being of the subject are, first, ὑπαρξις, existence, that is, the subject's standing or subsisting; this is the third mode of Aristotle and the logicians. Second, what is essential to the subject, pertaining to its definition and constitution; this is their first mode. Those concerning the nature of the subject are, first, the proper or accident (as they call it), which cannot be defined without mention of the subject; this is their second mode. Then, the cause and the caused, which is their last mode. According to the mode of hyparxis (existence), God is of himself, as substance or essence, and the Father is of himself as hypostasis, a subsisting person subsisting in that one essence of God, and the Son is of himself, and the Holy Spirit likewise; for each person subsists in the unity of the essence. According to τὸ αὐτῶδες (the self-same), God is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and conversely the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, indeed God subsisting of himself in the unity of the essence. According to the property (ἰδίωμα), the Father is not called God of himself (for this has nothing to do with that mode), but the Father of himself, that is, the eternal principle begetting the Son; and the Son too is not called God of himself, but is named the Son eternally begotten of the Father. According to the cause (αἴτιον), the Father can be called God of himself only improperly, as the cause of the Son; for the name of cause seems to imply a diversity of substance and a certain dependence of one on the other, and hence a difference between the cause and that of which it is the cause, in perfection or some power. Hence it follows that "God of himself" cannot be predicated of the Father as if his fatherhood were the cause of his being God, since the Father, as God and not merely as person, is the one cause of causes and the principle of principles, depending on no one, but having all things from himself, which are dependent. The Father therefore subsists of himself as God, and subsists as a person; likewise the Son subsists of himself as God, and subsists as a person by kath' hyparxin (by way of existence); and so the Holy Spirit. According to κατὰ τὸ χρονῶδες (the temporal), the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God: the name of God is predicated of the subsisting persons of itself. Any other modes of saying "of itself" do not pertain to this question at all. But the Samosatenian trick lies hidden here, in that he abuses the phrase "of itself", as he earlier abused the word "first". For he does not take that "of itself" simply and in the logical sense, but, through the other interpretation, he craftily lays a trap for pious minds, so that they will at once understand that the Father is God first and of himself, that is, not from another, while the Son is not God of himself or through himself, but is God from another by communication of grace. That this was Samosatenus' design is shown by the words that immediately follow, where he says, there is no other who is the Most High of himself, and so on. Yet, my good man, you are not ignorant that one thing is to be said of itself in the logical sense, and another thing is to be of itself; the former concerns the modes of predication, the latter the nature of things. Nor are you ignorant that the phrase "of itself" usually signifies one thing and "from himself" another, the former referring to essence, the latter to origin. Away with such quibbles and verbal riddles, by which the unlearned are not led to the truth but are deceived. He continues: because he is the one and only God. This is ambiguous, as we have also shown in Defence 2. For these words are said either of God essentially or of the person of the Father. If of God essentially, nothing is more true, for God in his essence is also called the holy and adorable Trinity. But if of the person of the Father, it is again ambiguous. For the words one and only either cling to the subject, so that "the one and only Father (excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit) is God", or they cling to the predicate, so that "the Father is the one and only God". We deny the former, for the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God as the Father is. As to the latter, we distinguish: for either God is taken essentially, and then "the Father is that God", that is, that person of the Godhead which is the Godhead, which is essentially the one and only God; and this is most true. Or the predicate is taken personally, as determined by the subject, as if you said, "the person of the Father is the one and only God"; and this statement we flatly deny, on the authority of God himself. He adds: besides whom there is no other who is the Most High of himself, and from whom are all things. We acknowledge this statement as true of God essentially, but as to the person of the Father we make a distinction. For if the verb is is used according to the nature of the essence, for what the Scholastics call "to stand under" (substare), since the essence of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one, and the Son and the Holy Spirit are altogether from no one as to the essence, then they are not from another as the Father is, or (as Samosatenus says) they are not from themselves, for they are one with the Father. But if it is used according to the notion of the person, so that "there is no other" means "that which subsists", and the comparison with the Son and the Holy Spirit is made, then, since the person of the Father is from no one, the person of the Son is from the Father, and the person of the Holy Spirit from both, it is rightly said of the Father, in this comparison of the persons with one another, that there is no other who is of himself, that is, from no one; for only the person of the Father is from no one. We have already spoken of the name of the Most High in Defence 2, section 6. But what is added afterward, and from whom are all things, is deceptive in two ways. First, because when all things is said, a relation and opposition properly arises between God and creatures; but here he sets up an opposition of the Father to the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by the term all things he also includes the Son himself, through whom all things are and who is above all things, ὑπερ́ανος (supra-celestial). Second, because he affirms that all things are from the Father alone, as God alone (excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit); that is, he makes the work of the whole essence a peculiar work of the person of the Father, which is common to the persons subsisting in the essence. This is contrary to the precept of the logicians, who derive the particular from the common efficient, as we have said several times before. But here they will say, "Yet these are the very words of Scripture: John 17:3, 1 Cor. 8:4, 1 Tim. 2:5, and other places besides." We acknowledge the holy Scripture, but what has been separated is confused, and its true meaning is omitted. We have spoken of each of these passages of Scripture in Defence 2, sections 4 and 10, and elsewhere in many places. From John 17 he will never prove that the Father alone is God, meaning the person of the Father alone, but that the Father is that God who alone is God in essence, which is also common to the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit. If Samosatenus had looked more deeply into the matter, he would see that he has committed the fallacy of division in this interpretation. For these words, that they may know you to be the only true God, are not predicated of the Father alone, of his person alone, but are said ἀπὸ κοινῶς (in common) of the Father and of the Son: that they may know you, he says, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, to be the only true God, namely the persons distinct in the unity of the essence. That this must be understood of Christ in that way is shown by what immediately follows in verse 5: glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made. To refer this prayer to a prior ordination is most unjust, and altogether alien to the words which I had with you, and to the whole substance of Christ's words. That passage also, 1 Cor. 8, there is no God but one, we most holily believe and confess. For God is an essential appellation; is means to subsist, and here it is said of the essence, not of subsisting, which belongs to the persons in whom the essence subsists and of whom the essence is predicated. Paul demonstrates this by opposing idols to the essence of God: We know, he says, that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no God but one. He confirms it by the following explanation: For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth (but they are called so equivocally, since they are not gods and lords as God is), as there are gods many and lords many (namely those who are said to be, but are not, as our God and Lord is), yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him. Someone might perhaps say that here there is an opposition of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. We deny it: nor would such an opposition have had anything to do with the Apostle's purpose and argument. The opposition is twofold: not of God the Father and the Son, but of the one God the Father and created things, and of the Lord governing and the things governed. Now when God is called Father in opposition to creatures, he is called Father essentially, and so the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are alike the Father of created things, as he is named throughout the Scriptures, Deut. 32:6, Matt. 5, 6 and 7, James 3:9, and elsewhere. For here God is called Father not personally, in relation to the Son, but essentially, in opposition to creatures. Therefore the efficient and final cause of all things, and of the holy Church, is most rightly attributed to him: of whom are all things, and we in him. This is the first opposition. The second opposition looks also to the mediator, through whom the things made by God and for him are led, by the same author, from beginning to end, so that God may be all in all. The mediator is the lordship and saving kingdom of Christ: the Lord mediator, God by nature indeed, but nevertheless the intermediate Lord by divine and voluntary dispensation, by whom are all things, and we by him, are directed from beginning to end. So, as we have settled the name of Father, so also we settle the word Lord. For sometimes it refers to the essence, according to which Father, Son and Holy Spirit are called one Lord, since he is Lord by nature; sometimes it refers to the person (of the Son), who as a person is Lord in a singular way, beyond the common and natural essence, namely by will and by the dispensation undertaken, which we have just touched upon. Therefore the Apostle sets the self-existent God (αὐτοθεὸς) over against the essence of idols made by human hands and art, and by this distinction establishes between...

units.la: P nam Filij, quæ persona singulari modo est Dominus, præter communem essentiæ & naturalem illum, nimirum voluntate & suscepta dispensatione, quam modo attigimus. Quapropter Apostolus essentiam Dei αὐτοθεὸς opponit idolorum manu & arte factorum essentiæ, & distinctione statuit inter dici & esse, quum his verbis utitur, esse qui dicuntur dij & in cœlo & in terra, ut de Deo secundum essentiam loqui ostenderet. Postremi loci ratio consimilis. Vnus enim Deus est, ait Paulus, vnus etiam Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Varia est huius loci interpretatio: & ut ea concedatur quam Samosatenus arripit, nihil vincet tamen. Primum enim vox Deus aut essentialiter accipitur, vt ante dixerat hoc bonum est & acceptum coram Deo Seruatore nostro, aut personaliter. Deinde vocem vnus alij de essentia intelligunt, vt quum dicitur, Iehoua Deus tuus Deus vnus est: alij de constantia & immutabili voluntate, vt Galat. 3. Deus vnus est, ibi constans idemque permanens. Qui ad vnitatem essentiæ referunt, sic argumentantur, Quorum vnus Deus est, alij pro alijs orare debent. Quorumuis hominum vnus Deus est, vt Rom. 3. Quorum ergo homines alij pro alijs orare debent. Qui vero ad vnitatem & constantiam voluntatis, alio modo. Sed his omissis concedimus, affirmamus, clamamus Deum vnum esse, vnicam Dei essentiam, optime nobis cum Paulo convenit: sed vnicæ personæ Patris diuinam essentiam esse, hoc nec Paulus vnquam dixit, nec nos concedimus. Cum Paulo dicimus Deum quidem esse vnum essentia: Patre vero esse personam vnam, in communitate essentiæ vnū Deum cū Filio & Spiritu sancto, ex Paulo & reliquis Scripturis didicimus. Iam de argumentatione Samosateni videamus. Qui vnus & solus Deus est, præter quem nullus est alius qui sit a seipso Altissimus, & ex quo omnia, huic nomen Dei per se primo tribuitur: Is autem est Deus Pater: Patri ergo per per se nomen Dei primò tribuitur. Multiplex vitium in maiore propositione est, in minore falsitas. In maiore primùm subiecto insunt plura interrogata, vt vocantur vulgo: tum ambiguè dicûtur omnia: quę si de essentia dicuntur omnia & essentialiter, bene est, concedi possunt: si de persona, exclusò Filio & Spiritu sancto, negantur omnia; hoc vno excepto, quòd Pater esse a seipso dicitur, id est, non ab alia persona: sinautem essentia & persona pro eodem habentur, vt ista membra omnia vnius suppositi dicantur esse, hoc verò Sabellianum est. Nec melius se habet ibidem praedicatum, quum nomen Dei per se & primò ei tribui dicitur ambiguitate & captione euidentissima, quam paulo ante demonstrauimus. Minor verò falsa est, qua mente a Samosateno adducitur. Etenim persona Patris secundùm suam (vt ita dicam) personalitatem nō est vnus & solus Deus, praeter quam nullus sit alius Altissimus, & ex qua sola sint omnia. Quòd si aut Pater nominatur essentialiter, vt ante diximus in Scriptura fieri, aut persona Patris dicitur Deus esse secundùm rationem essentiae, quae vna ipsi cum Filio & Spiritu sancto communis est, probamus hanc propositionem bene intellectam. Falsa igitur conclusio, Patri nomen Dei primò & per se tribui, exclusò Christo, quod Samosatenus voluit, & ex eodem ambiguo vitiosa. Nam Deus & Pater quum de essentia dicitur, de persona Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti dicitur synonymως, id est, vniuocè: sin autem de sola persona Patris, manet tamè immota συνωνύμως ratio, quia communis est, neque suppositione vnius personae in eo quod quid est fit remotio personae alterius. Essentia enim communem rationem habet in eo quod quid est: hypostasis verò, vel subsistentia, vel persona (vt verbis Damasceni vtar) neque quid est ostendit, neque quale quid est, sed tantùm quis est, & singulare indiuiduum de quo praep 2 dicatur essentia, determinat. Ex hac autē ἀσυλλογίστῳ argumentatione per contrarium infert Samosatenus verbis sequentibus, reliquos sive deos sive dominos, etiamq; Christum ipsum ab illo esse, illi debere quicquid sunt, & æquivoce ab eo appellari Deos. Antecedens falsum: nam personam & essentiam divinam pro eodem accipit contra auctoritatem Scripturæ: & falsa igitur consequentia. Primum enim falsum est omnes sive deos sive dominos æquivoce appellari: nam & Christus cum Patre Deus est univoce. Deinde & illud falsum, eamdem esse Christi cū aliis sive dij, sive dominis rationem: nam Christus Deus & dominus est, alij non sunt, sed dicuntur esse quod Deus est, ut ibidem affirmat Paulus. Tertiò eorum qui dicuntur dij & domini alij vere dicuntur esse, & falsò alij. Verè, quicunque vero iustoque ordine, aut applicatione, aut similitudine ita dicuntur, ut Angeli, Magistratusque, & siqui sunt eiusmodi: falsò autem, qui contrà. Ex his autem qui verè sunt, illi Deo debent quod dicuntur, cum habeant aliquā veram communicationē gratiæ: qui falsò, Satanæ & hominibus debent quod putantur esse. Itaque Christus, quà Filius æternus Dei Patris, Dominus & Deus cū Patre semper dicitur univocè: est enim Patri ὁμοούσιος, communem a natura cum Patre dominatū in unitate essentiæ obtinens: Quà autem caro factus est, eundem illum dominatum a natura possidet ut Deus, sed alterum quoque inferiorem dominationis modum voluntate assumsit homo factus, idque secundum eamdem œconomiam divinam & dispensationem qua homo factus est & inaniuit esse. Atque huc ferme pertinent omnes illi Scripturæ loci quos Samosatenus accumulat, postquàm subsistentiam divinā Christi coessentialem Patri belle sibi visus est sustulisse, ut nudum homine attributis divinis exornaret, velut operationes divinas producentem. Sed hæc singula suo deinceps
units.tr: the Son, who is Lord in a singular way, apart from the common and natural essence, namely by will and by the dispensation he has undertaken, which we have just touched upon. Wherefore the Apostle sets God himself [αὐτοθεὸς] over against the essence of idols, which are made by the hand and art of men, and he draws a distinction between being called and being when he uses these words: those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, to show that he speaks of God according to essence. The reasoning of the last passage is similar. For there is one God, says Paul, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. The interpretation of this place varies, and even if we grant the reading that Samosatenus seizes upon, it will win him nothing. For first, the word God is taken either essentially, as when he had said earlier this is good and acceptable before God our Saviour, or personally. Then, some understand the word one of essence, as when it is said, Jehovah your God is one God; others understand it of constancy and unchanging will, as in Gal. 3, God is one, where it means constant and abiding the same. Those who refer it to unity of essence argue thus: those of whom there is one God ought to pray for one another; of all men there is one God, as in Rom. 3; therefore all men ought to pray for one another. Those who refer it to unity and constancy of will argue otherwise. But setting these aside, we grant, affirm and proclaim that God is one, that the essence of God is single; this agrees well with Paul. But that the divine essence belongs to the single person of the Father, this neither Paul ever said nor do we concede. With Paul we say that God is indeed one in essence, but that the Father is one person, and that in the communion of essence there is one God with the Son and the Holy Spirit, we have learned from Paul and the rest of Scripture. Now let us look at Samosatenus's argument. He who is the one and only God, besides whom there is no other who is most high of himself, and from whom all things are, to him the name of God is first and through himself attributed; but he is God the Father; therefore the name of God is first and through himself attributed to the Father. The major premise has many faults, and the minor is false. In the major, first, the subject contains several questionable terms, as they are commonly called; then everything is said ambiguously. If all these things are said of the essence and essentially, it is well and may be granted; if of the person, with the Son and the Holy Spirit excluded, all are denied, except this one point, that the Father is said to be from himself, that is, not from another person. But if essence and person are held to be the same, so that all these members are said to belong to one suppositum, this is indeed Sabellian. Nor is the predicate any better there, when the name of God is said to be attributed first and through himself to him, with an ambiguity and deception most evident, as we demonstrated a little before. The minor is false in the sense in which Samosatenus brings it forward. For the person of the Father, according to his own personality (so to speak), is not the one and only God, besides whom there is no other most high, and from whom alone all things are. But if either the Father is named essentially, as we said above happens in Scripture, or the person of the Father is said to be God according to the reason of essence, which is one and common to him with the Son and the Holy Spirit, we approve this proposition when it is rightly understood. The conclusion, therefore, that the name of God is attributed first and through itself to the Father, with Christ excluded, which Samosatenus wanted, is false, and vicious from the same ambiguity. For God and Father, when said of essence, are said of the person of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alike, synonymously [συνωνύμως], that is, univocally; but if said of the person of the Father alone, the reason nonetheless remains unmoved and synonymous, because it is common, and by the supposition of one person no removal of another person takes place in what the thing is. For essence has a common reason in what it is; but hypostasis, or subsistence, or person (to use the words of Damascene) shows neither what a thing is nor what sort of thing it is, but only who it is, and determines the single individual of which essence is predicated. From this argument, which is not syllogistic [ἀσυλλογίστῳ], Samosatenus infers the contrary, in the following words: that the rest, whether gods or lords, and even Christ himself, are from him, owe to him whatever they are, and are called gods by him equivocally. The antecedent is false, for he takes the person and the divine essence as the same, against the authority of Scripture; and so the consequence is false. For first, it is false that all, whether gods or lords, are called equivocally, since Christ too is God with the Father univocally. Next, it is also false that Christ's standing is the same as that of the others called gods or lords; for Christ is God and Lord, while the others are not, but are said to be what God is, as Paul himself affirms in the same place. Thirdly, of those who are called gods and lords, some are truly so called and some falsely. Truly so are those who are called such in a true and just order, by application or by likeness, as angels, magistrates, and whoever are of that kind; falsely so are those who are the contrary. Of those who are truly so, they owe to God what they are called, since they have some true participation in grace; those who are falsely so owe to Satan and to men what they are thought to be. Thus Christ, as the eternal Son of God the Father, is always called Lord and God univocally with the Father, for he is homoousios [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father, holding by nature a common lordship with him in unity of essence. But as he was made flesh, he possesses that same lordship by nature as God, yet as man he also assumed by will another, lower mode of lordship, and this according to the same divine economy and dispensation by which he was made man and emptied himself. To this pertain almost all those passages of Scripture which Samosatenus heaps up, after he thought he had neatly removed the divine subsistence of Christ, coessential with the Father, so as to adorn a bare man with divine attributes, as one producing divine operations. But these single points we must annotate in their order, one after another.

units.la: inceps ordine opus est annotemus. I. Hæc verba sunt Dauidis Psal. 50. 1. in quibus euidenter posita est essentialis Dei appellatio: quæ non singularis est vnius personæ Patris, sed communis sanctæ & indiuisæ Trinitatis. Quòd si quis personaliter eam de Patre acceperit, tamen iure essentiæ (quæ eadem est Patris & Filij) Filio quoque communis futura est, quia Pater & Filius sunt vnum. Nã quod essentiale, id subsistentiarum etiam aut personarum commune est, eoque affirmatur de hypostasibus singulis vniuersaliter. Verumtamen si personaliter exponi (quod ego quidem probare non possum) oporteret, de Filio potius quàm de Patre diceretur. Est enim totus ille Psalmus Euangelicus, de Christo loquens, de regno, & de operatione eius adeò manifestè, vt mirum sit aliud quidiuis potiùs non adducia Samosateno de Patre dictum. Secundus locus, quòd Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi appellatur, plus habet speciei, quia de Deo Patre agitur personaliter. Sed falsa est tamen argumentatio ex falsa hypothesi: Qui Deus est & Pater Dei, ut vnus proprie & solus Deus est: Est autem ille Pater Christi: Ille igitur solus Deus. Negatur maior, vt antè demonstratum. Sed retorquetur contrà eodem modo: Qui Deus est & Pater Dei, eius Filius est coëssentialis Patri, & proprie natura Deus: aut (si forte seruari placet ipsa Pauli verba) Si Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi Deus est, etiam Dominus noster Iesus Christus Deus est, vnius cum Patre atque eiusdem essentiæ. Si negat Samosatenus, probat natura & Scriptura, Pater & Filius sunt vnum essentia. Sin figuratè hoc iubet intelligi, nos figuratum negamus esse, analogicum verò concedimus: nam quæ de Deo & rebus diuinis enunciantur, ea humano more dicuntur analogicè. Tertius locus, Patrē esse caput Christi, ex 1. Cor. 11. fallit elenchi ignoratione. Nam de persona Christi dicuntur ista non secundùm naturam diuina simpliciter, qua Filius Dei Deus æternus est, sed secundum illam dispensationem, qua factus est caro, & se in carne adunauit Ecclesiæ suę, de cuius ordine & ὁ τῆς ζωῆς agitur eo in loco, pro conditione vniuscuiusque. Fœminæ caput, inquit Apostolus, vir est: viri, Christus θεὸν θεοῦ... a Patre missus: Christi, mittens Pater. Quapropter vt Christus Mediator in Ecclesia se ordinat ad Patrem, ita vir tenetur se ordinare ad Christum, & fœmina ad virum, suumque ordinem religiose colere atque profiteri. Hoc enim Paulus ante docuerat dicens, Imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi. Illa autem iniqua est argumentatio, quæ ex ratione totius personæ de natura ipsius altera, aut ex opere voluntariæ dispensationis atque consilij de naturali (quod utrumque hic Samosatenus facit) concluditur. Nam secundum naturam Filius est æqualis Patri, secundum illam vero dispensationem Filius est minor Patre, & Pater est caput illius. Sic sequentia pleraque omnia. De hoc autem Defensione 2. segmento 7. plura. Libet hic corollarium ex Chrysostomo addere in hanc sententiam: Caput est coëssentiale suo corpori: Christus est caput viri: ergo coëssentialis viro. Item, Pater est caput Christi: coëssentiales igitur. 2. Negamus a Paulo dictum, quod solus Pater sit super omnes: nam exclusiva solus Ephes. 4. non comparet. Commune est autem trium personarum secundum essentiam, quod sint vnus Deus super omneis, &c. quod autem commune est quum de singulari dicitur, de communi quicquam non derogari ante ostendimus. Quod si ad solam personam Patris dictum restringi placuerit, nihil tamen Samosatenus effici. Nam ita respicitur ad ordinem illum quem Deus instituit, & Filius subijt voluntaria dispensatione, secundum quam Filius caro factus inaniuit se, & Pater maior est Filio: cum alioqui secundum naturam illam diuinam suam sit coëssentialis & coæternus Patri. Hîc ergo iterum fallacia elenchi obtruditur, & ad eamdem pertinent sequentia omnia. Facta enim voluntariæ dispensationis Samosatenus accumulat, vt naturam æternam Filij destruat, inconsequente argumentatione. Qui Deus est proprie, inquit a nullo factus, nec constitutus, nec electus, nec prædordinatus, nec sanctificatus a quoquam, nec exaltatus, nec missus, vel obediens alicui factus est, nec quemquam se maiorem habet: Christus autem factus est, constitutus, electus, &c. Non igitur Deus. Maior vera est de Deo, quà Deus: itaque secundum naturam diuinam vera est etiam de persona Christi. Sed alia plane ratio est secundum beneplacitum gratiæ gloriosæ ipsius & dispensationem illam misericordiæ, qua Deus homo factus est & manifestatus in carne voluntarie propter nos homines & salutem nostram, nobisque datus est Agnus Dei Deus. Nam secundum hanc rationem ille idem qui natura facit per se & propria virtute Deus, idem ergo vt Mediator homo factus est, filius Abrahami, filius Dauidis, filius mulieris, & filius hominis. sic sequentia omnia. Qui itaque diuina virtute constituit, eligit, prædordinat, sanctificat, exaltat, mittit, imperat, omniumque maximus est vt æternus Deus; idem diuino consilio & dispensatione voluntaria constitutus est, electus, prædordinatus, sanctificatus, exaltatus, missus, obediens factus & minor Patre, nimirum vt homo factus in tempore ad consummationem optatissimæ salutis nostræ, quam istis arietibus oppugnat Satan. Verum tamen vt semel moneamus quod iam superiore segmento demonstrauimus, turpiter hic disputator fallacijs accumulatis abutitur, quum ita arguit, Christus factus est homo, factus sapientia, iustitia, &c. igitur factus est. Nam primum differentia sunt argumentationum genera, quæ celat sophisticè, vt eo commodius irretiantur imprudentes. Prima enim illa propositio, Christum factum esse hominem, essentialis est: sequentes vero, accidentaria. harum vero propositionum ratio valde est differens. Deinde vero vt de prima dicamus priore loco, ambigua est loquutio illa, Christus factus homo: quam nos bene intelleciam accipimus vt illam, Sermo factus est caro, Deus est potest factus in carne, & siqua sunt eiusmodi. Nam suppositum est æternum Christus, Sermo, Deus, quod suppositum carnem dicitur assumsisse in vnitatem personæ: itaque non factus est Christus, quà Sermo Dei Deus est, sed quà homo, siue (vt loquitur Scriptura) caro. Sed ambiguo illudens Samosatenus quod de Christo secundum quid, puta secundum carnem, affirmamus, accipit simpliciter: quod de parte, accipit vniuersè, & ita concludit Christum vniuersè factum. Peccatum in argumentatione duplex. Præterea (vt ad alias transeamus) nec illæ veriores sunt, Christus factus est sapientia, iustitia, &c. ergo factus est. Mutatur enim prædicationis genus, cùm antecedens rationem habeat accidentalem, consequens essentiale fit. Quis sic vnquam argumentatus est? truncus factus est scamnum, truncus ergo factus est. Hic primùm iniqua diuisio fit ἀλλοιώσεως rerum quæ simul in prædicato coniunctæ sunt ad rei vnius significationem: deinde inconsequens est argumentatio mutato prædicationis genere. Nam factus est sapientia, &c. quum dicitur, prædicatum est actus & relationis accidentariæ de subiecto, siue applicationis ad nos qui credimus: quum autem simpliciter, factus est, prædicatum est de ortu essentiali eius: quorum prius verum est, posterius a vero differens & blasphemum in Filium æternum Dei. Illam itaque prædicationem, a nullo factus, æquè de Filio Dei atque de Patre veram agnoscimus, & probamus secundum illam diuinam subsistentiam qua Filius est cum Patre essentia vnum: nam quà a Patre est, genitus est, non factus. Secundùm humanitatem verò, quam assumsit in vnitatem personæ, Christum factum ex muliere, factum sub lege confitemur: proinde secundùm aliud & aliud eumdem hominem factum (hominem dico, non humanitatem) atque non factû agnoscimus. Factum denique sapientiam, iustitiam, &c. secundùm personam Ἰησοῦν, vt Mediatorem & Redemtorem nostrum.
units.tr: I shall take these up one by one in order. I. These are David's words in Psalm 50.1, where the essential name of God is plainly set down. It is not the peculiar name of the one person of the Father, but belongs in common to the holy and undivided Trinity. But even if someone understands it personally of the Father, it still belongs by right of essence (which is one and the same in the Father and the Son) to the Son as well, because the Father and the Son are one. For what is essential is common to the subsistences or persons, and so it is affirmed universally of each of the hypostases. Yet if it had to be expounded personally (which I, at least, cannot prove), it would be said of the Son rather than of the Father. The whole Psalm is indeed evangelical, speaking of Christ, of his kingdom and of his work so clearly that it is strange that Samosatenus should have chosen to adduce this passage as spoken of the Father rather than any other. The second place, where God is called the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, has more plausibility, since it speaks of God the Father personally. But the argument is false, drawn from a false premise: He who is God and Father of God, is properly and solely God, as one; but he is the Father of Christ; therefore he alone is God. The major premise is denied, as was shown before. But the argument can be turned back in the same way: He who is God and Father of God, his Son is coessential with the Father and by nature properly God; or (if it is perhaps preferred to keep Paul's own words): If the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is God, then our Lord Jesus Christ is also God, one with the Father and of the same essence. If Samosatenus denies this, nature and Scripture prove it: the Father and the Son are one in essence. If he insists that this must be understood figuratively, we deny that it is figurative, though we grant that it is analogical; for what is said of God and divine things is spoken analogically, after the manner of men. The third place, that the Father is the head of Christ, from 1 Cor. 11, fails through ignorance of the point at issue. For these things are said of the person of Christ not simply according to the divine nature, by which the Son of God is eternal God, but according to that dispensation by which he became flesh and united himself in the flesh to his Church, concerning whose order and ὁ τῆς ζωῆς [the order of life] the passage speaks, according to the condition of each one. "The head of the woman," says the Apostle, "is the man; of the man, Christ; θεὸν θεοῦ [God of God]... sent by the Father; of Christ, the Father who sends." Therefore, just as Christ the Mediator orders himself in the Church towards the Father, so the man is bound to order himself towards Christ, and the woman towards the man, and to observe and profess their order devoutly. For Paul had taught this before when he said, Be followers of me, as I am of Christ. That argument, however, is unfair which concludes from the character of the whole person that his other nature is so, or from the work of voluntary dispensation and counsel that his natural state is so (which is what Samosatenus does on both counts). For according to nature the Son is equal to the Father; but according to that dispensation the Son is less than the Father, and the Father is his head. And so with nearly everything that follows. I shall say more about this in the second Defence, section 7. It is worth adding here a corollary from Chrysostom to this effect: the head is coessential with its body; Christ is the head of man; therefore he is coessential with man. Likewise: the Father is the head of Christ; therefore they are coessential. 2. We deny that Paul said that the Father alone is over all: for the exclusive alone does not appear in Eph. 4.
