What is common to the three persons according to essence is that they are one God over all, etc.; and we have shown before that what is common is not taken away when something is said of the singular. But even if it is preferred to restrict the saying to the person of the Father alone, Samosatenus gains nothing by it. For it then refers to that order which God instituted, and which the Son undertook by voluntary dispensation, according to which the Son, made flesh, emptied himself and the Father is greater than the Son; although by his divine nature he is otherwise coessential and coeternal with the Father. Here again, therefore, the fallacy of ignorance of the point at issue is thrust in, and all that follows belongs to the same fault. For Samosatenus heaps up the facts of the voluntary dispensation in order to destroy the eternal nature of the Son, by an inconsequent argument: He who is God properly, says one, was made by no one, nor constituted, nor chosen, nor predestined, nor sanctified by anyone, nor exalted, nor sent, nor made obedient to anyone, nor has anyone greater than himself; but Christ was made, constituted, chosen, etc. Therefore he is not God. The major is true of God as God; so according to the divine nature it is also true of the person of Christ. But the reason is plainly different according to the good pleasure of his glorious grace and that dispensation of mercy by which God was made man and manifested in the flesh, voluntarily, for us men and for our salvation, and the Lamb of God, who is God, was given to us. For according to this reckoning he who by nature and by his own power is God through himself, the same, as Mediator, was made man, son of Abraham, son of David, son of a woman, and son of man. And so with everything that follows. Therefore he who by divine power constitutes, chooses, predestines, sanctifies, exalts, sends, commands, and is the greatest of all as eternal God, the same by divine counsel and voluntary dispensation was constituted, chosen, predestined, sanctified, exalted, sent, made obedient and less than the Father, namely as a man made in time, for the completion of our most desired salvation, which Satan attacks with these battering rams. Yet, to warn once more of what we have already shown in the previous section, this disputant shamefully abuses fallacies piled one upon another when he argues: Christ was made man, made wisdom, righteousness, etc.; therefore he was made. For first, the kinds of argument are different, which he cunningly conceals so that the unwary may be more easily ensnared. That first proposition, that Christ was made man, is essential; but the following ones are accidental, and the reasoning of these propositions is very different. Next, to speak of the first one in the first place: the phrase Christ made man is ambiguous; we rightly understand it as we take such phrases as the Word was made flesh, God who is able to be made in the flesh, and any others of that kind. For the subject that is eternal is Christ, the Word, God; this subject is said to have assumed flesh into the unity of person. So Christ was not made as the Word who is God, but as man, or (as Scripture speaks) as flesh. But Samosatenus, playing on the ambiguity, takes simply what we affirm of Christ in a certain respect, namely according to the flesh, and what is said of a part he takes of the whole, and so concludes that Christ was made in his entirety. The argument has a double fault. Moreover (to pass to the other points), these are no truer: Christ was made wisdom, righteousness, etc.; therefore he was made. For the kind of predication is changed, since the antecedent has an accidental ground while the consequent becomes essential. Who ever argued like this? The trunk was made a bench; therefore the trunk was made. Here first an unfair division is made of the alteration [ἀλλοιώσεως] of things which are joined together in the predicate to signify one thing; then the argument is inconsequent since the kind of predication has been changed. For when it is said was made wisdom, etc., the predicate is an accidental act and relation of the subject, or an application to us who believe; but when it is said simply was made, the predicate concerns his essential origin. The former is true, the latter differs from the truth and is blasphemous against the eternal Son of God. Therefore we acknowledge that the predicate made by no one is as true of the Son of God as of the Father, and we prove it according to that divine subsistence by which the Son is one in essence with the Father: for as he is from the Father, he is begotten, not made. But according to his humanity, which he assumed into the unity of person, we confess that Christ was made of a woman, made under the law; accordingly we acknowledge the same man to have been made (I say man, not humanity) according to one thing and not made according to another. Finally, made wisdom, righteousness, etc., is said according to the person of Jesus [Ἰησοῦν], as our Mediator and Redeemer.

units.la: 3. Inde ab his verbis ad finem huius loci vsque perpetua fallacia est ex elenchi ignoratione, quum enunciata quæ secundùm hoc dicuntur exponuntur secundùm illud, & veritas personæ, officij, beneficiorumque Christi hac confusione miserè inuoluitur. Nam tria concurrunt & simul incidunt semper in contemplationem personæ Christi ex quo factus est caro, secundùm quæ enunciationes singulas separatè aut coniunctim commodè accipi necesse est seruatis naturarum proprietatibus: primùm deitas siue natura diuina λόγου, vt Sermo æternus est æterni Patris, Patri ὁμοούσιος ᾧ συναΐδιος: secundò humanitas siue natura humana, quam in vnitatem personæ suæ assumsit ille æternus Sermo ex virgine Maria in tempore: nam propterea respectu prioris formæ essentialis, Filius Dei, respectu verò posterioris Filius hominis appellatur: postremò autem persona Filij Dei, Filij hominis, id est, Θεάνθρωπος, veri Dei, veri hominis, ex duarum naturarum compage (vt ita loquamur) & adunatione constituta. Hæc autem omnia, quorum respectu res non solùm differentes, sed etiam contrariæ secundùm hanc aut illam naturã de persona Christi verè & sanctè prædicantur, strenuè Samosatenus confundit, quia non credit, distinctáque a nobis dissimulat, quia non vult distingui, vt imperitis vincere videatur quũ viuus vidensque perit. Hæc, inquit, omnia prædicta Christo Filio Dei ex Maria nato (non alteri) tribuit aperte Scriptura, &c. Filio Dei, inquis, ex Maria nato? cur non ergo dicis, Filio Dei, Filio hominis? Quatenus enim Filius Dei est, non est natus ex Maria: quatenus item ex Maria natus, nō est Filius Dei: sed quà Filius Dei, coëssentialis est Patri, & cum Patre vnum, vnigenitus natura Filius, diuina hypostasis: quà Filius hominis, coëssentialis est matri, vnigenitus natura Filius virginis, humanum enhypostaton, quippe humanitate subsistente in persona λόγῳ vnione personali: non alter Filius Dei, alter hominis Filius, sed vnus idemque Filius Dei, filius hominis, persona vna ex duabus naturis constituta. Qui licet Deus sit & homo, inquit Athanasius, non duo tamen, sed vnus est Christus: vnus autem non conuersione diuinitatis in carnem, sed assumtione humanitatis in Deum: vnus omnino non confusione substantiæ, sed vnitate personæ. Nam sicut anima rationalis & caro vnus est homo, ita Deus & homo vnus est Christus. Hæc est fides catholica, hæc sanctorum Apostolorum professio: quos roganti Christo, quem me dicunt homines esse qui filius sum hominis? Simon Petrus respondens dixit, Tu es Christus ille Filius Dei viuentis, tu idem qui filius hominis: non duo supposita aut personæ duæ, sed vnum suppositum ex duabus naturis constans. Christus ergo omnia a Patre habet, totusque est Patris (vt ad Samosateni verba singula veniamus) tum quà Filius vnigenitus a Patre, vnum esse cum Patre habens, vt qui Patri ex hoc mundo discessurus diceret, mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea, tùm qua homo ex muliere sub Lege factus, vt esset ἄνθρωπος Mediator & Redemtor noster. Hic idem a Patre est factus filius hominis ex semine Dauid, ex muliere: nimirum qui Sermo erat est caro factus, & Deus in carne conspicuus: æternus ab æterno genitus secundùm diuinitatem, factus in tempore, Abrahami, & Dauidis, & Mariæ filius, secundùm humanitatem. Hic factus est a Deo Dominus & Christus in persona
units.tr: 3. From these words to the end of this passage there is a constant fallacy, an ignoratio elenchi: statements made with respect to one thing are explained with respect to another, and the truth about Christ's person, office and benefits is wretchedly entangled in this confusion. Three things always come together and fall at once under consideration of the person of Christ since he became flesh. Each statement, taken singly or jointly, must be rightly understood with respect to them, the properties of the natures being preserved. First, there is the deity, or divine nature, of the Word [λόγου], as the eternal Word is the eternal Father's own Word, consubstantial with the Father [ὁμοούσιος] and coeternal with him [συναΐδιος]. Second, there is the humanity, or human nature, which that eternal Word assumed in time from the virgin Mary into the unity of his person. For this reason he is called Son of God with respect to the former, essential form, and Son of man with respect to the latter. Last, there is the person of the Son of God and Son of man, that is, the God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], true God and true man, constituted from the joining, so to speak, and union of the two natures. All these things, with respect to which statements that differ and even contradict each other are truly and rightly predicated of the person of Christ according to this or that nature, Samosatenus vigorously confounds. He does not believe them, and he hides from us the distinctions that he does not wish to be drawn, so that he may seem to win over the unlearned, though, while alive and seeing, he perishes. "All these things spoken of," he says, "are clearly ascribed by Scripture to Christ, the Son of God born of Mary, and to no other," and so on. "The Son of God," you say, "born of Mary? Why then do you not say Son of God, Son of man?" For insofar as he is the Son of God, he was not born of Mary; and insofar as he was born of Mary, he is not the Son of God. But as the Son of God he is consubstantial with the Father and one with the Father, the only-begotten Son by nature, the divine hypostasis. As the Son of man he is consubstantial with his mother, the only-begotten Son of the virgin by nature, a human enhypostaton, since the humanity subsists in the person of the Word by personal union. He is not one Son of God and another Son of man, but one and the same Son of God, Son of man, one person constituted from two natures. "Although he is God and man," says Athanasius, "yet he is not two but one Christ; one, however, not by the conversion of the deity into flesh but by the assumption of the humanity into God; one altogether, not by confusion of substance but by unity of person. For as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ." This is the catholic faith, this the profession of the holy Apostles, who, when Christ asked them, "Whom do men say that I, the Son of man, am?", answered through Simon Peter, "You are that Christ, the Son of the living God": you are the same who is the Son of man. They did not say two supposita or two persons, but one suppositum consisting of two natures. Christ therefore has all things from the Father and is wholly the Father's (to come to Samosatenus's words one by one): both as the only-begotten Son from the Father, having one essence with the Father, so that he could say to the Father, on leaving this world, "All my things are yours, and yours are mine"; and as man, made under the Law from a woman, so that he might be our Mediator and Redeemer. This same one was made by the Father "the Son of man from the seed of David, from a woman": namely, the Word who was made flesh, and God made visible in the flesh; eternal, begotten from eternity according to the deity, made in time, according to the humanity, the son of Abraham, of David and of Mary. "This one was made by God Lord and Christ" in his person

units.la: Matt. 16.; Ioan. 17.; Rom. 1.; Galat. 4.; Actor. 2. sona sua; vt qui fecundùm diuinitatem per dispensatio-nem voluntariam & singularem gratiam, fecundùm hu-manitatem per gratiam vnionis omneis & singulas par-tes veri Domini & Christi ac Mediatoris præstiterit infe-fe vnitate personæ suæ ad redemtionem & salutem no-ftram. Huic Pater dedit nomen supra omne nomen,vt adore-tur, nimirum personæ Mediatoris & Redemtoris nostri, non huic aut illi naturæ,sed personæ toti fecundùm vtrâ-que naturam ipsius: tum diuinam, quia æternus ille Ser-mo, verus Deus,æqualis Deo & Patri, seipsum inaniuerat forma feruì accepta similis hominibus factus voluntate certa & dispensatione gratiæ: tum humanam, quia ha-bitu compertus vt homo fe summisit ipse, factus obediēs vsque ad mortem, eamque crucis in nostræ huius naturæ veritate, quam traditam morti atque cruciatam fuften-tabat λόγος in vnitate personæ ad perficiendum myfterîū salutis nostræ. Quapropter, inquit Apostolus, id est, pro-pterea quòd ille verus Deus & Filius Dei fecundùm natu-ram diuinam suam fe inaniuerat forma feruì accepta per dispensationem voluntariam, & fecundùm humanam fe ipse summiserat Legi & iustitiæ Dei factus fuerat obe-diens vsque ad mortem: propter has igitur causas, non eò solùm quòd Patri obediens fuit ad mortem vsque crucis, sed tum propter inanitionem deitatis, tum propter acer-biffimas perpeffiones humanitatis eius, totámque obe-dientiam totius personæ (quæ omnia inscitè Samofate-nus dirimit, vt suum dogma fulciat) Deus ipsum in sum-mam extulit sublimitatem, ac donauit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen, &c. puta & diuinitatem ab illa fui inanitio-ne potentissimè vindicando κατὰ φανέρωσιν, qua fe ipse inaniuerat dispensatione voluntaria certóque consilio nobis salutari: & humanitatem ab infirmitate & perpef-fionibus illius euehendo adeò magnificè, vt præter illam vnionis gratiam (quam in diuinitate Christi personaliter obtinet humanitas supra res creatas omneis) etiam in sese omnem plenitudinem gratiæ, & veritatis & gloriæ possidea, quantam natura creata potest percipere, & quantam nulla alia præter hanc percipit: quia supra omne nomen est cœlestium, terrestrium, infernorumque, & prout ita est, sic ab omnibus contemplatione diuinæ illius naturæ, & gratiæ immensæ persona Christi adoratur. Hic factus est nobis sapientia, iustitia, pax a Deo, nimirum persona illius secundum utramque naturam, distinctis ac nō confusis earum proprietatibus, secundum diuinā principaliter, secundum humanam instrumentaliter, secundum utramque regificè & admirabiliter operans. Idem est a Deo quoque datus nobis Magister, Pastor, Seruator, Rex, & caput, nempe ut Ιησους Χριστος secundum utramque naturam suam unus Christus. Similiterque in eo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ ac cognitionis abscondite, omnisque potestas data est ipsi in cælo & terra, ut Ιησου Χριστω seruatori nostro, cuius diuinitas sese inaniuerat ex dispensatione gratiæ, depressáque ex facto fuerat in humilitatem infimam humanitas propter nos homines & salutem nostram. Hæc igitur indigna turpisque fallacia est, quòd resadeò Scripturis testata, & ab Orthodoxis toties recantata omittitur, sine qua nec Deus verè Pater, nec Christus verè Deus esse, nec salus nostra unquam verè constare potest.
units.tr: Matt. 16.; Ioan. 17.; Rom. 1.; Galat. 4.; Actor. 2. (in his own person), so that he, who according to the deity by a voluntary and singular dispensation of grace, and according to the humanity by the grace of union, has perfectly performed all and each of the parts of the true Lord, Christ and Mediator, in the unity of his person, for our redemption and salvation. To this one "the Father gave a name above every name, that every knee should bow": namely, to the person of our Mediator and Redeemer, not to this or that nature, but to the whole person according to each of his natures: to the divine nature, because that eternal Word, true God, equal to God and the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made like men by a certain will and dispensation of grace; and to the human nature, because, found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, in the truth of our nature, which the Word sustained when it was delivered to death and crucified, in the unity of his person, to accomplish the mystery of our salvation. "Wherefore," says the Apostle, that is, because that true God and Son of God, according to his divine nature, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant by a voluntary dispensation, and according to his human nature had humbled himself under the Law and the justice of God, and had become obedient unto death: for these causes, therefore, not only because he was obedient to the Father unto death on the cross, but both on account of the emptying of the deity and on account of the most bitter sufferings of his humanity, and the whole obedience of the whole person (all of which the unskilled Samosatenus divides, to prop up his own doctrine), "God exalted him to the highest sublimity and gave him a name which is above every name," etc. That is, the deity is most powerfully vindicated from that emptying of itself which it undertook by a voluntary dispensation and a certain counsel salutary to us, openly displayed [κατὰ φανέρωσιν]; and the humanity is raised, from its weakness and sufferings, so magnificently that, beyond that grace of union (which the humanity obtains personally in the divinity of Christ, above all created things), it also possesses in itself all the fullness of grace, truth and glory that a created nature can receive, and that no other nature receives besides this one. For he is above every name of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and so, as he is, the person of Christ is adored by all in contemplation of that divine nature and of the immense grace. Here he "was made for us wisdom, righteousness and peace from God": namely, his person, according to each nature, with their properties distinct and not confused, working kingly and admirably in both natures: according to the divine principally, according to the human instrumentally. He is also "given to us by God as Teacher, Pastor, Saviour, King and Head", namely that Jesus Christ [Ιησους Χριστος] is one Christ according to each of his natures. And likewise "in him are all the treasures of wisdom and hidden knowledge, and all power is given to him in heaven and on earth", to Jesus Christ [Ιησου Χριστω] our Saviour, whose deity emptied itself by the dispensation of grace, and whose humanity was of necessity cast down into the lowest humility for us men and our salvation. This is therefore an unworthy and shameful fallacy, that a thing so attested by the Scriptures, and so often reaffirmed by the Orthodox, is passed over; without it neither God can truly be Father, nor Christ truly God, nor our salvation ever truly stand.

units.la: 4. Quòd autem ea ratione, & non alia (vt idem posteà loquitur) Dominus verè dicatur & Rex, tum Deus noster a Patre vnctus, cui & omnia subiecit: quòd, inquam, hac ratione & non alia Filius Dei sit Deus, &c. id Dei veritas & catholica Ecclesia pernegat. Etsi antequàm de ipsa dicimus, necessariò adhibenda est nobis distinctio, quā iusta docendi ratio seruari iubet: hic plura prædicata esse inter se differentia, ac non eadem ratione, quicquid Samosatenus afferat, ad Christum pertinentia. Vbi autem huiusmodi congeries vocum ab imprudentibus aut malitiosis hominibus obtruditur, nihil tam necessarium quàm vt singula singillatim atq; distinctè expendantur. Quis enim tam hebes est, qui vel naturæ luce non videat, siquis Deus & Dominus & Rex & vnctus appellatur, longè aliam rationem esse ex qua Deus dicitur, quàm ea sit ex qua Dominus, Rex, vnctus, &c. Quamobrem vt res sit euidentior, ita statuimus articulatè ad commodiorem institutionem omnium: 1. Eorum quæ de Christo prædicantur alia essentialia esse, vt vocantur, alia attributa personæ. 2. Quæcunque eiusmodi sunt, aut secundùm alteram eius naturam dici, aut secundùm vtramque, prout sunt adunatæ inter se personaliter. 3. Ea omnia etiã quæ secundùm naturam diuinam, aut secundùm humanam prædicantur, de persona in communi, tamquam suppositο vno atque eodem, prædicari, quamuis respectu naturarum inter se differentium. 4. Eorum quæ personæ sunt essentialia secundùm naturam diuinam ipsius, hæc communia esse sanctæ & individuæ Trinitatis, illa hypostatica, id est, huius vnius personæ propria & characteristica, vt veteres appellarunt. 5. Eorum quæ personæ sunt essentialia secundùm naturam humanam, alia esse naturalia quæ nobiscum a natura communia habuit, alia autem voluntaria cùm ad commoditatem naturæ alterius, tum ad cõmoditatem officij decenter conuenientia. 6. Attributa ferè in Scripturis salutaris officij respectu non alia prædicari, quàm quæ ad personam secundùm vtramque naturam pertinent; e quibus diuina principalis agens, humana instrumentalis est. 7. Horum attributorum alia ad causam finalem pertinere, vt quum dicitur Iesus, Seruator; alia ad officium ex dono & vocatione, vt quum appellatur Christus, Propheta, Sacerdos, Rex; alia ad actiones & perpessiones conuenientes officio ac fini propter quem est à Deo & Patre missus vt quum triumphali modo potestates traduxisse dicitur, & ipse mortem subijsse. 8. Hæc attributa omnia Filio Dei secundùm naturam diuinam (cui nihil in se addi aut detrahi potest) competere per dispensationem gratiæ, qua se ipse inaniuit voluntariè, vt idem sua natura summus infimè sese ad ea omnia quę fecit & perpessus est submitteret voluntate propria in assumta carne, sed natura vtraque semper integra permanente, & saluis vtriusq; proprietatibus. Ex his ergo legibus variè de istis prædicationibus quas Samosatenus congerit oportet iudicari. Nam primùm attributum, Christum esse Dominum, de persona ipsius secundùm naturam vtramq; est verissimum. Secundùm diuinam Dominus est ab æterno, essentiali dominatu, qui Filio cū Patre & Spiritu sancto communis est: & Dominus dispensatiuus proprio ac personali dominatu in tempore Ecclesiæ a Patre datus. Secundùm humanam Dominus est, non priore illo dominatu (est enim deitatis proprius & incommunicabilis) sed posteriore, Dominus a Patre factus per gratiam vnionis (vt vocant) in vnitate personæ, voluntaria dispensatione. Eadem plane ratione Christum Regem, qua Dominum, appellamus, vt Deus est, & vt ἀνθρωπος. Nam alioquin, vt homo simplex, Dominus & Rex frustra appellatur, licet dominetur regnetq; vt homo; quia nunquam in se aut per se vel ad momentu substitit humanitas, sed est semper ςυνπόςαλος, & subsistens in λόγῳ. Hæc igitur attributa, & siqua sunt eiusmodi, prout personæ Christi secundùm naturam diuinam competūt, modò essentialiter sunt accipienda, communiaque Patris & Spiritus sancti cum Filio agnoscenda: modò personaliter secundùm vtramq; naturam ad Christum Seruatorem nostrũ dicenda pertinere, vt personæ illius propria. pria. Sed quòd Deus est & appellatur persona Christi, id longè alia ratione quàm Samosatenus dicat, in Ecclesia obtinet. Nam factus quidē est Dominus & Christus, Act. 2.at non factus Deus, quod iste tamquam ex pari analogicè videtur cōcludere. Similium, inquiet, ratio similis. Est certè: sed hæc sunt dissimilia maximè. Deus enim est natura Dominus & Christus voluntate atque instituto, si ad personale dominium respexeris: Deus est absolutè, Dominus & Christus, relatè & respectu nostri: Deus est essentialiter, Dominus & Christus accidentarie: Deus est formaliter secundùm naturam diuinam suam, Dominus & Christus secundùm vtramque in vnitate personæ: & tu rationem horum, Samosatene, similem dixeris? At Christus, inquies, non est natura, absolutè, essentialiter, formaliterque Deus, sed communicatione a Patre. Respondeo, si communicatione, aut naturâ est, aut voluntate communicatio. Si communicatione naturæ Deus est, ergo Deus essentialiter, cum Patre vnum: si communicatione voluntaria gratiæ & instituto solùm, non ergo proprie & & vniuocè, sed figuratè est & æquiuocè appellatur Deus. Qui enim Deus proprè dicitur, hunc essentialiter formaliterque (vt loquuntur) oportet esse Deum. Non autem figuratè Christus appellatur Deus: proprie igitur. Quòd si proprie, ergo essentialiter est formaliterq; Deus. Tam enim verè est quod est, quàm verè est quod factus est: & tam proprie esse dicitur quod est, quàm proprie esse quod factus est. Est autē verè factus, & proprie factus esse dicitur Dominus & Christus: ergo tam verè est & proprie dicitur esse Deus, quā verè est & proprie factus esse dicitur Dominus & Christus. Quòd enim Deus est, id naturæ est: quòd Dominus & Christus est, id facturæ est atque instituti. Quapropter illum quidem factum a Deo legimus Dominum & Christum, sed Deum factum minimé. Verè autem & proprie Christum esse dicique Deum, iam supra in locum 1. & 2. demonstrauimus. Quod si vere & proprie Christum esse diciq; Deum Samosatenus contenderit, eo quòd diuinæ gratiæ κατ' ὑπερβολὴν a Patre communicationem habuerit: primùm negatur eum vere esse & proprie dici Deum, qui non sit essentialiter quod esse dicitur: deinde negatur alium hoc esse præter Deum, cùm Deus toties per Prophetas suos sit contestatus se gloriam suam non esse daturum alteri: postremò (vt cum Tertulliano ratiocinemur) si quod factus est Christus id propter nos factus est, factus est autem Deus, vt Samosateno quidem placere video, continuò factus fuisse Deus propter nos dicendus est. Finem autem quis homo nescit præstantiorem ijs rebus esse quæ finis causa fiunt, atque ad finem ordinantur? Nos igitur, auctore Samosateno, præstantiores Christo futuri sumus, siquidem Christus causa nostra factus est. Est autem hoc absurdum, falsum, impium, blasphemum consequens: ergo nec antecedens bona fide a viro bono probari potest. At, inquit, Pater ei subiecit omnia (seipsum tamen excipiendo) vt postremo nos regnum q; suum deuictis hostibus & morte reddat Deo & Patri, a quo accepit, vt sit ille Deus omnia in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15. Ex eo loco duo sunt quæ Samosatenus confirmare videtur velle: vnum, quòd Christus sit factus a Patre Deus, cùm Pater ei subiecerit omnia: alterum, quòd Deus Pater solus sit essentialiter Deus. De posteriore iam modò diximus. De priore igitur videamus. Ad priorem locum si ita argumentatur Samosatenus, Cui Pater subiecit omnia, is Deus est: Christo subiecit omnia: Christus igitur est Deus: totum argumentum damus, & damus eum vere esse Deum ac essentialiter, neque alteri gloriam illam diuinam dari potuisse. Sin autem sic argumentatur, Cui Pater subiecit omnia, hunc fecit Deum ipsi subjiciendo omnia: Christo subiecit omnia, omnia, &c. falsa est propositio maior, in Christum contumeliosa, & a natura propositionum aliena quæ necessariæ appellantur. Nulla enim iusta argumentationum lege confici illud potest, ut non nisi positis actibus ponantur subiecta a quibus procedunt illi. Actionum enim alii sunt natiuæ subiecti, perpetuæ, & necessariæ, aliæ secus. Hæ autem si in persona Christi expendantur, ita dicendum est: Secundùm actum natiuum, perpetuum, & necessarium, Pater gignit Filium, Deus Deum, non autem facit, aut fecit. Secundùm actum non natiuum, sed voluntarium, Pater Filium aut Deum non fecit, sed Filium illum suum Deumque nostrum, hunc fecit Dominum & Christum, eíque subiecit omnia. Subiectum enim & natiua adiacentia ac necessaria sunt natura simul: reliqua non item. Positis enim actibus (ut rectè docent Logici) ponuntur subiecta & adiacentia a quibus illi processerūt: non autem e diuerso positis subiectis ponuntur actus quilibet, sed natiui solùm ac necessarij. Atque hæc tota vis est argumenti quo Samosatenus vtitur, quam vim iam supra obtudimus. Quòd si eam adhuc infractam esse putauerit, cogitare eum peruelim hac ipsa quoq; argumentatione idem de Patre concludi posse quod narrat de Filio. Si enim hoc obtinuerit, positis subiectis, eorum actus quoslibet ponendos esse (quam rem expugnat naturæ, rationis, experientiæ, sensus etiam in nouitijs pueris veritas) & nobis vicissim hoc liceret dicere, quod absit: Pater omnia subiecit Filio: ergo non ante fuit, quàm omnia ei subijceret: proinde aut ab æterno subiecerit, aut fuerit Pater & esse cœperit in tempore: quorum neutrum Samosatenus noster accepturus est, si sibi constare volet. Præterea quandoquidem hic Deum proprie accipimus, etiam negatur valere propositionem illam qua ex ortu officij de ortu subiecti vel subsistentiæ concluditur, cùm eorum sit ratio maximè differens: officium enim ab instituto & voluntate est, persona vel subsistentia a natura est,& cætera quæ ante perstrinximus. Et natura quidem semper est in subiecto, nec ab eo natura sua abesse potest: officium nec semper est (acquiritur enim,ponitúrque commodè) nec semper inest subiecto, sed ab eo citra corruptionem illius abesse aut adesse potest, vt in hoc ipso exemplo mox demonstrabimus. Concludimus itaque, Christum Filium Dei, Deum ab æterno esse, non factum, sed genitum: Dominum verò non genitum, sed factum respectu dispensatiuæ huius dominationis, propter quam in plenitudine temporum caro factus est, & est Ἀνθρωπος ad salutem nostram.
units.tr: 4. As for the claim that the Lord is truly called King and our God anointed by the Father, to whom he also subjected all things, and that the Son of God is God only in this way and in no other (as the same writer says later), the truth of God and the catholic Church flatly deny it. Before we speak of the matter itself, however, we must make a distinction, which sound teaching requires us to observe. Many predicates are said of Christ, and they differ from one another; they do not all apply to Christ in the same way, whatever Samosatenus may assert. When a crowd of such terms is thrust upon us by careless or malicious men, nothing is more necessary than to weigh each one singly and distinctly. For who is so dull that he cannot see, even by the light of nature, that when someone is called God, Lord, King, and anointed, the reason by which he is called God is quite different from the reason by which he is called Lord, King, anointed, and so on? So that the matter may be clearer, we set out the following points in order, for the easier instruction of all: (1) Of the things predicated of Christ, some are essential, as they are called, and others are attributes of the person. (2) Whatever is of this kind is said either according to one of his natures or according to both, as they are united with each other in the person. (3) All the things that are predicated according to the divine nature or according to the human nature are predicated of the person in general, as of one and the same subject, even though the natures differ from each other. (4) Of the things that are essential to the person according to his divine nature, some are common to the holy and undivided Trinity, and others are hypostatic, that is, proper and characteristic of this one person, as the ancients called them. (5) Of the things that are essential to the person according to his human nature, some are natural, which he shared with us by nature, and others are voluntary, fittingly agreeing both with the advantage of the other nature and with the advantage of the office. (6) The attributes that Scripture predicates of the saving office are, for the most part, predicated only with respect to what pertains to the person according to both natures; of these, the divine nature is the principal agent and the human nature the instrumental one. (7) Of these attributes, some pertain to the final cause, as when he is called Jesus, the Saviour; some pertain to the office by gift and calling, as when he is called Christ, Prophet, Priest, and King; and some pertain to the actions and sufferings befitting the office and the end for which he was sent by God the Father, as when it is said that he led captivity captive in triumph and himself underwent death. (8) All these attributes belong to the Son of God according to the divine nature (to which nothing can be added or taken away), by the dispensation of grace, by which he emptied himself voluntarily, so that he, who is by his nature the highest, humbled himself to all those things that he did and suffered by his own will, when he had taken on flesh; yet both natures always remained whole, and the properties of each were kept safe. From these rules, therefore, we must judge in various ways the predications that Samosatenus heaps together. For first, the attribute "that Christ is Lord," said of the person of Christ according to both natures, is most true. According to the divine nature he is Lord from eternity, by an essential dominion, which is common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit; and he is Lord in dispensation, given in time to the Church by the Father, with a proper and personal dominion. According to the human nature he is Lord, not by that former dominion (for that is proper to the Godhead and cannot be communicated), but by the latter, having been made Lord by the Father through the grace of union (as they call it) in the unity of the person, by a voluntary dispensation. In exactly the same way we call Christ King as we call him Lord, both as he is God and as he is man [ἄνθρωπος]. For otherwise, as a mere man, he would be called Lord and King in vain, even though he rules and reigns as a man, because the humanity never subsisted in itself or by itself, even for a moment, but is always subsisting with [συνυπόστατος] and subsisting in the Word [λόγῳ]. Therefore these attributes, and any others of this kind, as they belong to the person of Christ according to the divine nature, are to be understood either essentially, and acknowledged as common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, or personally, according to both natures, as belonging to Christ our Saviour as proper to that person. But that Christ is God and is called God, in the Church, holds in a way very different from what Samosatenus says. For he was indeed made Lord and Christ (Acts 2), but he was not made God, which Samosatenus seems to conclude by a kind of analogy from equals. "The reasoning of like things is like," he will say. Certainly it is; but these things are most unlike. For God is Lord and Christ by nature, but Lord and Christ by will and appointment, if you look to personal dominion: God is so absolutely, Lord and Christ relatively and with respect to us: God is so essentially, Lord and Christ accidentally: God is so formally according to his divine nature, Lord and Christ according to both natures in the unity of the person. And will you, Samosatenus, call the reason of these things similar? But, you will reply, Christ is not God by nature, absolutely, essentially, and formally, but by communication from the Father. I answer: if the communication is by nature, or by will. If by communication of nature he is God, then he is God essentially, one with the Father; if only by voluntary grace and appointment, then he is not called God properly and univocally, but figuratively and equivocally. For he who is properly called God must be God essentially and formally (as they put it). But Christ is not called God figuratively; therefore he is called God properly. And if properly, then he is God essentially and formally. For he is as truly what he is as he is truly what he was made; and he is as properly said to be what he is as he is properly said to be what he was made. But he was truly made, and he is properly said to have been made Lord and Christ; therefore he is as truly and properly said to be God as he is truly and properly said to have been made Lord and Christ. For that he is God belongs to his nature; that he is Lord and Christ belongs to his making and appointment. Hence we read that he was made Lord and Christ by God, but by no means that he was made God. That he is truly and properly Christ and to be called God, we have already shown above in the first and second places. But if Samosatenus should contend that Christ is truly and properly to be called God because he received from the Father a communication of divine grace beyond measure [κατ' ὑπερβολήν], then, first, it is denied that he is truly and properly called God if he is not essentially what he is called; second, it is denied that anyone else is this, apart from God, since God has so often testified through his prophets that he will not give his glory to another; last, if (to reason with Tertullian) Christ was made what he is for our sake, and he was made God, as I see pleases Samosatenus, then it must be said that he was made God continually for our sake. But who does not know that the end is more excellent than the things that are done for the sake of an end and ordered to it? Therefore we, on the authority of Samosatenus, will be more excellent than Christ, since Christ was made for our sake. But this consequence is absurd, false, impious, and blasphemous; therefore the antecedent also cannot be approved by a good man in good faith. But, he says, "the Father subjected all things to him (excepting himself), so that at last he might deliver his kingdom to God and the Father, from whom he received it, after the enemies and death were overcome, so that God may be all in all" (1 Cor. 15). From that passage Samosatenus seems to want to confirm two things: first, that Christ was made God by the Father, since the Father subjected all things to him; second, that God the Father alone is essentially God. About the latter we have already spoken. Let us therefore look at the former. If Samosatenus argues to the first place in this way, "He to whom the Father subjected all things is God; the Father subjected all things to Christ; therefore Christ is God," we grant the whole argument, and we grant that he is truly and essentially God, and that the divine glory could not have been given to another. But if he argues in this way, "He to whom the Father subjected all things, the Father made God by subjecting all things to him; the Father subjected all things to Christ, all things," and so on, then the major premise is false, insulting to Christ, and alien to the nature of propositions that are called necessary. For no just law of argument can establish that the subjects from which certain acts proceed are posited unless those acts are posited. For some acts are natural and perpetual and necessary to their subject, while others are not. If these are weighed in the person of Christ, it must be said as follows: according to the natural, perpetual, and necessary act, the Father begets the Son, God begets God; he does not make or has not made him. According to the non-natural, voluntary act, the Father did not make the Son or God, but made that Son of his and our God Lord and Christ, and subjected all things to him. For the subject and the natural, adjacent, and necessary things are one by nature; the others are not so. For when the acts are posited (as the logicians rightly teach), the subjects and adjacent things from which they proceed are posited; but conversely, when the subjects are posited, not every act is posited, only the natural and necessary ones. And this is the whole force of the argument that Samosatenus uses, a force that we have already weakened above. But if he thinks that it is still unbroken, I would very much like him to consider that by this very same argument it could be concluded about the Father what he tells about the Son. For if this held, then, the subjects being posited, all their acts would have to be posited (a thing that nature, reason, experience, and even the truth of the senses in newborn children refute), and in turn we might be allowed to say, which God forbid: "The Father subjected all things to the Son; therefore he was not before he subjected all things to him; so either he subjected them from eternity, or he was the Father and began to be in time." Our Samosatenus will accept neither of these, if he wishes to be consistent. Moreover, since we here take "God" properly, it is also denied that the proposition holds by which, from the origin of an office, one concludes the origin of the subject or subsistence, since these have a very different reason: for the office comes from appointment and will, while the person or subsistence comes from nature, and the other things we have touched on before. And nature is indeed always in the subject, nor can it be separated from the subject by its nature; the office is not always present (for it is acquired and conferred as it is fitting), and it is not always in the subject, but can be present or absent from him without corruption, as we will show shortly in this very example. We conclude, therefore, that Christ, the Son of God, is God from eternity, not made but begotten; but he is Lord not begotten but made, with respect to this dispensatory dominion, for which, in the fullness of time, he became flesh and is man [ἄνθρωπος] for our salvation.

units.la: Alterum verò argumentum huic quasi succenturiatû Samosatenus complectitur ex verbis Pauli in hunc modum: Qui regnum Deo ac Patri traditurus est, & subiectus futurus ei, vs Deus factus est: Hoc autem factu-rus est Christus: ergo Deus factus est. Maior falsa est evidentissimè: tum demum futura vera, si ita dixeris, Qui regnum Deo Patri traditurus est & subiectus futurus ei, vs Rex factus est. Hæc, inquam, vera est propositio, si de persona Christi acceperis dictum Pauli. Sed in hac propositione ambigua sunt multa, quorum nomine conclusio evertitur: deinde plura rogata sunt, vt loquuntur vulgo, quæ ab Apostolo optimè distincta, hic a Samosateno pessimè confunduntur. Ambigua sunt hæc: primùm quòd dispensatiuum regnum Christi cum æterno illo & diuino conturbatur: cùm tamen hoc dispensatiuum sit ordinatum ad illud tamquam ad finem & complementû suum, & illud æternum sit huius dispensatiui finis. Etenim regnum dispensatiû Christi iam peruenit ad nos: de æterno, dum in hoc dispensatiuo degimus, oramus auctore Christo, adueniat regnum tuum. Secundò, quòd nomen Christi dicitur æquiuocè: dicitur enim Christus propriè quidem persona illa Filij Dei, figurate vero διὰ σωματικοχῆς caput cum corpore, Christus cum Ecclesia sua, quem orthodoxi Patres convenienter Scripturæ Christum mysticum appellabant. Christus autem in persona sua regnum illud dispensatione assumtum Deo & Patri traditurus est: idem vero in corpore carnis vel humanitatis suæ & Ecclesiæ suæ subiectus Deo & Patri futurus est, vt Defensionis 2. segmento 12. demonstrauimus. Atque hæc duo illa rogata sunt (vt cum vulgo Logicorum loquar) quæ a Samosateno confundi ante dicebamus, regnum tradere, & subiectum esse. Nam qua factus fuit rex Christus, in persona sua regnum Deo & Patri traditurus est: subiectus vero futurus est, qua regni subditos in vnum corpus adunauit sibi. Huius distinctionis ipse Paulus nobis est auctor locupletissimus. Postquam enim certitudinem resurrectionis nostræ futuræ confirmauit resurrectione Christi, velut capitis primitiarumque nostrarum, & conclusit dicens, quia per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectionem mortuorum esse: ne ad alia resurrectionis forte argumenta transcurreret non satis explicato resurrectionis Christi & regni eius, in quo resurrecturi sumus, mysterio, ordinem modumque illius visum est ei contextu vno percurrere. Vnusquisque, inquit, suo ordine: primitiæ Christus resurrectionis nostræ quam credimus, postea qui sunt Christi resurgent in aduentu ipsius. Deinde erit finis, puta dispensatiui illius regni & procurationis regiæ quam Pater commisit Filio, quum tradiderit ipsud regnum Deo & Patri, a quo acceperat vt seruaret electos suos. Atque hæc res non ante fiet, quàm aboleuerit omne imperium & omne potentiam & virtutem, vt tribus versibus proximè sequentibus exponitur. Postquam vero subiecta fuerint ei omnia, debellati hostes & adunati pij, tunc & ipse Filius cum Ecclesia (quæ est corpus & complementum ipsius) adunatus
units.tr: The second argument, which Samosatenus adds almost as a reserve to the first, he draws from the words of Paul in this way: He who is going to hand the kingdom over to God and the Father, and will be subject to him, has been made God; but Christ is going to do this; therefore Christ has been made God. The major premise is plainly false. It would be true only if you said, He who is going to hand the kingdom over to God the Father, and will be subject to him, has been made King. This proposition, I say, is true if you take Paul's words as referring to the person of Christ. But the proposition contains many ambiguities, and the conclusion is overturned because of them. Moreover, several things are assumed, as people commonly put it, which the Apostle distinguishes very well but which Samosatenus confuses very badly. The ambiguities are these. First, the dispensational kingdom of Christ is confused with that eternal and divine kingdom, although the dispensational kingdom is ordained toward the eternal one as toward its end and completion, and the eternal kingdom is the end of this dispensational one. For the dispensational kingdom of Christ has already come to us, while the eternal one we pray for, as Christ taught us, while we live in this dispensation: Thy kingdom come. Second, the name of Christ is used equivocally. Christ is properly the person of the Son of God, but figuratively, by a bodily figure [διὰ σωματικῆς κεφαλῆς], Christ is the head together with the body, Christ together with his Church, whom the orthodox Fathers rightly called the mystical Christ, in agreement with Scripture. Christ, in his own person, will hand over that kingdom, which he has taken up by dispensation, to God and the Father; but in the body of his flesh or humanity and in his Church he will be subject to God and the Father, as we showed in the second section of the Defence, chapter 12. These two things are the ones (to speak with the common run of logicians) that Samosatenus, as we said before, confuses: handing over the kingdom, and being subject. For insofar as Christ was made king, he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father in his own person; but he will be subject insofar as he has joined the subjects of the kingdom to himself as one body. Paul himself is a most weighty authority for this distinction. After he had confirmed the certainty of our future resurrection by the resurrection of Christ, as the head and first fruits of ours, and had concluded by saying, since by man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead, he thought it fit, lest he run on to other arguments for the resurrection without having fully explained the mystery of Christ's resurrection and of the kingdom in which we are to rise, to go through its order and manner in one passage. Each in his own order, he says: Christ the first fruits; then those who are Christ's, at his coming. Then comes the end, namely of that dispensational kingdom and royal administration which the Father committed to the Son, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, from whom he received it, that he might keep his elect. And this will not happen until he has abolished all dominion, and all power and might, as is set out in the three verses that immediately follow. But when all things have been subjected to him, the enemies overcome and the godly gathered together, then the Son himself together with the Church (which is his body and fulfilment) gathered together

units.la: Logicorum loquar subjcietur ei qui subiecit ipsi omnia, id est, regia illa procuratione quam accepit a Patre deposita, ipse cùm in persona sua secundùm carnem, tum in persona suorum secundùm corpus adscitum & mysticum ipsius, subiectus erit Patri qui omnia subiecit ipsi, regnúmque illud mediatorium dispensatione diuina tradidit, vt sit non quidem solus Pater,sed Deus omnia in omnibus, id est, diuina illa essentia, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus simpliciter & citra vllum praeterea mediationis actum sit in omnibus pijs ad vitam gloriámque vocatis in Christo omnia. Nā pijs & sanctis Deus est omnia, subsistentibus in Deo illa subsistentia gratiæ, qua æternùm in ipso ad vitam & gloriam æternam subsistemus. Quæ cùm ita sint,quis bonus non videat, obsecro, istas argumentationes nec per se cōsistere, nec per huiusmodi probationes falsò adductas atque expositas fulciri posse ? Ex his tamen summa præsidentia concludit Samosatenus in hunc modum, hæc est Christi solius prærogatiua & dignitas, &c. Et hac ratione, & non alia, Filius Dei est Deus, Dominus & Christus, Rex, Sacerdos, caput, Propheta, &c. quæ omnia quàm sint falsa & discrepantia a vero, antehac ostendimus. Nam Christus non est factus secundùm quod Deus : sed Christus Deus, qui verè & essentialiter Deus est, is factus est Dominus & Christus, rex, sacerdos, &c. quæ officia assumsit sibi, assumtáque fidelissimè est exsequutus, & adhuc exsequitur ad salutem nostram. De posteriore conuenit: prius, quamuis iam antè probatum, hac demonstratione concludemus : Quisquis verè Deus est, non est factus Deus : Christus autem verè Deus est: non factus igitur. Maiorem probant essentiales omnes de Deo prædicationes: quas fiquis de medio sustulerit, etiā teste natura tollit Deum. Et per conuersionem eiusdem propositionis, Quisquis id factus est quod est essentialiter, is non verè Deus est, est, sed factura siue creatura Dei: Christus autem vere Deus est, Filius Dei genitus, non creatus aut factus: Christus ergo id non est factus quod est essentialiter, siquidem vere Deus est. Est autem vere Deus: nam filius est Dei μονογενὴς, vnigenitus: & facti quidem caeteri, at non factus Christus secundum id quod Deus est: ergo est Deus essentialiter, vt pluribus ante ostendimus. Tandem concludit Samosatenus duobus absurdis, vt sanctissimam illam & catholicam doctrinam de Christo reddat odiosam. Etsi in propositione cauedus est ille scopulus, quem ante principio huius loci demonstrauimus, quum Samosatenus ait, qui Christum a seipso Deum esse credit, hunc duos Deos inducere, &c. Nam Christus secundum essentiam est a se & per se, at secundum personam a Patre est. A seipso Deus est Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus secundum esse, at secundum illud quod est subsistere, Pater a nullo subsistentiam habet, Filius non habet a seipso, id est, a nullo, sed a persona Patris tamquam principio suo habet subsistentiam suam personam Filij. Nam vna eademq; essentia tota est Patris, tota Filij & tota Spiritus sancti: est autem a nullo essentia: si ab aliquo esse dicitur, alius supra Deum Deus statuitur, & principium aliud: quod vel cogitare nefas. Sed absurda videamus. Prius est qui hoc sentit quod nos sentimus, hunc duos Deos inducere: posterius, afficere Patrem summa contumelia. Vtrumque absurdum negamus: prius, distincte, posterius simpliciter. Ad prius enim ita respondemus: Deus aut absolute dicitur de essentia substantiaue illa quae est ὑπόστασις, aut relate & determinate de subsistentia. Secundum priorem significationem falsò dicimur duos aut treis Deos inducere, qui vnam Dei essentiam constantissimè corde credimus, & ore confitemur. Secundum posteriorem, ambiguè & captio e dicimur duos item Deos inducere, pro eo quod est duas subsistentias siue personas subsistentes
units.tr: (to speak with the logicians) will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him; that is, he will lay down the royal administration he received from the Father. Then he himself, both in his own person according to the flesh, and in the persons of his people according to the body taken up and mystical to him, will be subject to the Father, who subjected all things to him and handed over that mediatorial kingdom by divine dispensation, so that God may be not only the Father, but God all in all, that is, the divine essence itself, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, simply and without any further act of mediation, may be in all the godly, called to life and glory in Christ. For to the pious and holy God is all things, since they subsist in God by that subsistence of grace by which we shall subsist in him eternally, to eternal life and glory. These things being so, who of good sense, I beg you, does not see that these arguments neither stand by themselves nor can be propped up by proofs falsely brought forward and set out in this way? Yet from these things Samosatenus concludes with great confidence, in this manner: This is the sole prerogative and dignity of Christ, etc. And by this reasoning, and no other, the Son of God is God, Lord and Christ, King, Priest, Head, Prophet, etc. How false all these things are, and how far they are from the truth, we have shown before. For Christ was not made God in so far as he is God; but Christ, who is truly and essentially God, was made Lord and Christ, King, Priest, etc., offices which he took upon himself, and which he has most faithfully carried out, and still carries out, for our salvation. Concerning the latter point we agree; but the former, although already proved before, we shall conclude by this demonstration: Whoever is truly God has not been made God; but Christ is truly God; therefore he has not been made. The major premise is proved by all the essential predications about God, which, if anyone removed them, would take away God, even by nature's own testimony. And by converting the same proposition: Whoever has been made what he is essentially is not truly God, but a thing made or a creature of God; but Christ is truly God, the Son of God begotten, not created or made; therefore Christ has not been made what he is essentially, since he is truly God. He is truly God: for he is the Son of God, only-begotten [μονογενής], the only begotten; and the rest are made, but Christ is not made according to what he is as God; therefore he is God essentially, as we have shown at greater length before. Finally, Samosatenus concludes with two absurdities, so as to make that most holy and catholic doctrine of Christ odious. Yet in this proposition we must beware of the rock which we pointed out at the beginning of this place, when Samosatenus says, whoever believes that Christ is God from himself, this man introduces two Gods, etc. For Christ is from himself and through himself according to his essence, but from the Father according to his person. As to being, God is from himself: the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. But as to that which is to subsist, the Father has his subsistence from no one, while the Son does not have it from himself, that is, from no one, but has his subsistence as the person of the Son from the person of the Father as his beginning. For the one and the same essence is wholly the Father's, wholly the Son's and wholly the Holy Spirit's; but the essence is from no one. If it is said to be from someone, another God is set up above God and another beginning, which it is wicked even to think. But let us look at the absurdities. The first is, he who thinks what we think introduces two Gods; the second, that he insults the Father with the greatest contumely. We deny both absurdities: the first in a distinct way, the second simply. For to the first we answer thus: God is said absolutely of the essence and substance, which is the hypostasis, or said relatively and in a determined way of the subsistence. In the first sense we are falsely said to introduce two or three Gods, since we most constantly believe in our heart and confess with our mouth the one essence of God. In the second sense we are said, ambiguously and captiously, to introduce two Gods likewise, meaning that there are two subsistences or persons who subsist

units.la: has profiteri in vnitate essentiæ, prout Filius & Pater sunt essentia vnum, Scripturis contestantibus. Quia enim simulatque nominatur Deus, continuò intelligitur essentialis illa forma deitatis quæ hypostasewn Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti communis est, illa autem essentialis forma est vnica, propterea male tres Deos nominat qui tres essentias constituunt deitatis. Cùm verò illa essentialis forma deitatis sit trium hypostasewn communis, etiam illius nomen de singulis hypostasibus optimè enunciatur, vt commune de suis particularibus enunciari solet. Verumtamen treis illas hypostases nobis religio est tres Deos dicere, ne videamur (quod Samosatenus criminatur falsò) treis essentias vel essentiales formas deitatis reipsa statuere: cùm illam vnicam essentiam seu essentiale deitatis formam non diuidamus re in personas siue hypostases, sed ratione solùm ex sacra Scriptura distinguamus personas illas in vnitate indiuisæ illius essentiæ. Tres itaq; Deos minimè, sed treis hypostases seu personas diuinas dicimus, quæ sunt Deus Pater, Deus Filius, Deus Spiritus sanctus, ratione tres personæ, essentia vnus Deus, ac non plures. Nam vox Deus proprie essentiam notat, quæ vna est: hypostasewn verò siue personarum singularitatem indicamus relatiuis appellationibus & notionibus illarum, quum Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum nominamus. Atqui, fortasse dixerit, supposita, quæ vnum sunt essentia, alia ab aliis diuisa sunt, & differentibus locus capiuntur. Respondeo, id quidem Physicè verum est, & necessariò verum in rebus corporeis: sed in formis intelligetibus & Metaphysicis solùm contingenter verum est; in diuinis nunquam. Itaque parentes quidem liberos extrudunt extra se, & singuli singulis locis capiuntur: sed spirituum alia est ratio, qui locum definitiuum capiunt, non ipsi capiuntur loco. Exemplum esto in dæmoniaco, de quo Marci 5. Luc. 8. nam eius spiritus habuit totum corpus ipsius, & idem tamen miseri hominis corpus legio daemonum legitur habuisse. Spiritus ergo suum locum νοητὸν & definitiuum capiunt, sed vnum eumdemq; locum aut singuli, aut multi, prout contigerit. Sed cum Deus essentia infinita sit, & in vnitate essentiae solummodo ratione inter se personae distinguantur, absurdum est diuisionem ponere vllam in ea essentia quae & infinita est tota vbique secundum perfectionem essentiae suae simul, & sola ratione distingui potest. Nam hae duae proprietates essentiales deitatis omni diuisioni aduersantur. Posterius absurdum, Patrem a nobis affici contumelia, vere absurdum est & absurde obijcitur. Nam Patrem is demum afficit contumelia qui perfectam sui imaginem ab eo genitam fuisse negat: hoc autem Samosateniani faciunt, vt perspicue Defensionis 2. segmento 6. docuimus. Nos autem, qui perfectā imaginem sui a Patre expressam fuisse agnoscimus, non contumeliose de Deo loquimur, sed honorificentissime glorificamus Patrem & Filium, credentes verbo Christi, qui discipulos suos hoc docuit, dicens, qui vidit me, vidit Patrem. Atq; haec ad prioris Samosateni verba. Posterior vero, quia his dictis non ita facile fidem sensit haberi posse, dedit operam argutijs quibusdam praeterea, his Grammaticis, illis Theologicis. Primum enim vt viam sternat doctrinae suae, inuestigat Hebraicam, & Graecam Dei appellationem: nec tamen admodum feliciter. Nomen Dei apud Hebraeos negat esse nomen substantiae aut personae proprium, sed auctoritatis, &c. De hoc nomine diximus aliquoties. Sed (ne actum agamus) quid ais, Samosatene? vtrum Dei nomen proprium, an figuratum est? Certe figuratum non est, proprium igitur. Dices, proprium a te non figurato opponi, sed appellatiuo nomini. At qui negas nomen esse substantiae aut personae:
units.tr: to profess in the unity of essence, since the Son and the Father are one in essence, as the Scriptures testify. For as soon as the name God is spoken, we immediately understand that essential form of deity which is common to the hypostases of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That essential form is one, so it is wrong to call them three Gods, as if they constituted three essences of deity. Yet since that essential form of deity is common to the three hypostases, its name is also rightly applied to each hypostasis, as a common name is customarily predicated of its particulars. Nevertheless, we think it wrong for religion to call those three hypostases three Gods, lest we appear (as Samosatenus falsely charges) to posit in fact three essences or essential forms of deity. We do not divide that one essence, or essential form of deity, in reality into persons or hypostases; we distinguish those persons only by reason, from Holy Scripture, within the undivided unity of that essence. So we do not speak of three Gods at all, but of three hypostases or divine persons, namely God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. As three persons they are one God in essence, and not many. For the word God properly denotes the essence, which is one; but we indicate the singularity of the hypostases or persons by the relative appellations and notions of them, when we name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But, perhaps he will say, things that are one in essence are supposed to be separated from one another, and different things occupy places. I answer that this is indeed true physically, and necessarily true of bodily things; but among intelligible and metaphysical forms it is true only contingently, and in divine things never. Thus parents indeed thrust their children out of themselves, and each child occupies its own place; but the case of spirits is different: spirits occupy a place by definition, and are not themselves contained by place. Let the example be the demoniac of whom we read in Mark 5 and Luke 8: his spirit possessed his whole body, and yet the same body of that unhappy man is said to have been possessed by a legion of demons. Spirits therefore occupy their place noētōn [intelligibly] and by definition, but either one or many occupy the same place, as it happens. But since God is an infinite essence, and the persons are distinguished within the unity of the essence only by reason, it is absurd to posit any division in that essence, which is infinite and wholly everywhere at once according to the perfection of its essence, and which can be distinguished only by reason. For these two essential properties of the deity are opposed to every division. The second absurdity, that the Father is insulted by us, is truly absurd and absurdly alleged. For the Father is insulted only by one who denies that he begot a perfect image of himself; and this is what the Samosatenians do, as we clearly showed in the sixth section of the second book of the Defensio. We, however, who acknowledge that a perfect image of himself was expressed by the Father, do not speak insultingly of God, but glorify the Father and the Son most honorably, believing the word of Christ, who taught his disciples this, saying: He who has seen me has seen the Father. So much for the first words of Samosatenus. The second, however, since he felt that these words could not so easily be believed, devoted effort to certain subtleties, some grammatical, others theological. First, to pave the way for his teaching, he investigates the Hebrew and Greek appellation of God, and not very successfully. He denies that the name of God among the Hebrews is a proper name of substance or person, but of authority, and so on. We have spoken about this name several times. But (not to waste time), what do you say, Samosatenus? Is the name God proper or figurative? Surely it is not figurative, so it is proper. You will say that proper is opposed not to figurative, but to appellative. But you deny that the name is of substance or person:

units.la: nomina autem quæ de substantijs dicuntur, nisi sint primæ substantiæ, etiā appellatiua Grammaticis dicta sunt. Tu proprietatis assertor loqueris improprie. Id fortasse tibi voluisti, non notari proprie simpliciterque substantiam Dei, vt fit illo Hebræo Iehoua. Hic vero duo tibi in mentem venire oportuit: vnū, proprie notari subiectum de quo agitur humano sermone, non solum nomine essentiali aut etiā characteristico & indiuiduali ipsius, verumetiam nomine (vt Scholastici vocant) connotante, id est, quo directe aliquid aliud spectatur, sed subiectum per consequentiam propriam & necessariam intelligitur: alterum, quæcunque attributa in Scripturis exstant Deum connotantia, ea vniuoce ad Deum pertinere, ad homines æquiuoce: proinde iudicem, sufficientem, fortem, &c. Deum appellari non κατ' ἐξοχὴν (si proprie loquamur) quia ἐξοχὴ est rerum congenerum quas vocant homogeneas; sed simpliciter, quia est, & ita vt dicitur est; cæteri esse ab eo habent tamquam principio per communicationem. Esto igitur: sit nomē auctoritatis, dignitatis, ac beneficentiæ, vt tu vis: at de Deo tamen enunciatur vniuoce: itaque si substantiam non notat, connotat tamen, & quidem proprie connotat; quod est ad rem præsentem satis. Subtilius vocem θεὸς exquirit, & proverbia adfert. Commeta hæc expugnare possem. Sed Grammatici viderint: nam ista pedibus per me trahantur licet. Quod in diuinis literis Dei nomine significari dicit, per eandem connotationem est quam modo diximus: sic mihi liceat cum vulgo Scholasticorum loqui. Summa: sic argumentatur hoc loco Samosatenus: Nomen Dei non notat essentiam subiecti de quo prædicatur: Christus subiectum est de quo nomen Dei prædicatur: ergo non notat essentiam Christi, puta diuinam esse eo quod appellatur Deus. Respondetur ad maiorem distinctione, in rebus creatis verum esse quod non notetur tur subiectum, quia transfertur per abusionem quamdā hoc nomen a subiecto suo, de quo vniuocè prædicatur, ad subiectum toto genere differens, &transfertur æquiuocè: at in diuinis aliter se habet, quia vniuoca est de Deo Nuius nominis prædicatio. Quapropter hoc modo arguimus, Nomen cōnotans vniuocè notat essentiam rei, Nomen Dei connotat vniuocè: Igitur essentiam notat in diuinis rebus. De Christo si neget Samosatenus diuino modo accipi oportere, ne longius abeamus, ex Ioanne & hoc ipso loco confirmatur. Nam iniquum est vnum nomen eodem in loco variè accipi, nisi cogat prædicationis modus: In hac autem sententia, Sermo erat apud Deum, & Sermo erat Deus, idem nomen bis prædicatur, nec varietatem cogit prædicationis modus: Eodem igitur modo accipiendum: ac proinde vt de Deo, sic de Sermone Dei essentiam diuinam connotat. Hic adfert Angelorum, principum, & Mosis exempla, probaturus essentiam minimè notari Dei appellatione. Sed quid hoc ad rem? nam vt prædicatis inest subiecti sui modificatio, sic etiam subiecta modum ostendunt prædicationum. Hæc subiecta sunt creata: ergo prædicationes dexterè intelligendæ pro ratione ipsorum. At Christus aliud subiectum est: quapropter nihil ad ipsum illa prædicati, quo de agitur, modificatio: vt ex Irenæo & Chrysostomo segmento 2. ostendimus. Negat Christum aliud subiectum esse, quum dicit, asserere ipsum ita Deum esse vt habeatur pro illo summo altissimóq; omnium auctore, extrema est impietas. At nos in eo collocamus pietatis arcem, & ibidem a Ioanne ipso collocari modò comprobauimus. Vt autem dictum suum pietati aduersum probet, duo colligit testimoniorum genera e Scripturis sacris: vnum, de Deo Patre: de Filio, alterum. Ex priore testimoniorum genere sic argumentatur: Solus Pater inuisibilis ac omnipotens Iehoua in Scripturs esse dicitur ille summus & altissimus auctor omnium: Filius ergo non est ille summus & altissimus omnium auctor. De hac argumentatione diximus ante satis Defensione 2. In summa, Antecedens huius enthymematis ambiguum est: & ita quod de uno sensu in antecedente potest affirmari sanctè, diverso sensu in consequente concluditur. Quamobrem antecedens distinguimus: negamus consequens. Antecedentis duo sunt æquivoca. Primum enim Deus appellatur Pater aut essentialiter (est autem Deus essentia unus, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus) respectu creaturarum, aut personaliter respectu Filij & relationis internæ illius quæ est inter Patrem & Filium. Priore modo interpretationis antecedens agnoscimus: posteriore minimè. Ad hunc autem consequens respicit. Secundo nomen solus aut est categorematicum, simpliciter notans subiecti solitudinem, velut carentis altero eadem natura aut conditione præditò; aut est syncategorematicum, respectu alicuius dictum. Si Pater solus dicitur categorematicè, propositio falsa: nam neque persona Patris est sola, neque essentia Dei sola, in quo viuimus, mouemur, & sumus. Sinautè solus appellatur syncategorematicè, aut statuitur solitudo in forma subiecti; aut in ratione prædicati. In subiecto: quemadmodum Augustinus dicit, Solum Patrem dicimus, non quia separatur a Filio, vel Spiritu sancto, sed hoc dicentes significamus, quòd illi simul cum eo non sunt Pater. Atque hoc sensu de Patre ἀπωδῶς verum, (vt in sequentibus etiam interpretationum modis) hoc dictū est sed falsum hypostaticè. In ratione prædicati aut excludit alium, aut aliud. Si alium personaliter, itidem falsum: si aliud, verissimum. nam quid adæquaretur Deo, aut consociaretur illi? Ex ambiguo nihil concluditur: quid falso facias? nam ex consequente argumentationis tuæ facilè deprehendimus quid tibi isto antecedente velis, quum Christum opponis Patri. Hac mente utrumque falsum. sum. Confirmaturus sententiam suam duos locos e Scripturis adfert, utrumque incommodè: nam eadem æquivocatione & ambiguitate conatur fallere. Sed de ijs iam diximus Defensionis 2. segmento 3. & 4. & 10. & alijs præterea locis. Inconsequens & falsa argumentatio.
units.tr: Yet names that are predicated of substances, unless they are primary substances, are also called appellative by the grammarians. You, an advocate of a property, speak improperly. Perhaps you meant that the substance of God is not signified properly and simply, as happens with that Hebrew name Iehoua. But here two things ought to have come to your mind. First, that the subject under discussion is properly signified in human speech not only by its essential or even characteristic and individual name, but also by a name that, as the Scholastics call it, connotes, that is, by which something else is directly regarded, while the subject is understood through a proper and necessary consequence. Second, whatever attributes are found in the Scriptures connoting God, these pertain to God univocally, and to men equivocally; hence judge, sufficient, strong, and so on are said of God not kat' exochēn [pre-eminently] (if we speak properly), because exochē [pre-eminence] belongs to things of the same kind, which they call homogeneous, but simply because he is, and is as he is called; the others have their being from him as from a principle, by communication. Granted, then, let it be a name of authority, dignity, and beneficence, as you wish: yet it is predicated of God univocally; so if it does not denote the substance, it nevertheless connotes it, and indeed connotes it properly, which is enough for the present matter. He investigates the word theos more subtly, and brings forward proverbs. I could overthrow these arguments. But let the grammarians look to them; for these may be dragged about by the feet, so far as I am concerned. As to what he says the name God signifies in the divine letters, it is by the same connotation that we have just described; so let me speak with the common usage of the Scholastics. In short, Samosatenus argues at this point thus: The name of God does not denote the essence of the subject of which it is predicated; Christ is the subject of which the name of God is predicated; therefore it does not denote the essence of Christ, namely that he is divine by the fact that he is called God. We reply to the major premise with a distinction: in created things it is true that the subject is not denoted, because this name is transferred by a certain abuse from its subject, of which it is univocally predicated, to a subject totally different in kind, and is transferred equivocally; but in divine things it is otherwise, because the predication of this name of God is univocal. Therefore we argue in this way: A connoting name univocally denotes the essence of a thing; the name of God connotes univocally; therefore in divine things it denotes the essence. If Samosatenus denies that Christ must be understood in a divine sense, this is confirmed, not to go farther afield, from John and from this very passage. For it is unfair for one name to be taken in various ways in the same place, unless the mode of predication compels it. But in this sentence, The Word was with God, and The Word was God, the same name is predicated twice, and the mode of predication does not compel a variation; therefore it must be taken in the same way; and so, just as in God, so in the Word of God it connotes the divine essence. Here he brings forward examples of angels, princes, and Moses, meaning to prove that the name of God does not in the least denote the essence. But what has this to do with the matter? For just as predicates contain a modification of their subject, so also subjects show the mode of their predications. These subjects are created; therefore the predications must be understood aptly according to their nature. But Christ is another subject; therefore that modification of the predicate under discussion has nothing to do with him, as we have shown from Irenaeus and Chrysostom in the second section. He denies that Christ is another subject when he says that to assert that he is God in such a way that he is regarded as that highest and most exalted author of all is the utmost impiety. But we place the citadel of piety in exactly this, and we have just shown that John himself places it there. And to prove his saying against piety, he gathers two kinds of testimonies from the sacred Scriptures: one concerning God the Father, the other concerning the Son. From the first kind of testimony he argues thus: In the Scriptures, the Father alone is called the invisible and almighty Jehovah, that highest and most exalted author of all; therefore the Son is not that highest and most exalted author of all. We have said enough about this argument before, in the second book of the Defensio. In short, the antecedent of this enthymeme is ambiguous, so that what can be affirmed soundly in one sense in the antecedent is concluded in a different sense in the consequent. Therefore we distinguish the antecedent and deny the consequent. The antecedent contains two equivocations. First, God is called Father either essentially (since God is one in essence, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) with respect to creatures, or personally with respect to the Son and to that internal relation which exists between the Father and the Son. We grant the antecedent in the first sense of interpretation, but not at all in the second; and it is to this that the consequent refers. Second, the word alone is either categorematic, simply denoting the solitude of the subject, as of one lacking another of the same nature or condition; or it is syncategorematic, said with respect to something. If the Father is called alone categorematically, the proposition is false; for neither is the person of the Father alone, nor is the essence of God alone, in whom we live, move, and have our being. But if alone is applied syncategorematically, the solitude is placed either in the form of the subject or in the nature of the predicate. In the subject: as Augustine says, We say the Father alone, not because he is separated from the Son or the Holy Spirit, but in saying this we signify that they are not the Father together with him. And in this sense, what is said of the Father is true apōdōs [in the way of a correlative], as also in the following modes of interpretation; but it is false as to the hypostases. In the nature of the predicate it either excludes another or something else. If it excludes another personally, it is likewise false; if something else, it is most true; for what could be equal to God, or associated with him? Nothing is concluded from an ambiguous premise. What would you achieve by a false one? For from the consequent of your argument we readily perceive what you wish by this antecedent, when you set Christ against the Father. In this sense both are false. To confirm his view, he brings forward two passages from the Scriptures, both to no advantage; for he tries to deceive by the same equivocation and ambiguity. But we have already discussed these in the third and fourth sections of the second book of the Defensio, and in other places as well. The argument is inconsequent and false.

units.la: His dictis, transiturus Samosatenus ad alterum testimoniorum genus de persona Christi, occupatione utitur non negare se quin Christus sit Deus, sed Deum esse inferiorem Patre, superiorem aliis omnibus qui dicuntur dij. Quod totum sub principium huius segmenti ante cofutauimus. Nam si Christum fatetur Deũ, aut proprie dicatur necesse est, aut figurate Deus: non autem figuratè, ut essentia, potentia, officijs, operationibus, effectis eius & testimonijs Scripturæ centies demonstratum: proprie igitur. Tum quod inferiorem dicit Patre, quà Christus Deus est, fallit elenchi ignoratione: nam quà Deus est essentialiter, & secundum naturam diuinam suam, æqualis est Patri: quà autem Mediator caro factus consilio suo, & secundum dispensationem voluntatis suæ, est inferior Patre. Nam qui Deus est natura, inaniuit sese voluntate gratiæ. Ingrati autem est animi, si eius naturam qui se abiecit tua causa, eo ipso nomine quòd abiecit sese, oppugnaueris. Sic κενὸς τροφεὰ ἀπολωνύει, quod vulgo dici solet. Quamobrem ut sequentibus verbis euehat Christum, nihil agit. Ut si quis hominem iugulet, ornet imaginem, sic Christo Samosatenus facit: naturalia destruit, prædicat accidētia & adiuncta eius. Atqui natura destructa, Samosatene, id nunquam effeceris, ut vere diuina de Christo prædicentur: nam quæ verè & essentialiter diuina sunt, ea sunt incommunicabilia: nec magis fieri potest ut creatura essentialiter res verè diuinas habeat, quàm ut creatura sit Deus. Res verè diuinæ sunt deitatis propriæ totius, solius, & semper, secundum perfectionem essentiæ eius. Has si Christus habet, (vt habet) verè Deus est secundùm perse-ctionem essentiæ illius: si non est Deus secundùm perse-ctionem essentiæ illius, nec res illas verè diuinas habet, vt-cunque hominem amplissima oratione extuleris. Te-stimoniorum de Christo summa est, ea prædicari in Scri-pturis de Christo quæ Deo essentiali non possunt competere: ex quibus concluditur Christum ergo non esse Deum essentialiter natura, sed accidentariè per communicationem gratiæ. Ne-gatur omnium consequentia: quia antecedens & conse-quens secundùm aliud & aliud dicta sunt. Nam quædam prædicantur de Christo, quà Deus essentialiter; atque hæc diuina sunt: quædam prædicantur de eodem, quà Θεάν-θρωπος, Deus & homo in vnitate personæ: atque hæc me-diatoria sunt: quædam verò quà homo similis factus fra-tribus suis, excepto peccato: atque hæc humana. Quem-admodum autem primus ille distinctionū gradus in per-sona Christi sequentes & inferiores non abolet: sic et-iam non aboletur sequentibus & inferioribus his, quos modò ostendimus. Concurrunt, non concertant: constituunt vnum opus suppositi vnius, non autem suppositum aut partes illius destruunt: quod Samosa-tenus hoc testimoniorum genere conatur agere. Nam vtrique naturæ Christi, velut differentibus subiectis, sua sunt adiacentia & actus necessarij: similiterque per-sonæ, velut supposito ex duabus illis naturis constanti. Hi autem actus & adiacentia distincta permanent, nec magis confundi possunt quàm ipsæ naturæ ad constitutionem personæ vnius adunatæ. Itaque a parte vna de altera nihil concluditur, aut contra alteram: nec a natura vna de altera, aut contra alteram in hoc argumento. Demonstratur illud hominis exemplo ex corpore & anima constituti. Nam si quis aut corporis attributa de anima enunciauerit, aut ex attributis corporis de anima itidem arguargumentetur, quis ineptientem ferat? Idem facit Samosatenus de persona Christi loquens, & applaudit sibi. Belle sane. At quis hoc argumentationis modo tandem non vincat hominem nihil nisi corporeum esse, ac pro-inde Samosatenum ipsum nihil nisi brutam pecudè censeri oportere? Quem hominem non pudeat istius infantiæ, simul atque in se ipse respexerit? Sed ad locos singulos veniamus.
