Primus locus est Heb. 1. & 3. vbi Christus cum Angelis, cum Mose comparatur, & illis anteponitur. Recte: sed anteponitur, mi homo, non solum propter dona gratiæ accepta in tempore, verum etiam, idque inprimis, propter veritatem naturæ diuinæ, & deitatem personæ: quod Apostolus utroque loco clamat potentissimè. Etenim capite 1. versu 1. appellatur Filius: versu 2. per eum Deus mundum condidisse: versu 3. esse dicitur effulgentia gloriæ & character personæ illius, sustinens omnia virtute verbi sui: versu 6. iubentur Angeli adorare illum, quod soli Deo deberi Christus ipse ex Mose docuit Matth. 4. tum versu 8. de Filio dicit Psaltes, Solium tuum, o Deus, in seculum seculorum: & alia quamplurima, quæ breuitatis causa omittimus. Est igitur anteponendus Angelis, Mosi, creaturis omnibus, non solum propter communicatam gratiæ plenitudinem, sed etiam propter naturæ illius diuinæ, quam ex Scripturis in Christo nouimus atque colimus, veritatem: non solum propter dona, vocationem, officia, beneficia, operationes, effectáque diuina illius, sed etiam propter naturam diuinam ipsius, quæ sola natura est subiectum in se per se capax istarum operationū; in carne vero sua, velut instrumento coniuncto, operans.
units.tr: Having said this, Samosatenus, about to turn to the second kind of testimony concerning the person of Christ, uses this evasion: he does not deny that Christ is God, but that God is inferior to the Father and superior to all the others who are called gods. This whole point we refuted at the beginning of this section. For if he grants that Christ is God, the name must be used either properly or figuratively. It is not used figuratively, since this has been shown a hundred times over from his essence, power, offices, operations and effects, and from the testimonies of Scripture. So it is used properly. Next, when he says that Christ is inferior to the Father, in so far as Christ is God, he commits a fallacy of ignorance of the question. For as God, essentially and according to his divine nature, he is equal to the Father. But as Mediator, made flesh by his own counsel and according to the dispensation of his will, he is inferior to the Father. For he who is God by nature emptied himself by the will of grace. It is ungrateful of a mind to attack the nature of one who humbled himself for your sake, precisely because he humbled himself. So κενὸς τροφεὰ ἀπολωνύει [the nurture of an empty man is lost], as the common saying goes. Therefore, in the words that follow, he achieves nothing in exalting Christ. He is like one who cuts a man's throat and then decorates his image. That is what Samosatenus does with Christ: he destroys what is natural and proclaims what is accidental and incidental. But once the nature is destroyed, Samosatenus, you will never succeed in making truly divine things predicated of Christ. For what is truly and essentially divine cannot be communicated. Nor can a creature possess essentially truly divine attributes any more than a creature can be God. The truly divine attributes belong to the whole of the Godhead alone and always, according to the perfection of its essence. If Christ has these (as he does), he is truly God according to the perfection of that essence. If he is not God according to that perfection, he does not have those truly divine attributes, however much you may extol the man in your lavish speeches. The sum of the testimonies about Christ is this: those things are predicated of Christ in Scripture which cannot belong to God essentially. From this it is concluded: therefore Christ is not God essentially by nature, but accidentally through the communication of grace. The consequence of all this is denied, because the antecedent and the consequent are stated with respect to different things. For some things are predicated of Christ in so far as he is God essentially, and these are divine. Some are predicated of the same person in so far as he is the God-man, God and man in the unity of person, and these are mediatorial. Others are said of him in so far as he was made like his brothers in all things, except sin, and these are human. Just as that first grade of distinction in the person of Christ does not abolish the later and lower ones, so too the later and lower ones, which we have just pointed out, do not abolish the first. They concur and do not contend. They constitute one work of one person, and they do not destroy the person or its parts, which is what Samosatenus tries to do with this kind of testimony. For to each nature of Christ, as to different subjects, belong their own accompanying properties and necessary actions, and likewise to the person, as to a supposit made up of those two natures. These actions and properties remain distinct, and they can no more be confused than the natures themselves can be confused in the one united person. Therefore nothing is concluded from one part concerning the other, or against the other, nor from one nature concerning the other, or against the other, in this argument. This is shown by the example of a man, who is made up of body and soul. For if someone should assert things belonging to the body of the soul, or argue about the soul from the attributes of the body, who would tolerate such a fool? Samosatenus does the same when he speaks about the person of Christ, and he applauds himself. Very fine indeed! But by such a mode of argument, who would not at last prove that a man is nothing but a body, and that Samosatenus himself ought to be judged nothing but a brute beast? What man would not be ashamed of such childishness, as soon as he looked into himself? But let us come to the individual passages. The first passage is Heb. 1 and 3, where Christ is compared with the angels and with Moses, and is set above them. Rightly so. But he is set above them, my friend, not only because of the gifts of grace received in time, but also, and above all, because of the truth of the divine nature and the deity of the person, which the Apostle proclaims most powerfully in both places. For in chapter 1, verse 1, he is called the Son; in verse 2, God made the world through him; in verse 3, he is said to be the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person, upholding all things by the word of his power; in verse 6, the angels are commanded to worship him, which Christ himself taught from Moses (Matt. 4) is due to God alone; then in verse 8 the Psalmist says of the Son, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; and many other things, which for brevity's sake we omit. He is therefore to be set above the angels, Moses and all creatures, not only because of the fullness of grace communicated to him, but also because of the truth of that divine nature which we know and worship in Christ from the Scriptures. He is set above them not only because of his divine gifts, calling, offices, benefits, operations and effects, but also because of his divine nature itself, which alone is the subject, capable in itself and through itself of these operations, while in his flesh, as a joined instrument, it operates.

units.la: Secundus locus est Ioan. 3. huic non admetitur Deus spiritum, itaque de plenitudine eius omnes acceperunt. Ioan. 1. Tertius, omnia dedit ei in manum Pater, Ioan. 3. Quartus, data est illi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, Matth. 28. Summa, Deus dedit illi spiritum sine mensura, omnia, potesta-tem omnem: ergo & Deum esse hæc donans dedit. Negatur consequens: nam Deum esse proprie & essentialiter, naturæ est: illis donis donari, est communicatæ gratiæ. Patrem autem dedisse illa dona Filio in Scripturis legimus: dedisse vt Deus sit, nusquam legimus. Ex illis autem adiacentibus quæ in tempore data sunt Christo non secundum naturam diuinam, sed humanam ipsius in persona Mediatoris nostri, inepte concluditur de natura diuina eius, vt ante ostendimus. Secundùm naturam diuinam, vt natura est, Christus nihil horum accepit simpliciter: sed tantùm secundùm personam, quà diuinitas secùdùm dispositionem gratiæ inaniuit sese assumta humanitate in vnitatem personæ. Sic varie peccatur in ista argumentatione. Nam primùm quod dicitur de Christo secundùm quid, affirmatur de eo simpliciter secundùm se: sic enim se habent inter se dispensatio & natura. Tum a qualitate ad substantiam non valet argumentatio, mutato prædicationis genere. Præterea Dei nomen sumitur æquiuocè: quia essentiam notat, vt ante diximus, hic autem de qualitatibus enunciatur: quod in rebus creatis fertur secundùm quamdam imaginem, in diuinis ferri nullo pacto potest. Postremò etiamsi daremus loquutionem istam, Deum Patrem dedisse Filio vt sit Deus (etenim dari potest, & sanctè prædicari) tamen æquiuoca loquutio futura est: nam dedit Pater illi Deum esse, quà Filius est, id autem est, generatione naturæ, & filiatione, vt loquuntur vulgo: dedit verò omnia, spiritum, omnem potestatem, ex horum locorum qui adducuntur sententia, per dispensationem voluntatis inanito Filio, communicatione gratiæ. Sed de his antè Defensionis 2. segmento 12. & aliis aliquot locis. Quintus locus est Philipp. 2. de exaltatione Christi, & sine exaltationis illius. Sic enim argumen-
units.tr: The second passage is John 3: God does not give the Spirit by measure to him, and John 1: of his fullness have all received. The third is John 3: the Father has given all things into his hand. The fourth is Matt. 28: all power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. In sum: God gave him the Spirit without measure, all things, all power; therefore, in giving these, God also gave him to be God. The consequence is denied. For to be God properly and essentially belongs to nature; to be endowed with these gifts belongs to communicated grace. We read in the Scriptures that the Father gave these gifts to the Son, but nowhere do we read that he gave him to be God. From those accompanying gifts, which were given in time to Christ not according to his divine nature but according to his human nature in the person of our Mediator, it is foolishly concluded concerning his divine nature, as we showed before. According to his divine nature, as it is nature, Christ received none of these things absolutely. He received them only according to the person, in so far as the deity, by the disposition of grace, emptied itself when the humanity was assumed into the unity of the person. Thus there are various errors in this argument. For first, what is said of Christ in a certain respect is affirmed of him absolutely and in himself. For this is how dispensation and nature relate to each other. Next, the argument does not hold from quality to substance, since the kind of predication has been changed. Moreover, the name God is taken equivocally, since, as we said before, it signifies essence, whereas here it is predicated of qualities. What in created things is borne according to a certain likeness can in no way be borne in divine things. Finally, even if we granted this way of speaking, that God the Father gave to the Son to be God (for it can be given and rightly predicated), it would still be an equivocal way of speaking. For the Father gave him to be God in so far as he is the Son, that is, by the generation of nature and by sonship, as people commonly say. But he gave him all things, the Spirit and all power, according to the sense of these passages cited, through the dispensation of his will, with the Son emptied, by the communication of grace. But these matters were discussed before, in section 12 of the second part of the Defence, and in several other places. The fifth passage is Phil. 2, concerning the exaltation of Christ, and the argument from that exaltation. For he argues thus:

units.la: {*} Sic in textu. argumentatur: qui exaltatur, & exaltatur ad gloriam Al-tissimi, idem non est altissimus: Christus exaltatur, idq; ad glo-riam altissimi: Non igitur Altissimus. Maior vera est, si idem ad idem ratione eiusdem dicitur de eodem Chri-sto. In hac autem argumentatione idem de eodem dici-tur: sed nec ad idem, nec ratione eiusdem dicitur. Non ad idem: nam alia est altitudo naturae diuinae, qua Chri-stus est altissimus, alia exaltatio personae, qua ἀνθρωπος Sermo propter nos caro factus per dispensationem gra-tiae supra res omneis creatas secundum naturam huma-nam euectus est. Nec ratione eiusdem: quandoquidem Christus, vt Deus simpliciter, non exaltatur, cum sit na-tura altissimus: sed exaltatur, vt Mediator & sponsor fa-ctus pro nobis dispensatione voluntatis suae, in persona sua, secundum naturam diuinam φανερώσει, vel mani-festatione, secundum nostram reipsa & veritate. Mino-rem itaque si de Christo secundum naturam illam enun-ciaueris simpliciter, falsa est propositio: si de persona qua-tenus inaniuit se & homo factus seipsum subiecit, &c. ve-rissima. Sed ab hac constitutione personae & inanitio-ne naturae argumentari contra naturae veritatem, insci-tum atque indignum est. Nam qui natura est altissimus, idem est abiectus dispensatione gratiae: qui natura est fi-nis omnium, ad cuius gloriam contendunt omnia, idem quasi natura cedens per dispensationem voluntatis suae gratiosae se adiunxit nobis, vt ad finem illum contende-ret, nósque secum in vno corpore perduceret. O homi-nes miseros, qui modum salutis suae oblatum in humili-tate carnis Christi abripiunt vltro, vt oppugnent euer-tantque amplitudinem maiestatis eius. Christus enim, quà Deus, finis est ad quem omnia contendunt, sed com-muniter cum Patre & Spiritu sancto in vnitate essentiae; quà homo vero factus, instaurator est & dux omnium ad finem: quà Deus, altissimus: qua Deus homo factus, trahens omnes post se & exaltaturus in æternum ad finem fidei nostræ, puta salutem animarum nostrarum in gloria. Hoc omnis lingua pia iam confitetur, & sancta illic confessura est, noscens personam illius Θεανθρώπου, & agnoscens beneficium. An ergo, Samosatene, salua his modis gloria altissimo illi Deo Patri omnium auctori futura est, si Filio eius naturam, qua idem est cum Patre, sustuleris? Hoccine de Filio verum, aut Patri gloriosum, si Filium dicatur ὁμοιούσιον, ac potius ἑτερούσιον genuisse? si Pater dicatur non misisse eum de cœlo? si ipse non venisse in carne, & inaniuisse in ea se? si non perfecisse redemtionem nostram dispensatione gratiæ, sed naturæ lege? si deniq; res divinas & operationes miraculosissimas, quas solus Deus potest facere, sine forma essentiali Dei & perfectione deitatis perfecisse? Quin potius gloriosum est Patri, quòd Filium gignat ὁμοούσιον: gloriosum, quòd misit unigenitum e cœlo ad institutionem nostram: gloriosum, quòd corpus aptauit ei ad communionem nostra: gloriosum, quòd dispositit inanitionem illius ad complementum nostrum: gloriosum, quòd perfecit redemtionem in Filio ad salutem nostram: gloriosum denique, quòd dispensauerit per eum miracula sua virtute essentiali deitatis eius. Quod autem Patri, idem etiam Filio est gloriae secundum unitatem essentiae diuinæ, & veritatem personæ. Hæc non ludicra cauillatio est, sed seria sanctáque gratiæ erga nos æternæ prædicatio, quum naturarum duarum integrarum unionem inter se agnoscimus: quam qui dissoluit, personam dissoluit, & salutem perdit in ea persona constitutam, & a Deo Patre in Christo exhibitam gratiosissime. Sextus locus est Col. 1. de quo Defensionis 2. segmento 6. diximus. Nasturtium, Samosatene, a te edi oportuit, quum ista scriberes. Quid enim? an nondum vides ex ipsa verborum serie Paulum ostendere amplitudinem tum personae Filij (quem dilectionis Filium appellauit) tum beneficiorum eius & redemtionis nostrae grauissima descriptione proprietatum eius, quae nemini homini possunt competere? Primùm enim proprietates personae Filij, quas in se habet, explicat duabus comparationibus: vna relationis internae, quòd imago est Dei inuisibilis, perfecta inquam imago & essentialis Patris, vt Defensione 2. fuit demonstratum: altera relationis externae, quòd primogenitus est omnis creaturae, ab quo in omnes fratres deriuatur omnis benedictio & sanctificatio, vt Hebr. 2. dicitur. Deinde verò vtriusque partis enarratio ordine contexitur & cōfirmatio ab operibus seu effectis illius: prout in rebus diuinis ab effectis ad causam mentes nostras opus est assurgere. Imaginem esse Dei inuisibilis, ab opere creationis, gubernationis, & sustentationis confirmatur, his verbis: Nam per eum condita sunt omnia quae in coelis sunt & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, siue throni, siue dominia, siue imperia, siue potestates, omnia per eum & respectu eius sunt condita: hactenus creationis opus. Sequitur gubernationis & sustentationis, estque ipse ante omnia, & omnia per eum consistunt. Per quem haec facta sunt, is necessario perfecta & essentialis est imago Dei Patris: Per Christum haec facta sunt: est igitur imago Patris. Post autem primogenitum esse omnis creaturae Christum demonstratur simili analogico, quum dicitur esse idem caput corporis Ecclesiae: & huius similitudinis analogia ostenditur a modo & fine ipsius. Modo: nam est principium auctor Ecclesiae suae, & primogenitus ex mortuis, eos principaliter a morte vindicans & vindicatos seruans. Fine autem: vt inter omnes teneat primas. Vtrum que asseritur de Christo, natura diuina, & operatio in carne, naturae illi diuinae respondens (vt loquuntur) proportionaliter. Nam proportionem essentiæ aut naturæ agentis sequitur operatio: huius operationes diuinæ sunt: ergo & natura est, quum operationum illarum potestatem habeat in se, & actus efficiat per se. Quo itaque argumento utitur Paulus Apostolus ad demonstrandam deitatem personæ Christi, eo tu, Paule Samosatene, ad oppugnationem eiusdem abutaris? At, inquit ille, falsa est hæc interpretatio. Nam si ita esset, hæc propria Christi dicenda essent: non sunt autem propria Christi, vt Apostolus ibidem exponit dicens, Quoniam placuit Patri vt omnis plenitudo in eo inhabitaret: falsa igitur interpretatio. Minorem negamus: nam proprium est personæ Christi, ac non cuiusquam alterius, omnem plenitudinem habere in se ad præstandum Mediatoris officium: de hac autem plenitudine agit diserte Paulus, & confirmant plane sequentia, & pacem per sanguinem eius facta, per eum reconciliare omnia sibi, &c. Sed non habet a se hanc plenitudinem, fortasse dixerit: non igitur propria ipsius. Ambiguum antecedens, & falsum consequens. Plenitudinem non solum hanc, sed infinitam diuinámque secundùm essentiam habet Christus a se, qua Deus: sed qua inanitus & factus caro, accepit & habet a Patre secundùm dispensationem gratiæ & beneplacitum diuinæ voluntatis. Consequens igitur re ipsa & argumento falsum. Re: nã quòd secundùm essentiam deitatis habet Christus a se, id secundùm dispensationem accepit a Patre, quantum ad mediationem opus. Argumento: nam falsum est axioma illud Samosatenicum, quod quis a se non habet, id non esse proprium illius: si vocem istam, a se, de principio & ortu acceperis. Nam ego principium & ortum quidem habeo a patre meo: sed meum esse mihi tam est proprium quàm suum fuit parenti meo. Aliud est de ortu & generatione re ipsius agere, aliud de constitutione & esse illius. Quòd si aliud sibi Samosatenus voluit, quid toties æqui-uocationibus tentat illudere? Hoc autem sensisse demō-strat loci, quo sermonem suum probare instituit, auctoritas. Falsa igitur, futiliáque omnia. Septimus locus est Hebr. 1. de quo Defensione 2. diximus, segmento 6.
units.tr: {*} As in the text. He argues thus: whatever is exalted, and is exalted to the glory of the Most High, is not itself the Most High. Christ is exalted, and that to the glory of the Most High. Therefore he is not the Most High. The major premise is true, if the same thing is predicated of the same Christ in the same respect. But in this argument the same thing is predicated of the same Christ, and not in the same respect or to the same thing. Not to the same thing: for the height of the divine nature, by which Christ is the Most High, is one thing; the exaltation of the person, by which the Word made flesh for our sake, ἀνθρωπος [anthropos], has been raised above all created things according to his human nature through the dispensation of grace, is another. Nor in the same respect: for Christ, as God simply, is not exalted, since by nature he is the Most High; but he is exalted as Mediator and surety made for us by the dispensation of his own will, in his person, and according to the divine nature, by φανερώσει [phanerōsei], that is, by manifestation, according to our nature, in fact and in truth. So if you state the minor simply of Christ according to that nature, the proposition is false; if of the person, insofar as he emptied himself and, made man, subjected himself, and so on, it is most true. But to argue from this constitution of the person and emptying of the nature against the truth of the nature is both ignorant and unworthy. For he who by nature is the Most High is himself humbled by the dispensation of grace; he who by nature is the end of all things, toward whose glory all things strive, the same, as though yielding his nature, by the dispensation of his gracious will joined himself to us, so that he might strive toward that end and lead us with him into one body. O wretched men, who snatch away of their own accord the means of their salvation offered in the humility of the flesh of Christ, in order to assail and overthrow the greatness of his majesty! For Christ, as God, is the end toward which all things strive, but in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of essence; as man, however, he has been made the restorer and leader of all toward that end. As God, he is the Most High; as God made man, he draws all after him and will exalt them forever to the end of our faith, namely the salvation of our souls in glory. Every devout tongue already confesses this, and holy tongues there will confess it, knowing the person of that God-man Θεανθρώπου [Theanthrōpou], and acknowledging the benefit. Is then, Samosatene, the glory of that Most High God, the Father and author of all, to be preserved in these ways, if you take away from his Son that nature by which he is one and the same with the Father? Is it true of the Son, or glorious for the Father, if it is said that he begot a Son ὁμοιούσιον [homoiousion], or rather ἑτερούσιον [heterousion]? If it is said that the Father did not send him from heaven? If he himself did not come in the flesh and empty himself in it? If he did not accomplish our redemption by the dispensation of grace, but by the law of nature? If finally he performed divine works and most wonderful operations, which God alone can do, without the essential form of God and the perfection of deity? Rather, it is glorious for the Father that he begets a Son ὁμοούσιον [homoousion]; glorious that he sent his only-begotten from heaven for our instruction; glorious that he fitted a body to him for our fellowship; glorious that he ordered his emptying for our fulfilment; glorious that he completed the redemption in the Son for our salvation; glorious, finally, that he performed his miracles through him by the essential power of his deity. And what is glory to the Father is also glory to the Son, by the unity of the divine essence and the truth of the person. This is no idle quibble, but a serious and holy proclamation of the eternal grace toward us, since we acknowledge the union of two whole natures; whoever dissolves this dissolves the person, and loses the salvation established in that person and most graciously exhibited by God the Father in Christ. The sixth passage is Col. 1., which we discussed in Defence 2, segment 6. You ought, Samosatene, to have set forth the nasturtium when you wrote these things. For what? Do you not yet see from the very sequence of the words that Paul sets forth the greatness both of the person of the Son (whom he called the Son of his love) and of his benefits and our redemption, by a most weighty description of his properties, which can belong to no mere man? For first he explains the properties of the person of the Son which he has in himself by two comparisons: one of internal relation, that he is the image of the invisible God, a perfect image, I say, and essential likeness of the Father, as was shown in Defence 2; the other of external relation, that he is the firstborn of every creature, from whom every blessing and sanctification is derived to all brethren, as is said in Heb. 2. Then the exposition and confirmation of each part is woven together in order from his works or effects, as in divine matters our minds must rise from effects to the cause. That he is the image of the invisible God is confirmed from the work of creation, government and preservation, in these words: For by him were all things created that are in heaven and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers; all things were created by him and with respect to him. So far the work of creation. There follows that of government and preservation: and he is before all things, and by him all things consist. He through whom these things were made must necessarily be the perfect and essential image of God the Father. Through Christ these things were made; therefore he is the image of the Father. Afterwards, that Christ is the firstborn of every creature is shown by a analogical likeness, when it is said that he is the same head of the body, the Church; and the analogy of this likeness is shown from his manner and end. From his manner: for he is the beginning, the author of his Church, and the firstborn from the dead, chiefly rescuing them from death and preserving those rescued. From his end: that he might hold the first place among all. Both things are asserted of Christ: the divine nature, and the operation in the flesh corresponding, as they say, proportionally to that divine nature. For operation follows the proportion of the essence or nature of the agent; his operations are divine; therefore he has a divine nature too, since he has the power of those operations in himself and effects the acts through himself. So with the argument which the Apostle Paul uses to demonstrate the deity of the person of Christ, you, Paul of Samosata, abuse it to assail the same. But, he says, this interpretation is false. For if it were so, these things would have to be said as proper to Christ; but they are not proper to Christ, as the Apostle explains in the same place, saying, For it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell. Therefore the interpretation is false. We deny the minor: for it is proper to the person of Christ, and to no one else, to have all fullness in himself to perform the office of Mediator; and of this fullness Paul speaks expressly, and the following words plainly confirm it: and having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things to himself, and so on. But, you may say, he does not have this fullness from himself; therefore it is not proper to him. The antecedent is ambiguous and the consequent false. Christ has from himself not only this fullness but an infinite and divine fullness according to his essence, as God; but as emptied and made flesh, he has received it and holds it from the Father according to the dispensation of grace and the good pleasure of the divine will. The consequent is therefore false both in fact and in argument. In fact: for what Christ has from himself according to the essence of the deity, he received from the Father according to the dispensation, as to the work of mediation. In argument: for that axiom of the Samosatenian, what someone does not have from himself is not proper to him, is false, if you take the word from himself as referring to principle and origin. For I indeed have my principle and origin from my father, yet my being is as much my own as it was my parent's. It is one thing to treat of origin and generation in fact, another of the constitution and being of a thing. But if Samosatenus meant something else, why does he so often try to trick us with equivocations? The context of the place where he sets out to prove his point shows that he meant this. So everything is false and futile. The seventh passage is Heb. 1., which we discussed in Defence 2, segment 6.

units.la: Octauus locus est Apocal. 5. vbi de Agno agitur, id est, Mediatore nostro, qui secundùm carnem assumtam in persona sua accepit a Deo & Patre ista omnia ex dispe-satione gratiæ. Duplex error (paucis dicam) hoc pacto committitur: vnus, quòd sermo de persona Filij Dei secundùm humanitatem dictus ad naturam superiorem inscite aut malitiosè rapitur abolendam: alter, quòd res dispensatione gesta in tempore itidem occupatur ad euer-tendam æternam illam naturæ diuinæ in persona Christi veritatem. Elenchus fallacissimus, & frequentissimus in isto scriptorum genere.
units.tr: The eighth passage is Revelation 5, where the Lamb is spoken of, that is, our Mediator, who in his assumed flesh received all these things from God the Father by the dispensation of grace. Briefly, two errors are committed in this way. The first is that what is said of the person of the Son of God according to his humanity is clumsily or maliciously taken to abolish the higher nature. The second is that what was accomplished in time by the dispensation is likewise seized upon to overturn the eternal truth of the divine nature in the person of Christ. This is a most deceptive argument, and a very frequent one in writings of this kind.

units.la: Nonus locus Ioan. 10. arx inuicta Samosateni est. Christus, inquit, non aliam deitatis filiationisque rationem sibi tribuit, quàm quæ a Deo sibi, vt homini, per sanctificationem concessa est: Est igitur Deus ratione duntaxat sanctificationis illius. Antecedens falsum. Nam Christus quidem instituit secum aliorum hominum coparationem, vt homo, quia hoc argumentū Iudæi vsurpauerant dicentes, quia tu, homo cum sis, facis teipsum Deum: sed instituta minoris comparatione, ostendit responsione sua se non hominem solùm agnosci, sed Deum etiam in vnitate personæ oportere: quæ duo Samosatenus iniquè diuidit, quamuis a Christo coniuncta. Nam de persona sua Christus secundùm naturam humanam (quam obiecerant Iudæi) dicit, quem Pater sanctificauit: at secundùm illam diuinam dicit, quem Pater misit in mundum: respiciens ad gratiosam missionem illam, qua Christus ex beneplacito Patris factus est caro, quia a natura est secundùm essentiam æternus Deus, secundùm personæ subfiftentiam Filius Patri ὁμοούσιον, in tempore caro factus. Proinde vtroque nomine demonstrat homines secum nullo iure comparari posse, neque naturæ, neque gratiæ dominorumque respectu: quemadmodum post argumentatione confirmauit. Nam & verbo ipsius, & operationibus credi oportere: operationibus,inquam,velut signis per quæ credatur verbo: verbo autem, vt personæ & naturæ latentis indici, secundum quam est in Patre & Pater in ipso vnitate essentiæ καὶ συνάλληλον περιχώρησιν, vt vocabant Patres: hanc deitatem personæ cum maiestate operum, tum veritate verbi hominibus sic esse expositam, vt nemo dubitare debeat de Filio, quin sit natura Filius vnigenitus; & de Patre, quin sit naturalis ipsius Pater. Sic ergo multis modis Samosatenus fallitur, & arci confidit ἀλλώτω. Primum membra diuidit coniunctissima, quem Pater sanctificauit & misit in mundum. Secundo comparationis vim & veritatem tollit: quia fit comparatio non solum sanctificationis secundum magis & minus, sed etiam naturæ personarum ex ludæorum hypothesi, cum alioqui nec persona Christi cum nostra merito, nec natura eius diuina cum humana debeat comparari. Tertio Patrem, qui Pater natura est Filij, & essentialis Pater, opere solum gratiæ Patrem esse intelligit. Quarto operum diuinorum deitatem eius testificantium argumentum ofcitanter omittit. Postremo non credit verbo, sed ea oppugnat quæ Christus dicit, nec vsquam alibi nisi de deitate personæ vnius cum altera & vnitate essentiæ legūntur dicta, Pater est in me, & ego in eo. Ista vero auctoritas (liceat iam vti Samosateni verbis) tam perspicua ac clara est, vt siquis illam cum Samosateno cauillari contedat, plusquam peruicacissimum se prodat. Nam ex parte mutilatur, & corrumpitur verborum sensus ex parte, vt ista obtineat interpretatio, quæ post Mosis, Aaronis, ronis, Principum exemplo impiè statuitur ad labefactan- dam veritatem personæ Christi. Decimus locus est Act. 2. Deus hunc fecit Dominum & Christum: fecit ergo Deum. Negatur consequens, vt paulo ante. Nam fallacia est consequentis: & mutatur prædicationis genus ab attri- butis & adiunctis de substantia concludendo, præsertim non natiuis & necessarijs, vt vocant Logici. Eiusdem generis sunt quæ sequuntur, quòd Pater locis innumeris vocetur Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Fallit enim Samosatenus elenchi ignoratione. Pater enim Deus est Christi, non secundùm naturam illam æternam qua Filius est coæternus & æqualis Patri (etsi ratione principij aliquo modo, sed tamen duriter, appellari posset) sed tum secundùm dispensationem illam qua Filius se inanivit ad opus Mediationis & redemtionis nostræ, tum secundùm naturam humanam ipsius, tum secundùm corpus mysticum assumtum, id est, Ecclesiam, quam ipse sibi suo sanguine comparauit. Illi ergo κόμμι Samosatenici omnino nihil ad rem, quum ex verbis Pauli & Christi ipsius se somniat triumphare. Hæc si faciunt Samosatenι inscienter, discant: sin verò scienter prudenter, resipiscant velim: quam ad rem oro mentem det illis Dominus, vt credant veritati. Sic duorum aliorum locorum habetur interpretatio. Quod itaque argutatur Christum sedentem ad dexteram Patris gubernare Ecclesiam, vt vicarium, non vt principalem Dominum, salsissimum est ex eadem elenchi ignoratione proficiscens, vt Defensione 2. docuimus. Nam Christus, quà Deus cum Patre & Spiritu sancto in vnitate essentiæ, gubernat vt principalis Dominus communiter cum Patre & Spiritu sancto æterna communis essentiæ naturæque diuinæ veritate: quà Mediator & honofactus, gubernat vt vicarius dispensatione singulari atque voluntate: quæ duo nullo modo inter se pugnare iam saepe demonstravimus. Contra hanc veritatem nihil, Samosatene, potes: quin finis ut possit apud te omnia veritas? Decimus tertius locus est 1. Cor. 15. de quo tum Definitionis 2. segmento 12. tum hoc ipso segmento ad prioris scripti Samosatenici verba diximus satis, iudicio nostro, & ex Dei veritate, ut confido in Domino. Decimus quartus locus est non uno, sed pluribus locis comprehensus, Christum semper in omnibus suis verbis ac factis omnem laudem & honorem Patri Deo suo (sic enim mauult Samosatenus captiose loqui, quam cum Scripturis dicere Deo Patri suo) detulisse. Primum falsa est propositio: nam etiam sibi Christus honorem vindicat, & eundem cum Patre: quemadmodum ipse dicit, omne iudicium dedit Filio: ut omnes honorent Filium, prout honorant Patrem: qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem qui misit ipsum: & similia multa. Secundo, etiam quatenus haec propositio vera est, fallit tamen Samosatenus, quum ex particulari statuit tolli communis rationem posse: nam secundum deitatem, honor unus idemque communis est Patri, Filio, & Spiritui sancto; qui honor quum de una aliqua persona praedicatur, non deminuitur de ratione communis quicquam. Ex particulari autem ad commune affirmatiuae propositiones duci possunt, negatiuae nunquam. Tertio, ut veram demus de caetero propositionem esse, laborat tamen ex elenchi ignoratione. Nam aliter Christus loquitur, ut Deus simpliciter in aequalitate naturae, aliter vero ut Mediator & homo factus, secundum dispensationem officio, secundum humanitatem natura minor & inferior Patre. Quid iis miseris, infirmis, fallacibus argumentis & probationibus facias?
units.tr: The ninth passage, John 10, is Samosatenus's unconquered stronghold. Christ, he says, claims for himself no other ground of deity and sonship than that which was granted him by God as man through sanctification: therefore God is only by reason of that sanctification. The antecedent is false. Christ indeed set up a comparison of himself with other men, as man, because the Jews had used this argument, saying, because you, being a man, make yourself God. But having set up the lesser comparison, he showed in his reply that he must be acknowledged not only as man but also as God, in the unity of the person. Samosatenus unjustly divides these two things, although Christ joined them. For Christ speaks of his own person according to the human nature (which the Jews had raised), whom the Father sanctified, but according to the divine nature he says, whom the Father sent into the world, looking to that gracious mission by which, by the Father's good pleasure, he was made flesh. For he is by nature, according to his essence, the eternal God, and according to the subsistence of the person, the Son, homoousios [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father, made flesh in time. Therefore by both titles he shows that men cannot rightly be compared with him, neither in respect of nature, nor of grace, nor of lordship; as he afterwards confirmed by argument. For he must be believed both in his word and in his works: in his works, I say, as signs by which the word is to be believed; and in his word, as an indication of the hidden person and nature, according to which the Son is in the Father and the Father in him, by unity of essence, and by mutual indwelling [καὶ συνάλληλον περιχώρησιν], as the Fathers called it. This deity of the person has been so set forth to men, both by the majesty of his works and by the truth of his word, that no one ought to doubt about the Son, that by nature he is the only-begotten Son, or about the Father, that he is his natural Father. So Samosatenus is mistaken in many ways, and relies on his stronghold in a different sense. First, he divides members that are most closely joined: whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world. Second, he destroys the force and truth of the comparison, because the comparison is made not only of sanctification by more and less, but also of the natures of the persons, on the Jews' hypothesis; whereas the person of Christ ought not rightly to be compared with ours, nor his divine nature with the human. Third, by the Father, who is the Father by nature of the Son and his essential Father, he understands a Father only by the work of grace. Fourth, he carelessly omits the argument from the divine works that bear witness to his deity. Finally, he does not believe the word, but attacks what Christ says; and nowhere else are words read about the deity of one person in the other and the unity of essence except The Father is in me, and I in him. This passage (I may now use Samosatenus's own words) is so plain and clear that anyone who contends with Samosatenus over it would show himself most obstinate. For the sense of the words is partly mutilated and partly corrupted, so that he may obtain that interpretation which, after the example of Moses, Aaron and the princes, is impiously set up to overturn the truth of the person of Christ. The tenth passage is Acts 2: God has made this man Lord and Christ: therefore he made him God. The consequent is denied, as a little before. For this is the fallacy of the consequent, and the kind of predication is changed, by concluding about substance from attributes and accidents, especially those that are not natural and necessary, as the logicians call them. Of the same kind is what follows, that the Father is called in countless places the God of our Lord Jesus Christ. Samosatenus is deceived by ignorance of the argument. For the Father is God of Christ not according to that eternal nature by which the Son is coeternal and equal to the Father (although in a sense, by reason of the principle, he might be so called, though harshly), but according to that dispensation by which the Son emptied himself for the work of our mediation and redemption, and according to his human nature, and according to the mystical body he assumed, that is, the Church, which he purchased for himself with his own blood. Those Samosatenian scraps [κόμματα] therefore have nothing at all to do with the matter, though he dreams that he triumphs from the words of Paul and of Christ himself. If the Samosatenians do this unknowingly, let them learn; but if knowingly and deliberately, I would wish them to repent; and in this matter I pray the Lord to give them a mind to believe the truth. Thus the interpretation of two other passages is established. Therefore what they quibble, that Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father, governs the Church as a vicar, not as the principal Lord, is most absurd, arising from the same ignorance of the argument, as we showed in the second Defence. For Christ, as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in unity of essence, governs as principal Lord, jointly with the Father and the Holy Spirit, by the eternal truth of the common essence and divine nature; as Mediator and made honourable, he governs as vicar, by a singular dispensation and will. We have often shown that these two things by no means fight against each other. Against this truth, Samosatenus, you can do nothing: unless perhaps truth itself may end up with everything for you? The thirteenth passage is 1 Corinthians 15, on which we have said enough, in our judgement and, as I trust in the Lord, by the truth of God, both in the twelfth section of the second Definition and in this same section, in reply to the words of the earlier Samosatenian writing. The fourteenth passage is comprised not in one place but in several: that Christ in all his words and deeds always ascribed all praise and honour to the Father, his God (for Samosatenus prefers to speak deceptively in this way, rather than with the Scriptures to say God the Father his God). First, the proposition is false: for Christ also claims honour for himself, and the same as the Father's, as he himself says, the Father has given all judgement to the Son, that all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father; he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him, and many similar things. Second, even insofar as this proposition is true, Samosatenus is nonetheless mistaken, since he concludes from the particular that the common reason can be removed; for according to the deity, the honour is one and the same and common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; and when that honour is predicated of any one person, nothing is taken away from the common reason. Affirmative propositions may be drawn from the particular to the common, but negative ones never can. Third, even granting that the rest of the proposition is true, he labours under ignorance of the argument. For Christ speaks one way as God simply, in equality of nature, and another way as Mediator and made man, according to the dispensation of office, and according to his humanity, in nature less and inferior to the Father. What can you do with such wretched, weak and deceptive arguments and proofs?

units.la: His positis, Samosatenus concludit tandem aphorismi duobus sermonem suum. Eorum prior huiusmodi est Omnes praerogativae ac excellentiae, quae in Scripturis Christo attribui
units.tr: These things being laid down, Samosatenus at last concludes his discourse with two aphorisms. The first is of this kind: All the prerogatives and excellences that are read as ascribed to Christ in the Scriptures

units.la: ban. 5. attribui leguntur, non uti Deo illi summo omnium auctori, sed uti Mediatori nobis a Deo constituto attribuenda sunt. Hunc bellum aphorismum negamus constantissime. Tollatur vniuersale signum: nos idem affirmabimus. Nam (ut ante diximus) eorum quae in Scripturis de Christo praedicantur, alia praedicantur de persona eius secundum naturam diuinam solum, alia secundum humanam solum, alia denique secundum vtramque simul, vel secundum totum (ut loquuntur) personae. Dicendum ergo Samosateno fuerat, non omnes, sed quaedam, indefinita voce. Sic verum fuisset dicturus: quod secus dixit, praestare non poterit, qui nihil contra veritatem potest. Nam secundum deitatem ante Ioannem fuit: secundum humanitatem post Ioannem venit: secundum vtramque naturam Mediator noster est, Agnus ille Dei qui tollit peccata mundi; qua Deus per se ac principaliter; qua homo, in se ac instrumentaliter. Alia quam plurima proferre possem: sed haec satis hoc tempore, ut omnes intelligant, siqui aphorismum istum mordicus teneant, eos plurimum erraturos: qui mediam viam hanc tenuerint, hos certa Scripturae vestigia veritatisque diuinae sequuturos.
units.tr: are to be attributed to him not as to God, the highest author of all, but as to the Mediator appointed for us by God. We most firmly deny this fine aphorism. Let the universal sign be removed, and we will affirm the same thing. For (as we said before) of the things that are predicated of Christ in the Scriptures, some are predicated of his person according to the divine nature alone, others according to the human nature alone, and others finally according to both together, or according to the whole of the person, as they say. Samosatenus ought therefore to have said not all but some, using an indefinite word. So he would have spoken truly; but what he said otherwise he cannot make good, since he can do nothing against the truth. For according to his deity he was before John; according to his humanity he came after John; according to both natures he is our Mediator, that Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world: by which he is God through himself and principally, and by which he is man, in himself and instrumentally. I could bring forward very many other things, but these are enough for the present, so that all may understand that those who hold firmly to this aphorism will go very far wrong, while those who keep to the middle way will follow the sure footsteps of Scripture and the divine truth.

units.la: Posterior aphorismus est, quando Christus a Patre huiusmodi potestatem, gloriam, maiestatemque acceperit, Petrum exponere epist. 2. cap. 1. nempe quando vocem illam pronunciauit in monte sancto, &c. Falsus, & fallens aphorismus. Omnino certe falsus est: nam & ante, & post accepit, & eo tempore vt Mediator est Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Ante accepit, per gratiam vnionis, reipsa: quapropter diu ante illud tempus dicebat Christus omnia tradita sunt mihi a Patre meo: item, Pater diligit Filium, & omnia dedit ei in manum. Post accepit manifestatione & exsequutione illius, vt dicit Apostolus eum declaratum fuisse Filium Dei in potentia secundum Spiritum sanElitatis per resurrectionem ex mortuis. Res enim tum dicuntur fieri, quum manifestantur, vt orthodoxi Patres optimè docuerunt. Illa autem declaratio quæ in monte sancto tribus Apostolis spectantibus facta est, particularis fuit manifestatio, huius communis manifestationis πραγματικὴ, vt verba Christi commonstrant manifestissimè, dicentis, Nemini dixeritis quod vidistis, vsque quo Filius hominis a mortuis resurrexerit. Falsus igitur aphorismus. Quid verò, quòd fallit ex elenchi ignoratione? Non enim sequitur, si Christo, vt Mediatori ἀνθρώπῳ per illud tempus data est potestas, &c. si tum accepit ille, non ergo eum ante secundùm deitatem fuisse, aut in se gloriam habuisse. Nam secundùm deitatem Christus gloriam diuinam essentialem habet, vt suum ipsius esse: secundùm humanitatem verò gloriam habet quam accepit; non vt natiuum & perpetuum adiacens, sed vt adiacens comparatum atque a Patre acceptum in tempore. Secundùm illam Christus dicebat Patri, gloriam habui apud te prius quàm mundus esset: secundùm hanc verò dicebat ibidem, Pater, glorifica Filium tuum, vt & te Filius tuus glorificet. Habes igitur qua ratione Christus æternùm sit gloriosus gloria essentiali & communi Patris & sancti Spiritus, vt Deus: & qua ratione idem sit gloriosus factus, vt Deus in carne patefactus, Mediator noster: quam distinctionem certissimam iam olim Samosatenus, Photinus, Arius, & alij summo opere cupiuerunt obscurare. Sed gratiæ agendæ sunt Deo auctori atque vindici veritatis suæ. SAMOSATENVS. 6. MS. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum. REPETIT, Verbum hoc quod erat Deus, id est, Iesum Christum in principio Euangelij, & antequam scilicet prædicationem ... cationem regni Dei suis Iudaeis manifestaret, soli Deo fuisse notum, hominibus vero incognitum. Quae repetitio etiam alia ratione nobis valde opportuna & utilis fuit. Per hanc enim declarare voluit, quàm nos tanti beneficij gratos esse oporteat, postquam Christus, uti Verbum, antea incognitus, nobis autem revelatus fuit.
units.tr: The second aphorism is: "when Christ received such power, glory and majesty from the Father," which he explains by 2 Peter 1, namely when the voice was uttered on the holy mount, etc. It is a false and deceptive aphorism. It is certainly false, for Christ, the man Jesus, who is the Mediator of God and men, received it both before and after that time. He received it before, in reality, through the grace of union; therefore long before that time Christ said, all things are delivered unto me by my Father; likewise, the Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into his hand. He received it afterwards through the manifestation and execution of it, as the Apostle says, that he was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead. For things are said to be done when they are made manifest, as the orthodox Fathers taught excellently. But that declaration which was made on the holy mount, with three Apostles looking on, was a particular manifestation; of this common manifestation it was the [pragmatic], as Christ's own words show most clearly, saying, Tell the vision to no man, until the Son of man be risen again from the dead. The aphorism is therefore false. But what of the fact that it also deceives through ignorance of the proper inference? It does not follow that, if power was given to Christ as Mediator, as man [anthropō], at that time, etc., and if he then received it, he therefore was not before, according to his deity, or did not have glory in himself. For according to his deity Christ has the divine and essential glory as his own being; but according to his humanity he has the glory which he received, not as a native and perpetual possession, but as something acquired and received from the Father in time. According to the former Christ said to the Father, I had glory with thee before the world was; but according to the latter he said in the same place, Father, glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee. You have, therefore, the reason why Christ is eternally glorious with the essential and common glory of the Father and the Holy Spirit as God, and the reason why the same Christ has been made glorious as God manifested in the flesh, our Mediator. This most certain distinction Samosatenus, Photinus, Arius and others long ago strove greatly to obscure. But thanks are due to God, the author and defender of his own truth.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXVS.

units.la: T O T A hæc interpretatio falsa est, atque a vero aliena, vt supra segmento 4. docuimus. Res verò ipsa nihilo plus veritatis habet. Quæ duo quia ibidem copiosè fuerunt exposita, unde peti a Lectore possunt, hic a repetitionis fastidio supersedebimus. Quòd autem hæc verba prior coniunxit antecedentibus iudicio suo, ac non Evangelistæ ordini obsequens, id consilio non satis iusto fuisse factum, segmento 4. & 5. ostendimus.
units.tr: This whole interpretation is false and alien to the truth, as we showed above in section 4. The thing itself has no more truth in it. Since these two points were set out there at length, where the reader can seek them, we shall here spare him the tedium of repetition. That the Samosatene joined these words to what precedes by his own judgment, and not in obedience to the order of the Evangelist, we have shown in sections 4 and 5 to have been done on a not sufficiently sound counsel.

units.la: SAMOSATENVS.
units.tr: SAMOSATENVS.

units.la: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est.
units.tr: All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.

units.la: H A C etiam particula abusi sunt mirè ad probandum Christum esse creatorem omnium, cœli terræq;. Sed in eo falsi sunt: primùm quòd vnum Deum esse Christum cum Patre somniarunt, illíque coaeternum & coæqualem, quare etiā creatorem cum illo vnum esse commenti sunt: secundò quòd creationis vocem non intelligerent de recreatione seu renouatione, reconciliatione, & recapitulatione, restauratiothough neque accipi quoque sæpe in Scripturis, vt Paulus docet, & superius colligere potuisti. Quod ad primum attinet, nemo piorum est qui degustauit sacras literas, qui vel vnum Deum esse Christum cum Patre, vel etiam creatorem esse cœli terræq; assereret. Vnus est enim Deus Pater, qui creauit omnia: alius ergo non est. Solus erat, & nemo illi aderat, quum crearet cœlos, Esaiæ 44. teste. Solus extendit coelos, Iobo teste cap. 9. Ille creator omnium ubique in lege, a Prophetis, Christo, & Apostolis prædicatur, tum in Symbolo Apostolico. Vide locos Deuter. 32. Esai. 40. 42. 44. Malach. 2. Sic Actor. 4. 14. 17.
units.tr: This particle too they have wonderfully misused to prove that Christ is the creator of all things, of heaven and earth. But they are wrong in this: first, because they dreamed that Christ is one God with the Father, co-eternal and co-equal with him, and therefore invented that he is also one creator with him; secondly, because they did not understand the word creation of re-creation or renewal, reconciliation and recapitulation, restoration, which is also often taken so in the Scriptures, as Paul teaches, and as you could gather above. As for the first point, there is no pious person who has tasted the sacred letters who would assert that Christ is one God with the Father, or even that he is the creator of heaven and earth. For there is one God, the Father, who created all things; there is therefore no other. He was alone, and no one was with him when he created the heavens, by the testimony of Isaiah 44. He alone stretched out the heavens, by the testimony of Job, chapter 9. That creator of all things is proclaimed everywhere in the Law, by the Prophets, by Christ, and by the Apostles, and so in the Apostles' Creed. See the passages Deut. 32, Isa. 40, 42, 44, Mal. 2. So also Acts 4, 14, 17.

units.la: Neque vero sola creatio: sed omnia opera quæ fecit Deus sub veteri Testamento, sive verbo iubendo & promittendo, sive Spiritu oris sui re præstando, tribuuntur illi uni Deo Christi Patri (ut Lucas Actor. cap. 13. apertissime docet) qui tandem impleuisse promissiones dicitur educto filio & dato ex semine Davidis, non ex aliquo Verbo Dei æterno. Moses etiam describit accuratè, & nemo illo melius (huic enim soli data fuit hæc provincia a Deo) omnium rerum creationem: singulos dies recenset quo quid factum sit: enumerat etiam animantia, bestias, insecta, herbas, & quidlibet suo genere: ubi, siquis Filius Dei adfuisset in creatione, an hoc præteriisset? Quemadmodum ubi ad restaurationem prolapsæ creaturæ venit, statim feminis mulieris, non æterni Filij, ad conterendum caput serpentis meminit. Et in historia Abraham meminit recuperandam benedictionem amissam per semen eius, Genes. 12. non per æternum quoque aliquem Christum dicit. Utrobique & ad maledictionem auferendam, & ad benedictionem conferendam (in quo omnia opera Christi comprehensa) feminis humani, non æterni alicuius Dei meminit: tum manna cœlestis, tum aquæ ex petra profluentis, agni Paschalis, serpentis suspensi, sine quibus Deus populum illum nec aluit, nec potauit, nec servauit. Describit structuram tabernaculi cum apparatu vario: sic sacrificia fusionem sanguinis, & partium orbis vel altaris, ad quam fiebat: quæ omnia erant umbra futuri Christi. In creatione vero cæli & terræ, omniumque per Christum (si qua esset) surdáne aure præteriret? Annon absurdissimum esset, res factas per illum omittere, futuras autem longè post accuratè describere? umbras nullas intermittere, & reptilia infectáque describere, Christum autem per quem facta essent omnia obliterare? terare? Quod ad nouam creationem attinet, hæc in no-uo Testamento vbique tribuitur Christo, per quem Deus hanc exsequutus est, de qua etiam hic Ioannes loquitur, omnia per illum Christum Deum Verbum, qui fuit caro, facta esse, & sine illo nihil factum quod factum fuisset: vbi quoque statim additam restrictionem vides, ne quis vniuersaliter de omnibus creaturis hoc diceiputet: addit enim, quod factum sit, intelligens de iis rebus quæ factæ sunt per eum. Nam ea exceptione innuit alia esse sine illo facta antequam educeretur ex semine Dauid, vt sub veteri Testamento fuisse diximus. Sed de noua creatione loquens Scriptura tribuit illi quòd per illum sint omnia & nos per illum, & nos creatos dicit in Christo ad bona opera, vt in illis ambulemus, 1. Cor. 8. Ephes. 2. Et 2. Cor. 5. scribit, si quis igitur est in Christo, noua creatura est: ecce nouam creaturam in Christo audis. Addit prætera, vetera prætereierunt, ecce nouafacta sunt omnia. en quoque omnia nova audis in Christo. Certè cœlum, terráque, mare, arbores, animantiáque omnia denuò creata non sunt per Christum: sed loquitur hic de spirituali renouatione & cum Deo reconciliatione per Christum: quemadmodum ibidem statim subdit dicens, hæc autem omnia (quæ scilicet sunt creata in Christo, & noua facta) sunt ex Deo, qui nos sibi reconciliauit per Iesum Christũ, deaitque ministerium reconciliationis: nempe quia Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, non imputando ipsis peccata ipsorum, posuitq; in nobis sermonem hunc reconciliationis. Hæc ergo creatio seu nouitas, omniáque noua seu noua creatura describuntur a Paulo, non cœli terræq; fabrica. Similiter & Ephes. 2. ait, vt conderet in semetipso in vnum nouum hominem faciens pacem, & vt reconciliaret ambos Deo per crucem. Similis est locus Ephes. 3. vbi dicit, omnia creata esse a Deo per Christum; qui locus de secunda creatione seu renouatione intelligitur, vt ex circumstantiis colligere facile est: quod & Calvinus aperte fatetur, quamquam in aliis locus aduersetur. Huic novae creationi per Christum servit & ille locus Colos.1. ubi mox a principio describitur Christus, non aliquis æternus, sed ille ex Maria natus, habens sanguinem, per quem habemus remissionem peccatorum. Meminit & ibi operum tenebrarum primum, ad quae destruenda venit Christus, 1. Ioan. 4. meminit & regni Christi, in quod translati sumus. Regnum autem hoc coepit in Christo homine: illi enim dicitur Luc. 1. dabit illi Deus (non ante dederat) sedem David patris sui, & regnabit in ea. non regnavit antea. Qui, & imago quoque Dei inconspicui, & primogenitus omnis creaturae dicitur: per quem Christum hominem omnia sunt condita, seu renovata, vel recollecta, aut recapitulata: quod idem esse ex Pauli verbis quivis colligere potest, quae ibi sequuntur vice expositionis, & Ephe.1.
units.tr: Nor is creation alone in question; but all the works which God did under the Old Testament, whether by commanding and promising in his word or by accomplishing them with the Spirit of his mouth, are attributed to that one God, the Father of Christ (as Luke most plainly teaches in Acts chapter 13), who is said at last to have fulfilled the promises when the Son was brought forth and given from the seed of David, not from any eternal Word of God. Moses also describes the creation of all things accurately, and no one describes it better (for this task was given by God to him alone): he recounts each day and what was made on it; he also enumerates the living creatures, beasts, insects, herbs, and whatever else in its kind. Where, if the Son of God had been present at the creation, would he have passed it over? Just as, when he comes to the restoration of the fallen creature, he at once mentions the seed of the woman, not of an eternal Son, to bruise the serpent's head. And in the history of Abraham he mentions the blessing that was lost being recovered through his seed, Gen. 12, and does not speak of some eternal Christ as well. In both places, both for removing the curse and for conferring the blessing (in which all the works of Christ are comprehended), he mentions the seed of man, not of some eternal God; likewise the heavenly manna, the water flowing from the rock, the Paschal lamb, the serpent lifted up, without which God neither fed, nor watered, nor preserved that people. He describes the structure of the tabernacle with its various furnishings; likewise the sacrifices, the pouring out of blood, and the parts of the circle or altar at which it was done; all of which were a shadow of the Christ to come. In the creation of heaven and earth, and of all things through Christ (if there were any such), would he pass it by with deaf ears? Would it not be most absurd to omit the things made by him, yet describe in detail those that were to come long afterwards, to pass over no shadows, and to describe reptiles and insects, yet blot out Christ, through whom all things were made? As for the new creation, this is everywhere in the New Testament attributed to Christ, through whom God accomplished it, and of which John also speaks here: that all things were made through that Christ, the Word who was God, who became flesh, and without him nothing was made that was made. Here you also see the restriction added at once, lest anyone take this universally of all creatures: he adds that was made, meaning those things that were made through him. For by that exception he hints that other things were made without him before he was brought forth from the seed of David, as we said under the Old Testament. But speaking of the new creation, Scripture attributes to him that all things are through him, and that we are through him; and it says we are created in Christ unto good works, that we should walk in them (1 Cor. 8; Eph. 2); and in 2 Cor. 5 it writes, if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature. Behold, you hear of a new creature in Christ. It adds further, old things have passed away; behold, all things are made new. Lo, you also hear that all things are new in Christ. Certainly the heaven, the earth, the sea, the trees and all the living creatures have not been created anew through Christ; but here he speaks of spiritual renewal and of reconciliation with God through Christ, as he immediately adds in the same place, saying, and all these things (namely, which are created in Christ and made new) are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, namely because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them, and has put in us the word of this reconciliation. This creation, then, or newness, and all new things or the new creature, are described by Paul, not the fabric of heaven and earth. Likewise Eph. 2 says, that he might create in himself one new man, making peace, and that he might reconcile both to God through the cross. A similar passage is Eph. 3, where he says that all things were created by God through Christ; this passage is understood of the second creation or renewal, as may easily be gathered from the circumstances, which Calvin also openly admits, although in other places he opposes it. This new creation through Christ is served also by that passage in Col. 1, where Christ is described at once from the beginning, not as some eternal being, but as he who was born of Mary, having blood, through whom we have remission of sins. There it also mentions the first of the works of darkness, which Christ came to destroy (1 John 4), and mentions the kingdom of Christ, into which we have been translated. This kingdom, however, began in Christ as man; for it is said to him in Luke 1, God will give him (he had not given it before) the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in it; he did not reign before. He is also called the invisible image of God, and the firstborn of every creature; through Christ as man all things were founded, or renewed, or gathered together again, or recapitulated; which anyone can gather is the same thing from Paul's words that follow there by way of explanation, and from Eph. 1.

units.la: In utroque autem loco eodem modo describit non caeli terraque creationem, quae solius Patris est, Christo tribuens, sed eorum quae in caelo & in terra sunt renovationem. Non enim tribuit Paulus Christo caeli & terrae creationem, sed pacificationem vel reconciliationem eorum quae in caelo & in terra sunt: ut & Hebr. 9. caelestia ait per Christum repurgata, non facta. Per Christum enim non solum Patrem se nobis Deus demonstravit, nos recipiendo pro filiis, sed & omne dissidium inter caelum & terram sustulit, Angelos (qui olim erant hostes nostri una cum Deo, & Adamo ingressum paradisi flammeo gladio prohibebant) non tantum amicos, sed etiam ministros fecit: qui gaudent super uno poenitente plus quam super semper multis iustis, & Angeli priorum intuentur faciem Patris in caelis semper, Heb.1. & Matth.18. Haec autem omnia data nobis in Christo, cui Deus ut capiti nostro subiecit omnia, cui introducto in orbe terrarum dictum, & adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei. Per hunc Christum quoque quaecunque erant maledicta in terra, per crucem mortemque in benedictionem vertit, ut nihil iam superfit in caelo & terra cuius inimicitiae nobis metuendae sint, postquam Christum fratrem nobis per omnia simile, caput universae creatura tura & dominum potestatem in cœlo & terra tenentem habe-mus. ⁵ Vt vero de Angelorum creatione Scriptura ta-cet, ita & de lapsu eorum, similiter etiam & de eorum resta-uratione paucis attingit. Restauratione quidem egebant, postquam illorum caput est Christus, postquam & Christus sine capite suo Patre nihil potest, Ioan. 5. Angelica natura etiam lapsu priorum Angelorum forte imminuta, ut & lapsu Adami humana corrupta natura. Hæc creatio seu reconciliatio per Christum facta in cælo & in terra plus nobis fructus attulit, & multo ampliorem gloriam Dei in nos patefecit illa priore quam habemus communem cum aliis creaturis.
units.tr: In both passages he describes in the same way not the creation of heaven and earth, which belongs to the Father alone, but the renewal of the things in heaven and on earth, and he ascribes this to Christ. For Paul does not attribute to Christ the creation of heaven and earth, but the pacification or reconciliation of the things in heaven and on earth. So also Heb. 9 says that the heavenly things were cleansed through Christ, not made. Through Christ God has shown us the Father, not only by receiving us as sons, but he has also removed every discord between heaven and earth. He made the angels, who once were our enemies along with God and who with a flaming sword barred Adam's entry into paradise, not merely friends but also ministers. They rejoice over one repenting sinner more than over many righteous persons, and the angels of these little ones always behold the face of the Father in heaven (Heb. 1; Matt. 18). All these things are given to us in Christ, to whom God subjected all things as to our head, and of whom it is said when he is brought into the world, "let all the angels of God worship him." Through this Christ, too, whatever was cursed on earth he has turned into blessing through the cross and death, so that nothing now remains in heaven and earth whose enmity we must fear, since we have Christ, a brother like us in all things, the head of the whole creation and the Lord holding power in heaven and on earth. Just as Scripture is silent about the creation of the angels, so it touches briefly on their fall and similarly on their restoration. They did need restoration, since Christ is their head, and since Christ too can do nothing without his Father (John 5). The angelic nature, too, was perhaps diminished by the fall of the former angels, just as human nature was corrupted by the fall of Adam. This creation or reconciliation made through Christ in heaven and on earth has brought us more fruit, and has revealed in us a much greater glory of God, than that former creation which we share in common with other creatures.

units.la: Ergo ut vetus Testamentum illa priorem creationem vni & soli Deo creatori omnium Patri tribuit, ita istam posteriorem creationem seu renovationem, seu recollectionem omnium in cœlo & in terra Christo facto noui testamenti Mediatori tribuit nouum Testamentum. Non enim dicit vsquam solum Deum omnia seruasse vel absoluisse, sed per Christum cuncta fecisse & reconciliasse: vnde & nos redemptos, iustificatos, sanctificatos, Deo reconciliatos, & vitæ æternæ hæredes factos (quod est nouæ creationis) per Christum noua Scriptura semper asserit (absque isto enim nihil horum factum est) tum etiam accessum nullum nos habere nisi per Christum ad Deum, ⁷ de quo sub veteri testamento altum silentium. ⁸ Vt quoque sub veteri Testamento suo ordine omnia opera creationis prioris &, quæ ad eam pertinet, conseruationis recensentur, Deo Patri vni tribuuntur: sic etiam in nouo Testamento omnia opera nouæ creationis per Christum facta recensentur quæ a Prophetis prædicta erant, neque intermissum quicquam quod nos scire expediret. Omnia inquit Lucas Actor. 1. se scripsisse, quæ Iesus cœpit (cœpit inquam) facere & docere (ecce initium operum & doctrinæ) vsque ad illud tempus quo in cœlum assumtus est, priùs constitutis testibus horum. Vide Matth. 4.
units.tr: Therefore, just as the Old Testament attributes that former creation to the one and only God, the Creator of all, the Father, so the New Testament attributes that later creation, or renewal, or recollection of all things in heaven and on earth, to Christ, made the Mediator of the new covenant. For nowhere does it say that God alone preserved or completed all things, but that all things were made and reconciled through Christ. Hence the new Scripture always asserts that we have been redeemed, justified, sanctified, reconciled to God, and made heirs of eternal life (which belongs to the new creation) through Christ, for without him none of these things has been done. It also asserts that we have no access to God except through Christ, of which under the old covenant there is a deep silence. Just as under the Old Testament all the works of the first creation, and those pertaining to its preservation, are recounted in their order and attributed to God the Father alone, so also in the New Testament all the works of the new creation made through Christ are recounted, which the Prophets had foretold, and nothing has been omitted that it would be useful for us to know. Luke says in Acts 1 that he has written of all that Jesus began (began, I say) to do and to teach (behold the beginning of his works and teaching), up to the time when he was taken up into heaven, after witnesses of these things had first been appointed. See Matt. 4.

units.la: Ad eundem quoque modum & Paulus de operibus huius novæ creationis scribens nouum testamentum statuit initium horum tum dictorum, tum factorum, Hebr. 1. quum nouissimis temporibus Deum ait loquutum esse per Filium, quod ante sub veteri testamento fecit per Prophetas. Sic & cap. 2. Hebr. vbi & doctrinæ salutis cœptæ prædicari a Christo, & operum eius summa recensetur. hoc ipsum & cap 12. Hebr. confirmat: Et cap 3. Christum facit administratorem domus Dei, cuius domus nos sumus.
units.tr: In the same way Paul, writing about the works of this new creation, also places the beginning of the new covenant at these things both said and done (Heb. 1), when in these last times God is said to have spoken through the Son, whereas before, under the old covenant, he did so through the Prophets. So also Heb. 2, where the summary of the saving doctrine begun to be preached by Christ and of his works is recounted. Heb. 12 confirms this very thing, and Heb. 3 makes Christ the administrator of God's house, whose house we are.

units.la: Mentiretur certè Paulus, & Lucas, tum alij Euangelistæ, vt Marcus, qui initium Euangelij Iesu Christi describit: si quid ante sub veteri testamento Christus vel docuisset Patres, vel etiam fecisset. Christus etiam ipse, si creasset cœlum & terram, non tacuisset id ud: ibi præcipuè, vbi contra Iudæos probat se filium Dei esse ex operibus communibus cum Patre: vbi tantum operum nouæ creationis meminit in sanando, viuificando, resuscitando, iudicando. Dixisset etiam, si verum fuisset hoc, vt Pater operabatur creando, ita & ego operabar: sed tantum de præsentibus loquitur, & Patrem sibi adiungit, quia Pater per eum omnia fecit: de præteritis tacet. Violare se ibi sabbathum negauit Christus, quia vt Pater omnia conseruando operatur, ita & Christus sanando in sabbatho hoc ipsum cum Patre egit.
units.tr: Paul would certainly be lying, and so would Luke and the other evangelists, such as Mark, who describes the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, if Christ had taught or even done anything under the old covenant before. Christ himself, if he had created heaven and earth, would not have kept silent about it, especially there, where against the Jews he proves that he is the Son of God from the works he shares with the Father, and where he mentions only the works of the new creation: healing, giving life, raising the dead, judging. He would also have said, if it were true, "As the Father worked in creating, so I too worked." But he speaks only of present things, and joins the Father to himself because the Father made all things through him; of past things he is silent. Christ denied that he was violating the Sabbath, because just as the Father works by preserving all things, so Christ, by healing on the Sabbath, was doing the very same thing together with the Father.

units.la: Sed & Prophetæ omnes de hoc alio secundo creatore tacent, vno contenti sunt Patre: opera autem Christi futura describunt Esai. 35. & 61. quæ Matthæi 2. & Luc. 4 quoque recensentur. Et hæc sunt opera nouæ creationis, seu restaurationis.
units.tr: But all the Prophets also are silent about this second creator; they are content with the one Father alone. They describe the future works of Christ in Isaiah 35 and 61, which are also recounted in Matth. 2 and Luke 4. These are the works of the new creation, or restoration.

units.la: Summa est, loquitur hic Ioannes de Christo ex Maria nato, per quem loquutus est Pater, non olim, sed nouissimis istis temporibus: vnde quoque Sermo vel Verbum dicitur.
units.tr: In sum, John here speaks of Christ born of Mary, through whom the Father has spoken, not in former times but in these last days; hence he is also called the Word or Speech.

units.la: De nouo testamento loquitur, cuius Christus homo, teste Paulo, est mediator: & Mediatori competit vt sint per illum omnia, non autem ex ipso. Hæc autem facta nouæ creationis describunt Euangelistæ quatuor, quæ per eum fecit Pater. Nam & Lucas scribit signa fecisse Deum per illum, dæmones expulisse, & omnes morbos sanasse, quia Deus erat cum illo illo nihil autem vsquam tribuitur Deo in Christo incarnato. Et Christus quoque sibi credi non vult si a seipso loquatur, vel faciat aliquid, sed propter opera quae egit Pater per eum, sibi credi voluit. Sic alias de Christo scribit Euangelista, bene omnia fecit. sed quae illa omnia? addit opera noui testamenti, nouae creationis in sanandis mutis & surdis, quae etiam Esaias ante multo praedixerat: & de creatione coeli terraeq; per Christum nusquam, cum omnibus Prophetis, vel verbo meminit. Sed & Ioannes cap. 1. inibi aperte ostendit gratiam & veritatem per Christum factam esse seu exsolutam, vt per Mosem Legem.
units.tr: He speaks of the new covenant, whose mediator, as Paul witnesses, is Christ the man. It belongs to a Mediator that all things be through him, not from him. The four Evangelists describe these deeds of the new creation, which the Father did through him. For Luke also writes that God did signs through him, cast out demons, and healed all diseases, because God was with him; nowhere is anything attributed to God in the incarnate Christ. Christ also does not wish to be believed if he speaks or does something on his own, but he wished to be believed on account of the works which the Father performed through him. So elsewhere the Evangelist writes of Christ that "he has done all things well"; but what were all those things? He adds the works of the new covenant, of the new creation, in healing the dumb and the deaf, which Isaiah had foretold long before. Nowhere does he mention the creation of heaven and earth through Christ, along with all the Prophets, not even in a word. But John 1 also there clearly shows that grace and truth were made, or brought, through Christ, just as the Law was through Moses.

units.la: Nequis ergo sibi somniet Filium Dei Christum aeternum, cuius generatio, vel unctio aeterna demonstrari non potest, sed nec vllum opus: tum quod aliquid acceperit a Patre, aut illi potestas data sit omnium. Isti enim ex Maria nato haec omnia tribuit Scriptura.
units.tr: Let no one, therefore, imagine that Christ, the eternal Son of God, has an eternal generation or anointing that cannot be demonstrated, nor any work of his, nor that he received anything from the Father, or that all power was given to him. For Scripture attributes all these things to him who was born of Mary.

units.la: M. S.
units.tr: M. S.

units.la: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est.
units.tr: All things were made by him, and without him was nothing made that was made.

units.la: DICTIO haec, omnia, non est referenda (vt vulgo fit) ad primam illam coeli terraeq; creationem. Nam Ioannes hic non de materialis ac visibilis huius mundi (de quo perfectissime scripsit Moses) sed de spiritualis mundi structura loquitur, quae non materialibus sed spiritualibus rebus, id est, Euangelij verbo construitur. Siquidem Christum (vt dictum est) ab effectu Verbum nuncupat, quod homines Euangelij doctrina spiritualiter instauret & regeneret. Vniuersalis ergo particula ista omnia, non est simpliciter intelligenda, vt ad visibilia ista trahatur: sed restringenda est ad negotium Euangelij iam tunc publicati ac recepti, quasi dicat, omnia quae nunc in Christi regno facta conspiciuntur (nam eo tempore quo Ioannes scripsit hanc suam de Iesu Christo historiam multi iam ad eius cognitionem venerant, ac ex potestate tenebrarum ad verum Deum conuersi erant) non aliunde facta sunt, quàm Christi solius opera, Euangelij, fui praedicatione. Nam & Christus ipse inquit, sine me nihil potestis facere. Sic Paulus ad Corinth. 2. cap 5. Siquis in Christo, noua creatura est: vetera praeterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia. & ad Ephes. cap. 1. vt omnia per Christum restauraret. & 3. capite, omnia creauit per Iesum Christum. Et hic creare pro instaurare Paulus vsurpat: vt multis etiam veteribus & modernis placuit.
units.tr: This word "all things" is not to be referred (as is commonly done) to the first creation of heaven and earth. For John is not speaking here of the material and visible world (about which Moses wrote most perfectly), but of the structure of the spiritual world, which is built not from material but from spiritual things, that is, by the word of the Gospel. For, as has been said, he calls Christ the Word from his effect, because he spiritually renews and regenerates people by the teaching of the Gospel. This universal particle "all things" is therefore not to be understood simply as drawing in these visible things, but is to be restricted to the business of the Gospel, already then published and received. It is as if he said: all the things that are now seen to be done in the kingdom of Christ (for by the time John wrote this history of Jesus Christ, many had already come to the knowledge of him and had been converted from the power of darkness to the true God) were made by no other means than the work of Christ alone, through the preaching of his own Gospel.
