For Christ himself says, "Without me you can do nothing." So Paul, 2 Corinthians 5: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; old things have passed away, behold, all things have become new." And Ephesians 1: "that he might restore all things through Christ"; and chapter 3: "he created all things through Jesus Christ." Here Paul uses "create" for "restore," as many ancient and modern writers have also thought.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXVS.

units.la: Hvivs loci interpretationem pro sua sapientia & auctoritate Samosatenus aggrediens, primùm affirmat proterue fatis omneis qui receptam illam de aeterno Dei Filio doctrinam sacram & catholicam defendunt, hoc loco abusos esse: deinde abusionis membra duo summatim proponit, quae post reliquo scripto multis & eodem ordine enarrantur. Ac primùm quidem si ipsa Mosis, Prophetarumque, Christi, Apostolorum, & Euangelistarum scripta expendimus, id sanctè coram Deo Patre & Domino Iesu Christo, qui venturus est ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos, possumus confirmare, non abuti eos Scripturae loco qui germanam sententiam eius, & reliquae Scripturae conuenientem afferunt: atque hanc interpretationem huius loci ita se habere. Deinde verò quos incusat abusionis Samosatenus! Deus bone. Apostolorum αὐτόπτας καὶ αὐτηκόους, qui eos viderunt, audiuerunt coràm, atq; coluerunt: quorum in numero Polycarpus suscepturus coronam matyrij in sua extrema oratione hac ipsam confessionem pronunciauit: tu proximos horum discipulos qui in Ecclesia quàm fidelissimè doctrinam eamdem a suis doctoribus acceptam tradiderunt sermone & scripto: quemadmodum exstant Irenaei luculentissima sima multa,& deijs vnum suprà segmeto 3. testimonium produximus : praeterea seculorum omnium ordine sequentium, in quibus homines Dei veritatem huius doctrinae natiuámque huius loci interpretationem summo consensu,fide,religione docuerunt:in summa,Ecclesiam illam catholicam inde a temporibus huius Euangelij in hac veritate doctrinae interpretationísque sanctissimè institutam,altam, atq; confirmatam:cuius vniuersitatem, antiquitatem,& consensionem in veritate Christi fundatam & veritate conseruatam illius facere debemus pluris, quàm Samosateniorum delirantium somnia. Hos homines hæc tempora,hanc Ecclesiam tu, Samosatene, hoc loco abusam dices? per te vnum a tetra abusione hūc locum vindicari? quis credat, nisi qui sciens prudens perire volet? Abusos illos? prudentes, an imprudentes abusos dicis? Si prudentes, impiè te auctore iudicéque fecerint : non fecerunt autem : ergo accusas impie. Si imprudentes, ij ergo fefellerint a quibus acceperunt, & his abusi fuerint. Scilicet Ioannes Polycarpum fefellerit, & alios quàmplurimos qui ab ipso coràm acceperunt, didicerunt, hauserunt huius doctrinae veritatem. O audaciam! Sic non discipuli solùm, sed ipsi etiam Apostoli abusionis auctores in rebus diuinis ad salutem vitámque æternam pertinentibus futuri sunt. Scilicet hic sacerdos veritatis, administer, interpres futurus est,qui palàm non dubitat damnare falsi Apostolos & Euangelistas, id est, homines ψευδάγγελος,notarios publicos diuinæ veritatis,omni exceptione maiores. Sed ad rē. Falsos duobus modis homines nostros interpretando hoc loco pronūciat: primùm quòd Christum esse vnum cum Patre Deum æqualem, coæternum, Creatorem cœli & terræ ex hoc loco pronunciant: secundò quòd creationem hanc de primo illo opificio materialis huius mundi, non de renouatione & instauratione acceperunt. Nos vero neutra in refuiffe fallos, aut adhuc falli confirmamus. Quapropter cùm de vtroque hoc dicto probando Samosatenus laboret sequentibus, age, de probationibus ad vtrumque allatis suo ordine videamus. Christum nec vnum Deum cum Patre, nec creatore esse cum Patre probaturus, primùm audacissima affirmatione in re comperta exploratáque vtitur, dicens, nemo piorum est qui degustauit sacras literas, qui vel vnum Deum esse Christum cum Patre, vel etiam creatorem esse cœli terræq; assereret. Nempe tibi, Samosatene, impij sunt quicunque hoc docent. At nos contra affirmamus neminem piorum esse, si modò sacras literas religiosè degustauerit, qui hoc non asseruerit. Affirmationem suam non probat Samosatenus: nos probauimus nostram Defensionis 2. segmento 2. & si opus est, amplius probaturi sumus omnium bonorum, omniumque ætatum consentientibus suffragijs. Quibus ætatibus inde ab Euangelij prædicatione aut neminem pium fuisse oportet (nam omnes contra quàm Samosatenus asserit docuisse constat) aut insigniter dare Samosatenum verba, & commenta sua imperitis fallendis obtrudere. Indignū hominis factum qui sanctissimos Dei seruos, testes Christi, & participes afflictionum eius ἀιροεατῶν maluit impietatis condemnare, quàm in se descendens gloriā æterno Dei filio tribuere. At quibus probationibus, obscuro?
units.tr: Attempting the interpretation of this passage with his own wisdom and authority, Samosatenus first asserts shamelessly that all who defend the received doctrine of the eternal Son of God as holy and catholic have abused this passage. Then he sets out briefly two parts of the abuse, which are afterwards explained in the rest of his writing, in the same order, with many words. First, if we weigh the writings of Moses, the Prophets, Christ, the Apostles and the Evangelists, we can solemnly affirm before God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, that those who bring forward the genuine meaning of this text, and one agreeing with the rest of Scripture, do not abuse Scripture, and that this interpretation of the passage is correct. Then, whom does Samosatenus accuse of abuse? Good God! The Apostles, eyewitnesses and earwitnesses [αὐτόπτας καὶ αὐτηκόους], who saw, heard and served him in person; among whom Polycarp, about to receive the crown of martyrdom, in his final prayer professed this very confession; then their disciples, who in the Church faithfully handed on in speech and writing the same doctrine received from their teachers, as the most lucid writings of Irenaeus still survive, of which we brought forward one testimony above in section 3; besides all the ages that followed in order, in which men of God taught the truth of this doctrine and the true interpretation of this passage with the greatest agreement, faith and piety. In sum, that catholic Church, holily established and confirmed in the truth of this doctrine and its interpretation from the times of this Gospel onward, whose universality, antiquity and agreement, founded in the truth of Christ and preserved by his truth, we ought to value more than the dreams of the raving Samosatenes. Will you, Samosatenus, say that these men, these times, this Church, have abused this passage? Will you alone claim that this text is cleared of foul abuse? Who would believe it, except one who knowingly and deliberately wishes to perish? Do you call them abusers? Do you say they abused it knowingly or unknowingly? If knowingly, they acted impiously by your authority and judgment; but they did not act so; therefore you accuse impiously. If unknowingly, then those from whom they received it deceived them, and they were misled by them. So John deceived Polycarp, and very many others who received, learned and drank in the truth of this doctrine from him in person. O audacity! Thus not only the disciples but the Apostles themselves would be the authors of abuse in divine matters pertaining to salvation and eternal life. Clearly this man, who is to be the priest, minister and interpreter of truth, does not hesitate openly to condemn as false Apostles and Evangelists those who are false messengers [ψευδάγγελος], public notaries of divine truth, greater than any objection. But to the matter. He pronounces our people false in interpreting this passage in two ways: first, because they derive from this passage that Christ is one God with the Father, equal and coeternal, Creator of heaven and earth; secondly, because they take this creation not as the restoration and renewal, but as that first work of the material world. We, however, affirm that they were not false in either respect, nor are they yet. Therefore, since Samosatenus labours in what follows to prove both of these points, come, let us see in order the proofs brought forward for each. Intending to prove that Christ is neither one God with the Father nor Creator with the Father, he first uses a most bold assertion about a matter already established and examined, saying: no one among the pious who has tasted the holy letters has asserted that Christ is one God with the Father, or even that he is Creator of heaven and earth. Indeed, Samosatenus, for you those who teach this are impious. But on the contrary we affirm that no one among the pious, if he has religiously tasted the holy letters, has failed to assert it. Samosatenus does not prove his assertion; we proved ours in section 2 of part 2 of our Defence, and if necessary we shall prove it further by the agreeing votes of all good men and of all ages. Yet from the preaching of the Gospel onward, either there must have been no pious person (for it is agreed that all taught otherwise than Samosatenus asserts), or Samosatenus is cunningly deceiving the unlearned and foisting on them his own inventions. A shameful deed in a man who preferred to condemn the most holy servants of God, the witnesses of Christ and sharers in his afflictions [ἀιροεατῶν] as impious, rather than to humble himself and grant to the eternal Son of God the glory due to him. But with what proofs, you ask?

units.la: Prima est, quòd vnus Deus Pater creator cœli & terræ passim in Scripturis dicitur. Agnoscimus, & idem affirmamus. Nam verè vnus est essentia Deus, ac non alius: vnus indiuisus, quamuis tres distinctæ personæ, vt Defensionis 2. segmento 3. expositum. Sed fallit Samosatenus æquiuocatione, quum ita dicit. Nam primùm vnus essentia est, non persona vna: quæ confundit iste. Deinde verò Deus Pater multis in locis dicitur essentialiter respectu spectu creaturarum, non autem personaliter respectu Filij quem genuit ab æterno Pater: atque hic ille est Elohim qui creauit cœlum & terram, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Postremò si etiam dicitur hoc de persona Patris distinctè, fit vario respectu, adeò ut nulla his verbis insit contradictio: nam Deus essentialiter Pater & Creator dicitur, quia communis est trium personarum in creandis rebus operatio: at Deus Pater personaliter Creator dicitur, respectu singularis termini a quo est principium creationis rerumque omnium. Nam communitas operationis non tollit singularem dispositionem personarum inter se, ad singularem dispositionis illius terminum in unaquaque, licet communi, operatione. Qua de re in Defensione 2. multis. Hunc igitur locum totum iusto sensu acceptum probamus, male obiectum vero religiosè distinguimus.
units.tr: The first is that one God, the Father, the Creator of heaven and earth is spoken of throughout the Scriptures. We acknowledge this, and we affirm the same. For truly God is one in essence, and not another; one, undivided, although there are three distinct persons, as was set out in section 3 of part 2 of our Defence. But Samosatenus deceives by equivocation when he speaks in this way. For first, there is one essence, not one person; this man confuses the two. Then, God the Father is called in many places essentially with respect to creatures, but not personally with respect to the Son whom the Father begot from eternity; and this is that Elohim who created heaven and earth: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Finally, even if it is said in this way of the person of the Father distinctly, it is said with a different respect, so that there is no contradiction in these words. For God is called Father and Creator essentially, because the operation of creating things is common to the three persons; but God the Father is called Creator personally, with respect to the single terminus from which the principle of creation and of all things comes. For community of operation does not remove the singular disposition of the persons among themselves, nor the singular terminus of that disposition in each, although the operation is common. On this matter there is much in Defence part 2. We therefore accept this whole passage in its right sense, and we religiously distinguish what is wrongly brought against it.

units.la: Secunda, quòd non solùm creatio, sed omnia opera quæ fecit Deus sub vetere Testamento, tribuuntur illi uni Deo Patri Christi, vt Actor. 13. Primùm non dicit Lucas, vni Deo Patri Christi: glossema est Samosatenicum. Secundò etiamsi dixisset ab uno Deo esse (quo sensu ante sumus interpretati) commune tamen non restringit aut derogat quicquam de particulari, aut particulare de communi: sed Pater fecit, Filius fecit, &c. cõmune opus dispositione particulari: quapropter ait Christus, quæcunque Pater facit, hæc etiam Filius pariter facit. Tertiò eo loco non agit Lucas de omnibus operibus quæ fecit Deus sub Testamento vetere, sed de præstitis promissionibus de mittendo Filio, quæ missio necessariò importat distinctionem personarum, & singularitatem operum intus in relatione interna consistentium: quia Pater mittit & excitat, Filius a Patre mittitur atque excitatur. Inanis igitur argumentatio. Quod autem cramben illam suam toties repetit, de filio dato ex semine Davidis, non ex aliquo verbo Dei æterno, duobus modis ineptum est. Nam primum res coniunctas opponit velut contrarias, naturam diuinam & humanam Christi, tamquam si non possent illæ simul consistere: cum tamen & hanc & illam substantiam esse nouerit, & nihil substantiæ aduersari. tum quæ de Christo dicuntur diuersa ratione, hic elenchum suum celans ratione eiusdem accipit artifex, vt circumueniat imperitos. Nam vtraque ratio est in una persona Christi, æternæ naturæ Sermonis illius, quà Deus, & temporariæ carnis, quà Deus in plenitudine temporum factus ex muliere: quę duo nec opponi possunt inter se ad mutuam euersionem, nec confundi ad euersionem personæ. Captiosa omnia.
units.tr: The second is that not only the creation, but all the works that God did under the Old Testament, are attributed to that one God, the Father of Christ, as in Acts 13. First, Luke does not say "to the one God, the Father of Christ"; that is a Samosatenian gloss. Secondly, even if he had said it was from the one God (in the sense in which we have interpreted it before), it nevertheless does not restrict or take away anything from the particular, nor the particular from the common; rather the Father made, the Son made, and so on: a common work by a particular disposition. That is why Christ says, whatever the Father does, these things the Son also equally does. Thirdly, in that place Luke is not dealing with all the works that God did under the Old Testament, but with the promises made concerning the sending of the Son, and that sending necessarily implies a distinction of persons and a singularity of works existing within the internal relation: because the Father sends and raises up, and the Son is sent and raised up by the Father. The argument is therefore empty. As for his often repeated little tale, of a son given from the seed of David, not from any eternal word of God, it is absurd in two ways. First, he sets against each other things that are joined together as if they were contraries, the divine and human natures of Christ, as if they could not exist together; yet he knows that both are substances and that nothing in substance is opposed. Secondly, he takes what is said of Christ in different respects in the same way, concealing his own fallacy by the artifice of a single respect, so as to deceive the unlearned. For both respects are in one person of Christ: the eternal nature of that Word, by which he is God, and the temporal flesh, by which he, God, was made in the fullness of time from a woman. These two cannot be set against each other so as to destroy each other, nor confused so as to destroy the person. All these things are captious.

units.la: Tertia probatio est ex Mose sumta. Nā Moses in Creatione mundi nullā mentionem fecit Christi; in promissis autē instaurationis semē mulieris, semen Abrahami nominat, & typos figurásque describit accuratissimē, quæ erant vmbracula futuri Christi, ac nō præsentis iā aut æterni Christi. Argumentatio hæc est: Qui tū futurus dicebatur & præsignificabatur, nondū erat: Christus futurus dicebatur a Mose, & præsignificabatur vmbraculis: Igitur nodū erat. Maior ambiguè dicitur: nā qui dicitur aut significatur futurus, is aut secūdùm substantiā futurus dicitur, significatūrq;, aut secūdùm modū & manifestationem illius: præterea aut secūdùm totū, si nihildum est illius, aut secundùm partē, si quid insuper est accessurum. Hinc minor exponenda: Christus non secundùm substantiam personæ suæ diuinæ futurus dicitur aut significatur, sed secundùm modū manifestationémq; illius in assumta carne: nec secundùm totum sui exstiturus dicitur significatúrue, sed tantùm secundùm illam (vt ita loquamur) particulam quam assumsit, nimirum carnem, de virgine Maria. Sic conclusionem bene intellectam non dubitabimus approbare: nondum erat Christus, nimirum mirum secundùm carnem ; sed erat tamen secundùm aeternam illam personæ diuinæ suæ veritatem. Sed absur-dum fuerit, inquit, Mosem non meminisse Christi, si quidem Christus fuit iam eo tempore. Respondeo primum cum Scholasticis, ab auctoritate negatiuè non valere argumentum: non meminit Christi, operumq; illius: non ergo fuit Christus. Secundò falsa est affirmatio, Mosem non meminisse Christi, tāquam eius qui iam tum esset: iam tum enim fuisse, & ab æterno esse, cùm alibi, tum etiam suprà segmento 2. ostendimus: atque etiam hoc ipsum a Mose quàm plurimis locis expressum fuisse euidentissimè, Genes. 1. & 3. & 11. & alibi. Sic erat quidem persona Christi, sed non erat semen quod assumeret ex muliere, Dauide, Abrahamo: ac proinde secundùm personam diuinâ erat, non erat autè secundùm naturâ nostram: hanc enim postea assumsit in tempore. Irrita cadunt igitur harum argumentationum tela: quibus certissimam illam interpretationem de creatione aspectabilis huius mundi conatur Samosatenus Christo & Ecclesiæ illius eripere.
units.tr: The third proof is taken from Moses. In the account of the creation of the world Moses made no mention of Christ, but in the promises of restoration he names the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham, and describes types and figures very carefully. These were shadows of the future Christ, not of a Christ already present or eternal. The argument runs: Whatever was spoken of and foreshadowed as future did not yet exist. Christ was spoken of by Moses as future and foreshadowed by shadows. Therefore he did not yet exist. The major premise is ambiguous. What is said or signified to be future is either future according to its substance, or future according to its mode and manifestation. It is also either future as a whole, if none of it yet exists, or future in part, if something more is still to come. So the minor premise must be explained: Christ is not said or signified to be future according to the substance of his divine person, but according to the mode and manifestation of that person in the assumed flesh. Nor is he said or signified to be going to exist as a whole, but only according to that part (so to speak) which he assumed, namely the flesh from the virgin Mary. Understood in this way, we shall not hesitate to approve the conclusion: Christ did not yet exist, namely according to the flesh; but he did exist according to that eternal truth of his divine person. But it would be absurd, he says, for Moses not to mention Christ, if indeed Christ already existed at that time. I answer first, with the Scholastics, that an argument from negative authority is not valid: he does not mention Christ or his works, therefore Christ did not exist. Second, the assertion that Moses did not mention Christ as one who already then existed is false. That Christ already existed, and was from eternity, we have shown both elsewhere and above in section 2. Indeed, Moses expressed this very thing in very many places, most evidently in Gen. 1, 3 and 11, and elsewhere. So the person of Christ did exist, but the seed which he would assume from the woman, from David and from Abraham did not yet exist. He therefore existed according to the divine person, but not yet according to our nature, for he assumed that later in time. The darts of these arguments therefore fall in vain, by which Samosatenus tries to snatch that most certain interpretation of the creation of this visible world away from Christ and from his Church.

units.la: Postquàm frustra operâ Samosatenus cōsumsit vt nostrā sententiā ad luculentissimū hunc locū euerteret, trāsit ad firmamēta interpretationis suæ. Hæc Ioannis verba, inquit, de recreatione, renouatione, reconciliatione, & recapitulatione, seu restauratione intelligenda sunt, quæ vbiq; Christo tribuitur, & per quē Deus hāc exsequutus est. Multa hic sesquipedalia ve ba, etiā re inter se differentia, ad rē vnā & eandem significandā. Sed nolumus in verbis curiosi esse: de re dicturi sumus. Negamus hæc Euangelistæ verba ad instauratione per Christum factam pertinere. Quibus argumentis hoc contendat assequi & conficere, videamus.
units.tr: After Samosatenus has wasted his effort in vain in trying to overturn our view of this most lucid passage, he moves on to the supports of his own interpretation. These words of John, he says, are to be understood of recreation, renewal, reconciliation and recapitulation, or restoration, which is everywhere attributed to Christ, and through whom God carried this out. Here there are many high-sounding words, even some differing among themselves, to signify one and the same thing. But we do not wish to be fussy about words; we shall speak to the matter. We deny that these words of the Evangelist pertain to the restoration made through Christ. Let us see by what arguments he undertakes to establish and accomplish this.

units.la: Primus probationum locus Noua creatio vbique in nouo testamento tribuitur Christo, eámque Deus per hunc exsequutus est: hæc ergo de noua creatione pariter intelligenda. Respondeo, per negationem consequentiæ. Hæc enim tunc demum valitura esset vt necessario vera, si ostenderetur vnicum esse actu Domini Iesu Christi: sed cum Iesu Christi actus non sit vnicus, immo potius multiplex, falsa est consequentia, neque ex antecedente isto confici vnquam potest. Præterea tribuitur hæc noua creatio Christo, velut proximo termino, vt ante dictum: sed eadem opus est commune Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti: quam communitatem vt Samosatenus confiteretur effecit veritas, quû diceret Deum hanc per Christum exsequutum esse. Vt autem communis renouatio, sic etiam creatio prima credenda est communiter a sancta Trinitate facta. Creauit igitur Christus mundum, ac non instaurauit solùm. Instar, Atqui restrictionem addit Ioannes, quod factum est, ne quis vniuersaliter de omnibus creaturis hoc dici putet, sed intelligat de ijs rebus quæ facta sunt per eum, quia aliæ sine illo factæ sunt in testamento vetere. Negamus istud ad rem pertinere. Nam primùm restringes istud glossema falsum est, quod factum est per eum, nec vllo ex loco eodem aut simili probari potest. Præterea stolida ist hæc restrictio est, quam vix balbutientes pueri, vix Battus agnouerit, sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est per ipsum. Te appello, Samosatene, si quid vnquam audisti infantius, prome. Postremò Hebræas, Græcas, Latinas aures probemus: cõsulamus, vtrum hoc genus loquutionis ad restrictionem pertineat, an vero ad enunciationem vniuersalitatis, οὐ καθόλου. Quum enim dicitur, nihil quod factum est, æquipollet hic sermo illi, nihil factum, vel nihil facti, vt nomen facti vniuersale sit, & nomen nihil vniuersale signum. Hæc tu restringes, Samosatene? nomen vniuersale coniunctum vniuersali signo? & nulla determinatione factum angustius? Sed quid mirum; si naturam vocum & enunciatorum mutas, qui mutas Dei veritatem? Summa, & hanc restrictionem stionem veram negamus esse, & alia sine Christo negamus facta, quod pro auctoritate hoc loco audes affirmare. Vellus quidem tibi, Samosatene, istic non carpitur: aliæ argumentationes & probationes adferendæ, si tibi vis haberi fidem.
units.tr: The first place of proof: New creation is everywhere in the New Testament attributed to Christ, and God carried it out through him; therefore these things are equally to be understood of the new creation. I answer by denying the consequence. This would necessarily hold true only if it were shown that the action of the Lord Jesus Christ is single. But since the action of Jesus Christ is not single, but rather manifold, the consequence is false, and it can never be drawn from that antecedent. Moreover, this new creation is attributed to Christ as the proximate term, as said before; but the same work is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Truth compelled Samosatenus to confess this commonality when he said that God carried this out through Christ. But just as the renewal is common, so the first creation too must be believed to have been made in common by the holy Trinity. Christ therefore created the world, and did not merely restore it. Further, John adds a restriction, "what was made", lest anyone think this is said universally of all creatures, but let him understand it of those things which were made through him, because others were made without him in the Old Testament. We deny that this pertains to the matter. First, this restrictive gloss, "what was made through him," is false, and it cannot be proved from any passage the same or similar. Moreover, this restriction is foolish, one which scarcely stammering boys, scarcely Battus, would recognise: without him was nothing made that was made through him. I challenge you, Samosatenus: if you have ever heard anything more childish, produce it. Lastly, let us test the Hebrew, Greek and Latin ears: let us consult whether this kind of expression pertains to restriction or rather to the statement of universality [οὐ καθόλου]. For when it is said "nothing that was made", this speech is equivalent to "nothing made" or "nothing of what was made", so that the noun "made" is universal and the word "nothing" is a universal sign. Will you restrict these things, Samosatenus? A universal noun joined to a universal sign, and nothing made narrower by any qualification? But what wonder, if you change the nature of words and statements, you who change the truth of God? In sum, we deny that this restriction is true, and we deny that other things were made without Christ, which you dare to assert on the authority of this passage. Indeed, Samosatenus, your fleece is not being plucked here at all. Other arguments and proofs must be brought forward if you want to be believed.

units.la: Ecce autem, his positis, tamquam re bene gesta, probata, euicta, confessa, excurrit ad nouæ creationis, siue renouationis per Christum enarrationem: & locos accumulans vbi de instauratione per Christum agitur (quam sanctè credimus, & participamus per gratiam, & docemus secundùm gratiam illius) videtur sibi probare hanc natiuam esse huius loci interpretationem, primùm propter locorum quibus hoc docetur copiam, secundò propter oppositionem quam instituit inter creationem nouam siue instaurationè per Christum, & illam veterem conditionem naturæ. Sed quàm infirmum vtrumque hoc sit probationum genus, paulo antè fuit demonstratum.
units.tr: Now, on these premises, as if the matter were well done, proved, established and conceded, he rushes on to the explanation of the new creation, or renewal, through Christ. Piling up passages where restoration through Christ is spoken of (which we believe devoutly, share through grace, and teach according to his grace), he seems to prove that this is the natural interpretation of the place. He argues first from the abundance of passages in which this is taught, and second from the opposition he sets up between the new creation or restoration through Christ and that old condition of nature. But how weak each of these kinds of proof is has been shown a little before.

units.la: Nam quod ad locorum qui adducuntur copiam, non est vnus locus, immò ne mille quidem loci lex sunt alterius in quo res diuersa agitur: sunt autem res diuersæ, creatio mundi, & instauratio: ineptum est igitur eos locos qui de re vna agunt, ad rei alterius locorumq; co pertinentium explicationem rapere. Sed, ne actum agatur, piumque Lectorem rogatum velim, vt ea solùm hoc loco adhibeat quæ proximè in primum probationis locum annotauimus.
units.tr: For as to the abundance of passages adduced: one passage is not the law of another in which a different matter is treated, nor even a thousand passages. But the matters are different: the creation of the world and restoration. It is therefore absurd to drag passages that treat one matter into the explanation of another matter and of the passages pertaining to it. But, lest the business be dragged out, I would ask the pious Reader to use in this place only those things which we have just noted at the first place of proof.

units.la: De oppositione verò quid dicturi sumus? Christum enim opponit Deo Patri, & opus creationis operi renouationis, tamquam si alterum altero euerteretur. Atqui, Samosatene, in causa persimili paulo antè ostendimus bifariam venire te contra istarum oppositionum leges. Nam primùm res coniunctas diuidis, & actus particulares facis ex communibus: tum ex operibus diuersis contraria facis, quamuis non affirmetur & negetur idem, ad idem, ratione eiusdem, eodémque modo & tempore. Frustra igitur laboras in probanda renouatione per Christum, quam credimus,sentimus,& docemus fideliter in Domino:fru-ftra opera consumis in creationis opere auertedo a Chri-sto,quod hic a loanne Christo tribuitur: vtrumque opus Christi est, & Christo in sacris literis sanctissime attribu-tum. Ex his autem omnino sequitur istud,quaecunque in hunc locum de renouatione & instauratione per Chri-ftum a te adducuntur, ea esse ἀπεςθαστιονυσα, nihil ad rem, atque ad locum pertinere:vt ante segmento 1.docuimus. Quapropter fiqua commode a te de renouatione dicta sunt, quamuis non huius loci, tamen libenter ea velut a Deo profecta relinquemus suo loco: quae autem a veritate discrepant, cursim destringemus, ne falso consentire, quum no contradicimus aut submonemus de eo, videamur cuiquam. 1. Hic locus 1. Cor. 8. aduersatur consilio Samofateni omnibus modis. Nam agitur de idolothytis:ostenditur neque idola,neque eorum quemquam qui dicuntur dij in coelo aut in terra quicquam in idolothyta posse,sed eum solum qui fecit omnia, tum in res quae idolis offeruntur, tum in idololatras potestatem omnem obtinere, cum omnia ab ipso,in ipso, per ipsum, & propter ipsum subsistant, vt idem ait Rom. 11. Quod opus commune trium personarum sanctae Trinitatis fiquis per suos personales (vt ita loquamur) terminos volet distinguere, omnia a Patre & in Patre subsistunt, velut principiali termino summo: per Filium vero fiue Dominum Iesum Christum, velut propinquiorem terminum, sapientiam Dei & potentiam Dei, sustinentem omnia verbo potente suo in hac administratione diuina, Hebr. 1. Extra chorum saltas, (quod aiunt) Samofatene, quum hanc interpretationem adtexis huic loco,& perdis Juculentiffimam grauissimamque Apostoli in hac causa argumentatione. 2. Peccatum hic duplex: primum oppofitio illa quam ante refellimus, perinde ac fi Christi vnus solùm actus effet (quod est ineptiffimum dictu) aut creatio omnium & renouatio Ecclesiæ tam contraria effent, vt ab vno eodemque auctore ἀδύνατον effet vtramque proficisci, quod ridiculum: deinde quòd res secundùm quid dicta accipitur simpliciter, & prauè locus exponitur. Sic enim verba Pauli habent, si quis est in Christo, noua creatura est: vetera præterierùt, puta in eo qui est Christi, noua facta sunt omnia in eo, quasi dicat, renouatus est per omnia. Hæc autem omnia sunt ex Deo, &c. Omnia igitur quum dicit Apostolus, non creaturas intelligit, sed quæ in creaturis, qualitates, ac non substantias. Proinde inepta oppositio est, quam pòst vsurpat Samosatenus dicens, Certè cælum, terra, mare, arbores, animantia, omnia denuò creata non sunt, &c. Alioquin de renovatione in Christo agi eo loco assentimur & docemus. De loco sequente Ephes. 3. suum cuique per me iudicium liberum, prout etiam a Caluino relinquitur. Sed inconsequens semper manet argumentatio: sic accipitur eo loco de Christo, ergo aliis etiam locis omnibus sic oportet accipi. Inepta ex particulari argumentatio.
units.tr: What shall we say about the opposition? He sets Christ against God the Father, and the work of creation against the work of renewal, as if one were overthrown by the other. Yet, Samosatenus, in a very similar case we showed a little before that you twice break the laws of such oppositions. For first you divide things that are joined together, and make particular actions out of common ones; then from different works you make contraries, although the same is not affirmed and denied of the same, in the same respect, in the same way and at the same time. You labour in vain, therefore, to prove renewal through Christ, which we believe, feel and teach faithfully in the Lord. You waste effort in the work of creation by turning away from Christ what John here attributes to Christ. Both works are Christ's, and both are most holily attributed to Christ in the sacred writings. From this it entirely follows that whatever you bring forward on this passage about renewal and restoration through Christ is beside the point [ἀπεςθαστιονυσα], nothing to the matter or to the place, as we taught above in section 1. Wherefore, if anything you have said about renewal is fittingly said, though not of this passage, we shall willingly leave it, as coming from God, in its own place. But what departs from the truth we shall touch on briefly, lest we seem to agree falsely with anyone when we do not contradict or warn about it. 1. This passage, 1 Cor. 8, is opposed to the design of Samosatenus in every way. The matter concerns things offered to idols. It is shown that neither idols nor any of those who are called gods in heaven or on earth can do anything with the things offered to idols; rather, he alone who made all things holds all power, both over the things offered to idols and over idolaters, since all things subsist from him, in him, through him and for him, as the same apostle says in Rom. 11. If anyone wishes to distinguish this common work of the three persons of the holy Trinity by their personal (so to speak) terms: all things subsist from the Father and in the Father, as the highest principal term; but through the Son, or the Lord Jesus Christ, as the nearer term, the wisdom of God and the power of God, sustaining all things by his mighty word in this divine administration, Heb. 1. You dance outside the choir (as they say), Samosatenus, when you attach this interpretation to this passage, and you destroy the most brilliant and weighty argument of the Apostle in this cause. 2. Here there is a double error. First, the opposition which we refuted before, as if Christ had only one action (which is most absurd to say), or as if the creation of all things and the renewal of the Church were so contrary that it would be impossible for both to proceed from one and the same author, which is ridiculous. Then, a thing said in a certain respect is taken simply, and the passage is wrongly explained. For the words of Paul are: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; old things have passed away, that is, in the one who is Christ's, all things are made new in him, as if he said he is renewed in all things. But all these things are of God, etc. Therefore, when the Apostle says "all things", he means not creatures but what is in creatures: qualities, and not substances. Hence the opposition Samosatenus then uses is inept, when he says: Certainly heaven, earth, sea, trees, living things, all have not been created anew, etc. Otherwise, we agree and teach that renewal in Christ is treated in that place. As to the following passage, Eph. 3, let each person have his own free judgment, as Calvin also leaves it. But the argument always remains inconsequent: it is taken of Christ in that place, therefore all other passages must also be so taken. An inept argument from a particular.

units.la: 3. Falsa oppositio, vt ante in probationem 2. huius segmenti ostendimus, & quam hic persæpe recantat κοκκύζων, adeò sibi in hac re allubescit: quamobrem idem etiam ad sequentia huiusmodi (nam frequentissimè recurrunt) dictum esto.
units.tr: 3. This is a false opposition, as we showed earlier in the proof of the second point of this section. The cuckoo [κοκκύζων] repeats it again and again and takes such delight in it on this matter. So what is said here should also be taken to apply to what follows of this kind, since these recur very frequently.

units.la: 4. Vera propositio, sed ambigua duobus modis. Eruncandũ vtrumque ambiguum. Prius est, quum dicit, in Christo homine. Nam hoc dictum aut simpliciter accipitur vt dictum se habet, pro eo quod est in persona Christi, qui est homo, idémq; Deus in vnitate personæ: aut accipitur cum exclusione latente quam Samosatenus dissimulat, pro eo quod est in persona Christi qui est homo solùm. Posterius negamus freti veritate Dei & auctoritate Scripturæ. Prio-
units.tr: 4. The proposition is true but ambiguous in two ways, and both ambiguities must be cleared up. The first lies in his words in Christ the man. This statement is either taken simply as it stands, to mean what belongs to the person of Christ, who is man and also God in the unity of his person; or it is taken with a hidden exclusion, which Samosatenus conceals, to mean what belongs to the person of Christ who is man only. The latter we deny, relying on the truth of God and the authority of Scripture. The former

units.la: y rem sentetiam intellectam commodè amplectimur. Alterum ambiguum est, quum dicitur regnum hoccapisse in Christo. Si enim Samosatenus id sibi vellet simpliciter principium huius regni a Christo esse, hunc unum esse regni illius principem, acquiescerem vltrò: sed aliud est quod machinatur, nempe tum primum exstitisse, quum Sermo factus est caro. Hoc autem salsissimum est: nam Sermo erat suppositum, ante quàm fieret caro, erat in principio, apud Deum, Deus operabatur, regnabat: quod hic negatur impie. At, inquit, dicitur Luc. 1. dabit illi Deus (non ante dederat) sedem Dauid patris sui, & regnabit in ea, non regnauit antea. Fallacia est, vt vocant, ex elenchi ignoratione duplex: nam vtrumque verum erat, sed non ratione eiusdem, nec semper de eodem tempore. Dederat Pater, & daturus erat: regnauerat Filius, & regnaturus erat. Dederat Pater secundum personam diuinam eius: daturus erat eidem personae secundum assumendam carnem. Regnauerat Filius Dei secundum diuinitatem suam: regnaturus erat secundum humanitatem suam re & manifestatione regni. Regnauerat semper in omni tempore secundum personam: post erat regnaturus etiam secundum carnem. Haec duo non sunt inter se contradicentia: quę tamen eadem arte ac potius imperitia Samosatenus velut contraria opponit, qua ante naturam diuinam humanae, opus diuinum humano, creationem nouam veteri oppositum; tamquam si in uno subiecto nunquam simul esse, aut ab uno subiecto, nimirum ἀνθρώπῳ, proficisci possent. Belle sane, & argutè omnia. De loco altero Coloss. 1. quem etiam torquet miserè, & adducit inepte, diximus suprà segmento 5. Quid plura? pergit in sua oppositione ex Col. 1. Ephes. 1 & tamquam Phoenix, in rogo suo sibi videtur viuere, coeli & terrae creationem soli Patri, renouationem verò Filio Deo a Patre facto vindicans, vtrumque falsò, & ex falsis hypothesibus quas antè reuici-mus, triumphos sibi de Filio Dei & de veritate somnians. Scilicet creationem Pater fecit, non ergo Filius. falsum: nam commune vsque adeò opus est vt quæcunque facit Pater, eadem Filius faciat pariter. Item dixero, renouationem fecit Filius: non ergo Pater. falsum: nam hoc quoq; commune opus est: non enim potest Filius a semetipso operari, nisi viderit Patrem facientem: Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat, ita etiam Filius quos vult viuificat. Ad eamdem falsam oppositionem relabitur argumento Hebr. 9. ex vnius facti affirmatione remotionem alterius non contrarij statuens, sed diuersi solum. Quis hominem literatum credat sic argumentari contra rationem, iustasque argumentandi leges euertere?
units.tr: in the sense understood we readily embrace. The second ambiguity lies in the words he has taken up this kingdom in Christ. If Samosatenus meant simply that the beginning of this kingdom is from Christ, and that he is the one prince of that kingdom, I would agree with him at once. But he is contriving something else, namely that the kingdom began only when the Word was made flesh. This is most false, for the Word was a subsistent person before he was made flesh; he was in the beginning, with God, God was working and reigning, and this is impiously denied. But, he says, Luke 1 says that God will give him (he had not given it before) the throne of David his father, and he will reign on it; he did not reign before. This is what they call a fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, and it is double: both statements were true, but not in the same respect, nor always about the same time. The Father had given, and was going to give; the Son had reigned, and was going to reign. The Father had given according to his divine person, and was going to give to the same person according to the flesh he would assume. The Son of God had reigned according to his divinity, and was going to reign according to his humanity, in fact and in manifestation of the kingdom. He had reigned always, at every time, according to his person; afterwards he was going to reign also according to the flesh. These two things do not contradict each other. Yet Samosatenus, by the same skill, or rather lack of skill, sets them against each other as contraries, as he sets the divine nature against the human, the divine work against the human, the new creation against the old, as if these could never be together in one subject or proceed from one subject, namely the man [ἀνθρώπῳ]. Indeed, all very fine and clever! As for the other passage, Colossians 1, which he also twists miserably and cites clumsily, we spoke of it above in section 5. What more? He goes on in his opposition from Colossians 1 and Ephesians 1, and like the phoenix he seems to himself to live on in his own funeral pyre, claiming the creation of heaven and earth for the Father alone, and the renewal for the Son as made by the Father. Both claims are false, and he dreams of triumphs over the Son of God and over the truth from false premises, which we have already refuted. Clearly, the Father made the creation, therefore not the Son. False: for the work is so common that whatever the Father does, the Son does equally. Likewise, if I say the Son made the renewal, therefore not the Father. False: this work too is common, for the Son cannot do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it; as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. Into the same false opposition he falls back in his argument from Hebrews 9, laying down that the affirmation of one fact removes another, not as a contrary but merely as a different thing. Who would believe that a learned man argues like this, against reason and overturning the just laws of argument?

units.la: 5. Etsi hæc nihil ad rem præsentem, quia tamen de restauratione Angelorum imaginatur & nugatur quædam in Christum ipsum & in Angelos iniuria contumeliosáque, non potuimus quin bona fide Lectorem monceremus. Duæ hîc enunciationes falsæ sunt: vna, Angelos instauratione eguisse: altera, argumento Christi hoc dictum de Angelis confirmari. Prius nusquam Scriptura dicit: non instauratione eguerunt, Samosatene, Angeli electi (non enim lapsi sunt) non lapsis autem non est instauratio, sed dono perseuerantiæ, & confirmatione diuina in bono: quod bonum in creaturis omnibus est natura mutabile, nisi a Deo sustentetur & subsistat in Deo. Mediatore ergo Angeli, ac non Redemtore; conseruatore, ac non instauratore eguerunt quod in Enchiridio ad Laurentium & alibi Augustinus optimè declarauit. Hîc verò quis ferat diuinaculum dicentem ista? Angelica natura lapsu priorum Angelorum forte erat imminuta.
units.tr: 5. Although these points have nothing to do with the matter at hand, still, since he imagines and babbles certain things about the restoration of the angels, to the injury and insult of Christ himself and of the angels, I could not help warning the reader in good faith. Two statements here are false: one, that the angels needed restoration; the other, that this saying about the angels is confirmed by an argument from Christ. The first is nowhere said in Scripture. The elect angels did not need restoration, Samosatenus, for they did not fall; and for those who did not fall there is no restoration, but the gift of perseverance and divine confirmation in good. This good is by nature changeable in all creatures, unless it is sustained by God and subsists in God. The angels therefore needed a Mediator, not a Redeemer; a preserver, not a restorer. Augustine has very well explained this in the Enchiridion to Laurentius and elsewhere. But here who could bear a fanciful man saying such things? The angelic nature was perhaps diminished by the fall of the first angels.

units.la: Priorum, inquis? ergo tibi sunt priores & posteriores tempore: hoc Scriptura non dicit. Deinde, forte erat imminuta, coniectura est, somnium: non augentur, minuuntur ue spiritales formæ, vt fit elementaribus. Tum imminuta lapsu aliorum: multo minus. nam si horum natura nec augeri perse (nam perfectionem habet in creaturis summam) nec minui potest (nam qui minuti sunt, eorum minutio semel in totum facta est) quanto minus per alium? Postremo, vt lapsu Adami natura humana corrupta est, sic illos minui potuisse. Negatur: est enim dissimile, toto genere, totaque ratione differens. Posterius vero plus etiam habet periculi, quia salutem attingit, quum dicit eos restauratione eguisse, postquam illorum caput est Christus, postquam & Christus sine capite suo Patre nihil potest. Quorum caput est Christus, qui egent instauratione: Angelorum caput est Christus: ergo. Maior particularis est: nam contra quorum caput est Christus, eorum quidam egent instauratione, puta qui homines sunt, quidam vero sola confirmatione in bono, puta qui Angeli. Itaque Christum Angelorum caput & Mediatorem esse damus, at instauratorem vel Redemtorem minime. Falsa igitur conclusio. Sed verba illa ex Ioan. 5. detorta ad hunc sermonem sunt indignissime, Christum sine Patre nihil posse: de quorum iusta interpretatione diximus copiose Defensionis 2. segmento 9. & alibi. Nam primum hoc loco mutilantur, quod est inquisitum: deinde in alienum sensum a mente & consilio Christi rapiuntur, vt locus ipse clamitat: postremo res plane dissimilis est. Ex loco autem mutilo, male expostio, atque dissimili, quid concludas boni? Pergamus ad alia.
units.tr: The first angels, you say? Then for you there are first and later angels in time; Scripture does not say this. Next, perhaps diminished is a guess, a dream. Spiritual forms are not increased or diminished as elemental things are. Then, diminished by the fall of others: far less so. For if the nature of these angels can be neither increased of itself (since they have the highest perfection among creatures) nor diminished (for those who have been diminished, their diminution was made once and for all), how much less can it be diminished by another? Finally, just as the human nature was corrupted by the fall of Adam, so they could have been diminished. This is denied. For it is unlike, differing in the whole kind and in the whole reason. What he says next carries even more danger, because it touches on their salvation, when he says they needed restoration, since Christ is their head, since even Christ without his Father can do nothing. Those whose head is Christ, who need restoration; the head of the angels is Christ; therefore. The major premise is particular: for, against it, of those whose head is Christ, some need restoration, namely those who are men, while others need only confirmation in good, namely the angels. Thus we grant that Christ is the head and Mediator of the angels, but by no means their restorer or Redeemer. The conclusion is therefore false. But those words from John 5, Christ can do nothing without the Father, are most unworthily twisted into this argument. We have discussed their proper interpretation at length in section 9 of the second part of the Defence and elsewhere. For first, the passage is quoted in mutilated form, and that is the very question; then it is dragged into a sense foreign to the mind and purpose of Christ, as the passage itself cries out; finally, the matter is plainly unlike. What good can you conclude from a mutilated passage, badly expounded and not even similar? Let us go on to other things.

units.la: 6. Ex hoc autem loco sic lubet argumentari: Qui minorem gloriam non cedit alteri, neque communicat, non cedit maiorem: Deus minorem non cedit alteri: ergo nec maiorem. Tum, gloria recreationis maior est quam fit creationis gloria: Deus creationis gloriam non cedit Christo, neque communicat: nec recreationis igitur gloriam Christo cedit, neque communicat. eat. Est autem falsum consequens: & antecedens igitur sal-sum, quod a Samosateno affirmatur. De sequente autem oppositione & diuisione communium Patri & Filio operationum, quàm sit iniqua, & falsa, & impia, iam sæpius est demonstratum.
units.tr: 6. From this passage he likes to argue as follows: He who does not yield a lesser glory to another, nor share it, does not yield a greater; God does not yield a lesser glory to another; therefore neither a greater. Then: the glory of re-creation is greater than the glory of creation; God does not yield or share the glory of creation with Christ; therefore he does not yield or share the glory of re-creation with Christ either. Let it be so. But the consequent is false, and so the antecedent too is false, as Samosatenus affirms. As for the following opposition and division of operations common to Father and Son, how unfair, false and impious it is, has already been shown many times.

units.la: 7. Falsum, vel Samosateno teste. Nam si per sacrificia & effusionem sanguinis ad Deum adibatur, illa autem fuerunt sacramenta quorum corpus est in Christo: quis Patres illos neget in Testamento vetere Deum Patrem per Christum adiuisse? Promissionibus, inquiet, typis, præfigurationibus. Non satis: nam præsens erat Christus, Exod.23. & 33. & 34. & 1. Cor. 10, & per nomen eius invocabatur Pater, Psalm. 80. Dani.9. & alibi. Non siluit de hac re in vetere Testamento Deus: sed hic voluntariè surdus & cæcus est miserabili cæcitate, quam curet in suis Dominus ille curator noster.
units.tr: 7. This is false, even by the testimony of Samosatenus. For if men approached God through sacrifices and the shedding of blood, and these were sacraments whose body is in Christ, who would deny that the fathers in the Old Testament approached God the Father through Christ? By promises, he will say, by types, by foreshadowings. That is not enough. For Christ was present, Exodus 23, 33 and 34, and 1 Corinthians 10, and the Father was called upon in his name, Psalm 80, Daniel 9, and elsewhere. God did not keep silent about this in the Old Testament. But this man is willingly deaf and blind, with a wretched blindness which that Lord, our healer, must cure in his own.

units.la: 8. Sequentia omnia ab eadem oppositione sunt, quam falsam & inanem esse antè ostendimus. Quæcunque autem adfert testimonia, ad fallaciam sunt appositá, partim a dicto secundùm quid (vt vocant) ad dictum simpliciter, vt Actor. 1. Matth. 4. Hebr. 1. & 2. (nam quæ de Christo secundùm carnem his locis dicuntur, simpliciter attribuuntur personæ toti & de toto personæ prædicantur) partim elenchi ignoratione, vt Hebr.3. & 12. nam quæ de persona dicuntur vniuersè, ea speciatim ad carnem Christi & tempus illius restringuntur certo consilio, vt aboleatur indignissimè beneficium Christi. Sed has argumentationes passim, diserte vero supra segmento 3. refellimus.
units.tr: 8. All that follows rests on the same opposition, which we have already shown to be false and empty. As for the testimonies he cites, they are all turned to fallacy: partly by moving from what is said in a certain respect (as they call it) to what is said absolutely, as in Acts 1, Matthew 4, Hebrews 1 and 2 (for what is said of Christ according to the flesh in these places is ascribed absolutely to the whole person, and predicated of the whole person); partly by the ignoring of the point at issue (ignoratio elenchi), as in Hebrews 3 and 12 (for what is said of the person in general is deliberately restricted to the flesh of Christ and to his time, so that the benefit of Christ may be shamefully abolished). But we have refuted these arguments here and there, and expressly above, in section 3.

units.la: 9. Hinc transit ad absurda Samosatenus: qui secundus est probationum locus, si quid absurda probant. Mentirentur, inquit, Apostoli, Euangelistæ, Christus. Negatur. Nam horum consilium in Euangelijs & alibi fuit plurimùm, vt de rebus a Christo in carne gestis agerent: atque hoc proprium est historiæ Euangelicæ. Hoc vero mendacium iure dici non potest, si vere narratur quod narratur, quamuis inde a bouo nō instituatur principium eius. Quae secundum quid dicta sunt, ea simpliciter ne accipiantur: integra erunt omnia. At Christus, si creasset caelum & terram, non tacuisset illud. Primum ab auctoritate negatiue (vt loquuntur vulgo) nihil efficitur: no dixit hoc, non est igitur hoc: fieri enim potest, vt alius quispiam dixerit. Deinde vero falsum est quod dicitur, Christum sibi creationem communiter cum Patre non asseruisse. Asseruit enim, & eo ipso loco asseruit quem hic Samosatenus obijcit. Dicens enim, Pater meus usque adhuc operatur, & ego operor, tria demonstrat manifestissimé: se communiter operari cum Patre, diuinitus operari vt Patrem, & indesinenter ab omni tempore & ante omnia tempora operari vt Deum. Communiter operari se cum Patre ostendit, quum occasione vnius operis dicit, Pater operatur, & ego operor: diuinitus operari vt Patrem, quum dicit praesente tempore (quod tempus est in Scripturis de deitate proprium, vt cui omnia sunt praesentissima) operatur, operor, qua de re supra segmenti 4. nota 11. aliquid diximus: indesinenter denique ab omni tempore & ante omnia tempora operari demonstrat dicens, vsque adhuc: nam ad illud vsque momentum siue terminum temporis se operatum quum dicit, se inquam & Patrem, attribuit sibi cum Patre omnium temporum antecedentium operationem. Quod si mentem Christi a nobis Samosatenus non vult cognoscere, saltem a Iudaeis audiat. Studebant enim, ait Ioannes, Christum trucidare, quia non solum soluebat sabbathum, sed & Deum dixisset Patrem suum, aequalem se faciens Deo. Singula haec senserunt Iudaei, Christum operari cum Patre, diuinitus operari, indesinenter ab omni tempore operari, denique per omnia Patri aequalem esse. Senserunt, inquam, Iudaei, ac non crediderunt: stupidior illis Samosatenus nec credit, nec sentit. Ergo, inquit, dixisset Christus, vt Pater operabatur creando, ita & ego operabar. Fallum: nam primùm non fuit hypothèsis de creatione, de qua si tum disertè specia-tímque dixisset Christus, responsuri fuissent Iudæi, nos de aliis, tu de cæpis loqueris: sed ex hypothesi optimè & conuenienter ad thesin assurgitur. Deinde verò de toto affirmat Christus, dicendo, vsque adhuc. Non est autem Samosatenus nescius, Quod tribuitur vel adimitur toti in quantitate, idem cuiuibet eius parti tribui vel adimi. Ergo & in creatione Christus operatus est cum Patre cō-muni operatione. At Christus tantùm, inquit, operum no-uæ creationis meminit. Negatur: nam omnia vniuersalia Christus enunciat quæ vnquam enunciari possunt, vsque adhuc, quæcunque, omnia, pariter. hæc communem æter-nitatem, vniuersitatem, æqualitatem sonant: vnitatem autem essentiæ demonstrat necessariò non solùm Patris & Filii appellatio, sed etiam operationum æqualitas. At de præsente dicit, de præteritis tacet. Negatur: nam præsente quidem tempore enunciat, sed de perpetuo, vt coniuncta vox, vsque adhuc, ostendit manifestò. Est autem præsens tempus simpliciter proprium deitatis, & summè proprie de ea enunciatur, vt segmento 4. ante docuimus. Falsa igitur restrictio.
units.tr: 9. Next Samosatenus turns to absurdities, which form the second line of his proofs, if absurdities prove anything. "The apostles, the evangelists, and Christ," he says, "would be lying." This is denied. For the purpose of these men in the Gospels and elsewhere was chiefly to tell of the things Christ did in the flesh, and this is the proper character of the Gospel history. Nor can it rightly be called a lie, if what is narrated is truly narrated, even though its beginning is not taken from the very start. What has been said in a certain respect must not be taken absolutely, and then all will be whole. But "Christ, if he had created heaven and earth, would not have kept silent about it." First, nothing follows from an argument from silence (as they commonly say): he did not say this, therefore it is not so; for it may be that someone else said it. Second, it is false that Christ did not assert that he shared the work of creation with the Father. For he did assert it, and he asserted it in the very passage which Samosatenus here objects to. For when he says, "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work," he shows three things most plainly: that he works in common with the Father, that he works divinely as the Father does, and that he works without ceasing from all time and before all times, as God. That he works in common with the Father he shows when, on the occasion of one work, he says, "The Father worketh, and I work." That he works divinely as the Father he shows when he says in the present tense "worketh, work" (which tense is proper to the Scriptures when speaking of the deity, since all things are most present to it); on this point we said something above, in section 4, note 11. Lastly, that he works without ceasing from all time and before all times he shows when he says "hitherto": for when he says that he, and the Father, have worked up to that moment or limit of time, he ascribes to himself, together with the Father, the working of all the times that went before. But if Samosatenus does not wish to learn the mind of Christ from us, let him at least hear it from the Jews. For, says John, "they sought to kill Christ, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God." The Jews understood each of these things: that Christ works with the Father, that he works divinely, that he works without ceasing from all time, and in short that he is equal to the Father in all things. They understood, I say, and did not believe; Samosatenus, more stupid than they, neither believes nor understands. "Therefore," he says, "Christ would have said that, as the Father was working by creating, so I was working too." False: for first, there was no question of creation, and if Christ had then said this expressly and particularly, the Jews would have answered, "You speak of other things, we of creation." But from the question the argument rises very well and fittingly to the thesis. Second, Christ affirms it of the whole, saying "hitherto." Now Samosatenus is not ignorant that what is attributed to, or taken away from, the whole in its totality is attributed or taken away from each of its parts. Therefore Christ also worked in creation together with the Father in a common work. But, he says, "Christ mentions only the works of the new creation." Denied: for Christ states all the universal words that can ever be stated, "hitherto," "whatever," "all things," "likewise." These words speak of a common eternity, universality and equality; and the unity of essence is necessarily shown not only by the names Father and Son, but also by the equality of their operations. "But he speaks of the present and is silent about the past." Denied: for he does speak in the present, but of what is perpetual, as the joined word "hitherto" plainly shows. The present tense is in itself proper to the deity, and is most properly predicated of it, as we taught above in section 4. The restriction is therefore false.

units.la: 10. Hoc aliud absurdum insidiosè dictum: Si Christus secundus creator esset, non tacuissent de eo Prophetæ omnes: Tacent autem. Maioris antecedens insidiosum est: Christus enim proprie nec secundus creator, nec secundus Deus appellatur: est enim vnus Deus, creator vnus, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, essentiæ vnitate: sed appellatur secunda persona deitatis vel essentiæ illius vnicæ, quam appellamus Deum. Minor omnino falsa est: quæ singulis fermè capitib. Esaiæ Prophetæ inde a capite 40. sæpius reuincitur. Sed de hoc alias. Quòd si opera instaurationis Prophetæ de Christo prædicarunt, non magis ex eo sequitur Christum non esse creatorem mundi communiter cum Patre, quàm si ex eo quòd hodie dicor ambulare, vellet quis concludere me igitur heri non vigilasse: adeò friuola & inanis oppositio est, vt ante demonstrauimus. Omnia certè sunt ab uno diagrammate, indocto tamen & futili. Postremò autem sequitur summa verè ἀλογίστως syllogismos qui antè positi sunt in unum contrahens arte & veritate pari, quam hactenus reteximus. Nam ex eo quòd Christus caro factus & ex Maria natus est secundùm carnem, concludit non ante fuisse, ne secundum personam quidem illam diuinam quæ erat in principio, & apud Deum, & Deus. Ex eo quòd Deus per ipsum his nouissimis temporibus nos alloquutus est, negat ante per eum loquutum esse. Ex eo quòd Sermo in novo Testamento dicitur (etsi dicitur etiam in vetere, vt ante docuimus) negat fuisse mediatorē veteris, contraquàm affirmat Paulus Rom.15. Galat.3. & alibi. Ex eo quòd Euangelistæ de Christo opera nouæ creationis descripserunt, negat opus creationis primæ ad Christum pertinere. Ex eo quòd Deus signa per illum dicitur edidisse, id est, Pater per Filium, negat Filium esse Deum, per singularem terminum operandi cupiens tollere vnitatem essentiæ. Ex eo quòd Christus vetat sibi credi, si quid a seipso loquitur aut facit, respiciens ad hypothesin Iudæorum ex specie hominis & studio suo de ipso iudicantium, seque illorum captui accommodans; concludit simpliciter ipsum non esse Deum. Ex eo quòd bene omnia fecisse dicitur signis contestantibus, concludit ergo signa tantum fecisse & creationem nouā. Ex eo quòd creationis cœli & terræ ipse non meminit, statuit non ergo eorum creatorem esse. Ex eo quòd gratiam & veritatem per ipsum factam docuit Euangelista, arguit nō ergo subftan-
units.tr: 10. Here is another absurdity, cunningly put: "If Christ were a second creator, all the prophets would have said nothing about him. But they do say nothing." The major premise is cunning: for Christ is properly called neither a second creator nor a second God. There is one God, one creator: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, in unity of essence. But he is called the second person of the deity, or of that one essence which we call God. The minor premise is altogether false, and it is refuted again and again almost in every chapter of the prophet Isaiah from chapter 40 onward. But of this elsewhere. And if the prophets foretold of Christ the works of restoration, it does not follow from this that Christ is not the creator of the world together with the Father, any more than if someone wished to conclude from the fact that I am said to walk today that I therefore did not stay awake yesterday. So empty and trivial is the opposition, as we showed before. All these things are certainly drawn from one diagram, an unlearned and worthless one. Lastly, he sums up the syllogisms set out above, reasoning in a manner truly irrational, with an art and a truth equal to what we have so far unravelled. For from the fact that Christ was made flesh and born of Mary according to the flesh, he concludes that he did not exist before, not even according to that divine person which was in the beginning, and with God, and was God. From the fact that God has spoken to us in these last times through him, he denies that he spoke through him before. From the fact that the Word is said in the New Testament (although it is said also in the Old, as we taught above), he denies that he was the mediator of the old covenant, contrary to what Paul affirms in Romans 15, Galatians 3 and elsewhere. From the fact that the evangelists described the works of the new creation in Christ, he denies that the work of the first creation pertains to Christ. From the fact that God is said to have shown signs through him, that is, the Father through the Son, he denies that the Son is God, desiring by a singular term of operating to remove the unity of essence. From the fact that Christ forbids himself to be believed if he speaks or acts of himself, looking to the Jews' supposition, formed from his appearance as a man and from their own zeal in judging him, and accommodating himself to their capacity, he simply concludes that he is not God. From the fact that he is said to have done all things well, with signs attesting it, he concludes that he did only signs and a new creation. From the fact that he himself makes no mention of the creation of heaven and earth, he decides that therefore he is not their creator. From the fact that the evangelist taught that grace and truth were made through him, he argues that therefore the substances and creatures were not made from the beginning by him.

units.la: Mar.7. substātias & creaturas principio ab ipso fuisse factas. Quorum pleraque (si ab ijs quæ ad carnem necessario pertinent discesseris) eodem iure & argumentationis modo de Patre prædicari possent: Gratiam & veritatem facit Pater (facit enim per Filium, vt Samosatenus agnoscit) non ergo fecit substantias, nec creauit omnia. & similia multa. Sed quia hæc omnia fermè sigillatim fuerunt ante confutata, & imbecillitas harum argumentationum cuiuis homini (qui mediocri iudicio præditus est) per se est expósita, non fumus in his rebus immoraturi diutius, sed Deum oraturi, vt imperitorum iudicia instituat, peritorum confirmet, vt in veritate ipsius possint fide & conscientia bona ex testimonijs verbi diuini constanter incedere ad gloriam ipsius, & alij alios ædificare in charitate Christi Seruatoris nostri. Eorum autem omnium quædam epitome in Manuscripto est. Cùm itaque nihil insuper eo contineatur quàm quod priore exemplari expressum est atque a nobis confutatum, ad alia, Deo auctore & duce, examinanda veniamus.
units.tr: Mark 7. Most of these (if you set aside what necessarily pertains to the flesh) could be predicated of the Father by the same right and the same mode of arguing: grace and truth are made by the Father (for he makes them through the Son, as Samosatenus acknowledges), therefore he did not make substances, nor create all things; and many similar things. But since almost all of these have been refuted one by one before, and the weakness of these arguments is in itself plain to anyone endowed with moderate judgment, we will not dwell on these matters any longer, but pray God to instruct the judgments of the unskilled, to confirm those of the skilled, so that they may walk steadfastly in his truth, in faith and a good conscience, from the testimonies of the divine Word, to his glory, and that they may build up one another in the charity of Christ our Saviour. A certain summary of all these things is in the manuscript. Since, therefore, nothing more is contained in it than what was set out in the earlier copy and has been refuted by us, let us come, God being our author and guide, to examine other matters.

units.la: SAMOSATENVS. 8.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 8.

units.la: In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum.
units.tr: In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

units.la: De eodem Christo ex Maria nato loquitur Ioannes, ostendens vitam hominum in eo stare. Qui enim in Christum credit, habet vitam æternam: qui vero non credit, non videbit vitam, & luce omni destitutus in tenebris degit, Ioan. 3. Loquitur ergo hic non de vita temporali, sed de æterna, vt 1. Ioan. 5. exponit dicens, quoniam vitam æternam nobis dedit Deus, & hæc vita in Filio eius est. Sic alias, vt Pater habet vitam in semetipso, ita dedit Filio vitâ habere in semetipso, vt & ille viuificet quos vult. Sic Christus ille homo vocat se viam, veritatem, & vitam, Ioan. 14. æternus ista de se ante hunc non dixit. Quod autem ad vitam animalem attinet, Paulus testatur Deum eam omnibus dare, & halitum; in ipso nos viuere, moueri & esse: cui vita etiam & habitationi in terra terminos praestituerit Deus. Quemadmodum ergo aliis titulis descripsit nobis Christum Dei filium ex Maria natum, non aliquem ante Mariam: ita quoq; & hoc titulo summo pingit eundem, cum in eo sit vita omnium, nemo praeter ipsum, & omnes per ipsum saluentur. Ille ipse est vita, ille habet verba vitae aeterna, ipse est panis vitae. Aeterno autem alicui Christo non homini nusquam ista tribuit Scriptura. Lucem quoque illum vocat, quia vt vivificat, ita & illuminat. Ille enim Christus homo de se testatur dicens, Ego sum lux mundi: qui me sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris: quamdiu fuero in mundo, lux sum mundi. Hanc lucem in tenebris lucentem tenebrae non apprehenderunt; immo eam fugiunt; ob hancque lucem spretam, quae venit in mundum, condemnationem esse iustam Ioannes asserit. Hunc titulum etiam Esai. 42. vt & Lucas cap. 2. Christo homini tribuit quum lux Gentium vocatur. Certum est autem eam lucem non lucere, neq; apprehendi, nisi ab haeredibus vitae: positurum enim se dicit Deus Christum in lucem, quia lux non fuit.
units.tr: John speaks of the same Christ born of Mary, showing that the life of men lies in him. Whoever believes in Christ has eternal life, but whoever does not believe will not see life, and, deprived of all light, walks in darkness (John 3). So he is not speaking here of temporal life but of eternal life, as he explains in 1 John 5: "God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son." Likewise elsewhere: as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself, so that he may quicken whom he wills. So Christ, that man, calls himself the way, the truth, and the life (John 14); the eternal one never said this of himself before he became man. As for animal life, Paul testifies that God gives it to all, and breath; in him we live, move, and have our being; and God has appointed the bounds of life and of our dwelling on earth (Acts 17). Just as Scripture describes Christ with other titles as the Son of God born of Mary, and not as someone before Mary, so too it paints him with this highest title: in him is the life of all, no one but he, and all are saved through him. He himself is life; he has the words of eternal life; he is the bread of life. Scripture nowhere ascribes these things to an eternal Christ who is not man. He is also called light, because as he gives life, so he also gives light. For Christ the man testifies of himself, saying, "I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness; as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world" (John 8). "The light shines in darkness, and the darkness has not grasped it"; rather, the darkness flees from it. John asserts that because this light was scorned when it came into the world, condemnation is just. Isaiah 42 and Luke 2 also ascribe this title to Christ the man, when he is called a light to the Gentiles. It is certain, however, that this light does not shine on, nor is it apprehended by, anyone except the heirs of life; for God says he will set Christ as a light, because there was no light before.

units.la: M. S. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum.
units.tr: M. S. In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

units.la: CHRISTVS vita dicitur, quia credentibus vitam dat aeternam. In hanc sententiam Christus ipse loquutus est, quum dixit, ego vitam aeternam do eis, & non peribunt in aeternum. Lux similiter dicitur, qui hominum mentes Euangelij praedicatione illustrat. Non intellexit ergo de vita naturali, de qua argutantur Philosophi, sed de vita qua Deus in nobis viuit per Christi Euangelium, vt ab ipso, per ipsum, & in ipso viuamus. Dictio, erat, refertur ad tempus conuersationis quam in carne gessit: nec aliud sonat haec dictio, erat, quam dicitur de Ioanne, Erat homo missus a Deo: item, non erat ille lux: sic, Baptista erat lucerna. Eodem modo vita est, vt lux: & sicut fuit lux mundi mundi quamdiu fuit in mundo, ita fuit vita quamdiu fuit in mundo.
units.tr: Christ is called life because he gives eternal life to believers. Christ himself spoke to this effect when he said, "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish" (John 10). He is likewise called light, because by the preaching of the gospel he illuminates the minds of men. So he did not mean natural life, about which the philosophers dispute, but the life by which God lives in us through the gospel of Christ, so that we live from him, through him, and in him. The word "was" refers to the time of the conversation which he had in the flesh. This word "was" means no more than when it is said of John, "There was a man sent from God," and again, "He was not that light," and "John was a lamp." In the same way, life is like light: just as he was the light of the world as long as he was in the world, so he was life as long as he was in the world.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: PRo instituto Samosatenus pergens primùm Christum hominem, siue ex Maria natum, nominat æquiuocè, vt persónæ æternæ illi diuinæ opponat humanam, & ex positione (vt loquuntur) naturæ vnius statuat remotionem alterius. Itaque (vt semel moneamus) in peccatum triplex hoc modo incidit. Primum est, quòd Christum hominem capriosè dicit pro humanitate Christi, cùm alioquin abstracta a concretis differre optimè Logici tradiderint. Secundum, quòd ex natura humana facit personam: id quidem certo consilio, sed contra veritatem. Nam Christus Θεάνθρωπος, Deus & homo, persona est, quæ persona æternùm est secundùm deitatem suã: natura verò humana, nunquam fuit nisi ἐνυπόστατος, inexistens in persona (vt loquuntur vulgo) ne ad momentum quidem. Tertium denique, quòd ex eo quòd dat Christum hominem esse, inconsequente argumentatione per oppositionem statuit non ergo æternum esse Deum essentialiter: quem errorem segmento 5. & 7. perspicuè cõfutauimus. His falsis hypothesibus superstruit huius loci & sequentium interpretationem: quapropter deinceps, quum idem incidet, huc sumus reiecturi. Duas autem illas enunciationes ab Euangelista positas ordine enunciat, sed eodem modo; nempe spiritualiter: quia nõ placet ipsi Christum Deum essentialiter, id est, Deum æternum appellari. Id autem vt assequatur, priori membro, In ipso vita erat, adtexit glossema suum, dicens, vita hominum. Hæc restrictio non est ab Euangelista: negamus. Non negamus vitam æternam in Christo esse: sed negamus esse hanc loci huius mentem. Cur negemus, ante segmento 2. & 3. aperte ostendimus, a cōsilio Euangelistæ, a perpetuo orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ consensu, a rei natura quæ agitur, a conditione loci, & similium comparatione. Cur autem de vita illa creante, sustentante, gubernante, ordinante, agente cuncta & singula vniuersè & particulariter non intelligatur? nam eam ipsam, vel Samosateno teste, Deus creaturis omnibus dare pro modo earum dicitur esse, subsistere, moueri, viuere in rebus creatis sunt indiuidualiter: in Deo communiter, velut in principio cōmuni omnium. In Deo ergo vita est: annuet Samosatenus. Christus est Deus: & hoc annuet. Ergo in Christo vita: de principio vitæ, a quo ad creaturas omnes vita communiter pertinet, negaturus est: de vita spirituali, dabit. Atqui plus est vita spiritualis illa quàm hæc temporaria, plus est illius quàm huius donatio, vt ipse proximè præcedente segmento confessus est. Ineptissimum. Atqui, mi homo, quæcunque hic prædicantur, absolutè prædicantur, conuenienter naturæ Dei. Si vita, omnis vita: Est autem in Christo vita: ergo omnis vita. Non est autem omnis vita, nisi in Deo: Christus ergo Deus. Si non est Deus, non est in ipso absolutè vita. Si est Deus, in ipso vita: si in ipso vita, Deus est. Demonstratio est necessaria, & termini ἀνλσροι, vt causæ efficientis semper agentis liberrimæ, & effectus eius perpetui. Video quid affectes, Samosatene: sed veritatem in simplicitate colimus: & quia Christus essentiales Dei proprietates per se in se habere dicitur (vt hoc loco vides, vtrouis modo vitam acceperis) Deum essentialiter Christum esse in sua persona agnoscimus. Vtramque vitam Christus in se habet: tu tollis alteram, quam tamen inferiorem esse altera confiteris. Quæ (malum) dementia est, vita digniore concessa personæ Christi, altera eripere quæ cum illa non sit dignitate comparanda? An hæc magis Dei quàm illa est? Sed ad cætera.
units.tr: To pursue his purpose, Samosatenus first calls Christ the man, born of Mary, by an ambiguous term, so as to set the human person against that eternal divine person, and by positing, as they say, the one nature he establishes the removal of the other. So (to warn once for all) he falls into a threefold error in this way. First, he says capriciously that "Christ the man" means the humanity of Christ, although logicians have taught very well that abstract terms differ from concrete ones. Second, he makes a person out of human nature: he does this deliberately, but against the truth. For Christ, God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], is a person, who is eternally a person according to his deity; but the human nature has never existed except as subsistent in a person [ἐνυπόστατος], as they commonly say, not even for a moment. Third, from the fact that he grants that Christ is man, he concludes by a faulty argument of opposition, "therefore God is not essentially eternal." We clearly refuted this error in sections 5 and 7. He builds his interpretation of this passage and the following on these false hypotheses; therefore, when the same error recurs, we shall refer back here. He states those two propositions set down by the evangelist in order, but in the same way, namely spiritually, because he does not wish Christ to be called God essentially, that is, eternal God. To achieve this, he adds his gloss to the first clause, "In him was life," saying "life of men." This restriction is not from the evangelist; we deny it. We do not deny that eternal life is in Christ, but we deny that this is the meaning of this passage. Why we deny it, we have shown clearly before in sections 2 and 3: from the intention of the evangelist, from the constant consensus of the orthodox Church, from the nature of the matter treated, from the context of the place, and from comparison with similar passages. But why should that life which creates, sustains, governs, orders, and acts on all things, universally and particularly, not be understood? For that very life, even by Samosatenus's own testimony, is said to be given by God to all creatures according to their kind: they exist, subsist, move, and live in created things individually, but in God commonly, as in a common principle of all. In God, therefore, there is life, Samosatenus will agree. Christ is God, he will agree to this too. Therefore in Christ there is life. He will deny this regarding the principle of life, from which life pertains commonly to all creatures; he will grant it regarding spiritual life.
