Yet that spiritual life is greater than this temporal life, its gift is greater than the other, as he himself confessed in the immediately preceding section. Most absurd! Yet, my friend, whatever is predicated here is predicated absolutely, and in a manner fitting the nature of God. If life, then all life. But there is life in Christ; therefore all life. But there is all life only in God; therefore Christ is God. If he is not God, there is not life absolutely in him. If he is God, then life is in him; if life is in him, he is God. The demonstration is necessary, and the terms are unlimited [ἀνλσροι], as with an efficient cause that always acts most freely, and its effect that is perpetual. I see what you aim at, Samosatenus; but we cultivate the truth in simplicity, and because Christ is said to have the essential properties of God in himself by himself (as you see in this passage, whichever way you take the life), we acknowledge that Christ is essentially God in his own person. Christ has both kinds of life in himself; you remove the one, though you confess that it is inferior to the other. What madness (for shame!) is it, having granted the more worthy life to the person of Christ, to snatch away the other, which cannot be compared with it in dignity? Is this more God's than that? But let us go on to the rest.

units.la: Lucem esse Christum eodem modo interpretatur, id est, spiritualem lucem ad vitam æternā. Quis negat? sed de hac non agitur simpliciter. Agitur de principio æterno lucis: Deus autē est lux, ait Ioannes, & tenebræ non sunt in illo: principium æternum lucis, lux essentialis, lucem rebus creatis fœnerans. Sed hoc principio posito, concludo, vt antè: Christus est Deus: & lux igitur. Si non hoc, nec illud: sin autem hoc, etiam illud. Negat Samosatenus? Quisquis negat, hunc & naturæ Dei, & diuinarum operationum dignoscendarum nescium oportet esse. Est enim causæ necessariæ semper agentis liberrimæ non impeditæ effectus necessarius: & ab hoc necessaria ad efficientem causam ipsius regressio. Ab hoc principio lux communicatione in humanum genus fusa est, primùm naturalis, integra, & obtenebrata, de qua in hoc versu: deinde gratiosa, tum oblata, sequente versu, tum percepta, versu 12. Hanc simplicissimam interpretationem Samosatenus dum fugit, tenebras luci conatur offundere, & ordinē fidelissimum lucis comitem in hoc capite conturbat imperitissimė. Sed de ordine, supra segmento 2. de luce, segmento 3. antehac diximus.
units.tr: Samosatenus interprets "Christ is light" in the same way, that is, as spiritual light leading to eternal life. Who denies it? But this is not the whole matter. The point at issue is the eternal principle of light: "God is light," says John, "and in him there is no darkness" (1 John 1). The eternal principle of light is essential light, lending light to created things. But once this principle is granted, I conclude as before: Christ is God, and therefore light. If not this, then not that; but if this, then that too. Does Samosatenus deny it? Whoever denies it must be ignorant of the nature of God and of how to recognise his divine operations. For the necessary effect of a necessary cause that always acts most freely and is not hindered is itself necessary, and from this effect there is a necessary regression back to the efficient cause. From this principle the light was poured out to the human race by communication: first natural, whole, and darkened (of which in this verse); then gracious, offered in the following verse, and then received (verse 12). While Samosatenus flees from this most simple interpretation, he tries to pour darkness over the light, and most unskilfully disturbs the most faithful order, which accompanies the light in this chapter. But we have spoken of this order above: concerning the light in section 2, and concerning the order in section 3.

units.la: Sed quando quidem Christum lucem spiritualem esse inter nos conuenit, & lucem illam veram; mirari satis non possum, cur Christum æternum esse neget, immò ante fuisse quàm conceptus esset in vtero virginis Mariæ. Nam si lux erat, si erat lux hominum, si in tenebris luxit, si illuminat omnem hominem venientē in hunc mundū, nemo lucem habuit nisi ab illa luce: Pij autem in testamento vetere habuerunt lucem: ergo ab illa luce. Est autem lux illa Christus: ergo a Christo habuerunt. Videns Samosatenus incommodum istud inexpugnabile, exceptionem commētus est, nempe lucem esse ab aduentu ipsius. Hanc exceptionem (falsam tamen, qua Deitatem Christi turpiter oppugnat) duobus modis voluit confirmare: primùm quòd lux Gentium appellatur: deinde quòd Deus prædixit se positurum esse Christum in lucem. Prior confirmationis locus concludit ex particulari: supponit enim idē genus oppositionis quod antè confutauimus:lux Gentium est, non ergo Iudæorum: lux noui Testamenti est, non ergo veteris. Si diceret Deus, lux Gentium solùm, Samosatenus vicisset, vt putat vicisse. Aliter Deus loquutus est. Posterior locus nihilo est firmior: nam ab accidente, siue ab actu & adiacente aduentitio concludit de esse subiecti, contra omnes naturæ & Logicæ leges; & de substantia ex accidente iudicat. Hoc verò argutari, non argumentari est. Sed vt Samosatenum molestia liberemus, age ex Esaia probationem certissimam & luculentissimam, quę dictum ipsius euertat, afferamus. Qui lux gentium datus est, olim diu fuerat Iudæorum lux, erecturus tribus Iacobi, & custoditos Israelitas reducturus: Christus lux gentium datus est: olim ergo diu ante fuit lux Iudæorum. Est enim æternus pastor & lapis Israelis, quem lapidem reprobauerunt ædificatores, & factus est caput anguli. Vt autè ante est lapis quàm structores ædificent, ita suppositum, id est, personam Christi ante fuisse constat, quàm caput anguli his temporibus vltimis efficeretur. Antè esse subiectum quàm carnem sumserit ostendimus: nimirum personam Christi: hoc autem effecto, quid restat quàm vt Samosatenus cedat, manumque porrigat veritati? Fac, o Deus veritatis, propter nomen tuum, per veram illam Lucem quæ erat in principio, & omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum a principio illuminat. De verbo autem, erat, segmento 2. suprá.
units.tr: But since it is agreed among us that Christ is the spiritual light, and that true light, I cannot sufficiently wonder why he denies that Christ is eternal, and indeed that he existed before he was conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary. For if he was light, if he was the light of men, if he shone in darkness, if he enlightens every man coming into this world, then no one has had light except from that light. But the godly under the Old Testament had light; therefore they had it from that light. Now that light is Christ; therefore they had it from Christ. Seeing that this difficulty could not be overcome, Samosatenus devised an exception, namely that the light came from his coming. He tried to confirm this exception (false, yet by which he shamefully attacks the deity of Christ) in two ways: first, because he is called the light of the Gentiles; second, because God foretold that he would place Christ for a light. The first proof of this confirmation concludes from the particular, for it assumes the same kind of opposition that we refuted earlier: "He is the light of the Gentiles, therefore not of the Jews; he is the light of the New Testament, therefore not of the Old." If God had said only "the light of the Gentiles," Samosatenus would have won, as he thinks he has won. But God spoke otherwise. The second proof is no firmer: from an accident, or from an act and an adjacent, adventitious thing, it concludes concerning the being of the subject, against all the laws of nature and of logic, and it judges the substance from the accident. This is not reasoning but quibbling. But that we may free Samosatenus from his trouble, come, let us bring forward from Isaiah a most certain and most clear proof that overturns his statement. "He who was given as the light of the Gentiles was long ago the light of the Jews, about to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved Israelites; Christ was given as the light of the Gentiles; therefore long ago, long before, he was the light of the Jews." For he is the eternal shepherd and the stone of Israel, the stone which the builders rejected and which has become the head of the corner. Just as the stone exists before the builders build, so it is plain that the person of Christ existed before he was made the head of the corner in these last times. We have shown that the subject existed before he took flesh, namely the person of Christ; and once that is granted, what remains but that Samosatenus should yield and stretch out his hand to the truth? O God of truth, for your name's sake, grant that through that true Light which was in the beginning, and which from the beginning enlightens every man coming into this world, [we may be led]. As for the word "was," see the preceding section above.

units.la: M. S.
units.tr: M. S.

units.la: SAMOSATENVS. 9. Et lux in tenebris lucet,& tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 9. And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

units.la: MERITO homines huius seculi tenebræ vocantur, quòd sine Christo vera luce nihil prorsus earum rerum cognoscant quæ ad salutem pertinent. Animalis homo enim non percipit quæ Dei sunt.Quòd verò Iudæi tam salutiferam non comprehenderint salutem, in causa fuit illorum ingratitudo, propter quam & grauissimè punientur, iuxta illud, Hoc est iudicium, quòd lux venit in mundum, & dilexerunt magis homines tenebras quàm lucem.
units.tr: RIGHTLY are the men of this age called darkness, because without Christ, the true light, they know absolutely nothing of those things which pertain to salvation. For the natural man does not perceive the things of God. But that the Jews did not comprehend that saving salvation was owing to their ingratitude, on account of which they will also be punished most severely, according to that saying: This is the judgment, that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.

units.la: Fuit homo missus a Deo, cui nomen Ioannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de luce, ut omnes per eum crederent.
units.tr: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for a witness, that he might bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him.

units.la: AD probationem manifestationis huius tam præclari luminis ponitur hic testimonium Ioannis Baptistæ, qui publicè testificatus est non de lumine aliquo substantiali ac æterno in Christo, ut multi falsò interpretantur, sed solummodò de spirituali vitali lumine Euangelij ipsius, ut ex progressu historiæ liquidò apparet. Vocat enim Christum Spiritus baptizatorem, ac Agnum Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, Christum, ac Dei Filium, &c.
units.tr: TO prove the manifestation of this so excellent light, the testimony of John the Baptist is here set forth, who publicly testified not concerning some substantial and eternal light in Christ, as many falsely interpret, but only concerning the spiritual, living light of his own Gospel, as is clear from the progress of the history. For he calls Christ the Baptizer with the Spirit, and the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, Christ, and the Son of God, etc.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: ETsi vera est simpliciter prioris loci interpretatio quam Samosatenus attulit, tamen ea in re peccatum est non mediocriter, quòd eam historiâ obscurat plane qua narratur quid mundus gesserit inde a principio, quamuis luce diuina Christi in viam revocatus, cùm naturæ ordinariis & extraordinariis testimonijs, de quibus Paulus in Actis, tum Verbi gratiosis. Sic ordinem rerum luculentissimum peruertit de industria, ut suo illi commento seruiat quod antè confutauimus, & ex vniuersali dicto facit particulare contra Ioannis mentem, & veritatis rerumq; gestarum ordinem hoc in loco instítutum.Cætera suo loco relinquimus. Huic autem incredulitati communi obiecit Deus remedium potentissimum, lucem Euangelij: cuius manifestationem & complementum iā olim promissum exspectatúmque coepit demonstrare ex facto per Ioannis Baptistæ prædicationem aducntu Christi in carne,id est, essentialis æternæque illius lucis quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, vt proximè præcedente segmento demonstrauimus. Hoc falsum interpretamentum Samosatenus vocat, dicēs agi de spirituali vitaliq; lumine Euangelij ipsius:hoc est, non hic agi de essentiali luce, sed de effectu illius. Atqui accidentia non sunt sine subiecto: nec igitur sine subiecto operatur. Tum,prout sunt operationes,ita est subiectum operans:hæc operatio diuina est:& subiectum igitur diuinum. Diuinum est, inquit,communicatione operationum, ac non essentiæ. Respondeo, quod diuinum est communicatione solum operationum,id nō habet res diuinas in seipso: Christus habet vitam, ac proinde res diuinas in seipso, vt ipse confirmat Ioan. 5. non ergo Deus est, aut diuinus communicatione solum. Si non communicatione solummodo operationum, ergo essentiâ Deus est. Sed de hac re plura in præcedente segmento. Confirmaturus suam illam distinctionem luminis,duo adducit probationum genera,progressum historiæ,& nomina attributa Christo. Progressus historiæ plane contrarium ostendit. Nam Ioannes missus est ad parandum viam Iehouæ: Christus ergo Iehoua. Christus lux vera est diuinitus:essentialis igitur. Illuminare omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum est Dei solius opus: Christus illuminat omnem hominem: ergo Deus, & quidem essentialiter. Sic sequentia omnia. Falsum igitur, quod de progressu historiæ ostentat. De nominibus iudicium idem. Baptizare spiritu opus deitatis est, est, essentialis deitatis: Christus baptizat spiritu, ac non minister ullus: Christi ergo quis esse neget essentialem Deum? Tum nemo tollit peccata cuiusquam, multo minus totius mundi, nisi Deus sit essentialiter: Christus autem tollit peccata mundi: Deus igitur: Non Deus, inquit, sed agnus Dei. Vtrumq;, inquam ego, & agnus Dei, & Deus in personae vnitate: Deus tollens peccata, essentiali virtute: agnus tollens peccata, corporis sui instrumento. Sed hic rursum impingit Samosatenus festiua illa oppositione sua, quam centies ante refellimus. Quod addit Christum, quasi dicat, Christus est siue vnctus, non igitur Deus: ab eadem falsa oppositione est: nam idem vngens & vnctus est, vt optime Damascenus loquitur, vngens deitate, vnctus humanitate sua. Lepidum vero illud est, quod obijcit Filium Dei appellari, vt probet non esse Deum. Atqui est Filius Dei vnigenitus, solus generatione Filius naturaque, non autem adoptione, regeneratione, & gratia: Filius est singulari modo, non communi, vt nos sumus. Est autem singularis filiationis modus (vt ita loquamur) generatio. Ex eo autem ita concludimus: Qui pater est gignit Filium essentia vnum, aequalem similemque persona: Deus Pater genuit Filium vnigenitum suum: est ergo Filius essentia vnus cum Patre, persona aequalis & similis Deo Patri suo. Hoc natura docet, quod nulla ars aut cauillatio potest reuincere. Est igitur Christus lux vera, verus Deus, & vita aeterna.
units.tr: Although the plain interpretation of the former passage which Samosatenus has brought forward is true, yet he has erred not a little in this matter, in that he obscures by his narrative the history which plainly relates what the world did from the beginning, though it was called back into the way by the divine light of Christ, both by the ordinary and extraordinary testimonies of nature, of which Paul speaks in the Acts, and by the gracious words of the Word. Thus he deliberately perverts the most clear order of things, so as to serve that fiction of his which we refuted before, and from a universal saying he makes a particular one, against the mind of John and against the order of truth and of the events recorded in this passage. The rest we leave for its own place. But against this common unbelief God has offered the most powerful remedy, the light of the Gospel, whose manifestation and fulfilment, long since promised and awaited, he began to show by the fact of John the Baptist's preaching and the coming of Christ in the flesh, that is, of that essential and eternal light which enlightens every man coming into this world, as we showed in the immediately preceding section. Samosatenus calls this interpretation false, saying that it is about the spiritual, living light of the Gospel itself; that is, he says that this passage is not about the essential light but about its effect. Yet "accidents are not without a subject; nor therefore does it operate without a subject. Moreover, insofar as they are operations, so there is an operating subject: this operation is divine; therefore the subject is divine." He says it is divine by communication of operations, and not of essence. I answer: that which is divine only by communication of operations does not have divine things in itself. Christ has life, and therefore divine things in himself, as he himself confirms in John 5; therefore he is not God, or divine, only by communication. If not only by communication of operations, then he is God by essence. But of this matter more in the preceding section. Intending to confirm his distinction of the light, he brings forward two kinds of proof: the progress of the history, and the names attributed to Christ. The progress of the history shows the very opposite. For "John was sent to prepare the way of Jehovah; therefore Christ is Jehovah." "Christ is the true light by divine nature; therefore essential." "To enlighten every man coming into this world is the work of God alone; Christ enlightens every man; therefore he is God, and indeed essentially." So all the following points. What he shows from the progress of the history is therefore false. The judgment on the names is the same. "To baptize with the Spirit is a work of deity, and of essential deity; Christ baptizes with the Spirit, and not any minister; who therefore could deny that Christ is essentially God? Again, no one takes away the sins of anyone, much less of the whole world, unless he is God essentially; but Christ takes away the sins of the world; therefore he is God." "Not God," he says, "but the Lamb of God." I say both: both the Lamb of God and God, in the unity of the person: God taking away sins by essential power, the Lamb taking away sins by the instrument of his body. But here again Samosatenus stumbles upon his witty opposition, which we have refuted a hundred times before. What he adds, "Christ," as if he were saying, "Christ is either anointed, therefore not God," rests on the same false opposition: for the one anointing and the one anointed are the same, as Damascene speaks excellently: anointing by his deity, anointed by his humanity. And that charming point is what he objects, that he is called "Son of God," to prove that he is not God. Yet the Son of God is the only-begotten, the Son alone by generation and by nature, and not by adoption, regeneration, and grace; he is Son in a singular manner, not in the common manner in which we are sons. And the singular mode of sonship (so to speak) is generation. From this we therefore conclude: "He who is a father begets a Son one in essence with him, equal and similar in person; God the Father begot his only-begotten Son; therefore the Son is one in essence with the Father, equal in person and similar to God his Father." Nature teaches this, which no art or quibble can overturn. Christ therefore is the true light, true God, and eternal life.

units.la: M. S. SAMOSATENVS. 10.
units.tr: M. S. Samosatenus, 10.

units.la: Non erat ille Lux vera, sed missus fuit vt testaretur de luce.
units.tr: He was not the true Light, but was sent to bear witness of the Light.

units.la: ERAT quidem & Ioannes lucerna ardens, vt infra cap. 5. legitur, idque non tam propter maximam vitae sanctitatem, quam quod Christum veram lucem vel ad digitum demonstrabat: sed tamen non erat ipsa lux vera, quae Euangelij praedi-
units.tr: Indeed John too was a burning lamp, as is read below in chapter 5, and this not so much on account of his very great holiness of life, as because he pointed out Christ, the true light, with his finger. Yet he was not himself the true light, which by the preaching of the Gospel would illuminate men's darkened minds.

units.la: 44 catione tenebrosas hominum mentes illustraret. Proinde sequitur,
units.tr: 44 Hence it follows:

units.la: Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum.
units.tr: The true light was coming into the world, which enlightens every man.

units.la: Solus ergo Christus est vera lux illa quæ Euangelij prædicatione hominum mentes a tenebris ignorantiæ Dei liberat, ac in veram resurrectionis vitæque æternæ lucem ac certam spem traducit. Quod autem hic dicitur Christum illuminare omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, tripliciter intelligi potest: Primum, quod quotquot ex hominibus huius mundi illuminantur ad vitam illam æternam, nō aliunde illuminentur quàm per Christi Euangelium: Secundo, quod per omnem hominem intelligat omnis generis homines: nempe quod non sit personarum acceptator, sed æque illuminet gentes atque Iudæos, tam doctos quàm indoctos, tam ignobiles quàm nobiles, tam fœminas quàm masculos, tam seruos quàm dominos, &c. iuxta illud Christi, quum exaltatus fuero, traham omnia ad me. Tertio, textus aliter legi potest; hoc nempe modo, Lux veniens in hunc mundum illuminat (spiritualiter scilicet) omnem hominem. Nam vox ista Græca, ἐρχόμενον, potest utrique accommodari, tam scilicet luci quàm homini. In hanc sententiam Christus ipse alibi dixit, Ego lux in mundum veni, ut omnis qui credit in me in tenebris non maneat.
units.tr: Christ alone, therefore, is that true light, which by the preaching of the Gospel delivers men's minds from the darkness of ignorance of God, and leads them into the true light and certain hope of the resurrection and of eternal life. As to what is said here, that Christ enlightens every man coming into this world, this can be understood in three ways. First, that as many of the men of this world as are enlightened to that eternal life are enlightened by no other means than through the Gospel of Christ. Second, that by "every man" he means men of every kind: namely, that he is no respecter of persons, but enlightens Gentiles and Jews alike, learned and unlearned, lowly and noble, women and men, servants and masters, and so on, in accordance with that saying of Christ, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself." Third, the text can be read in another way, in this manner: the Light coming into this world enlightens (spiritually, of course) every man. For that Greek word, ἐρχόμενον [coming], can be applied to either: that is, to the light as well as to the man. Christ himself said to this effect elsewhere: "I have come into the world as a light, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness."

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXVS.

units.la: PERTEXENS Samosatenus telam quam orsus est, Christum veram lucem esse pronunciat, quamuis non essentialem lucem: quod sanctè confirmauimus. Hoc discrimine posito, ferri possunt reliqua, præterquam huius membri interpretatio, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Nam quia hoc membrum vidit causæ suæ & commento obfuturum, posita signi vniuersalis æquiuocatione, aut etiam ambiguo, putauit se huic incommodo facile occursurum. Hoc illi incommodū est, quòd ita arguimus: Lux vera illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum: ergo nullum hominem non illuminat. Tum, homines autem fuerút inde a creatione: ergo lux vera inde a creatione illuminat. Vtrumque autem opus non est nisi veri Dei, qui Deus sit & lux sit essentialiter: Christus ergo, verus Deus, vera lux & essentialis est. Hæc declinare sibi Samosatenus videtur bellissimè adducta vocis, omnis, æquiuocatione, aut phrascos amphibolia. Aequiuocatione: nā omnis aut de toto in quantitate dicitur (prout nos accipimus) aut de communi quod totū in modo vocāt, pro eo quod est quiuis, ex quocunq; genere, cuiuscunq; modi: & ita Samosatenus, vt illi verissimæ argumentationi illudat. Sed nihil efficit hac distinctione sua. Nā quisquis illuminatur, illuminatur a luce: nemo homo non illuminatur: a luce igitur. Negat Samosatenus, quia hic agitur de spirituali luce, quę non est omnium. Primum falsam distinctionē esse hanc (suprà ostendimus segmento 9. & seq. Deinde spiritualis lux est instaurationis: ergo recum præcedente est eadem, quamuis modo & quantitate differens. Christus autem, vel Samosateno teste, est lux illa gratiosa instaurationis: ergo & lux naturæ est, quæ lux per nos amissa per eundem instauratur. Quòd si principium est vtriusque lucis (vt est) ergo illuminat omnem hominem (id est, non solum quemuis, sed quemque) venientem in hunc mundum. Sic vafritiei plus habet distinctio, quàm veritatis. Amphibolia vero adfertur duplex, a Grammaticis facile expedienda. Vna est καθ' ἑλλεψιν, illuminat omnem hominem, puta qui illuminatur: ellipsin non quidem inauditam, sed quæ non nisi ex necessitate summa adhiberi potest atque euidente: deinde quæ si recipitur, Ioannes pueriliter dicetur ταυτολογεῖν versu 11. & 12. quod vitium de Ioanne Euangelista ne iurati quidem omnes Samosatreni mihi persuaserint. Altera, καὶ συγχυσιν, quae tamen si obtineretur, ne pilum quidem Samosateni causam adiuuaret, quū ait vocem ἐρχόμενον cum nomine lucis aptari posse. Verū haec σύγχυσις admodum, violenta est nihil lucis orationi, nihil cōmoditatis ad rei intelligentiā, nihil deniq; opis ad causam Samosateniam adferēs: quo magis demirorab isto homine productam esse, vt inopiam magis sui iudicij, quàm inuentionis copiam (quod affectauit) ostenderet. Valeat igitur.
units.tr: Samosatenus, weaving the web he began, declares that Christ is the true light, though not an essential light; this we have soundly confirmed. With that distinction laid down, the rest may be let pass, except the interpretation of this clause, who enlightens every man coming into this world. For he saw that this clause would stand in the way of his cause and his invention, and he thought he could easily meet this difficulty by an equivocation in the universal sign, or even by an ambiguity. The difficulty for him is that we argue thus: The true light enlightens every man coming into this world: therefore it fails to enlighten no man. Then: But men have existed from the creation: therefore the true light has enlightened from the creation. Now this work belongs to none but the true God, who is God and light essentially: Christ, therefore, the true God, is the true light and is essentially so. Samosatenus seems to escape these conclusions by a very neat equivocation in the word omnis, or by an amphiboly in the phrasing. By equivocation: for omnis is said either of the whole in quantity (as we take it), or of the common, which they call the whole in mode, meaning whatever sort of thing, of whatever kind; and so Samosatenus mocks that most true argument. But he achieves nothing by this distinction of his. For whoever is enlightened, is enlightened by the light: no man is not enlightened: therefore by the light. Samosatenus denies it, because here the question is of spiritual light, which is not of all. First, this distinction is false (as we showed above in section 9 and following). Second, spiritual light belongs to the restoration: therefore it is the same as the preceding, though differing in mode and quantity. Christ, however, even on Samosatenus' own testimony, is that gracious light of restoration: therefore he is also the light of nature, which light, lost through us, is restored through the same Christ. But if he is the source of each light (as he is), then he enlightens every man (that is, not merely any man, but each man) coming into this world. Thus the distinction has more of cunning than of truth. The amphiboly, however, is alleged in two forms, which grammarians can easily dispose of. One is by ellipsis [καθ' ἔλλειψιν], he enlightens every man, that is, every man who is enlightened: an ellipsis not indeed unheard of, but one that can be admitted only from the greatest and most evident necessity; and further, if it were accepted, John would be said childishly to tautologize [ταυτολογεῖν] in verses 11 and 12, a fault which not even all the sworn Samosatenes could persuade me to attribute to John the Evangelist. The other is by confusion [σύγχυσιν], which, even if it were admitted, would not help Samosatenus' cause one hair's breadth, when he says the word coming can be joined with the noun light. But this confusion is very violent: it gives no light to the sense, no advantage to the understanding of the matter, and finally no help to the Samosatene cause. So much the more I marvel that this man put it forward, showing a lack of judgment rather than the abundance of invention which he aimed at. Let it stand, then.

units.la: SAMOSATENVS. II.
units.tr: SAMOSATENVS. II.

units.la: In mundo erat, & mūdus per ipsum factus est, & mundus eum nō cognouit. Ad sua venit, & sui eum non receperūt: Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, ijs qui credunt in nomen eius.
units.tr: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name.

units.la: MVNDVM hic vocat non cœli machinam & sphæras, sed homines. Quid enim hoc esset ad rem, Christum non esse cognitum a machina cœli & sphæris? Vox mundi apud Ioannem sæpe pro hominibus accipitur. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum daret, Ioan. 3. hominibus certè, nō sphæris cœlestibus. Sic non venit vt iudicet mundum, sed vt seruetur mundus per eum: Christus saluator mundi: tollit peccata mundi: dat vitam mundo & carnem pro mundi vita. In mundo ergo fuit, inter homines versatus est, & præcipuè inter Israelitas, quorum reformandorum & saluandorum causa primum venit. Christum autem ex Maria natum describit: nam illum æternum Christum confictum, inter homines versatum nusquam legimus. Qui ergo Christum venisse non in carne, sed ante carnem dicit, Antichristus est, 1. Ioan. 4. Intelligitur ergo de aduentu Christi, hominis videlicet in carne, in mundum. Sequentibus, Et mundus per ipsum factus est, de noua creatio- ne, vt audiuisti, loquitur. Per Christum enim nouus mundus sub nouo testamento, vt per Mediatorem noui testament, fa- bricatus est: docendo, quia fuit Verbum, magister, propheta: di- uinam vim in miraculis exercendo, quia Verbum fuit Deus: viuificando, quia fuit vita: & illuminando, quia fuit lux, Esai. 35. & 61. Lucæ 4. describuntur opera Christi, euangelizare pau- peribus, sanare infirmos, cæcos illuminare. Hæc est noui mun- di fabrica, & fabricatus nouus mundus a Christo: hæc est fa- brica, quam describunt omnes Euangelistæ, non Moses. Et ta- men hic fabricator summus huius mundi nō fuit agnitus, quia fuit vilis homo, caro, subiectus, despectus virorum. Quum esset in mundo, versaretúrque inter homines fabricans mundum, non agnoscebatur ab illo: quare & scandalizabantur in illo etiā discipuli eius, durum sermonem eius dicebant, deserebant eum, & Petrus etiam eum ter negauit, in illo principio nihil erat fir- mum in discipulis, & omnes discipuli fugerunt ab eo, & se solum esse desertum ab omnibus, Patre tantum excepto, dicebat.
units.tr: Here "the world" means not the machinery and spheres of heaven, but men. For what would it matter to the question that Christ was not known by the machinery of heaven and its spheres? In John the word "world" is often taken for men. So God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, John 3: certainly for men, not for the heavenly spheres. So he did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him: Christ the Saviour of the world; he takes away the sins of the world; he gives life to the world and his flesh for the life of the world. He was therefore in the world, he dwelt among men, and especially among the Israelites, for whose restoration and salvation he first came. But the one described is Christ born of Mary: for we nowhere read that the eternal Christ, fashioned in this way, dwelt among men. Whoever says that Christ came not in the flesh but before the flesh is Antichrist, 1 John 4. So it is to be understood of the coming of Christ, that is, of the man in the flesh, into the world. In the following words, "and the world was made through him," he speaks of a new creation, as you have heard. For through Christ the new world under the new covenant was fashioned, as through the Mediator of the new covenant: by teaching, since he was the Word, master and prophet; by exercising divine power in miracles, since the Word was God; by giving life, since he was life; and by enlightening, since he was light, Isaiah 35 and 61. In Luke 4 the works of Christ are described: to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the sick, to give sight to the blind. This is the fashioning of the new world, and the new world was fashioned by Christ; this is the fashioning which all the Evangelists describe, not Moses. And yet this chief maker of this world was not recognised, because he was a lowly man, flesh, subject, despised of men. When he was in the world, dwelling among men and fashioning the world, he was not recognised by them; wherefore even his disciples were scandalized at him, said that his saying was hard, forsook him, and Peter even denied him three times. At that beginning there was nothing firm in the disciples, and all the disciples fled from him, and he said that he was left alone by all, the Father alone excepted.

units.la: Quum autem esset glorificatus per resurrectionem, de- siisset q; versari inter homines, post Spiritum sanctum missum, amplior notitia eius & virtus se exeruit inter pios, quàm quum in mundo esset, vt ante audisti. Eo spectabat & illud Christi dictum, quum scandalizarentur in eo, vt vili, Quid si videri- tis (inquit) filium hominis (non aliquem alium) ascendentem vbi erat prius? Ioan. 6. hoc est, vbi hic filius hominis, qui vobis nunc sua vilitate est scandalum, exaltatus fuerit, seu demon- stratus Seruator mundi & Messias, per quem Deus omneus sal- uat, dederitq; ei illam gloriam Pater quam apud eum habuit ante mundi iacta fundamenta, vel in qua erat apud eum (dedit autem illi eam post resurrectionem locato in dextera) tunc tan- dem desinetis scandalizari: quod factum est in die Pentecostes. Exaltationem futuram obÿciebat vilitati suæ præsenti, præ qua non agnoscebatur a suis ad quos venit. Sicuti & Caiaphæ scandalt{z}ato in Christo vili, sed faciente interea se Filium Dei, quū scidit vestem, obȳcit illam exaltationem qua se filium hominis in nubibus cœli venturum cum maiestate sui asseruit.
units.tr: But when he was glorified through the resurrection, and had ceased to dwell among men, after the Holy Spirit was sent, his fuller knowledge and power showed themselves among the pious, more than when he was in the world, as you heard before. To this also looked that saying of Christ, when they were scandalized at him as a lowly man: "What if you should see the Son of man (not some other) ascending where he was before?" John 6. That is: where this Son of man, who now is a stumbling-block to you by his lowliness, shall have been exalted, or shown forth as the Saviour of the world and the Messiah, through whom God saves all; and the Father shall have given him that glory which he had with him before the foundation of the world, or in which he was with him (he gave it to him after the resurrection, when he was placed at the right hand); then at last you will cease to be scandalized. This came to pass on the day of Pentecost. He set the future exaltation against his present lowliness, by which he was not recognised by his own, to whom he came. Likewise Caiaphas, scandalized at Christ in his lowliness, yet while he was claiming to be the Son of God, tore his garment, and set against him that exaltation by which he asserted that he would come as the Son of man in the clouds of heaven with his majesty.

units.la: Quòd si vero quis de prima creatione hoc vellet intelligi, mundum hunc per illum factū, & illum fuisse in mundo olim, quod iam falsum esse ante probatum est: an non dicerent illi homines quos accusabat, quis nobis de Christo retulit quòd creauerit cœlos, vel fuerit ante mundum? Moses enim in creatione omnium de Christo tacuit. Christus etiam nullo verbo (etiamsi esset Verbum) se creatorem cœlorum esse patefecit: nam eum qui creauit omnia & Deum & Patrem suum esse, & verbis & reipsa testatus est. Frustra ergo quis hoc exprobrauerit illi populo.
units.tr: But if anyone wished this to be understood of the first creation, that the world was made through him, and that he was in the world long ago, which has already been proved false: would not those men whom he accused reply, "Who has told us about Christ, that he created the heavens, or was before the world? For Moses kept silent about Christ in the creation of all things. Christ too, in no word (even though he was the Word), revealed that he was the creator of the heavens; for he testified both by words and by deeds that the one who created all things is both God and his own Father." It would be in vain, then, for anyone to reproach that people with this.

units.la: Ioannes autem aliam creationem respiciens accusat Israëlitas, quòd quum venisset Christus ad eos sanandos, docendos, illuminandos, & suscitandos, tamen tenebræ, vbi luxit, eum non comprehenderunt, non fuit agnitus, nec receptus pro sua dignitate: a quibus vero fuit receptus, datam esse illis potestatem a Christo, vt essent filij Dei. Non leue illud beneficium Christus dedit, in quo eius summa prærogatiua & potestas accepta a Deo in mundo apparuit: nam hic Ioannes istius titulis prærogatiuam summam Filij Dei ex Maria nati tuetur, nequis leuis esse credatur. De æterno autem aliquo nihil somniat: qui nec fuit ante in mundo, nec docuit, nec miracula fecit, nec dedit potestatem cuiquam; cùm nec crederetur tunc in eum sub veteri testamento, sed expectabatur. Ioannis 14. quum ait, creditis in Deum, vt de re nota loquitur: & in me credite, vt qui non fui notus.
units.tr: John, however, looking to another act of creation, accuses the Israelites of this: when Christ came to heal, teach, enlighten and raise them up, yet "the darkness" did not "comprehend" him when the light shone; he was not recognised or received according to his dignity. Those who did receive him, John says, were given power by Christ to become the sons of God. Christ bestowed no small benefit here, and in it his supreme prerogative and the power he received from God appeared in the world. For here John, by the terms he uses, upholds the supreme prerogative of the Son of God born of Mary, lest he be thought of little account. But he dreams of no eternal being: one who was not previously in the world, who did not teach, perform miracles or give power to anyone, and who was not believed in under the Old Testament but was awaited. When he says in John 14, "You believe in God," he speaks of a known thing, as it were; and "believe also in me," as of one who was not yet known.

units.la: M. S.
units.tr: M. S.

units.la: In mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus est, & mundus eum non cognouit.
units.tr: He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world did not know him.

units.la: Hîc mundum per metonymiam pro huius mundi hominibus accipi nulli dubium esse debet. Est autem huius vocabuli frequens quens & multiplex vsus in Scripturis, & maximè apud Ioan-nem. Sed quantum ad præsentem locum attinet, sufficiet si no-scamus respectu diuersorum tripliciter accipi. Aliquando ergo in genere ac indifferenter pro hominibus tam renatis quàm nõ renatis vsurpatur: vt apud Matth.13. vbi Christus edisserens Zizaniorum parabolam dixit, ager est mundus: vbi evidenter apparet Christum mundi nomine bonos & malos huius mundi homines indifferenter comprehendisse. Aliquando pro regeneratis, ac spiritualiter per Euangelium renouatis; vt apud Paulum, Deus erat (inquit) in Christo mundum sibi reconci-lians: & Ioan 6. caro mea est, quam dabo pro mundi vita: & alibi, vt cognoscat mundus, quòd tu me miseris, & huiusmodi. nam ista verificari non possunt, nisi in solis regeneratis & electis. Tertiò pro non regeneratis & infidelibus: vt, væ mundo a scandalis: item, non pro mundo rogo, &c. cuius mundi alibi fit mentio, nunc princeps huius mundi eijcitur foras. Dum ergo Euangelista dicit, In mundo erat, perinde est ac si diceret, Christus versabatur inter homines huius mundi, qui mundus constat ex hominibus bonis & malis, ex fidelibus & infidelibus. Præterea dum dicitur, & mundus per ipsum factus est, nihil aliud infertur quàm si Ioannes dixisset, Homines isti qui nunc regenerati spiritualiterque renouati in Christi regno insunt: non aliunde id factum est, quàm beneficio Christiq. opera. Demum quum dicit, & mundus eum non cognouit, sensus erit, Homines autem qui mundo huic visibili sunt addicti eum non cognouerunt. Sed quia hoc paulo obscurius proposuerat, in hunc modum sese exponit, dicens,
units.tr: That "world" here is taken by metonymy for the people of this world is beyond doubt. This word is used in Scripture in many and varied ways, and especially by John. But as far as the present passage is concerned, it will be enough to note that, according to the different senses, it is taken in three ways. Sometimes it is used in general and without distinction for people both regenerate and unregenerate, as in Matthew 13, where Christ, explaining the parable of the tares, said, "The field is the world": where it is plain that Christ, by the word "world", included good and bad men of this world indiscriminately. Sometimes it means the regenerate, those spiritually renewed through the Gospel; as in Paul: "God was (he says) in Christ reconciling the world to himself"; and John 6: "my flesh is that which I shall give for the life of the world"; and elsewhere, "that the world may know that you have sent me," and suchlike. For these things cannot be true except of the regenerate and elect alone. Thirdly, it means the unregenerate and unbelieving: as in "Woe to the world because of offences"; likewise, "I do not pray for the world," etc.; of which world mention is made elsewhere: "now the prince of this world is cast out." So when the Evangelist says, "He was in the world," it is just as if he said that Christ lived among the men of this world, which world consists of good and bad men, of believers and unbelievers. Further, when it is said, "and the world was made by him," nothing else is implied than if John had said: those men who are now regenerate and spiritually renewed and dwell in Christ's kingdom owe it to nothing but the benefit and work of Christ. Finally, when he says, "and the world did not know him," the sense will be: those men, however, who are given over to this visible world did not know him. But because he had put this a little more obscurely, he explains himself in this way, saying:

units.la: Ad suos venit, & sui eum non receperunt: Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, ijs qui credunt in no-men eius.
units.tr: He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, even to those who believe on his name.

units.la: DECLARATIO est apertissimi superioris sententiæ,
units.tr: This is a plain explanation of the sentence above,

units.la: sed paulo commutato ordine ornatus gratia. Dum igitur Ioan-nes superius dixerat, in mundo erat: sic dicit, in sua venit, vbi obse quandum est ista verba Graeca, εἰς τὰ ἴδια, id est, in sua: quia etsi Christus missus est vt omnes seruet quantum in se est, tamē specialiter ad Iudaeos missus est, quod illius facta essent promissiones: ac si diceret, Christum veniendo ad Iudaeos venisse in domū suam. Sic enim alibi, quando Ioannes accepit Christi matrem in sua, eadem verba leguntur, εἰς τὰ ἴδια, in sua, habitatum in suā domum. Dum praeterea dixerat, & mundus per ipsum factus est, hic dixit, Quotquot autem eum receperunt, dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri. Demum vbi dixerat, & mundus eum non cognouit, hic habetur, & sui eum non receperunt.
units.tr: though with the order slightly changed for the sake of ornament. So when John said above, "He was in the world," he now says, "He came to his own"; here it must be noted that the Greek words are εἰς τὰ ἴδια, that is, "to his own things", because although Christ was sent to save all, so far as lies in him, yet he was sent especially to the Jews, since the promises were made to them: as if he said that by coming to the Jews he came into his own house. For elsewhere, when John takes the mother of Christ "to his own", the same words are read, εἰς τὰ ἴδια, "to his own", meaning into his own home. Further, where he had said, "and the world was made by him", here he says, "But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God." Finally, where he had said, "and the world did not know him", here it is put, "and his own did not receive him."

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXVS.

units.la: QVOD inde a principio huius capitis Samosatenus instituerat, vt sanctae huius grauissimaeq; narrationis ordinem conturbaret, in eodem consilio hic pergit diligentissime. Nec mirum: quia hoc nisi assequitur, omnino eorum quae captat nihil assequuturus est. Nam Ioannes ordinem ipsum naturae conuenientem persequens (vt ante segmento 2. & 3. docuimus) primum de rebus diuinis ad personam Christi in sese pertinentibus coeperat dicere: inde ad diuina opera eius erga res creatas descenderat, quorum alia in creandis rebus, alia in sustentandis & regendis sunt posita per vitam & lucem illius: quam primum naturae nostrae collatam, deinde (postquam amissa est) gratiose denuo operibus & sermone oblatam mundo narrauit Apostolus, turpissimeque inde a principio repudiatam ab hoc ingrato mundo. Nunc vero propter necessarium illud hyperbaton (quod distinctionis ergo commode interiectum est, versibus antecedentibus) regrediens Apostolus ad interruptam narrationem tionem suam, de oblata mundo luce amplius loquitur, eiusque a mundo repudiatae duos gradus ostendit, secundum rationem temporis & grauitatem facti optime ordinatos. Nam primum communitcr a mundo gratiam repudiatam exponit, hoc versu, deinde a gente Iudaeorum versu sequente, antequam ad tertium & vltimum genus manifestationis veniatur, nimirum in carne assumta personaliter: quae manifestatio facta est demum in temporum plenitudine, postquam opere & verbo diutissime omnes sollicitauisset. Hunc diuinum ordinem aeque imperite ac malitiose Samosatenus peruertens, prima cum medijs & media cum vltimis ita confundit, vt quisquis ordinem in explicatione eius quaesiuerit, oleum & operam (quod aiunt) miserè sit perditurus. Quod factum eo est indignius, quòd Euangelistae suauissimo, & grauissimo ordinis conuenientis (si quisquam est) typo hanc ἀλληγορίαν adfinxerit. Quod vel vnicum incommodum Samosateniani omnes si bene obseruarent, omnino a suis istis putidis commentis & cauillationibus abstinentes cederent diuinae veritati. Quam rem vt efficiat gratiosè Deus, oro & opto in Christo Iesu seruatore nostro. Pro eo quod igitur Apostolus ingratum hominum factum expositurus, resumtis argumentis antecedentium beneficiorū Christi, narrationem instituit ingrati animi tum omnium communiter, tum Iudaeorum singulariter, hic chimaeras & monstra supponit interpretationum. In mundo erat, inquit, id est, inter homines versabatur; & mundus per ipsum factus est, nimirum nouus: & mundus eum non cognouit. Atqui si nouus factus, quomodo non cognouit? Quid est Scripturae illudere, nisi hoc est? Haec sic interpretari, & ad carnem Christi ac tempus illius restringere, & argumento humanitatis naturam diuinam personae Christi tollere per ineptam illam oppositionem quam toties refellimus, nihil est aliud quàm veritatem salutémque voluntariè perdere falsarum interpretationum & fallacium argumentorum fuco. Lepida verò illa argumentatio est, quum Samofatenus dicit, Qui Christum venisse nō in carne, sed ante carnem dicit, Antichristus est, 1. Ioan. 4. Intelligitur ergo de aducntu Christi, hominis videlicet in carne, in mundum: quasi argumentetur ex maiore illa propositione hoc modo: Ioannes dicit Christum venisse: ergo venisse in carne dicit, ac non ante carnem: & contrà, vos orthodoxi ante carnem venisse dicitis: ergo Antichristi eftus. Maior ambigua, & falsa est, non Apostoli scribentis, sed huius argumentantis vitio. Ambiguitas duplex: vna in nomine Christi, altera in veniendi verbo. Chriftū enim personam illam diuinam, Sermonem illum intelligimus, qui erat in principio, erat apud Deum,& erat Deus,vt ante Ioannes loquutus est: Hic ψιλὸν hominem intelligit, qui tum primùm coepit esse, quum factus est caro ex virgine. Veniendi autem verbo singularem illam actionem intelligimus, qua se æternus ille Sermo adiunxit naturæ nostræ in vnitate personæ, & manifestum fiue confpicuũ in carne fecit: hic proceffionem a non esse(vt loquuntur) ad esse intelligit, tamquam fi Italico sermone,ac nō Græco Ioannes Euangelium suum conscripsisset. Nam apud Græcos inaudita est τᾶ ἐλθεῖν illa significatio, quicquid Samofatenus garriat. Falsum autē illud axioma est quod per oppofitionem (pro sua illa communi oppofitionum arte)hoc loco statuit, Qui Christum venisse ante carnem dicit, hunc Antichristum esse. Nam de Christo fecundùm personam agitur quæ æterna est, non de carne quam persona affumfit in tempore. Quòd fi quis diceret Christum in carne venisse ante carnem, merito exploderetur vt insani dictum: quis enim puer non videat illa esse contradictoria, nisi de carne per singularem dispensationem assumta(vt olim Christus & Angeli assumferunt) at non personaliter vnita alterum membrum intelligas? Sed persona Christi venisse dicitur, nō caro. Nam caro Christi siue humanitas,non est persona siue hypostasis, aut natura subsistens per se, sed natura est enhypostatos, inexsistens in persona, vt more Scholasticorum loquar. Atq; hæc diserte sua illa loquutione distinxit Ioannes, vt Samosateno ansam quam captat præcideret. Non enim carnem Christi venisse dicit (quod figuratū esset ἀνυπόλυ- λαγῆς dictum) non carnem Christum venisse siue hominem Christum (quod Apollinaristę sibi assumerent, & Samosatenus vsurpat) sed Christum, personam inquā Christi, venisse in carne, id est in humanitate assumta vnione personali, vt esset Immanuel, id est, nobiscū Deus, quod Prophetæ olim prædixerant: venisse inquam non mutatione loci in hunc mundum, non productione noua persone quæ ante non fuerit, non communicatione substantiæ, conuersione, aut confusione vlla, sed φανέρωσιν vel manifestatione personæ suæ diuinæ in carne, in qua factus est conspicuus qui in se est inconspicuus, vt loquitur Apostolus.
units.tr: Samosatenus, from the beginning of this chapter, set out to disturb the order of this holy and most weighty narrative, and here he continues with the same design most diligently. This is no wonder, since unless he achieves this he will certainly gain nothing of what he aims at. For John, following the natural order (as we showed before in sections 2 and 3), had first begun to speak of divine things pertaining to the person of Christ in himself; then he had come down to his divine works towards created things, of which some are placed in the creating of things and others in the sustaining and governing of them through his life and light. This light, first bestowed on our nature and then (after it was lost) offered again to the world by grace in works and in word, the Apostle has told of, and from the beginning it was shamefully rejected by this ungrateful world. But now, because of that necessary hyperbaton (which is conveniently inserted for the sake of clarity, in the preceding verses), the Apostle, returning to his interrupted narrative, speaks further about the light offered to the world, and shows the two stages of its rejection by the world, arranged very well according to the order of time and the gravity of the fact. For first he sets out in general the grace rejected by the world, in this verse; then, in the following verse, the rejection by the nation of the Jews, before we come to the third and last kind of manifestation, namely in the flesh assumed personally. This manifestation was made at last in the fullness of time, after he had long sought to move all men by work and word. Samosatenus, perverting this divine order as foolishly as maliciously, so confuses the first with the middle and the middle with the last that whoever seeks the order in his exposition will, as they say, lose his oil and labour miserably. This is the more shameful because he has fathered this allegory on the most sweet and most weighty pattern of the fitting order, if ever there was one. If all Samosatenians would observe this one drawback well, they would wholly abstain from their stinking inventions and cavillings and yield to divine truth. I pray and desire in Christ Jesus our Saviour that God may graciously bring this about. Therefore, since the Apostle, about to set forth the ungrateful deed of men, resumed the arguments of the preceding benefits of Christ and began a narrative of ungrateful minds, both in general of all men and in particular of the Jews, here Samosatenus supplies chimeras and monsters of interpretation. "He was in the world," he says, that is, he lived among men; "and the world was made by him," namely new; "and the world did not know him." But if it was made new, how did it not know him? What is this but mocking Scripture? To interpret these things in this way, and to restrict them to the flesh of Christ and his time, and by the argument of humanity to take away the divine nature of Christ's person through that foolish opposition which we have so often refuted, is nothing other than wilfully to lose truth and salvation by the paint of false interpretations and fallacious arguments. That argument is indeed a charming one, when Samosatenus says: "He who says that Christ came not in the flesh but before the flesh is Antichrist, 1 John 4. Therefore it is understood of the coming of Christ, namely of man in the flesh, into the world"; as if he argued from the major proposition in this way: "John says that Christ came: therefore he says that he came in the flesh and not before the flesh"; and conversely, "you orthodox say that he came before the flesh: therefore you are Antichrists." The major premise is ambiguous and false, and the fault lies not with the Apostle writing but with this arguer. The ambiguity is twofold: one lies in the name "Christ", the other in the verb "to come". For by "Christ" we understand that divine person, that Word who was in the beginning, was with God, and was God, as John said before; but Samosatenus understands a mere man, who began to exist when he was made flesh of the virgin. By the verb "to come" we understand that singular action by which that eternal Word joined himself to our nature in the unity of person, and made himself manifest or conspicuous in the flesh; but he understands a procession from non-being (as they say) to being, as if John had written his Gospel in Italian and not in Greek. For among the Greeks that sense of ἐλθεῖν is unheard of, whatever Samosatenus may chatter. Moreover, that axiom which he lays down here by opposition (according to his usual art of oppositions) is false: that he who says that Christ came before the flesh is Antichrist. For the question concerns Christ according to his person, which is eternal, not the flesh which the person assumed in time. If anyone should say that Christ came in the flesh before the flesh, it would rightly be rejected as the saying of a madman: for what child does not see that those are contradictory, unless you understand the flesh assumed by a singular dispensation (as Christ and the angels once assumed it), but not united with the person as another member? But it is said that the person of Christ came, not the flesh. For the flesh of Christ, or his humanity, is not a person or hypostasis, or a nature subsisting by itself; it is an enhypostatic nature, existing in the person, to speak in the manner of the Schoolmen. And John distinguished these things expressly in his phrasing, so as to cut off the occasion which Samosatenus seizes. For he does not say that the flesh of Christ came (which would be a figurative and ἀνυπόλυλαγῆς saying), nor that Christ's flesh or the man Christ came (which the Apollinarians took to themselves and Samosatenus uses); but that Christ, I say the person of Christ, came in the flesh, that is, in humanity assumed by personal union, so that he might be Immanuel, that is, God with us, as the prophets had foretold long ago. He came, I say, not by a change of place into this world, not by the production of a new person who had not existed before, not by a communication of substance, conversion or any confusion, but by the φανέρωσις, or manifestation, of his divine person in the flesh, in which he who is invisible in himself was made conspicuous, as the Apostle says. <context_after> </context_after>

units.la: Minor plane falsa est & cum veritate pugnas. Non enim hoc loco Ioannes dicit, In mundum venit: sed in mundo erat: Quumque dicit posteā, adsua venit, non dicit in carne venisse. Nam venit etiam aliter, & alio tempore, quàm in carne: sic falsa est ex particulari, siue ex distributo (vt vocant) argumentatio. Ac proinde quæcunque superstruuntur fundamento isti ex particulari & per elenchi ignorationem posito, ea nullas vires apud bonos merito habere possunt. Quid ergo ista sibi volunt, in mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus est? Nempe ingratum mundi animum in Christum Ioannes propositurus, duos amplissimos illos beneficiorum locos quos ante narrauerat summatim repetit ὕστερον πρότερον (qui ordo Hebraeorū est, memoriæ iuuandæ percommodus) vnum guberna-tionis, alterum creationis: quibus locis æquissimum fuerat homines adduci & rapi ad agnitionem Christi: in mundo erat (inquit) essentia, præsentia, potentiáque sua, regens omnia & sustinens verbo potente suo, vt Sermo æternus Patris apud Deum Deus: & mundus per ipsum factus est, id est, conditus creatusque in principio: quo iure, creationis inquâ & administrationis, mundus tenebatur omnino eum agnoscere, & non agnouit tamen. Sic & versus sequens. Sed hic nouus interpres occurrit dicens, non creationem mundi, sed instaurationem potius significari, quia per Christum nouus mundus sub Testamento nouo, &c. Quàm inconsequens sit hoc argumentationis genus, nouus mundus est per Christum, non igitur vetus per eundem est, ante ostendimus segmento 7. Nam ex particulari concluditur, & negatur diuersum, & tempora confunduntur, & ratio diuersa tollitur, quam in persona Christi necesse est obseruari: nam quà Deus, creauit mundum: quà mediator, instaurauit. Quis ex tot vitijs, obsecro, nectat bonam consequentiam? Hoc agnoscimus, a Christo nouas creaturas esse: quid hoc confitentibus, credentibus, acquiescentibus probari opus est? Sed hic Rhodus, hic saltus, quod aiunt, probari non esse a Christo creatio-nem omnium, quam simpliciter ex Ioanne & aliis haustâ in Ecclesia confitemur. De recreatione quam vocat, minimè contendimus, quam Christo Mediatori nostro ferimus acceptam: quæcunque ergo de ea commodè adferuntur, suo loco relinquimus. De creatione per Christum agitur. Quapropter hic artifex μιμητικῶς in suam scenam personas introducit, quæ probationes a nobis desiderent. Quod nemo docet, falsum est, inquiunt: Christum creauisse cœlos, aut ante mundum fuisse, nec Moses, nec Christus, nec quisquam docet: Falsum igitur. Minor planè falsa est. Nam creauisse cœlum & terram Moses narrat Deum Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctū, quem Elohim cap. 1. Iehouam Elohim, cap. 2. vocat̄ages de creationis argumento: Christus narrat Ioannis 5. vt ante segmento 7. docuimus. Ante mundum fuisse idē Moses per consequens narrat, qui mundum fecerit: Christus narrat Ioan. 17. quum se gloriam apud Patrem dicit habuisse prius quàm mundus esset. Quid? quòd vnicus ad Hebræos locus ex Testamento vetere vtrumque probat luculentissimè? Nam æternitatem primùm personæ, tum creationem ab eadem persona factam asserit his verbis, propositá Angelorum comparatione, De Filio verò dicit, Thronus tuus, o Deus, in seculum seculi: virga regni tui. Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea vnxit te, o Deus, Deus tuus oleo exsultationis præter consortes tuos. Et, Tu in principio, Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli. Ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes: & omnes vt vestimentum veterascent. Ac velut amictum circumuolues eos, & mutabuntur: tu verò idem es, & anni tui non deficient. Alia prætereà testimonia adferre possem: sed hæc pijs mentibus futura sunt satis: contentiosis ne sexcenta quidem studiū φιλονεικίας eximent. Atque hæc vniuersè de prioris scripti ad locum hunc interpretatione. Nunc ad singularia quædam excutienda veniamus. 1. Ad eumdem lapidem hic denuò offenditur, facta oppositione duarum naturarum in Christo: quæ, quia diuersæ, huic sunt visæ contrariæ & pugnantes inter se: vt bis aut ter etiam fit in hoc ipso loco. Sed de vanitate huius oppositionis iam dictum centies. 2. Hic ille ipse locus est, quem paulo ante ad demonstrandam æternitatem Christi protulimus: ab hoc autem interprete prolatum demirarer, nisi scirem ad mirabilem vim esse veritatis, quæ hanc confessionem huic homini expressferit. Hæc autem de manifestatione & demonstratione intelligi oportere ipsa verba Samosateni euincunt manifesto, quum ait, exaltatus fuerit, seu demonstratus seruator mundi, &c. Sic argumentatur: Qui alium quam se Creatorem omnium esse praedicat, se Creatorem negat : Christus Deum & Patrem suum Creatorem omnium testatur esse: Ergo se Creatorem negat. Maior ambigua est, & particularis: ex qua nihil iuste concluseris. Exempli causa, si quis alium quàm se dominum aedium, vel fundi esse dixerit, haec responsio duobus modis potest intelligi: nam aut alium secum dominum esse intelligit, si domus vel fundus communis est, neque se a communitate excludit; aut alium, non autem se, dominum esse intelligit, & excludit sese. Christus autem Deum & Patrem suum esse Creatorem pronunciat secundum rationem communis, non seipsum excludit ab illa communi operatione. Itaque nihil agit Samosatenus hac sua argumentatione. Quod autem Ioannes ad aliam creationem dicitur respicere, id ante negauimus, & falsi euicimus.
units.tr: The minor premise is plainly false and clashes with the truth. John does not say here, "He came into the world," but "He was in the world." When he says afterwards, "He came to his own," he does not say that he came in the flesh. Christ came in other ways and at other times too, besides coming in the flesh. So the argument from a particular case, or from a distribution (as they call it), is false. Whatever is built on this foundation, which rests on a particular case and on an ignoratio elenchi, can rightly have no force with good men. What, then, do the words "He was in the world, and the world was made by him" mean? Plainly John, about to set out the ungrateful attitude of the world towards Christ, briefly repeats the two very great benefits he had described earlier, in the order ὕστερον πρότερον [the later put first], which is the Hebrew order and very helpful for the memory: one is government, the other is creation. On these two points it was most fitting that men should be led and drawn to acknowledge Christ. "He was in the world" (he says), that is, present in his essence and power, governing all things and sustaining them by his powerful word, as the eternal Word of the Father, who was God with God. "And the world was made by him," that is, it was founded and created in the beginning. On the ground of both creation and governance, the world was wholly bound to acknowledge him, and yet it did not acknowledge him. The next verse is similar. But here this new interpreter steps in and says that "not the creation of the world, but rather its restoration, is signified, because through Christ there is a new world under the New Testament," and so on. How inconsequent this kind of argument is, namely, "The world is new through Christ, therefore the old world is not through the same Christ," we showed earlier in section 7. For a conclusion is drawn from a particular case, the opposite is denied, the times are confused, and a different aspect is removed, which must be observed in the person of Christ: for as God he created the world, as Mediator he restored it. From so many faults, I ask, what good consequence can be drawn? We acknowledge this, that new creatures come from Christ. Why does this need to be proved to those who confess, believe and assent to it? But here is the Rhodes, here the leap, as they say: it is not proved that the creation of all things is from Christ, which we simply confess as drawn from John and others and held in the Church. We do not at all contend about the re-creation, which he calls so, and which we bear as received from Christ our Mediator. Whatever is fairly said about it we leave in its own place. The question is about creation through Christ. Therefore this craftsman, mimicking, brings onto his stage characters who demand proofs from us. "What no one teaches is false," they say: "that Christ created the heavens, or was before the world, neither Moses, nor Christ, nor anyone teaches; therefore it is false." The minor is plainly false. For Moses narrates that God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (whom he calls Elohim in chapter 1, and Jehovah Elohim in chapter 2) created the heavens and the earth, and this is the argument of creation: Christ narrates it in John 5, as we showed before in section 7. Moses narrates by consequence that the one who made the world was before the world: Christ narrates it in John 17, when he says that he had glory with the Father before the world was. And what of the single passage in Hebrews, which proves both points most brilliantly from the Old Testament? For it asserts first the eternity of the person, and then creation by the same person, in these words, with the comparison of angels set out: "But of the Son he says, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom. Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands. They shall perish, but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old like a garment. And as a mantle thou shalt roll them up, and they shall be changed; but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail." I could bring other testimonies, but these will be enough for pious minds; not even six hundred would take contentious men away from their zeal for contention. So much in general on the interpretation of the earlier writing on this passage. Now let us come to examine certain particular points. 1. Here again they stumble on the same stone, by setting up an opposition between the two natures in Christ; because these are different, they seem to this man contrary and at odds with each other, as happens two or three times in this very passage. But the emptiness of this opposition has been said a hundred times already. 2. This is the very passage which we brought forward a little earlier to show the eternity of Christ. I should be amazed that this interpreter brought it forward, did I not know that there is a wonderful power of truth which drew this confession from this man. That these words must be understood of manifestation and demonstration is clearly proved by the very words of Samosatenus, when he says, "the Saviour of the world was exalted, or made manifest," and so on. He argues thus: "Whoever says that anyone other than himself is the Creator of all denies that he himself is Creator. Christ testifies that God, his Father, is the Creator of all. Therefore he denies that he himself is Creator." The major premise is ambiguous and particular, and nothing can rightly be concluded from it. For example, if someone said that anyone other than himself is the master of a house or an estate, this answer can be understood in two ways: either he means that another is master along with him, if the house or estate is common and he does not exclude himself from the community; or he means that another, and not himself, is master, and he excludes himself. But Christ declares that God, his Father, is Creator in the sense of a common function, and he does not exclude himself from that common operation. So Samosatenus accomplishes nothing by this argument of his. As for the claim that John is said to look to another creation, we denied that before and have shown it to be false.

units.la: Probaturus Christum nec aeternum esse, nec fuisse sub testamento vetere, tribus argumentis vtitur. Primum, Qui ante praedicationem Euangelij nec fuit, nec fecit quicquam, non est aeternus: Christus ante non fuit, nec fecit quicquam: non ergo aeternus est. Maiorem damus, minorem distinguimus. Christus ante no fuit secundum carnem, quàm plenitudo temporum aduenisset: at fuit Christus, seu persona Christi secundum diuinitatem aeternam, quae suo tempore induit carnem. Elenchus perpetuus est, ex quo conclusio falsa. Secundum, In quem non credebatur sub testamento vetere, is non erat: In Christum non credebatur: non erat igitur. Negatur minor: nam in Christum credidisse Patres sub testamento vetere, vel solus Dauid Psal. 2. & 16. & 45. & 102. & 110. docet apertis verbis, & Christus Apostolique confirmarunt. Tertium, Qui exspectabatur, nondum erat
units.tr: Wishing to prove that Christ is neither eternal nor existed under the Old Testament, he uses three arguments. First: "He who was not before the preaching of the gospel, and did nothing, is not eternal. Christ was not before, nor did he do anything; therefore he is not eternal." We grant the major premise and distinguish the minor. Christ was not before, according to the flesh, until the fullness of time had come; but Christ, or the person of Christ, according to his eternal divinity, did exist, and at his time he put on flesh. The argument is a perpetual elenchus, from which the conclusion is false. Second: "He in whom men did not believe under the Old Testament did not exist. In Christ men did not believe; therefore he did not exist." The minor is denied: for the Fathers under the Old Testament believed in Christ, and David alone teaches this in plain words in Psalms 2, 16, 45, 102 and 110, and Christ and the apostles confirmed it. Third: "He who was looked for did not yet exist"

units.la: Ioan. 8. Rom. 10. Hebr. 1. erat: Christus exspectabatur: Nondum igitur erat. Maior ambigua est: nam qui exspectabatur, aut futurus exspectabatur, aut venturus: futurus, si non erat; venturus, si non aderat. Christus autem exspectabatur, non futurus tum primum (erat enim) sed venturus in carne, secundum modum illum patefactionis qui exspectabatur. Falsa igitur conclusio: nam etsi non erat Christus secundum carnem, erat tamen secundum veritatem personae suae. His argumentationibus positis, Samosatenus quasi extra se raptus, ad aliam anchoram confugit, nempe ad notitiam Christi, quod non fuerit notus. Hoc autem quorsum, si certo constabat ipsi non fuisse Christum? Nam de eo qui non est, nec adhuc fuit, nemo dicit non esse notum, cum ne sit quidem. Dum vult iste homo subtilis esse, subtilitate diffluit. Deinde verbis Christi indigne abutitur ad istud suum commentum confirmandum. Nam Christus Apostolos his verbis compellans non agit de notitia illa communi, aut etiam singulari notitia fidei, ut eam tamquam prius ignoti habeant: noverant enim Christum, & fide aliqua noverant, ut verbis illis Petri demonstratur lotionem pedum a Christo recusantis: sed de confirmatione agit illius fidei aduersus scandalum crucis proxime obventurum: quemadmodum illa Christi verba vincunt manifestissime, ne turbetur cor vestrum: quibus illico subjicit, credituris in Deum, etiam in me credite. Quae cum ita sint, eo tantum pertinet haec interpretatio a Samosateno allata, ut ipse suo iuguletur gladio, cum haec euertat illam, & a Scriptura sacra potentissime vicissim euertatur.
units.tr: John 8, Rom. 10, Heb. 1. "...existed: Christ was looked for; therefore he did not yet exist." The major premise is ambiguous: for what was looked for was either going to be, or was coming. It was going to be, if it did not exist; it was coming, if it was not yet present. But Christ was looked for, not as one who was then about to be for the first time (for he already was), but as one coming in the flesh, according to that manner of manifestation which was looked for. The conclusion is false: for although Christ did not yet exist according to the flesh, he did exist according to the truth of his person. Having put forward these arguments, Samosatenus, as if carried out of himself, flees to another anchor, namely the knowledge of Christ, "that he was not known." But what does this mean, if it was clearly certain to him that Christ had not existed? For no one says that someone who is not, and has not yet been, is unknown, since he is not even at all. While this clever man wants to be subtle, he dissolves in subtlety. Then he shamefully abuses the words of Christ to confirm his own invention. For Christ, addressing the apostles in these words, is not speaking of that common knowledge, or even of the particular knowledge of faith, as if they had it before not knowing him: for they did know Christ, and knew him with some faith, as Peter's words show when he refused to have his feet washed by Christ. Rather, he speaks of the confirmation of that faith against the scandal of the cross which was about to come upon them very soon, as those words of Christ most clearly show: "Let not your heart be troubled," to which he immediately adds, "You believe in God; believe also in me." These things being so, this interpretation brought forward by Samosatenus serves only to make him be slain by his own sword, since it overthrows that interpretation and is itself most powerfully overthrown in turn by holy Scripture.

units.la: Altera interpretatio maiorem subtilitatē sectata, argumento quidem eadem est, sed modo interpretationis differens. Non contendam utrum haec metonymia, an synecdoche dicenda sit, ubi pars pro toto, vel totum pro parte sumitur: viderint Grammatici. Sed insignis est audaciæ,an impudentiæ?quòd vnico in versu, eóque per-breui, treis mundi significationes statuit: in mundo erat, nempe inter homines: & mundus per ipsum factus est, nempe hominū renouatorū & regeneratorū, per Spiritum & mundus eū nō cognouit, nempe hominū animaliū, qui mū-do huic visibili addicti sunt. Vt nō disputē quàm bene adferatur ista mūdi interpretatio; quàm alienū est, sic vno in loco ludi vnius vocis æquiuocationibus? Vel hic ipse interpretationis modus infirmitatē harū interpretationū arguit. Quid ergo est, in mundo erat? nempe essentia, præ-sentia, potentiaq; inerat mundo, vt verus illeDeus in quo vita erat & vita erat lux hominum. Quid, mundus per ipsum factus est? nempe creata mundi vniuersitas potentia diuina iplius, non exclufoPatre & Spiritu sanéto, vt qui sunt vnum, & operationem vnam efficiunt cõmuniter. Quid, & mundus eum non cognouit?nempe neipsi quidem mundi incolæ, quos lux illa communis hominum ad cognitionem ipsius prouocabat. Nam illud, non cognouit, priuationis est: hìc ergo demū restringitur mundi nomen ad eam partem mundi quam lux illa prouocabat, & cui habitus cognitionis fuerat inditus. Talia enim subiecta sunt, qualia permittuntur esse a prædicatis suis dexterè intelle&is. Sic non variat mundi significatio, sed tantùm postremo membro per synedochen communis ex necessitate prædicati restringitur. Hæc simplex interpretatio est, & euidente argumento: quia duo illa cõmunia Christi in mundum beneficia, gubernationis, inquam, siue prouidentiæ & creationis, plurimùm indignitatem humanæ istius ἀγνοίας siue ignorationis Dei & Christi amplificant.
units.tr: The other interpretation, pursuing greater subtlety, agrees with the first in substance but differs in its method of interpretation. I will not argue whether this should be called metonymy or synecdoche, where a part is taken for the whole or the whole for a part; let the grammarians decide. But it is a remarkable instance of audacity, or rather of impudence, that in a single verse, and a very short one, he sets up three meanings of "world": in the world he was, namely among men; and the world was made through him, namely of the renewed and regenerated men, through the Spirit; and the world did not know him, namely of the natural men who are devoted to this visible world. Leaving aside how well this interpretation of "world" is supported, how foreign is it to play with the equivocations of one word in one place? This very method of interpretation shows the weakness of these interpretations. What then is meant by, he was in the world? Namely, his essence, presence and power were in the world, as that true God in whom was life, and the life was the light of men. What is meant by, the world was made through him? Namely, the whole created universe by his divine power, not excluding the Father and the Holy Spirit, who are one and commonly effect one operation. What is meant by, and the world did not know him? Namely, the inhabitants of the world themselves, whom that common light of men summoned to a knowledge of him. For the words, did not know, express a privation. Here, then, the name "world" is finally restricted to that part of the world which the light summoned and into which the habit of knowledge had been implanted. For the subjects are such as their predicates, rightly understood, allow them to be. Thus the meaning of "world" does not vary, but only in the last clause is the general term restricted by synecdoche through the necessity of the predicate. This is a simple interpretation, and the argument is evident, because those two common benefits of Christ toward the world, namely his governance or providence, and creation, greatly magnify the unworthiness of that human ignorance [ἀγνοίας] or non-knowledge of God and Christ.

units.la: Cætera suo loco relinquimus; si duo exceperis. Vnum est, quod singulari applicatione confundit quodammodo historiam communem mundi cum singulari historia Iudæorum: quod malum tamen aliquo pacto, non satis, corrigit. Alterū, quòd Christum missum esse dicit, vt omnes seruet quantum in se est: quod ambiguè dictum voluissem ab eo amplius explicari. Non enim ignotum est, vocem, omnes, vniuersaliter, communiter, aut distributiuè accipi: & illud genus loquutionis quantum in se est, de Christo Filio Dei Deoque vero enunciatum non carere periculo, nisi commodè distinguatur in hoc argumento. Sed ad alia pergamus.
units.tr: I leave the rest to its proper place, except for two points. One is that he somehow confuses the general history of the world with the particular history of the Jews, a fault which is not sufficiently corrected in any way. The other is that he says Christ was sent so that he might save all, as far as lies in him; I would have wished this ambiguously stated matter to be explained more fully by him. For it is not unknown that the word "all" is taken universally, commonly, or distributively; and that this kind of expression, "as far as lies in him," said of Christ the Son of God and true God, is not free from danger unless it is carefully distinguished in this argument. But let us move on to other matters.

units.la: M. S. SAMOSATENUS.
units.tr: M. S. SAMOSATENUS.
