units.la: Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neq; ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt.
units.tr: Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

units.la: Hoc loco Ioannes Iudæorum supercilium retundit, qui gloriabantur se originem duxisse ab Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Iacobo. Concludit ergo nihil momenti habere in regno Christi, sed regeneratione vitæque nouitate opus esse.
units.tr: Here John breaks the pride of the Jews, who boasted that they had their origin from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He therefore concludes that this has no weight in the kingdom of Christ, but that regeneration and newness of life are needed.

units.la: ORTHODOXUS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: Hæc quoque nota probatur nobis, licet non plena sit loci interpretatio.
units.tr: This note also we approve, although the interpretation of the passage is not complete.

units.la: SAMOSATENUS.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS.

units.la: Et Verbum caro factum est, vel
units.tr: And the Word was made flesh, or

units.la: Et Verbum caro fuit.
units.tr: And the Word was flesh.

units.la: Qui Græcè norunt, vocem ἐγένετο norunt significare idem plerumque quod fuit, vt sit sensus, Christus ille, qui erat Verbum, Dei proloquutor seu interpres, & spiritu sine mensura vnctus, qui erat lux, vita, structorque noui mundi, qui quum ad suos venisset non fuit receptus: hoc Verbum, inquam, fuit caro, homo vilis, mortalis, despectus, maledictum etiam factus. Caro enim fere pro eo semper sumitur. Hoc dicit, nequis Christum sibi somniet, seu vnctum a Deo, qui non sit homo. Ideò & Ioannes præuidens alium Christum non hominem introducendum præmonuit dicens, Omnis spiritus qui Christum negat in carne venisse (non in carnem ait) ex Deo non est, impostor est & Antichristus, de quo audistis Antichristum venturum fuisse, & iam nunc in mundo esse. Quæ verba innuunt doctrinam hanc de Filio Dei fictò ante carnem, tempore Apostolorum iam exortam fuisse, & ante omnia Christum lucem veram sublatum esse, ut tandem omnia in tenebris vastaret Satan, ut Christus prædixit Ioan. 9. Certè in hus verbis Ioannis 1. capite nulla transsubstantiatio asseritur, neque aliqua unius Christi æterni cum altero temporali iunctura: unde etiam duas naturas, aut potius duos Christos introduxit Antichristus, visibilem & invisibilem, æternum & temporalem, unum hominem cum Deo copulatum, mortalem & immortalem, æqualem & minorem: qui creuit sapientia & ætate, tum qui non creuit: qui unus est cum Patre, & qui non unus: passus, & non passus pro nobis. Ista enim & multa alia portenta hinc stabiliuit Antichristus, de quibus nec somniauit Ioannes. Simplex est hic oratio, sed nunc obscurata per phantasmata Antichristi. Ioannes enim simpliciter illum Christum Verbum Deum, lucem, vitamque, structorem novi mundi, hominem fuisse docet, nequis vel Deum Patrem esse Messiam, vel Deum aliquem æternum, vel non hominem somniaret Christum. Contra Antichristum, & eius fictum Christum, editum hoc est Euangelium, quod Antichristus pro suo Christo æterno torquet. Talium verò phrasium plena est Scriptura, ubi vox ἐγένετο idem valet quod fuit. In eodem capite, paulo ante dicit de Ioanne, ἐγένετο ἄνθρωπος, fuit homo missus a Deo. Sic Ioann. 6. Sic de Christo Luc. 24. ὃς ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ, qui fuit vir verbo potens & opere. Sic Luc. 1. ἐγένετο &c. fuit in diebus Herodis Regis. Sic Marc. 1. Quod si quis diligens lector fuerit, plus mille locos colliget in novo Testamento ex Græca lingua: nusquam tamen hanc vocem pro incarnari, vel duas res aut naturas in unum iungi inuenies. Quin facilius inuenires pro converti, ut aqua factum vinum in Cana.
units.tr: Those who know Greek know that the word ἐγένετο often means the same as fuit [was], so that the sense is: that Christ who was the Word, the interpreter or spokesman of God, anointed with the Spirit without measure, who was the light, the life, and the builder of the new world, who when he came to his own was not received: this Word, I say, was flesh, a vile, mortal, despised man, even made a curse. For flesh is almost always taken for that. This says that no one should dream of a Christ who is not a man, or anointed by God as such. Therefore John, foreseeing that another Christ, not a man, would be introduced, warned beforehand, saying, Every spirit that denies that Christ has come in the flesh (he does not say into flesh) is not of God; he is an impostor and Antichrist, of whom you have heard that Antichrist would come, and that now he is already in the world. These words imply that this doctrine of a Son of God made before the flesh had already arisen in the time of the Apostles, and that before all else Christ the true light was taken away, so that at last Satan might lay waste everything in darkness, as Christ foretold, John 9. Certainly in these words of John, in the first chapter, no transubstantiation is asserted, nor any joining of one eternal Christ with another temporal one. Hence Antichrist also introduced two natures, or rather two Christs, one visible and one invisible, one eternal and one temporal, one man joined to God, mortal and immortal, equal and lesser, who grew in wisdom and age, and yet who did not grow; who is one with the Father, and who is not one; who suffered, and who did not suffer for us. For Antichrist established these and many other monsters from this source, of which John never even dreamed. This discourse is simple, but now it is obscured by the phantasms of Antichrist. For John simply teaches that that Christ was the Word, God, light, life, builder of the new world, and a man, lest anyone should dream that Christ was either God the Father, or some eternal God, or not a man. But against Antichrist and his fictitious Christ this Gospel was published, which Antichrist twists for his own eternal Christ. Scripture is full of such phrases, where the word ἐγένετο means the same as fuit. In the same chapter, a little earlier, he says of John, ἐγένετο ἄνθρωπος, there was a man sent from God. So John 6. So of Christ, Luke 24: ὃς ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ, who was a man mighty in word and deed. So Luke 1: ἐγένετο, there was, in the days of Herod the king. So Mark 1. If any diligent reader were to gather, he would collect more than a thousand such places in the New Testament from the Greek language; yet nowhere will you find this word used for becoming flesh, or for two things or natures being joined into one. Indeed you would more easily find it used for being changed, as the water made wine at Cana.

units.la: Quare pijs sedulò caveant sibi a talibus Antichristi impostoris: quibus non tantum ille Christus unicus verus Dei Filius ex Spiritu sancto conceptus, & ex Maria natus, & a Deo de coelo commendatus, & nunquam incarnatus vel ex duabus naturis conceptus, sublatus est; sed etiam tota Scriptura obscurata, ut nemo illam prae isto Christo fictitio intelligat. De nullo magis & diutius hucusque certatum, & ab initio, quam de istis naturis Antichristi, de quibus ne verbum quidem habetur in tota Scriptura, nec de communicatione idiomatum a Satana inventa.
units.tr: Therefore let the godly take care to guard themselves against such impostors of Antichrist, by whom not only that one true Christ, the only Son of God, conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of Mary, and commended by God from heaven, and never made flesh or conceived of two natures, has been taken away; but also all of Scripture has been obscured, so that no one understands it in view of this fictitious Christ. About no matter has there been more and longer contention, from the beginning, than about these natures of Antichrist, of which not even a word is found in all of Scripture, nor of the communication of properties, invented by Satan.

units.la: Quin & nunc in omnibus Ecclesiis Germanicis, Helueticis, Gallicis, de nullo alio contendunt, sicut ab initio Euangelij, quam de naturis. An vero putamus res tam necessarias non fuisse descripturos Apostolos, in quibus isti hodie proram & puppim religionis & salutis omnium locant? An tacuisset de Christo isto aeterno Pater? quem sub vetere Testamento nec ostenderat, nec promiserat unquam, nec vnxerat, nec in eum credere docuit: cum etiam Angelos saepe describat in veteri Testamento, & alias res leuissimas. Lux est Christus, vnus etiam magister, quo nemo clarius docet: nihil facilius est tota eius doctrina, si quis modo haec Antichristi blasphema commenta de Deo trino, & de Christo bino ab oculis abstergat. In hac sola doctrina Christi simplice, absque Patribus, Concilijs (cum per horum fumos obscurata sit lux) perseuerabat Ecclesia illa Apostolica purissima, in qua homines simplices, pij, & ardentes in fide & charitate erant, Luca teste. In hac quoque sola standum nobis erit ad finem, si volumus Christiani esse, id est, discipuli Christi, & ex Babylone exire, in Apostolicaque Ecclesia ad finem permanere.
units.tr: Indeed, even now in all the German, Swiss and French Churches they contend about nothing else, as from the beginning of the Gospel, than about the natures. But do we think that the Apostles would not have described such necessary matters, on which these men today place the prow and stern of religion and salvation? Would the Father have kept silent about this eternal Christ, whom under the Old Testament he neither showed, nor ever promised, nor anointed, nor taught to believe in? Yet he often describes angels in the Old Testament, and other very trivial things. Christ is light, and also the one teacher, than whom no one teaches more clearly; nothing is easier than his whole doctrine, if only one wipes these blasphemous inventions of Antichrist about the triune God and the binary Christ from one's eyes. In this simple doctrine of Christ alone, without the Fathers and Councils (since the light has been obscured by their smoke), that most pure Apostolic Church persisted, in which men were simple, godly, and burning in faith and love, as Luke bears witness. In this alone too must we stand to the end, if we wish to be Christians, that is, disciples of Christ, and to go out of Babylon and remain to the end in the Apostolic Church.

units.la: Quod si quis etiam Verbum factum carnem interpretetur, non pro vnione illa duorum in vnum, nec pro conuersione vnius in alterum, sed pro mutatione status seu conditionis summae potentiae Christo datae, non absurde (vt puto) faceret: vt respondeat loco illi Philip. 2. & Esaiae 53. de forma Dei & seruitum illi 2 Cor. 8. quod quum esset dives, factus sit pauper propter nos. Hic sensus enim omnium istorum locorum esset sibi correspondens. Quum Christus esset Verbum, primarius Doctor, & efset Deus tanta potentia praeditus ut omnia illi obedirent, & dæmones fugiendo, morbi cum morte cedendo, mare & venti sese pacando pro imperio Christi, esset que innocens sine peccato, sicut & Adam creatus ad imaginem Dei (hoc enim est esse in forma Dei, Paulo) quum ergo tantus tamque potens esset, missusque ad reconciliandum nos Deo per mortem, & ad exsoluendum peccatum (a quo ille, ut & ab omni dolo, erat liber, innocens, sanctus, pius, imaginem Dei referens, atque ita nec morti, nec maledicto vlli obnoxius) factus est tamen caro, vilis, & contemptus, & propter nos exinaniuit se hac Dei forma: quum esset æqualis Deo, formam serui suscepit, subiecit se sponte seruitu- ti non qualicunque, sed etiam maledictæ morti crucis, quum posset se potentia a Patre accepta tueri, nec tradere se illis quorum cogitationes ante nouerat, & manus eludebat, eosque iam capiendus coram virtute prostrauerat: Verbum illud Dei factum est, inquam, caro, id est, vilis, pauper, miser, maledictum, vermis & non homo, quasi omni potentia destitutus esset, morti se obiecit crucis obediens Patri factus: & hæc quoque est forma serui & paupertas spontanea. Quam ob causam etiam extulit illum Pater, dato illi nomine supra omne nomen, ut ab omnibus adoretur, resuscitauit eum, & ad dexteram suam sedere fecit, potentia in cœlo & in terra illi data. Et Ioannes post hanc vilitatem scribit, ut & Paulus, fuisse conspectam eius gloriam, non ut alicuius hominis vel Angeli, sed ut vnigeniti a Patre, iam non ut exinaniti vel in forma serui, sed plenigratiæ & veritatis. Nam ut aliquem Christum alium æternum ante Mariam fingant, qui fuit in forma Dei, vel diues, vel Verbum Deus, vel vita luxq, ut id probent, nullum locum habent Scripturæ, nullas diuitias eius possunt ostendere. De homine enim Christo in terris, tam potente & talia miranda patrante, hæc dici volunt Euangelistæ, non de alio. An non Paulo fuisset facilius loco formæ Dei dicere verum Deum & æternum, ut vult Antichristus? In forma enim enim Dei, tamquam Deus, imperabat omnibus. Id vero Paulus non fecit, quia de uno eodemq; filio Dei (quem Dominum & Christum fecit Deus) loquitur: illum qui non sit factus a Deo non demonstrat, neque duos Christos vsquam tradit. Vt enim vetus testamentum eum promittebat, figurabat, re non ostendebat: ita sub novo testamento, non sub veteri, natus, datus, demonstratus ab Angelis, Simeone, Anna, & a Deo Patre caelo aperto coram turbis proclamatus, quum iam proditurus esset (& non ante) ut se Verbum, Deum, lucem, vitamque ministerio suo docens faciensq; demonstraret. Eodem sensu uterq; redit: quum esset summus apud Deum, fuit infimus omnium: idem summus, qui factus vilis, non alius & alius: uti & doctiores Neoterici docent, praesertim Melanchthon, cuius verba hic placuit adjicere. Vide in vetusto illius commentario in primum Ioannis caput super illis verbis, & Verbum caro factum est, ubi sic ait: Porro omissis philosophicis disputationibus de incarnatione, breviter ita sentio, Ioannem tapeinōsin capere nasci, quum ait, Verbum caro factū est, id est quod Esaias ait, novissimus virorum: & Paulus 2. Cor. 5. pro nobis peccatum factus est: & Gal. 3. factus pro nobis maledictum. Quare quum carnem vocat, intellige extremā humiliationem Christi, &c.
units.tr: If someone also interprets "the Word became flesh" not as the union of two into one, nor as the conversion of one into the other, but as a change of state or condition, with the supreme power given to Christ, he would not, I think, be absurd. That reading would fit the passages in Philippians 2 and Isaiah 53 about the form of God and the servant form, and 2 Corinthians 8, "though he was rich, he became poor for our sake." The sense of all these passages would then agree with itself. Christ was the Word, the chief Teacher, and was God endowed with such power that all things obeyed him: demons fled, diseases and death gave way, and sea and winds were calmed at Christ's command. He was innocent and without sin, like Adam created in the image of God (for to be in the form of God, in Paul's words, is this). Since he was so great and so powerful, and was sent to reconcile us to God through death and to take away sin (from which he was free, as from all guile, innocent, holy, pious, bearing the image of God, and therefore subject neither to death nor to any curse), he nevertheless became flesh, lowly and despised. For our sake he emptied himself of this form of God. Though he was equal to God, he took the form of a servant and willingly subjected himself to a servitude of no ordinary kind, even to the cursed death of the cross, though he could have defended himself by the power he had received from the Father, and need not have given himself up to those whose thoughts he already knew, and he eluded their hands and, when they were about to seize him, struck them down by his power. That Word of God, I say, became flesh, that is, lowly, poor, wretched, accursed, a worm and not a man, as if stripped of all power. Obedient to the Father, he submitted himself to the death of the cross. This too is the form of a servant and voluntary poverty. For this reason the Father also exalted him, giving him a name above every name, that he should be worshipped by all; he raised him up and made him sit at his right hand, with power in heaven and on earth given to him. John, and Paul too, after this lowliness, write that his glory was seen, not as the glory of some man or angel, but as that of the only-begotten of the Father, no longer as one emptied or in the form of a servant, but full of grace and truth. For those who imagine some other eternal Christ before Mary, who was in the form of God, either rich, or God the Word, or life and light, have no passage of Scripture to support this, and can show no such riches of his. The Evangelists wish these things to be said of the man Christ on earth, so powerful and performing such wonderful deeds, and of no other. Would it not have been easier for Paul, instead of speaking of the form of God, to say "true and eternal God," as Antichrist wishes? For in the form of God, as God, he commanded all things. Paul did not do this, because he speaks of one and the same Son of God, whom God made Lord and Christ. He nowhere shows another who was not made by God, nor does he hand down two Christs. For just as the Old Testament promised and prefigured him, but did not display him in reality, so under the New Testament, not under the Old, he was born, given, and shown forth by angels, by Simeon, by Anna, and proclaimed by God the Father from an open heaven before the crowds, when he was about to be revealed (and not before), so that by his ministry he might show himself as the Word, God, light, and life, teaching and doing these things. Both expressions return to the same sense: though he was highest with God, he was lowest of all. The same one was highest, who was made lowly, not one and then another; as the more learned modern writers also teach, especially Melanchthon, whose words I have thought fit to add here. See in his old commentary on the first chapter of John, on the words "and the Word was made flesh," where he says this: "Moreover, setting aside the philosophical disputations about the incarnation, I think briefly that John takes 'became flesh' as the lowest humiliation [tapeinōsin ταπείνωσιν], as Isaiah says, the last of men; and Paul, 2 Corinthians 5, 'he was made sin for us'; and Galatians 3, 'made a curse for us.' Therefore, when he calls him flesh, understand the utmost humiliation of Christ, etc."

units.la: M. S.
units.tr: M. S.

units.la: Et Verbum caro factum est, seu potius Et Verbum caro fuit, id est, homo.
units.tr: And the Word was made flesh, or rather, And the Word was flesh, that is, a man.

units.la: INTERPRETES hoc modo exponunt: Verbum, id est, Filius Patri consubstantialis ac coaeternus factus est caro, id est, induit seu assumsit hominem. Sed nos quid Verbi nomine intelligendum sit, superius exposuimus: neque enim unquam ex verbo Dei, quod isti dicunt, probare poterunt. Observandum est igitur vocem istam Graecam, qua hic utitur Ioannes, duplici modo Latine reddi posse: nempe & verbum egeneto, id est, fa{s}tum est vel fuit. Ratio tamen contextus omnino postulat vt legatur, & Verbum caro, id est, homo fuit. Nam vltra quod superius Ioannes eadem voce Græca in hac significatione vsus est, quando mentionem faciens de Ioanne Baptista dixit, ἐγέ-νετο ἄνθρωπος, id est, fuit homo missus a Deo, &c. est & illud, quod optimè cohæret præcedentibus & sequentibus, estque optima expositio omnium præmissorum: quasi dicat Ioannes, Verbum hoc, de quo hactenus verba feci, quod lucem etiam ac vitam appellaui, cui testimonium perhibuit Ioannes Baptista, quodq; in mundo erat, ac in suam Iudæam veluti in propriam domum venit: hoc inquam Verbum, nempe Iesus ille Christus de quo in præsenti historia sum loquuturus, caro, id est, homo, & quidem mortalis, humilis ac despectus (nam per carnem huiusmodi hominem significari satis manifestum est) fuit: & hac ratione Christus ipse se filium hominis, id est, hominem sæpe vocat.
units.tr: The interpreters explain it in this way: the Word, that is, the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, was made flesh, that is, put on or assumed a man. But what is to be understood by the name Word we have explained above, for they will never be able to prove it from the word of God, as they claim. It must therefore be noted that this Greek word which John uses here can be rendered in Latin in two ways, namely, and the word egeneto [ἐγένετο], that is, was made or was. Yet the context of the passage altogether requires that it be read, "and the Word was flesh, that is, a man." For besides the fact that John earlier used the same Greek word in this sense, when speaking of John the Baptist he said, "there was [ἐγένετο] a man sent from God," etc. There is also this, which agrees very well with what precedes and follows and is the best explanation of all that has gone before: as if John were saying, this Word, of whom I have spoken so far, whom I have also called light and life, to whom John the Baptist bore witness, who was in the world and came to his own Judea as into his own home, this Word, I say, namely that Jesus Christ of whom I am about to speak in this history, was flesh, that is, a man, and indeed a mortal, lowly and despised man (for it is clear enough that by flesh a man of this kind is meant). In this way Christ himself often calls himself the Son of Man, that is, a man.

units.la: Quod si vertas, & Verbum caro factum est, non solum non cohæret textui, sed totum lectionis contextum euertit. Nam si ita legatur, oportuisset huiusmodi Verbum, antequam veniret Iudæus suis prædicatum, carnem fuisse factum: at hic legitur priùs venijse ad eos, deinde carnem esse factum. Adde quod si ita vertatur, & intelligatur de Filio æterno consubstantiali, vt isti volunt, non solum Scripturis probari non potest, sed toti Scripturæ maximè aduersatur. Nam cùm asserant esse Verbum illum Deum Iehouam, qui solus adorari debet & eum hominem esse factum: nònne hoc est Scripturam vniuersam inuertere, ipsamq; toti modo contemptui exponere?
units.tr: But if you translate "and the Word was made flesh," it not only does not cohere with the text but overturns the whole context of the reading. For if it were read so, the Word of this kind would have had to be made flesh before he came to the Jews and was preached to them; but here it is read that he first came to them and afterwards was made flesh. Add that if it is so translated and understood of the eternal consubstantial Son, as they wish, it cannot be proved from Scripture, and is most opposed to the whole of Scripture. For when they assert that this Word is God Jehovah, who alone ought to be worshipped, and that he has been made a man, is this not to turn the whole of Scripture upside down and expose it entirely to contempt?

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: THE ORTHODOX SPEAKER.

units.la: HORVM Euangelistæ verborum duplex adfertur interpretatio: quarum altera affirmatè enunciatur, altera συγχωρητικῶς. etsi hanc posterior interpres oppugnat simpliciter, vt sibi incommodam & sententiæ suæ. Prior interpreterpretatio est Verbum fuisse carnem: posterior, Verbum factum esse carnem. De utraque ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Two interpretations of the Evangelist's words are offered. One states the matter outright; the other states it by way of concession [συγχωρητικῶς]. The second interpreter attacks the first simply because it is inconvenient for him and for his own opinion. The first interpretation is that the Word was flesh; the second, that the Word was made flesh. We shall consider each in turn, beginning with the first.

units.la: In priore sequemur ordinem a Samosateno hoc interprete institutum. Nam primum sententiam suam proponit, tum confirmat prout potest, tandem accumulatis absurdis confutat nostram. Sensus est, inquit, Christus, hoc Verbum, fuit caro, homo, vilis, mortalis, despectus, maledictum etiam factus. Huius interpretationis vitia (ut dicamus paucis) tria animadvertimus: unum, in subiecti; & duo, in praedicati enarratione. In subiecto vitium est, quod Christus persona supponitur, quae tum primum coeperit esse, quum caro facta est, ac non persona divina essentialiter. In praedicato, vitiose nomen caro & verbum ἐγένετο exponitur. Cum enim nomen carnis substantiam proprie significet, cuius substantiae species proxime definitur, quū additur nomen homo (atque hoc aliquo modo verum est) illico attributa homini huic appinguntur toto genere differentia: tanquam si nomine carnis aequivocè diceren- tur multa ad categorias complureis pertinentia. Nam vilis, mortalis homo cum dicitur, attributa qualitatis sunt; quum vero despectus & maledictum etiam factus; haec continentur passionis categoria. Si ergo, Samosatene, nomine carnis tam multa & diversa significantur; putas ne idem de eodem, ut genus simul & ut accidens, enunciari posse? putas ne idem de eodem ut varia genera praedicari? Si putas, profer, quaeso, nomen contrarium quod ad certum genus referri possit. Id profecto nunquam quisquam effecturus est, data hac definitione carnis. Quod si substantia cum accidente, generaq; inter se hac circumscriptione confunduntur usque adeo ut nullum certum contrarium dari huius vocis aut species ἀντιδιηρημένη possit; non definitur nomen carnis, sed magis his loquutionibus obscuratur. De verbo ἐγένετο non melius quutionibus obscuratur. statuis: nam quo loco iubes exponi fuit, eodem tu ipse exponis factus est, quū dicis, fuit maledictum etiam factus. Quod verbum sive ad omnia tuæ definitionis membra retuleris, sive ad ultimum solum (in quo tamen plus excusationis futurum est) non potes quin euincaris ipse fundamenta doctrinæ tuæ euertere: qui idipsum in definitione tua ponis, quod tam constanter & tanta contentione extrudi iubes. Quæ cum ita sint, redundat tua illa definitio carnis: quam (si sapis) refectis omnibus attributis quæ placuit addere, hoc modo statues: caro, id est, homo, prout ab Apostolo nominatur Iesus Christus homo. Etsi hoc pium Lectorem velim observare, optimè Spiritui Dei placuisse ut hic potius diceretur, Verbum factum est caro, quàm Verbum factum est homo. Cur autem? quia homo simpliciter quum dicitur, persona intelligitur subsistens essentia sua in humanitate sua, vel in seipso secundum humanitatem suam: sed caro hic quum dicitur de verbo Dei vel sermone, intelligitur natura humana subsistens essentia sua in persona Filij Dei, ac non in seipsa, ut fit in omnibus hominibus progenatis naturæ ordine. Quapropter antehac dixi aliquo modo verum illud esse, quòd caro hic homine significet: nam respectu subsistentiæ caro Christi homo est: sed in ratione subsistendi (quem ὑπόστασιν ὑπάρξεως appellant Patres) discrimen intervenit quòd homo naturalis subsistit in se, humanitas Christi subsistit in persona Filij Dei, secundum unionem personalem humanitatis cum divinitate illius. Sequuntur probationes illius definitionis tuæ, quam modo expendimus. Prima, caro fere pro eo semper sumitur. Nego: nam est quidem dictio æquivoca: sed tamen nullum Scripturæ locum video, ubi sic possit coniunctè accipi: exemplum desidero. Si quod est, non possum meminisse: homo mostrum. Quòd statim excurrit Samosatenus ad suam illam toties recantatam oppositionem Filij æterni & hominis, tamquam si in uno suppósito non possent simul exsistere, puerile est: & eo amplius miror, quòd cosdum putant effugere absurdum (ut videtur) unum, in alterum aut potius idem video incidere. Nam non magis attributa purè divina creatæ naturæ inesse possunt, quam natura divina naturæ humanæ adunari: Hoc autem illis absurdum est: Et illud igitur absurdum esse oportuit. Ac proinde optimè e diuerso concludimus: Omnia attributa divina sunt propria deitatis: Quæ autem propria sunt deitatis non possunt naturæ creatæ cōpetere, aut inesse in se: ergo attributa deitatis non possunt naturæ creatæ cōpetere. Sed utraq; natura potest persona liter adunari, divina inquâ & humana, seruatis utriusq; in sese proprietatibus & cōmunicata operatione in suppositi siue personæ vnitate: illud ergo absurdissimū, hoc minimè absurdum est, quod ex verbo Dei credimus & confitemur. Non igitur alius Christus non homo (ut hic odiosè obijcit) a nobis introducitur, sed (quod maximè omnium est necessarium) natura diuina cum humana in vnitatem personæ dicitur adunata, vt in humana, per humanam, & cum humana suas diuinas præstet operationes verus Deus verus homo Christus, vnum suppositum, seu persona una.
units.tr: In the first I shall follow the order set by this interpreter, Samosatenus. First he sets out his own opinion, then he confirms it as best he can, and finally, after piling up absurdities, he refutes ours. "The meaning is," he says, "that Christ, this Word, was flesh, a man, lowly, mortal, despised, even made a curse." I note three faults in this interpretation, to put it briefly: one in the subject, and two in the explanation of the predicate. The fault in the subject is that a person is assumed for Christ who began to exist only when the flesh was made, and not a divine person in essence. In the predicate, the word flesh and the verb became are wrongly explained. For since the noun flesh properly signifies a substance, whose kind is then defined more closely, when the noun man is added (which is true in a certain sense), at once the attributes of a man are attached to it, differing entirely in kind, as if many things belonging to different categories were said equivocally of the one word flesh. For when we say "a lowly, mortal man," these are attributes of quality; when he says "despised" and "even made a curse," these belong to the category of passion. So, Samosatenus, if so many different things are signified by the word flesh, do you think the same thing can be predicated of the same thing both as a genus and as an accident? Do you think the same thing can be predicated of the same thing as various genera? If you think so, produce, I beg you, a contrary term that can be referred to a definite genus. Certainly no one will ever manage it, once this definition of flesh is given. But if substance and accident, and genera, are so confused with one another by this circumscription that no definite contrary of this word, or any opposed species, can be given, then the noun flesh is not defined at all, but is rather obscured by these expressions. Nor do you fare better with the verb became: for in the place where you order was to be explained, you yourself explain it as became, when you say, "was even made a curse." Whether you refer this verb to all the members of your definition, or only to the last (where there would be more room for excuse), you cannot avoid overturning the foundations of your own doctrine, since you put in your definition the very thing that you so constantly and so eagerly insist upon. Since this is so, your definition of flesh is superfluous. If you are wise, you will drop all the attributes you chose to add and state it in this way: flesh, that is, man, as the Apostle names Jesus Christ the man. Yet I would have the godly reader notice that it pleased the Spirit of God to say here, "The Word was made flesh," rather than "The Word was made man." Why? Because when man is said simply, a person is understood who subsists in his own essence, in his humanity, or in himself according to his humanity. But when flesh is said here of the Word or Speech of God, a human nature is understood, subsisting in its essence in the person of the Son of God, and not in itself, as happens in all men born in the natural order. Hence I said before that in a certain sense it is true that flesh here signifies man: for with respect to subsistence, the flesh of Christ is man; but in the mode of subsisting (which the Fathers call hypostasis of existence) there is a difference: natural man subsists in himself, while the humanity of Christ subsists in the person of the Son of God, by the personal union of the humanity with his divinity. Next come the proofs of that definition of yours which we have just examined. The first is: flesh is almost always taken for that. I deny it. For it is indeed an equivocal word, but I see no passage of Scripture where it can be taken in this conjoined sense; I want an example. If there is one, I cannot remember it: homo mostrum. What Samosatenus at once runs off to, his old opposition, so often retracted, between the eternal Son and man, as if they could not exist together in one suppositum, is childish. And I am the more surprised that they think they escape one absurdity (as it seems) only to fall into another, or rather into the same one. For purely divine attributes cannot inhere in a created nature, any more than the divine nature can be joined to a human nature. But this is absurd to them. Therefore that too must be absurd. And so, on the contrary, we rightly conclude: All divine attributes are proper to deity. But what are proper to deity cannot belong to, or inhere in, a created nature. Therefore the attributes of deity cannot belong to a created nature. But both natures can be united personally, divine and human, each keeping its own properties and sharing its operations in the unity of one suppositum or person. Therefore the absurd thing is that one, and the thing that we believe and confess from the Word of God is in no way absurd. Thus we do not introduce, as he odiously objects, another Christ who is not man. Rather (which is most necessary of all) the divine nature is said to be united with the human in the unity of one person, so that the true God and true man, Christ, in the human nature, through the human nature, and with the human nature, performs his divine operations, one suppositum or one person.

units.la: Secunda probatio : Qui docet dogma aduersus quod nos præmonuit Apostolus, is ex Deo non est, &c. Orthodoxi docent dogma eiusmodi: ergo. Minorem, quam negamus, probare volunt auctoritate Ioannis, dicentis, omnis spiritus qui negat Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est, impostor est & Antichristus. &c. hoc negant Orthodoxi: non igitur ex Deo sunt. Iterum falsa minor. Probare sibi videtur, dicendo, non ait in carnem venisse, vt vos affirmatis, sed in carne venisse dicit Ioannes. Atqui primum qui in carnem venisse dicit, non negat venisse in carne: nam venisse in carnem, & venisse in carne non sunt contradicentia: tantùm eo dilcrimen est, quòd venisse in carnem quum dicimus, cuidentius notamus ante fuisse suppositum quàm aut caro esset, aut suppositum veniret in carnem, atque hic scopulus ille est a quo tantopere & tanta contentione animi resilitis: venisse autem in carne quum dicimus, fit ad nos relatio, nempe quòd suppositum illud de quo agitur ad nos in carne venerit. Utrumque autem coniungimus, Christum venisse in carnem, quam assumsit in utero virginis Mariæ, & Christum in carne venisse ad nos, id est, in mundum atque in lucem prodijsse ex beatæ matris utero. Secundò non dicit simpliciter Ioannes (ut putas) qui negat Iesum Christum venisse in carne; sed dicit ἐληλυθότα, Iesum Christum qui venit in carne. Eodem enim, quo ante, respicit, quum diceret, Quis est mendax, nisi qui negat Iesum esse Christum illum? quemadmodum in Euangelio, hæc scripta sunt, ut credatis Iesum esse Christum illum, Filium illum Dei, &c. Tantum eo differt hic locus ab illis, quòd una amplius circumscriptio adijcitur a carne ipsius, omnis spiritus qui negat Iesum (hoc personæ nomen) Christum (hoc officij) qui in carne venit (hoc naturæ, cuius respectu adducebantur multi, ut carnis infirmitate & crucis scandalo offensi negarent hunc Iesum, hunc Christum eundem esse) is ex Deo non est, &c. Frustra itaque Samosatenus adtexit commenta sua, & nouam quamdam prisca Ecclesiæ proponit historiam: quam si velimus cognoscere, optimos illos & incorruptos antiquitatis testes ab ipsa antiquitate potius audiemus, quàm nouos homines, qui & in suis interpretationibus & in ijs quas adhibere solent historijs nihil nisi principium petunt, certis auctoritatibus, rationibus exemplisque destituti. Quæ contumeliosè in Christum, doctrinam, & nos vibrare audet, ea de industria omittimus. Tertia probatio, non probatio est, sed mera petitio principij: hunc Ioannis locum non obscurum, aut aut portentosum esse, sed clarum & simplicem. Obscurum fore, si transsubstantiationem aut consubstantiationem doceret naturarum: portentosum, si duas naturas aut potius Christos introduceret in quibus res contrariae inessent plane, &c. De obscuritate respondeo, nullum verbum esse in tota Ioannis historia, nullum in tota interpretatione nostra de transsubstantiatione sive substantiarum transmutatione. Negamus igitur: tum etiam regerimus, æquè obscurum esse atque παράδοξον, si quis transfusionem vel transportationem atque immigrationem proprietatum essentialium aut personalium de substantia una in alteram affirmauerit, quàm si transmutationem substantiarum inter se confirmaueris: propria enim, quæ quidem verè sunt propria, non emigrare e subiectis suis. Proprietatum autem immigrationem eiusmodi, & quidem diuinarum in naturam humanam (hominem Christum fallendi studio vocant) Samosatteniani tradunt, adeò vt ipsis auctoribus Christus purus putus homo Deus factus sit proprietatum diuinarum immigratione, secundùm quas vno momento & vno loco consistens omnes omnium hominum qui vbiuis locorum sunt animos corda & voluntates nouit, sermones & orationes audit, actiones videt, omnibus opem fert, &c. quæ solius deitatis propria sunt & essentialia. Obscurum ergo docent isti atque παράδοξον. Obscurum fore quod aiunt, si doceatur consubstantiatio sive iunctura (vt vocat) naturarum differentium, falsum est: nam nihil communius adunatione & coagmentatione in natura rerum. Fit vnio ex pluribus integris, perfectis remanentibus, vt in aceruis confusione, in ædium structura commensu & ordinatione: fit ex perfectis transmutatis, prout ex elementis fiunt corpora mista atque composita: fit denique ex imperfectis, non mixtis aut permutatis; vt ex membris fit corpus, ex anima & corpore fit homo, v-
units.tr: The second proof: Whoever teaches a doctrine against which the Apostle has warned us is not of God, etc. The Orthodox teach such a doctrine; therefore. They wish to prove the minor, which we deny, by the authority of John, who says: "every spirit that denies that Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; he is a deceiver and an Antichrist, etc." The Orthodox deny this; therefore they are not of God. Again the minor is false. He seems to prove it by saying: "John does not say that he came into the flesh, as you affirm, but says came in the flesh." But first, whoever says came into the flesh does not deny came in the flesh: for came into the flesh and came in the flesh are not contradictory. The only difference is that when we say came into the flesh we rightly note that the suppositum existed before either the flesh existed or the suppositum came into the flesh; and this is the rock on which you stumble so greatly and with such eagerness of mind. But when we say came in the flesh, a relation to us is made, namely that the suppositum of whom we speak came to us in the flesh. We join both: that Christ came into the flesh which he assumed in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that Christ came to us in the flesh, that is, that he came forth into the world and into the light from the womb of his blessed mother. Second, John does not say simply (as you suppose) "whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh," but says ἐληλυθότα, that is, "Jesus Christ who has come in the flesh." For he looks back to the same thing as before, when he says, "Who is the liar, but he who denies that Jesus is that Christ?" just as in the Gospel, "these things are written that you may believe that Jesus is that Christ, that Son of God," etc. This passage differs from those only in that one more circumscription is added, from his flesh: "every spirit that denies Jesus" (this is the name of the person), "Christ" (this is of his office), "who has come in the flesh" (this is of his nature, with respect to which many were led astray, so that, offended by the weakness of the flesh and the scandal of the cross, they denied that this Jesus and this Christ were the same), "is not of God," etc. So Samosatenus vainly adds his own inventions and proposes some new history of the ancient Church. If we wish to know it, we shall hear the best and uncorrupted witnesses of antiquity from antiquity itself, rather than from new men who, in their interpretations and in the histories they are accustomed to bring in, seek nothing but their starting point, lacking sure authorities, reasons, and examples. The insults he dares to hurl against Christ, the doctrine, and us, we deliberately pass over. The third proof is not a proof but a mere begging of the question: this passage of John is not obscure or monstrous, but clear and simple. It would be obscure if it taught a transubstantiation or consubstantiation of natures; it would be monstrous if it introduced two natures, or rather two Christs, in which contrary things were clearly present, etc. As to obscurity, I answer that there is no word in the whole history of John, and none in our whole interpretation, about transubstantiation or the transmutation of substances. We therefore deny it, and we also retort that it is no less obscure, and no less paradoxical, if someone affirms a transfusion, transport, or immigration of essential or personal properties from one substance into another, than if you asserted a transmutation of substances into one another. For proper properties, which truly are proper, do not emigrate from their subjects. But the Samosatenians teach this immigration of properties, and indeed of divine properties into the human nature (they call it "the man Christ," with the aim of deceiving), so that, by their own account, Christ, a mere man, was made God by the immigration of divine properties; by these, while remaining at one time and in one place, he knows the minds, hearts, and wills of all men who are anywhere, hears their speeches and prayers, sees their actions, brings help to all, etc., which are the proper and essential properties of deity alone. Therefore these men teach what is obscure and paradoxical. As for their claim that it would be obscure if a consubstantiation, or conjunction as they call it, of different natures were taught: this is false. For nothing is more common in the nature of things than union and joining together. A union is made from several wholes that remain whole and perfect, as in heaps by mixing, or in the building of a house by fitting and arranging; it is made from perfect things that are changed, as bodies that are mixed and compounded are made from the elements; and finally it is made from imperfect things, not mixed or changed, as a body is made from its members, and a man from soul and body; ...

units.la: Cbnione quam dicimus personalem. Non ergo obscurum aut alienum esse potest, siqua hic quoque unio deChristo prædicatur, sed singulari modo: quia non natura ( si proprie velimus loqui ) sed persona assumsit naturam in vnitatem personæ suæ. Quod itaque de adunatione dicitur naturarum, siue naturæ ad personam assumentem, naturale est, licet supernaturalis ortus: & quum dicitur his verbis, Sermo factus est caro, non obscure dicitur, sed tam perspicue quàm dici hoc mysterium potest. Quod autem forte portentosum obijcit, si aut duæ naturæ introducuntur, aut duæ personæ prædita contrarijs proprietatibus in vno suppositu, negamus prius, posterius concedimus, atque affirmamus, quod Samosateno dolet. Duæ, inquam, naturæ coëunt in vnum suppositum personali vnione, quo in suppositu qualitates plane contrariæ coalescunt, & in vnaquaque natura integræ permanent, quamuis in persona adunatæ. Sic vnus & idem homo visibilis est secundum corpus, secundum anima inuisibilis; mortalis est secundum corpus, secundum anima immortalis: crescit per spatia secundum corpus, secundum anima non crescit, &similia multa. Quemadmodum autem duæ imperfectæ naturæ in homine coagmentantur seruatis proprietatibus ad suppositi vnius constitutionem in carne & anima subsistentis virtute Dei; sic etiam persona Christi, quæ naturæ est perfectissimæ, assumsit naturam humanam in vnitatem personæ virtute sua: atque hæc adunatio facta est in ipso seruatis proprietatibus naturæ vtriusque, ad suppositi vnius constitutionem in persona illa diuina & carne assumta subsistentis virtute sua ipsius. Sic vnus & idem Christus homo visibilis est secundum carnem, secundum deitatem inuisibilis: temporalis secundum carnem, secundum deitatem sempiternus: verus Deus verus homo in vnitate personæ ( etsi hæc non sunt contraria, cum substantiæ non sint contrariæ inter se, sed qualitatum contrariarum sint subiecta solùm) mortalis secundùm carnem, secundùm deitatem immortalis: minor Patre secundùm carnem, æqualis Patri secundùm deitatem; qui creuit ætate & sapientia secundùm carnem, secundùm diuinitatem non creuit: qui vnum est essentia vel vnus cum Patre Deus, & qui non est cum Patre vnus secundùm personam, non aliud, sed alius, vt dicebant Patres: qui denique passus est pro nobis secundùm carnem, idem secundùm deitatem ἀπαθὴς permanens. Hæc, vir bone, portentosa non sunt, non ab Antichristo impiè stabilita, non delirantium somnia: sed naturæ vsu euidentissima, a Deo per singularem gratiam effecta pro nobis, & ab Ecclesia inde a principio Euangelij fide religiosè percepta, & sanctis laboribus, vigilijs, ieiunijs, perpessionibus, martyriisque contestata: quæ Samosateni, Photini, Arij, aliorumque phantasmata niituntur obscurare, & Satanas διὰ τῶν πτεγνασμάτων τῆς πανουργίας eripere.
units.tr: The union that we call personal. Nothing obscure or foreign can therefore be meant if this union is also asserted of Christ, though in a singular way: for it was not the nature that assumed (if we wish to speak properly) but the person that took the nature into the unity of its person. What is said, then, of the joining of the natures, or of the nature assumed into the assuming person, is natural, although its origin is supernatural. When it is said in these words, "The Word was made flesh," it is not said obscurely but as plainly as this mystery can be stated. As for his objection that it is perhaps monstrous, "if either two natures are introduced, or two persons endowed with contrary properties in one suppositum," we deny the first and grant the second, and we affirm what vexes Samosatenus: two natures, I say, come together into one suppositum by personal union, and in that suppositum qualities that are altogether contrary coalesce, while in each nature they remain whole, though joined in the one person. Thus one and the same man is visible according to the body and invisible according to the soul; mortal according to the body, immortal according to the soul; he grows in stature according to the body, and does not grow according to the soul, and many similar things. Moreover, just as two imperfect natures are joined in man, their properties being preserved, into the constitution of one suppositum subsisting in flesh and soul by the power of God, so also the person of Christ, which is of most perfect nature, assumed the human nature into the unity of its person by its own power; and this union was made in him, the properties of each nature being preserved, into the constitution of one suppositum subsisting in that divine person and the assumed flesh by his own power. Thus one and the same Christ is visible man according to the flesh, invisible according to the deity; temporal according to the flesh, eternal according to the deity; true God and true man in the unity of the person (although these are not contraries, since substances are not contrary to one another, but serve only as subjects of contrary qualities); mortal according to the flesh, immortal according to the deity; less than the Father according to the flesh, equal to the Father according to the deity; he who grew in age and wisdom according to the flesh did not grow according to the divinity; he who is one in essence or one God with the Father, and who is not one with the Father in person, is not "another" but "other" (alius), as the Fathers said; and finally he who suffered for us according to the flesh, the same remaining impassible [ἀπαθὴς] according to the deity. These things, good sir, are not monstrous, nor were they impiously established by Antichrist, nor are they the dreams of madmen; they are most evident from the use of nature, effected for us by God through his singular grace, and religiously received by the Church from the beginning of the gospel's preaching, and attested by holy labours, watchings, fastings, sufferings and martyrdoms. These are the things that the fantasies of Samosatenus, Photinus, Arius and others strive to obscure, and that Satan seeks to snatch away "through the artifices of trickery" [διὰ τῶν πτεγνασμάτων τῆς πανουργίας].

units.la: Sed illud quod ait Samosatenus portentosum foret, si duo Christi, id est, duo supposita duæ̈ue personæ in vnitatem personalem dicerentur assurgere: quod neque vnquam ab hominibus nostris dictum est, neque a bonis comprobatum.
units.tr: But what Samosatenus says would be monstrous, namely if two Christs, that is, two supposita or two persons, were said to come together into a personal unity, is something that was never said by our people, nor approved by sound men.

units.la: Quemadmodum etiam id omnino portentosum est, quum proprietates vnius essentiæ in essentiam alteram dicuntur immigrare, quod isti homines non dubitant affirmare. Nam si Christus homo solùm est secundùm essentiam suam, vt isti volunt, & tamen in hac sua humanitate & per humanitatem Deus est, resque diuinas operatur in omnibus, omnia vno momento ac non successiuè in infinitum videns, audiens, cognoscens, operans, &c. nonne ex facto proprietates diuinæ in naturam humanam transfiuerunt? Quòd si prout sunt essentiæ, ita operantur, & modus operandi quem res vnaquæque habet, modum τὸ εἶναι sequitur illius (vt certè verum est) quis non miretur portenta Samosatenicæ istius doctrinæ, qua Christus nobis & tota salus eripitur? Quod si nos rationibus humanis pugnare dicant, quibuscum hæc mysteria nihil commune habeant:cogitent ipsi an non rationibus humanis, ijsque cæcis, in ista opinionum portenta quæ tuentur deuenerint: cogitent has rationes non ex hac humili tantùm natura terrenarum rerum depromtas esse, sed principia naturalia esse & communes notiones a recta ratione impressas mentibus nostris, & ad quamlibet naturam communiter rerum physicarum, metaphysicarum, diuinarumque pertinentes: cogitent denique has rationes Scriptura teste iam olim fuisse confirmatas, quum per Prophetas toties dixerit, ego sum, ego sum, & non alius Deus præter me: Gloriam meam alteri non dabo: maledictus homo, qui suam fiduciam collocat in homine, & similia multa. Non est portentosum, quod putas Samosatenę, duas naturas coalescere, aut personam sibi naturam assumere: sed portentosum illud est (si quicquam) quod dicis, propria essentialia in naturam atque essentiam aliam & differentem transmeare: in primis autem diuina, quæ omni modo & omni tempore sunt incommunicabilia, cùm neque Deus aliud fieri possit, nam esset mutabilis: neque aliud fieri Deus, nam nec vnus foret Deus, nec simplicissimus: quod vel cogitare est impium. Det mentem vobis ad ista Dominus ille misericors & immutabilis. Verum itaq; in sese illud est quod concludis, Ioannem simpliciter illū Christum, Verbum, Deum, lucem, vitamque opificem mundi (sed hoc membrum de industria transponis, vt nouæ illi tuæ interpretationi de nouo mundo adhibeas fulcrum) docere homi-nem fuisse: at non hominem solùm. Nam suppositum est Sermo, Filius æternus Dei, de quo inde a principio dixit Euangelicæ narrationis suæ: appositum, caro, hoc ver-su:quam su: quam carnem assumsisse dicitur in vnitatem personæ siue suppositi. Quod autem postea subijcis, ne quis vel Deum Patrem esse Messiam, &c. id ita accipio. Qui Christum hominem esse docet, is Christum negat esse Deum Patrem, vel Deum æternum, vel non hominem. Illud autem Ioannes docet: hæc igitur negat. Maior ex parte ambigua, sed tota falsa est. Ambiguè dicitur Deus Pater: aut essentialiter respectu creaturarum, quarum principium est diuina essentia: aut personaliter respectu Filij. Christum autem negamus esse Deum Patrem personaliter; nam est Patris Filius: sed essentialiter idem est Deus, Pater, principiúmq; omnium cum Patre & Spiritu sancto. Hoc posito, negamus propositionem totam: nam Ioannes vtrumque de Christo, sed diuersa ratione docet. Ac proinde Christus est homo: & quà homo, nec Deus Pater est, nec Deus æternus est, nec etiā nō homo: quà autē Deus est, secunda persona deitatis, idem & Deus Pater est omnium, & Deus æternus, & non homo: quà autem suppositum vel persona vna, idem est Deus & homo; Pater omnium, & in omnibus primas tenes vt in numero omniū cōprehensus; æternus, & principium habens; adde etiam, si placet, homo, & non homo in vnitate personæ: nam Deus est. Quum enim dicitur non homo, indefinitè dicitur: indefinitum autem hoc enunciatum, non homo, definimus in persona Christi, quum appellamus Deum. Hic purus putus elenchus est, quo Samosatenus vtitur: atque eodem modo suauiter sibi figmētum fingit, quum hoc Euangelium editum fuisse dicit contra Antichristum (quod verum est) & contra veritatē personæ Christi, quem diuinitate æternum esse, humanitate verò in tempore natum ex sacris Scripturis didicimus. Hanc blasphemam audacemque affirmationem ipsa rerum operationúmque natura, ipsa Ioannis verba, ipse narrationis ordo, omnia denique confutant potentissimè, vt antè demonstrauimus. Quarta probatio ex vocis ἐγένετο interpretatione petita est. Vox ἐγένετο, inquit, amplius mille locis in Scriptura idem valet, quod fuit: non ergo est incarnari, vel duas res aut naturas in unum iungi. Non dicit, non ergo est factum esse, quod fuerat dicendum ad confutandam interpretationem nostram: sed, non ergo est incarnari, &c. De argumentatione ergo enthymematica illa videamus. De numero locorum nihil dicemus: nam loquitur hyperbolicè. de enthymemate ita statuimus, id esse simpliciter verum, si rectè intelligatur. Sed tamen adhibenda in antecedente distinctio. Nam γένεσθαι verbum, aut significat esse factum & γιγνόμενος factus, expressamque ortus notationem habet (atqui haec propria est significatio) aut metaleptice significat esse, quia res in natura sunt ex quo factae sunt; & tamen vi naturali vocis manet eadem ortus principiique notatio, siue (vt Scholastici vocant) connotatio. Sic quando dicitur ἐγένετο fuit homo, notatur fuisse hominem, sed connotatur factum fuisse hominem: quis enim homo non factus? γιγνόμενος; ortum & principium habens aliunde? Aliter se habet verbum εἶναι, quo simpliciter notatur esse rei citra ortus & principij notationem vllam. Prior itaque significatio propria est verbi γένεσθαι, posterior figurata. Consequens autem concedimus, non quia vi antecedentis conficiatur (id enim falsum est) sed quia per se verum est, neutram harum per se verbi γένεσθαι significationem esse. Restat igitur, vt loquutio haec aut proprie exponatur, Verbum caro factum est, aut metaleptice, Verbum caro fuit, quam interpretationem Samosatenus hic tentat retinere. Nos altera defendimus. cur autem? 1. quia propria est. 2. quia etiamsi daretur figurata interpretatio, tamen idipsum quod Samosatenus fugit connotatione complectitur. 3. quia sic Ioanes ipse distinguit in hac narratione ratione tota ab imperfecto ὤ, quo esse notatur subiecti sine ratione vlla principij aut ortus illius. Nam de simplice esse dicit Ioannes, in principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & verbum erat Deus. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum in ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum. Erat lux illa vera, quae illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum: In mundo erat: & de Ioanne Baptista, non erat ille lux vera. haec omnia verbo ὤ. Sed de eo quod factum est, aut quod ex antefacto est, altero verbo semper vtitur, nimirum γίνεσθαι. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum est: & mundus per ipsum factus est : qui autem receperunt ipsum, dedit eis hoc ius vt Filij Dei fierent: & de Baptista, erat homo missus a Deo. 4. quia etiamsi hoc isto verbo γίνεσθαι significaretur, tamen si ponè sequitur nomen substantiuum, fieri significat (ac non esse) simpliciter & necessario, vt quum aqua facta vinum dicitur Ioan. 2. quum quaerit Apostolus, ergo quod bonum est, mihi factum est mors? Rom. 7. quum dicit, Christus factus fuit nobis sapientia a Deo, & iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemtio, 1. Cor. 1. Christus pro nobis factus est exsecratio, Galat. 3. & similia multa. 5. quia rei natura postulat, & narrationis ordo quem ante declarauimus. Quod si aliter accipi sententiam oporteret, nempe pro esse simpliciter, fuisset dicturus Ioannes, ὁ λόγος ὤ σάρξ, non autem ἐγένετο, quemadmodum paulo ante dixerat, ἡ ζωὴ ὤ τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, & similia. Non enim hic de eo agitur quod iam tum erat Sermo, sed de eo quod tum primum factus est, quum assumsit carnem in unitatem personae. Quod autem facilius inuentum iri hoc verbum dixerit pro eo quod est conuerti, hoc interpretis huius nostri paradoxis oportet deputari, qui ex vnius loci expositione particulari nō dubitat de altero, quamuis in dissimili argumento, similiter concludere; & posita generali significatione verbi specialem affirmare. Fieri enim, genus est: conuerti, species. Nő autem continuo speciem poni constat posito genere, vt hic videtur affirmare. Sequuntur deinceps absur-da, quibus orthodoxa nostra doctrina tandem oppugna-tur. Horum primum illud est quod in praefatione Samo-fatenus posuerat. Christum vnicum verum Dei Filium, &c. hac doctrina tollit. Si verum pro essentiali accipit, vt faci-mus, quid amplius oppugnat? Ii non, certe nos quoque su-mus veri filij Dei, quicunque hoc ius a Patre accepimus credentes in nomen Christi, vt ante proxime enunciauit. Sed, vt ad rem, negamus hoc absurdum sequi: nec ante-cedens vllum est ex quo istius absurdi consequentia osse-di possit. Nam quod oppositionem statuit naturarum, & posita vna euerti putat alteram, id quàm ieiunū & puerile sit, iam saepe ostendimus. Natura vna nō euertit alte-ram vnione personali in nobis: nam hac vnione persona humana constituitur. Itidem ergo in Christo natura per-sonae diuinae alteram euertere dicenda nō est vnione per-sonali. Sed ex Samosatenica illa proprietatum essentia-lium transfusione quae absurda sequantur, ipsi viderint: nos quidem ante destrinximus. Secundum absur-dum est, totam Scripturam obscurari, vt nemo illam praeijto Christo fictitio intelligat. Negatur: nec probari potest. Nam ab Ecclesia orthodoxa semper ita fuit perspicue intelle-cta inde a temporibus Apostolorum, & a nobis intelligi-tur pro demenso donationis Christi. Quod si recta est haec doctrina nostra, aut ijs recta est quibus nondum oculos dedit ad videndum Deus, & pro quibus supplices oramus Dominum vt oculos mentis ipsorum per gratiam illu-minet, aut ijs quibus Deus huius saeculi excaecauit men-tes, ne irradiet eos lumen Euangelij gloriae Christi. Iniquè autem, immo iniquissimè vitiū tenebrarum & caecitatis mentes humanas possidentis perspicuae Scripturarū luci adscriadscribitur. Inepta fallacia est a non causa ut causa, quem-admodum vocatur vulgo. Quid enim? Solem ne dicat obscurare, si lucem Solis caeco obiecero? Nec in Scriptura vitium est, nec in nobis, quod quidem hanc causam attinet; sed in natiua & voluntaria hominum caecitate, abs qua eos cupimus secundum Deum liberari, nostraque officia eis liberandis ex charitate offerimus. Tertium est hoc perpetuum fuisse & adhuc esse in Ecclesia contentionum seminarium, quod de istius naturis & de communicatione idiomatum (Satanae inuentum vocat) exponitur. Egregium argumentum, eiusdem artis cum antecedente. Atqui vulgo dictum illud est verissimum, veritas odium parit. Veritas a Christo est, a Scriptura, a nobis: & miraris veritatem hanc a Satana, ab administris eius, a mundo, a caecis (quorum semper magnus est numerus) oppugnari? an ergo malis taceri & dissimulari veritatem propter odia agnascentia, quam ad salutem credentium propalari? Aliter Ioanni praecipiebat Angelus, Ne obsignauerus, inquiens, verba prophetiae libri huius: tempus enim prope est. Qui nocet, noceat adhuc: & qui sordidus est, sordescat adhuc: & qui iustus est, iustificetur adhuc: & sanctus sanctificetur adhuc. Haec doctrina de duabus naturis in Christo & de communicatione idiomatum (cuius exempla in nobis ipsis perpetua sunt, & in sermone nostro) non commentum Satanae, sed cruciamentum est, quia firmissimum est subsidium salutis nostrae, quam inuidet Satan. Noftrate dictum est, viro bono plus non esse pacis, quam per vicinum licuerit. Tandem te auctore & viros bonos, & veritatem tolli e medio oportebit, velut contentionum semina, si argumentationes istae processerint. Etsi quid multis opus est? in omnibus Ecclesiis, Germanicis, Helveticis, Gallicis de hac re contendi negamus: in nonnullis, minime diffitemur: sed dolemus, & gregem Christi ad sanctam pacem in vnitate spiritus colendam reuocamus. Qua fide bonis obijcis, quod operarij faciunt imprudentes aut mali? Quartum & postremum absurdum est, non fuisse tacituros Apostolos, non ipsum Deum Patrem de hac doctrina nostra, & persona Christi. Certè, nec tacuerunt, nec tacent: sed surdis canitur mysterium. Non tacuerunt Apostoli in Testamento novo. Nam hoc ipsum est quod dicunt Filium Dei factum esse ex muliere, ex femine Dauidis, Sermonem factum carnem, Deum in carne factum conspicuum, & similia multa: quae isti homines vtut circumagant, nunquam tamen effecturi sunt quin veritas ipsa sint, & secundum veritatem ipsam a nobis recte intelligantur. Non tacuit Deus in Testamento vetere: nam & per Moisem aperte ostendit, vt suprà segmento 3. demonstrauimus, & promisit Adamo & Patribus. Quum enim serpenti diceret, semen mulieris conteret caput tuum, audientem Adamum & Euam consolabatur, non de simplice aliquo homine, qui Satanam attriturus esset (nam homo victus, & prostratus qui fecisset? aut homo integer, si quis detur, Satanam qui vicisset tam nostro quàm suo nomine? cùm nec Angelorum iustitia & sanctitas transcendat personam ipsorum, vt de ea cum alijs communicent) sed Dei opus de Deo homine enunciat Christo Iesu, quem Apostolus notauit diserte dicēs, Deus pacis conteret Satanam sub pedes vestros cito. Quum Abrahamo diceret, & semini tuo, Christum & ostendit praesentem secundum diuinitatem, & promisit venturum secundum carnem, & vnctum esse docuit symbolica confessione Patrum & typis legalibus, & Patres iussit in eum credere. Sic Isaaco, Iacobo, alijs. Solum tertium caput ad Galatas audaces istas affirmationes potest conuellere. Abrahamo, inquit, dictae sunt promissiones & semini eius. Non dicit, & seminibus, vt de multis multis; sed vt de vno, & femini tuo, qui est Christus. Hoc autem dico, pactionem priorem ratam factam a Deo respicientem in Christum, Lex quæ post annos quadringentos triginta cæpit, non facit irritam, vt vanam reddat promissionem. Et paulo post, Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus. Hæc enim de omnibus promiscuè dici qui sub lege & sub gratia, demonstrat comparatio antecedentis membri, quum ait Apostolus, Non igitur Lex addita est aduersus promissiones? absit. nam si data fuisset Lex quæ posset viuificare vere ex Lege esset iustitia. Ex eo infert, non est autem data Lex quæ posset viuificare; igitur contrà conclusio facienda, Omnia sub peccato Scriptura Legis conclusa esse, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus, tam qui sub lege, quam qui sub gratia. Crediderunt ergo, & fide Iesu Christi, id est, quæ in Iesum Christum est, crediderunt. Possem ex aliis locis, præsertim ad Hebræos multa: sed hæc in præsentia satis.
units.tr: In the same way, it is utterly monstrous to say that the properties of one essence migrate into another essence, which these men do not hesitate to affirm. For if Christ is man only according to his essence, as they wish, and yet in this his humanity, and through his humanity, is God and performs divine works in all things, seeing, hearing, knowing, and working all things in one moment and not successively, without limit, etc., have not the divine properties passed over into the human nature as a result? But if things act as they are, and the mode of acting that each thing has follows its mode of being [τὸ εἶναι], as is certainly true, who would not marvel at the monsters of this Samosatene doctrine, by which Christ and all our salvation are snatched from us? If they say that we fight with human reasons, with which these mysteries have nothing in common, let them consider whether it is not by human reasons, and blind ones at that, that they have arrived at those monstrous opinions which they defend. Let them consider that these reasons are drawn not merely from this lowly nature of earthly things, but are natural principles and common notions impressed on our minds by right reason, pertaining in common to every nature of physical, metaphysical and divine things. Let them consider, finally, that these reasons were confirmed long ago by the testimony of Scripture, since through the Prophets it has so often said: "I am, I am, and there is no other God besides me. I will not give my glory to another. Cursed is the man who places his trust in man," and many similar passages. It is not monstrous, as you think, Samosatene, that two natures should coalesce, or that a person should assume a nature to himself; but that is monstrous (if anything is), what you say: that the essential properties pass over into another and different nature and essence. Above all, the divine properties, which are incommunicable in every way and at all times, since God cannot become anything else (for he would be changeable), nor can God become something else (for then he would not be one God, nor most simple). To think even this is impious. May that merciful and unchangeable Lord give you understanding of these things. Now, in itself, what you conclude is this: that John simply taught that that Christ, the Word, God, light, and life, the maker of the world (but you deliberately transpose this clause, so that you may use it as a prop for your new interpretation of a new world), was a man, and not only a man. For it is presupposed that the Word, the eternal Son of God, of whom from the beginning he spoke in his Gospel narrative, was joined with the words "flesh" in this verse, which is said to have been assumed into the unity of person or supposit. As for what you add afterwards, "lest anyone should suppose that God the Father is the Messiah," etc., I take it thus: "He who teaches that Christ is a man denies that Christ is God the Father, or the eternal God, or not a man. But John teaches the latter; therefore he denies these." The major premise is partly ambiguous, but the whole is false. "God the Father" is used ambiguously: either essentially, with respect to creatures, whose principle is the divine essence, or personally, with respect to the Son. We deny that Christ is God the Father personally, for he is the Son of the Father; but essentially he is the same God, Father, and principle of all, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Given this, we deny the whole proposition, for John teaches both things about Christ, but in different respects. Accordingly, Christ is man, and as man he is neither God the Father, nor the eternal God, nor yet not a man; but as he is God, the second person of the Godhead, he is also God the Father of all, and the eternal God, and not a man; and as he is a supposit or one person, he is both God and man, the Father of all, and holds the first place among all things, as one comprehended in the number of all; eternal, and having a beginning; add also, if you like, man and not man in the unity of person, for he is God. For when it is said "not man," it is said indefinitely; and we define this indefinite statement, "not man," in the person of Christ when we call him God. This is the pure and simple sophism which Samosatene uses; and in the same way he pleasantly fashions a fiction for himself when he says that this Gospel was published against Antichrist (which is true) and against the truth of the person of Christ, whom we learn from the holy Scriptures to be eternal in his divinity, but born in time in his humanity. The very nature of things and of their operations, the very words of John, the very order of the narrative, in short, all these refute this blasphemous and bold assertion most powerfully, as we have shown before. The fourth proof is drawn from the interpretation of the word "came to be" [ἐγένετο]. "The word 'came to be,'" he says, "in more than a thousand places in Scripture has the same force as 'was'; therefore it is not to become flesh, or to join two things or natures into one." He does not say, "therefore it is not 'was made,'" which ought to have been said to refute our interpretation, but "therefore it is not to become flesh," etc. Let us therefore look at this enthymematic argument. We will say nothing about the number of places, for he speaks hyperbolically. About the enthymeme we hold this: it is simply true if it is rightly understood. But a distinction must be applied to the antecedent. For the verb γένεσθαι [to become] either signifies to have been made, and γιγνόμενος [becoming] means made, and has the clear notation of origin (and this is its proper meaning); or metaleptically it signifies to be, because things exist from the time they were made; and yet by the natural force of the word there remains the same notation of origin and beginning, or, as the Scholastics call it, connotation. Thus when it is said ἐγένετο, "was made" [ἐγένετο], that a man was, it is noted that he was a man, but it is connoted that he had been made a man; for what man is not made, or becoming, having his origin and beginning elsewhere? The verb εἶναι [to be] is otherwise, by which the mere being of a thing is noted without any notation of origin or beginning. The former signification, therefore, is the proper one of the verb γένεσθαι, and the latter is figurative. We concede the consequent, not because it follows from the antecedent by force (for that is false), but because it is true in itself that neither of these meanings is the proper meaning of γένεσθαι in itself. It remains, therefore, that this expression must be explained either properly, "The Word was made flesh," or metaleptically, "The Word was flesh," which interpretation Samosatene here tries to maintain. We defend the first. Why? (1) Because it is the proper one. (2) Because even if a figurative interpretation were granted, it would still embrace by connotation the very thing that Samosatene avoids. (3) Because John himself, in this whole narrative, thus distinguishes the imperfect ἦν [was], by which the being of the subject is noted without any reason of beginning or origin. For John speaks of simple being: "In the beginning was [ἦν] the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world. He was in the world"; and of John the Baptist, "He was not that light." All these are expressed with the verb ἦν. But of what has come to be, or of what has come from something before, he always uses another verb, namely γίνεσθαι [to become]. "All things, he says, were made by him, and without him nothing was made that was made; and the world was made by him; but to as many as received him he gave the right to become the sons of God"; and of the Baptist, "There was a man sent from God." (4) Because even if the meaning of γίνεσθαι were signified by this word, nevertheless, when a substantive noun follows, it means to become (and not merely to be), simply and necessarily, as when "water is made wine" is said in John 2; when the Apostle asks, "Has then what is good been made death to me?" Romans 7; when he says, "Christ was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption," 1 Corinthians 1; "Christ was made a curse for us," Galatians 3; and many similar passages. (5) Because the nature of the thing requires it, and so does the order of the narrative which we have set out before. But if the sentence had to be understood otherwise, namely in the sense of simply "to be," John would have written ὁ λόγος ἦν σάρξ [the Word was flesh], and not ἐγένετο [became], as he had said a little earlier ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων [the life was the light of men] and similar things. For here it is not a matter of what the Word already was, but of what he then first became, when he assumed flesh into the unity of person. As for the claim that this word would more easily be found to mean what is "converted," this must be assigned to the paradoxes of this interpreter of ours, who, from the particular exposition of one passage, does not hesitate to conclude similarly about another, though in a dissimilar matter; and, having posited the general meaning of a word, affirms a specific one. For to become is a genus; to be converted is a species. But it is not at all certain that a species is posited when the genus is posited, as he here seems to affirm. There follow next the absurdities by which our orthodox doctrine is finally attacked. The first of these is what Samosatene had put in the preface: "The one true Son of God, Christ, etc., by this doctrine removes." If he takes "true" as meaning essential, as we do, what more does he attack? Certainly not us; for we too are true sons of God, all of us who have received this right from the Father, believing in the name of Christ, as he said a little earlier. But, to come to the point, we deny that this absurdity follows, and there is no antecedent from which the consequence of this absurdity can be inferred. For his claim that the natures are set in opposition, and that when one is posited the other is thought to be overturned, how empty and childish this is we have often shown. One nature does not overturn the other by personal union in us; for by this union a human person is constituted. Likewise, therefore, in Christ the nature of the divine person ought not to be said to overturn the other by personal union. But what absurdities follow from that Samosatene transfer of essential properties, let them see for themselves; we indeed have already set them out before. The second absurdity is that "the whole of Scripture is obscured, so that no one can understand it unless he has first accepted the fictitious Christ." This is denied, nor can it be proved. For it has always been understood clearly by the orthodox Church from the times of the Apostles, and by us it is understood according to the measure of the gift of Christ. If this doctrine of ours is right, it is right either for those to whom God has not yet given eyes to see, and for whom we pray as suppliants that the Lord may illuminate the eyes of their minds by grace; or for those whom the God of this age has blinded in their minds, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them. But the vice of darkness and blindness, which possesses human minds, is unjustly and most unjustly ascribed to the clear light of the Scriptures. It is a foolish fallacy, a non-cause taken as a cause, as it is commonly called. For what? If I place the light of the sun before a blind man, do I say that the sun is obscured? The fault lies neither in Scripture nor in us, so far as this cause is concerned, but in the natural and wilful blindness of men, from which we desire that they be freed according to God, and to whose liberation we offer our services out of charity. The third absurdity is "that this has been and still is a perpetual seedbed of contentions in the Church, the doctrine which is set forth concerning the natures of this one and concerning the communication of properties" (he calls it an invention of Satan). A striking argument, of the same kind as the preceding. But the common saying is most true: truth breeds hatred. The truth is from Christ, from Scripture, from us; and are you surprised that this truth is attacked by Satan, by his ministers, by the world, by the blind (whose number is always great)? Or should truth rather be silenced and concealed by evil men, on account of the hatreds that arise, rather than made known for the salvation of believers? The angel instructed John otherwise: "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let him who is unrighteous still do wrong, and let him who is filthy still be filthy; and let him who is righteous still practise righteousness, and let him who is holy still be holy." This doctrine of the two natures in Christ and of the communication of properties (whose examples are perpetual in ourselves and in our speech) is not an invention of Satan, but a torment to him, because it is the firmest support of our salvation, and Satan envies us it. It has been said by one of our own, that a good man should have no more peace than his neighbour allows. Finally, if these arguments prevail, on your authority both good men and the truth will have to be removed from the midst, as seeds of contention. But why need there be many words? In all the Churches, German, Helvetic and French, we deny that there is contention over this matter; in some we by no means deny it; but we grieve, and we call the flock of Christ back to cultivating holy peace in the unity of the Spirit. By what faith do you impute to good men what the careless or wicked workmen do? The fourth and last absurdity is "that the Apostles would not have kept silent, nor God the Father himself, about this doctrine of ours and the person of Christ." Certainly they neither kept silent nor are silent; but the mystery is sung to deaf ears. The Apostles did not keep silent in the New Testament. For this is precisely what they say: "the Son of God was made of a woman, of the seed of David; the Word was made flesh; God was made manifest in the flesh," and many similar things; which these men, however they twist them about, will never bring it about that they are not the truth itself, and are not rightly understood by us according to the truth itself. God did not keep silent in the Old Testament either: for he also clearly showed it through Moses, as we demonstrated above in section 3, and he promised it to Adam and to the Fathers. For when he said to the serpent, "The seed of the woman shall crush your head," he consoled Adam and Eve as they listened, not with reference to some simple man who was to crush Satan (for what could a defeated and prostrate man do? Or what integrated man, if any were given, could have conquered Satan in our name as well as his own, since not even the righteousness and holiness of the angels surpass their own person so as to share it with others?), but he declares the work of God, the God-man Christ Jesus, whom the Apostle clearly pointed out when he said, "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." When he said to Abraham, "and to your seed," he both showed Christ present according to his divinity, and promised that he would come according to the flesh, and taught that he would be anointed by the symbolic confession of the Fathers and by the legal types, and commanded the Fathers to believe in him. So too with Isaac, Jacob, and the others. Only the third chapter to the Galatians can overturn these bold assertions. "The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' who is Christ. Now I say this: the covenant previously ratified by God, with respect to Christ, which the law, coming four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul, so as to make the promise void." And a little after: "Scripture has shut up all things under sin, so that the promise through faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe." For that these things are said indiscriminately of all, both those under the law and those under grace, the comparison of the preceding clause demonstrates, when the Apostle says, "Is the law then against the promises?
