God forbid. For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be by the law." From this he infers: "But the law which could give life has not been given; therefore the conclusion must be drawn the other way: Scripture has shut up all things under the law so that the promise through faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers, both those under the law and those under grace." They therefore believed, and believed in Jesus Christ, that is, in what is in Jesus Christ. I could cite many more passages from other places, especially from the Epistle to the Hebrews; but for the present, these are enough.

units.la: Quòd itaq; concludit lucem esse Christum, neminem clarius docere, nihil facilius tota eius doctrina, verum est, vbi capacia subiecta sunt, id est, oculos habetia. Nam quæ oculos habent, ea cum Nazianzeno semper confitebuntur se non posse vnum Deum cernere quin tres personæ circumfulgeant, non posse treis personas cernere quin videant & agnoscant vnicam essentiam & maiestatem Dei: at de Christo bino falsum esse commentum falsò obiectum testabuntur palàm, & nos aperte antehac confutauimus. Sequentia quàm sint a vero aliena, Defensionis 2. segmento 2. & alibi ostendimus.
units.tr: That he concludes Christ is the light, that no one teaches more clearly and nothing is easier than his whole doctrine, is true where the recipients are capable, that is, where they have eyes. Those who have eyes will always confess with Nazianzen that they cannot see the one God without the three persons shining round about, and cannot see the three persons without seeing and acknowledging the one essence and majesty of God. But that the false fiction of two Christs has been falsely laid against him, they will openly testify, and we have clearly refuted it before. How far the following points are from the truth we have shown in section 2 of the second part of the Defence and elsewhere.

units.la: Venio ad alterum interpretationis locum: in quo Samosatenus statuit etiamsi detur illa expositio verborum Ioannis, Verbum esse factum carnem, tamen carnis vocem non de substantia naturæ huius, sed de qualitate abiectissima intelligi oportere, ad quam Christus seipsum demisit. Negamus hoc proprie significari carnis appellatione, & vllu exemplum adferri posse interpretationis istius. No id quidem negamus, carnis appellatione pro locoru qui adducutur natura etia abiectione maximam & conditione misera interdum(vt Scholastici vocat) connotari: sed proprie semper notatur caro & persona carnea, velut subiectum istarum qualitatum quae de supposito carneo praedicantur. Imperite ergo nomen subiecti de puris accidetibus exponitur, vt accidetia fine subiecto coftent, secudum noua quamdam Logica imaginaria. Deinde vero abiectionis persone Christi partes duae a se inuice turpiter dirimuntur, vt abo-leatur persona diuina eius. Cum enim abiectionis Christi partes sint duae: vna, secudum quod persona diuina Christi sese inaniuit assumens carnem; altera, secundum quod in carne submisit sese factus obediens ad mortem vsque crucis, vt optime distinxit Apostolus; substantia tollitur personae, & qualitates solae ac perpessiones in hac interpretatione recensentur. Haec autem duo reprehendimus aperte in hac expositione, & falsam esse propterea ostendimus, quod Scripturis aduersentur. In hac autem enarrationis parte primu Lectores pios obseruare velim, quisnam sit illius modus. Nam pro eo quod Rhetores in causis turpibus aut falsis eos qui dicunt iubent inuoluen-dis & obscurandis rebus maxime occupari, ne verum queant auditores per inuolucra & velamenta cernere, hic contra huic interpreti vfuuenisse video: qui qua in re se explicare studuit, in ea se miserè implicarit, & tanquam in maeandro circuitionum repetitionumque oberrarit. Vix veritatem videas in sermone ita laborare, quia co-mes ipsi est simplicitas: praesertim vero in rebus sacris, de quibus vere praedicari illud potest, fidem nostram non consistere in sapientia hominum, sed in potetia Dei: proinde orationem in hoc argumento non ambitiosam, sed sim-
units.tr: I come to the second place of interpretation. Here Samosatenus holds that even if that explanation of John's words, the Word was made flesh, be granted, the word flesh must still be understood not of the substance of this nature but of the most abject condition to which Christ lowered himself. We deny that the word flesh is properly used in this sense, and we deny that any example of this kind of interpretation can be cited. We do not deny that, in the passages that are adduced, the word flesh sometimes implies the nature itself, together with abasement and a wretched condition (as the Schoolmen call it). But flesh and a fleshly person are always properly meant, as the subject of those qualities which are predicated of a fleshly suppositum. So this man clumsily explains the name of the subject as referring to mere accidents, as if accidents could exist without a subject, on some new imaginary logic. Next, the two parts of Christ's abasement are shamefully torn apart from one another, so that his divine person is abolished. For Christ's abasement has two parts: one, in so far as the divine person of Christ emptied himself by assuming flesh; the other, in so far as, having been made in the flesh, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, the death of the cross, as the Apostle distinguished so well. In this interpretation the substance of the person is taken away, and only qualities and sufferings are listed. We openly find fault with both of these points in this exposition, and we have shown that it is false for the reason that it contradicts the Scriptures. In this part of the exposition I would first have pious readers notice its manner. For whereas orators, in base or false causes, bid those who speak to be especially busy in wrapping and obscuring matters, so that the hearers may not be able to see the truth through the wrappings and veils, here I see the reverse in this interpreter. In what he tried to explain, he entangled himself miserably, and he wandered as in a maze of circuits and repetitions. Scarcely could you see the truth labouring in such speech, since simplicity is its constant companion; especially in sacred matters, of which it can truly be said that our faith rests not in human wisdom but in the power of God. Therefore, in this subject, a plain and not an ambitious style must be kept.

units.la: Philip. 2.
units.tr: Philip. 2.

units.la: 1. Cor. 2. simplicem retinendam. Deinde vero dicta quædam incidunt singularia, quæ dissimulare non possum, ne forte imprudentes eis decipiantur ad subuersionem suæ fidei. Primum est, quòd Christum esse Verbum & Deum pronunciat, neutrum essentialiter intelligit, sed communicatione gratiæ, per quam officio verbum est & dignitate Deus: Quas res iam antè satis refellimus. Secundum, quòd eundem esse innocentem dicit sine peccato, sicut & Adamü creatum ad imaginem Dei: quod verum quidem dictum est, sed non sufficiens. Aliter enim se habet in Christo innocentia, vacuitas peccati, & imago Dei, atque in Adamo: cùm in Adamo humana fuerint omnia, in Christo supra quàm humana, & in persona Filij Dei subsistentia: ex quo id consequutum est quod optimè dicebat Augustinus, potuisse Adamum nō peccare, vtpote mutabilem; sed Christum, etiam in nobis, non posse peccare, vt qui diuina virtute sua sit immutabilis. Tertium, quòd hoc ipsum esse dicit quod Paulo dicitur esse in forma Dei. Nam forma Dei proprie essentialis est, eaque unica: quæ si interire posset aut mutari, interiret aut mutaretur essentia. Nam cùm in simplicibus & ἀύλοις (quæ sunt metaphysica) idem sit forma & id cuius est forma, quis de Deo simplicissimo aliud sentire possit? Christus autem, persona inquam Filij Dei est in forma Dei, & est æqualis Deo: ac proinde secundùm essentiam unus est cum Patre & apud Patrem unitate formæ siue essentiæ, secundùm personam vero est æqualis Patri. Hic autem noster de forma accidentali accipit, quæ potest adesse & abesse citra corruptionem subiecti: cuiusmodi forma in Deo nulla est, cùm sit essentia verè atque in totum simplicissima. Præterea formam Dei interpretatur imaginem eius, vt in Adamo fuit: sed hanc interpretationem refellit planè oppositi membri comparatio, vbi dicitur sese inaniuisse forma serui accepta, similis hominibus factus. Nam duo illa distinguit euidentissimè in Christo, quà homo, quæ iste inscitè confundit, formam essentialem, & similitudinem siue imaginem: quarum prior substantiæ, posterior relationis est, toto genere differentes. Taceo, quòd nusquam forma Dei in Scripturis sic potest accipi, aut vllo exemplo & authoritate confirmari. Falsa igitur interpretatio, qua & formam Dei essentialem, & formam serui obscurauit, quum ad accidentia vtramque retulerit contra mentem Pauli & ordinem verborum ab eo institutum. Quartum, quòd narrat post hanc vilitatem gloriam eius fuisse conspe-ctam vt vnigeniti a Patre, angustius quàm debeat. Nam etiam in ipsa vilitate gloriam eius Apostoli & pij conspexerunt, non illo solùm facto transfigurationis quam merito extollit Petrus, aut inde a resurrectione, quod omnes Apostoli & Euangelistæ testantur, verumetiam toto vocationis curriculo, quum ex operationibus diuinis quas faciebat, & quas etiam diuinitus cum eis communicabat, gratiam illam vnionis non obscurè animaduerterent personæ diuinæ cum natura humana assumta, in ea, atque per eam operantis in vnitate personæ: quam rem tum Iudæis aliquoties, tum discipulis non dubitauit exponere, quum ipsorum cor angustia occuparet ne ad gloriam eius respicerent. Hoc verò non est alium Christum æternum ante Mariam & carnè ex ea assumtam confingere, sed eundem Christum colere verum Deum æternum, genitum, non factum, & hominem in tempore factum, non genitum, in vnitate personæ. Sed iam tempus est rationes eius, quas ad suam istam interpretationem formæ Dei, & formæ serui ac carnis confirmandam adfert, expendamus. Prima ratio. Annon Paulo fuisset facilius loco forma Dei dicere verum Deu& æternum? quæ sequuntur, zelo præpostero dicit, quia iuuat homi-
units.tr: 1. Cor. 2. Plain speech must be kept. Next, certain singular statements occur which I cannot pass over, lest unwary readers be deceived by them to the undermining of their faith. The first is that he declares that Christ is the Word and God, understanding neither essentially, but by a communication of grace, by which he is the Word in office and God in dignity. We have already refuted these points sufficiently. The second is that he says that the same Christ is innocent and without sin, as Adam too was created in the image of God. This is indeed true as far as it goes, but it is not sufficient. For innocence, freedom from sin, and the image of God are otherwise in Christ than in Adam: in Adam all things were human, but in Christ they were more than human, and subsisted in the person of the Son of God. From this follows what Augustine rightly said, that Adam, being mutable, could not sin, but Christ, even in us, cannot sin, since by his divine power he is immutable. The third is that he says that this very thing is what is said of Christ by Paul, that he was in the form of God. For the form of God is properly essential, and it is one only; if it could perish or be changed, the essence itself would perish or be changed. For since in simple and immaterial [ἀΰλοις] things, which are metaphysical, form and that of which it is the form are the same, who could think otherwise of the most simple God? But Christ, that is, the person of the Son of God, is in the form of God and is equal to God; and accordingly he is one with the Father in essence, that is, in unity of form or essence, with the Father, and according to person he is equal to the Father. Here, however, our author takes it as an accidental form, which can be present or absent without corruption of the subject; but in God there is no such form, since he is truly and wholly most simple essence. Moreover, he interprets the form of God as his image, as it was in Adam; but this interpretation is refuted by the plain comparison with the opposed member, where it is said that he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men. For in Christ, as man, the apostle very clearly distinguishes those two things, which this man foolishly confuses: the essential form, and the likeness or image; the former belongs to substance, the latter to relation, and they differ in kind entirely. I say nothing of the fact that the form of God can nowhere in Scripture be taken in this sense, nor confirmed by any example or authority. Therefore the interpretation is false, which has obscured both the essential form of God and the form of a servant, since it has referred both to accidents, contrary to the mind of Paul and the order of words he set down. The fourth is that he says that after this lowliness his glory was seen as that of the only-begotten of the Father, in a narrower sense than it ought to be. For even in that lowliness the Apostles and the godly saw his glory, not only in that act of transfiguration which Peter rightly extols, or from the resurrection onwards, as all the Apostles and Evangelists testify, but throughout the whole course of his calling. From the divine works which he performed, and which he also communicated to them by divine power, they clearly perceived that grace of union, by which the divine person operated with the assumed human nature, in it and through it, in unity of person. This he did not hesitate to explain both to the Jews on several occasions and to the disciples, when anxiety had taken hold of their hearts so that they did not look to his glory. But this is not to invent another eternal Christ, before Mary and the flesh assumed from her; rather it is to worship the same Christ, the true eternal God, begotten and not made, and man made in time, not begotten, in unity of person. But now it is time to weigh his reasons, which he brings forward to confirm his interpretation of the form of God, and of the form of a servant and of flesh. The first reason: Would it not have been easier for Paul to say, instead of "form of God," true and eternal God? What follows he says with a perverse zeal, because it pleases him to curse man

units.la: { } Ioan. 5. & 10. Ioan. 14. hominem maledicere: nos iuuat benedicendo vincere. Quapropter omittamus. Quorsum ista? nam primum hoc dicit per æquiualens: nam forma Dei vnica est, verus & æternus Deus: secundò pertinuit hoc ad commoditatem maximè oppositionis institutæ, quam Paulus ibi persequutus est grauissimè: postremò nego futurum fuisse facilius: nam formam Dei dicens (est autem vniuoca) omnia complectitur: sin verum & æternum Deum dixisset, subortus aliquis Samosatis aut aliunde partus obganniuisset verum quidem & æternum esse, sed tamen communicatione Deum. Sed ô acumen hominis. Forma Dei, inquit, dicitur æquiuocè: in forma enim Dei tanquam Deus imperabat omnibus,&c. Video iam te, mi homo, nec Græcè nec Latinè agere, sed Italicè: quapropter id a te addi oportuit, Forma Dei nostratibus Italis dicitur æquiuocè: sed vestras æquiuocatio est, catachresis vestra, Græcis, Latinis auribus inaudita. Hanc igitur æquiuocationem tuis proba qui nec Græcè nec Latinè sciunt: nam qui Græcè & Latinè scient, si boni sient, ab æquiuocatione ista abhorrebunt. Cætera verba sunt ad rauim vsque recantata, quæ ante refellimus: sed etiam millies palato quidem tuo repetita placebunt. Secunda ratio ex comparatione veteris Testamenti desumta est. Vetere Testamento promittebatur, figurabatur, re non ostendebatur: in nouo natus, datus, demonstratus, &c. Hoc iam ante sæpe confutauimus. Elenchus est duobus modis fallens, respectu substantiæ & modi. Nam substantia Christi consideratur aut secundùm personam simpliciter qua Deus, aut secundùm carnem assumtam, aut deniq; secundùm totum personæ, ex quo Deus factus est in carne corpicuus. Modus autem duplex, ante carnem assumtam, & in carne, pro temporum ratione. Olim promittebatur figurabaturq; tum secundùm carnem, tum etiam secundùm totum personæ Deus in carne conspicuus, Mediator noster, sed ita vt re ostenderetur secundùm personam diuinam, quà Deus, & a sanctis Patribus crederetur perciperetúrque: sic prius membrum ambiguum ex parte,& falsum est. In nouo autem Testamento natus est secundùm carnem,datus & demonstratus,& similia,secundùm totum personæ. Hæ res commodè distinctæ habent euidentiam: confusæ, magis ac magis abingenijs aliud agentibus conturbantur & damnosa obscuritate implicantur. Tertia ratio. Eodem sensu vterque redit, &c. Negatur: nam prior interpretatio de substantia est personæ simpliciter, & ortu carnis a persona assumtæ: posterior de accidentibus quæ Filio Dei secundùm carne contigerunt, & accidentibus varijs, quorum alia ad qualitatem personæ pertinent, alia ad actiones & perpessiones ipsius: ac proinde admirabilis etiam in posteriore hac interpretatione ponitur æquiuocatio, quum summa rerum genera in eadem voce confunduntur præter iustam omnium sermonum legem. Naribus trahantur oportet qui istis interpretationibus tam inconsideratè acquiescunt. Etsi præterire non possum silentio, quod ante in nostris hominibus Samosatenus damnabat segmento 2. id hoc in loco ab ipso commissum esse, & varias vnius loci interpretationes ferri. Certè etsi id omnium est longè optimum quod est verissimum ac simplicissimum, veritas autem simplicitasque typum habent perpetuum suù in Scriptura sacra, tamen duo ab infirmitate nostra nobis contingunt incommoda in Scripturis sacris, quamuis perse cuidentissimis: vnum, quòd verum non ita peruidemus vt est opus, quia lucem habentes inchoatam so-lùm ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: alterum, quòd huic hæc veritatis pars a diuina luce tribuitur cognoscenda, & illi illa, vt charitatem & coniunctionem nem inter nos ex nostræ tenuitatis & necessitatis conscientia in communione sanctorum discamus colere. Quapropter de errantibus miseranter, de aliud adferentibus prudenter, de omnibus amanter iudicandum, lucisq; diuinæ amplior reuelatio semper a Deo exspectanda expetendáque in Christo Iesu. Sed pergamus. Quarta ratio. Sic doctiores Neoterici docent, præsertim Melanchthon, cuius verba reliquo hoc in loco subiecta sunt. Primùm negamus hanc doctissimorum quorumque neotericorum interpretationem esse; & falsum esse res ipsa loquitur. Quid enim dicimus? a quibus accepimus? quibus adhæremus? nonne Neoterici quique (vt vocantur) cum Ecclesia orthodoxa prisca ex Scripturis sacris se hanc doctrinam hausisse profitentur? Deinde negamus hanc simpliciter esse Melanchthonis & mentem & interpretationem. Fallis duobus modis, Samosatene, qui & res coniunctas diuidis, & eas quæ per consequentiam hauriuntur statuis velut interpretationis caput. Quod si bona fide agere est, omnino in hoc misero seculo bonam fidem dixero periisse. Diuidis coniuncta (vt nihil de posterioribus editionibus, quas tu dissimulas non omnino belle pronunciem) quum dicta Philippi de incarnatione præterfilis, quæ autem sunt incarnationis consequentia ex eo accumulas. A prioribus metuis, ad posteriora confugis veteratorie. Nam in principio illius loci ita ait Philippus: Mirari queas, cur cum de ingressu Verbi in mundum antea dixerit, non prius etiam de incarnatione loquutus sit. Respondeo, quamquam de ingressu in mundum loquutus est, tamen omnia quæ de eo dicta sunt, ad verbi potentiam, non ad infirmitatem carnis Christi referri debuerunt: quia caro Christi non illuminat, non viuificat, non renouat, &c. Ideo nunc tandem de incarnatione loquitur. Hactenus interpretationis caput, vt ante appellauimus. Pòst sequitur μεσιτα, quod tu velut caput arripis, cùm sit pes aut pedis articulus manans de capite, quum Philippus ait per μεταβασιν, Sed & hoc apto ordine subiectum est: quia sicut in Christo verbum caro factum est, ita in nobis carnem fieri oportet: id demum est renasci, quoad verbum cogitatio humana tantum est, non Filij Dei. Hoc argumento μεταφορας proposito, quò transit Philippus allegorica accommodatione quadam, instituit enarrationem illius respectu personæ Christi, vt capitis; & nostræ, vt membrorum eius. Quapropter dicit, Porrò omissis philosophicis disputationibus de incarnatione, &c. quæ Samosatenus hunc in locum intulit. In his autem verbis vides primùm incarnationem Sermonis statui, sed omitti certo consilio de ea disputationes; postea vero transiri ad illam rerum necessario ex carne consequentium accommodationem, quam tu abreptus studio non videris observasse. Nam quum ait, ita breuiter sentio Ioannem παρεναγωσεις capere Nasci, de natiuitate piorum loquitur cuius antè meminerat dicens, ex Deo nati sunt: quum postea subijcit, vti quum ait, Verbum caro factum est, id est quod Esaias ait, &c. accommodationem instituit nati Christi allegoricè cum natiuitate nostra. est enim hæc ἀπόδοσις institutæ similitudinis. Quemadmodum autem in simili intelligendo falsus es, sic etiam vocem ταπεινώσεως æquiuocè accipiens loco abuteris. Non enim hîc de reali humiliatione Christi, ac ne de Christo quidem Philippus in hac similis parte loquutus est, sed de verbali & Rhetorica figura, quam Seruius in Virgilium Aeneid. I. sic explicat, Apparent rari nantes in gurgite vasto (pro eo quod est in pelago) Tapinosis est, inquit Seruius, id est, rei magnæ humilis expositio. Prudenter tamen Virgilius humilitatem sermonis epitheto subleuat, vt hoc loco, vasto, addidit. Tu autem, Samosatene, hæc omnia fortiter præterfiliens, non potes commodè argumentari a dicto secundùm dùm quid, vt vocant, ad dictum simpliciter: neque hæc verba tua cuiquam bono, si iudicium adhibuerit, vnquam probaturus es. Atque eadem est omnium sequentium ratio, quæ tu ex Philippo adhibuisti mutila, vt libellum hunc tuum ementitæ auctoritatis specie & suffragio quasi extorto viri optimi concluderes.
units.tr: Ioan. 5. & 10. Ioan. 14. It pleases a man to curse; it pleases us to conquer by blessing. Therefore let us pass these things over. What is the point of this? First, he says this by equivocation: the form of God is one, the true and eternal God. Second, this served the convenience of the opposition that Paul pursued so gravely there. Last, I deny that it would have been easier. By saying "form of God" (which is univocal) he embraces everything. But if he had said "the true and eternal God," some Samosatene or someone born elsewhere would have snarled that he is indeed true and eternal, yet God only by communication. But oh, the cleverness of the man! "The form of God," he says, "is said equivocally: for in the form of God, as God, he commanded all things, etc." I see now, my friend, that you are speaking neither Greek nor Latin but Italian. You ought therefore to have added that "the form of God is called equivocal by us Italians." But your equivocation is your own catachresis, unheard of by Greek and Latin ears. Prove this equivocation, then, to your own people, who know neither Greek nor Latin. Those who know Greek and Latin, if they are good, will shrink from that equivocation. The rest of your words have been recanted to hoarseness, and we have refuted them before; yet repeated a thousand times they will please your palate. The second reason is taken from a comparison with the Old Testament. In the Old Testament it was promised and figured, but not shown in reality; in the New it was born, given, demonstrated, etc. We have often refuted this already. The argument is misleading in two ways, with respect to substance and to mode. The substance of Christ is considered either according to the person simply as God, or according to the assumed flesh, or finally according to the whole person, from which God became visible in the flesh. The mode is twofold: before the flesh was assumed, and in the flesh, according to the circumstances of the times. Formerly he was promised and figured, both according to the flesh and according to the whole person, God made visible in the flesh, our Mediator; but it was so that he was shown in reality according to the divine person, as God, and was believed and perceived by the holy Fathers. Thus the first member is in part ambiguous and false. But in the New Testament he was born according to the flesh, given and demonstrated, and similar things, according to the whole person. These matters, conveniently distinguished, have clarity; when confused, they are more and more disturbed by minds busy with other things and entangled in harmful obscurity. The third reason: each returns in the same sense, etc. This is denied. For the former interpretation concerns the simple substance of the person and the origin of the flesh from the assumed person; the latter concerns the accidents that befell the Son of God according to the flesh, and various accidents, some pertaining to the quality of the person, others to his actions and sufferings. Therefore a remarkable equivocation is set up even in this latter interpretation, since the highest kinds of things are confused under the same word, contrary to the just law of all speech. Those who so carelessly acquiesce in such interpretations ought to be dragged by the nose. Yet I cannot pass in silence what Samosatenus condemned in our people in section 2, that here it has been committed by him, and that various interpretations of one passage are offered. Certainly, although that which is most true and simplest is by far the best, and truth and simplicity have a constant type in holy Scripture, yet two disadvantages befall us from our weakness in the holy Scriptures, however clear they are. One is that we do not see the truth as clearly as we ought, since, having only a light just begun, we know only in part and prophesy in part. The other is that this part of the truth is given by divine light to be known by one person and that part by another, so that from awareness of our own slightness and need we learn to cultivate love and fellowship among ourselves in the communion of saints. Therefore we must judge the erring with pity, those who bring forward something else with prudence, and all with love; and a fuller revelation of divine light is always to be expected and sought from God in Christ Jesus. But let us proceed. The fourth reason: so the more learned moderns teach, especially Melanchthon, whose words are set out in the rest of this passage. First, we deny that this is the interpretation of all the most learned moderns, and the matter itself shows that it is false. For what do we say? From whom have we received it? To whom do we cling? Do not the moderns, as they are called, profess together with the ancient orthodox Church that they drew this doctrine from the holy Scriptures? Next, we deny that this is simply the mind and interpretation of Melanchthon. You err in two ways, Samosatene: you both divide what is joined together and set up as the head of the interpretation what is drawn from it by consequence. If this is acting in good faith, I would say good faith has perished altogether in this wretched age. You divide what is joined (not to mention the later editions, which you conceal and which I cannot fairly pronounce on), when you pile up from the incarnation the things that follow from it, while passing over Philip's words on the incarnation. You fear the earlier passages and flee craftily to the later. For at the beginning of that passage Philip says: You may wonder why, when he had earlier spoken of the Word's entry into the world, he did not first also speak of the incarnation. I answer: although he spoke of the entry into the world, all that is said of it ought to be referred to the power of the Word, not to the weakness of Christ's flesh, because Christ's flesh does not enlighten, does not quicken, does not renew, etc. Therefore now at last he speaks of the incarnation. So far the head of the interpretation, as we called it before. Next comes μεσιτα [mesita], which you seize upon as the head, when it is a foot, or the joint of a foot, flowing from the head. For Philip passes by metabasis to: But this too is subjoined in a fitting order: for just as in Christ the Word was made flesh, so in us the flesh ought to be made; this is indeed to be born again, so far as the Word is concerned; the human thought is only that, not the Son of God. With this metaphor proposed as the argument, Philip moves on, by a certain allegorical application, to set out an explanation of it with respect to the person of Christ as head, and to ours as his members. Therefore he says: Moreover, the philosophical disputations about the incarnation being set aside, etc., which Samosatenus has inserted into this place. In these words you see, first, that the incarnation of the Word is laid down, but that disputations about it are set aside by a deliberate plan; afterwards he passes to that application of the things necessarily following from the flesh, which you, carried away by zeal, do not seem to have noticed. For when he says: I think briefly that John takes the figure "to be born" in this way [παρεναγωσεις], he speaks of the birth of the godly, of which he had earlier spoken, saying: they were born of God. When he afterwards adds: as when he says, the Word was made flesh; this is what Isaiah says, etc., he sets up an allegorical application of the birth of Christ to our birth; for this is the apodosis of the similitude he has set up. But just as you were wrong in understanding the similar part, so you also misuse the word ταπεινώσεως [tapeinoseos], taking it equivocally in that place. For Philip is not speaking here of the real humiliation of Christ, nor even of Christ in this similar part, but of a verbal and rhetorical figure, which Servius explains in his commentary on Virgil's Aeneid I, thus: "Apparent rari nantes in gurgite vasto" (for "in the sea"). "Tapinosis est," says Servius, "id est, rei magnae humilis expositio. Prudenter tamen Virgilius humilitatem sermonis epitheto subleuat, ut hoc loco, vasto, addidit." You, Samosatene, passing over all this boldly, cannot properly argue from a statement made in a certain respect to a statement made absolutely; and you will never persuade any good man, if he exercises judgment, that these words of yours are valid. Indeed, the reasoning of all that follows, which you have taken from Philip in mutilated form, is the same: you wish to conclude this little book of yours with the appearance of a false authority and with the support, as it were extorted, of an excellent man.

units.la: Interpres alter, iudicio suo, limam accuratiorem adhibens, primùm de more negat Verbum Dei æternam personam diuinam esse, qua de re sæpius a nobis dictum: deinde aggreditur verbi Græci ἐγένετο interpretationem, & nominis caro. De vtroque in præcedentem diximus, atque hæc commenta refellimus. Postremò argumentis oppugnat nostram illam, Verbum caro factum est, interpretationem. Ea sunt duo, quæ expediemus paucis. Prius: Si ita legatur, oportet hoc Verbum, antequam veniret Iudæis suis prædicatum, carnem fuisse factum: at prius venisse ad eos legitur hic quàm sit caro factus. consequens igitur falsum. Respondeo, verè falsum est consequens (neque enim ex antecedente conficitur) & falsa tota argumentatio. Nam vtrobique vitium est ex elenchi ignoratione, & verbi, venio, æquiuocatione. Prius venerat ad Iudæos (vt Philippi verbis vtar) secundùm potentiam diuinitatis suæ: tum venit secundùm infirmitatem carnis: prius venit sine motu, diuino modo: post venit, per generationem carnis & exhibitionem sui ipsius in carne, humano modo: venit humanitus, qui venerat & semper aderat diuinitus. Quid hac misera argumentatione facias? Posterius argumentum nihil est aliud quàm pura petitio principij, supponi Filium Dei æternum, atque hoc falsum esse. Sed hoc genus argumentationis amplius centies falsi reuicimus. Nec maioris momenti absurdum illud est quod ex eodem fonte profluit, hac nostra doctrina de Filio Dei Scripturam vniuersam inuerti, & exponi contemtui. Negatur: desideratur probatio dicti, non adfertur vlla. Quum itaque adferetur, rum Deo volente viderimus. Etsi quoties confutata, convicta, explosa haec omnia?
units.tr: Another translator, applying a finer file of his own judgement, first denies in the usual way that the Word of God is an eternal divine person, a point we have often made. He then takes up the interpretation of the Greek ἐγένετο [egeneto, "became"] and of the noun caro, "flesh." We spoke about both in the preceding part and refuted these inventions. Finally he attacks our interpretation, "The Word was made flesh." There are two arguments, which I shall dispose of briefly. The first: If it is read thus, this Word must, before coming to his own people, have been proclaimed as having been made flesh; but it is read that he came to them before he was made flesh; therefore the consequent is false. I answer that the consequent is indeed false, for it does not follow from the antecedent, and the whole argument is false. In both places the fault lies in ignorance of the point at issue (ignoratio elenchi) and in an equivocation on the word venio, "come." He had come to the Jews earlier (to use Philip's words) according to the power of his divinity; then he came according to the weakness of the flesh. Earlier he came without motion, in a divine manner; afterwards he came through the generation of the flesh and the manifestation of himself in flesh, in a human manner. He came humanly who had come and always was present divinely. What can you make of such a wretched argument? The second argument is nothing but a plain begging of the question: that the Son of God is eternal is assumed, and this is false. We have refuted this kind of argument more than a hundred times as false. Nor is the absurdity of lesser weight which flows from the same source: that by this doctrine of ours about the Son of God the whole of Scripture is overturned and exposed to contempt. It is denied; a proof is wanted, and none is offered. When it is offered, we shall see, God willing. Yet how often have all these things been refuted, convicted and driven off?

units.la: SAMOSATENVS. 14.
units.tr: SAMOSATENUS. 14.

units.la: Et habitauit in nobis, & vidimus gloriam eius, gloriam quasi vnigeniti a Patre.
units.tr: And dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father.

units.la: CARNEM fieri est maledictum & peccatum fieri vt tolleretur maledictio in carne nostra. Ita quod ait, habitauit in nobis, significat hic quod Philipp. 2. dicitur, in similitudinem hominum factus, habitu inuentus vt homo: & Hebr. 4. habemus Pontificem tentatum per omnia: idque ita vt nouissimus hominum a Propheta vocetur. Et vidimus gloriam eius. Antithesin facit Ioannes: vt ante de humiliatione Christi, sic hic rursum de glorificatione loquitur. Gloria praeter omnia miracula Christi, est resurrectio eius a morte, Ephes. 1. neque aliud miraculum aut opus Christi salutare nobis est praeter hoc, vt Matth. 16. non dabitur eis signum, nisi Ionae Prophetae: & Rom. 10. Si in corde credideris quod Deus eum suscitauit ex mortuis, saluus eris. Quid autem est credere resuscitatum a mortuis? regnare, vicisse mortem, & fregisse portas inferi, sustulisse peccatum, tueri nos, iudicaturum incredulos. Haec gloria resurrectionis est, qua glorificat Christus omnes credentes sibi. Haec Philippus Melanchthon: qui etiamsi tuetur Christum aeternum incarnatum, tamen in expositione verborum Ioannis, Verbum factum caro, nobiscum consentit.
units.tr: To be made flesh is a curse, and to become sin so that the curse might be taken away in our flesh. Thus what he says, "dwelt among us," here signifies what is said in Philippians 2: made in the likeness of men, found in fashion as a man; and in Hebrews 4: we have a high priest tempted in all things; and in such a way that he is called by the Prophet the last of men. "And we beheld his glory." John makes an antithesis: as before he spoke of the humiliation of Christ, so here again he speaks of his glorification. Beyond all the miracles of Christ, the glory is his resurrection from the dead (Eph. 1). Nor is there any other miracle or saving work of Christ for us apart from this, as in Matt. 16: "no sign shall be given them but the sign of the prophet Jonah"; and in Rom. 10: "If you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." What, however, is it to believe that he has been raised from the dead? It is to reign, to have conquered death and broken down the gates of hell, to have taken away sin, to keep us safe, and to be about to judge the unbelieving. This is the glory of the resurrection, by which Christ glorifies all who believe in him. Thus Philip Melanchthon; and although he maintains that the eternal Christ was incarnate, nevertheless in his exposition of the words of John, "The Word was made flesh," he agrees with us.

units.la: M. S.
units.tr: M. S.

units.la: Et habitauit in nobis, & vidimus eius gloriam, gloriam quasi vnigeniti a Patre: plenus gratia & veritate.
units.tr: And dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

units.la: VERBVM hoc per quod omnia facta sunt, quod manifestatum est Iudaeis, & quod homo fuit, nempe Christus Iesus, nobiscum nobiscum habitauit & conuersatus est: qui quamuis huius mun-di hominibus inglorius & contemptus fuerit, nobis tamen maximè gloriosus fuit. Nam vidimus illius miraculosam gloriam: erat enim plenus gratia & veritate in omni genere diuinarum virtutum. Nonne ex his verbis manifestum fit Ioannem hic non intellexisse de illo aeterno Filio (neque enim huiusmodi verba illi accommodari possunt) sed de illo visibili Dei Filio homine Iesu Christo? Et ad clariorem intelligentiam loci huius consideretur locus apud Lucam cap. 24. vbi legitur quòd Iesus Nazarenus fuit vir Propheta potens opere & sermone coram Deo & toto populo: vbi etiam ponitur dictio illa ἐξήρετο in ea significatione in qua ponitur hic a Ioanne. Obseruanda est hic praeterea vox, Vnigeniti: hic positam esse, primùm ad significandum Christum extra rerum ordinem, hoc est, ex virgine natum esse: secundò propter excellentiam ac plenitudinem perfectionemque donorum spiritualium nullis aliis concessorum praeterquàm vni Christo, de cuius plenitudine nos omnes accepimus: ipse enim immediatè a Deo omnia accepit, nos autem mediatè per ipsum: tertiò quòd Christus magis dilectus & charus Deo fuerit: quae phrasis vsitata est in Scripturis. Hinc Dauid vocat Solomonem vnigenitum, quamuis multos haberet filios, Paralip. 29. Prouerb. 4. Item Genes. 22. vocatur Isaac vnigenitus non tantùm quia solus & miraculosè natus esset, sed quia fuit a Patre vnicè dilectus. Hanc esse genuinam, quam attulimus interpretationem agnoscent, qui diligenter perpendent cætera omnia quae in Ioanne sequuntur. Sed, vt res clarior reddatur, exemplo agamus. Ad hunc modum se Ioannes hic habet quemadmodum si quis metaphoricè scripturus Moysis historiam, quando Israeliticum populum ex Aegypto liberauit, ista diceret. In principio erat liberator (ab effectu enim libet liberatorem appellare) & liberator erat apud Deum (dum scilicet adhuc mundo pro liberatore populi manifestatus non esset Moses) & Deus erat liberator (constitutus enim fuit Deus super Pharaonem) In populo Israelitico erat, ac populus Israeliticus per ipsum liberatus fuit, & populus Israeliticus ipsum non cognouit (murmurauit enim contra ipsum Mosem, & volebat lapidare eum) & liberator fuit caro (id est, homo abiectus humilis, ac contemptus) Nam mos Dei est exerere virtutes suas per viles, abiectos, ac contemptos homines, vt hac ratione illustrior eluceat ipsius gloria.
units.tr: This Word, through whom all things were made, who was manifested to the Jews, and who was a man, namely Christ Jesus, dwelt and conversed among us. Although he was without glory and contemptible to the men of this world, nevertheless to us he was most glorious. For we beheld his wonderful glory: he was full of grace and truth in every kind of divine virtue. Does it not become plain from these words that John here did not understand this of that eternal Son (for such words cannot be applied to him), but of that visible Son of God, the man Jesus Christ? And for a clearer understanding of this passage, let us consider the passage in Luke 24, where it is written that Jesus of Nazareth was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; where also that word ἐξήρετο [exēreto, "was taken up"] is used in the sense in which John uses it here. Here one must further observe the word "only begotten": it is placed here, first, to signify that Christ was born outside the order of things, that is, that he was born of a virgin; second, on account of the excellence, fullness and perfection of the spiritual gifts granted to no one else but to Christ alone, from whose fullness we have all received, for he received everything immediately from God, while we receive it mediately through him; third, that Christ was more beloved and dear to God, a phrase which is in common use in the Scriptures. Hence David calls Solomon "only begotten," although he had many sons (1 Chron. 29; Prov. 4). Likewise Isaac is called "only begotten" in Gen. 22, not only because he alone was born, and that miraculously, but because he was uniquely loved by his father. Those who carefully weigh all the other things that follow in John will acknowledge that this is the genuine interpretation we have offered. But, so that the matter may be made clearer, let us illustrate it with an example. John here stands in the same relation as if someone, writing the history of Moses metaphorically, when he freed the Israelite people from Egypt, were to say these things: In the beginning was the liberator (for it is permissible to name the liberator from the effect), and the liberator was with God (that is, while Moses was not yet manifested to the world as the liberator of the people), and God was the liberator (for he was set up as God over Pharaoh). In the Israelite people he was, and the Israelite people was liberated through him, and the Israelite people did not know him (for they murmured against Moses himself and wanted to stone him), and the liberator was flesh (that is, a lowly, humble and despised man). For it is God's custom to show forth his virtues through vile, abject and despised men, so that his glory may shine forth more brightly by this means.

units.la: ORTHODOXVS.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: Ex antecedentibus Melanchthon persequutus consequentium interpretationem, quia de incarnatione: pluribus non statuerat dicere, hic primùm summatim repetit quid carnem fieri significet, non proprie (est enim incarnari, quod ante nominauerat) {sed κατὰ τὸ ἀκόλουθον}, vt ante diximus, ex consequentia. Quapropter illud, habitauit in nobis, interpretaturus, vtramque simul apponit explicationem, propriam ex loco Philip. 2. & consectariam ex Hebr. 4. & Esai. 53. quæ omnia quid aduersum nos? Etsi detruncat Philippi verba: sed hoc quoque quid ad nos? De sequentibus iudicium idem. Hæc omnia sanctè a Philippo dicta, commodè accipi necesse est, non incommodè præter veritatem rei & sententiam auctoris detorqueri, aut primarijs interpretationibus secundarias, vt facit Samosatenus, adæquari. Sic enim audet concludere: nos vtrumque ex verbis & sententia auctoris cùm hîc, tum alibi perspicuè testata improbamus.
units.tr: Having followed Melanchthon through the preceding passages to the interpretation of what follows, since he had decided not to say more about the incarnation, here he first briefly restates what it means for the Word to be made flesh. This is not strictly proper usage (for "to be incarnate" is what he had named before), but is taken {in the sense of what follows} from the context, as we said before. So, in order to interpret "dwelt among us," he sets out two explanations side by side: the proper one, from Philippians 2, and the consequential one, from Hebrews 4 and Isaiah 53. What is all this against us? Even if he mutilates Philip's words, what does that matter to us? The same judgment holds for what follows. All these things said by Philip so soundly must be received in a fair sense; they cannot be twisted unfairly, against the truth of the matter and the author's meaning, nor can secondary interpretations be made equal to the primary ones, as Samosatenus does. For he dares to conclude thus: we reject both interpretations, as the words and meaning of the author clearly attest here and elsewhere.

units.la: Secunda interpretatio omnino est eiusdem generis, quod ante confutauimus. Quòd autem æternum illum Filium Dei verum Deum homini visibili Dei Filio Iesu Christo opponit, ferrâ per eamdem (quod aiunt) lineam reciprocans, quàm ieiuna sit ac futilis hæc oppositio, ante demonstrauimus aliquoties: cùm persona sit vnica ex vtraque natura constans, quarum naturarum oppositio ratione solùm, ac non re (quod hic facit) institui potest. neque enim partis vnius positio remotio est alterius, neque naturæ similiter: sed contrà posita parte essentiali altera ponitur, &posita natura essentiali vna, altera ponitur ex quo primùm cœpit esse in constituendo supposito.
units.tr: The second interpretation is entirely of the same kind as the one we refuted before. As for his setting the eternal Son of God, true God, against the visible man Jesus Christ, the Son of God, while he drives back and forth along the same line (as they say), we have shown several times before how empty and futile this opposition is. For the person is one, made up of both natures, and the opposition of the natures can be set up only in thought, not in reality (as he does here). For the position of one part is not the removal of the other, nor is it so with the nature. On the contrary, when one essential part is posited, the other is posited too, and when one essential nature is posited, the other is posited from the moment it began to exist in constituting the person.

units.la: Locum Lucæ 24. miror vehementer ab homine arguto in hanc sententiam adductum esse. Bifariam peccat, dum eo abutitur. Nam primùm sermo est hominum in fide titubantium, quorum cor rei nouitas inexspectata & crucis scandalum conturbauerat: vt increpatio Christi luculentissimè ostendit, exclamantis, ô carentes mente & graues corde ad credendum, &c. Huiusmodi testium sermoni fidem quis habeat? quis ex eo sermonem suum firmare iure possit? Deinde verò, quid si eos dicamus nesciuisse Christum? sic enim Samosatenus ipse confirmat in exemplo simili, segmento 4. Postremò, vt demus ratum haberi sermonem illorum oportere, quis non videt eodem relabi Samosatenum quò ante, & ex positione naturæ vnius inferre negationem alterius? vir propheta est: non igitur Deus. Falsa est oppositio in eo supposito, quod per dispensationem gratiæ Dei ex vtraque natura credimus & profitemur constitutum. Nihil itaque hoc loco agitur. De voce ἐγένετο diximus segmento præcedente.
units.tr: I wonder greatly that a clever man was led to this opinion by the passage of Luke 24. He errs in two ways in abusing it. For first, the speech is of men wavering in faith, whose hearts the unexpected novelty of the thing and the scandal of the cross had troubled, as Christ's rebuke shows most clearly when he cries out: "O foolish men and slow of heart to believe," and so on. Who would trust the speech of such witnesses? Who could rightly confirm his own speech by it? Next, what if we say that they did not know Christ? For Samosatenus himself confirms this in a similar example, in section 4. Last, even granting that their speech must be held valid, who does not see that Samosatenus falls back into the same error as before, and from the position of one nature infers the denial of the other: "He is a prophet, therefore not God"? The opposition is false on the supposition that, by the dispensation of God's grace, we believe and profess the person to be constituted of both natures. So nothing is accomplished here. As for the word "was made," we spoke of it in the preceding section.

units.la: Admiranda verò & profunda est hominis istius sapientia in voce vnigeniti exponenda. Vnigenitum enim hîc Christum tribus nominibus docet appellari, natiuitate extraordinaria, donorum excellentia, & dilectione singulari Dei. Primam interpretationem negamus, quia a matre vninatus (si ita loqui licet) vel vnicus natus dicereretur: dicitur autem vnigenitus; & vt peruersa hæc glosa in mentem cuiusquam venire non posset, Spiritus sanctus addidit, vnigeniti a Patre. Immò, inquit iste, vnigeniti a matre. Perge porrò, Samosatene, in hunc modum, & ementire proterue verba veritatis, si quidem non loquens, sed latrans audire voles. Secunda & tertia interpretatio figurata est, prior metaphora, posterior metalepsi constans. Atqui nō est hic figurae locus: nam vetat sic nomen hoc accipi additamentum sequens, a Patre. hac determinatione apposita figurae illae tuae excluduntur auctore Spiritu Dei. Tum quid hoc rei est? eamdem vocem eodem loco propriam & figuratam significationem habere simul? etiam figuratas complureis vario respectu eidem voci eodem loco accommodari sine vlla necessitate? Hoc nemo iustus Grammaticus aut Logicus fecerit: ne Rhetor quidem, sed testis aliquis fortasse comicus, aut ex ganea recens. Nunc abi, & roga numquis melius cum ratione insanire possit. Hanc quidem multiplicem copiam & flumen tuarum interpretationum minime probant sequentia, neque vocis aut loci expositionibus (quas adfers) suffragantur. Restat exemplum, quo rem a se declarari dum Samosatenus putat, declarat infantiam suam, ne quid dicam grauius. Ita est, inquit, quasi quum de Mosè historiam aliquis hoc modo pertexuerit. In principio erat liberator, &c. At primū vniuersè nego: nam exemplū est dissimile, quod manifesto euincitur Sermonis seu Verbi enarratione, quam supra segmento 3. attulimus, & prius ex Irenaeo, Chrysostomo, aliisque docuimus. Secundo etiam negantur membra comparationis istius singula, & dissimilia esse ex ijs quae ante singulos in locos annotauimus, demonstratur manifestissime. Nam neq; illa est principij determinatio, neq; esse apud Deum vsquam hac significatione legitur, neque vox Dei simpliciter hoc sensu vsurpatur, neque modus essendi (vt ita loquar) idem est, nec denique omnia sequentia eodem respectu aut consimili praedicantur. Id res ipsa loquitur. Postremo infirmitatem huius ipsius exempli, quod nouus interpres tam clarum esse pronunciat, arguit euidentissimè factum istud; quòd versus aliquot silentio praeterit, quos institutæ narrationi suæ se accommodare nõ posse commodè sentiebat. Quam rem si praestare aliqua ratione potuisset, an verò fuisset omissurus, quin exempli sui historici per omnia partibus partes narrationis huius exsultans gaudio conformasset? Quæ cùm ita sint, humanis commentis omnibus omissis, veritati Dei, quam nobis de Christo Filio suo, vero æterno Deo & vero homine, testificatus est, sanctè acquiescendum est, & in ea perue-stiganda atque consequenda omnis labor religiosè consumendus, vt in illo æterno Dei Filio hîc viuentes atque morientes, immortalémque vitam beneficio eius illic consequuti Deum Patrem glorificemus æternum cum Filio & Spiritu sancto, qui Deus est vnicus benedictus in secula. Veni, Domine Iesu.
units.tr: Truly wonderful and deep is this man's wisdom in explaining the word "only-begotten." For he teaches that Christ is called only-begotten by three names: by an extraordinary birth, by the excellence of his gifts, and by the singular love of God. We deny the first interpretation, because he would be called "only-born" (if I may so speak) from his mother, or simply "born only." But he is called "only-begotten," and so that no one could come upon this perverse gloss, the Holy Spirit added "only-begotten of the Father." "Nay," says this man, "only-begotten of the mother." Go on, Samosatene, in this manner, and shamelessly lie against the words of truth, if indeed you wish to be heard not as a speaker but as a barker. The second and third interpretations are figurative: the first is a metaphor, the latter consists of a metalepsis. Yet there is no place here for figure, for the following addition, "of the Father," forbids the word to be taken this way. By this added qualification those figures of yours are excluded, the Spirit of God being the author. Then what kind of thing is this: that the same word in the same place should have at once a proper and a figurative meaning? And that several figurative senses, in different respects, should be fitted to the same word in the same place without any necessity? No just grammarian or logician would do this, nor even a rhetorician, but perhaps some comic actor, or one fresh from the drinking-table. Now go away, and ask whether anyone could rave more reasonably. Indeed the following words in no way support this manifold abundance and flood of your interpretations, nor do they agree with the explanations of the word or passage that you offer. There remains the example by which Samosatenus thinks the matter is made clear, and by it he makes his own childishness clear, not to say anything harsher. "It is so," he says, "as if someone had woven the history of Moses in this way: In the beginning was the liberator, and so on." But first, I deny the whole comparison; for the example is unlike, which is plainly proved by the explanation of the Word or Speech that we brought forward above in section 3, and earlier taught from Irenaeus, Chrysostom and others. Second, the individual members of this comparison are denied, and it is most manifestly shown that they are unlike what we noted before at each place. For neither is that a definition of "beginning," nor is "to be with God" anywhere read in this sense, nor is the word "God" simply used in this meaning, nor is the mode of being (so to speak) the same, nor, finally, are all that follow predicated in the same respect or a similar one. The thing itself speaks to this. Lastly, the weakness of this very example, which the new interpreter declares to be so clear, is proved most evidently by this fact: he passes over in silence several verses which he felt could not fittingly suit his intended narrative. If he could have managed this in any way, would he not have omitted them? Or would he not rather, exulting with joy, have made the parts of his historical example conform part by part to this narrative in every respect? Since these things stand thus, all human inventions being set aside, we must humbly rest in the truth of God which he has witnessed to us concerning his Son Christ, true eternal God and true man, and in searching out and attaining it every labor must be devoutly spent, so that, living and dying here in that eternal Son of God, and having obtained immortal life there by his benefit, we may glorify God the Father eternally, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is the one blessed God for ever. Come, Lord Jesus.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.
